Advantage: Reducing the number and leveling the speed of


vehicles will result in safer and more pleasant


neighborhoods. There will be fewer accidents, and vehicle


emissions will be reduced by eliminating stop-start traffic.


There are enough different customer segments that want this:


the residents, the local traffic authority, the police, the


environment. The last one is not, strictly speaking, a


customer segment, but it will be a beneficiary of this


initiative.


Purpose-advantage-measurement finishes with a measurement.


In this case you could measure average speeds, the time it


takes for a vehicle to traverse the neighborhood, and the


number of reported accidents (evenly flowing traffic has been


shown to reduce collisions between vehicles). The measurement


is along these lines:


Measurement: The number of cars entering the regulated areas


will not exceed 250 vehicles per hour and will travel within


## 第 104 页


the posted speed limits. Traffic accidents will be reduced by


15% from current numbers. Residents’ complaints will go down


by 25%.


Note that there is still no mention of how this is to be


achieved, only what must be achieved. With this measurement,


you can go back to the stakeholders and confirm whether this


is indeed solving the real problem. From the residents’


complaints, it appears that it is.


However, when you present these outcomes to your


stakeholders, it is possible that they realize that’s not


what they wanted at all. In that case, you rework the


purpose-advantage-measurement until you achieve agreement.


You must have this agreement to ensure that you are solving


the real problem, and that the rest of the development effort


will deliver the right solution.


Review


Finding the real business problem and making sure that


everyone understands it goes a long way toward a successful


development project. It stands to reason that if a project


does not solve the right problem, then any solution it


## 第 105 页


produces will be useless. On the other hand, useful solutions


are used—they do something that their customers need.


The Blastoff is the beginning of the journey, and the


decisions you make early on are the ones that have the


greatest impact. One decision—determination, really—is what


problem are you solving? Note that this is the problem, not


the solution. Solutions are easy to find; problems are a


little bit harder. Perhaps this is why so many projects skip


the problem bit and jump straight into a solution.


The business problem to be solved is independent of any


potential solution. So, the best place to start is to look


for the essence of the problem. (We’ll have a lot more to


say about essence in Chapter 16, The Essence of the Problem.)


Look at your statement of the business problem your solution


is meant to solve. Does it contain any technology? Does it


mention web, phone, software, cloud, internet, laptop, app,


server, mesh, or anything else that is a way of doing


something and not the something to be done? If it does, then


it sounds like it is a description of a solution, and not a


statement of the problem. Rewrite it, and keep rewriting,


until you have erased any trace of any possible


implementation. That’s when you have reached the essence of


the problem.


## 第 106 页


And if you don’t have a technologically agnostic problem


statement, or any statement at all, do not go past this point


until you do. You can only reach a destination when you know


what the destination is. Yours is to solve your customer’s


business problem—but first you have to understand it.


Development projects fail for many reasons: politics,


incompetence, lack of resources, and so on. But when it comes


to successful projects, with the exception of some


serendipitous accidents, none has ever succeeded without


first understanding the real business problem it was meant to


solve.


Resources


A Guide to the Business Analysis Body of Knowledge (BABOK


Guide), put out by the International Institute of Business


Analysis, is a comprehensive guide to business analysis and


requirements discovery. Chapter 2 covers planning a


project’s business analysis.


How Big Things Get Done by Bent Flyvbjerg and Dan Gardner


(Macmillan, 2023). This is an excellent book, and while it is


not about IT projects specifically, the authors have very


## 第 107 页


useful things to say about starting any project in the right


way.


Be a Great Problem Solver—Now! by Adrian Reed (Pearson,


2016). This is a quick read and has some terrific tips for


getting a project underway.


5 Whys: The Effective Root Cause Analysis by Oliver Roderich


(self-published, 2021). A simple approach to finding the real


problem.


Practical Project Initiation: A Handbook with Tools by Karl


Wiegers (Microsoft Press, 2007). This is about building a


solid foundation for your project. The author discusses some


of the key project initiation practices.


## 第 108 页


Chapter 4. The Value of Solving the
Problem


In the previous chapter, we talked about finding the real


problem. It is not always easy to do that, so you might


prefer to come at it another way. Solving the customer’s


real problem will provide value to him. So perhaps you might


try starting by thinking about what value your solution will


bring to your customer.


Start with a simple question: Does your customer value your


solution? Simply because you deliver some software (or


service or product) does not necessarily mean that the


customer receives any value. The customer can only receive


value if you solve the real problem. So, it follows that the


real problem to solve is the one whose solution enables the


customer to realize value when he uses it. The real problem


and customer value are inseparable—discover the problem and


it will lead you to the value. Conversely, if you understand


what your customer values, it leads you to the business


problem that the customer wants solved.


What Does Your Customer Value?


## 第 109 页


In this part of the book, we are talking about the Blastoff,


and how its role is to establish the foundation for your


requirements activity. This foundation is vital to your cause


—it is where you determine whether your efforts will deliver


the right solution. Part of being right is that the solution,


when delivered, enables your customer to realize value from


it.


Customer value is your customer’s perception of whether he


received enough in return for his investment. We all


experience this almost every time we buy something. You must


have eaten at a restaurant and afterward thought, That was


far too expensive for the quality of the food. You didn’t


receive enough return for investing in the price of the meal


—it was poor value for money. That jacket you bought years


ago and still wear a lot—that’s good value for money. And


that smoothie maker you don’t use all that often but got for


a low price—to you, that’s still good value for money.


Of course, value is not always monetary value. We receive


value when something provides a pleasant experience, or saves


us time when we use it. Sometimes we value convenience.


Sometimes we value something because it has a pleasing


appearance, or makes us, in our opinion, appear better or


smarter.


## 第 110 页


Your customers make the same kind of value decisions.


Sometimes they are concerned with the price of your solution.


For example, if the customer spends $100 to buy your solution


off the shelf, does she perceive that she gets more than a


hundred dollars’ worth of value from it? Sometimes the cost


of development must be considered when assessing value. For


example, if a company spends $1 million developing an


actuarial solution, does the increase in accuracy of its


statistics and calculation of insurance risks and premiums


bring a benefit to the company?


In the previous chapter, we discussed goals and how you could


state goals using the purpose-advantage-measurement


construct. Value and advantage are the same thing, but we


can look more deeply into value. For example, you saw this in


the previous chapter as part of a purpose-advantage-


measurement statement:


Advantage: Reducing the number and leveling the speed of


vehicles will result in safer and more pleasant


neighborhoods. There will be fewer accidents, and vehicle


emissions will be reduced by reducing stop-start traffic.


This was stated as an advantage, but it can only be


advantageous if someone values it. So, who values it?


## 第 111 页


• Value to residents: Quieter streets, more careful driving


meaning the streets are calmer, people feel safer and are


less worried about their children’s safety when walking on


the sidewalks and crossing the streets


• Value to police: Constant-speed traffic, which has been


shown to produce fewer accidents, thus fewer accidents to


attend and fewer speeding tickets to write


• Value to the environment: Less pollution, as there are


fewer emissions from steady-speed cars than from cars in


stop-start conditions


• Value to the sponsor (this is the road authority): Safer


streets, fewer complaints from residents, and less wear on


the street surface


Not all of these can be monetized, but the well-being and


environmental values make this a worthwhile project. Note


that in the above scenario, the environment and the police


were recipients of value. The police and the environment


would not always be involved, but you should always look


beyond the obvious customer to find others that could value


your solution.


## 第 112 页


Most of the time you provide a solution to enable your


customers to do their work. Value comes when your solution


gives your customers an advantage when they use it. That is,


the customers will be able to do their work in a better way.


Work often means sitting at a desk using a computer to do


daily tasks. To provide value, your solution must make these


tasks easier, more effective, faster, or more accurate, or it


must provide extra functionality that enables the customer to


do something that he could not do before.


Work can also include using an app to do online banking, get


a boarding pass, or pay for something. Work can include some


of the millions of things we humans do every day.


The point of understanding customer value is straightforward:


During the Blastoff, you are establishing whether or not to


go ahead and acquire a solution. One of the factors that you


consider is whether that solution will bring value to the


customers doing their work.


Functional Value


You enable functional value when your solution has


functionality that solves the customer’s business problem.


If the problem was so severe that it threatened to cripple


## 第 113 页


the business, then your customer will obviously place a high


value on your delivered functionality (providing it solved


the problem). And if it does solve the problem, your customer


might also be willing to spend more on your solution and


still perceive it as valuable.


Sometimes functional value is achieved when your solution


improves the customer’s business; usually by making some


business process(es) easier or cheaper. This kind of


improvement can be quantified, which makes it easier for your


customer to assess value.


A value statement describes the value your


customer receives when you solve her business


problem.


You might consider writing a value statement. This is not


strictly necessary, but the point of your project is to


deliver value, and if you cannot articulate that value, then


perhaps the project is not valuable.


A value statement clarifies the situation. It describes the


value the customer receives when you solve his problem. This


value statement guides the team in their requirements


## 第 114 页


discovery and development. You can write your value statement


any way you like, but we suggest something like this:


As a [type of customer]


I receive value when [outcome for the customer].


Functional value statements might be:


As a bank customer,


I receive value when I can see a projection of my current


balance alongside my expected debits for the remainder of the


month.


As a subscriber to a music streaming service,


I receive value when my family can share the music.


As a sales supervisor,


I receive value when all of my salespeople have immediate


access to current inventory and can submit their customer’s


order from wherever they are.


As head of claims,


## 第 115 页


I receive value when the average time needed for an accurate


claim’s adjustment is less than 15 minutes.


The functional value might be delivered to the customer when


your solution makes a business process cheaper or faster or


more accurate:


As a delivery service to distribution centers,


I receive value when all my deliveries are completed within


30 minutes of the scheduled time.


We can conclude from this value statement that deliveries to


the distribution centers were previously not very punctual,


which might have had serious consequences. The functionality


that provides accurate deliveries is valuable—it helps


retain customers. If your solution makes money or saves money


for your customer, then customer value will be proportional


to the increase in revenue or savings. Of course, your


customer will include the cost to develop or buy your


solution in her assessment of value.


You might well have more than one functional value statement;


just don’t have 50 of them.


Psychological Value


## 第 116 页


Psychological value is provided when your solution brings


benefits such as pleasure, satisfaction, and convenience.


Later in this book we talk about non-functional requirements


such as usability and humanity requirements—psychological


value is closely linked to that type of requirement. We also


talk later about customer experience; that is also part of


psychological value.


In many cases, projects are run to develop a solution whose


main purpose is to provide a more


pleasant/novel/exciting/easy/accessible/learnable/convenient/


[insert your own adjective here] experience for its intended


user. These are psychological values.


Value statements like this are appropriate:


As a supermarket,


I receive value when my customers find they prefer to use the


self-checkout devices instead of the manned checkout desks.


That kind of value statement would need to be augmented by a


measurement:


As a supermarket,


## 第 117 页


I receive value when my customers find it attractive to use


the self-checkout machines,


And I will know this if within three months of their


introduction to the stores, 65% of checkouts are completed


using the self-checkout devices when human checkout operators


are available.


Or:


As a music streaming service,


I receive value when my customers enjoy streaming from my


service,


And I will know this when I have 85% customer retention.


Receiving Value


Figure 4.1 shows how value varies according to who or what


receives the value. There is often more than one party who


might receive value from your solution. It is worth


considering them as part of determining that you are solving


the real problem.


## 第 118 页


![embedded_p118_12.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p118_12.jpeg)


Figure 4.1 Value from the solution comes in different ways


to different parties.


## 第 119 页


The Sponsoring Organization


The sponsoring organization usually wants the solution for


its employees, and it is willing to pay for it. The


organization either builds the solution through its in-house


IT department or buys a ready-made solution. In some cases,


the organization might commission a third party to build the


solution.


Regardless of how it acquires the solution, value to the


sponsoring organization comes when the solution improves the


work of its employees. For example, the solution might


enable the employees to do their work more efficiently and


save money, enable them to do work that they could not do


before and generate revenue, or enable their work to fit more


readily into the organization’s infrastructure.


Naturally, the cost of buying or building the solution must


be commensurate with the value of having the solution.


Additionally, it might take several years before the


investment in the solution pays off.


Your task as a business analyst is to help estimate the


impact your solution will have on the workplace, and to help


estimate the cost of acquiring it.


## 第 120 页


The Building Organization


The building organization—Microsoft, Adobe, Oracle,


Salesforce, and thousands of others—receive value when


customers buy their solution. The building organization


receives value when it sells enough of its solution to offset


the development costs and provide enough revenue to realize a


profit. To assess this value, you must estimate the revenue


from sales. Estimating sales is beyond the remit of most


business analysts, but your part is to provide information


regarding what potential customers would value.


One source of information on consumer value comes from Bain &


Company. This management consulting firm built an excellent


analysis of consumer values incorporating 30 elements of


value. These are arranged in a hierarchical pyramid based on


Maslow’s hierarchy of needs. The four levels of the pyramid


are Functional, Emotional (we call this one psychological),


Life Changing, and Social Impact. A link to Bain & Company is


listed in the Resources.


Some organizations provide their solutions for free. These


are the open-source providers that build their solutions


using enthusiastic volunteer labor, and then distribute the


solution freely. No money changes hands; the value comes from


## 第 121 页


the satisfaction of providing an exemplary solution and


having customers use it.


The other type of building organization is the one that


builds a solution on commission from a sponsoring


organization. These are software houses and outsourcing


companies. Value is received by simply charging enough for


the commission to make a profit.


The Customer as User


The customer as user is someone who is usually given the


solution to help him do his work. Here you are looking at the


value of making his work better. This might be enabling the


employee to make better decisions, do the work more quickly,


or make it more convenient, easier, or more error-free. You


would assess the value mainly by productivity gains.


The Customer as Purchaser


The customer as purchaser is someone who buys the solution


and receives value when it does something useful for her. For


example, she might edit her photographs, or use a word


processor to write a novel. Or she might receive value if the


solution she bought is a game and she enjoys playing it. How


## 第 122 页


much value she receives would depend on how useful or


enjoyable the solution is to her.


Other Recipients of Value


There may be others. The solution might be something that is


beneficial to the environment. For example, it could be a


solution that reduces the number of deliveries that are made


by the organization. It could be a solution that contributes


to the local community. Let’s say that an HR solution


provides as a by-product a web page of employees who are


willing to spend some of their time volunteering for local


charities or volunteer organizations.


Usually, solutions are built to bring value to the sponsoring


organization, but we can always hope that others get some


value too.


Review


Customer value needs to be part of your requirements


activity. The purpose of any development project, whether it


is to develop software, a consumer product, a service, or


anything else, is to solve a business problem and by doing


so, provide value to the customer of the solution. The


organization sponsoring the solution must also receive value


## 第 123 页


from the solution. If it does not provide value, then it is


less than worthless—it has cost money to build, but nobody


needs it.


Take the time to state up front what value your project


intends to deliver. Please keep in mind that simply building


the software/product/service does not necessarily deliver


value. The value statements keep you and your team focused on


what you are trying to achieve. Which means that all the


time, effort, and money expended during the project is aimed


at providing the business value.


Resources


Bain & Company’s Customer Values Analysis. At the time of


writing, you can find this well-presented analysis at


https://media.bain.com/elements-of-value/#.


Value Proposition Design: How to Create Products and Services


Customers Want by Alex Osterwalder, Yves Pigneur, Greg


Bernarda, and Alan Smith (Wiley, 2014). This is a companion


to their Business Model Generation, and it explains the tools


and processes needed to create solutions that your customers


want. There is an online companion at


https://www.strategyzer.com.


## 第 124 页


Return on Software: Maximizing the Return on Your Software


Investment by Steve Tockey (Addison-Wesley, 2008). This is a


comprehensive introduction to software engineering economics.


It should be a part of every software project.


## 第 125 页


Chapter 5. Goals-Scope-Stakeholders


The Goals set down the desired future state of the


customer’s business, along with the business advantage of


meeting the goal. For example, it should be 15% faster or


cost 12% less; it should take no more than 15 minutes on


average to process a claim; it should provide a customer


experience that results in a 40% retention rate. Scope is


the problem space. It is the part of your customer’s


business that is to be improved—fulfillment, patient


tracking, monitoring production line temperatures, or


whatever it might be. Stakeholders are the people who are


involved in that part of the work—they do it, they know


things about it, they are impacted by it, and they have


ambitions for it.


The goals, scope, and stakeholders are established during the


Blastoff. Figure 5.1 shows how the goals are the determining


factor for the scope of the problem space. People—we are


calling them stakeholders—work in or have an interest in the


problem space. These stakeholders in turn are the people who


influence or determine the goals. This is not an infinite


loop, but you could expect to go around it a couple of times


before your goals-scope-stakeholders stabilize.


## 第 126 页


![embedded_p126_13.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p126_13.jpeg)


Figure 5.1 The goals-scope-stakeholders trinity is the


foundation for your project. The goals of the project


establish the scope of the business problem to be solved. The


scope establishes the stakeholders who need to be involved,


and the stakeholders in turn establish the goals for a


solution that improves their business.


You are establishing these elements early in the project. The


intention is to give the project a solid foundation and


provide a clear direction for the project team. However,


there will of course be times when circumstances warrant


adjusting one of two of these elements. When this happens you


must make the change, but the point is that you remain in


## 第 127 页


control and that the team knows precisely what they are


trying to achieve.


Goals


We have yet to see a project succeed with unclear goals. From


time to time, happy accidents occur when the project team, or


a lone person, stumbles upon a winning solution. The


microwave oven, penicillin, Velcro, chewing gum, saccharin,


and so on—are all fortuitous accidents. But let’s face it,


you’re unlikely to stumble upon an enterprise resource


planning system or accidentally build an email client. If you


plan on succeeding, you need a clear and unambiguous—and


ideally ambitious—goal to aim for.


Keep in mind that the goal is not to build a


piece of software.


It is supremely important to keep in mind that the goal is


not to build a piece of software—it is to solve a business


problem. You might do that by building some software, but


that is not your goal. Solving the business problem is.


It is more than likely that you are given a goal at the


beginning of a project. The goal is usually derived when


## 第 128 页


management makes the business case for a project to solve a


business problem or take advantage of an opportunity. Despite


the goal being handed down from on high, it is not immutable.


A real goal must demonstrate value, and you must


be able to measure it.


Start by examining the goal. Our colleague Nick de Voil


suggests examining it out loud with key stakeholders, even if


they’ve already been through a round of discussions pre-


project. It never hurts and often helps a lot to revisit this


to ensure that it does in fact deliver value to your


customers. Moreover, this value must be able to be measured


in some way. Goals that are not measured are not helpful. For


example, the goal “We aim to increase our mindshare with the


customer by synergizing core competences” is not a real


goal; you cannot ever tell if you have met it or not. To be a


real goal it must demonstrate value, and you have to be able


to measure it.


For example, the value might be measured along these lines.


• Our solution reduces the cost of connecting a new


subscriber by 12%.


## 第 129 页


• Our solution makes the claims process 15% faster.


• Our solution reduces our required staffing to one agent per


500 subscribers.


• Our solution has a turnaround time of less than one second.


The value might be qualitative.


• Our solution improves the user experience.


• Our solution has a more pleasing design than our


competitors’.


• Our new solution is better liked than the old one.


At first, the items in the above lists might seem a little


touchy-feely, however they can all be measured once you have


established what people mean by what they are saying. For


example, qualitative goals can be measured by things such as


the following:


• Customer retention


• Customer satisfaction


• Customer surveys


## 第 130 页


• Voluntary usage uptake


• Lack of requests for modification


• And more


Obviously, these measurements are taking place after the


product has been built. Isn’t it then too late to discover


that the customers hate it and are turning to a competitor?


Yes, of course. Which means that you must make certain that


your qualitative goals can be met before building your


solution.


You can do two things. If your product is a bet-the-


existence-of-the-organization-on-it product, then you would


build multiple prototypes and test those against a


representative sample of your customer segment. The resources


spent on this kind of testing pay off handsomely if it


prevents you from putting the wrong product on the market.


The second thing is knowing the measurement of success. If


you, as a business analyst or UX designer, know how the


solution is going to be measured, then you put considerable


effort into making sure that it meets its quantitative and


qualitative measurements.


## 第 131 页


Purpose-Advantage-Measurement


As we are talking about the goals of the project, it is worth


revisiting the purpose-advantage-measurement way of


formatting the goal that we met in the previous chapter. When


you are trying to discover the real goal, think of it in


terms of these three components. Each of these focuses on one


aspect of the goal. When you put these three together, it


becomes evident whether the goal statement provides an


unambiguous guide for the project.


The purpose is what you are trying to achieve by doing the


project. For example:


The purpose of the project is to help college students find


and buy used or discounted textbooks, and to sell the


textbooks when they are no longer needed.


The purpose of the project is to optimize the routes for the


delivery drivers.


The purpose of the project is to minimize the time needed to


check out in our fashion stores.


The purpose is not enough on its own. Purpose, advantage, and


measurement are needed together to state the goal. The


## 第 132 页


advantage justifies the purpose—it asks why the purpose is


important. For example:


Lower-priced textbooks result in students paying less for


their books. These might be bought from brick-and-mortar


stores, or online. Students selling their books after use


further reduces costs.


Optimized routes result in more deliveries being made, with


less fuel consumption and thus less pollution.


A faster checkout makes the checkout experience more


enjoyable and reduces or eliminates the number of customers


who abandon their baskets when they see the checkout is


taking too long.


The other aspect of stating the advantage is to evaluate


whether or not it is worth pursuing, and whether the return


on investment is appropriate for the necessary expenditure of


resources.


The measurement has two reasons. It makes the purpose and


advantage clearer, and it gives the project team the ability


to know when the problem has been solved. For example:


## 第 133 页


Students pay on average no more than 40% of new-book prices


for their textbooks. This is measured taking into account the


cost of purchased books and sold books.


The measurement for the checkout project at the fashion


stores is this:


Checkout—paying and bagging—on average takes no more than


45 seconds, not counting the customer time needed to produce


a credit card or phone.


Purpose-advantage-measurement is a tool for discovering the


real goal. It is an exploratory tool, intended to help


stakeholders with diverse views of the problem to converge on


an agreed goal. A single sentence stating the goal is


infinitely arguable. But by having three elements of the


goal, stakeholders find it easier to discuss, understand, and


subscribe to each piece.


Additionally, a goal expressed as purpose-advantage-


measurement enables the team to keep the project on track and


to know when they have built a successful solution. It also


provides a clear view of the desired outcome of the project.


Achievable Goals


## 第 134 页


We have talked about how to formulate the goals, but that is


not quite enough. You also need to know if you can achieve


that goal. There is little point in starting a project if the


goal is to enable travel from New York to London in seven


minutes—you’re never going to achieve it.


We suggest that you look at the constraints surrounding the


problem space to see if there are any that would cripple the


project. Constraints are not just time and money, but


business conditions and the technological ecosystem. There is


a full discussion of constraints in section 3 of the Volere


Requirements Specification Template in Appendix A.


Additionally, there is not much point in having a goal that


cannot be achieved within the timeline and the budget. Of


course, it is difficult, if not impossible, to set a


realistic budget until you know the size of the problem you


are dealing with. Next up, we discuss scope and how you can


know the extent of the problem to be solved.


Scope


Your customer needs to do some work that—directly or


indirectly—is beneficial. Your customer wants to improve


that work, and you want to provide a solution to help her do


## 第 135 页


that. However, your solution can only be useful if it fits


seamlessly into the customer’s business. That is, it becomes


a natural part of the business activities that surround it.


To this end, it is important that you think of the scope of


your investigation as being the extent of the problem space;


that is, the part of your customer’s business that she


wishes to improve. Eventually, through your investigation,


you learn enough about the work being done within the problem


space to determine a solution. The scope of the solution is


some, and sometimes all, of the problem space.


Setting the scope is very much about determining the boundary


of the problem space. Anything inside the boundary is


something that you must study and understand. Anything


outside can be ignored (up to a point). However, the


interface between the inside and outside is critical and


needs to be well-defined.


The scope of the problem space is determined by the goals of


the project. The goal is to bring about some desired future


state of the work being done. So, you must consider a problem


space wide enough for you to find a solution that can meet


the goals. Consider the abstract context diagram shown in


Figure 5.2.


## 第 136 页


![embedded_p136_14.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p136_14.jpeg)


Figure 5.2 This is a context diagram. You use it to define


the scope of your problem space. The internal functionality


of this problem space is hidden for the moment; the intention


of the model is to define the boundary of the work being done


and its interface with the outside world.


The problem space to be studied includes any of the work


that can be affected by your solution and is under your


customer’s control. If you are building a solution intended


## 第 137 页


to automate part of some existing work, then the scope of


your study should include those parts of the existing work—


human activities, together with any automated systems—that


could potentially be affected by the eventual solution. For


embedded systems, there may be no human activity in your


work, but the scope must include any devices that can be


changed or in some way affected by the current development.


Even if you are building an electro-mechanical device, such


as an NFC card and phone reader, where most of the human


participation occurs outside the solution boundary, your work


context must still include the work that the human will be


doing with the device. After all, you need to discover what


the customer making the payment would like to do with the


machine, not just what is currently possible.


If your intended solution includes, either partially or


entirely, a ready-made component, then that must be inside


your problem space, along with any human activities, business


processes, or other components, whether they are ready-made


or you intend to build them.


The work to be studied includes anything that can


be affected by your solution.


## 第 138 页


While we are talking about the context diagram, note its


limited, but nevertheless crucial, aim. It shows only the


flows of information entering or leaving the work. It does


not attempt to show the activities within the problem space.


Likewise, it does not explicitly show who or what is doing


the work, although this information might be inferred.


As is true of many models, the context diagram is an


abstraction that shows a single view. In this case, it shows


only the work of the problem scope, the flows of information


(and sometimes the material) going to and from it, and the


adjacent systems that make up the ecosystem of the work.


As an example of setting the scope of the problem to be


studied, let’s look at a simple piece of work that you are


probably familiar with: a tapas restaurant.


Carmen’s Taperia


The deal at Carmen’s establishment is that the place mats


double as the menu. Customers sit at their table and either


they mark the dishes they want on the place mat or the waiter


makes suggestions and marks the mat as needed. The waiter


also takes the customer’s drink order.


## 第 139 页


The waiter then takes the marked-up mat back to the waiter


station and enters all the ordered dishes. She also enters


the drink order into the bartender’s system. The food order


is printed on tickets for the chefs and is also added to the


display for the pass. (If you’re not familiar with


restaurant terminology, the pass is where the cooked food is


checked and its presentation finalized before it is passed


over to the waiters.) Thus, the pass is the focal point of


communication between the wait staff and the kitchen. It is


usually presided over by the head chef, or in this case,


Carmen herself. She also keeps an eye out for dishes that are


taking too long to be prepared or delivered.


Carmen’s operation is shown diagrammatically in Figure 5.3.


## 第 140 页


![embedded_p140_15.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p140_15.jpeg)


Figure 5.3 A rich picture of food ordering and delivery to


customers at Carmen’s Taperia


Carmen’s goals are to reduce the errors and ensure rapid


delivery of the food. Additional goals are to sell more food


## 第 141 页


and provide a richer experience that encourages customers to


come back. The activity where the waiters enter the food and


drink orders is currently error prone, and she would like to


improve monitoring the orders at the pass and ensure their


rapid delivery to the tables. You have been hired as a


business analyst to help bring about a solution for Carmen.


Keeping in mind Carmen’s goals, think about the scope of the


work you need to study to find a solution to meet those


goals. The scope defines the extent of the problem space and


so should include all the activities that could influence


your choice of a future solution.


Don’t be tempted to presume to know the


solution.


Don’t be tempted to presume to know the solution. For


example, a presumed solution here would be to scan the place


mats and print the orders for the chefs. Or for the customers


to use their phones to scan a QR code and enter their orders


on an app. However, if you concentrate exclusively on a


presumed solution, you miss the richness of the surrounding


business.


## 第 142 页


For example, an important part of the business from Carmen’s


point of view is the interaction between the waiters and


their customers. Carmen wants the interaction to be friendly.


She wants the waiters to be knowledgeable about the food so


that they can answer customers’ questions and suggest new


things for them to try. “The gambas al ajillo [prawns with


garlic] are fantastic today, and you’ve got to try the


chipirones [baby squid]. Have you ever tried our albóndigas


[meatballs]? I’ll get the chef to make you a sample—it’s


on the house.” Carmen knows her food is good, and if some


new dish surprises and delights customers, then she will see


them again. On the other hand, if you presume the solution is


to have the menu on a smartphone app, it all but eliminates


interaction with the wait staff. Peering into the small phone


screen, customers are more likely to pick dishes that they


already know, and they might never get to taste Carmen’s


berenjenas con miel (a tapas from Córdoba; fried eggplant


with honey), which are absolutely delicious.


The Ecosystem


The business ecosystem is the part of the world that


connects and interacts with the problem space that you are


studying.


## 第 143 页


First, there is no such thing as a piece of work that has no


connection to the outside world—it does not make any sense.


Everything is connected to its ecosystem. For example, your


house or apartment exists within an ecosystem that supplies


electricity and water to it and drains wastewater from it.


The internet is part of its ecosystem. You pay rent for your


dwelling, and this payment goes to your landlord, which is


part of your dwelling’s ecosystem.


Within your dwelling, you may have a room thermostat,


possibly a smart one. The ecosystem for this device includes


the heating and/or cooling systems—they are switched on or


off by signals from the thermostat. The air temperature of


the room is part of the ecosystem, as it is sensed by the


thermostat. The thermostat might be connected to the


electricity or connected to the internet. All of these things


make up the thermostat’s ecosystem.


Everything is connected to something.


Everything is connected to something. It is these


“somethings”—devices, services, systems, businesses,


people, and so on—that are of immediate interest. We call


them adjacent systems, and they connect to the work by


## 第 144 页


delivering data or material to it or receiving data/material


from it.


Adjacent systems behave like any other systems: They contain


processes and consume and/or produce data. You are interested


in them because they are often consumers of the information


or services provided by your work, or because they supply


information or material needed by your work. You can see


these relationships by looking at the data flows on a context


diagram, as demonstrated in Figure 5.4. It is through these


informational connections that the adjacent systems influence


the work.


## 第 145 页


![embedded_p145_16.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p145_16.jpeg)


Figure 5.4 The context diagram for Carmen’s Taperia. Note


that the waiters and the food and drink preparation are


inside the scope. The work’s ecosystem here is made up of


## 第 146 页


the suppliers and the customers. These are shown as adjacent


systems.


Note that in Figure 5.4, there are no data flows going to the


suppliers to order food or drinks. This is because the


ordering activity is outside the scope you are considering.


For that reason, it is not shown in the rich picture in


Figure 5.3.


However, suppose that when she sees the context diagram,


Carmen thinks about the difficulty of ordering supplies and


the time needed to do it. She would like to change the scope


to include the ordering activity within the problem space.


Now, ordering data flows would be shown going to the Drinks


Supplier and the Food Supplier. Note that this change has


altered the goals a little and will affect any cost estimates


that have been made at this stage.


To find the adjacent systems, you sometimes must venture


outside your own organization. Look to the customers for your


organization’s products or services. Look to the outside


automated systems and organizations that supply information


or services to your work. Look to the other departments that


have connections to the work. Within reason, the wider you


## 第 147 页


make your investigation, the more useful your solution is


likely to be.


Do not be limited by what you think might be the


limits of an IT system. Instead, try to find the


farthest practical extent of any influence on the


work.


You will usually find that your work is also closely


connected to one or more IT systems, often within your own


organization. Sometimes you are making an enhancement to an


existing IT system. In this case, the IT systems, or the


parts that you are not changing, are adjacent systems. The


interfaces between your work and the existing IT systems are


critical. Although these interfaces may prove difficult to


describe, unless you define them clearly you can never know


the extent of your work, and eventually the extent of your


product.


One of the interfaces you are interested in is the


interaction with Carmen’s customers. You must understand and


define this interface if you are to understand its


functionality. In other words, you are studying what happens


during the interaction so that you know that any future


solution will fit comfortably with the way this restaurant


## 第 148 页


runs. It is important to keep in mind that this is the scope


of the work you are about to study, or if you like, the scope


of the problem space. Note that this is not the scope of a


solution.


Also note that the chefs are included in your scope despite


the fact that Carmen has no intention of automating the


cooking. A large part of the attraction of this restaurant is


the imagination that goes into the tapas, along with the


skill of the preparation. Carmen wants to retain that, but


there could well be opportunities for improving your solution


by better understanding the needs of the chefs, how they


interact with the pass, their scheduling needs, and so on.


For example, if they have some easy way of knowing that the


same dish has been ordered by three different tables at more


or less the same time, then it stands to reason they might


want to cook all three at the same time. Would the chefs like


to see the trends in that day’s orders? Do they need to be


reminded if individual dishes on a table’s order have not


been cooked or dispatched? It is only by including the work


of the chefs within your scope that you will ask such


questions and discover better, richer requirements.


During the Blastoff and in the early stages of analysis, it


is important to focus on understanding the problem. So, your


## 第 149 页


context diagram should be about the scope of the problem. It


is too early to fixate on any presumed solution.


Zone of Influence


When you are thinking about the scope of the problem, you


should also be thinking about the scope of the goals. Part of


the goal is always to improve your customer’s business area.


However, this goal by itself is possibly not enough. A common


reason for wanting to improve a business area is to influence


the behavior of part of the ecosystem.


Let’s revisit Carmen and her restaurant serving up Spanish


tapas. The context diagram in Figure 5.4 shows a central area


called Problem Space for Carmen’s Taperia. This is the space


you plan to study with the goal of improving it. To improve


it you will introduce your solution, which will change that


space. Carmen wants you to make this improvement, so we shall


call that space a zone where you have a charter to change.


In this zone you may make the necessary alterations. Figure


5.5 shows this zone.


## 第 150 页


![embedded_p150_17.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p150_17.jpeg)


Figure 5.5 The charter to change zone and the zone of


influence have been overlaid on the context diagram. Anything


outside these zones is considered unchangeable. Here we see


that Carmen wants to heavily influence her customers and have


## 第 151 页


a slight influence on her food supplier. The drinks supplier


cannot be influenced or changed in any way.


Carmen’s goals are a little wider than the charter to


change. She wants to influence the behavior of her


customers. She cannot order her customers to do something—


they are not employees (if they were, they would be in the


charter to change zone)—but your solution should do things


to influence the customers.


Previously you read “An important part of the business from


Carmen’s point of view is the interaction between the


waiters and their customers.” Her goal here is to influence


the customers so that they try new things and to make the


restaurant experience better. So, you include the customers


in your zone of influence. A little of the Food Supplier


adjacent system is included—the potential for influence is


limited—but none of the Drinks Supplier is—it is a large


multinational company and impossible to influence. (Carmen


buys from this supplier because she gets better prices.)


Including some or all of an adjacent system in your zone of


influence means that you pay attention to the requirements


for the functionality that is part of the interaction with


that adjacent system. In Carmen’s case, you spend some


## 第 152 页


effort eliciting the requirements for the functionality that


produces the flows of information that go to and from


Carmen’s customers. In this case, these flows are carried by


the waiters, and so the functionality is to provide the


waiters with all the information they could possibly need to


influence the customers.


To influence a customer’s behavior, the solution provides


functionality that has the potential to cause a change in the


way the customer interacts with the organization. A well-


known example is Amazon Prime. Amazon offers a subscription


to Prime membership that entitles the Prime customer to perks


such as next-day delivery and some free video and music.


Amazon did not order the millions of Prime customers to pay


the annual subscription—it can’t do that. Customers are not


part of the charter to change zone, but the functionality on


the customer-facing side of the organization influences


(persuades, if you like) a change in customer behavior.


When you are setting your scope, you need the goals. The


goals guide you—almost command you—when setting your


charter to change and your zone of influence.


Your charter to change zone is that part of your client’s


business that she wants you to change. This zone includes any


## 第 153 页


automated solution you produce, and the people and devices


that surround the automation. They have to change their work


practices to fit in with the new automation.


Your zone of influence is whatever parts of the surrounding


ecosystem your solution should have some kind of influence


on. The zone of influence is almost always made up of humans


—it’s hard to influence a machine—and any influence is


voluntarily accepted by the included adjacent systems.


By all means, draw these zones on your context model. They


are determined by the goals of the project. However, you


might find that your zones cause you and your stakeholders to


rethink and somewhat modify the goals. As we said earlier,


your requirements process is not a procession, but a flexible


framework to guide your requirements discovery.


A Presumed Solution


We have shown you an example of a context diagram of the


problem space in Figure 5.4. Now let’s look at the downside


of presuming a solution and ending up with a context diagram


that shows only the solution. Consider the context diagram


shown in Figure 5.6, where the scope is restricted to the


presumed solution.


## 第 154 页


![embedded_p154_18.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p154_18.jpeg)


Figure 5.6 This is what not to do. The scope here is too


narrow—it shows only the presumed solution.


## 第 155 页


One of Carmen’s goals is to reduce the errors and ensure


rapid delivery of the food. Let’s say that someone has leapt


to a presumed solution of scanning the place mats and


printing the orders for the chefs. The context diagram in


Figure 5.6 shows the restricted scope of this presumed


solution.


People think about how to solve the problem


rather than what the problem is.


Why has this happened? It is usually because people think


about how to solve the problem rather than what the problem


is. (As a business analyst, you will have experienced your


users telling you a solution rather than the problem that


needs to be solved). So, they take their presumed solution as


the starting point for the requirements.


What’s wrong with this? The big problem is that it misses


too much of the business activity that would benefit from


being studied. If you were to understand the work being done


by the waiters and chefs, you would most likely come up with


a solution that could improve their work while retaining the


spirit of the taperia, which Carmen has gone to a lot of


trouble to build up. By excluding these people and their work


from the scope, you risk delivering a very sterile,


## 第 156 页


unimaginative solution that fails to take advantage of the


rich opportunities of a wider scope.


By including the waiters and chefs in the scope of study, it


does not mean that you intend to automate them. It does mean


that any solution you devise will be much more attuned to


their work. It means that your solution could well provide


functionality that helps them do their work more effectively.


Let us conclude this section on scope by saying there are


some important things to keep in mind when deciding the scope


for your project.


• Step back—see the wider view and understand what the


business is doing.


• Understand that there is a difference between the business


problem to be solved and a presumed solution.


• The wider your scope of study is (within reason), the


better your solution will fit into the real world.


For the sake of your requirements and development effort, it


is important to set the scope as firmly as possible and as


early as possible. You cannot guarantee that it will not


change for the duration of the project, but if you want to


## 第 157 页


avoid scope creep—the usual suspect for runaway projects—


then set it as accurately as possible in the first instance,


and carefully control any changes. The context diagram is


useful. Make good use of it.


The Context Diagram


The context diagram is versatile. It does the following.


• Demonstrates the scope or extent of the business area to be


studied (you can also call this the problem space)


• Shows all the data entering and leaving that business area


• Arbitrates on what is in and what is not in the scope of


development


• Determines the business events (more on these later)


• Helps estimate the cost of the project


• Indicates the complexity of the business area


• And on the soft side, is a focal point for your work


Despite its versatility, the notation for the context diagram


is simple. You probably figured out how it works from the


## 第 158 页


examples given above, but it’s worth a closer look at the


mechanics.


The diagram works on the straightforward principle of data


in-process-data out. Figure 5.7 shows this simplification.


![embedded_p158_19.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p158_19.jpeg)


Figure 5.7 The incoming data, and sometimes material, is


transformed by the process and becomes the outgoing data.


If you were to extend this principle of data in-process-data


out to any business area (or problem space), it would appear


as in Figure 5.8.


## 第 159 页


![embedded_p159_20.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p159_20.jpeg)


Figure 5.8 An abstract view of the context diagram. The


context diagram of your problem space will look something


## 第 160 页


like this. It shows the data in and out, and the business


ecosystem in which this piece of business exists.


Around the periphery of the business area are the sources and


consumers of the data. These are called adjacent systems


(they are also known as external entities or terminators).


Just as your business area is a system, it is surrounded by


other systems. These adjacent systems both produce data to be


used by your piece of business and are the recipients of data


produced by the business.


The important part about adjacent systems is that they are


outside the scope of your control; you do not have permission


to change them, but you can influence them, or negotiate with


them if changes to their input or output need to be made.


Otherwise, they are off-limits, and your interest only goes


as far as the data that they produce or receive.


It is useful to note that the person normally called the end


user is not an adjacent system, but is part of the business


area you are studying. The reason for this is that you must


understand that person’s work and therefore must include it


inside your scope.


## 第 161 页


Let’s have a look at a couple of other examples of context


diagrams.


The functionality of the Young Musicians Site context diagram


shown in Figure 5.9 would mainly be about the website, and


obviously automated. However, there would also be some manual


work done inside the circle. Humans would be needed to


monitor context to ensure that the site’s standards are


being upheld, to arbitrate in case of disputes of authorship


of songs (this happens a lot), and to monitor the activity.


This is all to say that the central circle on a context


diagram usually contains a mixture of manual and automated


processes.


## 第 162 页


![embedded_p162_21.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p162_21.jpeg)


## 第 163 页


Figure 5.9 A music site for young musicians. The site is for


unsigned or independent musicians to upload samples of their


work in the hope of being noticed. If you look at the flows


of data that enter and leave the work area, you can more or


less work out what this piece of business is doing.


Now turn to Figure 5.10. The scope here is a driverless


subway train. The various sensors (shown as adjacent systems)


that surround this piece of work are separate from the train


and are not part of the same analysis and development effort.


The train must receive data from these adjacent systems to


function correctly and safely.


## 第 164 页


![embedded_p164_22.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p164_22.jpeg)


## 第 165 页


Figure 5.10 The context diagram for a driverless subway


train. It would be more complicated in reality, but this is


sufficient for the purpose here.


When you build a context diagram for a problem space, all its


functionality is hidden for the moment; the diagram exists to


set the scope of the problem, not to show how it works. Later


you expose the inner workings when you start trawling or


prototyping the business events. However, in case you are


curious, the functionality for the subway train would include


• Responding to temporary trackside signals (these could be


set by track maintenance workers or others)


• Checking that upcoming points are correctly set for the


train’s destination


• Checking that the track ahead is clear


• Stopping the train according to the platform guide beacons


• Starting the train when the doors are correctly closed


after loading


• Checking that passengers on the platform are clear of the


train


## 第 166 页


• Checking passengers inside the train for unusual activity


• Relaying any emergency passenger signals


• Ensuring that the train’s speed is consistent with the


controller’s advice


• And so on


If you are going to draw only one model for your project,


then make it the context diagram. Why? Because in the first


instance, it is helping you and your key stakeholders decide


the precise business problem you are trying to solve.


You can use the context diagram alone to give you a quick


indication of complexity. A diagram with 100 flows in and


out of the business area is obviously more complex and thus


more expensive than one with 30 flows at its periphery.


(Don’t be afraid to draw such a model. If there really are


100 flows, then they must be shown. We have seen plenty of


examples of this.)


Each flow on the context model indicates some


work to be done by the business.


## 第 167 页


Each flow represents some work to be done by the business


area. We’ll talk about this more when we get to business


events, but for the moment, consider an incoming flow called


Request to open an account. The work to be done here is


whatever is needed to establish the account and welcome the


new customer to the company. There would be a different


amount of work to be done by, say, a change of address


request.


If you go around the context diagram and for each incoming


and outgoing data flow, estimate the complexity of the work


to be done for that flow, use a simple scale such as small-


medium-large. For example, let’s say that you have 10 large,


20 medium, and 30 small work items. What remains is to know


(or to estimate) the effort needed for each of these


categories and do the multiplication.


The context diagram is also an instant arbiter of scope


questions:


“Is this feature in or out of our scope?”


“There’s no data entering the business area that is needed


for the feature, so it must be out of scope, or we have


missed some data.”


## 第 168 页


“Is our project responsible for time reporting?”


“No, but you can see how the output data gives the


information to the controller’s office (presumably an


adjacent system) for them to calculate the time records.”


A little later we will see how the context diagram helps to


determine the business events, but for now let’s turn to


something else: the people involved in your project.


Stakeholders


We began this chapter by talking about the trinity of goals-


scope-stakeholders. We have looked at goals and scope, so


let’s turn to the next part, the stakeholders.


A stakeholder is anyone with an interest in, or an effect


on, the outcome of the solution. The customer, the person (or


organization) who will ultimately possess and use your


solution, is the most obvious stakeholder. There are others.


For example, the project sponsor is a stakeholder; a subject-


matter expert is a stakeholder; a security expert; someone


who benefits from the solution’s functionality, such as the


manager of people who use the solution to do their work; the


marketing department; and so on.


## 第 169 页


Stakeholders are the source of the requirements.


You are trying to solve a business problem, and that probably


means talking to many people. The people who are potential


sources of requirements are your stakeholders. You must


ensure that you include those who are authorized to make


decisions, as well as those who are not authorized but have


knowledge about the work.


The stakeholder map (Ian Alexander, one of its originators,


calls it an “onion diagram”) in Figure 5.11 identifies


common classes of stakeholders that might be represented by


one or more people in your project. There are potentially


dozens of types of stakeholders for any project, and you can


find a comprehensive list in the form of a spreadsheet in


Appendix B, Stakeholder Management Templates. You can use


this spreadsheet to manage your stakeholders by identifying


who they are and what involvement you need them to have.


Check out Appendix B soon, but for the moment we’ll look at


some of the stakeholders in the diagram. Keep in mind as we


do that some roles will overlap, or individuals may have more


than one role.


## 第 170 页


![embedded_p170_23.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p170_23.jpeg)


Figure 5.11 The stakeholder map shows the organizational


rings surrounding the intended solution and the types of


stakeholders who inhabit these rings. Use this map to help


determine which stakeholders are relevant to your project.


## 第 171 页


You can use this generic diagram as a starting point for


talking about your stakeholders and discovering which are


relevant to your project and which others you need to add.


At the center of the stakeholder map is The Intended


Solution. Notice that it has a vague, cloudlike shape—this


is intentional. At the start of the requirements activities,


you cannot be certain of the precise boundaries of the


solution, so for the moment we will leave it as being vaguely


defined. Surrounding the intended solution is a ring


representing The Operational Work Area—stakeholders who will


have some direct contact with the solution inhabit this


space. In the next ring, The Rest of the Organization, you


find stakeholders who benefit from the solution in some way


even though they are not part of the operational area.


Finally, the outer ring, The Outside World, contains any


external (to the organization) stakeholders who can influence


the solution or have an interest in it.


It is helpful to discuss some of the more important


stakeholders.


The Customer


Your customers are the people you must satisfy with your


solution. After all, the customers are the people with the


## 第 172 页


power to reject it.


The customer is the ultimate possessor of the solution.


Customers can possess it by being


• The manager of a department who buys or commissions the


solution for the people working in the department


• The user of the solution, possibly working for the manager


• Someone who directly purchases your solution


• Someone who pays to use the solution


Perhaps you already know the names of your customers, or


perhaps there are hundreds or thousands of unknown people who


might be persuaded to pay for your solution. In either case,


you must understand them well enough to know what work they


are doing, what they find valuable, and what they will pay


for. If you are developing open-source software, you still


have a customer; the difference is simply that no money


changes hands.


There are several customer roles; we wrote about them in the


previous chapter. We mention them again, as each of them has


different requirements.


## 第 173 页


The customer as purchaser is someone who is putting up his


money to possess your solution. His requirements are those


that ensure that he receives value from it. For example, he


pays to have your password manager app on his phone, and you


must discover what capabilities he needs.


The customer as sponsor is the person who sponsors the


acquisition of the solution. This person usually has users


working for her, and so her requirements are about ensuring


that the staff can work effectively to produce the outcome


needed by her department. There is more on this role in the


Project Sponsor section below.


The customer as user is the person who possesses the


solution because he uses it to do his work. His requirements


are those that define the functionality he needs to do his


work.


We’ll shorten the role to “users,” and by that we mean the


people who will ultimately be the hands-on operators of your


solution. In the case of solutions that are not software


products, the users are the people performing the service (or


whatever your solution is). The better your understanding is


of your users, the better your chance is of specifying a


suitable product for them.


## 第 174 页


The Project Sponsor


The sponsor is financially responsible for the


development of the solution.


On the simple basis that “money talks,” the sponsor—more


accurately, the sponsor’s budget—is paying for the


development and has organizational authority over the


solution’s requirements. You cannot proceed without a


sponsor. If no one is representing the interest of the


organization, if no one is putting their hand up and saying


“This is my project,” then there is little point in


proceeding. If nobody is steering, the ship goes on the


rocks.


Your sponsor might have different roles within the


organization. For example, the sponsor could be part of the


following.


• User Management: If you are building a solution for in-


house consumption, the most realistic sponsor is the manager


of the users who will ultimately operate the solution. This


department is the beneficiary of the solution, so it is


reasonable that the cost of construction is borne by the


departmental manager.


## 第 175 页


• Marketing Department: If you build products for sale to


people outside your organization, the marketing department


might assume the role of sponsor and represent the eventual


customers of the solution.


• Product Management: If you have a product that is


continually being upgraded to meet market demands (such as a


phone operating system), the budget for its development would


be with a product manager or a strategic program manager—one


of those would be the project sponsor.


Consider your own organization—its structure and job


responsibilities. You have to identify the person who takes


organizational responsibility for your project. Our project


will not succeed without her.


The Business Analyst


The business analyst’s responsibility is the discovery and


analysis of the requirements. This usually involves


determining the business problem that has caused the project


to be initiated. When the business problem is correctly


identified and understood, the business analyst studies the


activity in the problem space. The objective is to identify


the solution to the problem and produce the requirements for


that solution.


## 第 176 页


The business analyst’s tasks include producing correct


requirements and/or stories. To be usable, requirements and


stories must be accurate. We shall talk a lot more about


writing accurate requirements and stories later. For the


moment, we can say that they must be measurable, testable,


verifiable, and agreed to by the appropriate stakeholders.


You will find the rest of the skills and responsibilities of


the business analyst in the remainder of this book.


The Product Owner


The product owner is one of the Scrum roles. Scrum is an


agile software development method that uses iterative and


incremental construction of the solution, or “product” in


Scrum parlance. Much has been written about Scrum and we


don’t need to repeat it here. The Resources section at the


end of the chapter has some references.


The primary duties of the product owner are to prioritize the


product backlog and to decide what the development team needs


to be working on. In other words, the product owner decides


which features or capabilities are to be constructed during


the next iteration cycle, or “sprint.”


## 第 177 页


The product owner role is included as a stakeholder because


of the product backlog. This is a collection of stories yet


to be developed. Stories (sometimes called “user stories”)


are the replacement for requirements in the Scrum world.


Throughout this book, we use the terms “stories” and


“requirements” almost interchangeably. They’re not the


same—requirements are usually more detailed than stories.


You’ll see lots of examples of both as we look more at


requirements discovery.


Scrum has nothing to say about how the product backlog and


its stories come into existence. That is the role of the


business analyst: It is he who works closely with


stakeholders to discover the needs of the business and writes


those needs as stories or requirements, and often (and


wisely) a combination of both. There is a lot more on how


this works, and how you can synchronize the work of the


business analyst and the product owner, in Chapter 35, Story


Map, where we talk about story maps as a better way of


organizing a product backlog.


The product owner has only a marginal role in requirements


discovery, but a very active role in constructing the


solution (the product). The product owner is included as a


stakeholder because she must become very aware of the goals


## 第 178 页


and desired business outcomes of the initiative. The product


owner is responsible for the development team constructing


their product in accordance with the goals set by the key


stakeholders in conjunction with the business analyst. The


product owner also liaises with the business analysts


throughout development to ensure that the product backlog is


being prioritized in line with the priorities of the customer


segments and the business events. More on these in a little


while.


Other Stakeholders


To find all the requirements, you need to talk to some more


people. Your contact with these stakeholders might be


fleeting, but it is nevertheless necessary. Any of them may


potentially have requirements for your product.


“Every context is composed of individuals who do or do not


decide to connect the fate of a project with the fate of the


small or large ambitions they represent.”—Bruno Latour,


ARAMIS or the Love of Technology (Harvard University Press,


1992)


The problem that you often face in requirements projects is


that you fail to discover all the stakeholders, and thus fail


to discover some of the requirements. You night also fail to


## 第 179 页


discover some aspects of the problem, goals that need to be


satisfied, and constraints that need to be respected. In


other words, you need to find everybody with an interest in


the solution to discover their requirements.


We list our stakeholders in section 2 of the


Volere Requirements Specification Template. You


can find this template in Appendix A. The list


acts as a checklist for finding the appropriate


stakeholders. You will also find the Stakeholder


Management Template in Appendix B.


Let’s consider some other stakeholders. You can see these on


the stakeholder map shown in Figure 5.11.


• Consultants—both internal to your organization and


external—are people who have expertise that you need.


Consultants might never touch or see your product, but their


knowledge becomes part of it.


• A functional beneficiary is someone who receives something


useful from the activity (or the functionality) of the


solution, such as a periodic report or ad hoc alerts. It


could also be someone whose work is improved by the fact that


someone else is using the solution. For example, a manager


## 第 180 页


can monitor his budgets more effectively because his staff


are able to make better projections by using the solution.


• A political beneficiary is someone who achieves the


perception of power because the solution has been developed.


This might be a person who is in a position of authority, and


so her requirements cannot be ignored (no matter how much you


may want to ignore them).


• A financial beneficiary is someone who is better off


because of the solution. This person might be a shareholder


or similar whose stock in the organization is more valuable


when the product sells. Or the solution saves money by making


a business process more efficient, and thus helps the budget


of its manager.


• Product managers and program managers are responsible for


the ongoing development of a product. Your company might, for


example, produce accounting software, and this must be


constantly upgraded to keep up with changes in the law, but


also to provide new and better facilities to keep ahead of


the competition.


• Subject-matter experts may include domain analysts,


business consultants, business analysts, or anyone else who


## 第 181 页


has some specialized knowledge of the business subject.


Consequently, these experts are a prime source of information


about the work.


The greatest problem concerning stakeholders is


the requirements you miss when you don’t find


all the stakeholders.


• Regulators include people such as government inspectors,


any kind of safety inspectors, technical inspectors, or even


possibly the police. It may well be necessary to build


inspection capabilities into your product. If your product is


subject to any regulatory act, then inspection is crucial, as


are the requirements from the inspectors.


• Marketing and sales are the stakeholders representing the


marketplace. When you are building a product for commercial


sale, trends in the market are a potent source of


requirements, as is a deep knowledge of the likely consumers.


• Lawyers are the stakeholders for most of your legal


requirements. Each year the world is filled with more and


more laws. Complying with all of them is daunting but


necessary.


## 第 182 页


• Hostile stakeholders are internal people who do not want


the project to succeed. Although they may not be the most


cooperative individuals, you would be wise to consider them.
