Also consider the people who threaten your product: the


hackers, defrauders, and other malevolent people. You will


get no cooperation from them, but you should consider how


they might mistreat your product.


Also consider the adjacent systems and the data flowing to


and from them on the context diagram. Look at each adjacent


system: Who represents its interests, or who has knowledge of


it? When the adjacent system is an automated one, who is its


project leader or maintainer? If these stakeholders are not


available, you might have to read the adjacent system’s


documentation, or its code, to discover whether it has any


special demands for interacting with your product. For each


adjacent system, you need to find at least one stakeholder.


Review


The Project Blastoff is there for you to set a solid


foundation for your requirements discovery. We described the


goals-scope-stakeholder trinity. When your blastoff is


successful, these three are coordinated to give you the


target for your requirements. Are the requirements in scope?


## 第 183 页


Are they contributing to the goal? Are they valuable to the


stakeholders?


The Blastoff is also part of your requirements discovery. By


determining the scope of the problem, you are determining


where your requirements are to be found and which


requirements are not part of the problem.


It’s helpful to think of the goal as the highest-level


requirement. This is what your project aims to achieve. The


goal is not to build a piece of software or some other


product, but to solve a business problem, and in so doing,


improve the customer’s business.


The goal sets the target, and every requirement that you


discover is subordinate to the goal and in some way


contributes to the goal.


The scope describes the extent of the problem space. It


shows what is inside and what is outside the problem you are


analyzing. We suggest using a context diagram to illustrate


the scope and be the arbiter of where you study and what is


outside your problem.


The scope and the goals are vital to your project. Without


them you are doomed to wander in a fog of uncertainty. So, it


## 第 184 页


is important that they be given enough attention to ensure


their correctness.


Getting the stakeholders right means that you find the right


people—those with the knowledge and authority—to answer


your questions and provide the basis for deriving the right


requirements.


Before leaving this, we should mention cost. It is only when


you know the scope of the problem that you can begin to


estimate the cost of, or the effort needed for, the solution.


To do otherwise is to invite calamity later when the project


runs out of budget or time.


Goals, scope, and stakeholders are the trinity that will pay


you back for getting them right.


Resources


The Agile Guide to Business Analysis and Planning: From


Strategic Plan to Continuous Value Delivery by Howard Podeswa


(Addison-Wesley, 2021). This book is about how product owners


and business analysts can maximize the value delivered to


stakeholders by integrating business analyst competencies


with agile methodologies.


## 第 185 页


“$1 Million Wasted Every 20 Seconds by Organizations Around


the World” by Vanessa Andres (https://bit.ly/40gvMwg). This


article discusses a study conducted by Project Management


Institute that shows that on average, organizations globally


waste 9.9% of every dollar due to poor project performance


and that around one in three projects (31% globally; 28% in


Canada) do not meet their goals.


Business Analysis Agility: Delivering Value, Not Just


Software by James Robertson and Suzanne Robertson (Addison-


Wesley, 2018). This book looks closely at how real value is


the result of solving the business problems that the


stakeholders really need to have solved.


## 第 186 页


Chapter 6. Customer Segments


A customer is the ultimate possessor of your solution. She


might have your solution on her computer or device, having


paid for it or gotten it for free; or she might have bought


or commissioned the solution for her staff to use. For the


purposes of segmentation, let’s say that a customer is


someone who, directly or indirectly, uses your solution to do


some kind of work.


You are interested in the work that people need to do with


your solution. For example, a customer might be using your


solution all day to schedule the transportation of consumer


goods from his company’s distribution center to retail


stores. Or the customer’s work might be more fleeting, such


as logging on to request a report. Or the customer might come


to your website to browse your offerings and buy something


from you, or to chase up a delayed delivery. There are


thousands of possibilities for customers using your solution.


There is also the possibility that you have thousands of


customers.


However many customers you have, they do not necessarily


behave the same way. They have different motivations, and


## 第 187 页


some of them are using your solution to do different things.


To provide the appropriate solution, you can’t aim at


everybody (try to please everybody and you’ll please


nobody). There is a need to segment your customers and


investigate the business problem of each of the segments.


As an example, buyers and sellers on eBay are two different


segments, each with different tasks to do and different


aspirations. It would not make sense if you were to try to


discover the requirements for both sets of people at the same


time.


The most useful way to segment your customers is to consider


their needs and what they want to do with your solution. It


might be necessary to further segment on demographics—for


example, by age, income, or education. You will do this only


if it makes a difference to the way that different


demographic groups might use your solution.


Having identified the segments, you can prioritize them so


that you can choose the order in which you work on them.


Customers and Their Segments


The customers we are talking about are your customers as


users and/or customers as purchasers. We’ll just call them


## 第 188 页


“customers” from here on. There are lots of customers and


they are not all the same—so you must subdivide them in


order to provide accurate requirements.


Customers are humans, and different humans have different


aspirations and values. Also, different humans are trying to


do different things. So, the possibility exists that your


solution cannot be a one-size-fits-all solution, but a


nuanced solution that provides different functionality, and


possibly different behavior, for different segments of


customers.


You start segmenting your customers according to their


needs. You could think of their needs as what they are


trying to achieve or the business problem they are trying to


solve. You might also consider their pain points, or


obstacles to achieving their goals. Disregard, for the


moment, the detailed tasks they do; you don’t yet know if


these tasks are appropriate or if they are merely the


customary things that the customers have always done but


won’t necessarily do in the future.


Consider this situation: You are the lead business analyst


for a large multinational container shipping and transport


company. There are about 20,000 employees around the globe.


## 第 189 页


As you know, containers are those huge steel boxes that you


see stacked up on container ships. When they reach their


destination port, they are offloaded to be picked up by


trucks to carry them inland. Containers are designed to be


stackable to make them transportable by ships, and to be the


right size to fit on the back of a truck or a railroad car.


A manufacturer will fill a container with the goods, do the


customs paperwork, and then seal the container. The transport


company (that’s your organization) picks up the container


and either delivers it directly by road or rail or takes it


to the container terminal for onward shipping to its


destination country.


Many of the 20,000 employees are potential customers for your


solutions. For example, some of your customers work at


arranging bookings for containers to be delivered to


manufacturers so that they can fill them with the goods they


want shipped. You also have customers who are concerned with


scheduling the trucks to drop off and pick up the containers.


Other customers predict the need for containers by area and


ensure that there is a supply of empty containers to meet


demand. Others arrange the ships and dock facilities and so


on. Still more customers bill for the company’s services.


## 第 190 页


The problem your company faces is that it has grown up with a


patchwork of solutions, and these solutions are very


inefficient at sharing data and communicating with each


other. This often results in the same data having to be input


to several different parts of your company. This patchwork


has led to employees not having ready access to the


information they need, and in some cases, salespeople have


inadvertently arranged contracts for containers or shipping


capacity that did not exist.


An initiative has been launched with the goal of making all


data seamlessly available to all employees (wherever


authorized). Another goal is for solutions to share their


data so that there is very little duplicated data in the


organization.


The last thing you want to do at this stage is to presume a


solution, which would have one huge data store in the cloud.


Someone might go far enough to suggest one large solution for


the whole of the company.


Instead of thinking about solutions, let’s look at the


customer segments. Your customers are the employees engaged


one way or another in the moving of containers to their


destinations around the world. The first approach to


## 第 191 页


segmentation would be to look at the activities the employees


are doing. You might start with their departments or


divisions to give you a first attempt at segmentation. You


might adjust these segments as you learn more.


For example, the Shipping department could be one segment,


the Scheduling department another. The Predicting department


(these are the people who predict demand) has different


activity (and needs), but it connects closely with the


activities (and needs) of the shippers and the schedulers.


Each of the segments we have discussed—and perhaps a dozen


more that we have not listed—have different needs. Each


segment needs to be investigated separately, as each require


a different solution.


Without customer segments, you would be faced with trying to


find the requirements for 20,000 people—truly impossible.


With segments, you have a manageable business problem to


solve for each segment. Naturally, once you have a few


segments under your belt, you will find that overlaps and


similarities smooth the way for you.


Think of your own project situation. Once you have more than


a few dozen people who will ultimately possess your solution


## 第 192 页


—these are your customers—it is likely that you have a need


to segment them. Treating all the customers equally means


that your requirements discovery will be very much less than


optimal, as will the eventual solution.


One other reason for segmenting your customers, as we shall


see in a while, is to prioritize the segments and work on


your requirements discovery for the highest-priority


segments. Figure 6.1 illustrates this division and


prioritization.


![embedded_p192_24.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p192_24.jpeg)


## 第 193 页


Figure 6.1 The universe of customers is divided into


segments according to their business needs, and in some


cases, their business behavior. Each segment is studied


separately, beginning with the highest-priority segment.


Personas


Having segmented your customers, it is appropriate to


consider the possibility of using personas. You create a


persona to put a human face on a segment so that you and your


team can better visualize the needs and behaviors of the


people who make up the segment. Archetypes are the same


thing, except the segment is treated as an abstract entity


and is given a name to represent the segment’s grouping of


characteristics.


A persona is a virtual character that personifies


a customer segment.


A persona is an invented personality, an imaginary but


nevertheless archetypical representative of a customer


segment. You derive the persona through customer research or


by surveying the segment to understand their motivations,


goals, behaviors, and what they need to do with your


solution. Alternatively, you and your team can discuss from


## 第 194 页


your collective experience the attributes of the segment and


form your persona from that. The degree of precision needed


varies in proportion to both the size of the customer segment


and the criticality of the product to be built.


Why use an imaginary character when there are potentially


thousands of real people out there? Because for a mass-market


product, or one that is to be used by more than a dozen


different people, you don’t know, and can’t get to know,


all the potential users. But you can know one really well.


That is your persona, and although imaginary, his attributes


guide your requirements discovery. Almost always, a persona


is a better representation of your customer segment than a


human proxy.


Most teams write a one- or two-page description of the


persona’s behavior patterns, goals, skills, attitudes, and


environment. It is also usual, and indeed desirable, to


include enough personal details—including an invented name—


to make the persona seem real to you and your team.


A team discovering the requirements for a book-finding app


wrote this:


## 第 195 页


Alessia is 27 years old. She works in a large city in the


finance industry, drives a small electric car, is a casual


user of social media (about 20 minutes a day), reads (two to


three hours a day) mainly on her tablet but enjoys the


occasional hardback, spends time out with her girlfriends, is


educated to degree level, thinks of herself as mildly


adventurous, and is always keen to discover new authors. She


has disposable income but is careful what she spends it on.


There could be a lot more, but you get the idea by now. You


will also find it useful to have a photograph—you can find


thousands of photos in the online stock photo agencies.


Select one that the team agrees is their mental image of your


persona. The team picked Figure 6.2 as the kind of person


they think of as Alessia.


## 第 196 页


![embedded_p196_25.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p196_25.jpeg)


Figure 6.2 The team’s photo of their persona. The team


developed their persona through research into the customer


## 第 197 页


segment and interviews with potential customers.


A persona helps the team understand the customer segment and


think about the segment’s needs. When team members can see a


photo and speak about the persona by name, it brings to life


what otherwise would be abstract data about customers. The


question to ask is not what a set of data wants, but “What


does Alessia want?” Or “What would Alessia do in this


situation?” Or “What information does Alessia need for this


interaction?”


Personas avoid what Alan Cooper (see Resources) calls the


“elastic user,” whereby different stakeholders define the


characteristics of the product to be everything they have in


mind, and to accommodate their own assumptions about the kind


of user they are building for. The result is usually too many


requirements, some of which conflict with other requirements,


and a solution that, by trying to satisfy everyone, satisfies


none of its intended audience.


Having a persona also prevents designers from defining the


customer as themselves. This “self-referential” approach


(see Figure 6.3) almost always yields idiosyncratic results,


with most of the real customers failing to appreciate or use


the product.


## 第 198 页


![embedded_p198_26.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p198_26.jpeg)


Figure 6.3 The self-referential user considers only herself,


and inadvertently disregards the wishes or needs of the real


audience.


You probably use some consumer products that fit extremely


well with your personal preferences. This is not because the


product’s builders know you personally, but because they


## 第 199 页


selected a persona whose attributes matched (more or less)


yours. In contrast, if you try to write the requirements for


a product to suit your complete universe of customers, the


functionality would be so cumbersome as to make the solution


so unwieldy that nobody would use it—trying to suit


everybody ends up suiting nobody.


The lifelike attributes of the persona give the business


analysts and stakeholders a target at which to aim their


solution. Persona attributes such as computer literacy,


attitude toward technology, cultural taboos, viewpoints, and


so on act as a guide to your team.


For example, a few years ago we had the local government


council for one of the London boroughs as a client. Part of


the council’s responsibilities is to provide meals at home


for aged people and others who are not able to provide for


themselves. We worked with the team who manage this service,


whose objective was to make improvements to the meals and how


they were delivered. We jointly derived a persona (we called


her Elsie), partly from council data and partly from the


personal experience of the social workers. We arrived at a


consensus persona that was felt to be archetypical of the


meal recipients. The team then began asking, “What service


does Elsie really want?” and “How would she react if we


## 第 200 页


provided this service instead of that?” The answers were a


revelation to many of the team members; up until now they had


been designing this service to suit what they wanted to


deliver. Elsie—her photo smiled down on the team—gave them


answers that made for a far better and well-received service.


See Figure 6.4.


## 第 201 页


![embedded_p201_27.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p201_27.jpeg)


Figure 6.4 The team used a persona to represent their


customers. By treating the persona as a real person, they


were able to uncover a superior vision of what the future


business should be.


## 第 202 页


Personas are close to vital when it comes to agile


development and prototyping. We have seen some agile teams


where anybody can contribute stories or requirements. This


naturally leads to solutions that lack focus and are often


idiosyncratic. On the other hand, a well-developed persona


assists the team to be much more precise on the needs of the


solution. And if your development team sits down with a


single human customer, that customer must be exceptional;


otherwise, we urge you to consider a persona as an


alternative.


Prioritizing the Customer Segments


A quick glance at a list of your customer segments usually


reveals a difference in the importance of the segments. If


you only have one or two segments, then prioritizing them is


easy. But when you are faced with a longer list of segments,


things become slightly more difficult.


Prioritize your customer segments by value.


Customer segments differ in their value to your organization,


so it makes sense to prioritize them by value, and to


discover the requirements and develop a solution for the most


valuable one first.


## 第 203 页


Before we go any further, we need to remember that value can


mean different things at different times to different


people. You can think about value to the customers, but as


the organization is paying for the development of your


solution, it is probably best to start by thinking about what


provides value to the organization.


Consider the container shipping company you met earlier. The


project is about infrastructure and providing the appropriate


data for each business unit. Value to the organization is


delivered when you have finished the project, but that is a


long way off—it’s a very large business problem. The reason


for deriving the customer segments for this organization is


to give you a starting point.


As this project is largely about sharing data, the most


valuable place to start is the source of the data. There is


no actual source of data; it doesn’t bubble up from the


ground like an alpine spring. But the segment that creates


most of the data is the part of the business doing the


scheduling. These customers arrange the movement of


containers and so generate the data about where the


containers are and where they are going to be once delivered.


Sure, the sales segment generates income for the company and


therefore could be considered as the most valuable, but the


## 第 204 页


salespeople have to know the availability of containers in


order to sell their service. They need data from the


schedulers to do that.


Prioritizing segments is not easy, and obviously management


needs to be involved. For example, there might be a segment


or two where meeting their needs does more to achieving the


desired business outcome than others. Your task as a business


analyst is to provide information and advise management about


the relative value of the segments for the right decisions to


be made.


The container company’s segments are complex when it comes


to value, so let’s look at a different and simpler


situation. This time we can just use revenue.


Gotham Coffee Roasters is a new but growing business


supplying coffee beans to the discerning people in the city.


Looking at this business you can see reasonably distinct


customer segments.


• Direct personal buyers: These people come into the shop to


interact with the staff to find the most suitable beans to


match their tastes, and to discover new blends and new


## 第 205 页


single-origin coffee. The beans can be ground if the customer


wishes.


• Online buyers: These customers usually know what beans


they want, and they value convenient ordering and quick


delivery.


• Cafes & bars: These customers are concerned with freshness


and guaranteed continuity of supply.


• Resellers: These are the stores (usually food shops) that


stock Gotham’s beans and sell them to their customers.


Glancing at the above list, you can see that while parts of


the customers’ interactions are overlapping, there are also


distinct differences that require different solutions.


However, there are also commonalities between the segments,


so solutions for each segment will not be completely unique.


Gotham’s accounting people tell you that direct personal


buyers are the biggest revenue generators; the stores and the


personal engagement are very popular. The online segment is


next in size, and growing; people apparently like the


convenience of buying online. The cafes & bars segment and


the resellers segment are currently smaller than the others.


## 第 206 页


You could illustrate this situation as we have done in Figure


6.5.


## 第 207 页


![embedded_p207_28.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p207_28.jpeg)


Figure 6.5 A graphical representation of the proportional


revenue of the Gotham customer segments. There is no need to


## 第 208 页


have such a graphic apart from wanting to emphasize the


relative value of the customer segments.


Revenue is a good starting point for prioritizing the


segments in this case, but it pays to step back and see if


there are other factors that should be taken into


consideration. For example, is there a desire to grow one


segment? Suppose that Gotham’s management feels that having


a bigger online presence would be a desirable way to grow the


business. In other words, value here means “future value,”


or perhaps “desired value.” In this case, you might begin


with requirements discovery for the online segment and leave


the others aside for the moment.


Prioritizing the customer segments is not the sole


responsibility of the business analyst. Rather, it is a joint


effort involving management, marketing (if appropriate), the


product owner, and other stakeholders. It is advisable to


prioritize as early as possible in the project. Doing so


means that you are discovering the requirements and


developing the solution for the most valuable segments first,


and so the organization reaps the advantage that your


solution delivers as early as possible.


Review


## 第 209 页


Identifying, characterizing, and prioritizing customer


segments enables a more focused requirements discovery. When


you segregate your customers by their needs and aspirations,


the result is segments with clearly defined needs. If you


construct a persona for the segment—and we urge you to do so


—then requirements discovery becomes more straightforward


because you only have to discover one persona’s


requirements. Your own thoughts as to what the solution


should be are subordinated to the “thoughts” of the persona


you have generated for the segment. This means a sharper set


of requirements.


Your segments should be prioritized. We suggested that you


use business value, but sometimes just the estimated number


of people in the segment can set the priorities. However you


do it, working on the highest-priority segments brings you


the highest-value solution.


Of course, there will be overlap of the requirements for the


segments, but you will be more efficient by discovering all


the requirements for the highest-priority segment, and going


ahead and developing those requirements. The requirements for


subsequent segments lie in the differences between the


customer segments.

techniques to help you define and refine your value


proposition for specific customer segments.

## 第 211 页


Chapter 7. Business Events


Business events are the building blocks of business solution


design and development. They are also the unit of work that


forms the most effective way to discover the requirements.


But we are getting ahead of ourselves. Let’s start with the


business problem you are trying to solve. You have already


partitioned using customer segments, which gives you focused


chunks of the problem to deal with and the priority in which


you deal with the chunks. Now we’ll look at using business


events to give you the ideal partitioning for your further


investigation.


Business events are significant happenings that trigger a


response from the activity within your problem space. See


Figure 7.1.


## 第 212 页


![embedded_p212_29.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p212_29.jpeg)


Figure 7.1 Business events happen when a significant actor


outside the business does something that requires a response


from the business. Here we see a customer enrolling in a


service, someone buying something, some goods being


delivered, and so on. There is also a time-triggered business


## 第 213 页


event: At the end of each week, the business problem space


produces a report for an outside actor.


Note that the examples that follow talk about the whole of


the problem space. This is done for pedagogical reasons: It


is easier to discuss business events if they are not layered


on customer segments.


We’ll use business events for the remainder of our


investigation and development of the solution. The response


to each event is investigated, and the result of this


investigation is the discovery of the requirements for that


part of the problem.


Understanding the Work


In some situations, you have a large number of customers, and


they have differing needs. In the previous chapter, we


discussed how you can partition them into customer segments.


For our purposes here, we will treat each customer segment as


a separate piece of work.


There will be some overlap between the segments. The work of


each is probably not completely unique, but it is different


enough that it is more effective to look at each separately


and jump over any duplication you find.


## 第 214 页


When we talk about a piece of work, consider it to be either


the work of a customer segment or the entirety of your


business problem space. The examples of work that follow in


this chapter ignore customer segments and assume that you are


studying the whole of a business problem space.


The work is the activity happening within the problem space.


We have defined the problem space by the data that enters and


leaves it (we did this in Chapter 5, Goals-Scope-


Stakeholders, when we set the scope of the work and built a


context diagram). Now we want to investigate the work that


goes on inside that problem space. This is the work or


activity that is responding to the incoming data and


producing the outgoing data.


The work includes human tasks, software, machines, and low-


tech devices such as telephones, photocopiers (remember


those?), manual files, and notebooks—in fact, anything that


is used to produce the customer’s goods, services, or


information.


The Scope of the Work


Your context diagram shows how your work fits


within its business ecosystem.


## 第 215 页


Most business areas exist to provide services or products to


the ecosystem that surrounds them. The ecosystem is


represented on the context diagram by the adjacent systems.


The adjacent systems could be automated systems, or customers


who buy from or subscribe to the work, or departments,


organizations, or other parties that place some kind of


demand on or make some kind of contribution to the work.


To provide services or products, the work receives


information and signals from the ecosystem, uses these inputs


as raw material for its business processes, and responds by


sending information, signals, services, or products back to


the ecosystem.


As an example, Figure 7.2 shows the context diagram for a


piece of work (you can also call this the problem space) that


sells capsule coffee and the machines that use the capsules.


This work is fully automated—that is, it is online—and it


takes the orders from the customers, processes their


payments, and passes the orders to the Fulfillment Center for


shipping capsules and machines to the customers. The work


shown here is surrounded by its ecosystem: the adjacent


systems that either supply the data necessary for this work


or receive services and information from the work.


## 第 216 页


![embedded_p216_30.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p216_30.jpeg)


Figure 7.2 The context diagram showing the scope of the


work. The central area of the diagram represents the work


## 第 217 页


being done in the problem space. The outside world, the


ecosystem, is represented by the adjacent systems—Customer,


Fulfillment Center, Payment Processor, and so on. The named


arrows represent flows of information between the adjacent


systems and the work.


What Are Business Events?


Every piece of work responds to things that happen outside it


—it’s that simple. For the sake of clarity, because we are


discussing the work done by the business, we call these


happenings business events. This idea is shown in Figure


7.3.


## 第 218 页


![embedded_p218_31.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p218_31.jpeg)


Figure 7.3 A business event and its response. A business


event happens at the moment the adjacent system—an entity


outside the business—decides to do something and indicates


this to the work by providing the triggering data flow. When


this data arrives, the work responds by processing the


incoming data and by retrieving and recording stored data.


## 第 219 页


Let’s look at an example of a business event. Suppose that


you are a customer for the capsule coffee company we showed


you a moment ago. Let’s also suppose that your supply of


capsules is running low, and in order to continue enjoying


your morning coffee, you decide to restock. You do this by


ordering capsules from the coffee capsule company. That


moment—the instant you realized that you needed more


capsules—is the business event.


Of course, a business event goes unnoticed unless you tell


the business about it. In this case, you signaled the work by


placing an order for some capsules, and if it was not already


on file, you provided your credit card, shipping address, and


so on. This incoming flow of data triggers a response within


the coffee seller’s work. The response is to charge your


credit card, record the sale, and send a message to the


Fulfillment Center to ship the capsules to you. In this


organization, the physical goods—capsules and machines—are


held by the Fulfillment Center, and no physical material


(just data) enters the work.


It might seem a little overcomplicated to think separately


about the business event and the triggering data flow, but


there is a reason for doing so. The business event in this


case is Customer needs capsules. Suppose that you examine


## 第 220 页


this happening, and as usual for a business analyst you ask


why: Why does the customer need capsules? Why did he run low?


Perhaps a better business analysis question is “Why was he


allowed to run low?” Could the work have forestalled the


situation by automatically replenishing, or running a


subscription service, or something similar? Are coffee


consumption habits predictable enough to auto-replenish? Is


there a nonintrusive way for the customer to be reminded that


his stock of capsules is low? Remember, the real business


event is Customer needs capsules. The closer you get to that,


the better.


By thinking about the actual event and why it came about,


you give yourself the opportunity to discover more about the


activity of the adjacent system. The coffee customer is in


your zone of influence, so you should be studying him.


Another coffee business event: The customer needs help with


his membership, or wants advice on types of coffee, or wants


to know when his order will arrive, or has some other query.


That’s the business event—The customer needs help. However,


he will remain un-helped unless he has some way to inform the


work that the business event happened. This brings us to the


triggering data flow. You can see this triggering data flow


called Help Request on the context diagram in Figure 7.2.


## 第 221 页


When the work receives this flow, it can respond to the


business event. It fires up its AI chatbot and through a


conversation, provides the answers the customer needs.


The customer does not own or control the coffee company.


Nevertheless, in both examples he makes the company respond


by processing his incoming flow with the activities to


produce the needed outcome.


In some cases, the adjacent system where the business event


occurs is an automated system. There’s nothing unusual about


this, and you will find that most companies have multiple


software systems, and they are constantly passing signals and


data between them. Each time this happens it is a business


event, and for the system on the receiving end of the data,


this is a triggering data flow. It triggers a response just


as if the adjacent system were a human.


Business Use Cases


The work area (you can also call this the problem space)


always responds to the business event. This response is the


processing done to satisfy the request from the outside. It


could also be the processing needed to satisfy the business


policy that is invoked whenever any time-triggered or


conditional event occurs.


## 第 222 页


In short, the response is processing of some kind, and we


call this chunk of processing a business use case (BUC).


It doesn’t matter whether the processing for the business


use case is done by people or machines, or any combination


thereof. It is simply processing. You can describe it in


several different ways, and you will see examples of these as


we go through the book.


The business use case starts at the point where the work is


made aware that the event has happened: This is the arrival


of the triggering data flow. The processing continues until


several things have been achieved. The first is that all


necessary data has been retrieved and stored. The second is


that the desired business outcome of the BUC has been


achieved.


Figure 7.4 is a process model that illustrates the BUC for


the business event Customer orders coffee. There are several


different notations for this kind of model, and you might use


a different one for your own work. Don’t worry about the


notation; instead, focus on the functionality and the


outcome.


## 第 223 页


![embedded_p223_32.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p223_32.jpeg)


Figure 7.4 A process model of the business use case that


responds to the business event Customer needs coffee. The


work becomes aware of the event when it receives an incoming


data flow, and then responds by activating processes to


achieve the desired business outcome.


The business event happens when the Customer needs coffee and


generates the triggering data flow Capsule Order. It does not


matter whether this data flow is generated by the customer by


filling in a screen, sending an email request, telephoning,


or walking into a brick-and-mortar shop. The result is


incoming data that is represented by the envelope icon in the


starting event (that’s the circle at the extreme left of the


model). When this data arrives, it triggers the response from


the work.


When a business event happens, the work becomes


aware of it by the incoming triggering data flow


and responds by initiating a business use case.


## 第 224 页


The first of the responding activities shown in Figure 7.4 is


the one that checks that there is sufficient stock on hand to


fulfill the customer’s order. The database symbol shows that


the activity is accessing stored data. (We’ll ignore for the


moment the exception of there not being enough stock.) The


next activity is to get an authorization from the credit card


company, and then it goes on to record the sale and deduct


the ordered quantity from inventory (again, the process


accesses stored data).


There are two outgoing data flows from this BUC; one goes to


the customer to acknowledge that the order is accepted and


will be shipped, and the other goes to the Fulfillment Center


where the capsules will be picked off its shelves and shipped


to the customer. You can see these incoming and outgoing data


flows on the context diagram in Figure 7.2.


The desired outcome for the business event has been


achieved: The capsules will shortly be on their way to the


customer, and the stored data about sales and inventory has


been updated.


The outcome for each of your business use cases should


contribute in some way to the goals of the project. If it


## 第 225 页


does not, then it is a sign that the business event is not


needed or is outside the scope of your project. Finally, you


need to check that all the goals have been met. They can only


be met if your scope is correct and you have discovered all


the business events.


In the above example, the triggering data flow, Capsule


Order, originated with the customer who is outside the work.


Thus, we refer to this, naturally enough, as an external


business event. Now let’s look at another kind of business


event.


Time-Triggered Business Events


Time-triggered business events are initiated by the arrival


of a predetermined time or date. For example, your bank


generates a statement of your banking activity on the last


day of every month, or your insurance company sends you a


renewal notice a month before the anniversary of your policy.


“The arrival of a predetermined time” could also mean that


a certain amount of time has elapsed since another event


happened. For example, you are sent a reminder if two weeks


have elapsed since you were sent the original bill. Note that


it does not matter whether the customer receives the output


by paper or electronic means.


## 第 226 页


The usual response to a time-triggered business event is to


retrieve previously stored data, process it, and send the


resultant information to an adjacent system. The coffee


capsule company sends out a monthly Club News Bulletin to all


its club members. This gives general coffee advice, announces


new coffee, and sometimes offers club members discounts on


some capsules. The business event is Time to send out Club


News Bulletin.


The response to this business event is to retrieve the copy


that the copywriter has generated over the past month and


stored in a database within the capsule company’s work. The


response also includes an AI module that looks at the sales


figures, and where appropriate decides whether to offer a


discount on the slow-selling capsules. All that information


is formatted and emailed to the customers who have signed up


to be members of the club. This response is illustrated in


Figure 7.5.


## 第 227 页


![embedded_p227_33.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p227_33.jpeg)


Figure 7.5 A time-triggered business event, this one


happening every month. Data stored by previous business


events (data stores are shown as named parallel lines) is


retrieved, processed, and sent to an adjacent system(s). Here


we see the Newsletter Copy and the Capsule Sales data being


retrieved, processed, formatted, and sent to the Club


Members.


Once the predetermined time for the event arrives, the


work’s response is to do whatever is necessary to produce


the output. This almost always involves the retrieval and


manipulation of stored data. Once again, we use the response


to the time-triggered business event—the business use case—


as our unit of study.


## 第 228 页


Conditional Business Events


Conditional business events happen when a condition is met.


This condition is usually established by a business rule.


For example, recall the business event where a customer


orders capsules from the coffee company. If you glance back


at Figure 7.4—the process model of the response—there is an


activity called Record sale and reduce inventory. There is a


business rule that specifies the inventory threshold that


triggers restocking. If a customer order depletes the


company’s inventory such that it reaches the threshold, it


triggers the business event Need to resupply capsules. The


response to this event is to predict how many capsules are


needed and to place the order with the Capsule Supplier. You


can see the outgoing order on the context diagram shown in


Figure 7.2.


Data Conservation


Data conservation is a fancy name for “what comes out must


have gone in.” If you look back to Figure 7.5, you can see


that the process to generate the monthly newsletter uses


three data stores. These are called Newsletter Copy, Club


Members, and Capsule Sales. Note that a data store could be


anything—automated or manual—that can hold data. As long as


## 第 229 页


it can retain its data over time, we’ll call it a data


store.


The data in these stores is put there by external business


events. The Club Members data store is added to whenever a


customer wants to join the club. There is a data flow on the


context model (Figure 7.2) called Club Application. This


contains data about the applicant and is stored in the data


store Club Members by the processes of the BUC. Similarly,


the Capsule Sales data store is added to whenever a Capsule


Customer buys coffee.


The data that comes out of a business must have


gone into it somehow.


But how does the Newsletter Copy get there? There is no flow


on the context model to bring that data into the work area.


All the data stored within the work area has to come from the


outside, which it does whenever there is a business event.


The triggering data flow carries the data into the work where


it is processed and stored.


The lack of an incoming data flow carrying the copy means


that we have a data conservation error, or more plainly, we


have missed a business event. If the coffee company uses


## 第 230 页


generative AI to produce the copy for the newsletter, there


must still be a prompt coming from the outside to tell it


what to write about, and some data it needs for its language


model.


At this stage, that is, early in the project, it would be


relatively easy to correct the context diagram and carry on.


However, if you discover these data conservation errors later


in the project, it will be more serious. It will cause


considerable rework to incorporate the missed business events


and their stored data.


Why Business Events Are a Good Idea


We may seem to be going to a lot of trouble to describe


something that may, at first glance, seem obvious. But this


attention to the subject provides a framework for discovering


and managing your requirements. Consider that business


events:


• Are significant happenings. Business events are more than a


mouse click. They represent something that is important to


the business.


• Are a natural partitioning theme. They represent the


outside world’s view of the problem space.


## 第 231 页


• Are objective. They are determined by the work’s


interactions with the outside world.


• Are the ways your outside customers see your business.


• Ignore internal partitions—departments, systems,


technological items, and so on. These hold no interest for


outside customers.


• Stop you, to some extent, from plunging into a presumed


solution.


• Are cohesive partitions with minimal interfaces between the


pieces.


• Are the ideal partition for the discovery of the


requirements. You can investigate each event independently of


the others.


• Can be used later as implementation units.


Finding the Business Events


Business events are significant happenings that cause the


work to respond in some way. To get the work to respond,


there can be a triggering data flow, or for a time-triggered


## 第 232 页


and conditional event, there is a resultant data flow on the


context diagram.


Let’s make use of that with a different case. Figure 7.6


shows the context diagram for a piece of work that predicts


when ice will form on roads and schedules trucks to treat the


roads with deicing material before they freeze. Look at the


diagram and note the information flows that connect the


adjacent systems to the work. For example, the flow called


Changed Road is the result of the event that occurs when the


Road Engineering department either builds a new road or makes


significant alterations to an existing one. The engineering


personnel advise the work of the change so that the


scheduling work can update its own stored data about roads.


The flow called Road Deicing Schedule is the outcome of a


time-triggered business event: Every two hours, the work


produces a schedule of the roads to be treated and sends it


to the Truck Depot.


## 第 233 页


![embedded_p233_34.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p233_34.jpeg)


## 第 234 页


![embedded_p233_34.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p233_34.jpeg)


Figure 7.6 The context diagram for the Ice Breaker work.


Note the flows of data entering and leaving the work. These


indicate the presence of business events.


Each flow that enters or leaves the work is the result of a


business event; there can be no other reason for an external


communication to exist. Looking at each flow, you can


determine the business event that caused it. In some cases,


several flows may be attached to the same business event. For


example, when the Truck Depot advises that a scheduled truck


has broken down or will be withdrawn from service (input flow


Truck Breakdown), the work responds. Because one of the


trucks is now out of service, the other trucks must be


rescheduled to compensate for the shortfall, and the


resultant outgoing flow is the Amended Deicing Schedule.


Table 7.1 shows a list of business events and their input and


output flows for the deicing work. Compare it with the work


context diagram in Figure 7.6 and reconcile the business


events with the data that flows to and from the work.


## 第 235 页


Table 7.1 List of Business Events and Their Associated Input


and Output Flows for the Road Deicing Work


## 第 236 页


![embedded_p236_35.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p236_35.jpeg)


## 第 237 页


![embedded_p236_35.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p236_35.jpeg)


Admittedly, you need some knowledge of the work to figure out


the business events. To this end, we advise you to start the


process of determining business events during blastoff, when


the key stakeholders are present. In most situations, you


find the stakeholders know the business events (they may not


know them by that name, but they will know what they are).


Try to identify all the business events during the blastoff.


You might miss one or two, but you will find them when you


begin to study the work.


Ready-made Solutions


Business events also apply when using ready-made solutions. A


ready-made solution is something that already exists and can


potentially solve your business problem. It might be a


solution to the whole of the problem, or it can be a


component that contributes part of the solution. Ready-made


solutions can be bought, subscribed to, or acquired as an


open-source solution. They can also be legacy solutions.


These are whole or partial solutions that your organization


## 第 238 页


has already built or bought. Ready-made solutions are also


known as off-the-shelf (OTS) solutions, as commercial off-


the-shelf (COTS) solutions, and sometimes as packages. In


short, anything that we plan to use without building it from


scratch we call ready-made solutions.


If your project proposes to use a ready-made solution or


ready-made components then they must respond to the same


business events as would any other type of solution. However,


with the ready-made solution, your task is slightly


different. Instead of discovering what the response to a


business event is, you are discovering whether the outcome of


the response from the ready-made solution is what you need it


to be.


Figure 7.7 is the conceptual view of a proposed ready-made


solution. The purpose of the diagram is to illustrate that


the ready-made, “out of the box” solution responds to


business events. The task is to assess the outcome of each


event and compare it with the organization’s desired


outcome. The desired outcome would include the data produced


by the response, along with the correctness of the algorithms


used by the ready-made response.


## 第 239 页


![embedded_p239_36.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p239_36.jpeg)


## 第 240 页


Figure 7.7 The ready-made solution (shown as an open


cardboard box signifying an “out of the box” solution) is


assessed as to whether the business events it handles match


the needed business events and whether the outcome of each


event matches the organization’s desired outcomes.


The objective is to assess whether the business events are


suitable, whether the response conforms to the


organization’s desired behavior, whether the response needs


some modification to be made to the ready-made solution, or


in some cases whether the organization needs to change to fit


the ready-made solution.


We’ll revisit this later when we look at the Trawling


activity in Part IV.


Review


Business events allow you to carve out a rational and


cohesive piece of the problem space for further study.


Instead of trying to understand the whole of the problem at


once, you digest it one business event at a time. Naturally,


it’s more effective to analyze moderately sized chunks.


These responses—we’re calling them business use cases or


## 第 241 页


BUCs—are independent of each other, so they make an ideal


partitioning theme.


By using business events to partition the problem space, you


are taking an external view of it. You are not relying on how


it happens to be partitioned internally at the moment, or on


someone’s idea of how it might be partitioned in the future.


Instead, you partition the work according to the most


important view of the work: how the outside world sees it.


Later, we will suggest that you develop and deploy the


solution one business event at a time. But let’s not get


ahead of ourselves. Before doing anything more, we should


prioritize the business events.


Resources


Essential Systems Analysis by Steve McMenamin and John Palmer


(Yourdon Press, 1984). This book introduced the ideas of


essence and business events. Unfortunately, it is now out of


print.


Business Analysis Agility: Solve the Real Problem, Deliver


Real Value by Suzanne Robertson and James Robertson (Addison-


Wesley, 2018). This companion book also looks at business


events.


## 第 242 页


Business Analysis Techniques, 3rd Edition by James Cadle,


Debra Paul, Adrian Reed, David Beckham, and Paul Turner (BCS


Learning and Development Ltd., 2021). This has a slightly


different take on business event analysis.


## 第 243 页


Chapter 8. Prioritizing the Business
Events


Not all business events are equally valuable to your


customer, nor are they equally urgent. While you eventually


must discover the requirements for all of them and implement


all of them, you obviously cannot do all of them at the same


time. And there is no need to.


At some stage early in your development cycle, you should


stop, step back, and prioritize the business events you have.


It makes sense when you are discovering the requirements to


favor those events that yield the best return. The best


return in this case comes from economically developing the


events that are the most valuable to your organization and


your customers.


Keep in mind that you might have already divided the problem


space according to customer segments. So here you would be


prioritizing the business events within each customer


segment.


This chapter is about the factors to consider when


determining which parts of the problem are to be given the


most and/or earliest attention.


## 第 244 页


Priority, Priority, Priority


In the previous chapter you saw the context model for a


company selling coffee capsules, and we discussed a few of


its business events. The context model for this company is


reproduced in Figure 8.1, but this time it has been annotated


with the numbers of the business events. The numbers of the


events do not signify priority; they are simply identifiers.


They have been put in this order for reading convenience


only. You must put them in priority order.


## 第 245 页


![embedded_p245_37.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p245_37.jpeg)


Figure 8.1 The business shown here sells coffee capsules and


machines that use the capsules. The numbers attached to the


## 第 246 页


data flows identify the business event associated with that


flow.


This business is straightforward. Customers order coffee and


pay at the same time. Either the work holds their credit card


or the card number is submitted along with the order. A


separate payment company processes the transactions.


Authorized orders are sent to the Fulfillment Center, which


packages and ships the physical goods. Customers can join the


club, which gives them a newsletter and occasional discounts.


From time to time, the capsule and machines in the


Fulfillment Center are damaged or lost. When this happens,


Fulfillment advises the work of the actual quantities of


goods.


However, don’t spend time figuring out how this business


works. The point of it is to look at the business events and


prioritize them.


The numbers on the context diagram are a cross reference to


the following list of business events. Note that some of the


business events have multiple flows:


1. Capsule Customer orders coffee


2. Capsule Customer applies to join club


## 第 247 页


3. Capsule Customer orders coffee machine


4. Capsule Customer requests help


5. Time to publish Club News Bulletin


6. Time to forecast stocking needs


7. Time to order more capsules from the Supplier


8. Time to order more machines


9. Fulfillment Center advises actual stock levels


Take a few moments to check this list against the context


diagram, and then consider which of the business events you


would give the most priority to. You are just guessing at


this stage, but it is worth the few moments to consider which


of the events bring the most value to the business.


There is no single right answer to prioritization—it depends


on multiple factors. Each organization, each project, each


sponsor, and each product owner has its own priorities and


preferences. While we cannot say which prioritization factors


are right for your project and team, we can show you some of


the factors that have proved useful over time.


## 第 248 页


Prioritization is affected by the people doing it. It should


not automatically be a management decision. Sometimes fitting


in with legacy solutions means different priorities, and


these are in the domain of the business analyst, the product


owner, and possibly some of the development team. Sometimes


dependencies between events dictate priorities, again the


domain of the business analyst. Then of course there are


management factors such as revenue. The sponsor might need


certain events before others. And there would be other people


involved.


For the sake of simplicity, let us say that the people


involved in the prioritization exercise are the key


stakeholders. There is no fixed definition for this term, but


most development initiatives have a subset of the


stakeholders who are much closer to the initiative and have a


greater interest in its outcome.


For example:


• The manager of the department where the solution will be


deployed


• The product owner


• At least one of the business analysts


## 第 249 页


• The project sponsor


• The product manager


• The program manager


Key stakeholders vary from project to project, and exactly


who is key is usually dependent on the organizational


structure. The nature of the solution also influences who is


key.


In short, you, the business analyst, need to find the people


who are key to the project and invite them to prioritize the


business events.


Estimating Effort


There is another factor needed to prioritize effectively: the


amount of effort required for each business event. This


effort estimation technique is borrowed from agile


development where the team estimates “story points.” We’re


in the Blastoff here, and we don’t have stories yet.


Instead, we’ll use the story point technique to estimate the


effort needed for each of the business events. Let’s change


the name to event points to make it easier to visualize. You


are estimating each business event with the intention of


## 第 250 页


understanding how much effort it needs to complete the


analysis and requirements tasks.


You have a list of business events. We looked at determining


these in the previous chapter. Each business event has a


business use case. The BUC is the functionality needed to


achieve the outcome of the business event. It takes effort to


uncover and analyze this functionality, and to write


requirements, or stories, for a solution to implement it. You


need to know how much effort.


Start your estimating with a smallish team of business


analysts. During Blastoff, at best you have a brief


description of a BUC, but you also have the experience of the


team. Depending on their experience, they have some idea of


what is involved.


To estimate the effort for a business event, the team holds a


“planning poker” session. Each team member is given a set


of “poker” cards with values 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20, 40, and


100 event points. These numbers come from Mike Cohn (see


Resources). Some teams use T-shirt sizes—S, M, L, XL—but


Cohn’s numbers, based on the Fibonacci series, are probably


better.


## 第 251 页


The team starts with a business event, and someone who knows


a little about it gives a brief introduction to it. Then each


team member uses his experience to allocate the number of


event points. Event points represent the effort needed to


complete the business analysis for that business event.


This is illustrated in Figure 8.2.


## 第 252 页


![embedded_p252_38.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p252_38.jpeg)


Figure 8.2 Estimating the effort required for each business


event, and awarding them event points


Estimating effort means considering the complexity of the


BUC, the amount of work required, risks associated with the


BUC, and the amount of uncertainty about it. Other factors


## 第 253 页


are an assessment of how difficult it will be to get access


to the stakeholders, and how much outside knowledge will be


needed. Each team member privately makes his best estimate of


the effort needed for this business use case to be fully


understood and its requirements to be written. He then


selects the poker card with the number of event points that


represents his estimate of required effort. He puts this face


down on the table.


When all members have made their estimate for an event, the


cards are turned over and discussed. The discussion continues


until the team reaches a consensus on the event points for


the business event. Note that this is not the average of the


cards, but the consensus value that the team arrives at. If


someone gives the event a high score, then he is asked if he


knows something that others don’t. If the numbers are widely


dispersed, then after a discussion, the cards are played


again. And it is worth restating that you’re looking for a


consensus, not the average.


You are estimating effort, not time. Event points are not


absolute units—you can’t say that 1 event point will take


four hours or cost $1,000. You are allocating points on a


relative basis—8 event points require a little over half the


effort of a business event with 13 event points.


## 第 254 页


We’ll make several uses of event points. The first is


prioritization.


Prioritization Factors


To prioritize, the key stakeholders consider some of the


following factors, listed here in no particular order.


• Expected revenue: Back in Chapter 6, Customer Segments, we


suggested you prioritize your customer segments using


expected revenue as one (perhaps the most important) of the


prioritization factors. It is a little more difficult to


estimate the expected revenue from an individual business


event, but with some help from your accounting department,


you can usually make reasonable estimates of revenue per


event.


• Business value: This might simply be revenue, but it can


also mean the contribution the business event makes toward


the goals and benefits of your project.


• Required effort: Is the value of a business event—


expressed in event points—worth the effort needed to analyze


and implement it? Consideration is given to whether it’s


better to do the big-effort or small-effort events earlier.


## 第 255 页


• Data dependencies: When business events happen, the


triggering data flow brings data into the work and stores it.


This stored data will be subsequently needed by another


business event. You would need a rudimentary data model, or a


CRUD table (we’ll talk about CRUD in a subsequent chapter),


to know your data dependencies, but this might be a


worthwhile prioritization exercise to help the eventual


implementation.


• Minimum viable product: If your project intends to develop


a minimum viable product (MVP), then the product owner


liaises with the business analyst and management to decide


which business events are to be part of the MVP. These events


are pushed to the top of the list, leaving the remainder to


be developed at some later time. Naturally, the remaining


events are prioritized before proceeding with them.


• Adjacent systems: Some of the adjacent systems on your


context diagram are more important to the business than


others. The business events that affect these adjacent


systems can thereby be given a higher priority.


• MoSCoW or MuSCoW: This means Must have (crucial); Should


have (important but not crucial to success); Could have (nice


to have but not essential); and Won’t have yet (include


## 第 256 页


these when time permits). MuSCoW doesn’t tell you how to


assign a priority; it is just there to give you a label for


your priority assignment.


• Risk: This applies to business events that carry the


possibility of failure. Perhaps they involve some new,


untried technology, or perhaps customer acceptance of the


event is yet unknown. Risky business events should be done as


early as possible. There is no point in spending most of your


budget and then discovering that something cannot be done.


• Market impact: Is this event one that is innovative and


new, and is intended to have a significant impact in the


marketplace? If so, move it higher on the list.


• Time needed to develop: These are early days, and we are


not yet thinking too much about the implementation of this


part of the solution. However, sometimes the nature of the


business event suggests that it will be difficult or time-


consuming to implement. This is really a product owner’s


call as to whether to do the time-consuming things early or


late.


• Visibility: Sometimes you find your project running late,


or sometimes you have a threat to your funding. You need a


## 第 257 页


success story, or something that brings attention to your


solution. Pick the flashiest, most client-pleasing business


events and, providing they are not excessively time-


consuming, move them up the charts.


Having looked at some of the prioritization factors, you


might care to reconsider the priorities for the capsule


company’s business events. You saw this a little earlier.


Event 1, Capsule Customer orders coffee, is certainly the


revenue earner, and for this reason you might want to start


with it and devote a little time to ensuring it is the best


buying experience for the customer. However, event 9,


Fulfillment Center advises actual stock levels, is the one


that establishes the data needed for event 1. This event


happens when the fulfillment people adjust their stock counts


for damage or loss, and when a new shipment of capsules


arrives from the supplier. This event informs the work of the


actual stock counts, so it would be the highest priority if


you want to establish data dependencies.


You might think about the adjacent systems, and Capsule


Customer is the most important of all. For this reason, you


might consider all the events connected to the customer as


## 第 258 页


top priority and work on them first. These are the ones that


make the most obvious contribution to the project’s goals.


There is no single right answer, but using the prioritization


factors, you and your key stakeholders can reach agreement on


the priority of the business events.


Your own list of business events for a project that you are


doing at work would likely be longer than the above list.


This makes the prioritization task a little harder, but the


longer the list is, the more necessary it is to prioritize.


The priorities of the business events can change. As you


discover more about the work and the business problem, you


might need to alter your thinking about priority. Similarly,


it is quite possible that the problem space changes. By


having the priority factors and your list of priorities, you


and your stakeholders have a mechanism for reprioritizing.


Approval Voting


Approval voting is an electoral system that is particularly


effective when multiple parties or candidates are contesting


an election. It is especially suited for those European


countries that have lots of smaller political parties, and is


used in some American cities.


## 第 259 页


You start with the candidate business events. You have a list


with, say, 20 to 40 business events on it, and you want to


reach a consensus with the key stakeholders as to the


relative importance of these events.


Approval voting works by stakeholders giving one vote for


each of the business events that they approve of and want


to see implemented early. Each stakeholder can vote for as


few or as many of the events as they approve of. (Voting for


every event nullifies that stakeholder’s votes.) The winner


is the one that has collected the greatest number of approval


votes.


The advantage here is that the winner is a consensus of the


key stakeholders. But it’s not just the winner you are


concerned with. Approval voting gives you the chance to see


the distribution of approval votes, and it clearly shows the


ranked support, or lack thereof, of each of the business


events.


Approval voting is possibly the fairest way of determining


priority. It can be thought of as a popularity contest, but


if some events are popular with a significant number of key


stakeholders, those events must be crucial, and thus high


priority.


## 第 260 页


Business Analysis Planning


You now have two things to use for planning the business


analysis work. One is the event points—representing the


effort needed for an event—and the other is the priority in


which the business events are to be tackled.


Starting with the highest priority, you need to allocate


events to team members. It makes sense to give the one with


the highest event count to the team member who is most


productive. We know there is a significant difference between


people when it comes to productivity. You only need to look


around your office to see this.


For the sake of illustration, let’s say there are three team


members, and we’ll call them Alpha, Beta, and Gamma. Alpha


is more experienced and is good at getting the work done.


Gamma is young and inexperienced, and so is not yet as


productive as Alpha. Beta is somewhere in between the others.


The top three events on the priorities list have event points


of 3, 8, and 13. You give Alpha the 13-pointer, and Gamma


gets the 3-point event. When you estimated the event points,


difficulty and uncertainty were two of the factors you used.


## 第 261 页


What better than to ensure that Alpha—and other Alphas in


the team—tackle the difficult, uncertain events.


As time goes on, you can begin to get a sense of the speed,


in terms of event points, the team is achieving.


Review


On a personal level, you prioritize when you decide whether


to go to a movie or have an early night. You prioritize when


you decide your monthly spending budget. Your government


prioritizes when it decides the national budget.


Prioritization, as we are discussing here, means determining


what is valuable to the organization and the project. This is


the important stuff, and you do it early. This way, when you


run into the inevitable deadline problems, you’re left with


the less consequential stuff. It also has a psychological


effect that the team works on the best stuff early in the


project when enthusiasm is highest.


Prioritization is illustrated in Figure 8.3.


## 第 262 页


![embedded_p262_39.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p262_39.jpeg)


Figure 8.3 The business events are prioritized, and the


highest-priority events are trawled and prototyped to


discover the requirements. The process is iterative.


Prioritize early; prioritize often.


Prioritization varies from project to project—the


prioritization factors vary according to the situation. They


also change throughout the project. This means that of course


## 第 263 页


you prioritize early, but you also prioritize often. Whenever


there is a change to the scope, the stakeholders, or the


goals, it is an indication that there might be a need to


reprioritize. As you progress with your project, things


change, and some of these will change your ideas on what is


important.

planning poker here to estimate business events.


Agile and Business Analysis: Practical Guidance for IT


Professionals, Second Edition, by Lynda Girvan and Debra Paul


(BCS, The Chartered Institute for IT, 2024). This covers


various agile techniques, including MuSCoW prioritization of


requirements.


ProjectManagement.com. This website


(https://www.projectmanagement.com/#_=_) is not strictly


about business analysis and requirements, but it has a range

of articles, blogs, and resources on project management. You


can find information on task prioritization techniques,


including those applicable to business analysis.


International Institute of Business Analysis (IIBA). The IIBA

## 第 265 页


Chapter 9. To Go or Not to Go?


We have left this discussion on whether to proceed or not


until this last chapter of Part II, Project Blastoff.


However, that does not mean that any project should leave it


until late to decide whether going forward is the right


option. To go or not to go is a question that should be


asked early and often.


Back in Chapter 5, we discussed goals-scope-stakeholders.


Right there is a point at which you have an idea as to the


viability of the project and whether it is sensible to


proceed. Again, when you look at the real problem to solve,


you must ask if this is the right problem to solve. Does


anybody really need this? Or should you be looking at another


part of the business for a more advantageous opportunity?


In Adrenaline Junkies and Template Zombies (see Resources),


together with our Guild partners we wrote about “dead


1


fish” projects. From day one, this type of project has no


chance of meeting its goals, and most people know it but say


nothing. Despite all the other dead fish littering the beach,


this one presses ahead.


## 第 266 页


1


The Atlantic Systems Guild (https://systemsguild.eu) is a


transatlantic partnership of thinkers and practitioners in


the business analysis and systems domain.


Dead fish projects happen because people are discouraged from


asking, “Should we proceed with this? Should we go or not


go?” And yet, given that most projects fail in some way,


this is a question that should be asked again and again.


Somehow it is seen as shameful to question the legitimacy of


a project, and even more shameful to cancel one.


We have now looked at all the things you can do in the


Project Blastoff. Using these as ammunition, it is time to


put aside any embarrassment and ask if going ahead or


stopping the project is the most beneficial thing to do.


Each time you and your team come together to decide whether


or not to proceed, there are a couple of things to consider.


1. The likelihood that the project will be successful. That


is, the project delivers a solution that provides the desired


business outcome.
