2. Whether the solution will provide a return on investment.


Over the lifetime of the solution, it brings enough benefit


## 第 267 页


to warrant the cost of developing it.


It is worthwhile to look at both in some detail. We


understand that business analysts are not always involved in


this kind of work, but they should be. The business analyst


is usually impartial—she has no political investment—and is


the closest person to the business problem. The role of the


business analyst here is to supply the information that


enables enlightened decisions to be made as to project


viability.


The Likelihood of a Successful Project


Too many projects end up as dead fish. As previously


mentioned, these are hopeless cases and drag on for months


despite the team’s objection to the smell of the dead


carcass. The bizarre thing here is that all too often, the


team knew at the outset that the project was doomed and would


end up metaphorically rotting with the other carcasses on the


beach.


Let’s avoid that. There are some simple enough checks that


reliably indicate the likelihood that your project will be


successful, or that you are better off to abandon it now.


Goals


## 第 268 页


There should be a limited number of goals. We have found


that up to five (no more) well-stated, measurable goals can


steer the project. More goals than that defeats your ability


to focus on the important things and to keep your


requirements discovery consistent with the goals.


Then you should ask if the goals are clear and unambiguous.


Fudge words and corporate buzzwords are danger signals.


However, when the language is concrete enough that everybody


can agree on its meaning and thus the goal, your success


likelihood indicator moves up a notch.


Does the goal indicate a desired business outcome that will


bring an actual benefit to the customer and to your


organization? Further, is this benefit measurable? The simple


thing to look for here is whether the goal contains numbers.


A goal that says “Lower production costs by 4%” can be


tested to determine the effectiveness of the solution,


whereas “Streamline production” is so vague that almost any


solution would qualify.


The reason for having measurable goals is to establish a


precise target, and for you and your client to be able to


objectively say when you have successfully completed the


project.


## 第 269 页


Risk


Risk is not necessarily a bad thing—we face risks every


day. Just leaving your home to go to work involves some risk:


Your car won’t start, the train will be late, you will be


assigned to share an office with someone you don’t like. But


still, you go to work each day because you know the risks and


consider the outcome (your salary and job satisfaction) to be


worth the risks.


Similarly with development projects: Taking risks is


necessary if you are to make advances. Nothing was ever


gained without some risk of failure. Bill Gates and Paul


Allen knew they were taking a risk when they dropped out of


Harvard to start Microsoft. Jeff Bezos knew the risks when he


quit his Wall Street job to start Amazon. The point is that


there is a difference between calculated risk and


recklessness.


But each day people plunge into projects where they have no


idea of the risks involved, and thus no idea whether the


intended outcome is worth taking the risks.


Have you ever worked on a project where nothing


went wrong?


## 第 270 页


Have you ever worked on a project where nothing went wrong?


Neither has anyone else. But did you ever try and figure out


ahead of time what could go wrong and do something to prevent


it from going wrong, or at least allow for the mishaps by


budgeting for them? This, in its simplest sense, is risk


management.


The criticality and the cost of your project determine the


formality of your risk management. For short, sharp projects,


it’s probably enough to sit down with the team and ask:


“What kind of mishaps has the organization had with this


type of project before? What is the possibility of that


happening again? [The answer is not zero.] How severe was the


impact of the mishap? Do we need to take mitigating action,


or can we deal with it when or if it arises?”


A short list of common project risks might be helpful, shown


here in no particular order:


• Inaccurate estimation of cost


• Vague goals


• Too little time allocated to the project


• Inappropriate people on the project team


## 第 271 页


• Incompetent people on the team


• Knowledgeable or skilled people leaving the project team


• Difficulty of recruiting project team members


• Aggressive deadlines


• Failing to discover the real business problem


• Scope creep


• Lack of stakeholder involvement


• Inadequate knowledge of the technology involved


• Unmet expectations


• Poor project management


• External risks—changes in the market, new laws, and so on


• Poor user uptake of the delivered solution


• Absence of any risk management (yes, it’s a risk)


• Inadequate resources


• Absence of project sponsorship


## 第 272 页


• Poor productivity


All of the above, and more, have happened and are happening


today on development projects. It is folly to deny that none


of the above will apply to your project.


For large, mission-critical projects, it is reckless to


proceed without formal risk assessment done by a competent


risk specialist. The cost of doing it is amply repaid when it


reveals risks that, if manifested, could have the potential


to cause the whole project to fail.


Whatever the scale, you, your team, and your management need


to be aware of risks that might become problems. You can also


identify early-warning signs that a risk is coming to


fruition and whether you wish to take mitigating steps.


To know if risks are becoming obstacles, Adrian Reed points


out the value of having a tripwire. Tripwires were


originally wires strung about a foot off the ground around


the perimeter of your camp so that if the enemy, or a grizzly


bear, tried to sneak up on you in the dark, they would trip


over the wire and set off an alarm. In projects, a tripwire


is a condition that you set in advance. If this condition is


## 第 273 页


met, it triggers a warning that you need to pay attention to


something.


For example, you might set a tripwire about the state of the


project. Your tripwire might say that ten business events


must be analyzed and implemented by the end of the year. The


wire can be tripped for several reasons: lack of stakeholder


commitment, incompetent people on the team, uncertainty of


purpose, lack of skilled personnel, and so on. Whatever the


reason, if you don’t achieve your ten business events, the


wire is tripped and you regroup and reevaluate.


Risk is a double-edged sword. You try to avoid some risks,


but most opportunities carry risk. Say you are about to


implement a radical change to the way your company processes


its payroll. If you pull it off, it will save tens of


thousands of dollars each year (by being more effective, not


by reducing employees’ salaries). The technology needed to


do this is as yet untried, but the potential savings mean


that this is a risk worth taking. You would of course monitor


the risks and perhaps set a tripwire or two.


Tim Lister, our partner in The Atlantic Systems Guild, summed


this up very simply: “Risk management is project management


for grown-ups.”


## 第 274 页


Cost


One of the factors that determine whether your project should


be allowed to go ahead is whether its cost in time or money


is affordable given the benefits.


Estimating cost is not within the jurisdiction of the


business analyst. (If you want to know more about it, there


are several references in the Resources section.) However, as


a business analyst you are the responsible adult in the room


when cost estimates are presented. Somebody has to be the


grown-up, because most projects fail to deliver within


budget. Flyvbjerg (see Resources) points at IT projects that


have exceeded budget by more than 400%. According to Gartner


studies, 75% of all US IT projects fail to deliver on time


and within budget. Other studies have shown that


(coincidentally) 75% of IT people do not expect their


projects to succeed.


What’s going wrong here? Clearly a large share of the blame


must lie with the expectations for the project. Many projects


start with seriously underestimated costs. Why? Because


people want to do the project, and deflating the budget and


inflating the advantages is a very common way to convince


management to run the project.


## 第 275 页


As a business analyst, you cannot prevent that from


happening, but you can point out that the estimates are low.


For example, look at the number of business events, or the


number of flows on the context diagram. If you were to divide


the budget by the number of events, does the average cost per


event fall on the “reasonable” side of the ledger, or the


“fantasizing” side?


Viability


Viability is about whether or not the project has a chance


of succeeding. It is not viable to leap off a tall building


with the expectation of flying, and yet many projects


metaphorically do so.


The point here is that the estimate of time or money needed


must be within the budget. If not, either the budget is


increased, the scope of the project reduced, or the project


abandoned. We are talking about viability here, and an


inadequate budget of time or money means that the project is


anything but viable.


As a business analyst, you spend time with the stakeholders.


This means you are in a position to assess the cultural


viability of the project. Is it likely to produce a solution


that will fit with the users’ acceptable way of working?


## 第 276 页


Will it be a good match with the prevailing organizational


culture?


Technical viability is assessed by asking if the


organization has the skills to construct any potential


solution. If the team is not familiar with the likely


technology, then the viability of the project is compromised.


You should also consider the risks that were mentioned above.


If there is a strong chance that one or more of these is


likely to become a serious problem, then you need to question


the viability of the project.


Ready-made Solutions


For ready-made solutions, the decision to go or not to go is


similar to what we have been describing. Your assessment


takes in the cost of the ready-made, if needed the cost of


modifying the ready-made or changing the organization, and


the desirability of the ready-made’s outcome for each


business event.


Modifying the organization to fit the ready-made happens


more and more often. The cost to consider here is the cost of


disruption. The people doing the work have to learn new


procedures, which usually brings a certain amount of


## 第 277 页


uncertainty. This affects productivity for a little while


after the ready-made is deployed. Organizations don’t go


from 0 to 100 in a day; it takes time before productivity is


back up to previous levels.


The other cost that might affect viability is whether there


are human costs associated with the ready-made. Do people


have to do extra tasks because of the ready-made? Do they


need training? Do backup and security bring extra work? These


things should be brought up as part of your decision to buy


or build.


Develop the Business Case


It is unlikely that in the commercial world, you would embark


on a project if there were no financial reward for doing so.


Perhaps in the military the emphasis would not be on money,


but a defense department would want to quantify their return


on investment—the number of incoming enemy missiles


intercepted and destroyed, the improved range or accuracy of


an artillery piece, or some such. Whether it’s commercial,


military, medical, government, or internal, we should expect


some kind of return for the money and effort we put into


developing our solutions.


## 第 278 页


The role of the business analyst is expanding—they are no


longer limited to writing requirements. What we are about to


discuss might be thought of as a management task, but our


experience points to business analysts becoming more and


more involved in developing the business case for the


project.


The business case is the justification for your project. It


balances the advantages of completing the project and


delivering a solution with the disadvantages of not having


the solution. The objective is to present the information


needed for the organization to decide whether your project is


a worthwhile investment.


Business cases often make recommendations but should not be


used as a sales pitch for a preferred solution. The business


case should be a presentation of the facts. If the facts are


clear enough and presented coherently, then arriving at the


right decision is more likely.


There is no fixed format for a business case, so when you


write yours, or contribute to one as a team effort, you can


write it pretty much any way you see fit. However, we suggest


the following set of items make a solid business case.


Business Problem


## 第 279 页


The best place to start your business case is with the


business problem you are proposing to solve. We looked at


this in previous chapters when we discussed goals, essence,


and the real problem. You should elaborate a little on the


business problem by including some background. The background


should demonstrate why this is a problem. Describe this


succinctly; there is no need to rabbit on for page after


page. If the problem exists, it will be easily recognized by


your readers. You should connect your description of the


business problem to the scope, stakeholders, and goals that


we looked at earlier. For example:


Orders are taking too long to reach the customers. We are


losing customers as a result (5% fewer customers this


financial year, revenue is down 6.5%). Six of our competitors


are beating us on the time they take to deliver. Our


warehouse and its equipment are up to 15 years old, and our


fleet of delivery vehicles, and the drivers, are older than


average for our industry.


Sometimes the business problem is an opportunity. That is,


instead of something needing correcting, there is an opening


of some kind that can be taken advantage of. You can treat


business problems and opportunities as the same thing.


## 第 280 页


Value Proposition


You should write a value proposition: a statement of the


solution the organization proposes to offer. The value


proposition is a promise of the value the solution will


provide to a customer segment. Thus, the purpose of the value


proposition is to enable a customer to assess the benefits of


possessing your solution.


A value proposition might also propose value to


stakeholders other than the customer. These are values that


would be realized to these ancillary stakeholders when the


customer uses the solution. For example, previously we spoke


of a traffic regulating solution. The customer for this is


the road authority; the ancillary stakeholders who would


receive value from the solution are the residents and the


police.


Previously we discussed goals, and how goals should be


quantified: “Customers are able to acquire a mortgage in


less than 15 minutes”; “The cost of claims processing will


be reduced by 12%”; and so on. The goal is the value of


having your solution.


You might go further with your value proposition and add


value drivers: the major capabilities of your solution that


## 第 281 页


help to bring about the value. For example, you’re proposing


a solution to allow commuters to use their debit cards,


phones, watches, and so on to pay their fare on a Metro


system. The value of this is the convenience of fare paying:


The time taken for commuters to buy tickets is zero, the


customer satisfaction is estimated above 80%, and the cost of


fare collection is reduced by 65%.


The value drivers here are


• Connections to debit card payment systems


• Connections to other payment systems


• Automated entry/exit barriers


These give weight to your proposal of value.


Don’t confuse these value drivers—you might think of them


as features— with benefits. The automated barriers are a


feature; the benefit is faster, cheaper access to the Metro.


Risks and Assumptions


All projects face risks; we discussed this earlier. We


suggest that you include in your business case the most


impactful risks. You should also include the risk of not


## 第 282 页


developing a solution. For example, “Our competitors are


developing similar solutions, and we risk losing customers if


we don’t have our own solution.”


Assumptions are part of the business case. Sometimes you are


basing your case on assumptions such as “The price of oil


will remain over $100 per barrel”; “People will continue


working from home and not commute”; or “Younger people will


reduce their social media usage by at least 50%.” It is


important to bring your assumptions into the light—your


management must be aware of them to either endorse or refute


them. Figure 9.1 illustrates balancing risk with advantages.


## 第 283 页


![embedded_p283_40.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p283_40.jpeg)


Figure 9.1 The business case is an assessment of whether the


advantages that the solution will bring outweigh the costs


and risks of building or buying a solution.


Options


## 第 284 页


Here you show the options that have been considered for the


project—including those that were discarded and those still


under consideration. Options can be to buy, build, borrow,


enhance, revert to manual, outsource the problem, outsource


the solution, abandon the commerce, use a sister


organization’s solution, and so on. One option that should


always be considered is to do nothing and ignore the problem.


It’s obviously the cheapest thing to do, and over the years


might have saved a few overeager teams from developing


sunroofs for submarines.


This section should show the feasibility of the options.


These can be any of the following.


• Technical: Do we have the technical resources to buy and


install, or build a solution?


• Business: Does it fit the organization? Is the market the


right market and ready for this?


• Financial: Do we have the money to build this option, and


what is its return on investment?


• Better alternatives: Are there things that the


organization could better invest in?


## 第 285 页


Cost


We previously said that estimating the cost of development is


beyond the remit of business analysts. However, it is in


someone’s remit, and you should ensure that the estimate of


cost is based on something tangible. You as the business


analyst can provide tangible assets such as a context


diagram, a list of business events, and perhaps a first cut


of a data model. All these have factual, countable elements


that should be used as input to the estimate.


If you wish to know more about estimating, we refer you to


the Resources section at the end of the chapter.


Keep in mind that cost is often wildly underestimated, for


political reasons. For example, management might balk if the


real costs were presented, and so they are artificially


reduced. You need only look at the statistics for cost


overruns in IT projects to confirm this. The purpose of a


business case is to evaluate whether it is worthwhile


developing a solution. The whole case hinges on having


realistic estimates of cost, so having hysterically


optimistic reduced costs is entirely self-defeating.


Some agile projects like to start out without an estimate of


cost, with costs being estimated cyclically as the project


## 第 286 页


proceeds. This might seem attractive, but if eventually the


cumulative costs outstrip the advantages, then it turns into


a poor choice.


It is possible to estimate costs within a reasonable degree


of accuracy. Take advantage of justifying the project on a


realistic projection of cost.


Return on Investment


Here you set out the financial justification for the project.


First, the value—we looked at this a moment ago. Value is


the benefit that the customer receives from having your


solution. At this stage (we are still in the Blastoff), you


do not know exactly what your solution will be. But that is


not the point—the point is to determine whether your


organization wants to spend the money and resources to


discover what solution will best serve the business need, and


then build or buy that solution. The benefit can exist


without you knowing exactly how you will achieve it.


The cost of investigating the problem and finding a solution


is naturally a significant part of your business case. You


state your expectations of cost, along with the resources


needed.


## 第 287 页


A cost that should not be overlooked is the disruption cost


of your solution. If, say, your solution is to be deployed


in-house, then your users’ productivity will plummet for a


period while they learn the new solution, come to grips with


their new business process, overcome the natural resistance


to change, and so on. The disruption cost should not be


ignored, as it is usually significant. To think that users


will be 100% effective on day one of the new solution is


delusional.


The return on investment (ROI), simply put, is the benefit


received from having the solution, less the cost of acquiring


the solution.


Of course, you have to take into account the lifetime of the


solution. It is unlikely that you receive a positive ROI in


the first year—usually it takes longer for the benefit to


overcome development or purchase costs. As part of


determining the ROI, you must consider the expected lifetime


of the solution. If the product will no longer be relevant in


five years’ time, then the returns must be achieved before


then.


Almost all installed solutions are modified over the years,


sometimes extensively so. The expected maintenance costs for


## 第 288 页


your solution need to be part of your determination or ROI.


Resources Needed


It is still early days, and you cannot precisely know the


skills, people, and technology that will be needed to build


or buy a solution. But you are making the business case, and


so must give some indication of the resources that might be


needed along the way.


Your organization has likely undertaken similar projects


before, so sitting down to coffee with a few project leaders


and product owners would give you a reasonable idea of the


needs based on organizational history.


The reason for this section of the business case is that your


management needs to assess whether these skills and people


are available or could be hired.


Time


Consider your window of opportunity. A business case cannot


be made to develop a solution if it will take two years, and


you know that in two years’ time the solution will be


irrelevant.


## 第 289 页


Your window of opportunity is closed by factors beyond your


control. The business ecosystem for your proposed solution is


constantly changing. The technological environment is also


(rapidly) changing. Market sentiment, the law, and your


customers are constantly changing. You cannot expect the


world to stand still while you develop your solution.


The time that is most important to your business case is the


time between you delivering the solution and the time it


becomes irrelevant or superseded. That is the time when you


achieve ROI; that is the time to talk about when writing your


business case.


Preferred Option


It might be apparent, given all the information you have


provided so far, that there is a solution that is noticeably


more suitable than any of the other options. In this case it


is as well to declare it, but don’t use this section to


promote a presumed or pet solution.


Justification


This is the executive summary of the business case. You write


your conclusion saying that one of the options is justified


and this is why.


## 第 290 页


To Go or Not to Go


Before we leave this topic, it must be mentioned that there


are many other ways that help assess the viability of


starting a project to solve a business problem: techniques


like SWOT, fishbone diagrams, pestle, and many more. There is


no coverage of these techniques here, but to see the most


complete list of them, we refer you to James Cadle and Debbie


Paul’s book, Business Analysis Techniques (see Resources),


where they cover 123 of them.


However, we find that writing a good business case is


sufficient in most situations. The main purpose of the


business case for you is in collecting the information needed


to present the case. Once you have done that and written the


case in a coherent and truthful way, it more or less makes


the go/no go decision for you.


If the case is feasible and is approved by the person paying


for it, then you can proceed with confidence that your


solution, whatever it is and whenever you deliver it, will


bring a benefit to its customer. And because it is feasible,


you will be more likely to be able to deliver it.


## 第 291 页


In short, the business case gives you the answer: to go or


not to go.


An Agile Approach to Blastoff


The Project Blastoff provides a justification for starting


the project. However, there are some projects where the team


prefers not to do much up-front planning. Instead of debating


the wisdom of this approach, let us look at how you might


pull it off.


We suggest that it is unwise to start a project without a


solid foundation, and we think it is lunacy to start one


without a business case. The business case is the


justification of the project, and if you have no


justification for the project, then you have no business


doing it.


There are parts of the business case that are essential for


any kind of enterprise. These are things that, should you


set out without paying at least some attention to them, you


might find yourself wandering in the desert.


Projects fail unless they know the business problem they are


solving. Not just an assumed solution to the problem, but the


actual problem. The scope of the problem is also needed.


## 第 292 页


Projects without some ideas of the scope are doomed to almost


eternal scope creep, and spending time developing solutions


for things that are not part of the problem the customer


needs solved.


Estimating the cost and time for the project is sometimes


shunned in favor of estimating at the beginning of each


cycle. But this cannot work unless there is some scale of


commitment established at the beginning of the project.


Without some limit to the project, it is possible to run up a


huge bill with little to show for it.


In any event, it is hard to make the business case if the


benefits of the solution are unknown or not quantified, and


the cost of achieving that solution is indefinite.


However, Figure 9.2 shows an approach to running an agile


project and keeping the up-front planning to a minimum.


## 第 293 页


![embedded_p293_41.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p293_41.jpeg)


Figure 9.2 An agile approach to the blastoff


The cycle starts with the Reduced Project Blastoff. This


would, at a minimum, establish the business case for the


project. One of the elements of the business case is the


advantage to be gained from having the solution. Unless your


project is pure research, then it should only exist if there


is some measurable advantage to it. Additionally, it is only


an advantage if the lifetime cost of the solution is less


than the benefit from having the solution.


## 第 294 页


The scope of the problem must also be established. Without


an agreed boundary to the problem, any project is rudderless


—it is impossible to tell what is in and what is out of


scope, and when to stop discovery and development.


A truncated business case and a defined scope—preferably


using a context diagram—is the bare minimum for a Reduced


Project Blastoff.


But let’s start with that. The next activity, Go or No Go,


is to decide whether to go ahead or to stop the project.


Should you go ahead, then the highest-priority business event


(or events) is investigated to discover its requirements.


This of course depends on you having a list of the business


events, but that is easy enough if you have a context


diagram.


This event is developed and then comes a Mini Blastoff. The


activity here is to assess whether the lessons learned from


the previous cycle give you any reason to update the business


case. Perhaps you learned that things are going to be much


more expensive due to technological problems. Or you learned


that some of the features you planned are not needed.


Whatever you learned is used to update the business case.


## 第 295 页


You also use what you learned to estimate the effort needed


for the next cycle. Note that you are estimating the effort


required to discover and deliver one business event. As we


have previously mentioned, a business event is a stand-alone


chunk of functionality, and therefore ideal for a cycle.


(We’ll have a lot more to say on this in Chapter 35, Story


Map, when we talk about using story maps to synchronize


requirements discovery and implementation.)


You might also reassess the priorities of the business events


here.


When you have updated (if necessary) the business case and


estimated the effort for the next cycle, you again decide the


go/no go question. And if you decide to go, then you discover


the next lot of requirements. And then the next. And so it


continues and continues to continue until you either decide


that not going ahead is the wisest thing to do or run out of


business events, or because you’re doing this on a


prioritized list of events the next one is so low priority


that you decide not to do it and all subsequent events.


A cyclic process is a learning process. Each time around you


learn something new about the requirements and the solution.


## 第 296 页


You also learn about the effort required. Instead of one


blastoff, you have many mini blastoffs.


Review


Some organizations, hopefully not yours, are repeat


offenders. Project after project fails to deliver, or is


abandoned partway through, or, and this is the worst offense,


restarts the project, making exactly the same mistake.


The mistake here is launching a project when the chances of


it delivering something of value are close to zero.


Of course, this does not apply to all organizations, only


those whose teams, or managers, are so anxious to rush in and


build something that they fail to stand back and consider


whether they should continue or walk away.


Does the business case give ample justification for doing the


project? Is there a realistic business case in the first


place? Does this project face unnecessary risks (remember


that all good projects have some risk; otherwise, they would


not make any advances), or have the risks been considered? Is


the cost reasonably accurate, and does it indicate that the


project will bring a suitable return on the investment of


doing the project?


## 第 297 页


In short, will the project deliver a business solution that


repays the effort expended to build it?


Finally, have you and your team stood back and carefully


considered whether you should go ahead, or stop before any


serious money is wasted?


Resources


Essential Systems Analysis by Steve McMenamin and John Palmer


(Yourdon Press, 1984). This book introduced the ideas of


essence and business events. Unfortunately, it is now out of


print.


How Big Things Get Done by Bent Flyvbjerg and Dan Gardner


(Macmillan, 2023). Flyvbjerg is not talking about IT projects


directly, but what he has to say about the up-front planning


work should be required reading for all business analysts and


project leaders. He has something to say about projects that


should never have been started.


Making Risk Management Work: Engaging People to Identify, Own


and Manage Risk by Ruth Murray-Webster and Penny Pullan


(Routledge, 2022). The central theme of this book is that


successful risk management is not merely a matter of


following processes and procedures but involves creating a


## 第 298 页


culture where everyone in the organization understands,


identifies, and takes responsibility for managing risks.


Waltzing with Bears: Managing Risk on Software Projects by


Tom DeMarco and Tim Lister (Dorset House, 2003). This book


provides a practical and insightful approach to understanding


and mitigating risks in the software development process. The


authors argue that risk is not a bad thing—we must take


risks if we are to advance. The book emphasizes the need for


proactive risk management rather than trying to eliminate


risk entirely.


Predicting the Unpredictable: Pragmatic Approaches to


Estimating Cost or Schedule by Johanna Rothman (Practical


Ink, 2015). This book emphasizes the importance of pragmatism


and offers a real-world perspective on estimation,


acknowledging that software development projects are not


always predictable and that perfection in estimation is not


the goal. Instead, the focus is on providing valuable,


actionable estimates that support effective decision making


throughout the project life cycle.


Return on Software: Maximizing the Return on Your Software


Investment by Steve Tockey (Addison-Wesley, 2004). The author


sees software development not just as an expense, but as an


## 第 299 页


investment that should provide a return. Tockey emphasizes


the need to think strategically about software projects,


considering their potential long-term benefits.


Adrenaline Junkies and Template Zombies: Understanding


Patterns of Project Behavior by Tom DeMarco, Peter Hruschka,


Tim Lister, Steve McMenamin, James Robertson, and Suzanne


Robertson (Dorset House, 2008). This book introduces the


concept of the “dead fish” project.


Business Analysis Techniques: 123 Essential Tools for


Success, 3rd Edition, by James Cadle, Debra Paul, Jonathan


Hunsley, Adrian Reed, David Beckham, and Paul Turner (BCS


Learning and Development Ltd., 2021). The authors discuss 123


business analysis techniques.


## 第 300 页


Part III: Prototyping for


Requirements


Prototypes, as we are using the term here, are explorations


of the problem space. You can think of them as experimenting


with the problem by proposing a solution. History is full of


such experiments: Some were tried and abandoned for being


impractical; some were tried and, while not developed, led to


further experiments in a different, successful direction; and


some showed that the product under consideration was


worthwhile and viable.


We are using prototypes to rapidly explore the problem,


explore the customer’s perception of the problem, and ensure


that we are indeed solving the right problem.


Sometimes the customer doesn’t know what is


needed and won’t know it until he sees it.


Traditionally, once you have the blastoff deliverables of


scope, stakeholders, and goals, you start asking requirements


questions of the stakeholders. But when you are prototyping


for requirements, you are asking the questions in a different


## 第 301 页


way. You are giving your customer something visual, something


more engaging than a list of questions, something that better


demonstrates the impact of the proposed requirements. You


know your prototyping effort is working when the customer


treats a prototype as if it is real—even though she knows


it’s not—and comes up with requirements that would make it


work even better.


The process schema shown in Figure P3.1 highlights the


Prototype for Requirements activity. However, it is not


intended to be used exclusively or in isolation. The Trawl


for Requirements activity (the more traditional way of


discovering requirements) is a parallel activity. You will


almost certainly use both. The results from your prototyping


efforts determine how much of each you use.


## 第 302 页


![embedded_p302_42.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p302_42.jpeg)


Figure P3.1 Prototyping is used to discover requirements


that are added to the central requirements repository (your


specification, or story map, or backlog, or whatever way you


store your requirements). The more traditional Trawling


activity is also discovering and adding requirements to the


## 第 303 页


repository. Later, when we look at Designing and Developing,


we’ll again use prototyping to experiment with business


solutions.


Before going further, we must point out that “prototype”


is the wrong word. Most dictionaries have it that


“prototype” means the first, or preliminary, version of a


solution from which other forms are developed. For the


purposes of this book, we go along with common IT practice


and say that a prototype can be anything from a rough sketch


(preferred) through to a piece of software that might turn


out to be the forerunner of the solution to be built. It


might also be some kind of physical model or demonstration,


or any other form that makes it possible for people to share


ideas. It doesn’t really matter. What matters is how you use


your “prototype” to find all the right requirements and


confirm that you are solving the right problem.


ISO 9241-210: “A prototype is a representation


of all or part of an interactive system that,


although limited in some way, can be used for


analysis, design and evaluation.”


We are talking about sacrificial prototypes. They are


sacrificial because you do not intend to have your prototypes


## 第 304 页


evolve into the solution. You are using the prototypes to


explore the problem, and after the exploration, you throw


away the prototypes but keep the knowledge.


These are probably just sketches of possible candidate


solutions. You are using these sketches to question your


customer about the impact of the candidate solution. You ask


questions like: Why does this candidate solve the right


problem? What would you do if you had this solution, and why


would you do it? Would this candidate cause problems in other


areas of your business? Does this candidate trigger other


ideas? Then you ask yourself what you learned about the


problem and what you learned about the requirements for the


solution to the problem. This is illustrated in Figure P3.2.


## 第 305 页


![embedded_p305_43.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p305_43.jpeg)


Figure P3.2 The business analyst and the customer explore


the business problem using sacrificial candidate solutions.


## 第 306 页


Sometimes using prototypes brings out better answers when you


are trying to uncover the real business problem to be solved.


By looking at some visual representation of a possible


solution, your customers are better able to envision the


impact and the suitability of the solution, and whether it


addresses their real business problem. While there is no


guarantee that your candidate will morph into the final


solution, you are presenting the customer with something that


appears to be more real than abstract questioning.


## 第 307 页


Chapter 10. Generating Sacrificial
Candidate Solutions


Sacrificial candidate solutions are there for you to explore


your customer’s business problem. They are “sacrificial”


as they will most likely be discarded after they have served


their purpose of discovering and experimenting within the


problem space. You keep the knowledge but throw away the


candidate.


They are “candidates” because you generate several of them,


and test each to see what effect it would have on the problem


space. They are “solutions” because they could potentially


act as a solution, but their purpose here is to give you a


vehicle for learning more about the business problem.


It is important to have multiple candidates. The usual


practice is to look for one right answer; find an answer and


then stop. Job done. In fact, we might not even look for the


one right answer—we might presume the answer and proceed as


if it is the right answer. It might be, but more often, it


might not be. There is always the “second right answer.”


This was proposed by Roger von Oech (see Resources). Instead


of looking for the answer, look for answers. Plural. Instead


of digging in and defending the first answer, think about


## 第 308 页


rephrasing the question, think about using the Creative


Triggers (coming up soon) and looking for the second (and


third and fourth) right answers, which will probably—almost


certainly—be a better solution.


Generating multiple sacrificial candidates means that you and


your stakeholders have to think more, but you also have to


look at the problem differently. Instead of one solution, you


have a choice of solutions to pursue.


Multiple Candidates


The idea behind generating multiple candidates is that a


single candidate is simply not enough to open your mind to


all the possibilities. If you only have one candidate, then


it is probably the presumed solution, and you have not


thought enough about the problem. With only one candidate you


are denying your customer (and yourself) the opportunity to


explore the business problem. It is, after all, this


exploration that reveals the real problem and uncovers the


requirements that otherwise would have remained hidden.


“If you want to have a good idea, have lots of


ideas.”—Linus Pauling


## 第 309 页


Consider the candidates shown in Figure 10.1. The business


problem here is that college students must acquire the


textbooks that are required reading for their courses. The


diagram presents five alternative candidate solutions. They


range from the simple and obvious of buying the book at a


store, through using an Espresso Book Machine to print the


book in the store. The point of having five (and sometimes


more) candidates is that you and your stakeholders probe each


of them to look for viability and whether they are solving


the right problem and producing the right outcome for the


customer. Importantly, have you and the stakeholders


understood the problem?


## 第 310 页


![embedded_p310_44.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p310_44.jpeg)


Figure 10.1 Consider the five candidates that were generated


for the same business problem. The business is students


getting their required textbooks.


## 第 311 页


The idea is to have ideas because ideas can morph into other


ideas. Candidates, once seen and examined, can be changed to


become something else. A good example of this is the iPhone.


The iPhone is a product that was so good, and in 2007 (the


time of its release) so extraordinary, that it sold so well


that within a year all the major electronics companies were


pushing out their own iPhone copies. Yet the iPhone didn’t


start out as a phone. It began as a project to develop a


tablet (much later to become the iPad), and it was after some


of the Apple designers talked about how they hated their


clunky, keypad-driven phones of the time that the idea came


to combine a phone with the touchpad technology of the


tablet. The rest is history.


“If you haven’t found it yet, keep looking.


Don’t settle. As with all matters of the heart,


you’ll know when you find it.”—Steve Jobs


When you are prototyping, you are generally working closely


with your customer. If you find that the customer is not


asking lots of questions and coming up with requirements, it


could be a sign that he doesn’t recognize how your


prototypes are part of his world. If this is happening to


you, rework the prototype with enough characteristics that


## 第 312 页


your customer recognizes it. These characteristics could be


specific technology, names of people, places, jobs, existing


systems...anything that the customer relates to. This often


kick-starts the communication, and the customer now


recognizes that this is real; it is his problem you are


talking about.


Just as prototypes and ideas can change, the problem you are


looking at might change as well. When your customer sees a


candidate, she says, “What is the problem that this solution


is solving? It is not exactly my problem.”


In Chapter 14, Probing and Exploring the Candidates, we


discuss how you probe your candidates to find their


suitability and applicability. This probing looks at such


things as the impact of the candidate solution, whether it is


feasible, whether it solves the right problem, and so on. But


to have meaningful probes, there must be several candidates.


When there is only one candidate and the probe reveals flaws,


you become locked into improving it instead of using it as a


springboard to find new and better ideas.


Don’t Be Pygmalion


Pygmalion was a character in Greek mythology. The legend


tells how Pygmalion, a sculptor, made an ivory statue that


## 第 313 页


represented his ideal of womanhood. The statue was so


beautiful and so perfect that Pygmalion fell in love with it.


We tell the story here to say that it is important not to


become so enamored with your prototypes that you block out


any criticism of them. A candidate is there for you to


explore ideas, not to fall in love with.


By the way, Pygmalion’s story has a happy ending. At the


altar of Aphrodite, Pygmalion wished for a bride who was


“the living likeness of my ivory girl.” When he returned


home and kissed the statue, he found that she was now a


living woman and that she was, happily, in love with


Pygmalion. They married and had one or two children (the


myths are none too clear on this point). However, you don’t


have the goddess Aphrodite looking out for you. So please


don’t fall in love with your prototypes. They won’t come


to life.


It is important that you see your candidates as sacrificial.


Think of yourself as another character from Greek mythology,


Medea. Medea marries Jason of Golden Fleece fame, and later


kills their children. Your candidates are only as long as


they help you and your customer explore the business problem


and see how different solutions can have different outcomes.


## 第 314 页


Naturally enough, you are searching for the outcome that is


most beneficial for your customer.


“Daring ideas are like chessmen moved forward.


They may be beaten, but they may start a winning


game.”—Johann Wolfgang von Goethe


Time Flies, But You Are the Pilot


Prototyping is not meant to be eternal. Obviously, coming up


with new sketched prototypes takes time, and time is a finite


and valuable resource. Timeboxing the prototyping activity is


one possibility, but we like to think that the team will know


when they have exhausted the possibilities. If a day or two


go by with no new candidates emerging, then it is probably


time to concede that there are no more. Don’t be in too much


of a hurry to pull the plug on the prototyping activity, but


don’t let it go on once it has ceased being useful.


Review


The idea is quite straightforward: Generate multiple—three


or four or five or more, if you like—candidate solutions for


your customer’s business problem. The idea is less to find a


solution than to explore the problem. You are exploring by


## 第 315 页


testing each of the candidates against the problem to see


what you and your customer learn. You could of course just


ask questions about the problem, but your customer might


answer according to his own idea of a solution to the


problem. By presenting and probing each candidate solution,


you are inviting the customer to think beyond his own


presumed solution and see a bigger and better picture.


It is possible that one of your candidates goes on to be


further refined and eventually turn into the delivered


solution, but for the moment, we are concerned with rapidly


exploring the problem space and learning as much as we can


about it. For it is only by understanding the real problem


that you can come up with the right solution.


Resources


Thinkertoys: A Handbook of Creative-Thinking Techniques by


Michael Michalko (Ten Speed Press, 2006). This book presents


creative-thinking techniques for approaching problems in


unconventional ways. On the entertainment side, it has dozens


of useful hints, tricks, tips, tales, and puzzles.


Be a Great Problem Solver—Now! by Adrian Reed (Pearson,


2016). This looks at generating a range of possible solutions


## 第 316 页


for business problems. The author also explains the trap of


selecting the first solution that comes along, and looking


for long-lasting answers.


A Whack on the Side of the Head: How You Can Be More Creative


by Roger von Oech (Grand Central Publishing, 2008). One of


the original books on how to have good ideas.


Prototyping: A Practitioner’s Guide by Todd Zaki Warfel


(Rosenfeld Media, 2009). This looks at techniques for


prototyping and has a review of many tools used for


prototyping.


TED Talks (https://www.ted.com). There are many talks on


creativity and innovation.


## 第 317 页


Chapter 11. Prototypes, Prototypes,
Prototypes


Let’s start by reiterating that we are talking about


sacrificial prototypes, and they are being used for the


moment as aids to discover and explore the problem and its


requirements. The effort you put into these prototypes is


mainly done by your brain, not your hands.


There is no point in building elaborate prototypes. These are


sacrificial; you’re going to throw them away once they have


done their job. We are talking about sketched prototypes.


Build no more than you need to get your idea across and to


allow your customer to see what you’re getting at and assess


whether it is solving the correct problem.


Some of the prototypes you sketch might later be developed


into the final product, but only once you and your customer


are certain that it is satisfying the real business


requirements. For the moment, keep thinking of sacrificial


candidates.


“Prototypes are requirements bait.”—Steve


McMenamin, CIO, Hawaiian Electric


## 第 318 页


This chapter gives an overview of some of the types of


prototypes available to you. We have no way of knowing which


of them will appeal to your customers, and for the moment,


neither do you. So try them, and find the ones that your


customers relate to and that you feel happiest with. You are


trying to find and use prototypes that conform in some way to


the artifacts and experiences that are most familiar to the


customers. They will respond more appropriately when there is


some visual representation that they can criticize and change


and discuss and argue about.


One more thing: In Part II, Project Blastoff, we spoke about


business events, and how these events are the drivers of your


customer’s business—your customers will recognize them. The


response to each of the events is a stand-alone piece of


functionality, and that makes it an ideal candidate for a


prototype.


Types of Prototypes


What follows are some prototyping techniques that we and


others have found useful. Pick ones you like the look of, and


try them. Pick one you have not used before, and try it. Try


not to fall back on the same old ones you have been using


## 第 319 页


before—see what you learn by trying one not yet familiar to


you.


Give them a prototype they recognize.


Sketches/Low-Fidelity Prototypes/Wireframes


Drawing is 73,000 years old, and you would think that after


all that time we would be good at it. With a few exceptions,


we’re not. But the good news is that we don’t have to be


good, just expressive. Drawing—or as we prefer, sketching—


is nothing more than putting together a picture of your


candidate prototype. It does not have to be great art; in


fact, it should not be. There is value in having rough,


unfinished diagrams: Your customers are more likely to make


suggestions and ask for changes. That is exactly what you


want. If your drawing is too polished, then it conveys the


message that it is the design of something, that it is


finished and cannot be changed. It’s not finished, and it


definitively can be changed. It’s a rough sketch that


invites change. These rough sketches are often referred to as


lo-fi prototypes or wireframes.


In order to explore a business problem, you are sketching a


picture of a proposed solution. So your sketch should show as


## 第 320 页


much of the business as is needed to understand that problem.


Don’t restrict yourself to just a screen; show the wider


ecosystem. The objective is to ensure that you are solving


the right business problem: The more you show of the


business, the better the chances of seeing the right problem.


The sketch shown in Figure 11.1 illustrates this idea.


![embedded_p320_45.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p320_45.jpeg)


## 第 321 页


Figure 11.1 The sketch of a candidate solution to assist


with customs inspections of goods-carrying trucks at


international borders


The sketch shown in Figure 11.1 illustrates the prototyping


approach to requirements discovery. The sketch is about


trucks carrying goods across international (and sometimes


state) borders. The customs officials of the arrival country


need to be satisfied that the goods are allowed into the


country, that any applicable duty and taxes are paid, and


that the goods are manufactured to be compatible with


national standards. There are typically delays for trucks at


borders, as the process of checking the truck’s cargo


manifest is cumbersome and slow. The intention is to reduce


or eliminate the time taken and still retain the integrity of


the customs checks.


Note that the sketch has a wider scope than just the software


product on the customs officer’s computer. The scanner is


located several miles short of the border. This is to give


the officers time to review the truck’s manifest when it is


transmitted ahead. Depending on their findings, they will


either wave the truck through—they already have all the


necessary documentation—or decide to stop the truck for


## 第 322 页


further checks. Perhaps they need to open the truck to


inspect the cargo.


All of the above would be explained when the analysts and the


customers get together to discuss this candidate solution.


They probe the candidate looking for good requirements, for


places where the proposition would not work, and for places


where it fails to address the complete business problem.


For example, consider the electronic cargo manifests carried


by the trucks.


• How can they be standardized in places like Europe where


there are several dozen countries sending trucks to other


countries, not all of them within the European Union?


• How can all the manifests be made to communicate with this


country’s scanners?


• What happens if the manifest is not scanned?


• How do the officers at the border post recognize which


trucks are allowed to proceed and which are to be stopped?


• Does the manifest have to be in the truck? If it is


electronic, could it be transmitted from the shipper’s


## 第 323 页


office ahead of the truck starting its journey?


• Is the manifest “always on”? That is, can the scanner


automatically detect it without any action by the driver?


• What about fraudulent or erroneous manifests?


We’ll stop there. It seems that the business analysts have


more work to do. However, it does appear that this candidate


solution is exposing more of the actual business problem. So,


the sketch has served its purpose so far. You would go on to


build more complete and detailed models as your knowledge


about this piece of the business grows.


The above example is not a particularly complicated candidate


solution—it is more likely that your sketches will, of


necessity, be more elaborate. But this example serves to


illustrate the possibilities provided by sketching.


You could also sketch a wireframe of the customs officer’s


screen such as shown in Figure 11.2.


## 第 324 页


![embedded_p324_46.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p324_46.jpeg)


Figure 11.2 A wireframe of a candidate solution to the


customs business. This wireframe demonstrates to the


stakeholders the kind of data that is associated with the


candidate.


## 第 325 页


A wireframe, in IT usage of the term, is a very quick


mockup of a screen. A wireframe is intended to show the


functionality of the solution and should not go into details


of screen design. That comes later—while you are exploring


the problem, you must dissuade your customers from getting


into it. Your wireframe is intended only to demonstrate to


your customer how she could work with the candidate.


Go through the wireframe with the customer. For the one shown


in Figure 11.2, you would look at the information and verify


whether this is feasible. For example, the wireframe shows


the truck’s license plate and a silhouette of the kind of


vehicle. Is this enough for a customs officer to recognize


and stop the truck? Should the solution be expanded to


include an automatic license plate reader and lower a barrier


to stop the truck? Is the manifest detailed enough? If not,


what information is needed, and how would that be acquired?


A wireframe like this raises lots of questions, which is


exactly the point of having it.


Before we leave sketching and wireframes, we should mention


that we love the spontaneity of sketching on physical


whiteboards and paper with the customers around the table.


However, there are some terrific collaborative automated


## 第 326 页


drawing tools available. If you work remotely or are a member


of a distributed team, you spend a lot of your work time


electronically. Having easy-to-use collaborative whiteboards,


wireframe builders, and design tools helps your analysis of


the business a lot.


Storyboards


Storyboards are borrowed from the movies. Before shooting a


movie, the director gets together with a storyboard artist.


Using the script, the director decides how each scene is to


be shot. This is drawn by the artist and shows where the


actors are in relation to the camera, what dialog is to be


spoken for that scene, and what directions are to be given to


the actors. At the end of the exercise, the storyboard shows


the complete movie, scene by scene. It becomes the shooting


script, or plan for the movie.


You probably don’t have anything as glamorous as movie


actors and elaborate sets in your workplace. However, just as


the movie storyboard shows the activity of the movie, your


prototype storyboard shows the activity of your candidate


solution.


Let’s say that your client wants to enhance the home


security solutions that her company sells. You have been


## 第 327 页


given a vague description of the problem: She “would like to


automate more of it.” Of course, you could leap in and


automate all sorts of things, but it is wise to find out what


part of the solutions she is thinking about. The candidate


solution shown as a storyboard in Figure 11.3 is intended to


give your otherwise vague client something to start the


conversation with. By showing your client this storyboard,


you are first trying to identify the scope of the problem.


![embedded_p327_47.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p327_47.jpeg)


## 第 328 页


Figure 11.3 This storyboard demonstrates the functionality


for a candidate home security solution. The text under each


panel describes the action for that phase of the candidate.


You walk the client through the story, and then start to pick


it apart. She likes the first two panels. This indicates that


this is part of the business problem. Then you get to the


third panel, and she becomes hesitant. Food is not part of


the security problem as she sees it. So, you cross out the


third panel and the part of the fourth one that talks about


cooking.


What you have learned is part of the scope of the business


problem, and where your investigation should concentrate. For


example, the second panel mentions a “random lights


program.” For this to be convincing, it should not be random


at all, but should mimic the normal pattern of lights for the


household. You can dig into this after the walkthrough.


This is a security solution, so the fourth panel might raise


some concerns. If it senses the car and unlocks everything,


could that be misused? For example, could another car with


the same security product drive by the house and


unintentionally unlock it? How can the client sell this to


customers who don’t keep their car in the garage?


## 第 329 页


There is more to explore, and the point of the storyboard—


indeed, any prototype—is to be a vehicle to help you and


your customer explore the business problem.


The role of the storyboard is to illustrate the functionality


of a candidate solution in a recognizable way, and to invite


questions and criticism. You get together with the


appropriate customers, walk them through the story, and probe


the candidate until you have agreed either that it is not


viable because it is solving the wrong problem, or that it is


a potentially workable solution solving the right business


problem and worthy of further investigation.


You can enhance the commentary part of the storyboard if you


wish to include more information about the action taking


place for each scene. For instance, you might include a


rationale for the action, or any notes of open questions


attached to the scene.


You can also find storyboarding software to help you build


your boards; these would be useful if you are part of a


remote or distributed team. And when you have a quiet moment,


check out some of the examples of movie storyboards on the


Web. After that, you might then be tempted to add a superhero


## 第 330 页


to your own storyboards, but only if they are smart enough to


understand the real business problem.


Mind Maps


A mind map is a combination of drawing and text that mimics


the way your brain stores information. It does this by using


links between the words and pictures to represent the


synaptic connections our brains use.


As an example, let’s look at a mind map that our friend,


Joanna Kenneally, drew when she was planning her business.


The business provides advice and recipes for people who dine


alone at home. This market segment usually does not have


well-stocked larders and fridges, and sometimes they find it


hard to buy food in quantities suitable for one person.


Additionally, they might not be good cooks. Our friend’s


business, Good Food for One, provides recipes and advice on


cooking when one is on one’s own. Joanna’s mind map is


shown in Figure 11.4.


## 第 331 页


![embedded_p331_48.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p331_48.jpeg)


Figure 11.4 A mind map drawn while planning the business


Good Food for One. This Web-based business provides recipes,


shopping advice, and cooking tips for people who cook and eat


alone. Mind map by Joanna Kenneally. Used by permission.


Note the quick sketches and the hastily scribbled words in


Figure 11.4. Joanna was in a hurry. She wanted to start her


business right away and needed a quick prototype of what it


would do. She wanted to record all her ideas and see if they


came together to form a viable business. This mind map is not


all that legible—she was drawing it for herself, not you.


And that will be true for many of your mind maps.


## 第 332 页


Mind maps are useful devices for organizing your thoughts and


gathering those of your customer. You can see the result of


your thinking in one diagram—you get an overview and details


at the same time—with each of your subtopics teased out to


show divergence and connections. Drawing small pictures on


your mind map helps; they obviate the need to have words and


have the advantage of being more easily remembered than


words.


The mind map provides enough information—shown as keywords


and links between those keywords—for your customer to get


the overall picture. The value here is that it becomes


easier to see if things have been missed, if there is


sufficient functionality displayed to make a useful solution,


and if the parts will come together as a coherent whole


solution. You might find it more useful to draw your mind


maps in collaboration with the customer and other


stakeholders.


Process Models


Process models have been around for a long time in one form


or another. However, their antiquity does not diminish their


usefulness. There are several competing notations for process


models; the most commonly used notations are Unified Modeling


## 第 333 页


Language (UML) and Business Process Modeling and Notation


(BPMN). However, when using them as a prototyping tool, we


suggest you ignore their finer points and elaborate notation


and focus on drawing models that communicate clearly with


your customers.


You can build a model in isolation and afterward show it to


the customers for their confirmation, but you’ll get a


better result by sketching your process model in their


company.


Keep in mind that you are sketching a candidate solution.


Note the word “candidate.” When you are sketching your


process model you have no real idea whether the candidate


will make it through to further development.


So, what is a process model? A process model demonstrates a


business process. Business processes are usually made up of


activities arranged in a sequence of some kind. Business


process models use various notations to mirror the flow of


these activities, but a rectangle representing an activity is


the most commonly used, with arrows to show the sequence of


activities.


## 第 334 页


The candidate solution shown in Figure 11.5 is a proposal for


a forum for people to give away things that are still usable


but no longer needed—furniture, outgrown children’s toys,


games, clothing, books, and so on. While establishing a


central point for the exchange of no-longer-needed stuff is


thought to be a good idea, it needs to be tested. This model


will be discussed by the main stakeholders of the


organization, and then further experimented with to ensure


that it is a viable solution to the real business problem.


Having the candidate solution in a visual form, in this case


a process model, gives participants a more accessible way to


see and discuss its ideas.


## 第 335 页


![embedded_p335_49.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p335_49.jpeg)


Figure 11.5 A process model of a candidate solution. Begin


at the starting circle and read the sequence of activities


until you reach the end circle. The notation is simple enough


for almost all stakeholders to immediately grasp the meaning


of the diagram.


You will find that process models can be gainfully used later


in the development cycle when you are designing how the


pieces of your solutions fit together. They can also be used


when Trawling for Requirements, which is coming up in Part


IV. We have a lot more to say about process models there.


## 第 336 页


Scenarios


A scenario is pretty much a process model without the


pictures. We are using the term “scenario” to describe a


series of steps that together achieve some business


objective. You can use a scenario as a prototyping tool, and


simply describe each step of your candidate solution. You


would do this when either you don’t like drawing or your


client prefers text to pictures. Take this example of a


prototype process for managing a company’s fleet of


vehicles:


1. Record all purchased vehicles into the fleet database.


2. Categorize the new vehicles as cars, vans, and trucks


according to the company guidelines.


3. For all trucks, allocate to heavy goods yards in


proportion to managers’ requests.


4. Attach the appropriate classes of driver’s license to


each truck vehicle record.


5. Allocate vans to warehouses proportionally to managers’


requests and projected demands.


6. Reserve 10% of the cars to be carpool cars.


## 第 337 页


7. Allocate cars to employees considering company, rank, and


date of request.


8. Check the employees’ driver’s licenses and notify them


of their allocation.


You would use this scenario to walk your stakeholders through


your prototype. For each step, you ask if this is solving


their problem. For example, step 4 talks about the


appropriate license required for each category of truck. Are


there exceptions to this? Do the company’s records of


drivers carry an indication of the licenses? Is this step


solving a problem that needs to be solved? These questions


(and others) about the scenario help you and your


stakeholders discover and explore the real business problem.


Scenarios have the advantage that they are immediately


recognizable to your customer, so walkthroughs and probes do


not have to overcome any notational issues. They are also


easy to change, so you and your customer can make updates on


the fly as you explore your candidate and whip it into shape.


Scenarios can also be useful later in the development cycle.


We’ll talk later about story maps, and you’ll see how the


scenario lends itself to being readily converted to stories.


## 第 338 页


Slogans and Elevator Pitches


• “The ticket you don’t have to buy”


• “Let the customers approve their own loans”


• “Renew without renewing”


• “Sign up in 60 seconds”


• “Banking with inbuilt budgeting”


• “Fleet management for dummies”


The list could go on, but you get the idea. The idea of the


slogan touting the benefit was best demonstrated with


Apple’s iPod slogan, “1,000 songs in your pocket”. This


was of course aimed at potential customers for the iPod, but


consider its value as a description of a product that you


must develop. It’s all there; all you must do is come up


with a device that is small enough to carry around and can


store music (and presumably play it to the person carrying


the device).


A slogan doesn’t pretend to be a complete description, but


as we are dealing with candidate solutions, why not try using


a slogan to tout one of your candidates?


## 第 339 页


The elevator pitch is so named as it is a short description


of the candidate, short enough that you can tell it to


someone while traveling in an elevator. Elevator pitches are


two or three sentences long and should be made up of a short


statement of the problem, followed by a short statement of


how your candidate would solve the problem. For example:


“Did you know that most employees spend about five hours per


day on their email, and on average, only 46% of them manage


to clear their inbox each day? Our proposal is to have an


automated solution to observe people’s email behavior over


time, to see which messages they treat as important and which


they consider unimportant. As the solution learns the value


that an employee puts on each type of message and each


sender, it begins to sequence the employee’s inbox in value


order. It continues to observe and improve.”


The value of an elevator pitch is that you can write one in a


few minutes.


Cardboard Boxes


## 第 340 页


![embedded_p340_50.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p340_50.jpeg)


## 第 341 页


![embedded_p340_50.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p340_50.jpeg)


The next time you buy an appliance and it comes in a large


cardboard box, don’t recycle the box; keep it. Cut a


rectangular hole on one side to represent a computer screen


or a phone and have one of the business analysts get inside


the box. The analyst plays at being the candidate solution


and responds to verbal directions given by the customer.


The customer is playing through a typical transaction or work


scenario.


The rest of the team watches this interaction and notes any


gaps in the conversation, whether the analyst’s script fails


to cater to the customer’s needs, or whether there are some


missing pieces.


Cardboard box prototyping is highly playful and relatively


fast. You and your team decide the proposed functionality


that the cardboard box possesses. This is told to the analyst


inside the box who plays at being the software. You cue the


customer to attempt some piece of work by saying something


like “The cardboard box is your new system. Use it to try


and do the things you need to do to manage the fleet and


transfer licenses in and out.”


## 第 342 页


Techniques like cardboard box prototyping might seem to have


a degree of silliness about them. That is not a bad thing—


people who play enjoy themselves and are frequently more


productive.


Fun helps people to relax, enjoy themselves, and


be more productive.


Videos or Video Walk-throughs


There is no doubt about the attraction of video. Humans are


visual beings—we are attracted to images, both still and


moving. We spend a lot of our time watching some form of


video; many people say they learn more easily by watching


videos. The popularity of YouTube as a learning resource


attests to this.


## 第 343 页


![embedded_p343_51.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p343_51.jpeg)


Since we like learning by watching videos, it stands to


reason that presenting a candidate solution to your customer


can be done using a video presentation.


The simplest form of this is having someone hold your phone


and film you explaining your solution. Of course, it can be


more elaborate. There is quite a lot of animation software


available that can be used to make convincing demonstrations


of your candidate. Alternatively, you can use screen or voice


recordings to make your prototype.


## 第 344 页


However, you must think of video as a presentation tool. That


is, once you’ve made your video, it is a fixed entity with


very little ability to be changed on the fly.


Hi-Fi Prototypes


High-fidelity prototypes are built using software tools and


produce results that have the appearance of working software


products. They can either be presentation prototypes, be


built using content management systems, or be more functional


and built using whatever programming language(s) your


organization uses. They are attempting to be a partial


version of a potential product.


The hi-fi prototype (we call it “hi-fi” because it is high


fidelity and faithful to the look of the finished product)


looks real and appears to be a working product. There is a


downside, however. Stakeholders might be tempted to


concentrate on its appearance and possibly forgo making


functional improvements. To do so would defeat the purpose of


requirements prototyping.


Putting aside the slight risk of stakeholders


misunderstanding their role in the prototyping activity, the
