hi-fi prototype has a lot to offer. It is interactive, which


encourages users to explore its capabilities. The icons and


## 第 345 页


data displayed on the screen are representative of the data


and icons used to do the actual work. The stakeholders should


feel at home with the prototype: They should be able to click


around, update data, and be told whenever they make an error.


In other words, the prototype can be a realistic simulation


of their real work. An example of a hi-fi prototype is shown


in Figure 11.6.


## 第 346 页


![embedded_p346_52.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p346_52.jpeg)


Figure 11.6 Hi-fi prototypes look like the real thing and


are often built with content management systems. They provide


very realistic prototypes, and customers usually have no


trouble experimenting with them.


## 第 347 页


However, always keep in mind that the purpose of a


requirements prototype is to explore the problem. When your


customers are clicking around, exploring the candidate


solution, you are constantly questioning them about the


problem this solution is meant to solve.


Review


The types of prototypes you can build are limited only by


your imagination, as are the candidate solutions you are


proposing. Keep in mind that the purpose of these prototypes


is to explore the problem space and the solution space. To


that end, you must regard your prototypes as sacrificial.


Quick sketches are easy to throw away—you have not invested


time and effort (apart from thinking effort) into them.


Elaborate prototypes are harder to discard and there is a


tendency to defend them from criticism and changes. So, make


them quickly, and change or discard them quickly.


Of course, some of your prototypes might go on to be


developed into the solution you deliver to your customer, but


for the moment they are exploratory vehicles.


Used wisely, prototypes have a significant role to play in


your requirements discovery.

The Back of the Napkin: Solving Problems and Selling Ideas

(https://www.ideo.com/search?query=prototypes) prototype


examples of the many different kinds of prototypes it has

## 第 350 页


Chapter 12. Ready-Made Solutions


Most development efforts include some ready-made solutions.


Whether your development intends to deliver a consumer


product, a service, or software, some—perhaps almost all—of


it will be bought and not built. You might prefer to call


this an off-the-shelf (OTS) solution, and it does not matter


whether you are buying it (commercial off-the-shelf or COTS),


you are getting it free as open-source software, you are


subscribing to a cloud computing service or software was a


service (SAAS), or it is a legacy solution. Because it


exists already, let’s just call it “ready-made.”


In this part of the book, we are discussing prototypes and


how they are involved in exploring the problem space and


discovering requirements. To satisfy these requirements, you


intend to build something or to buy something, often a


combination of both. The prototypes you build of candidate


solutions must therefore include and demonstrate any


potential ready-made components.


When the whole of the solution is intended to be ready-made,


your prototypes are used to explore its outputs and outcomes.


Before you get something off the shelf, you need to know that


## 第 351 页


it works and satisfies the business problem—just the same as


if you built it yourself.


A ready-made solution is only useful if it fits within your


customer’s business activities. The intention of the


prototypes we are discussing here is to explore how a ready-


made would help solve the customer’s business problem.


Most ready-mades require configuring or customizing. The


prototypes you are experimenting with here help to discover


the requirements for this customization, and any other


requirements for integrating it into the customer’s business


environment. In some cases, your prototypes might demonstrate


the effectiveness of changing the customer’s business area


to accommodate the ready-made.


Prototyping with Ready-Made Solutions


In previous discussions about prototypes, we made no mention


of whether the functionality of the prototype would be built


or bought. So, now let’s look specifically at prototypes in


which the intention is not to build, but to acquire ready-


made components for some or all of the solution. These


prototypes differ from those discussed previously in only one


aspect: The ready-made is treated as a black-box piece of


## 第 352 页


functionality that sits somewhere in the sketch. The


intention is to show how a business solution would operate


using a ready-made to do some or most of the work.


The roles of these prototypes is severalfold.


• The prototype is used to determine the suitability of a


ready-made solution. Does it fit into the customer’s


business, and will it deliver the results needed for that


business?


• The prototype demonstrates the result, given each of the


proposed configurations of the ready-made solution. In other


words, you are modeling outcomes and testing them against the


customer’s expectations and real business needs.


• Prototypes can also be used to assess the suitability of


ready-made solutions in various combinations and


configurations.


• When assessing suitability, you would also assess how much


configuration or customization is viable, necessary, and


economic.


• The prototypes are used to assess the feasibility of


changing the business process to fit the ready-made solution.


## 第 353 页


• Your prototypes are part of the input to the acquisition


process and might be used to help formulate your Request for


Proposal (RFP).


Let’s look at these.


Suitability


Look at the prototype of a business process shown in Figure


12.1. The ready-made solution is shown as a cardboard box


representing an “out-of-the-box” solution. This one is in


the middle of the process and is being assessed for


suitability. Note the data in and data out components on the


model. These are there to help you assess whether the input


data can be manufactured by the activity on the left, and


importantly, whether the output data from the ready-made is


suitable for the remainder of the activities in this business


process.


## 第 354 页


![embedded_p354_53.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p354_53.jpeg)


Figure 12.1 The diagram is a prototype showing a business


process. The first process in the chain is intended to be


custom-built. The cardboard box icon is used to represent the


ready-made or “out of the box” solution. The process


continues with another custom-built component, followed by a


manual activity, before the process reaches its conclusion.


In this case, you assume that the ready-made solution is some


component that is available on the market, or as an open-


source product. It can also be a piece of legacy software


that the organization already owns. Whichever it is, you are


testing the prototype for its suitability. Suitability is


determined by whether the ready-made solution can transform


## 第 355 页


the input data to the desired output data. It doesn’t matter


how it does it, as long as the result is correct.


You could also use this prototype as a model of the desired


future business. In this case, the prototype shows a business


process that the team knows they can put together, providing


they can acquire a ready-made solution that meets their data


requirements. In this way, the prototype helps you to


discover the requirements for the ready-made.


Figure 12.1 shows a prototype of a situation where two


processes (the ones on either side of the ready-made) must be


built to accommodate the ready-made. In this case, the


functionality of the ready-made is such that it appears


worthwhile to adapt the business to fit it instead of the


other way round. Subsequent exploration and probing will


reveal the feasibility of this approach. Keep in mind when


doing this that the prototype, including its ready-made, is a


candidate solution. There might be other, better candidates.


Impact


Systems thinking helps you to assess the impact that any


activity has on connected activities. A simple example: I


have a payment activity and decide to change it to stop


accepting credit and debit cards. This alteration has an


## 第 356 页


impact on the buying activity; customers now must pay cash.


This in turn would impact the browsing activity: A lot of


customers would not shop with me, because they cannot pay


using a card.


“Systems thinking is not worrying about the


first or second consequence of an action, but the


third, fourth and fifth.”—Steve McMenamin,


personal communication


Figure 12.2 is a prototype model of a ready-made component


that has been inserted into an existing business system,


probably to replace an aging legacy system. The aim of the


prototype is to illustrate the impact of the ready-made.


## 第 357 页


![embedded_p357_54.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p357_54.jpeg)


Figure 12.2 A ready-made solution is plugged into an


existing business. The diagram uses shading to illustrate


activities that are impacted by the ready-made.


## 第 358 页


The ready-made becomes part of six business use cases, shown


as BUC1, BUC2, and so on. The shading shows the extent of the


negative impact on each of the BUCs. Negative impact means


that you must configure or customize the ready-made, or


rebuild the connected activity to accommodate the ready-made.


Let’s start with BUC1. This BUC is fine as it is; the lack


of shading signifies that you have determined that there is


no negative impact caused by the ready-made.


BUC2 has a problem. There is some impact (shown by the


shading) that requires some modifying action. This could be


to modify the activity or to modify the ready-made (the


diagram does not show which).


The required modification might be a simple configuration.


Configuration is when the ready-made includes the ability for


the customer to use parameters. These might change the


appearance of forms or reports, or change the terminology,


screen layouts, simpler parts of the functionality, and so


on. The ability to be configured is usually built into ready-


made solutions, is quite straightforward, and mostly can be


done quite quickly.


## 第 359 页


Customization requires more effort. It means your developers


have to reprogram part of the ready-made’s code. This is


done only when configuration cannot produce the required


functionality. The problem with customizing is that some


modifications can take the ready-made out of the upgrade


path. That is, for each new release you must re-add your


customization modifications.


BUC3 is also problematic. The shading on the activity closest


to the ready-made indicates that there is a need for some


kind of change with either the activity or the ready-made. If


the change must be made to the activity, and it is a manual


activity, then the person or people who do that activity need


to have their work description altered. If the activity is


automated, then it must be reprogrammed. Alternatively, it


might be the ready-made that needs to be configured or


customized.


BUC3 also communicates with the outside world. Let’s say


that the arrow connecting the ready-made to the adjacent


system is some kind of data flow—an invoice, a report, a tax


return, or something else. The shading in the adjacent system


indicates that there is some negative impact—the data in the


flow is not what the adjacent system is expecting. The


consequence of this impact is that either the ready-made is


## 第 360 页


modified to produce the data flow that is required by the


adjacent system, or you have to negotiate with the adjacent


system to get it to accommodate the data in the form in which


the ready-made produces it.


BUC4 shows a different kind of problem. There is an impact on


the activity adjacent to the ready-made, and this impact has


an impact on the next activity in the flow. This is the


“ripple effect.” It is so called because one activity can


impact another, and another, and the impact travels like


ripples on the water and can reache quite distant activities.


This is where systems thinking comes in—the art of looking


at all the components of a system to see how any one of them


can affect any of the others. Sometimes, because of the


ripple effect, an activity is impacted by a ready-made even


though it is several activities away from the ready-made.


Your task is to assess what is needed to correct the


situation shown in BUC4 and make that part of your assessment


of the suitability and viability of the ready-made.


BUC5 shows no impact, and thus the ready-made is suitable


straight out of the box. BUC6 shows some negative impact to


both the activity and the adjacent system that supplies data


to the activity. Again, you assess what needs to be done to


## 第 361 页


make the ready-made acceptable to the organization, or


whether the situation is so critical that the ready-made is


not suitable to become part of the business system.


The purpose of this kind of prototype is to assess the


impact. For a situation such as the one shown in Figure 12.2,


you evaluate whether the advantage of the ready-made is


sufficient to justify the needed modifications. The


modifications can be adjustments to manual activities or


automated activities, configuration or customization of the


ready-made, or negotiations with the adjacent systems.


You would also build prototypes of alternative ready-mades—


there are always several to choose from—and gauge their


impact. Most of the time, the ready-made with the least


impact is the one to acquire. Here you measure impact by the


effort needed to configure or customize, and the downside of


having a customized ready-made (you have to re-customize


after each upgrade).


This evaluation is best done using business use cases. We


spoke about these back in Chapter 7, Business Events. Each of


these has a defined starting point (the business event) and a


defined ending. The data at either end of the BUC is also


defined. Your evaluation is based on the difference between


## 第 362 页


the desired data and the data needed and produced by the


ready-made.


Does It Solve the Problem?


We should now turn our attention to whether the ready-made


solution solves the business problem. Keep in mind that you


are exploring the problem space. You use candidate solutions


that include ready-made components to do this. And like any


other prototype, it must solve the real business problem.


Figure 12.3 illustrates a prototype in the form of a process


model. In the middle of this candidate process you have


proposed a ready-made component. The activities on either


side of the ready-made can be existing activities, or ones


you intend to build. The question now is whether this


prototype of a process solves the business problem.


![embedded_p362_55.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p362_55.jpeg)


Figure 12.3 A prototype showing a ready-made component as


part of a business event


## 第 363 页


This prototype is about one business event and is triggered


by the arrival of the leftmost data flow. You need to add a


definition of this flow of data to ensure that the activity


can function correctly. Similarly, the data that leaves the


activity and enters the ready-made must be whatever the


ready-made expects. And so on for all the activities if you


are to determine the correctness of their functionality.


Having determined that the prototype is functionally correct,


you turn to looking at the problem space to see that it is


solving the right problem.


Your exploration of the problem space using this prototype


would be along these lines.


• Does this prototype solve the real business problem?


• Does it suggest a different problem would be the right one


to solve?


• Does the ready-made component included in the prototype


change your thinking about the problem to solve?


• Does the ready-made include functionality that suggests a


better way of solving the problem?


## 第 364 页


• Does it have functionality that suggests a different


business problem to solve?


• Does the prototype indicate that you should build a


different prototype for this problem?


• What else did I learn from the ready-made that helps


discover the real problem?


And then of course:


• Does the ready-made produce the correct outcome for this


business process?


Let’s say that you have probed the problem using some


prototypes that include ready-made components. Let’s also


say that you have found that, with a few adjustments, one or


more of them work correctly and solve the business problem.


Now you can choose one of the available ready-made solutions.


Choosing Ready-Made Solutions


Prototyping can help you to choose your ready-made solutions.


Let’s look at how this works.


Figure 12.4 shows a variation on the context diagram. We


discussed this diagram when we talked about the Blastoff. For


## 第 365 页


simplicity’s sake, this context diagram shows one ready-made


solution. (It could also be a collection of them, but the


effect for our purposes here is the same.) In this case, the


scope shown in the diagram is the part of the customer’s


business that you are studying prior to installing your


solution. The ready-made solution can be real or desired. It


is real if you know that it exists; it’s on the market or


available through open source. It could also be a legacy


component. It can be a desired ready-made in that you do not


know if such a solution is on the market, but you would like


to choose one that has the capabilities that the prototype


calls for.


## 第 366 页


![embedded_p366_56.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p366_56.jpeg)


## 第 367 页


Figure 12.4 The diagram is a prototype of a ready-made


solution in your customer’s business. The ready-made is


shown as a cardboard box within the scope of the problem


space, which is indicated by the large circle.


The prototype indicates the business events by showing the


flows of data coming from and going to the outside world. The


outside world is portrayed by the adjacent systems, or the


squares around the periphery. Earlier (in the Blastoff) we


discussed business events and how they involve one or more


flows of data connected to an adjacent system.


For example, suppose that you want to subscribe to a service


provided by a business such as a movie service, a newsletter,


or live news. This business event is Customer wants to


subscribe. The business knows this event has taken place


because the customer sends a flow of data containing his


enrollment details. You show this flow of data on your


context diagram.


You know the data content of the flows that are attached to


the business events. You know this because they exist in the


current incarnation of the business; it has been processing


them for some time. If the piece of business is completely


new, then you have to learn what data the adjacent systems


## 第 368 页


need to supply or expect to receive. In the case of the


subscription, the data would be your personal details, a


credit card, your preferences, and so on.


This means the context diagram, its business events and flows


of data, are your starting point for assessing the ready-made


solution.


The context diagram is your starting point for


assessing the ready-made solution.


You make use of the data flows by matching the inputs and


outputs to and from the proposed ready-made. You are


assessing whether they are suitable in their current form,


whether they need to be modified, or whether the ready-made


needs to be configured or customized. Alternatively, you


might need to build some processes to adjust the data to or


from the ready-made. By knowing the data content of the


existing flows, you can match them to the flows needed or


produced by the ready-made.


When we are talking about “existing,” we recognize that


most software development projects are replacing or enhancing


some existing pieces of the customer’s business. Usually,


your client has been in business for some time, so the


## 第 369 页


existing business processes, for better or worse, can be used


as the starting point. Your prototypes should reflect the


existing reality.


Naturally enough, you want the ready-made solution to be able


to handle all the business events. If it cannot do so, then


you need to discover the requirements for processing the


uncatered-to business events and assess the cost and


inconvenience of either configuring or customizing the ready-


made, or building additional software.


In Figure 12.5, you see prototypes of alternative solutions.


Solution A uses only ready-made components. This arrangement


requires more detailed analysis—you need to determine that


all of the interfaces between the ready-made components are,


in fact, compatible. This kind of solution would probably


require significant configuration or customization to make it


functionally workable.


## 第 370 页


![embedded_p370_57.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p370_57.jpeg)


Figure 12.5 Alternative prototypes. Solution A uses only


ready-made components. In solution B, the ready-made solution


is surrounded by existing or to-be-built activities.


For solution B, other activities surround the ready-made


solution. The activities can be existing ones that are to be


reused by the new solution, or activities that you intend to


build. They can be automated or manual activities. This


arrangement gives you the opportunity to study the activity


that would surround the ready-made and ensure that it


synchronizes with the rest of the business area. Either the


business area can be adapted to fit the ready-made or the


## 第 371 页


ready-made can be adapted to fit the business. Most likely,


you’ll use a combination of the two.


Prototypes give you a preview of possible solutions using


ready-mades. Rather than buy a ready-made and then wonder


what to do with it (don’t laugh, it’s happened many times),


your prototype gives you the opportunity to explore how well


the ready-made fits into the organization and how well it


solves the business problem. Moreover, it does that without


spending much money.


A Strategy


Most of the ready-made solutions that you are considering are


large and complicated (if the problem was small and easy, you


would probably build the solution yourself). Rather than


assess the whole of the ready-made solution, it’s best to


decompose it into manageable chunks, and business events are


the most convenient chunks to use.


If you start by building a context diagram as we discussed


above, it reveals the business events. Alternatively, you


can, in conjunction with your customer, construct a list of


business events. Your ready-made supplier should be able to


match your list of business events with the transactions


carried out by the ready-made.


## 第 372 页


You probably want to build a table for the next part. We show


an example of such a table in Figure 12.6. The table should


list all the business events relevant to your problem space.


For each event, assess whether the ready-made caters to it,


and if so, how closely its input and output match your


customer’s existing or desired input and output.


## 第 373 页


![embedded_p373_58.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p373_58.jpeg)


Figure 12.6 A table showing the fit of the business events


with the proposed ready-made solution


The idea is to show, event by event, the fit of the ready-


made solution against your business needs.


## 第 374 页


You can be as elaborate as you want. You can show the fit of


each business event, whether it matches or needs


customization, additional functionality, changes to the


business procedures, and so on. The objective of the list is


to give you a picture of how well the ready-made solution


fits into your customer’s organization, or how much of a gap


there is between the ready-made and the organization’s


needs.


You might also consider allocating points for fit, deducting


points for configuration (which is usually easy), and


deducting a greater number of points for customization (which


is generally harder). The points would vary according to the


cost and inconvenience of the configuration or customization.


Certainly, if you are assessing competing ready-mades, a


point scoring approach will serve you well.


We shall leave this here. There is more to working with


vendors to assess the capabilities of ready-made solutions,


but that is getting a little far off the topic of


prototyping. However, what you do with your prototypes, the


list of business events, and their data inputs, outputs, and


outcomes make a valuable contribution to your RFP, a common


way to approach vendors. We have more on RFPs later.


## 第 375 页


Review


Prototyping should be thought of as exploratory modeling. You


build prototypes, which are sketches, storyboards, process


models, or some other quick-and-dirty model of a candidate


solution. You use these to explore the problem space.


When it comes to including ready-made components in your


prototype, you are transitioning from a prototype where there


are no constraints to one where there is a very real


constraint. The ready-made exists, and it is more or less


fixed. Its functionality must therefore contribute to solving


the business problem. Which in turn means that you must spend


some time understanding the functionality of the ready-made


before including it in your prototype.


You are building these prototypes to help you understand the


business problem and whether the ready-made can help to solve


it. Your prototypes model this situation and help you to


assess whether the ready-made is a good enough fit or whether


it needs customization. Alternatively, your prototype might


reveal that the most effective course of action is to change


the organization to accommodate the ready-made.


## 第 376 页


Ready-mades are rarely the dream solution that, right out of


the box, is a perfect fit with the organization. Your


prototyping efforts provide crucial information, not only on


the requirements for the ready-made and their customization,


but also on what the organization can expect should it decide


to deploy the ready-made.

Software Requirements, Third Edition, by Karl Wiegers and Joy


Beatty (Microsoft Press, 2013). Karl and Joy have some things


to say about COTS solutions.


Off-the-Shelf IT Solutions: A Practitioner’s Guide to


Selection and Procurement by Martin Tate (BCS, The Chartered


Institute for IT, 2015).


“How to select a software vendor using the Request for


Information (RFI) and Request for Proposal (RFP) technique,”


an article available on the website of UK business management


consultant Blackmetric (https://blackmetric.com/downloads).


Bridging the Gap has articles on specifying requirements for


COTS or SAAS projects (bit.ly/3QOYMs7).


## 第 377 页


Chapter 13. Creative Candidate Solutions


Too many people think that coming up with good ideas and


innovative solutions is someone else’s job. It’s not


someone else’s; it’s yours. Every business analyst, product


owner, developer, product manager, and business stakeholder


must consider that innovation is a crucial part of their job.


We are not here merely to build things the customer asked


for, but to challenge, to provide alternatives, to come up


with original ideas that are beyond—and better than—what


the customer asked for. After all, if no innovation occurs,


then any new solution will be much the same as whatever it


replaces.


The business analyst’s task is not to deliver exactly what


is asked for, but to find something better.


For example, look at your phone. How many of the apps that


you see were the result of someone asking for it, and how


many are there because the designers came up with a great


idea that proved to be very useful (or entertaining)? And


while you’re looking at your phone, consider how many people


asked for a flat phone with a touch screen to replace the


keypad phones that went before it. Almost nobody, and yet


each year, over a billion touch screen phones are sold.


## 第 378 页


We must innovate; that is beyond questioning. Yet many people


do not consider themselves to be innovative or inventive.


It’s not true; you can be innovative—but you might need a


little help.


In this chapter, we look at a few techniques that can help


you to come up with innovative solutions. As we said several


times so far when talking about prototypes, you need to come


up with multiple candidate solutions. Read on to find out how


you can come up with fresh ideas for your candidates.


Creative Triggers


Creative triggers provide inspiration for innovation. Think


of the trigger as a guide to an idea—the trigger is not the


idea, it’s what to have an idea about. The triggers are


there to, well, trigger an idea for you.


The following triggers might sound too general, and perhaps


too obvious. They are, but they belong to that category of


things that are obvious once they are pointed out.


Participation


People like to participate. The success of social media


attests to people’s desire to participate and share their


## 第 379 页


photos and opinions and read what other participants have to


say. From a business analyst’s point of view, you should


think of customers as people who want to participate in the


business. People want to do things for themselves that


previously were done for them. Air travel, banking, and


shopping are all examples of this.


People like to participate.


Companies such as Amazon encourage customers to participate


in their business by writing reviews of products they have


bought. On Amazon, you can say anything you want about a


product. The company makes no attempt at censorship, except


for filtering for profanities and blatant advertising. Other


customers read these reviews and often make buying decisions


based on what other participants have said. Shoppers tend to


trust reviews from their peers more than those from


outsiders. This and other kinds of participation involve


customers more closely with a business, and thus, they are


more likely to be repeat customers.


1


Monzo, a UK neobank, has a community page. Its customers


participate by posting messages about their good experiences


or difficulties with the bank. When you read the messages,


you get the sense that Monzo’s customers enjoy participating


## 第 380 页


in the community, they enjoy helping each other when there


are problems, and they like the sense of belonging. The Monzo


app also has many articles on how to manage your money.


Clearly, the company has thought about connecting to its


customers and encouraging their participation. In a crowded


field, Monzo is currently the largest UK neobank.


1


Neobanks are smaller, more nimble banks that operate


exclusively online through their smartphone apps and


sometimes their websites. They occasionally target a


particular market segment or community. They are also known


as “fintechs” and “challenger banks.”


For your project, ask the team and the stakeholders: “What


can your solution do to provide more customer


participation? How can we involve the customer in the


work?”


Convenience


People love convenience; what’s more, they are willing to


pay for it. We pay much more to buy a mobile phone than to


buy a landline one. We do this because it is infinitely more


convenient to carry a phone around with us instead of being


constrained by a cord connected to the wall. We also hate


## 第 381 页


inconvenience. Studies have reported that up to 97% of


consumers say they have backed out of making a purchase


because of the inconvenience of the purchasing and/or


checkout process.


In several countries, particularly Australia, Mercedes-Benz


dealers are located very close to airports. Why? Convenience.


People who buy Mercedes cars are especially likely to be


affluent people, and especially likely to be people who fly


on business. The near-airport dealer provides a convenience:


When the car must be serviced, the owner takes it to this


conveniently located dealer, and the dealer drives the owner


to the terminal to catch her flight. When the owner returns,


the dealer picks her up at the terminal with the car fully


serviced. The car has been washed, and any clothing left on


the back seat has been dry-cleaned.


These benefits might at first seem trivial, but put yourself


in the position of a Mercedes owner: You are most likely


affluent and busy. Anything—and that means anything—that is


more convenient is welcome. People value convenience and are


willing to pay for it.


But it is not only the busy Mercedes owner who values


convenience; the user of your proposed solution also values


## 第 382 页


her convenience just as we all do. Think of the devices and


services you own that are there primarily to make your life


more convenient. Think of how convenient online shopping is


(see Figure 13.1).


![embedded_p382_59.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p382_59.jpeg)


Figure 13.1 Online shopping is convenient, and is increasing


its share of the retail market each year as more and more


people turn on to its convenience.


Ask what it is that your solution can do to make life more


convenient for its user. Think about your favorite consumer


products—they are probably your favorites because they are


## 第 383 页


so downright convenient. Or look at the way that successful


software products work; the most successful are almost always


the ones that are convenient to use and provide the most


convenience. Ask what it is that the customer is trying to


do. Then ask what your solution can do to make the task easy


and convenient for them.


Often, less is better. When people sign up for your service,


can you take out any requests for information that are not


absolutely essential? Can you find a shorter, more convenient


way for people to sign up? As an example, many neobanks ask


potential customers to send a video of themselves and their


passport in the same take. That is much more convenient than


finding a notary to sign an affidavit that the potential


customer has correctly identified himself, and then mailing


that in.


Are there some steps in your business process that can be


reduced or eliminated? Can you remove things from your


website that are rarely if ever used? People find uncluttered


sites more convenient and gravitate to them. As an example,


look at the sparseness—and the success—of Google’s home


page.


## 第 384 页


And then we must pay for things. If your solution requires


its customers to make a payment, then the process must be as


convenient as possible. That seems obvious, but how many


times have you found that paying for something online is


anything but convenient? And did you ever go back to that


store? Think hard about your own solution’s payment process.


Build prototypes of it and reduce it to the bare minimum.


By making your solution as streamlined and convenient as


possible, you make life easier for your customers, probably


keep them longer, and make your own life easier when your


customers don’t need as much support. Best of all, your


customers will love your convenient solution.


Connections


We love to be connected. No, let’s be honest here: We are


addicted to being connected. The number of users (about one-


third of the world) and the amount of time they spend on


social media attest to an almost pathological need to tell


our friends and followers about our lives and thoughts.


People check their phones 150 times per day (this is ten


times more than they laugh). Surveys have found that more


than half the population consider themselves to be highly


addicted to their smartphones. These people leave their


## 第 385 页


phones on 24/7, and often sleep with the phone beside the


bed.


Given that your customers—if they are like most of the


modern world—are people who value connectedness, it seems


sensible to give them as much of it as you can. Your next


question must be, “What can my solution do to build a better


connection between my organization and its customers?”


Alternatively, the question might be, “What can my solution


do to build better connections between my customers or


users?” See Figure 13.2.


![embedded_p385_60.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p385_60.jpeg)


## 第 386 页


Figure 13.2 The stronger the connections you can establish


with the solution’s customers, the better.


Having people participate in the work makes for a stronger


connection. Travelers book their own flights and transport,


we use an app to have a taxi or car service come and pick us


up, we shop online and arrange for the delivery, and even in


supermarkets we select our own goods from the shelves (there


used to be sales staff to do that for us) and then check


ourselves out (there used to be checkout people to do that


for us). We participate in lots of business activities and


don’t seem to mind doing so.


Putting your business on a smartphone app is connecting to


your customer. The traveler who booked her own flight has the


boarding pass on her phone. Updates on the flight status,


gate number, boarding time, and alerts when it is time to go


to the gate all connect the customer more closely to the


business. And when she feels connected to an airline, she is


more likely to continue flying with that airline.


Being responsive establishes a closer connection. The


response your solution makes is its message. Customers


measure organizations by the way they respond. For example,


the vacuous phone announcement, “All of our agents are


## 第 387 页


currently busy. Your call is important to us, so please stay


on the line and we will respond as soon as we can,” damages


the connection between the customer and company. Companies


that promptly answer the phone, or at least offer to phone


back, connect strongly to their customers.


When you are prototyping candidate solutions, check each one


for responsiveness. What opportunities does the candidate


have to be more responsive to its user, or what can it do to


connect more strongly? Remembering the customer’s name,


preferences, and previous orders is a way of remaining


connected. Can you build in any additional information


messages to the user? An example would be keeping people


informed on the status of their orders. Or can you offer a


better help facility? Does the candidate tell its user what


it is doing? Can you find a better way to connect your


candidate to its end user? Can your candidate solution make


the customer feel ownership of the solution? That is about


the strongest connection you can make.


Software support websites are another example of


connectedness. Someone with a problem asks a question about


their problem, and other people, hopefully experts, offer


their advice on how to solve the problem. With a few


exceptions, they are not paid to do this; they do it because


## 第 388 页


they enjoy participating and connecting with other people.


People who use these support sites usually feel more attached


to the software product.


Information


Think about your business customer: He wants information,


wants more of it, and wants it without delay. If you don’t


believe that, then look at the astonishing success of Google.


What is Google’s product? Information. Almost half of the


total internet population uses Google each day to find


information. The billions of daily hits on Google indicate


that our thirst for information is relentless and


unquenchable.


This dictum also applies to your customers. They know that


many organizations are willing to supply as much information


as they want, so you must specify your product in a way that


it tells the customer everything he needs or wants to know.


But the product must do more than just pump information at


the customer; it has to deliver useful information. Some of


this makes your product more convenient—you provide all the


information needed to make it easier for the customer to


carry out the transaction.


## 第 389 页


Information enables people to make decisions.


Information enables people to make decisions. Figure 13.3


shows a London bus stop. Public transport is both ubiquitous


and heavily used in London. At the time of writing, the


London bus fleet is almost 9,000 buses and 19,000 bus stops.


Many of the stops are equipped with a sign like this showing


in real time the expected arrival of the buses.


![embedded_p389_61.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p389_61.jpeg)


Figure 13.3 The electronic readout of expected bus arrival


times. The 453 has just left and the 30 to Marble Arch is


“due.” You can see it arriving. If you want to get to


Sudbury, you have a minute to wait, and if you just missed


the 453 to Marylebone, there is another in three minutes.


## 第 390 页


This kind of information enables passengers to make


decisions: Do I wait for the bus? Do I walk to the nearby


Tube stop? Do I hail a taxi? The effect of these signs is


that passengers at bus stops are much more patient because


now they know where their bus is. They don’t become anxious


wondering if one will ever come for them, and they don’t


spend time looking down the street for their bus. They know


when it is arriving.


Now consider the solution you are working on. What


information can it provide, and what can you enable its


customer to do with that information? Information without


enabling action is probably not useful.


Feeling


Systems and products are accepted or rejected based on how


the consumer feels about them. This might at first seem to be


very subjective, but an awful lot of buying decisions and


acceptances are subjective. When you deliver your solution to


its customers, they have to feel good about it and feel good


about using it; otherwise, there is a strong possibility they


will reject it. For example, you must know someone who bought


a phone and then realized they didn’t like it and couldn’t


wait to get rid of it. Or someone who bought any other kind


## 第 391 页


of product—particularly clothing—and after a while realized


that they didn’t feel good about it and dumped it. (This


someone might have been you.) Or have you ever, when


comparing apps for your computer, selected the one that made


you feel good about it?


Making a solution feel good is about making it as usable and


convenient as possible. See the situation as your customer


sees it. What is he doing when he comes to use your solution?


By understanding the viewpoint, the goals and desires of the


customer, and taking the trouble to think about the customer,


you are in a better position to think about what you can


provide to make her feel good about your solution. We don’t


mean pleasing colors and catchy music, but actions that are


natural and logical and that fit into her world.


Lastly, you must make your user or customer feel that you are


being responsive to his needs. That is, your solution must be


innovative enough to make your customer feel that you have


understood his request and are doing all you can to provide


the most appropriate answer. Your response is the strongest


message you can send to your customer. Your customers measure


you by the way you respond to them—how you answer their


questions, how you support them, how you keep them informed


## 第 392 页


about your products and services. Responsiveness makes your


customer feel better about your solution.


Speed


We want things to be fast. Figure 13.4 shows the door close


button in an elevator. Why do people press this button? They


want the door to close a few seconds before it would


automatically close. Why? What are they going to do with


those few seconds? We don’t need to save time; we just want


the door to close more quickly.


## 第 393 页


![embedded_p393_62.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p393_62.jpeg)


## 第 394 页


![embedded_p393_62.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p393_62.jpeg)


Figure 13.4 The door close button in an elevator. This


button is often repeatedly pressed in the hope of having the


door close more quickly. In many cases, the button is not


connected to anything and has no effect. It’s there to make


people think they’ll be on their way sooner.


Most drivers exceed the speed limit a few times in their


driving day. Why? The speed limit is there to ensure safety,


yet people apparently want speed more than safety. We grow


impatient if we must wait more than a day for something we


bought online to arrive. We click repeatedly if a website


does not respond instantaneously. We sigh deeply and roll our


eyes if the person ahead of us at the checkout line seems to


be taking too long.


Using the speed trigger, you ask what your candidate solution


can do to make it be faster or appear faster to its customer.


Can you make it faster by cutting out a step or two from the


business process? Can you make it appear faster by providing


some form of distraction if you know your solution needs time


to extract information from distant databases? Can you hold


information so that the customer does not have to reenter it?


## 第 395 页


In short, think of anything that makes the solution appear—


or be—faster.


What Would Your Grandchildren Do?


![embedded_p395_63.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p395_63.jpeg)


## 第 396 页


This trigger is simple: Imagine the solution that your


grandchildren will use. Of course, you cannot see into the


future—technology is evolving so quickly that it’s


difficult to imagine what you’ll be using in five years’


time, let alone 40 or 50 years.


However, the question is meant not to be answered, but to


be asked. It’s there to let you dream up creative solutions


without bothering too much about what’s possible. It’s hard


to think of a world without, say, electricity. Yet people


before the 19th century would have struggled to imagine a


world with electricity. But being difficult does not mean


that it’s impossible.


The best part of this technique is that it encourages you to


make giant mental leaps. We tend to think in evolutionary


terms—next year’s phone will be an improvement on this


year’s, and the year after that another improvement. Now


let’s jump over the next few years; your grandchildren


won’t have phones. What will they have? You try to imagine


it, and whatever you come up with, let it influence your


candidate solution.


Focusing on grandchildren (you could even try great-


grandchildren) directs you to think into the unconstrained


## 第 397 页


and unknown future. This is a technique that asks you to


avoid thinking about constraints in your current world, and


project into some imaginative future world.


Lateral Thinking


Lateral thinking is a problem-solving technique that can


also be used to come up with better, more innovative


solutions. The term “lateral thinking” was first used by


Maltese psychologist Edward de Bono. It involves rejecting


traditional step-by-step logic, or “vertical thinking,” and


looking at the problem with an unconnected, or lateral,


view.


As an example of lateral thinking, answer this question: A


person falls out of a 40-story building and survives. How?


Vertical thinking will focus on the obvious answers: a


parachute, a magic landing pad, Superman plucks him out of


the air, and so on. But none of those are the right answer.


Lateral thinking means that you ignore the progression of


vertical answers given above and approach the problem by


questioning all the components and assumptions. In this case,


the person survives because he fell out of a ground floor


window. Previously you might have assumed that because the


building is 40 stories, he went off the top.


## 第 398 页


A man walks into a bar and asks for a glass of water. The


bartender pulls out a gun and points it at the man’s head.


The man says, “Thank you,” and walks out. Why? The answer


to this will not be found by using any of the components of


the problem. What is the answer? Keep reading, it’s at the


end of the chapter.


The value of lateral thinking is that it asks you and your


team to look for solutions by thinking about the problem


completely differently. Ignore all the obvious and


predictable solutions, and see the problem “sideways,” or


laterally. You will be pleasantly surprised.


Removing Constraints


A constraint is a restriction on the problem space. It is


not a physical restraint, like a pair of handcuffs, but some


stated or unstated limitation on the project, the design of


the solution, or the way in which it must be solved. When you


pretend for the moment that the constraint can be removed


or significantly altered, you can often uncover a new and


better solution. For example:


“What if we had only $1,000 to spend to develop a


solution?”


## 第 399 页


“What could we do if we only had three months to develop a


solution?”


“What if we did not have to obey the law?”


“What if we did not have to deliver the parcels?”


“What could we do if . . . ?”


Not all constraints are real; some are assumptions. People


assume that because something has “always been done this


way” that it always must be done that way. Challenge this


assumption by asking what happens if you remove it. Sometimes


the assumption is wrong, and the constraint turns out not to


be real. In this case, you can remove it.


Removing constraints as we mean it here is an innovation


technique. It’s not that you will remove the constraints


(sometimes you do), but imagining the situation if the


constraint did not exist often leads to different ways of


thinking about the problem. This in turn leads to different,


more innovative solutions. See the example in Figure 13.5.


## 第 400 页


![embedded_p400_64.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p400_64.jpeg)


Figure 13.5 Metro systems all over the world probably asked


“What if travelers didn’t have to buy a ticket?” which led


to ticket barriers accepting debit cards.


For example, suppose there is a constraint that says you must


make a profit. Take this constraint and ask, “What if we


gave our product away?” This at first might seem


counterproductive and pointless, but think about solutions


where the product is given away. The most obvious example is


Google, which gives away its search facility. The search


engine cost Google a considerable amount of money to build


and run, but by giving away its search facility, it can


attract a huge audience and make an eye-watering profit from


advertising to that audience.


## 第 401 页


Amazon most probably said something along the lines of “What


if we didn’t charge people for delivering their goods to


them?” which led to Amazon Prime and its free delivery and


hundreds of thousands of loyal subscription-paying customers.


Whenever you encounter a constraint, challenge


it. Is it a real constraint? And what would


happen if you removed it?


Consider the newspaper you read on your tablet device or


phone. When newspapers first went online, almost all of them


put out a daily edition, just as they had been doing for


their print version. Then somebody asked, what happens if we


remove the constraint of the daily edition? It means we


don’t have to wait until tomorrow to publish a breaking


story. Removing this constraint meant that online newspapers


could move to the hybrid model where the daily edition is


supplemented by, and often replaced by, new stories covering


breaking news.


Constraints are all around us and sometimes taken for


granted, like obeying the law. You have to look hard to find


them, and when you do, ask what happens if you take them


away.


## 第 402 页


Combination


Combination means taking existing components and recombining


them in different ways to make something new. Johannes


Gutenberg changed the world when he combined the wine press


with a coin stamp to make his movable type printing press.


Today a phone has been combined with a camera to the joy of


the millions of selfie takers. The hybrid car, combining


electric and internal combustion engines, is another example


of successfully combining two technologies.


Anything you need probably already exists.


The raw materials for combination are the technology,


solutions, processes, ideas, and so on that have already been


built. There is so much stuff out there that it is safe to


say that anything you need already exists. The raw materials


should not only be thought of as individual components lying


about but could be complete systems or processes. Your team


might use only parts of these systems or use them in their


entirety. We wrote about ready-made solutions in Chapter 12


and elsewhere. Combining ready-mades with existing solutions


often provides an innovative result.


## 第 403 页


However, the raw material does not always come in a neatly


labeled box ready to use. You might have to look at the


abstract essence of whatever it is to see how, by changing


the subject matter, you can use it as one of your components.


The task here is to take a moment with your team and ask if


you really have to build something from scratch, or if you


can take some existing components and combine them in a new


way to make all, or most, of your new solution.


Review


None of the techniques mentioned above are magical fairy dust


that will make you the most inventive person since Thomas


Edison. They are, however, triggers that might just give you


the inspiration that results in a better solution.


The objective is to come up with several candidate solutions.


If one of the techniques makes that easier, then good. If one


of them makes you look at the problem differently, then


better.


There are of course lots more creativity techniques. The


intention in this chapter is to describe some of the most


used ones. But it helps to keep on looking for other


## 第 404 页


creativity techniques and ways of thinking that help you to


discover new ideas.


The answer to the lateral thinking puzzle of the man walking


into the bar and asking for water is that he had hiccups.


Resources


Creative Confidence: Unleashing the Creative Potential Within


Us All by Tom Kelley and David Kelley (Crown Currency, 2013).


The founders of IDEO explore how creative thinking can be


harnessed to create innovative software products.


The Innovator’s Toolkit: 50+ Techniques for Predictable and


Sustainable Organic Growth by David Silverstein, Philip


Samuel, and Neil DeCarlo (Wiley, 2012). As the title says,


these are tools to help you innovate. The book goes on to


explain why, when, and how to use them.


The Creative Contrarian: 20 “Wise Fool” Strategies to Boost


Creativity and Curb Groupthink by Roger von Oech (Wiley,


2021). The author uses the analogy of the wise fools who were


consulted by kings and emperors to find ways of overcoming


entrenched and obsolete solutions. This is most appropriate


for finding better, more innovative ways of solving the


business problem and avoiding the presumed solution.


## 第 405 页


Lateral Thinking: A Textbook of Creativity by Edward de Bono.


This is the classic book on this subject. De Bono shows how


to avoid “vertical thinking”—that is, serial problem


solving—and come at business problems “laterally.” The


results are creative and ingenious solutions.


Design Sparks (https://designsparks.io; from Bayes Business


School) is an AI-enabled online tool to help you find more


creative solutions. You start with your problem statement,


then Design Sparks uses AI and established creative problem-


solving techniques to respond with inventive directions.


These are curated by CebAI’s design and creativity experts.


## 第 406 页


Chapter 14. Probing and Exploring the
Candidates


At this stage, you have multiple prototypes of sacrificial


candidate solutions. You have multiple candidates because it


is important to have a range of alternatives; they facilitate


a more thorough exploration of the problem space. Besides,


having alternative candidates helps to avoid falling in love


with your sole prototype.


The prototypes are candidates—they are proposals generated


to explore the problem space, not be a forerunner of


something you build. Calling them “candidates” means that


you have a number of them, each one trying to solve the


problem in a different way. However, until they are proven,


each of them remains a hypothesis, and you are probing to


prove whether the hypothesis is true.


Candidates are sacrificial. You have built them as a learning


experience: If a candidate does not teach you anything, then


you discard it. We are probing the candidates, not so much as


a test to see if the candidate solution works, but to explore


the problem it is proposing to solve.


## 第 407 页


We often call these “safe-to-fail probes.” We have borrowed


the term from Dave Snowden (see Resources), and the


implication is that you are not betting everything on any


candidate. You have not invested a lot of time building a


candidate, so not much is lost if it isn’t useful. It might


seem unproductive to generate candidate solutions and then


test them to destruction, but if the result is that you solve


the right business problem, every hour spent is doubly


worthwhile. Having said that, your probing should be done as


quickly as possible.


Probing


You are examining multiple candidate solutions to explore


the problem space, and hopefully, some of your candidates


lead you to more adventurous, alternative problem spaces. The


objective is to study the problem by seeing how well, and


why, a candidate would solve the problem. Conversely, you


learn something when a candidate doesn’t solve the problem.


You and your client are exploring the problem space. It’s


not unusual to hear something like this: “I don’t know what


I need, but I will know it when you show me something that I


don’t need.” These candidate solutions are there to help


you uncover the real problem.


## 第 408 页


You are probing to determine whether the candidate does one


of the following.


• Reveals nothing new about the business problem.


• Reveals that you are solving the wrong problem.


• Reveals that you are solving a different problem. However,


the candidate is innovative and so attractive to your


customer that he prefers to change his requirements to fit


the candidate.


• Confirms that you are solving the right business problem


and the outcome of your candidate is what is desired.


You are also exploring the candidates for their suitability,


desirability, and feasibility within the business ecosystem.


In addition, you are using the candidates to explore the


problem space and ensure that the candidate is addressing the


customer’s real business problem.


• Is it solving the right problem, and is it the right


problem to solve?


• Ask the customer, “How does this solve your problem?”


• Ask, “Why does it solve your problem?”


## 第 409 页


• Is the premise of the candidate correct?


• Or was it assumed and is not representative of the real


problem?


• Does the candidate solution have the correct functionality?


• Is the outcome of this candidate the desired outcome?


• Is it acceptable to its customers and users?


• What is the impact of this candidate on the surrounding


business ecosystem?


• Does this candidate provide real business benefit to the


customer?


• Is it economically feasible?


• Is it needed? Does the functionality contribute to the


customer’s business? Will it be used?


Let’s look at some of these using the business of Athena’s


Wines. The wine business is competitive, and wine buyers have


a lot of choice as to where they buy their wine. Athena’s


customers appreciate the high-quality wine she sells, and


they also appreciate convenience. (See the reference to


## 第 410 页


convenience as a creative trigger in the previous chapter.)


Athena has done some research, and one of its findings is


that wine customers are very appreciative of fast delivery.


Athena sees a business opportunity if she can provide fast


and convenient home delivery of her wine.


So, at this stage the business goal looks like this:


Purpose: To provide a fast, convenient home delivery service


for Athena’s wines within the city


Advantage: An increase in customer satisfaction with her


business


Measurement: Any order can be delivered within four hours,


and customer approval is above 85%.


Athena feels that if she introduces a service that her


customers appreciate, or become dependent on, she will


establish a closer, more permanent link to them. And if her


customers like the service, they will tell others. The


intangible benefit for this initiative is closely connected


customers, leading, she hopes, to tangible benefits of more


sales and improved customer retention.


## 第 411 页


Figure 14.1 is a candidate solution for Athena’s business


problem in the form of a storyboard.


## 第 412 页


![embedded_p412_65.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p412_65.jpeg)


## 第 413 页


![embedded_p412_65.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p412_65.jpeg)


Figure 14.1 This storyboard prototype shows a candidate


solution for a wine company. Take a quick look at it—we are


going to probe it to demonstrate how prototypes are used to


explore the problem.


Let’s talk through this candidate to see how it addresses


the business problem.


In panel 1, the customer’s order is received in the existing


brick-and-mortar shop. Customers like to talk to Athena about


the wines they are selecting, so many of them come to the


store. They can also order on the phone or through Athena’s


website or app.


In panel 2, the order is sent to the warehouse, where it is


picked and made ready for dispatch. The order is not


immediately dispatched, as panel 3 shows, but waits for two


hours to see if other orders come in that can be delivered at


the same time.


In panel 4 the time has arrived, and the warehouse staff load


the order (or orders) into the autonomous vehicle, which then


navigates its way to the delivery address. Once there (panel


5), the vehicle phones the customer to come out and collect


his wine (panel 6).


## 第 414 页


Does the Candidate Solve the Right Problem?


The purpose of this sacrificial candidate is to help you


determine if it solves the right problem. So, you now have to


question the problem that this candidate purports to solve.


This prototype is about delivery, so the first question to


your customer, Athena, is about whether her real problem is


the delivery of the wine.


She has said she wants “a service that her customers


appreciate, or become dependent on, and that will establish a


closer, more permanent link to them.” The autonomous


delivery candidate looks cool, but is it the best thing to


establish “a closer link to the customers”? Also, is making


closer links Athena’s real problem? You use this candidate


to question Athena as to whether the outcome of autonomous


delivery is the outcome she needs.


For example, is the right problem to solve the one about


establishing a relationship with the customers based on


convenience and speedy delivery? Or could the right problem


be about ensuring that the customers get wines that they


like? Should you be proposing a candidate to Athena where she


curates individual customers’ selections (perhaps with a


little help from AI) so that they always get wines they


## 第 415 页


enjoy, yet have an interesting variation between orders? In


other words, customers will come to be assured that


everything they buy from Athena fits their tastes.


Or could the right problem be about the range of wine that


Athena carries? For example, could you prototype another


candidate where customers have access to a huge selection of


wines, many of which Athena does not stock? The autonomous


delivery vehicles from the earlier prototype could be used to


pick up wine from another wine merchant’s stock before


delivering it to the customer.


The point of any candidate is to cause you and Athena to


carefully consider whether you are attacking the right


problem. If it turns out to be the wrong problem, the


candidate is still valuable because it has led you in a


better direction.


Discard the candidate; keep the knowledge.


Let’s press on with our probing.


Does the Candidate Solution Have the Correct Functionality?


Let’s revisit the autonomous delivery candidate shown in


Figure 14.1. The question now is, does it work? That is, does


## 第 416 页


this candidate’s functionality achieve the right outcome?


Panel 1 is fine—Athena’s customers have been ordering from


the website for some time. Some of her customers prefer to


phone or come in and discuss the wine with Athena. She likes


this, as it allows her customers to explore different wines


and maintain a personal connection with her business.


Panel 2 is about picking the wine in the warehouse. This


relies on the correct information being given to the


warehouse staff, so you should satisfy yourself that the


output of panel 1 is suitable. Getting the right bottles off


the shelves and into cartons can be achieved. The business


has been doing that for some time.


So far, so good.


Panel 3 is about waiting for an amount of time. This time


delay is proposed to allow other orders to come in so that


the vehicle can deliver to multiple addresses during a trip.


Keep in mind that Athena operates in a densely populated


city. While waiting is very easy to functionally achieve—


just do nothing—it might cause other problems. For example,


customers will know that this wine merchant has autonomous


## 第 417 页


delivery vehicles and will probably expect to have their wine


quite soon after they order. People hate to wait.


On the other hand, some customers might prefer to phone in or


tap in their order while they are at work and ask for


delivery in the evening. Autonomous vehicles can run all


night and there is no need to pay penalty rates to human


drivers.


So, we have to say that the functionality as it stands—a


two-hour wait—is problematic. Probably the best thing to do


is to have some functionality whereby Athena can set the


delivery time to take into account her customers’ requested


times.


In panel 4, the warehouse staff load the vehicle. This might


not work if the delivery is earmarked for the evening and the


staff have gone home for the day. Another potential problem


with this activity is whether there are enough autonomous


vehicles available. This would conflict with the goal of fast


and convenient deliveries.


Panel 5 has the vehicle arriving at the destination address


and phoning the customer with a message that it is outside


## 第 418 页


and to come and get their wine. What happens if the customer


is not at home?


The customer comes out to retrieve their wine in panel 6.


Functionally, this is straightforward—get a couple of


cartons out of a vehicle and carry them inside. However, one


of the questions you ask is whether the solution is


acceptable to all customers. For example, elderly or disabled


customers might not be able to manage it, and some customers


might not be willing to come out into the street and retrieve


their wine. We’ll come back a little later to this one.


We also need some functionality to ensure that each customer


retrieves his own wine from the autonomous van and not


somebody else’s. Additionally, it must stop people from


putting anything into the van.


So, with a few corrections, this candidate would be


functionally correct.


But that is not enough.


Exploring


Let's look a little into using this prototype to explore the


problem and solution.


## 第 419 页


Is the Outcome of This Candidate the Desired Outcome?


The outcome of this candidate is that an order of wine can be


delivered at almost any time of the customer’s choosing,


provided they are willing to retrieve it from the autonomous


vehicle.


For this you must go back to Athena, the wine business owner.


• Is that the outcome she wants?


• Or have the analysis team presumed that this is a desirable


outcome?


• Does this outcome significantly improve her business?


• Will it attract new customers, or at the least, provide a


better experience for her existing customers?


• Will the cost of the solution outweigh the benefits, both


tangible and intangible?


• What risks are incurred if she were to go ahead with this


solution?


In an earlier chapter we wrote about the goals of the


project, and discussed how the goal should be measurable.


## 第 420 页


Assessing the outcome of a candidate is measuring how close


it comes to fulfilling the project’s goal. The autonomous


vehicle service would go some way toward Athena’s goal of


fast, convenient delivery.


Earlier we questioned Athena’s goals and proposed some


alternatives—curating a customer’s selection and accessing


a wide range of wines. If either of these had been determined


to be the right goal, then prototypes of these candidate


solutions would be questioned in the same way as we are


questioning the fast, convenient delivery candidate.


You might find that when you come to explore outcomes as we


are doing here, it reveals that the candidate is solving the


wrong problem, and that the goal is not what was originally


thought.


This candidate does not offer any outcome other than


delivery. The ordering and warehousing parts of the solution


are already in place, and this candidate does not appear to


improve them in any way. Sometimes candidates offer ancillary


outcomes, but that does not appear to be the case here.


This is now in the hands of Athena and her goal. Either she


wants the outcome of this candidate—fast delivery at most


## 第 421 页


times of the day—or the candidate has missed its mark.


Either way, you have learned something about the problem


space, and hopefully learned something that triggers a new


and different candidate.


Is This Candidate Acceptable to Its Customers and Users?


Part of the delivery candidate is that the end customers must


come out and unload the vehicle themselves.


• Will they be happy to do that? If they have settled in for


the evening, would they want to come out into the cold to


carry in their wine?


• Are they the kinds of people who would find that


acceptable?


• Are they people who are able to carry boxes of wine into


their homes?


• Would they feel safe unloading a wine-carrying vehicle at


night?


• Would they feel that unloading the vehicle is a good trade-


off for getting their wine quickly and at convenient times?


## 第 422 页


These are the kinds of questions that you and your team need


to ask. After all, if the wine customers refuse to unload the


autonomous vehicle, then the candidate solution is worthless.


What Is the Impact of This Candidate on the Surrounding
Business Ecosystem?


When you install a solution in your customer’s business, it


has an impact on that business; it disrupts it in some way.


If your solution interacts with external customers, then it


impacts their activity. This impact might be beneficial, or


it might not. In any event, understanding and assessing the


impact is vital if you are to provide the right solution.


Which is why we suggest that you assess the impact while the


solution is still a candidate.


Figure 14.2 shows a candidate solution surrounded by its


business ecosystem. The solution must interact with the


elements of the ecosystem, and some elements interact with


other elements. The elements might include internal


operations, or external suppliers, or external receivers of


something from the organization.


## 第 423 页


![embedded_p423_66.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p423_66.jpeg)


Figure 14.2 The candidate solution has to fit into the


business ecosystem. Note the connections of the candidate to


the ecosystem and the interconnectedness of the elements of


the ecosystem.


Figure 14.2 shows The Market, which represents either the


external customers for this organization or any other group


## 第 424 页


of people who are external yet interact with the


organization.


Other Software Systems must be assessed if they interact with


this candidate. It might require a painstaking search through


the documentation of the software to assess the impact of the


candidate.


A candidate usually interacts with people, who can be inside


or outside the organization. The impact here is the effect it


has on their job or their way of working. Sometimes the


impact might be functional—they must do something different


to accommodate the candidate—or it might be personal in that


it affects their feeling for the job and the way they think


about their job.


Your client wants the candidate to have a beneficial impact,


which could be that the candidate enables people to do their


jobs more easily: A business process can be made faster or


cheaper which could make it easier and quicker for external


customers to make their transactions with the organization.


Perhaps the candidate can save the organization money, or it


causes external customers to buy more of the organization’s


product. Perhaps the candidate takes advantage of a business


## 第 425 页


opportunity and provides a way for the organization to


operate in a new market.


Beneficial impacts are what drive your development effort.


And of course, the benefit must be greater than the cost of


achieving it. Most beneficial impacts can be costed—money


saved by a better process or extra revenue generated. Some


are harder to evaluate purely financially. For example,


taking advantage of a new technology might be done purely to


keep up with the competition. This has a financial advantage,


but it is over a longer term and harder to evaluate. Giving


your customers the ability to do something they could not do


before might not have an immediate financial gain but could


nevertheless be quite beneficial.


Most candidates have some negative impact. They would cause


disruption, require retraining of the users, and so on.


However, any negative impact must be substantially overcome


by the benefits; otherwise, you should discard the candidate.


Does This Candidate Provide Real Value?


Consider Athena of the wine business, as she is paying for
