your development efforts. She would receive value if this


candidate solution resulted in either an increase in the


number of her customers, more wine being sold, or an


## 第 426 页


improvement to the experience for her wine-buying customers


that resulted in better customer retention. To predict


whether any of those factors will come to fruition, you need


to do a little research on the wine-buying customers. Do


those customers feel there is value in having their wine


delivered more promptly, and delivered at more convenient


times? Would this value be lessened by having to go and


retrieve the order from the delivery vehicle? Some wine


customers might consider that to be a negative value.


Your customer research would survey the audience with


questions such as these.


• Do you need fast home delivery?


• Do you want to unload the autonomous vehicle yourself?


• Would this service make you more likely to buy your wine


from Athena?


• Would it cause you to recommend Athena’s Wines to somebody


else?


• Would you become a customer of Athena’s just to receive


this service?


## 第 427 页


You are attempting to assess whether this solution will


provide value to the wine customers, and as a result bring


value to Athena. The size of the investment in the solution


obviously dictates how much effort you put into this


research. Your marketing department might also hold strong


views on the value of your candidates. Somehow, and it is not


always easy, you need to assess value.


This assessment must be honest. When you read about failed IT


projects, a recurring theme is that the projected value of


the solution was overstated. Often ludicrously so. Be honest


and careful assessing value, as the success of the initiative


depends on it.


Let us say that customer response has been mainly negative,


and so it is looking a little shaky for this candidate. It


does not appear to provide enough value for either Athena or


her customers for it to be taken any further. But let’s


press on with our exploration.


Is This Candidate Economically Feasible?


It is plain that a solution is of little value to your


organization if the cost to construct it and operate it


outweighs its economic advantages. There is an exception


where the solution produces intangible benefits that the


## 第 428 页


organization is willing to pay for. Either way, you must


assess the (tangible and intangible) economics of any


candidate.


In Athena’s case, you go through each panel in the


storyboard and estimate its cost. In this case, the first two


panels introduce nothing new—it is safe to assume that your


client has existing mechanisms for taking the orders and


warehousing—but the third panel, the one about waiting two


hours, may introduce some cost.


What does it cost to have an order sitting in the warehouse


for two hours? Does this cause some kind of lost opportunity?


For example, do the wine customers want their wine to be


delivered as soon as possible after they order it? The


intention of the two-hour wait is to potentially reduce


delivery costs by delivering several orders in one trip. If


that happened often, then fewer autonomous delivery vehicles


would be needed. This means you compare the savings in


delivery costs against the potential for harm caused by the


two-hour delay.


Panel 4 in Figure 14.1 introduces the autonomous delivery


vehicle. You would now need to assess the cost of purchasing


or leasing the required number of vehicles. Add to that the


## 第 429 页


cost of maintenance, insurance, and the real estate cost of


housing them when they are not out delivering wine. To be


economically feasible, these costs must be considerably less


than the extra revenue the service brings.


Double-Loop Learning


Normally, we solve problems in a single-loop manner. That is,


each time we fail to solve the problem we go back and try to


solve it again, each time using a different or modified


solution to the problem. When a probe reveals that a


candidate solution is not viable, you go back and either


select a different candidate or use what you have learned to


modify and improve the candidate. Thus, the candidate


solution changes for each single loop of the cycle.


Be willing to admit that you might be wrong,


question everything, and revisit your assumptions


about the problem you’re trying to solve.


Double loop means that instead of repeatedly trying to


solve the same problem, you loop further back to the


original problem and question it. Could it be that you are


trying to solve the wrong problem? Could it be that there is


a better problem to solve? Could the original problem be


## 第 430 页


incorrectly defined, and by correcting it, would you have a


more relevant problem to solve? Or could it be that your


attempts to solve it prompt the customer to realize that this


is not the right problem to solve? Figure 14.3 illustrates


this double-loop approach to problem-solving.


![embedded_p430_67.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p430_67.jpeg)


Figure 14.3 Double-loop learning. The attempt to solve the


problem using a safe-to-fail probe reveals that the problem


was not solved. A single loop goes back and probes a


different solution. A double loop goes back and questions


whether you are trying to solve the right problem.


## 第 431 页


Let’s go back to Athena and her wine business. In Figure


14.1, you saw the candidate solution that used autonomous


vehicles to deliver the wine orders. Let’s say that the


exploration of the autonomous delivery vehicles revealed that


while it is possible to implement such a system, it would


have a low uptake by customers, and so it is not going to


bring much value to Athena’s business. This discovery is


valuable. You haven’t spent a lot of time on your


prototypes, but you have learned a lot. The prototype has


been sacrificed to the pursuit of understanding the real


business goal.


So, now you do a double loop back and question Athena about


the business problem she’s trying to solve. Here’s where it


gets interesting.


We’re in a double loop here, so we’ve stepped back to


question the goal of the project. Does it conform with the


goals of the company? In line with most commercial companies,


Athena has a goal of making a profit. This delivery project


has its own goal, which is not necessarily to make a profit,


but it must contribute to the company’s overall goal.


The double loop means that you ask Athena if fast delivery is


the right goal. It seemed like a good idea at the time (as do


## 第 432 页


many projects), but it’s only the right goal if the wine


customers value it. When we probed the candidate, it turned


out that customers placed little value on autonomous vehicles


and speedy deliveries.


We referred to these as safe-to-fail probes. Safe-to-fail


means that the project does not fail even when a candidate


fails. Let’s call the delivery candidate a failure, but


it’s really a success. You’ve saved Athena an expensive and


potentially damaging development effort that would have


resulted in an unwanted solution.


Also consider the knowledge you gained by probing the


candidate. During the probe, some of Athena’s customers said


that they don’t value speed so much as they value


convenience. What her customers really want is to arrange


convenient delivery times and to know when the delivery will


arrive.


“I need to order it now but don’t want it delivered until


Saturday.”


“I don’t get home from the office until 7 p.m., so I want


it delivered between 7 p.m. and 10 p.m.”


## 第 433 页


“I sometimes have to wait around for a delivery that is


coming that day. If I knew exactly when it would reach me, I


could go out to run errands and be back in time.”


This example might seem exaggerated, and indeed it is, but it


is also not far away from situations that, in our experience,


occur frequently. We have exaggerated a little and simplified


a lot to illustrate what can happen when a project sets out


to solve a problem that is not the right problem.


You will find that probing candidates can be difficult.


People are stubborn when their ideas are challenged. People


are reluctant to let go of cherished ideas regardless of the


evidence stacked against them. People tell you you’re


wasting time finding the real problem and it’s better to get


on and build something.


Let’s say we have overcome resistance, and everyone is


accepting that we were solving the wrong problem. We’ll


return to building some candidate solutions to help Athena’s


customers order wine and have it delivered at a convenient


time. Figures 14.4 and 14.5 are prototype sketches of


candidate solutions you and the team subsequently put


together.


## 第 434 页


![embedded_p434_68.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p434_68.jpeg)


Figure 14.4 A process model of the ordering process


The process model shown in Figure 14.4 would need a little


enhancing. For example, when the customer selects the


delivery time it would be more efficient for this activity if


it started with the company offering a default time, which


would be the time it knows deliveries are to be made in the


customer’s area. The process should also allow customers to


cancel if they cannot get a convenient time slot, and you


would also need another process for people to rearrange their


delivery times, and perhaps more. We’ll ignore these for the


sake of brevity.


## 第 435 页


![embedded_p435_69.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p435_69.jpeg)


Figure 14.5 A prototype screen to experiment with and probe


to determine if it satisfies the wine customers’ requirement


to know when their wine will be delivered


You would use the prototypes shown in Figures 14.4 and 14.5


to explore a little more. Is it feasible to offer delivery at


any time the wine customer wants? Does the business have to


use autonomous vehicles to deliver outside normal working


hours? Could delivery be done by having a special


relationship with a small delivery company that is willing to


## 第 436 页


deliver at almost any hour? Is Athena’s problem not just


getting the wine to her customers, but being able to make a


profit by having the capacity for on-demand delivery?


We can leave it here. There would most likely be more


exploration and probing to do, but by now you have the point


that although they are prototypes of candidate solutions,


they are actually devices for discovering more about the


problem.


Review


It is important to generate multiple candidate solutions.


You cannot hope to satisfactorily explore the problem space


with only one. If there is only one, then it is almost


certainly a presumed solution. This means that little if any


thought has gone into establishing the real business problem,


and the team is rushing into the first solution that presents


itself.


Among your solutions, you might consider including a wild-


card candidate. This is a candidate that is far-fetched,


playful, gravity-defying, and almost impossible to deliver.


It might not make the grade in the end, but along the way it


## 第 437 页


might inspire some better ideas and fresh approaches to the


problem.


“Play is the highest form of research.”—Albert


Einstein


It is also important that you think of your candidates as


sacrificial. You are not betting the farm, or your own ego,


on a candidate solution. If you throw one away, there is a


reason to do so, and that reason is usually that you have


learned more about the problem and discovered that this


candidate doesn’t fit the problem. It’s okay to be wrong


early. It’s expensive if you’re wrong late.


You are probing to find flaws. If a candidate is flawed, you


might be able to repair it and re-present it for another


probe. Or you might pick another candidate. That’s single-


loop learning.


It is more valuable when flaws in the candidate cause you to


go back and rethink the problem. That’s double-loop


learning.


When you are prototyping, you are building multiple


sacrificial candidate solutions, examining them, and probing


## 第 438 页


them, possibly to destruction. Why? It’s a learning


experience. When it helps you and your customer to uncover


the right business problem and the best solution for it, it


is valuable learning indeed.


Resources


Cynefin: Weaving Sense-Making into the Fabric of Our World by


Dave Snowden and friends (Cognitive Edge – The Cynefin Co.,


2020). The Cynefin Framework is designed to help deal with


uncertain, complex systems. We find the thinking behind the


Framework useful for probing candidate solutions.


Return on Software: Maximizing the Return on Your Software


Investment by Steve Tockey (Addison-Wesley, 2008). Tockey


discusses the engineering economy and how software


practitioners can appreciate the organizational ramifications


of their candidate solutions.


Teaching Smart People How to Learn by Chris Argyris (Harvard


Business Review Press, 2008). This book is aimed at business


in general, but the author’s discussion of double-loop


learning is powerful and applicable to business analysts.


## 第 439 页


Chapter 15. Using Prototypes as the
Specification


Sometimes it is possible that a candidate prototype can serve


as the specification. But only sometimes, and regardless of


what we say here, this should not be used as your mainstream


approach. There are too many opportunities for a prototype to


mislead the developers, which would defeat the point of using


it as a specification.


However, when your project is smaller and not mission


critical, and when the application domain is well understood


by the developers, you might get away with this. You probably


will have to add some more detail, but judiciously using a


prototype as the specification can sometimes work.


It is worth repeating that prototypes, as we are suggesting


you use them, are intended to ensure that you are solving the


right problem. They help you interrogate the customer about


his problem, not his solution.


Let’s say that you have been prototyping your customer’s


problem and by now have several prototypes. (See Figure


15.1.)


## 第 440 页


![embedded_p440_70.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p440_70.jpeg)


Figure 15.1 By now, you have several prototypes of the


different business events. Some of these might be used as the


specification for development.


We have suggested that most of your prototypes are about one


business event. The business event triggers the work to


respond with a chunk of functionality (which we call a


“business use case” or “BUC”). The BUC represents one


transaction from the point of view of the outside world—your


## 第 441 页


external customers or similar. Because it is a discrete unit


of functionality, it is an ideal unit for development.


Let’s see how this might work.


The Prototype as the Specification


Let’s look at an example. This one is a neobank and it wants


to add a facility to help customers save money for a special


purpose: a vacation, a house deposit, an engagement ring, or


something else. The team built the prototype shown in Figure


15.2. They proposed to call the feature a “pot,” as in the


pot of gold at the end of the rainbow. The pot is a separate


account within the customer’s main account and is treated


individually. That is, it does not show up as part of the


customer’s balance, and it is not available to be spent


unless the customer deliberately releases the pot. Pots earn


interest at a slightly higher rate than regular savings


accounts.


## 第 442 页


![embedded_p442_71.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p442_71.jpeg)


Figure 15.2 The prototype for a savings pot feature for the


neobank. The team chose to use a process model to show the


candidate functionality.


The activities in the prototype start with the bank customer


requesting to open a pot. This activity would include some


checks that a pot is appropriate. For example, if the


customer has a balance of, say, only $5, then there is little


point in him having a pot. There will be some business rules


that apply to this activity. We discuss business rules fully


in Chapter 24, Other Trawling Techniques, but briefly they


are the “laws” that the business has established for


itself. You would need to find all the relevant business


rules and attach them to this activity for the developers to


know what to build.


## 第 443 页


The next activity is the customer naming his pot. This is to


give the customer a connection to the particular purpose for


which he wants to set aside money. It would be more inspiring


to have a pot named “Tropical Holiday” than one simply


named “pot.” If the customer wants it, a start date for the


pot can be set. You would attach this brief description along


with any other details to this activity.


Then the customer sets the rules for the pot. For example, he


might want to lock away the money (from himself) until


vacation time rolls around, or Christmas is on the horizon,


or there is a special birthday or anniversary coming up, or


he is just saving for some luxury item. You would have to add


a description of this activity for the developers to build


the right solution.


The deposit amounts in the final activity specify whether an


amount is to be deposited in the pot whenever his salary is


banked, or if payments made from the main account are rounded


up and the spare change goes into the pot. There can be other


ways of building the pot which the customer specifies here.


Again, you need to describe this activity in enough detail


for the developers to build the right solution and add any


business rules that apply to this activity.


## 第 444 页


So far, so good. You could almost hand this prototype to the


developers, with the addition of the details mentioned above.


You would also add information about how the pot connects to


the existing customer accounts database. There will be some


security issues, the look and feel must be consistent with


the rest of the bank’s app, there might be some operational


issues, and so on. It would be worthwhile to look at the


Volere Requirements Specification Template (see Appendix A)


and use it as a checklist for the other non-functional


requirements.


This candidate solution is relatively straightforward and


should be able, with the enhancements mentioned above, to be


handed over to the development crew.


However, before doing so, you should consider the risks


involved. If this piece of business is crucial to the


existence of the organization, then under no circumstances


should you consider the prototype to be the specification. If


your business rules are numerous and complicated, then this


shortcut is not for you. On the other hand, if the domain is


well-understood, the developers are familiar with the type of


application to be built, and the product owner is confident


that the right solution will be built, then go ahead.


## 第 445 页


Whatever you do, don’t do it without honestly considering


the risks.


What to Do with the Prototype


The preceding chapters looked at building and probing


prototypes. So now, let’s see how you make use of what you


have been reading. For the sake of convenience, the Volere


process that has also been discussed elsewhere is shown again


in Figure 15.3.


## 第 446 页


![embedded_p446_72.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p446_72.jpeg)


Figure 15.3 The Volere process showing its activities


In preceding chapters, we have been talking about using the


goals and the scope established by the Project Blastoff to


build prototypes as a way of exploring the business problem.


We must stress that the intention of these prototypes is to


## 第 447 页


prompt your customer to give you (and possibly himself) a


better, more correct understanding of his problem.


The prototypes are throwaways. Once they have helped you


discover the real business problem, they have served their


purpose. Normally, you would switch to trawling for


requirements to find the details of the problem space.


However, in some cases, as we have just seen, prototypes can


have a further purpose. You have several options for how to


proceed, as illustrated in Figure 15.4.


## 第 448 页


![embedded_p448_73.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p448_73.jpeg)


Figure 15.4 The options available for further use of a


prototype. For option A, the prototype is discarded, but its


scope and problem are trawled. Option B’s prototype is used


during the Trawling activity, and for option C, the prototype


can be used for Designing and Developing.


Normally, when the prototype has done its job and you are


satisfied that the real business problem has been discovered,


## 第 449 页


you would trawl the problem space exposed by your prototype.


You can discard the prototype—it has done its job. This


situation is shown as option A in Figure 15.4.


Normally, the prototype would reveal the scope of the


business problem, which should be in accordance with the


scope determined during the project blastoff. However, it is


not uncommon to find that the initial scope needs to be


adjusted because of discoveries made during the prototyping


and probing efforts. It is also quite possible that your


prototyping has changed your understanding of the business


problem, and that requires the scope to be reworked.


Typically, you would have been building your prototypes, one


for each business event. We discussed business events in


Chapter 7, Business Events, when we were discussing the


Project Blastoff. If you jumped over that part, it is worth


revisiting it for the discussion about business events. They


are the backbone of your requirement and development efforts.


As each business use case is a discrete unit of functionality


for the complete solution, you can treat each prototype as a


separate case when deciding what to do with it.


Option B in Figure 15.4 is when the prototype has revealed


the real problem and its scope, and the solution demonstrated


## 第 450 页


by the prototype is a good basis for trawling its


requirements. To put that another way, the prototype shows a


solution that has the right scope and the right


functionality to solve the problem. So, in this case, you


keep the prototype as a reference for your trawling when you


discover the detailed requirements for that solution.


In some cases, the prototype can be used as a development


specification with some additions. This is shown as option


C. There is a discussion above on how to do that. Keep in


mind when doing this that your prototype must fit with the


overall design of the business solution. It is obviously


necessary to have consistency between the various parts of


the total solution.


Subsequent chapters discuss the activities mentioned above.


Please jump to whichever of them would be most useful to you.


But before you leave, there is one more thing to consider.


Evolutionary and Sacrificial Prototypes


The preceding chapters have discussed building sacrificial


prototypes of candidate solutions. The reason for building


the prototypes (you should always build several of them) is


to propose a solution that might solve the problem. As you


## 第 451 页


probe this candidate solution, you and your customer learn


more about the problem. It is sacrificial—you fully intend


to discard it if it doesn’t solve the problem or it doesn’t


reveal any more of the problem.


You might keep a successful candidate prototype to serve as a


focus for the exploration of the business problem. If it


illustrates the problem or shows insights that are useful,


then add it to your requirements repository.


However, in some cases your prototype could be


evolutionary. See Figure 15.5.


## 第 452 页


![embedded_p452_74.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p452_74.jpeg)


Figure 15.5 The suggested way of using prototypes to


incrementally build the complete solution


So far, the prototype is a sketch of a solution, a “paper”


prototype, if you will. It shows enough of the needed


functionality for you or your developers to turn this into a


piece of code to make a very rudimentary version of the


solution you intend to deliver. You know from your


prototyping and probing activities that it is solving the


right business problem. The few hours spent prototyping now


pay off—you can proceed with complete confidence.


## 第 453 页


Go back to the customer with this rudimentary version and


work with him to refine it. To do this you might need some of


the trawling techniques that are discussed in subsequent


chapters. The aim is to have your prototype evolve into the


delivered solution.


You can think of this process as being both evolutionary and


incremental. Each business event evolves into its final form.


Then, it is added incrementally to the end solution.


Review


This is a book about requirements. Requirements are a crucial


part of any development effort. If the requirements are not


right, then your solution cannot be the right one. However,


you would like to discover the requirements as quickly as


possible. This means developing your requirements to the


point that the correct product can be built.


In some cases, it might be possible that the prototypes you


built to explore the problem can be a significant part of the


requirements. Naturally enough, you need to enhance the


prototype with the relevant business rules and the


appropriate non-functional requirements. You must be honest


about the risk of doing this, but it might be worthwhile.


## 第 454 页


A further use of your prototype as a specification is when


your developers can use it to build a rudimentary version of


the intended product, which is subsequently developed


iteratively. It is necessary for the customer, and probably


other stakeholders, to be closely involved in this iterative


development, as each increment of the product serves as a


prototype. If the increment does not produce the right


result, then you discard it and rework it. Again, you must be


aware of the risks associated with this approach.


Your prototypes are intended to be experiments. Sometimes


they can be more than that.


This brings us to the end of the prototyping chapters. There


are several types of prototypes you can build, and there are


several ways of using these prototypes. Experiment with them


and decide which is best for you and your project.


## 第 455 页


Part IV: Trawling for


Requirements


Trawling is metaphorically dragging a net—much like a deep-


sea trawler’s fishing net—through the customer’s business


to learn about and scoop up its requirements. You might think


of this as illustrated in Figure P4.1.


## 第 456 页


![embedded_p456_75.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p456_75.jpeg)


Figure P4.1 Trawling is metaphorically dragging a net


through your customer’s business to scoop up its


requirements.


## 第 457 页


The requirements you are trawling for are the requirements


for a solution to the customer’s business problem. As


mentioned before, the problem can be an opportunity, the need


to replace a legacy solution that can no longer cope with the


demands placed on it, a change to the technology, or a change


to the business environment that necessitates a new solution


or modification to an old one. Or simply that something is


broken.


Whatever the cause, we call it a business problem. To find a


solution for it, you must first understand that problem.


This is trawling: going through your customer’s problem


space, investigating it, modeling it, and doing whatever it


takes for you, the business analyst, and your customer to


reach a clear and unambiguous understanding of that business


problem. From your understanding of the functionality and


data used by the business problem, you derive the


requirements for its solution.


The requirements we are talking about here fall into three


main categories. Functional requirements are the things that


your solution must do. For example, it must record a bank


deposit, calculate interest on a savings account, accept an


application for an account, and so on. Non-functional


## 第 458 页


requirements specify how the functionality must be carried


out; for example, how fast, how secure, how easy to use, how


private, and so on. Constraints are restrictions that your


solution must comply with. For example, it must run as an app


on a phone, it must use data from an existing legacy system,


and so on.


You can see a complete description of all the requirement


types in Appendix A, The Volere Requirements Specification


Template.


Let’s say that you have had a successful Project Blastoff—


or achieved enough of the Blastoff outcomes to be sufficient


—and you are happy to start looking at the problem space.


Alternatively, you might have been doing some Prototyping for


Requirements and find that you need to look more closely at


some of the business processes that the prototypes have


revealed, or there are questions that your prototypes are not


answering. So you Trawl for the Requirements. Figure P4.2


shows how these activities relate to each other.


## 第 459 页


![embedded_p459_76.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p459_76.jpeg)


Figure P4.2 The Trawling activity involves working with the


customers and discovering their business needs. These are


usually recorded as requirements or stories and added to the


requirements repository.


## 第 460 页


Trawling and prototyping should not be seen as mutually


exclusive activities. They overlap to some extent, and you


will most likely find yourself switching from one to the


other for the same area of study. Prototypes can help you


explore the problem, and trawling can help you uncover the


complete details of the business. They are not meant to be


separate activities, but complementary ways of discovering


the real requirements.


Trawling is conventional business analysis. That is, you’re


asking questions, running workshops, writing scenarios, or


using any of the other trawling techniques. All of them are


designed to discover requirements, but it is unlikely that


you use all of them. At least, not on the same project.


As you are going through this section, please keep in mind


that you should only do as much trawling as you need to.


After all, the fisherman’s (or woman’s) goal is to catch


enough fish, not to catch all the fish in the ocean. That may


seem obvious, but too many projects seem to become locked


into their trawling and carry on with it far beyond what is


needed.


After you’ve done some trawling on a particular subject, ask


yourself if you have learned enough to understand what


## 第 461 页


contributes most to the overall goals of the project. If


you’re not sure, then it’s an indication that you need to


do some more trawling.


What follows are a number of chapters, each dealing with a


different trawling technique. Pick the techniques that you


think will deliver the best value to you. You can always come


back later to find others that might be equally useful.


The best guidance is to use the trawling techniques that work


best with the people you are trying to communicate with. If


you find that a technique is not helping you discover


requirements or that people seem to be irritated or vague,


then change your approach rather than sticking with whatever


it is you’re using. Some people respond well to direct


questions and other people prefer that you quietly observe


their work and ask for clarification later. Some people know,


and are very clear about, what they need (although this is


not nearly as common as one would hope). Other people need


examples to help them discover what they really need.


The point is that you should try the techniques in the


following chapters and use the ones that are most effective


for you and your customers.


## 第 462 页


Chapter 16. The Essence of the Problem


We have been spending some time talking about how a problem


and a solution are different things. For example, there is a


difference between “search” and “find.” The essence of


the problem is to find something; searching is merely one way


of doing it. You might want to know David Bowie’s birthday—


you can search for it using a search engine. That’s a


solution. But the essence is to know his birthday, and you


can come to know it in other ways. For example, you could


write to the David Bowie fan club, speak with people who knew


him, or look it up in the register of births in Brixton,


where he was born. Regardless of how you solve it, the


essence is to know his birthday. (It’s January 8, by the


way.)


The essence is an abstraction, it’s conceptual, it has no


real-world technology, and that is what makes it such a


powerful requirements tool. By shaking off any implementation


technology, both current or proposed, human or


organizational, you are left with only the problem itself, or


as we are expressing it here, the essence of the problem. You


could say that the essence is the soul of the problem, but


not its body.


## 第 463 页


This chapter is about finding the essence of your customer’s


business problem, and about the difference between a problem


and a solution. Unless you fully understand the former, the


latter cannot be right.


The Problem


A lot of flawed solution development happens because the team


and the stakeholders confuse the problem with the solution.


Stakeholders frequently ask for a solution without stating


the problem it is meant to solve. Development teams often


rush into a solution because they presume that it is the


right solution, or it’s the solution they feel they should


build. These projects often don’t end well.


A problem is an abstract thing. A solution is a


physical thing.


It is useful to keep in mind that the difference between a


problem and a solution is that a problem is an abstract thing


whereas a solution is a physical thing. The problem has no


physical incarnation; it exists only in the mind. The


solution exists in some tangible artifact: It’s the computer


on your desk or the device in your hand; it’s the software


running on your device; it’s the consumer product you bring


## 第 464 页


home from the store; it’s the list of instructions for an


employee to follow.


If you are to solve the right problem, first you have to find


it. To do that, you need to take a solution-free view of the


problem. Let’s consider abstraction as a way of doing that.


Abstraction


The writer Yuval Noah Harari, in his book Sapiens, talks


about how Homo sapiens were able to dominate their close


neighbors, the Neanderthals, and might have caused the


Neanderthals’ extinction. The reason behind this is that,


probably because of a random genetic mutation, sapiens became


able to believe in abstract ideas. An example of a useful


abstract idea here is government and authority. These are


abstract concepts that we have, and we all (more or less)


believe in them. Sure, you can see government buildings,


watch the people’s representatives debate the great issues


of the day, and you can see written constitutions, but you


cannot actually see or touch government. Government itself is


an idea, an abstraction. It’s an agreement that we have some


elected people run our country and make the rules for living


together. And the forms that governments take—democracy,


monarchy, totalitarianism—are also abstractions, as are


## 第 465 页


capitalism and socialism. You cannot see, hear, touch, or


smell any of them. You cannot see or touch authority. Yes,


there are traffic lights, but it is the abstraction that a


red light means stop that regulates traffic and keeps you


safe on the streets.


Back to the sapiens and their domination of the Neanderthals.


Because of abstractions such as authority and hierarchy, the


sapiens could organize themselves. They were smaller and


weaker than the Neanderthals, but when it came to a mass


fight, the sapiens used their organization and tactics (both


abstract concepts) to win the day. “Thag, you take your


troop and go to their left, and Rog, you take this group and


feint right, while Gan takes his boys to the top of the cliff


and throws rocks at them.”


It probably wasn’t exactly like that, but note the


abstractions that we take for granted: the authority of the


person giving instructions, forming soldiers into a troop;


the feint; the tactics; and so on. Without the ability to use


abstractions, the Neanderthals were unorganized individuals


and were no match for the organized sapiens and their


tactics. So, we can say that you, a descendant of the sapiens


(and not of the Neanderthals), are here today because of


abstraction.


## 第 466 页


Another example of an abstraction—and possibly another


contributor to you being here today—is marriage. Sure, there


are rings and wedding cakes, but you cannot touch or see


marriage itself. It is an idea, an agreement between two


people. Yes, it has legal status, but law itself is an


abstraction. It’s something that we humans made up for the


greater good. The company you work for and its hierarchy are


abstractions, as are all other ideas that we subscribe to.


Before we disappear down the rabbit hole of abstraction,


let’s see how it affects us when it comes to the business


problem we are meant to be solving.


Essence


Back in Chapter 3, Understand the Real Problem, we included a


quotation from Abe Lincoln about sharpening his axe before


starting to chop down a tree. This notion of preparedness


brings up a quotation from Albert Einstein in which he said


that if he had only one hour to save the world, he would


spend 59 minutes defining the problem. The reason for


spending time on the essence—an abstraction—is to discover


the real problem and avoid what happens in many organizations


where people waste their entire 60 minutes building solutions


to the wrong problems.


## 第 467 页


When you are trawling for requirements, much of what you hear


is a customer’s or other stakeholder’s idea for a solution,


but not a description of the underlying problem to be solved.


This could be a terrific solution, but more likely it is a


solution limited by the stakeholder’s experience and


imagination. Moreover, as yet, you and your stakeholders have


no idea whether it is solving the right problem. Your task as


the requirements discoverer is to interpret what your


stakeholder is saying and make the necessary abstractions to


uncover its essence.


Separate the essence of the problem from any


proposed solution.


How the work physically accomplishes its functionality—the


technology, the instruments, the computers, the people, and


so on—is its implementation, as illustrated in Figure 16.1.


## 第 468 页


![embedded_p468_77.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p468_77.jpeg)


Figure 16.1 The essence usually lies buried under its means


of implementation. The task is to strip away the physical


artifacts to uncover the essential problem.


For example, you might be streaming your music, playing music


stored on your phone, playing a vinyl record, have the radio


## 第 469 页


on, or be at a live concert. The essence is the same: You’re


listening to music. Music is still music no matter how you


produce or reproduce it. You arrive at the essence of the


problem by ignoring the current or proposed implementation,


and underneath that you can find its essence, which is the


fundamental reason that the work exists.


“Perfection is achieved, not when there is


nothing more to add, but when there is nothing


left to take away.”—Antoine de Saint-Exupéry,


Wind, Sand and Stars (Reynal & Hitchcock, 1939)


There are several reasons for finding the essence. The


first, and most important, reason is that you solve the right


problem: This is obvious but often overlooked. The second


reason is that finding the essence means you avoid the


presumed solution. Unfortunately, people tend to express


their needs in technological terms: “I need a content


management system”; “I need a mobile device app”; “I need


a drop-down menu”. These presumed solutions are often


“flavor of the month, bright shiny object” solutions that


might solve the problem but are far more likely to


disappoint.


## 第 470 页


The essence exists regardless of any


technological implementation.


Ask Why—Again, and Again, and Again


You can often reverse engineer the essence from a


technological implementation by asking why repeatedly until


you arrive at a statement that is clear of any technology and


is the essence of the problem.


Asking why is standard practice that is


ingrained, or should be, into every discoverer of


requirements.


Asking why is standard practice that is ingrained, or should


be, into every discoverer of requirements. It is probably the


most effective technique for getting to the essence of the


problem. Some people say that you should ask why five times.


This might get you the right answer, but if repeated too


frequently, will get your face slapped. We prefer to think of


it as asking why as many times as you need to until you


arrive at an essential answer and are satisfied that you have


discovered the right problem.


For example, consider this story we came across:


## 第 471 页


As a university professor


I want to search for a book by title


So that I can check its price and availability


Let’s ask why a few times.


I want to search for a book by title


Why does he want to search? “Search” is a solution to


something; it’s not the problem. Why does he search? Because


he wants to find. Finding something is the real business


problem. Can you find it without searching? Sure, but that’s


not the point. Let’s go on with uncovering the essence:


Why does he want to find a book?


He’s putting together a reading list for his students.


Why does he want to search by title?


He explains that’s what he’s always done. But that implies


that he already knows which book and does not leave any scope


for finding new books.


Why is he looking for a particular book?


## 第 472 页


Because he wants it to be part of his reading list.


Why does he want to check the price?


Because the university sets a book budget for courses.


Why does he think the price he finds is the price students


will pay?


(Students might find a secondhand copy of the book or be


given one.)


Why does the university’s budget apply?


The university wants students to be able to afford the books


they need for their courses. This means that it’s necessary


to limit the amount of money students have to pay.


Why does he check the availability of the book?


Because students have to be able to buy it.


Does “availability” mean available everywhere?


Or just the place the professor is searching?


By now it is obvious that the professor has not told you the


real business need. So, let’s jump right to what the


## 第 473 页


essential story should have been. You can see the difference


between the professor’s presumed solution and the essential


problem that we arrived at by asking why:


As a university professor


I can assemble a reading list for my students


So that the list contains my preferred books, the books are


available, and the students can acquire the books within the


university’s budget for my course


Compare the essence with the solution given originally. You


can imagine how the solution for the essence would bring far


more value that the originally-proposed solution.


Asking why works in many situations. You are trying to get


past the presumed solution, past people telling you how they


think the problem should be solved, to get to the real


business problem.


Technological fossils are technological solutions that have


been part of a system for many years, and yet the reason for


them has long since disappeared. For example, look at your


credit cards. Do any of them have raised numbers? Why are the


numbers raised? The embossed numbers were introduced to be


## 第 474 页


used with carbon-paper card imprint machines. You probably


don’t know what those are, because they disappeared 25 to 30


years ago when chip-and-pin cards were introduced. And yet,


raised numbers still seem to be a requirement for some card


issuers.


Technological fossils are things that are mistakenly accepted


as essence. Part of finding the essence of the problem is to


look for these fossils in your customer’s organization. You


can uncover them by asking why. If you don’t get an answer


that relates to essence, you probably have a fossil.


The moral of this story is that for any piece of technology—


no matter how beguiling, state of the art, and attractive it


is—you must abstract out the technology and see its


underlying essential purpose. Or, to paraphrase President


John F. Kennedy, “Ask not what your technology can do for


you, ask what you’re trying to do with the technology.”


Referred Pain


“Referred pain” is a medical term. It concerns pain that is


felt in one part of the body, but the cause of the pain lies


elsewhere. The most common example is sciatica. The symptom


is a pain felt in one or both legs, but the problem is a


## 第 475 页


slipped disk pinching a nerve in the spine. Treating the leg


will do nothing to eliminate the underlying problem.


Take the example of referred pain shown in Figure 16.2. The


staff at a large organization are complaining that they are


on hold for far too long before they can speak to the


internal help desk. You could attack this problem by hiring


more people to man the help desk. You could eliminate waiting


on hold by implementing a register-and-call-back system. You


could play calming music for the caller.


![embedded_p475_78.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p475_78.jpeg)


## 第 476 页


Figure 16.2 Referred pain. The symptom of the problem is


with the help desk, but the cause of the problem lies


elsewhere.


These solutions address the symptom and leave the cause of


the problem untouched—they are treating the referred pain.


The root cause of the problem has nothing to do with the help


desk; it is with people needing the help desk. By


investigating why staff need help, you could, or should, be


able to improve the organization’s systems. By making its


systems easier to use and more comprehensible, you reduce the


need for help. Perhaps your investigation uncovers a lack of


training. If the staff were better trained, they would be


more productive, need less help, and, as a bonus, not waste


their time on hold waiting for the help desk. Treating


symptoms—playing music, in this example—without


understanding and addressing the root cause is only


superficially effective at best. Before you can solve the


problem, you need to uncover the essence of the problem.


Disguised Problems


Sometimes problems are deeply disguised. Consider this


example: Store managers at a supermarket chain are concerned


with the age of their point-of-sale (POS) system. Some of


## 第 477 页


them say that customers have been complaining about long


checkout lines (see Figure 16.3). The IT department has


suggested developing a new POS system.


![embedded_p477_79.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p477_79.jpeg)


Figure 16.3 What causes long supermarket checkout lines?


What is the disguised problem here? The IT department seems


to be solving the problem that it wants to solve. It is keen


to develop a new POS system, but it is far from clear that a


new system would do much to alleviate the real problem.


Why would it not? The POS system is old, but does that


necessarily mean it is slow? And would that be the only cause


of long checkout lines? Probably not. Consider these possible


causes of long checkout lines.


• There are not enough checkout registers.


• There are not enough checkout clerks.


• The checkout clerks are too slow.


## 第 478 页


• The barcode scanners malfunction frequently.


• The people hired to pack the customers’ bags are not fast


enough or are in the parking lot fetching abandoned shopping


carts.


• The design of the checkout area is slowing things down. (We


have observed a checkout line where the shopping carts were


too wide to fit through the checkout, causing shoppers to


carry their goods to the belt.)


• The lines are long but fast moving. This still qualifies as


“long checkout lines” even if it does not inconvenience


customers.


• The environment in which shoppers wait in line is


unpleasant, which causes them to think they spend a lot of


time in line.


• There are sweets displayed near the lines, and parents have


trouble restraining their kids from grabbing the sweets. This


kind of annoyance makes any wait seem longer.


• People in individual lines always think that other lines


are moving faster than theirs. This might lead shoppers to


complain of “long lines.”


## 第 479 页


This list could be longer, but let’s stop there. Admittedly,


the list is speculative, but it points out that until the


real cause of the “long lines” is known, it would be folly


to spend money rushing into developing a new POS system. The


right problem to solve might well still be hidden, and the


right solution to the right problem might well be far cheaper


than a new POS system.


Suppose you interviewed the supermarket’s customers and


found that “long checkout lines” means people perceive that


the lines move too slowly. You might solve this quite easily


by having one feeder line that branches to individual


checkouts as they become available. This system of queuing


appears to be faster because people are moving more quickly,


and it might make people stop complaining. It would be worth


trying—the cost would be little more than a few retractable


queue barriers. If complaints lessened where it was tried,


then you’re on your way toward knowing the real problem.


You might also consider approaching the problem laterally.


People are complaining about the time spent checking out, so


why not consider slowing it down and have one lane designated


as the “slow lane”?


## 第 480 页


The objective is to cater to people—sometimes older people—


who feel pressured once they get to the checkout to do it as


quickly as possible. Some people are worried that they are


“in the way” and want to avoid keeping people behind them


in the queue waiting. Some of them are lonely and want to


take as long as they possibly can to prolong the conversation


at the checkout. Customers for this lane might also be people


with an impairment that slows them down, people who suffer


anxiety attacks, parents with several young children to


control who want extra time, or people who simply don’t care


how long checkout takes and welcome a leisurely approach.


By having a dedicated slow lane, staffing it with somebody


who is sympathetic to the people using it, and warning people


in a hurry that this is the slow lane, you might remove other


sources of friction and cut down on the number of complaints.


It is worthwhile spending a little time exploring a solution


such as this.


Without observing the situation, interviewing real customers,


and unmasking the disguised problem—the essence of the


problem—any money spent is likely to be wasted.


Review


## 第 481 页


Getting to the essence of the problem is quite possibly the


most valuable thing you can do for your project. By scraping


away the presumed solution, the existing solution, the bright


shiny technology being proposed, you get to the underlying


essence.


This underlying essence is the real problem. It exists


regardless of how anybody chooses to implement it. The


essence is the right problem. That’s the one you have to


solve.


Everything in your project relies on solving the right


problem. This sounds incredibly obvious, but the thousands of


development projects that fail each year attest to the fact


that this is not always observed.


However, by understanding essence, by asking why enough


times, by looking past the assumed solutions, you can ensure


that your project solves the right problem and delivers the


right solution.


Resources


Essential Systems Analysis by Steve McMenamin and John Palmer


(Yourdon Press, 1984). This is the book that introduced the


concept of essence. Whether you know about this book or not,


## 第 482 页


it has been hugely influential in the field of business


analysis.


Critical Thinking: A Concise Guide, 3rd Edition by Tracy


Bowell and Gary Kemp (Routledge, 2009). Critical thinking is


about challenging and questioning information that is


presented to you instead of just accepting it. This is an


important skill for a business analyst trying to get to the


essence of the problem.


The Root Cause Analysis Handbook: A Simplified Approach to


Identifying, Correcting, and Reporting Workplace Errors by


Max Ammerman (Productivity Press, 1998). Understanding the


root causes of a problem is another way of getting to the


essence of it. This book presents a walk-through example that


illustrates root cause analysis and shows how to implement


it.


The Critical Thinking Community, The Foundation for Critical


Thinking (https://www.criticalthinking.org). This online


resource offers articles, courses, podcasts, and teaching


materials on critical thinking.


Khan Academy (https://www.khanacademy.org). Khan Academy


provides excellent free courses on a number of subjects—


## 第 483 页


math, science, and so on. In this case, we are suggesting


their critical thinking courses.


## 第 484 页


Chapter 17. Business Events and Business
Use Cases


Business events are events that are significant to the piece


of your customer’s business that you are now studying.


Business events are also significant to requirements


discovery because whenever a business event happens, the


business must respond to it.


The response to a business event is a business use case or


BUC. The BUC is a collection of the activities and data


needed to satisfy the instigator of the business event. If


the business event is a customer wanting to listen to a piece


of music on a streaming service, then the response—the BUC—


is to locate the music and stream it along with some


recommendations for future listening.


You are interested in business use cases because when you are


building prototypes, trawling, discovering the requirements,


specifying, and implementing, BUCs are the most convenient


and consistent unit of functionality.


Business Events


## 第 485 页


You met business events back in Chapter 7, Business Events,


when we were discussing the Project Blastoff; however, they


are so important to what you are doing that it will be


helpful to have a short recap here.


As Figure 17.1 illustrates, most business events are


triggered in the outside world. That’s where your business


customers, other computer systems, and other organizations


trigger business events. Because they start outside the


problem space, we call these external events.


## 第 486 页


![embedded_p486_80.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p486_80.jpeg)


Figure 17.1 An example of a business event. The business


event happens the moment the plane reaches a point where the


pilot should request permission to land. The pilot then


radios Air Traffic Control for permission. The response to


this incoming request is that the controller arranges a


## 第 487 页


landing slot and radios the outgoing data back to the pilot.


(Note that this is very much a simplification of what


actually happens with ATC.)


Another type of business event happens because of the passage


of time. It’s called a time-triggered event, and it happens


when a certain date is reached, a certain time of day is


reached, or a certain amount of time has elapsed since


something else happened. Figure 17.2 shows an example of a


time-triggered business event and its BUC.


## 第 488 页


![embedded_p488_81.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p488_81.jpeg)


Figure 17.2 A time-triggered business event. This one is


initiated when a predetermined date is reached. In this case,


this organization sends customers their monthly credit card


statements on the 15th of every month. It does not matter


whether the statements are sent via mail, email, or a link.


The response to the event Monthly statement due date has


## 第 489 页


arrived is to retrieve the customers’ transactions for the


month and collect them into statements, which are sent to the


customers.


Conditional business events, the third type of event, happen


when a condition is met. For example, most countries have a


law that requires banks to report any personal deposits


exceeding a specified amount. Let’s say the amount is


$10,000, and one day Ron Slick deposits $50,000 into his


account. Ron might have been up to no good, and the tax


people would like to know about it. Because Ron’s deposit


exceeded the $10,000 reporting condition, it triggers a


conditional business event, Report deposit to the tax


authority. Or suppose that your point-of-sale (POS) system


deducts each sale from inventory, and during the processing


of a sale it detects that the number of blue jeans in


inventory has fallen below the allowed threshold. In other


words, a condition has been met, and this triggers the


response that will request more jeans be brought up from the


stockroom.


What Is a Business Event?


We will be using the term “business event” a lot over the


course of this book, so you should be clear on what it means.


## 第 490 页


A business event is a happening—a time has been reached, a


condition has been met, or in the case of external events, an


adjacent system decides something. For example, in Figure


17.3, you see someone deciding to insure her car. Of course,


if she wants to get the car insured, she must notify the


insurance company. She does this using the triggering data


flow Insurance Application. It is called a “triggering data


flow” because—fairly obviously—it is made up of data, and


it triggers a response from the insurance company: setting up


the policy, arranging premium payments, and so on.


## 第 491 页


![embedded_p491_82.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p491_82.jpeg)


Figure 17.3 The business event happens when the owner


decides to insure her car.


Note that the business event happened the moment she decided


to insure the car. We are talking about business analysis


here, so as an analyst you must be inquisitive and ask, What


was going through her mind at that moment? For example, how


did she pick the insurance company? Was it random, or was it


after carefully comparing the policies and rates of different


## 第 492 页


companies? Go further with your analytical role and ask if


you (actually your client’s organization) can do that for


her. Extending the work by offering a comparison site could


be very good for your customer’s business. There are


probably other possible opportunities.


Consider buying a book. Suppose you are in a brick-and-mortar


bookstore (they still exist, and most are thriving). You’ve


picked a book off the shelf, and you decide you want to buy


it. That moment of decision is the business event. Of course,


for this business event to mean anything you must inform the


bookstore that you wish to buy the book.


It is important to see the business event and the


triggering data flow as separate (but connected) things.


The business event is what happens; the triggering data flow


is what the business needs to learn in order to respond to


the event.


Giving business events a good name is helpful. The general


way of doing this is to form the name from the adjacent


system name plus what happened. For example, in Figure 17.3,


the name would be Car owner wants to insure her car.


## 第 493 页


You would normally determine the business events and list


them during the Project Blastoff. This is so that you have a


better understanding of all the pieces within the scope of


your task. To make the development project more responsive to


your client’s needs, you prioritize the events. We talked


about how to do this prioritization in Chapter 8,


Prioritizing the Business Events.


Let’s assume you have a prioritized list of the business


events that are part of your problem space. Remember, you


might have assigned the priority based on some combination of


factors that add up to the best value. So, let’s start


trawling your most valuable events.


The Business Use Case


The business use case—the BUC—is probably the most


convenient chunk of functionality to trawl. It is not an


arbitrary unit but is clearly delineated. It has a known and


defined starting point—when the incoming data arrives at the


edge of the business—and a defined ending point—when all


the appropriate processing has been done, stored data has


been retrieved and/or stored, and any needed data has been


sent to the outside world. This is illustrated in Figure


17.4.


## 第 494 页


![embedded_p494_83.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p494_83.jpeg)


Figure 17.4 The response to any business event is a business


use case. The BUC is a collection of activities that process


the incoming data and continue to do so until all the


activities that make up the BUC have completed their tasks,


all the stored data has been retrieved and/or stored, and any


outgoing data has been dispatched.


A business use case is the response to a business event. It


is always a collection of identifiable activities and the


data that is needed by the activities or stored by the


activities. Because it is this collection of activities and


data, you can say that it is a collection of the requirements


needed to respond to the business event.


## 第 495 页


The business use case is a collection of the


requirements needed to respond to the business


event.


You can readily isolate a business use case because it has no


processing connections to other BUCs; the only overlap


between BUCs is their stored data. Therefore, different


analysts can investigate different parts of the problem space


without the need for constant communication between them.


This isolation of each business use case makes it easier to


identify the stakeholders who are experts in that part of the


work, and they can (with your help) describe it precisely and


in detail.


Business events are known to the stakeholders (they’ll know


what they are without necessarily knowing the term “business


event”), and they can show you how the organization


processes the BUCs. For example, it would be easy enough to


find someone in your favorite bookshop who can take you


through the process of selling a book, or someone in your


insurance company who can show you how the company processes


a claim. You can sometimes see the activities within the BUC,


and there is always a stakeholder or two who can describe


them for you. You are using the BUC as a guide to find your


## 第 496 页


way around the customer’s world and identify the pieces that


functionally belong together to support a cohesive piece of


the business policy.


Trawling the BUCs


You are trawling the BUC to discover the real business


problem and to discover the requirements for a future


solution. Subsequent chapters discuss how you can trawl. For


the moment, we are establishing what you are doing. Consider


Figure 17.5.


![embedded_p496_84.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p496_84.jpeg)


## 第 497 页


Figure 17.5 The business analyst and the customer select


from the prioritized list of business events. They trawl each


business event’s BUC. The output can be any recording of the


BUC’s functionality.


We must stress that you get the best results if you trawl one


business use case at a time. You are doing several things


when you’re trawling:


• Establishing that the BUC contributes to solving the right


business problem


• Establishing that the BUC is the desired response to the


business event


• Discussing the BUC with the stakeholders to explore whether


there is a better response


• Ensuring that any ready-made solutions work correctly


within the BUC


• Discovering the requirements or stories for the BUC


The output from the Trawling activity is input into the


Design and Development activities. (Figure 17.5 shows how the


Trawling activity fits into the overall process.) The record


## 第 498 页


of the BUC is a statement of what the response is to be. When


you design and develop, you decide how it is to be.


The Desired Future BUC


Sometimes you have a piece of your customer’s business that


does not exist at the moment, but the customer wants it to


exist. Or possibly it does exist, but the customer wants any


future solution to be different. In this case, you need the


people with their vision of the future to describe what they


have in mind.


This works when you start with the business events and for


each of them, you model what their desired future


incarnation is to be. When the intention is to use ready-


made solutions to be part or all of the solution for this


BUC, then the ready-made, naturally enough, becomes part of


any model you build of the desired future state. However, you


need to tread a fine line between using ready-mades and


leaping into a presumed solution. Your models of the future


state should ensure that you are getting to the essence of


the problem.


Figure 17.6 shows the requirements discoverer using a


storyboard with the customer.


## 第 499 页


![embedded_p499_85.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p499_85.jpeg)


Figure 17.6 The customer describes how he wants the future


BUC to work. The business analyst is recording the desired


future state using a storyboard. Note that the analyst is


modeling one BUC. This BUC is the response to the business


event Customer wants to open a bank account.


Using a storyboard to illustrate the problem space allows


your customer to confirm the situation and discuss whether


this is the best approach to solve the problem, and whether


it provides value to the organization.


## 第 500 页


The desired future BUC is a significant achievement. It is


for this BUC that you write your requirements or stories. We


have a lot to say about requirements and stories later, but


for the moment, the emphasis is on establishing a coherent


partitioning and framework for your requirements and stories.


Prototyping and BUCs


In earlier chapters, we looked at the idea of using


prototypes to help uncover the real problem and some of the


requirements for a future solution. The intention of the


prototyping activity is to model the business use cases one


at a time. You won’t necessarily model all of them, and


sometimes it is convenient to combine BUCs, but your


analytical task will be more focused if each of your


prototypes concentrates on a single BUC.


The advantage to you is that you know the start and end


points for your prototype. This would be clear if you had


used, say, a process model for your prototype, as illustrated


in Figure 17.7. The starting event (the circle on the left of


the model) represents the business event. The flow of


activities makes up the business use case, and the end state


is when all the data has been retrieved and stored, and


outgoing messages sent.


## 第 501 页


![embedded_p501_86.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p501_86.jpeg)


Figure 17.7 A process model is used to prototype a candidate


solution. The advantage of using BUCs here is that the start


and end points are very clearly defined.


Describing the BUCs


You need to describe the functionality of the BUC. This is so


that you and your stakeholders can arrive at a recorded


agreement on what the BUC has to do in order to make the


correct response to the business event.


The BUC description contains the processes, the data, the


decisions, and the outcome of the BUC. You can describe these


in a number of ways. For example, the process model shown in


Figure 17.7 has four activities. These are chunks of


functionality, and the names of the activities are sufficient


to describe what the BUC does.


## 第 502 页


Alternatively, you could use a scenario to describe the BUC.


A scenario is a list of steps, and each one is some piece of


functionality that contributes to achieving the processing


goal of the BUC. A simple example is to take each of the


activities of the process model shown in Figure 17.7 and


arrange them in a numbered list. Normally, your scenarios


would be a bit meatier, but you get the idea. In Chapter 20,


Scenarios, we’ll look in more detail at scenarios.


You can also use stories (coming up soon), data models, and


almost anything you wish as long as your description sets


down the functionality needed to achieve the objective of the


business use case.


Review


Business events and business use cases allow you to carve out


cohesive pieces of the problem space for study, modeling, and


prototyping. By coming to an agreement with your customer


about the functionality to be done by each of the BUCs, you


come to an understanding of the optimal solution to support


that functionality. And it is from these BUCs that you write


the requirements.


## 第 503 页


If you are using ready-made solutions, they too respond to


business events. Additionally, they must respond to your


customer’s business events in a way the customer finds


acceptable. There is no real need to trawl the internal


workings of the ready-made solutions, but your responsibility


is to ensure that the input and output data closely match the


needs of your customer’s business.


Business events give you an external view of the


customer’s business. This is because the business events


are happenings, and many of them happen in the systems that


surround your problem space. You are not relying on how it


currently happens to be partitioned internally, or on


someone’s idea of how it might be partitioned in the future,


or “features” or some other arbitrary partition. Instead,


you chunk the problem according to the most important view of


it: how the outside world sees it. This means that you end up


with a solution that is more responsive to the real demands


of the outside world, and thereby more valuable to its owner.


You will probably go on to implement your solution one BUC at


a time. There is more on implementation in subsequent


chapters, but for the moment, it is useful for you to have


the necessary functionality grouped into BUCs.


## 第 504 页


The chapters that follow discuss some of the approaches you


can use to trawl your BUCs.


Resources


Object-Oriented Software Engineering: A Use Case Driven


Approach by Ivar Jacobson (Addison-Wesley, 1992). This book


introduced the idea of use cases. We have modified


Jacobson’s approach considerably, marrying use cases to


business events, to make them more useful for business


analysis.


Essential Systems Analysis by Steve McMenamin and John Palmer


(Yourdon Press, 1984). McMenamin and Palmer originated the


idea of using business events and event partitioning for


analysis work. They referred to them as “events.” We have


called them “business events” to make the intention more


meaningful. They also introduced the idea of essence. Sadly,


this book is out of print.


Business Analysis Agility: Solve the Real Problem, Deliver


Real Value by Suzanne Robertson and James Robertson (Addison-


Wesley, 2018). This delves into finding the essence of the


problem, and then designing a suitable business system to


implement the essence.


## 第 505 页


Chapter 18. The Brown Cow Model


The Brown Cow model is a way of organizing your thinking.


When you’re trawling the problem space, you are working with


your customers, your stakeholders, and your team and


examining different aspects of the business problem and its


solution. The Brown Cow model is a way of compartmentalizing


these aspects so that everybody concerned is clear on exactly


what is being discussed and what each aspect contributes to


understanding the problem and the solution.


Previously, we looked at the essence of the problem. The


essence is an abstraction that removes any physical


implementation devices to reveal the underlying policy of the


business problem. It would be advantageous to have an orderly


way of keeping these two viewpoints—how something is done


and the essence of what is done—separate but linked. This is


the role of the Brown Cow model.


1


How Now, Brown Cow?


1


In case you were wondering, the model gets its name from


the phrase “How now, brown cow?” This is used in English


elocution lessons to teach students their rounded vowel


sounds. It isn’t clear when or where the phrase originated,


## 第 506 页


but “how now” is an archaic greeting. How-Now is the first


quadrant of the Brown Cow model, and thus gave the model its


name.


Figure 18.1 shows the Brown Cow model. There are two axes.


The horizontal axis divides What from How, and the vertical


axis divides the current situation, or Now, from the proposed


solution, which we will call Future. Each quadrant of the


model focuses on a single viewpoint. This is particularly


useful during team discussions when different people are


talking about different aspects of the problem. Use the model


to refocus and help people understand each other. You get


people to focus with questions like “Are we talking about


what’s happening with the customer’s problem at the moment,


or what she wants to have in the future?” “Is this supposed


to be a technological view of the solution, or an essential


view?”


## 第 507 页


![embedded_p507_87.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p507_87.jpeg)


Figure 18.1 The Brown Cow model showing the four viewpoints


of the problem space


Sometimes people talk about “As is” and “To be.” Taking


only those two views is inadvisable because they ignore the


important difference between the physical and the essential


thinking about the problem. “As is” and “To be” encourage


## 第 508 页


rushing from one solution to another and discourage creative


thinking. They ignore what “could be.”


How-Now


Start with the bottom-left quadrant of the model shown in


Figure 18.1. This is the How-Now quadrant, and as its name


suggests, it shows how things are happening at the


moment[md[or, if you like, the current implementation of


your customer’s business.


This How-Now model of your customer’s business shows the


physical devices used to process the business activities—


things like the computers and software (let’s think of
