software as a physical thing for the moment), the people,


possibly their departments, transportation devices, machines,


and so on. The aim of such a model is to establish a


baseline, to ensure that you are studying the correct part of


your customer’s business, and to have the stakeholders


recognize their work, as illustrated in Figure 18.2.


## 第 509 页


![embedded_p509_88.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p509_88.jpeg)


Figure 18.2 The analyst and the customer establish the


current technological way of working.


Do not spend more time than necessary modeling in this


quadrant. Your aim is to get enough of an understanding of


## 第 510 页


the current situation to be able to move on. This is, after


all, a view of something you are planning to change.


Do not spend more time than necessary on modeling


the How-Now quadrant.


What-Now


Moving above the line, you get to the What-Now quadrant. The


word “what” means just that: what the business is doing,


and not how it is doing it. In other words, this is the


essence of the current problem space.


If you took the How-Now view and abstracted it by stripping


away all its technological devices, you’d arrive at its


essence. You would see the things that have to be done no


matter how they are done or who does them. This view, the


What-Now view, enables you and your customer to see the real


business being conducted at the moment, without the


distraction of its technology.


It’s necessary to have a clear view of the current essence


because a lot of it must be included in any future solution.


Many development projects are renewal projects—an old,


tired, creaking solution is being replaced by a new and


## 第 511 页


hopefully better one. In this case, you should consider


minimal models of the How-Now view, only enough to help you


discover its essence—the What-Now—of the problem space.


This view gives you the underlying business policy and


business rules of the current solution.


There is often a realistic proposal that the future solution


will include ready-made components or that the entire


solution is a ready-made one. (Ready-made components can be


off-the-shelf [OTS] solutions, software as a service [SaaS],


open source, or something else. The point is that you don’t


build it yourself; it is made for you.) Having a clear and


agreed-upon understanding of the current essence is vital if


you are to select the right ready-mades. Any future ready-


made solution must be capable of processing most or all of


the current essence. You allow, of course, for reasonable


customization and configuration of the ready-made (we looked


at this in Chapter 12, Ready-Made Solutions), or reasonable


modifications to the current business processes. But the


starting point for selecting a ready-made solution should


always be the current essence.


We’ve started talking about the future, so let’s move


there.


## 第 512 页


Future-What


Although many projects are renewal projects, it is highly


unlikely that anyone would just take what they have at the


moment and reimplement it using a new technology. Admittedly,


there are some projects in which the objective was to rewrite


a suite of old COBOL applications in a modern language


(younger readers will have to ask their parents what COBOL


is), but they were usually done because there are very few


COBOL programmers today; they retired long ago.


Often, your customer wants what she has now along with some


enhancements and some alterations. Moving away from the What-


Now view and adding your customer’s changes gives you the


Future-What.


The Future-What is the most important quadrant of


the model.


Note the name: The Future-What is the essence to be


implemented. Without seeing the essence of the new business,


you risk any future solution not solving the right business


problem. This means the Future-What is the most important


quadrant of the model. You might choose to start with this


one and revert to the Now views if you need to. If you have a


## 第 513 页


good handle on the idea of essence, then we urge you to start


with this one.


If your project is a greenfield project—one starting


completely from scratch, with no legacy solutions—then


Future-What is the place to start your planning. You need to


start with What. There is little point in thinking about


solutions (How) before you know the essential business to be


carried out.


If using a ready-made solution has been mandated, then it


should not be thought of as technology, but treated as


essence. This means that any ready-mades you plan to use show


up in this essential, Future-What view.


The two What or essential views involve “above-the-line


thinking.” (The line being the horizontal one diving How


from What.) In the abstract, essential world, you are


unconstrained by technology and are free to imagine what


could be. Here is where you challenge the existing policies,


the work practices, the “but we’ve always done it this


way” mindset. Here is where you use creativity and


innovation to explore new and different ways to achieve the


organization’s goals.


## 第 514 页


We looked at deriving innovative solutions in Chapter 13,


Creative Candidate Solutions. The creative techniques that


can be used when prototyping are entirely appropriate when


moving into the Future-What view.


We urge you to consider above-the-line thinking as an


opportunity to bring about a better piece of business for


your customer. Time is usually a scarce resource on projects,


but spending time on the Future-What viewpoint is never time


wasted.


Future-How


The Future-How shows the technology and people (and any other


devices) you plan to use to bring the essence into the


physical world. You are moving from the abstract to the


tangible. You are showing how the business will work in the


future.


This quadrant usually overlaps with the work of the solutions


architect, and sometimes the enterprise architect. You are


treading in their domain when you start to allocate the


essence to the available processors. Those architects can be


very helpful with this view.


## 第 515 页


Future-How is the technological view of the solution you plan


to build. It shows the software or hardware components, the


people, and any other device you plan to use. This is the


view that is the basis for your detailed requirements. And


because you based your future implementation on the essence


of the problem, you can be confident that your requirements


are the right ones.


How to Use the Brown Cow Model


First, the Brown Cow is intended to be used as a thinking


framework and not a procedure. We have spoken about the


quadrants in a sequence, but the intention is not to


slavishly build a model for each quadrant. If yours is a


replacement project, then there might be some advantage to


looking at each quadrant, but only if you are getting some


value from each view. Otherwise, jump in and out of the


quadrants wherever you need that viewpoint.


Some teams keep the skeleton of this model in a visible


location so that team members can refer to the viewpoint they


are discussing. When you build models—process models,


prototypes, scenarios, and so on—it can be useful to tag


them with the view they portray.


## 第 516 页


You don’t have to build elaborate models. A list of business


events and their outcomes is often enough to serve as an


essential model for the whole of the problem space. The


details of the processing of each business use case can be


done later.


Additionally, you don’t have to build models at all. Brown


Cow is a tool to allow you to compartmentalize your thinking,


or to direct your thinking to the quadrant that is most


useful to you and your team at the time. How you record your


thinking is a choice that you and your team make. Models are


convenient, but whichever form works for you is the right


one.


Prototypes usually take the Future-How view—they are


solutions, after all. You should derive the essence from your


prototypes to ensure that you are solving the right problem.


Prototypes are meant to be disposable, so not much harm is


done if you discover that one of yours does not satisfy the


required essence.


Now the bad news: Some projects start with the Future-How


and never leave it. When you start in this quadrant you’re


starting with a presumed solution. There is no reference to


the actual business rules and policy that the solution must


## 第 517 页


incorporate. There is every possibility that this presumed


solution is solving the wrong problem.


We strongly suggest in these situations to take the proposed


solution and extract its essence. In other words, you reverse


engineer it into the Future-What, as illustrated in Figure


18.3. By doing so, you can see whether the presumed solution


covers the complete essential business policy.


## 第 518 页


![embedded_p518_89.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p518_89.jpeg)


Figure 18.3 Reverse engineering the essence from a presumed


solution


## 第 519 页


We suggest that you capture the essence of the proposed


solution with a list of business events and their outcomes.


You examine these outcomes and ask if they contribute to the


goals you established in the Project Blastoff. You might also


build a context diagram of the proposed solution and compare


that with the one you built during the blastoff. Now you can


have an informed conversation with your stakeholders and


resolve the discrepancies.


Review


The Brown Cow model is a framework for thinking. Each


quadrant represents a different viewpoint of the same problem


space or solution space. The advantage to you is that you can


clearly differentiate between the views you’re taking at any


given time.


We must stress that the viewpoints are not intended to be


taken in a sequence where it is not practical or effective to


do so. However, in some cases, you may choose to work


methodically through the four viewpoints, starting with the


How-Now and ending with the Future-How. But this would be


because you need to untangle a complicated situation, and


separating the viewpoints helps everybody have a clear vision


of what’s happening.


## 第 520 页


It is, of course, not necessary to build models (or some


other representation) for each quadrant. You might choose to


do that for only one or two of the segments. The intention of


the Brown Cow is to aid your thinking about the problem.


Whether you commit your thinking to a diagram is up to you.


Whatever you do, it is a matter of necessity to think


clearly, and being able to separate your viewpoints is very


much a part of that clarity.


The emphasis in this book is on solving the right problem.


Being able to separate viewpoints, and in particular,


separate the essential—the what—from the implementation—


the how—gives you a much better chance of seeing the real


problem. This means you spend a lot of your time thinking


“above the line.” This is the horizontal line on the model


that separates the What from the How, or the essence from the


implementation.


Brown Cow is a thinking tool, and so should be a vital part


of your trawling activities.


Resources


You can see Suzanne explain the Brown Cow model at


https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ckWaVRkM3dI&t=239s.


## 第 521 页


Chapter 19. Workshops


Workshops are one of the most commonly used trawling


techniques. A workshop will typically involve you, the


business analyst, and the right combination of specialized


stakeholders, all of whom have an interest in the solution.


Workshops can cover any scope, but you will probably find


that they are particularly helpful when you concentrate on


one business use case. We discussed before how the business


use case, the BUC, is the collection of functionality and


data that respond to the business event. A workshop is


particularly useful for the stakeholders to discuss what they


want and need this BUC to be.


Workshops bring about synergy—interaction that produces


results that are greater than the sum of the results


individuals could produce on their own. The participants work


together to come to a consensus on what is needed and wanted.


This synergy between the participants also brings ownership


and engagement. When people feel they have contributed—in


any way whatsoever—they have a stake in the success of the


outcome. If your workshop is about a solution, then the


participants own that solution and will now do what’s needed


to make it succeed.


## 第 522 页


Most of all, workshops are a time for exploration and


discovery. They should be freewheeling affairs where


everybody contributes and all ideas are exposed for better or


worse until the optimal result is achieved.


BUC Workshops


Let us assume that you have called a workshop to explore the


required functionality of a business use case and to discover


some or most of its requirements. Of course, you hold


workshops for other purposes, but as we are concerned with


requirements discovery, let’s focus on that kind of


workshop. Figure 19.1 illustrates such a workshop.


## 第 523 页


![embedded_p523_90.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p523_90.jpeg)


Figure 19.1 The workshop records the proposed functionality


of the business use case using models, scenarios, sketched


prototypes, or other means.


Outcomes


Your workshop should focus on outcomes. One outcome should


be an imaginative and functionally correct BUC description


## 第 524 页


that is ready for further exploration for its requirements


and eventual development.


There is also the outcome of the BUC. That is, when it is


implemented, the BUC produces a result that is beneficial to


the organization and/or the customer. Another outcome of the


BUC is that it works correctly within the constraints of the


customer’s organization. That is, it must not disrupt


(within reason) other business processes. A little bit of


systemic thinking can be useful here.


Sometimes you do not have access to the real customers to get


their needs. In this case, you would use a persona. We


discussed personas in Chapter 6, Customer Segments, where we


described a persona as “an invented personality; an


imaginary but nevertheless archetypical representative of a


customer segment.”


When the team has built a persona, the team members are


familiar with the attributes of the persona and use that


knowledge to discuss how the persona would react to some of


the suggestions. What would the persona expect from this BUC?


Would the persona accept it?


## 第 525 页


Your authors know of teams that have a physical


representation of their persona in their workshops. The most


striking was the team that had a life-size cardboard cutout


with a photo of their persona (found on the internet) as its


face. It was slightly surreal when team members talked to the


persona. It was also effective.


Regardless of your representation of the persona, the outcome


of the BUC being discussed by your workshop must be that it


works correctly, satisfies the customer’s (in this case, the


persona’s) needs, is beneficial, and is an attractive


business solution. A well-run workshop should be able to


achieve all of these goals.


Outputs


Along with the outcome, the workshop produces outputs. In


Figure 19.1, the team is writing a scenario. Scenarios are


coming up in the next chapter, but in the meantime, they are


a step-by-step description of the BUC’s functionality: Step


1, do this; Step 2, do that; Step 3, do something else; and


so on.


You might also build a process model (coming up in a few


chapters). This is a graphical representation of the


functionality of the BUC. There are other models, and they


## 第 526 页


will appear in subsequent chapters. It doesn’t really matter


which model you use as long as all the meeting participants


understand it.


One other useful output from the workshop is a collection of


business rules. Business rules are the internal “laws” that


govern the activities of the organization. These will be


cited by the appropriate participants and should form part of


your requirements repository. Business rules are focused on


the organization. They originate internally or are imposed by


external organizations—governments, regulators, and so on—


and any solution you build must comply with them. Many of the


requirements for your solution are derived from the business


rules, as obviously, it is a requirement that business rules


are followed.


Non-functional requirements often come out of workshops. When


you are discussing and exploring the BUC it is common for


people to come up with non-functional requirements that apply


to the functionality under discussion. For example, for a BUC


in which a customer is making a bank transfer, your workshop


participants would likely want to talk about security and


usability, the enterprise architect would want to talk about


interoperability with the bank’s payment system, and the


marketing person would want to talk about look and feel. Your


## 第 527 页


task is to capture these non-functional requirements and add


them to the growing collection for the BUC.


Mechanics of a Successful Workshop


There are a few things you can do to make your workshops


effective. None of this is rocket science. And although it is


certainly not the fun part of workshops (the discussion


part), it is nevertheless important.


The Right Participants


Your workshop participants must be people who have a genuine


interest in the business use case under discussion.


Representatives of the customer segment should be part of the


workshop’s makeup. They can be human representatives, or it


can be your persona. The objective is to have knowledge of


the customer and what the customer needs the solution to do


for him. Your workshop should be made up of willing


participants, preferably influential ones.


The right people are those who can either make the decisions


or have the business or technological knowledge to support


the decisions. The people who do the work and their leaders


make up the former group. Business analysts, product owners,


and developers are among the latter group. Your organization


## 第 528 页


is unique, so the right people have different roles and


titles, but you can recognize who they are by asking each


participant at the beginning of the workshop what they think


they can contribute to the workshop, why they are interested,


and what they would like to get from the workshop.


We realize how hard it can be to get the right group, but


without the right attendees, your workshop cannot be


effective.


The Right Workshop Space


This is obvious, but it helps a lot. Simply put, it is


difficult for participants to contribute effectively if they


are constrained by their environment.


If your workshop is online, ensure before the workshop that


everybody is comfortable with the technology. It is annoying


and a waste of time to participants if they have to wait


while somebody fumbles with their computer’s settings to


load the software or get their microphone or camera to work.


And although people have been using this technology for some


time, it still happens that someone’s settings have changed


and now interfere with the online meeting.


## 第 529 页


Collaborative whiteboards are useful for workshops. When


every participant has a pen, they can write on the whiteboard


at their moment of inspiration. Just ensure before the


workshop that everybody’s operating system allows them to


use your chosen whiteboard and that everybody is familiar


with the way it works.


When you are able to bring people together in the same


physical room, take the time to check the room if you are not


already familiar with it. It is frustrating to participants


when they discover that the whiteboard pens are missing or


have run out of ink, or there’s no flipchart paper, or they


cannot see the screen showing a remote participant. You


almost always have to rearrange the furniture so that


everybody is comfortable. These are small things, but they


distract from your aim of getting the maximum value from your


workshop.


A Facilitator


Someone has to be in charge. Someone has to coordinate


people’s comments and contributions. This would normally


be you, the business analyst, but occasionally, people prefer


to bring in someone with facilitation skills. We would not


for a moment suggest that you hire an expensive outside


## 第 530 页


facilitator, but often in organizations there is somebody who


is able and willing to facilitate your meeting. This is


particularly effective if the number of participants becomes


too large for you to handle.


The Discussion


The discussion should be a facilitated free-for-all.


That’s contradictory, but it indicates the lively atmosphere


of a good workshop. The facilitator encourages everyone—


including the shy ones—to participate. The participants


introduce their ideas whenever they have them.


The discussion is about a business use case. The intention is


to capture its business needs and what its most beneficial


outcome could be. This means discussing the needed


functionality and the business rules that regulate or require


that functionality.


Workshops work because they are a forum for the interested


parties to contribute their ideas on the composition of the


BUC. They discuss what the BUC should do and how it should do


it. This is the time to introduce innovations and new ideas


that will make the BUC more valuable.


## 第 531 页


In short, the discussion brings together the thinking of the


people who are most qualified to decide on the best BUC.


Visual Artifacts


Humans respond to what they see. Our environments and our


evolution have resulted in people whose visual sense is their


strongest stimulus.


Your workshops should be visually active. Building


diagrams, models, and prototypes on screens and whiteboards


provides a focus for your participants. If people merely sit


around the table and talk, the meeting is far less productive


(possibly inconclusive) than if they have the focus of


something visual to aim their remarks at. This is shown in


Figure 19.2.


## 第 532 页


![embedded_p532_91.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p532_91.jpeg)


Figure 19.2 A workshop using a visual artifact as the focus


for the participants


These visuals can be prototypes, scenarios, process models,


stories, story maps, or anything that captures the ideas


coming from workshop participants.


## 第 533 页


Some people are reluctant to draw anything in public, so many


workshops find it effective to have someone act as a scribe.


The scribe records what is being said and draws diagrams as


the participants describe their ideas.


Having visual representations gives people not only a focus,


but a sense of progression as they see their ideas


transformed to a visual reality.


Draw, don’t talk. Of course, you must talk, but draw while


you’re talking.


A Call to Action


Your workshop should end with a call to action. Actually,


many actions.


During the workshop, you discuss many issues. Most of these


require some further action, or actions, that should not be


done during the workshop but taken offline. Each action must


have an owner—someone who is responsible for ensuring that


the action is carried out. Each action preferably has a


deadline, and the owner agrees that the allowed time is


reasonable.


## 第 534 页


The call to action is a list of everything that requires


further work. Make sure everyone is given this list so that


they all know what has to be done, who is doing it, and when


it will be done by. This is the kind of information that


fuels project teams.


Review


Workshops are where the facilitator (this could be you, the


business analyst) brings together the right group of


knowledgeable stakeholders to discuss a business use case.


The intention of the workshop is to discover the


requirements for the BUC.


The requirements are not necessarily the detailed, atomic


requirements that are delivered to the developers. More


likely, the requirements are represented by models and


scenarios that define the intended functionality at a higher


level.


The workshop is a discussion using visual artifacts. These


artifacts—process models, wireframes, scenarios, and so on—


are built while the discussion is going on. They are the


result of the discussion, a record of the discussion, and


also the output of the workshop. It is later that the


## 第 535 页


business analyst will derive the detailed requirements from


the workshop’s output.


This chapter was intended to introduce workshops and provide


the basic information to get you started with them. Once you


have a workshop or two under your belt, you will want to know


more about the conduct of workshops. We refer you to the


books listed in this chapter’s Resources section.


Resources


Requirements by Collaboration: Workshops for Defining Needs


by Ellen Gottesdiener (Addison-Wesley, 2002). Refreshingly,


this gives a lot of emphasis to the human side of software


development. The book explains how to plan and conduct


requirements workshops so that the requirements are more


effectively defined through collaboration.


Making Workshops Work: Creative Collaboration for our Time by


Penny Pullan (Practical Inspiration Publishing, 2021). This


gives step-by-step guidance for running engaging, effective


workshops. The author is very visually oriented, and her


simple graphics are used to illustrate and communicate the


findings of your workshops.


## 第 536 页


Chapter 20. Scenarios


For each business event, there is a response: the business


use case, or BUC. In this chapter, we will discuss recording


the functionality of the BUC, and by doing so, discovering


its requirements. Here, we’ll look at using scenarios to


record this functionality. We looked at workshops earlier. A


scenario is often used in workshops to capture the thoughts


of the participants as you’re discussing the desired


functionality for a BUC.


A scenario is a limited series of functional steps that are


needed to complete the work of the BUC. They are written in


plain text; they describe the business needs rather than the


technological ones and can be understood by business


stakeholders with no technical training.


The scenario starts out as a requirements discovery tool.


Later, it is used to show the developers how the atomic


requirements hang together. We should mention that you can


add exceptions and alternatives into your scenarios to make


this tool quite utilitarian. We’ll look at these as we go


along.


## 第 537 页


In short, scenarios are easy to understand, are useful and


flexible, and make a valuable requirements tool for your


Trawling activity.


What Is a Scenario?


The scenario describes the actions of a business


use case.


A scenario, to give it its proper meaning, is an outline of a


plot, or a postulated sequence of steps. In requirements


work, we use this term to mean the plot of a section of the


work you are studying. The use of “plot” in its literary


sense is intended to imply that you break the work into a


series of steps or scenes, and by explaining these steps,


you explain the work.


Previously, we discussed how to partition the problem space


using business events. Each business event has a functional


response: the business use case. You write a scenario for


most, if not all, of the BUCs.


Consider the following scenario, which is the response to the


business event A movie fan wants to go to the movies:


## 第 538 页


1. The moviegoer asks for movies based on her previously


recorded preferences.


2. The moviegoer filters the movies based on the time of the


screening and the location of the cinema.


3. Reviews of the shortlisted movies are provided on demand.


4. The moviegoer selects a movie.


5. The moviegoer buys a ticket online.


6. Ticket details and a QR code are sent to the moviegoer’s


phone.


7. The moviegoer can elect to send messages to selected


friends with details of the movie and an invitation to join


her at the movies.


8. The moviegoer checks parking availability and public


transport options for the cinema.


9. The moviegoer sets an alarm to remind her when it is time


to leave for the movies.


How would you use this? In several ways.


## 第 539 页


If you need to record the current way that your customer does


her work, then you can interrogate and record the results in


a scenario format. Ask “What do you do next?” and “What


comes after that?” and add the responses to your growing


scenario. This is the How-Now view from the Brown Cow model


discussed in Chapter 18, The Brown Cow Model. You don’t


always need to do this, but it can be a useful way to arrive


at a consensus on the work.


Or, probably more usefully, you could use the scenario to


elicit what the customer wants to do in the future. At the


same time that your customer is telling you what she thinks


she wants, you are looking for the essence of it, and trying


not to simply record her presumed solution.


When you are in a workshop, the scenario can be used to


record a consensus of the participants’ views and ideas.


Just like the individual customer, you are always suggesting


and shaping and innovating to arrive at the optimal flow of


the work.


For the moviegoer’s scenario, you would go back over it


looking for improvements. You are looking to see if any of


the steps can be replaced with a more essential version.


There is still some technology in the scenario—buying the


## 第 540 页


ticket online; receiving the ticket on a cellphone—but as


these are mandated by external entities, which means there is


no feasible alternative, it is okay to include these


technological items. In fact, you are treating them as agreed


constraints.


Scenarios with Ready-Mades


If your project intends to use a ready-made (off-the-shelf,


open-source, legacy, etc.) solution, then your scenario is


used to show the customization steps and any additional steps


to make the ready-made work in the customer’s environment.


For example, let’s have a business event where an existing


bank customer wants to set up an additional special-purpose


account. The BUC scenario would be as follows:


1. Perform in-house security check on the application.


2. Ready-made account solution (with configuration) opens the


account.


3. New account routed to existing ready-made customer


resource management (CRM) solution.


4. Generate app page for the new account.


5. Send acknowledgment message to the customer.


## 第 541 页


Step 1 is there because the bank’s policy is to do its own


security checking and not rely on an outside service. The


security checking can be done immediately with no break to


consult with a human, so it is considered to be a single


step.


Step 2 is done by the ready-made (you would give it its real


name). The functionality of the ready-made does not have to


be documented by your scenario; it’s all hidden inside and


you don’t have to worry about it. This is, after all, the


reason you’re buying the ready-made. As long as you know the


data in and data out, you can ignore its internal


functionality. However, the scenario mentions


“configuration.” Most ready-mades need some kind of


configuration to work as desired. You have to tell it the


rules for accounts and prices, what exception handling you


want, and so on. We suggest that you specify the required


configuration using a separate but linked document.


Step 3 is the way this bank operates and is not part of the


accounts ready-made. However, the bank has an existing CRM


ready-made. In this case, the communication between the


accounts solution and the CRM is already established, and


there is no need for any special implementation.


## 第 542 页


Steps 4 and 5 are things the bank wants to do when its


customers open a new account. These will need to be developed


in the usual way.


Using Scenarios


You need to reach a consensus on your scenarios. Often, the


most expedient way is to write the scenario and then present


it to the customer and the stakeholders. You invite


criticism; you invite changes. You make changes to help


everybody reach an agreement that this is what the solution


will do whenever this business event occurs.


Write your scenarios using from three to ten


steps.


Write your scenarios by breaking the functionality of the


business use case into a series of steps, with each step


being some meaningful and recognizable activity. Ideally, you


should aim for between three and ten steps. These numbers are


not carved in stone, and nothing untoward will happen to you


if you use more than ten steps. However, if you end up with


dozens of steps, either you have a gigantic business use case


(impossible for normal commercial work) or you are writing


your scenario with an unnecessarily meticulous level of


## 第 543 页


granularity. The aim is to keep the scenario simple enough to


be readily understandable. Three to ten steps usually


achieves this goal.


The next example is the business use case for checking a


passenger onto an international flight (see Figure 20.1).


This business event happens when the passenger arrives at the


check-in desk. Either he has not checked in online, or for


some other reason—like dropping off bags—he needs to go to


a check-in desk. Here’s Sherri, one of the agents describing


the check-in process. Keep in mind that she is describing the


current way of working—the How-Now view of the work—which


you are using to start your investigation:


“I call the next customer in line. When he gets to my desk,


I ask for some kind of identification of his flight. I can


get the record locator (that’s the six alphanumeric


characters code) from the QR code on the passenger’s phone,


or if they have not checked in online, I ask for their name


and the flight they are on. Most people don’t know the


flight number, so I usually ask for their destination. They


must know that!


“I make sure I have the right passenger and the right


flight. It would be pretty embarrassing to give away someone


## 第 544 页


else’s seat or to send a passenger to the wrong destination.


Anyway, I locate the passenger’s flight record in the


computer. If he has not already given it to me, I ask for the


passenger’s passport. I check that the picture looks like


the passenger and that the passport is still valid.


“If the computer has not already assigned a seat, I find


one. This usually means I ask whether the passenger prefers a


window or an aisle seat, or, if the plane is already almost


full, I tell him what I have available. Of course, if the


computer has assigned a seat, I always ask if it is okay. One


way or another we settle on a seat, and I confirm it with the


computer system. If needed, I can print a paper boarding pass


at this stage, but I usually do the bags first.


“I ask how many bags the passenger is checking and, at the


same time, verify that he is not exceeding the carry-on


limit. Some people are unbelievable with what they want to


carry into a fairly space-restricted aircraft cabin. I ask


the security questions about the bags and get the


passenger’s responses. I print out the bag tags and securely


attach them to the bags, and then I send the bags on their


way down the conveyor belt.


## 第 545 页


“Next, if the passenger does not have a boarding pass on his


phone, I print one. This means that I have done everything as


far as the computer is concerned. But there is one more thing


to do: I have to make sure that everything agrees with the


passenger’s understanding. I read from the computer screen


where he is going, what time the flight is, and what time it


will board, and if a gate has been assigned I tell him that


too. I also read out how many bags have been checked and


confirm that their destination matches the passenger’s


destination. I hand over any documents and wish the passenger


a good flight.”

Figure 20.1 An airline check-in for an international flight.


As we go through the scenario for this case, see if it


matches your experience of checking in for a flight.


Now, sketch out the scenario. Break the story down to the


steps that you consider to be the best ones to capture the


normal path through the story. There are no hard-and-fast


rules about how you accomplish this—just write whatever


seems logical to you. After all, you are the person who is


going to use the scenario; it might as well fit with your


view of the work. Later you will adjust it with your


## 第 547 页


subsequent activities, but for the moment let us suppose that


this is your first draft:


1. Find the passenger-booking record using the QR code from


the passenger’s phone or ask for the passenger’s name and


flight.


2. Check that this is the right passenger, flight, and


destination.


3. Check that the passport is valid and belongs to the


passenger.


4. If the passenger is not checked in, allocate a seat.


5. Ask the security questions.


6. Check the baggage onto the flight and print and attach the


bag tags.


7. Print the boarding pass (if needed).


8. Do a final check of the flight details and tell the


passenger to “Have a nice flight.”


In a workshop, stakeholders are invited to


participate and revise the scenario until it


## 第 548 页


represents a consensus of what the work should


be.


Confirm this scenario with the interested stakeholders. It is


in plain English (or whatever language you’re using) so that


the stakeholders can participate and revise this scenario


until it represents a consensus view of what the work


should be. Once a consensus is reached on the work, start to


formalize the scenario. Along the way, you will learn more


about the work.


The first part of the formalized scenario identifies it and


gives it a meaningful name.


Business Use Case Name: Check passenger onto flight.


Next, you add the start-up mechanism—the trigger—for the


business use case. It usually consists of some data or


request (often both) arriving from outside your work area.


There are also time-triggered business use cases, in which


case you state the time condition (an hour or a date is


reached, an amount of time has passed since another business


use case, and so on) that initiates the use case.


## 第 549 页


Trigger: Passenger arrives at the desk with passport and


flight ID or destination.


Now add any preconditions that must exist when the business


use case is triggered. Preconditions indicate the state of


the work at initiation. Usually, this means certain other


business events must have occurred before this business use


case makes any sense.


Preconditions: The passenger must have a reservation.


The check-in desk is not the place to be if you do not


already have a reservation. While it may seem like good


customer service to allow passengers to make a reservation at


the check-in desk, the amount of time needed for this


transaction would no doubt annoy the other passengers


standing in line.


Actors are the people or systems that connect to or do the


work of the business use case. Usually, one actor triggers


the business use case, and then one or more others


participate in the work.


Actors: Passenger (trigger), check-in agent.


## 第 550 页


The passenger triggers the business use case by arriving at


the check-in desk; he is also the recipient of the business


use case’s output. The passenger interacts with the agent to


carry out the work of the business use case. Although the


agent manipulates any automated product being used, that


action should be thought of as simply the current


implementation; it has no binding significance. The essential


business is triggered by the passenger, who, in some future


incarnation, might be more closely involved. Self-check-in


seems obvious, but don’t leap to the first solution that


comes along. The point of the requirements investigation is


to make sure you understand the work before choosing a


solution.


The Essence of the Business


The scenario now represents the current incarnation of the


work. If you think back to the Brown Cow model from earlier,


this scenario belongs to the first quadrant of the model: the


How-Now view of the work.


To move above the line and look at the What-Now and Future-


What views, you must consider the essence of the problem. To


do so, go back over the scenario and eliminate any


## 第 551 页


technological bias while simultaneously asking the question:


“What does the business really need to do?”


The essence is not a better solution to the


problem. It is the real problem.


The essence is not a better solution to the problem. It is


the real problem. You find the real business problem when you


eliminate all the technological camouflage that normally


makes up a description of some work.


Assume for the normal case that everything works


perfectly.


Also, for the moment, consider only the normal case scenario.


The normal case (sometimes called the happy path) is when


everything works perfectly. Of course, everything does not


always work perfectly, so later you go back over the same


scenario and explore the exceptions and alternatives.


Let’s revisit the check-in scenario, and this time change


the language to be technologically neutral. The How-Now


version is:


## 第 552 页


1. Find the passenger-booking record using the QR code from


the passenger’s phone, or ask for the passenger’s name and


flight.


The passenger and the record locator are both constraints on


the work. The passenger comes from outside the work. The


record locator is a constraint imposed by the current


computer system. In this case it is a real constraint, not


because a computer system uses it (the computer system


belongs to the airline and therefore can be changed), but


rather because it is used by travel agents and other bodies


outside the scope of the organization. For this reason, we


accept that it is a constraint. However, the record locator


is merely a means to an end. The essence of the work is to


find the passenger’s reservation. Let’s rewrite step 1 to


reflect this understanding:


1. Locate the passenger’s reservation.


Stating it in the essential manner, without the technological


artifacts, allows us to think of better ways to implement it.


If you want to rush ahead, you can see that there are several


possibilities for the future solution. Machine-reading the


passport or face recognition spring to mind as a way for


passengers to identify themselves.


## 第 553 页


But for now, put those ideas for future technology aside and


consider that the essence of the problem is to connect the


passenger with his reservation. The How-Now scenario reads:


2. Check that this is the right passenger, flight, and


destination.


This step focuses on ensuring that the passenger is who he


says he is and that the reservation matches his expectations


for the flight. Let’s write the essential step 2:


2. Ensure that the passenger matches the reservation.


Next, the How-Now scenario checks the passport:


3. Check that the passport is valid and belongs to the


passenger.


The passport step contains no technology (apart from the


passport, which is a constraint); therefore, we can consider


it to be the essence and we do not change it. However, you


need to specify what is meant by valid, so this warrants a


few words of explanation. We suggest enhancing this step by


adding the appropriate business rules:


## 第 554 页


3. Check that the passport is valid and belongs to the


passenger.


3.1 The passport must be current.


3.2 The passport must not expire within three months of the


end of the complete trip.


3.3 The passport must be valid for travel to the destination


country.


3.4 Visas (where needed) must be current.


3.5 There must be no “refused entry” stamps from the


destination country.


Alternatively, you might simply leave this step as it was and


refer to notes to complete the business rules for step 3.


3. Check that the passport is valid and belongs to the


passenger.


See procedure guideline CAA-175.


This is the essence of the problem. There is an unyielding


constraint that the passenger has a passport—this is


international travel you are dealing with. Ignore for the


## 第 555 页


moment countries within the Schengen Agreement; that is,


countries that allow travel between them using an identity


card only. These are alternatives and you’ll come back to


them later. The airline’s management needs to enforce the


rules on passports because the airline is responsible for


returning any passengers who are refused entry at the


destination country. All in all, this seems like a mandatory


constraint, so keep it as part of the essence.


The same technique of scrubbing away the technology and


getting to the essence is employed for later steps in the


scenario. Keep working through it until you and your


interested stakeholders agree that it is an accurate, but not


yet detailed, portrayal of the essence of the work. When you


are finished, it should look something like this:


Business Event: Passenger decides to check in.


Business Use Case Name: Check passenger onto flight.


Trigger: Passenger arrives at the desk with passport and


flight ID or destination.


Precondition: Passenger must have a reservation.


Actors: Passenger (trigger), check-in agent.


## 第 556 页


1. Locate the passenger’s reservation.


2. Ensure that the passenger matches the reservation.


3. Check that the passport is valid and belongs to the


passenger.


See procedure guideline CAA-175.


4. Allocate a seat if not previously allocated.


5. Get the correct responses to the security questions.


6. Check the baggage onto the flight.


7. Give the passenger the boarding pass and proof that the


bags have been checked in.


8. Wish the passenger a pleasant flight.


You should add an outcome to the scenario—that is, the


desired situation at the successful conclusion of the


business use case. Think of it as the stakeholder’s


objectives at the time he triggered the business use case.


Outcome: The passenger is recorded as checked onto the


flight, the bags are assigned to the flight, a seat is


## 第 557 页


allocated, and the passenger is in possession of a boarding


pass and bag reclaim information.


We have left the outcome of the BUC until the end. We have


done that for symbolic reasons. That is, you get to the end


of the processes for the BUC, and this is the outcome you


have achieved. You could, however, put the outcome at the


beginning of the scenario and call it the desired outcome.


Think of it as the process steps you are about to read are


all aimed at achieving this desired outcome. Whether you put


the outcome at the beginning or the end, you should think of


it as the center of interest for the business use case.


Alternatives


Alternatives arise when you offer an intentional


choice of user actions.


Alternatives arise when you wish the user to have a choice of


possible actions. These choices are intentional; they are


wanted and defined by the business. They usually exist to


make the work of the business use case more attractive and


convenient to the actors. When you buy things online, for


example, you can decide whether to place your selected goods


in a shopping cart awaiting checkout or bypass the shopping


## 第 558 页


cart and have them shipped right away by clicking “Buy


now.” These deliberate choices offered by the vendor are


alternatives.


In the airline check-in commentary above, for some countries,


passengers did not need passports and could use an identity


card. Treat that as an alternative.


The work reacts differently depending on which alternative is


selected. Suppose that you are sending a small package to


someone and want to use the postal service. You buy the


postage online through the postal service’s website, but


before you print the shipping label showing the postage paid,


you have a choice of how to get your package into the post.


One option is to take it to the post office. In this case,


you will be offered the location of the nearest post office


and several others nearby. You could elect to drop it in one


of the drop-off boxes scattered around the city, in which


case the site tells you the nearby ones. You could elect to


have your mail carrier collect it; in which case you book a


pickup day and pay a small fee. The following is part of a


scenario. Let’s say that you are up to step 5.


5. Arrange getting your package into the postal system.


## 第 559 页


Alt 5.1 Take the package to the post office.


Alt 5.1.1 Provide nearby post offices.


Alt 5.1.2 Include post office QR code on mailing label.


Alt 5.2 Use a drop-off box.


Alt 5.2.1. Warn the customer about the maximum size of


parcels for drop boxes.


Alt 5.2.2 Provide nearby drop boxes.


Alt 5.2.3 Include drop-off QR code on mailing label.


Alt 5.3. Collection.


Alt 5.3.1 Select a collection day from those available.


Alt 5.3.2 Inform the customer of the fee and add it to the


postage.


Alt 5.3.3 Add collection instructions and QR code to the


mailing label.


6. Print mailing label.


## 第 560 页


You find alternatives by examining each step of the normal


case. Look for instances where the step may be carried out


differently, or the user or customer can be given a choice.


These choices are sometimes interesting from the point of


view of improving the work or providing a better service.


Exceptions


Exceptions are unwanted but inevitable deviations


from the normal case.


Exceptions are unwanted but inevitable deviations from the


normal case. They are unwanted in the sense that the owner of


the work would rather that they did not happen, because they


have the potential of preventing the actors from achieving


the desired outcome of the BUC. Nevertheless, we know that


they will happen from time to time, so we have to cater to


them. For example, a passenger might have a dead battery on


his phone and cannot retrieve his boarding pass, an online


customer might forget his password, or a passenger could


arrive at the airport having left his passport behind.


We must pause here to urge you to delay looking for


exceptions until you are satisfied with the normal case (or


happy path) scenario. It is far too easy for stakeholders to


## 第 561 页


get carried away with exceptions, and your workshop can be


quickly derailed by needlessly chasing exceptions that might


never happen. It is only when you have agreed to the normal


case that you can methodically work through it by looking for


the exceptions and deciding what to do about them.


The goal of the exception scenario is to show how the work


handles the exception: in other words, which steps must be


taken to rejoin the path of the normal case (if possible).


You can write a separate scenario to show the exceptions,


but in most cases, it is more convenient to add the


exception steps to your normal scenario.


You find the exceptions by examining each step of the normal


case and asking questions such as the following.


• What happens if this step cannot be completed, or does not


go to completion, or comes up with a wrong or unacceptable


result?


• What can go wrong at this step?


• What could happen to prevent the work from reaching this


step?


• Could any external entity disrupt or prevent this step?


## 第 562 页


• Could any technology used to implement this step fail or


become unavailable?


• Could the end user fail to understand what is required of


him, or misunderstand the information presented by the


product?


• Could the end user take the wrong action—intentionally or


unintentionally—or fail to respond?


There are many questions you can ask, each of which seeks to


find a different potential error. We suggest that you make a


checklist of the questions pertinent to your particular


situation and add to it each time a new project discovers new


questions.


We have also seen some successful attempts to use automation


to help with this task. Our colleague Neil Maiden at City


University in London developed a scenario presenter that


works with a normal case scenario to automatically generate a


list of potential exceptions. It also uses rich-media


scenarios where additional information in the form of


photographs, movies, sound, and so on is integrated into the


scenario.


## 第 563 页


We know from experience that the exceptions have the


potential to necessitate a great amount of remedial rework if


they are not found at requirements time, so look carefully


for things that could go wrong. You can ignore the scenario


in which the work is struck by a meteor, or giant flying


squids eat the internet, but almost anything else is


possible.


Misuse Cases and Negative Scenarios


Misuse cases show negative or harmful possibilities, such as


someone abusing the work or attempting to defraud it.


Examples include users deliberately entering incorrect data,


customers using stolen credit cards, and pranksters making


fictitious calls or transactions, planting a virus or other


malware, or engaging in any of the myriad other things that


can be done to harm the work.


“Maybe ‘abuse cases’ sounds like a bad pun,


but the idea of the Negative Scenario (Burglar


impersonates householder, Alarm Call Center


Operator colludes with Burglar, etc.) is


important.”—Ian Alexander, Scenarios, Stories,


Use Cases: Through the Systems Development Life-


Cycle


## 第 564 页


It may be helpful here to think in terms used by novelists


and to use the idea of the protagonist and the antagonist.


The protagonist is the hero or main character of the story:


the good guy, the user, the person using your solution as


shown in your normal use case scenario. While you want your


protagonist to win, you should also think of your protagonist


as someone who is forgetful, slow, distracted, or not paying


attention. Go through the normal case scenario, and for each


step, ask what could be done incorrectly. It may be simpler


to write a new scenario for each misuse, as the ramifications


of a misstep may be complex enough to warrant their own


separate story.


Examine all the steps for the normal case and ask


if there is a possibility of someone opposing or


misusing that action.


So much for the protagonist. The antagonist is the person


who opposes the work, seeks to harm it, or wants to defraud


it. Hackers and fraudsters are the most commonly thought-of


examples of antagonists. Examine all the steps for the normal


case and ask if there is a possibility of someone opposing or


misusing that action. In this case, the ramifications upon


## 第 565 页


discovering an antagonist’s misuse may be to simply stop the


execution of the business use case.


Whether you annotate the normal case with the misuse steps or


write a separate misuse scenario depends on the complexity of


the situation and the comfort level of the stakeholders.


Review


We have been discussing how to write a scenario; a natural


language tool for describing a business use case. The


intention of the scenario is to help you and your


stakeholders come to a mutual understanding of the


functionality of a business use case. Writing the BUC


scenario tests whether sufficient study has been done or


whether the business analyst needs to investigate further.


You can, if it is helpful, write a scenario for each Brown


Cow segment. The How-Now segment gives you a view of how the


work is done at the moment. This is useful as a starting


point, as it gives your stakeholders a recognizable snapshot


of part of their work. The What-Now segment shows the essence


of that work, and you use it to ensure that the problem it


solves is indeed the real business problem.


## 第 566 页


The Future-What scenario describes the desired essential


activity. This view shows what the solution must do to


achieve the goal of the project. It improves on the What-Now


by incorporating the improvements desired by the customer.


The Future-How view brings the abstract essence into the


real, technological world. It shows how the physical


processors (computers, humans, devices, etc.) implement the


essence. It is this view that forms the basis for writing


your detailed requirements.


Your scenarios start out as a trawling tool and eventually


morph into a specification tool.


Resources


Scenarios, Stories, Use Cases: Through the Systems


Development Life-Cycle by Ian Alexander and Neil Maiden


(Wiley, 2004). This book explores the use of scenarios and


provides techniques for effective scenario writing.


Writing Effective Use Cases by Alistair Cockburn (Addison-


Wesley, 2000). Although primarily focused on use cases, this


book provides valuable insights into writing effective


scenarios for business analysis.


## 第 567 页


Chapter 21. Stories


Traditionally, stories are used by agile teams to specify a


piece of functionality to be developed. While they are


waiting to be developed, they are assembled into a backlog.


These stories are known as “user stories.” However, as we


are discovering requirements, it is premature to be thinking


about users. The term “user” implies that you envisage


someone sitting in front of a computer, which in turn implies


that you have a solution in mind. As you are in the process


of discovering the business problem, it is definitely


unhelpful to be thinking about the solution.


In this chapter, we show you how to make use of stories in a


different way. These are not “user stories,” but stories


about requirements. This is a trawling technique, so while we


use the format of the user story, we’ll drop the “user.”


We start by writing stories for the business events, and so


we’ll call them “business event stories.”


The Business Event Story


Business events are happenings in the real world that cause


the solution space to respond. Just to remind you, a business


use case (BUC) is the chunk of functionality that your


## 第 568 页


solution uses to process and complete the response to the


business event. For example, a customer wanting to renew her


insurance is a business event. The processing needed to


accomplish the renewal—checking the terms, accepting the


payment, sending out the policy documents, and so on—is the


business use case.


So, this is where you begin to write stories—at the business


event level. These are stories that are descriptors of the


business use cases. As business event stories are high-level


stories, there is some detail to be added later.


Some people refer to high-level stories as “epics.”


However, there is no satisfactory definition of an epic apart


from “a high-level story that may contain other stories or


epics.” This is not useful—it means an epic could be almost


anything. The definition does not provide any scope, or any


boundaries to the amount of functionality it might cover.


So, instead of using this vague, overused, and imprecise


term, we use the business event as the basis for our stories.


You know exactly what a business event is: You know why it


is triggered, where it starts, where it ends, and exactly how


much functionality makes up the response to the business


event. If you write a story for the business event, then


## 第 569 页


it’s a story that is a bounded, independent, traceable


descriptor of the solution’s response to the business event.


The response is triggered the moment an external entity


initiates a request and ends when the request is completely


fulfilled.


A business event story is a bounded, independent,


traceable descriptor of the solution’s response


to the business event.


The business event story is bounded and independent in that


the functionality it includes is not connected to any other


business event stories. It is traceable because all the


business events have one or more data flows on the context


diagram, and the context diagram is where it all begins. See


Figure 21.1.


## 第 570 页


![embedded_p570_93.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p570_93.jpeg)


Figure 21.1 The business events show on the context diagram


because there are one or more boundary data flows associated


with each event. The business event stories can be derived


using the adjacent system and the functionality of the


response to the business event. There is one story for each


business event.


## 第 571 页


You have probably spotted that this bounded, traceable story


is an ideal candidate for a development iteration or an


implementation unit. But that’s just a bonus to come later;


for the moment, we are concerned with discovering the


requirements that are needed to solve the business problem.


For each business event, you write a story. It looks like


this:


As a [customer segment]


I can [functionality that responds to my business event]


So that [business value].


The customer segment is the adjacent system that initiates


the business event. The flow on the context diagram triggers


the functionality of the story. Of course, at this stage the


functionality is simply a summary description—you’ll


explore it and discover its details later. However, it should


be an accurate description of the functionality needed to


provide the business value described in the last line.


Note the scope of the business event story. It begins with


the adjacent system that triggered the event, describes the


response the business makes, and states the business value


## 第 572 页


generated as a result. In other words, business event


stories are about the business.


The business event story gives an overview of the


functionality. Later, you might need to break it down in


order to see its functional composition. This is illustrated


by the data model in Figure 21.2.


## 第 573 页


![embedded_p573_94.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p573_94.jpeg)


Figure 21.2 This is an extract from the Requirements


Knowledge Model, which is discussed in detail in Appendix C,


Volere Requirements Knowledge Model. This part of the model


## 第 574 页


shows that the scope of the work can be subdivided into


Business Events, and for each business event, you write a


Business Event Story. These will later be broken down into


the functionality that makes up the response to the business


event.


Figure 21.2 shows entities called Functional Story, Detailed


Task, and Atomic Requirement. This is the way we organize the


breakdown of the top-level Business Event Story, and they are


needed when you start to develop your solution. We shall come


back to these in a lot more detail when we discuss story maps


in Chapter 35, Story Map.


Until then, let’s stick to business event stories.


The Story Format


As mentioned above, the suggested format of a story is as


follows:


As a [customer segment]


I can [some functionality that responds to my business event]


So that [business value].


Let’s look at the story elements more closely.


## 第 575 页


“As a”


As a [customer segment]


The first part of the story points at the customer segment,


which can be a person, some people, a system, or an


organization that receives the benefit of the story. The


customer segment is also the initiator of the business event.


Or to put it another way, this is the adjacent system from


the context model. See Figure 21.1.


Be as descriptive as you can, and whatever you do, don’t


write “As a user.” That is meaningless and gives no


indication as to what the solution should be doing, who it


should be doing it for, or why it should be doing it. On the


other hand, “As a cargo loader” or “As a rider wanting to


find a rental bike” or “As a bank customer wanting an


overdraft” or “As a professional photographer” gives a


clear pointer to what the story is about.


As we suggested in Chapter 6, Customer Segments, you might be


using a persona for your requirements discovery. A persona is


an archetypal representation of a customer segment and is


intended to give a human face to the characteristics of the


population of the customer segment. You might prefer to


personalize the story by writing “As Alice,” or whatever


## 第 576 页


name you have given to the persona representing the customer


segment.


To get good requirements, you need to ask some analytical


questions.


• Is this customer segment important? You obviously don’t


want to spend time in the early stages developing solutions


for unimportant customers. Ask if this customer segment makes


a significant contribution to meeting the goals of the


project.


• Does the importance of the customer segment align with the


priority given to the business event when you prioritized the


events during the blastoff?


• Is this customer segment the real initiator of the business


event, or should you be looking at someone further away from


the problem space?


• Is this the real beneficiary of the story? Or should you


investigate further and find the real one?


• Do you know this customer segment well enough to know what


it needs and what will be beneficial?


## 第 577 页


You might have to come back to some of these questions after


you have written more of the story.


When your business event is time triggered, don’t write “As


a clock.” The “As a” should cite the beneficiary. Time-


triggered business events usually have to do with reports,


statements, reminders, and so on. The beneficiary of these is


usually the receiver of the output of the business event


story.


For example, let’s say that the business event is Time to


remind policyholders that their insurance is about to expire.


This would happen a month before the anniversary of each


policy, and the beneficiary of the event is the policyholder:


As a policyholder


I can be reminded of the expiration of my policy


So that I can renew in time and maintain continuous coverage.


Examples of other beneficiaries: Producing monthly bank


statements is a staple of most banks. The customer segment in


this case is the bank customer. The benefit is that the


customer is updated with her financial position. A monthly


(or weekly, or daily) sales report is produced for someone’s


## 第 578 页


benefit. That person, or group of people, is named in the


“As a [customer segment]” line of the story; for example,


“As the Sales Director”.


The reason for going to a little trouble over the beneficiary


is that the beneficiary must be important to the goals of the


solution. This importance helps with prioritization. For


example, “As the Chief Operating Officer” immediately makes


the story important; “As the facilities superintendent,”


not so much. Be as descriptive and accurate as possible, it


helps you discover the real requirements.


“I can”


I can [functionality that responds to the business event]


Here are examples of what to write:


As a music fan


I can open an account with the streaming service


As a tax compliance officer


I can be informed of all bank customers who have made


deposits over $10,000


## 第 579 页


Resist writing “I want.”


The functionality should be a description of what a solution


will do to enable the beneficiary to achieve a business goal.


You must also ensure that you are writing about the needed


functionality and ignore how it would be done. Whatever you


write on this line, ask if it is a solution masking the real


need. Remember that there is a difference between a problem


and a solution, and that by writing “I want” instead of “I


can,” you are in danger of adding a solution to this part of


the story.


Here is an example of what not to write:


As an iOS user


I want to sync data with an Apple Watch


So that I can track calories burned more accurately


Note the “I want” line. Syncing data is a solution; Apple


Watch is a solution. By filling this line with a solution,


the actual functionality is pushed onto the “So that” line.


Tracking calories is an activity; it has a verb. However, you


still don’t know why this guy wants to track his calories.


## 第 580 页


Is he trying to balance calories burned with calories


ingested? If so, then this solution is not going to work.


Where are his ingested calories? And what does syncing data


have to do with calories? What is this “data”? It remains


unsaid. This story is unlikely to lead to a solution that


will satisfy anyone’s needs. And while we’re looking at it,


the “As a” line is completely useless. It gives no


indication as to why this story is important. Anybody with


any requirement can be an iOS user.


If you delete the solution about the Apple Watch and write


the following (which, incidentally, was written as part of


the original story, so it appears to be needed):


I can track calories burned more accurately


tracking burned calories more accurately seems worthwhile,


but more accurately than what? Perhaps we could turn it into


this:


I can track my burned calories


The story would then make sense if it ran something like


this:


As a health-conscious person


## 第 581 页


I can track my burned calories


So that I can ensure my daily caloric intake is balanced with


calories burned.


The story is improving, and it now suggests that we can take


it further. For example, is the “So that” line the real


business value? If you asked why, you would find that this


person is concerned about putting on weight. So, let’s


rewrite the story as follows:


As a health-conscious person


I can ensure my daily caloric intake is balanced with


calories burned


So that I maintain my healthy weight.


Keep in mind all the time that you are discovering


requirements. Your stories are aimed at eliciting the real


needs of the business problem. Revisit your stories as we did


above, and ensure that the end result is a story that


demonstrates an important business value.


Keep in mind all the time that you are


discovering requirements. Your stories are aimed


## 第 582 页


at eliciting the real needs of the business


problem.


To this end, the story’s functionality should be a complete


but not detailed description of what has to be done to


respond to the business event. For example:


As a music fan


I can establish an account


So that I can stream music from the service.


As a policyholder


I can renew my insurance at the best available rate


As a highway patrol officer


I can be alerted if any vehicle in my vicinity is stolen or


otherwise of interest


And so on. You have to work with your customer to be certain


that the functionality is what is needed; in other words, you


are discovering the requirements.


“So that”


## 第 583 页


Now we arrive at the most important part of the story: its


rationale. Some people leave this out, and worse, some


authors advocate leaving it out. Don’t. Without it, you


cannot know if your story is correct or even useful. The line


is:


So that [business value].


Let’s take this story from a receptionist at a busy health


clinic:


As a medical receptionist


I can use any one of five different patient attributes


So that I can quickly locate any patient regardless of


their means of identification.


This looks like a reasonable justification for this story.


You have to talk to the receptionist and determine if it is


solving an important problem. The receptionist tells you that


when patients arrive, they don’t always have their patient


number, but they will have a date of birth, an address, an


appointment time, or their Social Security number or National


Insurance number (or the equivalent depending on the


country). This is a busy practice, and the receptionist needs


## 第 584 页


to quickly and accurately identify people and flag their


records for the doctor/nurse/practitioner. This rationale


aligns with the goals of the project. It makes a constructive


contribution to the eventual solution. It’s a valid story,


and the rationale (“So that”) provides real business value.


We left the highway patrol officer’s story without a


rationale. The complete story is:


As a highway patrol officer


I can be alerted if any vehicle in my vicinity is stolen or


otherwise of interest


So that I can locate and stop the stolen vehicle as rapidly


as possible to question the driver and passengers.


This provides business value to the officer, as well as to


the police service (which is your customer for this project).


In some cases, a business event has more than one


beneficiary. For example, an insurance policyholder receives


a business benefit when he renews his insurance: His


insurance coverage continues. Additionally, the insurance


company benefits from the revenue. You could continue this


line and say that an employee of the insurance company


benefits because she remains employed, and so on.


## 第 585 页


As a rule, stick to the beneficiary who receives business


value directly from the outcome of the business event. If you


absolutely need to, append other beneficiaries to the


business event story.


On the other hand, consider this story and its rationale:


As a marketing manager


I want a content management system


So that I can manage and provide quality content and


experience to my readers.


This story does not give us any real business value. Why does


this manager want to “provide quality content and


experience”? Surely the benefit comes when potential


customers (not “readers”) respond to the marketing


overture. The fact that someone is reading the literature is


almost irrelevant. They might be reading it for their own


amusement and have no intention of buying anything, or they


are idly passing the time in the dentist’s waiting room.


The content management system is a presumed solution, and


so should play no part in a requirements story. Perhaps the


objective might be achieved with a content management system,


## 第 586 页


but there might be alternatives that are better suited to the


real purpose. Regardless, by including it in the story, the


writer omitted the business value and gave the business


analyst no chance to assess the importance of the story.


Presumed solutions should not be part of your


stories.


It gets worse. The frivolous “So that” line spoke of
