quality content. This too is a presumed solution; it’s


presuming that if the content is high quality, it will be


more effective. This might be true, but equally might not.


Additionally, would the employment of the content management


system guarantee high-quality content?


And what did he mean by “quality content” anyway? You


should talk to a real marketing person before specifying


“quality content and experience” and determine the real


business value of this story. Otherwise, you have no idea if


this story makes any real contribution to the goals of the


organization.


Let’s try to rescue this story by rewriting it as follows:


As a marketing manager


## 第 587 页


I can have enticing marketing material sent to potential and


existing customers


So that I achieve an improved take-up rate.


Your development project is intended to produce business


value. Writing stories that have no business value is


pointless.


In case you’re wondering, the examples of poor


stories in this book have not been carefully


constructed by your authors to illustrate the


points. They are other people’s stories being


cited as good examples of how to write a story.


Keep in mind that you are using stories as an aid to


discovering requirements. We have discussed above how you


interrogate each part of the story to ensure its correctness.


You can also interrogate the story as a whole. For example,


you can ask analytical questions such as: “Why do you want


to do that?”, “Where is the business benefit?”, “Is that


really the initiator of this business event?”, and so on,


until you arrive at the real business need. See Figure 21.3.


## 第 588 页


![embedded_p588_95.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p588_95.jpeg)


Figure 21.3 Stories are being used here to examine the


problem and discover the requirements.


Stories alone are insufficient to serve as the requirements


for your solution. However, they can be very useful to you in


your efforts to discover all the requirements.


Review


Writing a story for each business event gives you a


collection of high-level stories that cover all the


functionality needed by the problem space. Each business


## 第 589 页


event has a purpose, and this is reflected in the “So that”


line of the business event story. Your analytical efforts are


to ensure that the “So that” rationale describes actual


business value and that it aligns with the goals of your


project. Or to say that a different way, the collection of


“So that” justifications delivers the goal of the project.


Once the business event story is accepted, you dig deeper


into the details of the functionality for the event. This


means that you have to do some trawling—workshops,


interviews, process models, stored data, and so on—to


uncover the atomic requirements. Later, the developers add


technological requirements to your business requirements (see


Figure 21.4). Following chapters look at these topics.


## 第 590 页


![embedded_p590_96.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p590_96.jpeg)


Figure 21.4 The stories discussed in this chapter are


stories about business needs. When these are known to solve


the right business problem, the developers take over and


extend the business stories with stories needed for


implementation reasons.


For the moment, concentrate on the business event stories. If


these accurately define the business outcome of the event,


then they are the foundation for what is to come. By getting


## 第 591 页


these stories right, you give yourself every chance of


delivering the correct, most valuable solution.


Resources


User Stories Applied: For Agile Software Development by Mike


Cohn (Addison-Wesley, 2004). The author is concerned with


writing “user” stories aimed at agile development. However,


his knowledge of stories is worth pursuing.


Agile Alliance (https://www.agilealliance.org). This


organization provides resources on topics from user stories


through articles, webinars, and conference materials.


The Mountain Goat Software Blog


(https://www.mountaingoatsoftware.com/blog). Mike Cohn’s


blog contains valuable insights and articles on user stories.


## 第 592 页


Chapter 22. Business Process Models


Business process models demonstrate a set of activities that


together achieve a business objective. Business process


models can be in a number of forms—for example, UML activity


diagrams, BPMN diagrams, data flow diagrams, or flowcharts.


What you use or call them doesn’t matter. It’s what you do


with them that matters.


If you are familiar with process models, skip ahead. If not,


take a look at the simple process model depicted in Figure


22.1. The process model shows the business activities—each


one a recognizable chunk of functionality—and the sequence


in which they are organized to achieve the goal.


![embedded_p592_97.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p592_97.jpeg)


Figure 22.1 An example of a process model from DC Comics


Process models are a tool to help you find requirements. Once


you have drawn your process model and agreed on it with the


customers and stakeholders, you can readily derive your


requirements or stories from it. The activities on the model


provide a suitable amount of functionality to qualify as a


## 第 593 页


story. Or if you are writing detailed requirements, you can


extract them from the relevant activities on the process


model.


As Figure 22.2 shows, you can use process models in various


situations. They are useful for prototyping when you want to


show the functionality of a candidate solution. They are used


in the Trawling activity when you might want to model the


current state of the work under study or you’re proposing


some future process to your customer. Solution designers


might also use process models to illustrate how their design


achieves its purpose.


## 第 594 页


![embedded_p594_98.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p594_98.jpeg)


Figure 22.2 Process models are used in several of the


requirements discovery activities.


Process models are a tool to help you discover the right


requirements and/or stories. And as we mentioned above, you


can derive your requirements and stories directly from the


## 第 595 页


process model. In some cases, with willing developers, you


might be able to develop the needed software directly from


the process model.


Our approach to process models for requirements work is an


informal one. We have no interest here in formal process


models using elaborate notation. Process models for the


business analyst are quick sketches aimed at eliciting


information. Let’s start by looking at their notation.


Notation


Before we go too far, we should warn you not to get involved


in notation wars. Sometimes people get very passionate about


issues such as whether and how to show data, whether a


process should be a circle or a rectangle or a rectangle with


rounded corners, how conditions should be shown, and so on.


You’re a business analyst; your process models are for you


to communicate with. As long as your customer and other


stakeholders understand your diagrams in the same way,


you’re using all the notation you need.


However, it is useful to know that there are two popular


notations: Unified Modeling Language (UML) and Business


Process Model and Notation (BPMN). You can use either to


## 第 596 页


document, or invent, a business process. BPMN has the most


comprehensive modeling vocabulary, but you should only use a


minimal subset—just as much as you need to communicate with


the stakeholders. BPMN and UML, when used in a cut-down form


for trawling purposes, are not that dissimilar. Use whatever


subset of either notation works for you and your


stakeholders.


You should be sketching your models, so hand-drawn diagrams


are all that are needed. Please don’t spend time and money


on one of the dedicated apps for drawing these things. You


need nothing more than a pencil and paper, or a whiteboard,


virtual or real. We propose that you draw the models as


you’re talking to your customer, your team, and other


stakeholders.


Activity Diagrams


This is a quick introduction to basic activity diagrams.


Figure 22.3 shows all that you need, probably more than you


need, in a UML activity diagram.


## 第 597 页


![embedded_p597_99.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p597_99.jpeg)


Figure 22.3 The basic notation of the UML activity diagram


In Figure 22.4, note the initial icon called the “start


event.” This is the happening that triggers the process—it


## 第 598 页


is in fact a business event. This is convenient, as most of


the time you draw a process model of a business use case, or


the response to one business event.


![embedded_p598_100.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p598_100.jpeg)


Figure 22.4 A subset of the BPMN model


## 第 599 页


You probably won’t use much of the notation shown in Figures


22.3 and 22.4. We want you to know that the notation is


there, but we will use a subset for our examples.


Data Flow Diagrams


Data flow diagrams are the simplest and most natural and


minimal notation to show business processes.


The data flow model differs from other process models in that


it shows the data that is input and output from each


activity. Including the input and output from a process


guides the person creating the diagram into a more


“natural” functional partitioning. The activities are


natural in that they are whatever is required to transform


one piece of known data into another.


The example shown in Figure 22.5 repeats the airline check-in


process we discussed in Chapter 20, Scenarios.


## 第 600 页


![embedded_p600_101.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p600_101.jpeg)


Figure 22.5 A data flow model of the airline check-in


process that was shown as a scenario in Chapter 20


The notation of the data flow model is this: Around the


periphery are the adjacent systems that you first saw in the


context model when we were discussing scope in Chapter 5.


They are exactly the same when used here. The activities are


shown as circles. The arrows represent flows of data between


## 第 601 页


the activities; the name attached to each data flow indicates


the contents of the flow.


The other notation is the parallel lines enclosing stored


data. Stored data can be either a complete database or


individual entities/classes from your data models. For


reference, the notation is shown in Figure 22.6.


![embedded_p601_102.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p601_102.jpeg)


Figure 22.6 An overview of the data flow notation


We encourage you to draw data flow models one business event


at a time. However, when there is a need to show a wider


## 第 602 页


business area, perhaps the entire problem space, the data


flow model works very well. You would possibly want to do


this when looking at the How-Now or “As is” view of the


work in order to establish the starting point and help define


the scope.


Figure 22.7 shows an example of looking at the wider scope.


![embedded_p602_103.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p602_103.jpeg)


## 第 603 页


Figure 22.7 A data flow model illustrating the full extent


of a problem space


Data flow models are very business friendly, and we believe


that the addition of recognizable data flows helps


stakeholders have a rapport with your models of their work.


Business Events and BUCs


Business events are an important idea, and we have spent some


time discussing them. The advantage of combining business


events and process modeling is that the business event gives


you well-defined start and end points for your models.


In Chapter 20 we looked at scenarios, and you saw the example


of an airline passenger and his bags being checked onto a


flight. Please refer back to that scenario if you wish and


compare it with a process model of the same business use case


in Figure 22.5. Consider your stakeholders and consider what


you need to communicate. In some cases, a scenario would be


preferable, and in others, a diagram will best convey the


needed information. A scenario can be more detailed, but in


some cases, the higher level of abstraction that a diagram


provides is preferable. We leave it to you to experiment and


## 第 604 页


decide which form of representation is most appropriate for


the situation.


Figure 22.8 shows the business use case where the passenger


checks onto a flight. It is triggered by the passenger


arriving at the desk, bringing with him the data needed to


check in. It ends when the outcome of the BUC has been


achieved. That is, the passenger and his bags are


successfully checked onto the flight. It means that all the


data has been processed and the needed parts of the data have


been stored, the outputs—boarding pass, bag tags—have been


produced, and there is nothing left for this BUC to do.


## 第 605 页


![embedded_p605_104.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p605_104.jpeg)


## 第 606 页


![embedded_p605_104.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p605_104.jpeg)


Figure 22.8 An activity diagram showing a passenger checking


in for a flight. This is the equivalent of the scenario and


the data flow model shown previously.


In Figure 22.8, note the swimlanes, the dotted lines that


divide the work between the participants. Swimlanes are


optional, and they are a double-edged sword. They provide a


clear explanation of who is doing what in the current


implementation—the How-Now view. However, it is highly


likely that different processors will be used in a future


solution; in which case the swimlanes can be misleading. And


they must never be taken as a constraint. They are there to


explain the current work and must not be considered


unchangeable. We suggest that when you are modeling the


essential view—What-Now and Future What—you omit swimlanes.


The activity diagram shows parallel processing. For example,


the Check Bags and Print Boarding Pass activities can be


performed at the same time. The black bar shows the point at


## 第 607 页


which processing can be split and become parallel. This is


called a fork node.


The activity diagram also shows a join node—the second


black bar on Figure 22.8. This symbol means that all


processing must reach this point before proceeding. In the


case of the airline check-in, the entire process cannot end


until both the bag tags and the boarding pass have been


printed.


Diamonds can be used to denote decisions, just as they are in


traditional flowcharts. We tend to leave them out where the


conditions are obvious or can be shown by attaching guard


conditions (the words in brackets at the exit of an


activity). When using activity diagrams during requirements


work, simplicity is more useful than correct and complete use


of the notation.


When to Use Process Models


The short answer is whenever you like. A better answer is


that whenever you are discussing a business process, you


should consider sketching a process model.


When You are Getting Started


## 第 608 页


Suppose your customer sells a product that is quite


specialized. Your client’s customers make customized orders.


You could start with a very simple process model, as shown in


Figure 22.9.


![embedded_p608_105.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p608_105.jpeg)


Figure 22.9 This was sketched early in the project as a


high-level model to illustrate the business flow.


The activities in Figure 22.9 are high level—they simply


group the detailed processing into useful chunks. A high-


level model such as this is used to start the discussion with


your stakeholders. The first activity, Customize the Order,


## 第 609 页


is a human activity where Kevin and the customer decide on


the customization of the product. The activity is annotated


to indicate that it is a human activity. This is a


complicated activity and will need some trawling to see if it


could be improved. Fulfill the Order and Shipping are both to


be done by ready-made components. This is flagged by the


addition of the “out of the box” symbol. Finally, Hesta in


accounting does the billing manually.


The two activities to be done by the ready-mades do not have


to be specified in detail (you can think of them as black


boxes), apart from any configuration and the data interfaces


into and out of them.


This model would be used by the requirements discoverer to


get an agreement from the client that this is the correct


response to the business event Customer wants to place an


order, and to highlight the areas where further investigation


is needed.


When You Are Prototyping with Models


Prototyping, as we use the term for requirements discovery,


is building a number of candidate solutions. These are probed


and explored to determine if they solve the right business


problem. We discussed prototyping in earlier chapters.


## 第 610 页


Let us say that your client is a fashion retailer and wants


to have an innovative way for her customers to shop, one that


will attract younger, more trendy shoppers. Now let’s say


that you and your team brainstorm candidate solutions. So


that you can discuss them and show them to your client, you


sketch process models such as the one shown in Figure 22.10


as part of your prototyping sessions.


![embedded_p610_106.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p610_106.jpeg)


Figure 22.10 A sketched candidate prototype using a process


model


## 第 611 页


You have annotated your process model with some figurative


elements to make it potentially more attractive and


understandable to your client. You could use this model to


explain to your client that the clothing displayed in the


store is currently grouped according to designer, as it is in


many large department stores. As a result, a shopper in one


designer’s area would not know what was available in other


areas. This solution allows shoppers to be made aware if


there are alternatives to the item they have picked off the


rack. Perhaps the idea of a robot delivering clothing might


be a little bit startling to a shopper, but then, it might be


fun to have a friendly robot following you around the store


carrying the clothing you have selected so far.


You would discuss and argue these things with your team and


your client, changing the process model as needed, and


probing it to ensure that this candidate is viable. Keep in


mind that this process model is a prototype. If it doesn’t


work out, you discard it and go on to the next one.


When You Are Doing How-Now Modeling


One of our clients, a medical insurance organization,


realized it had grown so quickly that it lost control of its


internal business processes. Members of each department were


## 第 612 页


more or less making up their processes as they went along and


building ad hoc software to suit themselves. This resulted in


very little coordination between different departments, and


soon enough, management realized the business was inefficient


due to its tangled and overlapping processes.


We started by having the people who worked in different


departments sketch process models of some of their most


important processes. These models were depictions of what


existed at the moment—the How-Now view.


When they brought these models together, it became obvious


that there was a lot of redundancy due to different


departments duplicating some—quite a lot, actually—of their


business processes. They used the models to put together a


What-Now view—the essence of the business. The duplication


and overlap were eliminated, and data that could be shared


was centralized. The resultant set of essential process


models was then used as the basis for further improving and


then reimplementing their systems.


Review


Process models are a trawling tool that are at their best


when proposing, documenting, or demonstrating a business


## 第 613 页


process. Much of your analytical work has to do with business


processes: what has to be done when a student wants to


register at a university; what activities are needed when a


cargo agent needs to book an air shipment; and so on.


A process model gives you a graphical way to show a business


process to your stakeholders. The diagramming notation is not


so complex as to be daunting to those unfamiliar with it.


Which is, by the way, why we have been urging you not to


become involved with the rich language of BPMN and UML and to


stick to a basic subset that uses only a few symbols.


We spoke about process models back when we were discussing


prototyping. A process model can be a great way to


demonstrate a proposal. After all, your prototypes are


candidate solutions, which are almost always a business


process.


Process models also play a part in process improvement. By


building a graphical model of an existing process, it becomes


easier for your stakeholders to locate the chokepoints,


redundant activities, and inconsistencies.


The ability to see the process laid out in graphical form


also makes it easier to see the essence. For each activity on


## 第 614 页


a model, you ask why. Why is this process here? What does it


contribute? Is it part of an essential policy, or is it there


for some technological or organizational reason?


Finally, there is communication. Once your stakeholders


become familiar with, or at least unafraid of, the


diagramming notation, you can demonstrate and communicate


more fluidly. Showing your client an essential process model


and using it to explain a proposed new way of working brings


clarity to the conversation. Sure, you need words to fill in


the details, but the model provides the road map for your


communication.


Resources


BPMN Quick and Easy: Using Method and Style. Process Mapping


Guidelines and Examples Using the Business Process Modeling


Standard by Bruce Silver (Cody-Cassidy Press, 2017). As the


(rather long) title suggests, this is an entry to BPMN, and


also provides style rules for building your models.


Learning UML 2.0: A Pragmatic Introduction to UML by Russell


Miles and Kim Hamilton (O’Reilly, 2006). This demonstrates


UML and describes how to draw UML models. The activity


diagram is the one you would use most. The book also


## 第 615 页


discusses how to use UML as a prototyping tool or during the


Trawling activity.


There are also endless online resources for UML and BPMN.


## 第 616 页


Chapter 23. Stored Data


Every organization, every solution, every system stores data.


Your phone (a solution) stores data: Your phone numbers are


data, your messages are data, your banking app stores data,


your to-do list is data, your calendar, your settings, your


notes . . . the list is endless.


We process data all the time. When you make a payment using a


card, phone, or watch, you are processing data. The data


representing your money is moved from your account to the


recipient’s account. When you look at your card statement,


you are looking at stored data that has been processed and


stored for every transaction in the past month.


Data is all around us; it is part of every problem space and


solution. Knowing more about it helps you learn more about


the processes that surround the data, as well as the


requirements for the processes and the data.


Data and process are joined at the hip. You can’t have one


without the other. There is no such thing as data that is not


processed; there is no process that is not processing data.


Both have requirements, which is what we are interested in


here.


## 第 617 页


Before going too far into this, we have to say that the


business analyst is not designing a database. The business


data models that we are discussing here are input to the


database design process, but for the moment, let’s talk


about the business data.


As we are concerned only with business analysis, we shall


stick to modeling the essential stored data. Also, because we


are concerned with business analysis and requirements


discovery, we are using a simplified notation for our data


models. You will also come across class diagrams (from UML),


entity relationship diagrams, and other notations. By all


means use those if your company so decrees, but the models


you see here are sufficient for your trawling.


When you are trawling, you are usually trawling for business


processes. All processes use data one way or another, so


discovering the data is a way of discovering the processes.


Alternatively, discovering the processes also discovers the


needed data.


Let’s look at stored data and how it is connected to


requirements.


Data Models


## 第 618 页


Data models are an abstraction of the real world. A data


model is made up of entities that reflect real-world things.


(You can use the UML term “classes” if you prefer.) In the


real world, things are connected, so the data model shows


relationships (associations in UML) between the entities.


For example, you have a bank account—a thing—and it is


linked to your debit card—another thing.


These things can be represented by data. The debit card has


a number, your name, expiry date, CCV, and so on. These data


items—we’ll call them attributes—belong to an entity,


which naturally enough you would call Debit Card. Your bank


account also has an identifying account number, account


balance, and so forth. Because it is a thing that is uniquely


identifiable, it too is an entity. When you buy something,


the transaction must be recorded (another entity) so that the


transaction amount can be debited from your bank account.


If you are trawling this business, the aforementioned things


become entities on your data model.


Entities don’t stand alone; they are linked to other


entities by relationships. Relationships represent some


real-world associations needed by the business. These


relationships are established by business processes. For


## 第 619 页


example, when your bank issued you a debit card for your


account, it established the relationship between the card and


the account. When you use your card to buy something, the


transaction has to be linked to your card and your bank.


Figure 23.1 shows the resultant data model.


![embedded_p619_107.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p619_107.jpeg)


Figure 23.1 Three entities and the relationships that model


the activity of your debit card


The big deal about data models is that by trying to build one


for the data stored in your problem space, you have to


discover the data entities and how they relate to each other.


It is by questioning what the data is and how the pieces are


## 第 620 页


linked that you discover more about the business you are


investigating.


Let’s look at an example. Some countries are introducing


charges for heavy trucks using their highways. This is


beginning to happen in European countries, but it is a


possibility for some cash-strapped states in the United


States to raise a little revenue from trucks driving through


interstates within their borders. The countries or states do


not want to install toll barriers—barriers slow down


traffic. Instead, they probably want some electronic sensing


system to detect trucks on their highways.


Let us say that you are trawling this piece of business to


find its requirements. These requirements will eventually be


used to construct a (probably automated) solution.


What entities spring to mind? Truck is an obvious one, as is


Road. You need these two because you are charging the truck


for using the road. The entities on the data model are not


themselves data—they have no alphanumeric value—but they


can be thought of as “containers for attributes.”


Attributes are the individual items of data that have an


alphanumeric value: a date, an amount of money, a name, the


price of something. Each attribute must belong to its


## 第 621 页


relevant entity. You can’t have an attribute of, say, credit


card number, in an entity called Stock Item.


The entity Truck would have attributes including the license


plate number, the country or state issuing the license plate,


the type of truck, its weight, and so on. This entity on your


data model represents not just a single truck, but all the


trucks that may use the roads. This is why the word “class”


can be used to refer to entities; it’s the class of the


thing of which there are many instances. Because there are


many of these things, each one must have a unique identifier.


In this case, the license plate together with the country or


state of issue identifies an individual truck. By the way,


you need the state or the country as part of the identifier,


as it is not beyond the bounds of possibility that a plate


from one state could have identical characters to that from


another.


The next data entity to represent a real-world thing is the


Road. The Road would have data attributes such as a road


identifier—Interstate 70, county road 57, European or


national road numbers —and some geographical data, permitted


uses, and so on. The road identifier is needed because there


are lots of roads in the problem space.


## 第 622 页


Now we have to link these two things. However, they don’t


directly relate to each other for the purpose of this


business. Sure, a truck can drive on a road and a road can


carry a truck, but the business charges for each instance


that a truck uses a road. This means we need another entity,


this one a conceptual or intangible one, which we call


Journey. See the partial model in Figure 23.2.


![embedded_p622_108.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p622_108.jpeg)


Figure 23.2 The partial data model reflecting the narrative


of the business as we have it so far


There is more of this model to come, but let’s pause here


and consider what we have. Keep in mind that we are trying to


## 第 623 页


understand a business and find its requirements by building a


model of the data that it stores.


So far, we have three entities on this model; Road and Truck


are obvious. The third entity, Journey, needs some


explanation.


A truck will drive along many roads, and a road will carry


many trucks. When you investigate the business, you find that


it needs to keep track of which truck drove along which


roads. This is data and thus needs an entity to store it, so


you create the Journey entity to contain it. Naturally


enough, there has to be a new instance of Journey created


whenever a truck drives on a road.


The lines between the entities represent the relationships


(associations in UML terminology) between them. Note the


characters attached to the relationship line: “1” means a


single instance, and the “⁕” means many instances of the


entity.


An instance of Journey can belong only to one Road—you


can’t be simultaneously using several roads—whereas over


time a road will experience many instances of Journey. An


instance of Journey can only be created by a single truck,


## 第 624 页


but the truck will use roads many times, and for each time


there must be a new instance of Journey to record that


particular usage.


To show this you put an “⁕” at the Journey end of the


relationship, and as there can only be one Truck making an


individual journey, you mark the Truck end of the


relationship with a “1”. Similarly, an instance of Journey


can only be made on one Road, but a Road will be used many


times, so that is tagged with a “1” and a “⁕”. It’s


easier to call this a “one to many” relationship. These


cardinality (or multiplicity) notations are there to tell


you a little more about the business.


Let’s get on with the requirements for this piece of work.


The data model and the business policy are mirrors of each


other. To carry out the policy, any business needs data. You


can find functionality by finding the data, or having found


some data, determine the functionality that uses it.


You interview the road authority and ask about their business


policy for charging for a Journey. Do they charge for the


distance a truck travels on a road, or the time spent on the


road? Does the weight of the truck come into the charging


calculation? Does the truck’s cargo affect the charge?


## 第 625 页


The answers to these questions bring a need for data.


The road authority tells you that they intend to charge for


the distance traveled on a road, which is probably the most


viable way to do it. However, roads can be very long—


hundreds or thousands of miles/kilometers—and a truck might


not traverse the full distance. Ideally, you would charge the


truck from the exact point it entered the road to the exact


point it left the road. However, to monitor every possible


entry and exit from a highway would be prohibitively


expensive and problematic. The stakeholders tell you that


there are already gantries (or overhanging signs) erected


across roads to provide signage—distances to cities along


the way, upcoming exits, traffic conditions, and so on. As


these exist, they have known geographic locations, and it is


probably feasible to add scanners to monitor truck activity.


This means the gantries can be used as checkpoints for


measuring distance. It is not as precise as entry/exit


monitoring but is deemed to be good enough. A scanner every


50 miles or so would be sufficient.


Now we need more data, specifically about the Gantry. When a


truck passes its first gantry it establishes a new instance


of Journey, which is attached to the Gantry entity. As the


truck passes subsequent gantries, they too are attached to


## 第 626 页


the Journey entity. This continues until the truck stops


passing gantries and the distance traveled can be calculated.


Figure 23.3 shows the revised data model.


![embedded_p626_109.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p626_109.jpeg)


Figure 23.3 This version of the data model introduces the


gantry. Gantries have scanners attached to detect trucks. The


gantries are needed to determine the distance of a truck’s


journey on a road.


## 第 627 页


The data model is mirroring the business policy. It also


gives you requirements. For example, there is now a


requirement to establish the gantries in the solution. There


will in fact be a new business event to establish a gantry,


and another to delete it, change it, and so on.


Similarly, the data attributes of Journey need to be used


(you cannot have data that is not processed, just as you


cannot have a process with no data). The attribute Distance


Traveled is the basis for charging. From the relationships,


you know which truck made the journey and which road was


used. This information is used to send out an invoice. Your


solution must retain a history of the invoices, so more


stored data in the form of another entity is needed. This one


is attached to Journey because that is what you are billing


for.


![embedded_p627_110.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p627_110.jpeg)


You are discovering requirements, either by deriving them


from a data model or by using the data model to drive your


discovery. Let’s question the cardinality of the


## 第 628 页


relationship between Journey and Invoice. Is it—reading left


to right—one to one, meaning that one invoice is sent for


one journey (i.e., as soon as the truck’s journey has ended,


an invoice is generated)? Or is the cardinality many to one,


meaning that one invoice is sent for a collection of all the


journeys a truck made within a billing cycle? You go back to


the stakeholders to discuss this. It’s an issue you have to


resolve, as it would be easy to presume the wrong approach.


You write your requirements for whichever approach is


selected.


Then we have the problem of the invoice—who exactly is


invoiced? You can’t send an invoice to a truck, so


presumably it must go to the truck’s owner. Now it becomes


more complicated. Some—probably most—of the truck owners


are large haulage companies and have many trucks. Should the


authority send an invoice for each journey, or for all the


journeys the owner’s trucks have completed in the billing


cycle?


Consider the data model as it is shown in Figure 23.4. This


represents what we know so far on the business policy and the


data needed to support that business policy. If the road


authority had wanted to charge for the weight of the truck,


then more data would be needed as an attribute of the Truck


## 第 629 页


entity. Additionally, if the truck’s cargo influences the


road-charging calculation, we would need another entity


called Cargo with a relationship with the Truck.


![embedded_p629_111.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p629_111.jpeg)


Figure 23.4 The completed (so far) data model of the road-


charging business


## 第 630 页


But let’s leave it here. The point of the exercise is that


you can discover the stored data and the functionality needed


to process that data at the same time. And discovering one


helps you discover the other.


You can discover the stored data and the


functionality needed to process that data at the


same time. And discovering one helps you discover


the other.


Business Events


Business events are significant to the data model because it


is business events that bring data into our solutions, and


then later process the data and send it to the outside


world. These flows of data into and out of the business area


are shown on the context model (see Figure 23.5). Each flow


on this model is connected to a business event.


## 第 631 页


![embedded_p631_112.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p631_112.jpeg)


Figure 23.5 The context model for the road-charging problem


space


This is a simplified view of this piece of work; the real


thing is much more complicated. However, this will suffice


for our purposes.


An important business event occurs when a truck passes a


gantry. We can assume that the gantry scanners have license


plate recognition technology to identify each truck as it


passes. This business event triggers the incoming flow Truck


## 第 632 页


Detected, the data of which would include the truck license


plate number, the time the truck passed the gantry, and


probably more. The response to this business event is to


create a new instance of the Journey entity, or to update the


Journey entity if one had already been created by the truck


passing an earlier gantry on this road. The Journey entity is


linked to the Truck and Gantry entities. These will later be


used to calculate the invoice.


The business cannot magically know about trucks, so the


trucks have to be registered. This is another business event


that establishes the Truck entity and connects it to the


Owner. This ownership needs to be established if the business


is to send the right invoice to the right owner.


Another business event would establish a new owner, and so


on. Following is the list of business events derived from the


context model, in no particular order:


1. Owner wants to open an account


2. Owner wants to register a truck


3. Truck passes a gantry


4. Time for invoices to be sent


## 第 633 页


5. Road Maintenance builds a new road or changes one


6. Road Maintenance installs a scanner in a gantry


Hang on to that for a moment while we look at the CRUD check.


CRUD Check


The CRUD check—Create Read Update Delete—is used to ensure


that you have all the business events, and that all the data


entities are relevant and correctly used. It works like this:


Every entity must be Created. They don’t magically fall out


of the sky; they have to be created and it takes a business


event to create one. Creating an entity makes no sense unless


it is used, so there must be at least one business event to


Read the entity. Some of the entities are Updated (by


business events) and some might be Deleted (also by business


events). So, we are using the entities from the data model


and the business events to build the CRUD table.


At this point, let’s take a small diversion.


You don’t have to build the data model to find the entities.


As previously mentioned, an entity is something that is


identified. It is also a thing that itself has no


## 第 634 页


alphanumeric value, but attributes of data with values are


attached to it. This means you can make a list of the


entities by looking for things in the problem space that are


identified and about which data is kept. For example, an


account always has a unique account number. A truck has a


license plate and state of issue, which uniquely identifies


any truck. Roads have numbers and the authority has data


about them. All these things are entities, and you can build


a CRUD table by simply listing them. End of diversion.


Next, you populate the CRUD table by listing all the entities


in the first column. Then, ask what business events process


it. All data must be processed in one way or another, so


you’re asking which business event creates, reads, updates,


or deletes that entity of data.


Figure 23.6 shows a populated CRUD table. It uses the


entities from the data model shown in Figure 23.4 and the


business event numbers from the list above.


## 第 635 页


![embedded_p635_113.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p635_113.jpeg)


Figure 23.6 The CRUD table showing the entities and the


business events that create, read, update, or delete them.


This table is complete with what you know to date. As you


progress with your investigation, you will fill in more of


the table.


The CRUD table is a check of the completeness of your


knowledge to date. Its purpose is to find any missing


business events and data entities. For instance, the table


shows that the Account entity is created by business event 1


## 第 636 页


when an Owner wants to open an account so that her trucks can


legally use the roads. It is read by business event 4 when it


is time for the invoices to be sent.


We have intentionally omitted the housekeeping business


events. These are things like Owners changing their details—


address, company name, and so on. We have left out all the


deletions—a gantry is removed, an account is closed, a truck


is taken out of service, and so on. These are omitted to make


it easier for you to see what is happening by not having


cluttered models. But you can expect your models back at work


to be more cluttered.


If you look through the table, you can see the combination of


business events and data entities that complete the work of


this piece of business. Or not quite. Note that there are


some blank cells on the table. These indicate that something


is missing.


For example, the Invoice entity is created by business event


4, but there are no other events that use it. Data that is


created should be read; otherwise, it has no purpose. In this


case, the lack of a read business event can be explained if


there is another solution—say, an adjacent accounting


## 第 637 页


solution—that uses the Invoice entity. Otherwise, the blank


cell would indicate a missing business event.


The Gantry entity is neither updated nor deleted—we said we


have omitted the housekeeping events. The Journey entity is


updated by business event 3. This is the business event that


happens when a truck passes a gantry. The business use case


responding to the event calculates and updates the Distance


Traveled attribute.


And so, you work through the CRUD table. You’re looking for


entities that are not read, updated, or deleted. If there is


not a business explanation for this, the explanation is that


you are missing a business event. If there is an entity that


is read without being created, then the explanation is


certainly a missing business event. By the time you have


worked over the whole table, you can be certain that you have


all the events and all the data.


Review


The world sometimes seems to be divided into two kinds of


business analysts: those who model process and those who


model data. But there is every reason why you should become


## 第 638 页


an analyst who models process and data and, ideally, does it


in parallel.


Data models are revealing. The stored data of a piece of


business reflects its business policy. You store data because


you need it to run the business, and the data is stored,


read, updated, and deleted by business processes. These


processes exist because of the business events that the


business responds to. Data is brought into the business by


the triggering data flow belonging to a business event and


leaves the business on the outgoing flow of a (usually time-


triggered) event.


You can look at a data model and ask what business event


creates, reads, updates, or deletes this entity.


Alternatively, you can look at the data attributes of data


flows connected to business events and ask what entities of


data these belong to.


Data entities represent the things that are important to the


business. Anything that is uniquely identified or has data


stored about it is important and so becomes an entity on your


data model. The relationships between the entities are


determined by the processing done by the business. That is,


whenever a business event happens, the responding BUC will


## 第 639 页


form or update a relationship. To do this, it will create


and/or read the entities that it is linking.


When you come to build or buy your solution, it requires


stored data to support its functionality. This probably means


a database. The business data model we have been discussing


here is a conceptual model. However, it shows the necessary


data, and that makes it the foundation of the database


design. The database designers take your conceptual model and


add the technological pieces to turn it into a database


design. However, database design should not influence the way


in which you see the business’s stored data. Your model is


of the essential data needed to support the business


activities, and you are using it for requirements discovery.


Resources


Data Modeling Made Simple: A Practical Guide for Business and


IT Professionals by Steve Hoberman (Technics Publications,


2009). Hoberman is an engaging writer and his take on data


modeling is both straightforward and comprehensive. He shows


you how to model data and, importantly, when and why you


should.


## 第 640 页


Data Modeling Essentials by Graeme Simsion and Graham Witt


(Morgan Kaufmann, 2004). This is the third edition of this


popular book, and it takes you through the basics and theory


of data modeling, discusses the stages of applied data


modeling, and addresses advanced subjects including business


rules.


Any of the books on UML discuss the class diagram. This is


UML-speak for data models.


## 第 641 页


Chapter 24. Other Trawling Techniques


We have been looking at different methods of trawling for


requirements. You will use some of these methods a lot, most


noticeably workshops, scenarios, and process models. There


are also other techniques that are equally useful but that do


not need an entire chapter to themselves.


The task of discovering requirements needs a certain amount


of flexibility. If one technique is not working for you and


your stakeholders, then switch to another. Use several at the


same time. Additionally, some approaches are more appropriate


to different circumstances. We advise you to have a well-


stocked toolbox so that no matter what the target, you always


have the appropriate tool.


Two very important tools are the ones on either side of your


head. Listening is where you learn the most, provided you’re


listening and not just hearing. Listening is caring about


what is being said and listening beyond the words to the


sometimes-unspoken essence of the conversation. And of


course, that gray thing you have between your ears is equally


important.


## 第 642 页


Another useful tool is “Why?” Asking why repeatedly is one


of the most effective ways to discover requirements. It is


only by arriving at the underlying—and often unspoken—


essence of the problem that you are you able to discover the


right problem to solve and the right requirements to solve


it.


There are other practices that are useful for requirements


discovery. However, these are practices that are not often


used but people have written whole books about them. We feel


it is beyond our remit to try to deal with these things


exhaustively here—things such as ethnography, or studying


the situation through close observation of the participants,


seeking to understand their motivation; family therapy, or


understanding that you don’t have to get people to agree


with each other, but you do have to get them to communicate


with each other (we could use a lot of that in our


legislatures); the Soft Systems methodology; systems


thinking; psychology; and more. These are soft sciences,


which are hard to describe and learn but can be useful when


the problem is complex and its participants are unsure. Most


of these are referenced in the Resources section at the end


of the chapter.


## 第 643 页


What follows are some techniques that are not so soft and


that at some stage will be useful to you.


Apprenticing


Apprenticing—based on the old idea of masters and


apprentices—is a wonderful way to observe and learn the work


as it really happens. In this case, you are the apprentice,


and the user of the current solution assumes the role of


master craftsman. You sit with the user at her place of


work, learning the job by making observations, asking


questions, and perhaps doing some of the work under


supervision. This technique is also sometimes known as “job


shadowing.”


Apprenticing is particularly useful for in-house


work. The underlying assumption for apprenticing


is that users are currently doing work, and you,


as the business analyst, have to understand their


work and the purpose behind it. This work could


be clerical, commercial, graphic arts,


engineering, or almost anything short of brain


surgery.


## 第 644 页


It is unlikely that many users, sitting in a conference room


or on a remote call, can explain what they do in enough


detail for you to understand the work and thereby capture its


requirements. When users are away from their work, they tend


to generalize. While generalizations can be useful, they do


not provide all the detail you need for your requirements


discovery.


“Nobody can talk better about what they do and


why they do it than they can while in the middle


of doing it.”—Hugh Beyer and Karen Holtzblatt,


Contextual Design: Defining Customer-Centered


Systems


Nor can you expect users to have the presentation and


teaching skills needed to present their work effectively to


others. Conversely, almost everyone is good at explaining


what they are doing while they are doing it. Apprenticing


cannot take place in high-security environments (unless you


have the appropriate clearance), nor will it be effective in


very high-pressure, busy situations like air traffic control.


Most of the time you are talking to people in normal offices


and workplaces. It is here that a user can do a running


commentary of the work as it happens, and that commentary


## 第 645 页


provides the details that might otherwise be lost. While she


is working, the user can describe her task precisely and tell


you why she is doing things. If the explanation is not clear,


the apprentice (that’s you) asks questions: “Why did you do


that?” “What does this mean?” “How often does this


happen?” “What happens if this piece of information is not


here?” You also get to see the things that can go wrong, the


special cases, and the workarounds she uses when things are


not normal. Through the process of apprenticing, you come to


see all the cases and the actions the user takes for each of


them.


Apprenticeship can be combined with modeling. As you observe


the work and the user explains it, you sketch a model of the


tasks and their connections with the other tasks (see Figure


24.1). As you build your models, you feed them back to the


user and confirm that they are correct. You use this feedback


to raise questions about any areas of uncertainty. These


models would certainly be about the How-Now, but they might


well serve as the starting point for envisioning the future,


improved solution.


## 第 646 页


![embedded_p646_114.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p646_114.jpeg)


Figure 24.1 The requirements analyst learns the work while


sitting at the user’s desk, sometimes building models of the


work while learning it.


## 第 647 页


When you are apprenticing, you are an interpreter as well as


an observer. When you are looking at the current work, you


must abstract away from what you see to overcome the user’s


close connection to the physical incarnation of the work. In


other words, the artifacts, the technology, and other inputs


that are currently used must be seen as a product of a


previous solution designer. But times have changed. Today it


may be possible to do things in ways that were impossible


yesterday. Better ways may now be available that take


advantage of up-to-date technology, ways that use streamlined


processes, ways that simplify the work or automate some or


all of it.


But first you have to abstract. While you are learning the


work by seeing it done in real-world conditions, you are


abstracting from the current technology to find the


underlying essence of the work. We looked at essence a little


earlier, and if you need a refresher on finding the essence


of the business, feel free to divert back to Chapter 16, The


Essence of the Problem.


Needless to say, apprenticing is about finding the real


problem that your future solution should solve.


Interviewing


## 第 648 页


Interviewing is used by almost all projects, as


it is really a part of all elicitation


techniques. Despite its omnipresence, we suggest


that you do not use interviewing as the only way


to discover requirements. Rather, you should


conduct interviews in conjunction with the other


techniques discussed in this chapter and


elsewhere.


Interviewing the stakeholders is a technique that is commonly


employed but is not without its problems. Just as with


apprenticing, the interviewer relies on the interviewee to


know—and be able to verbalize— knowledge of the work.


Interviewing may work very well when people are knowledgeable


about their work, but that knowledge is often restricted to


their own immediate area. There are likely to be few people


in the organization who understand enough of the business to


be the sole person to describe it for you.


Some business analysts draw up a questionnaire and send it to


the stakeholder in advance of the interview. While this


preparatory step gives some structure to the subsequent


interview, we have found few stakeholders who are motivated


enough, or who have time enough, to fill in a questionnaire


## 第 649 页


prior to meeting the analyst. We suggest that you send a


brief agenda listing the topics that you wish to cover in


your interview along with the planned duration of the


interview. This notification at least gives the stakeholder a


chance to think in background mode, to have needed material


close by, or to ask subject-matter experts to be present.


Stakeholders should not remain completely passive while being


interviewed. Instead, you must involve them by building


models—process models, scenarios, and so on—during the


interview. This approach of creating something visual


provides a feedback loop between you and your stakeholders,


and it means you can test the accuracy of what you are being


told.


Try these guidelines to make your interviews more effective.


• Set the interview in context—explain the scope of what you


wish to cover. This step is necessary to avoid the


stakeholders talking about something irrelevant to your


purpose. It also gives them a chance to withdraw gracefully


if they have not prepared for the interview.


• Limit the duration of the interview to the time stated in


the agenda. We find that interviews running for more than an


## 第 650 页


hour (90 minutes tops) tend to lose focus.


• Use business use cases as an anchor for the interview.


Stakeholders recognize business use cases (although they may


not necessarily call them by that name), and it makes for


more directed conversations if you talk about their work one


business use case at a time.


Feed back your understanding. Build models while


you are interviewing the stakeholder.


• Ask a question (more on this in a moment), listen to the


answer, and then feed back your understanding.


• Draw models and encourage the customer to change them.


There are plenty of models you can use to help you


communicate your understanding of a process—for example,


data flow diagrams, activity diagrams, and rich pictures. You


can also construct data models for information and mind maps


to link different subjects. (Rich pictures are covered later


in this chapter; there is a citation for mind maps in the


Resources section.)


• Use the stakeholders’ terminology and artifacts, both


conceptual and real. If the stakeholders do not use their own


## 第 651 页


language, then you force them to make technological


translations into terms they think you will understand.


Sadly, this usually leads to misunderstandings. By contrast,


if you ask questions about their terminology, you inevitably


make new discoveries.


• Thank the stakeholders for their time, and tell them what


you learned and why it was valuable. After all, they have


lots of other things to do. Talking to you is not the reason


they are employed, and they often view the interview as an


interruption to their work.


• Write down what you were told. We guarantee you’ll have


more questions


Asking the Right Questions


Let’s look at this by using an example. Say that you’re


working on a project to build a solution to manage the


deicing of roads in winter. (You saw this project in Chapter


7, Business Events.) The solution must involve a network of


weather stations that sense temperature and pressure. Let’s


say that you are interviewing the chief engineer.


The business event you want to explore this time is Road


engineering installs a new weather station. Your questions


## 第 652 页


should focus on what the work does to respond to this


business event.


Business Analyst: “What happens when your engineers install


a new weather station?”


Chief Engineer: “They let us know where the new weather


station is located, and we keep a record of it.”


BA: “How do you keep this record?”


CE: “I’ll show you the spreadsheet that we use.”


BA: “Thank you. I’d like a copy of it, if possible. I see


that you keep track of the weather station number,


geographical coordinates, and installation date. What else do


you keep track of?”


CE: “We have another computer system where we have the


maintenance history for each weather station. There are some


double entries, but that’s the way it is.”


BA: “Is there any data you record that you don’t have any


use for?”


CE: “Yes, we record information about the crew that


installed the station and how long they took to do it. Nobody


## 第 653 页


ever looks at that. It’s a hangover from earlier days.”


BA: “Are there any other facts about the weather station


that would be useful to you?”


CE: “Well, we would like to know the manufacturer and


performance of each weather station.”


BA: “What do you mean by performance?’


CE: “Which weather stations need the most maintenance. This


would help in planning which new technology we spend our


budget on. However, we’ve never been able to do that in the


past.”


BA: “Would it be acceptable to you if you had a new system


that integrates all the information about the weather


stations, their maintenance, and their performance?”


CE: “What, you mean all on one screen?”


BA: “Possibly. It would be something that makes it possible


for you to track a weather station and its lifetime


performance.”


CE: “That sounds great, but I’d have to check it with some


of the engineers.”


## 第 654 页


BA: “Well, once I’ve made sure that I have all the facts


about the weather stations properly defined, then I could do


a quick mockup to show the engineers our ideas. How would


that be?”


CE: “I like the idea.”


BA: “Thanks for your time. I’ll go back and review my notes


and the samples you have given me, and I’ll send you a brief


summary of this interview. I might need to phone you with a


couple of questions. Then, I’ll make an appointment to


explore the mockup with the engineers. Is this approach okay


with you?


CE: “Yes, it is. Thank you.”


The Brown Cow viewpoints help you explore the


business use case as it is now, its essence, and


what it might be in the future.


In this interview, the business analyst uses the Brown Cow


viewpoints to help explore the business use case. He starts


by asking how the work is currently done (How-Now) and


discovers the spreadsheet and the other computer system for


maintenance of the weather stations. He asks, “What else do


## 第 655 页


you keep track of?” to discover the attributes that are


recorded (What-Now) when a new weather station is installed.


The question about “What other facts” and the one about


unused data are designed to uncover data that is not


currently recorded or is recorded and not made use of


(Future-What). Raising the idea of an integrated system and a


mockup (Future-How) is signaling the chief engineer that


there will probably be a better way of doing things once the


BA has properly understood the business of installing weather


stations.


Note that the BA used a lot of open questions. These begin


with “What,” “How,” “When,” “Where,” “Why,” or


“Who” (the “W” words), and they encourage the stakeholder


to give a detailed answer rather than simply “Yes” or


“No.”


Listening to the Answers


Being a good listener means being able to understand someone


else’s meaning behind their words. This is difficult. We


assign meanings to words based on our own assumptions,


experience, and preoccupations.


Also, especially when conducting an interview, we are often


afraid of silence. Silence might be interpreted as lack of


## 第 656 页


experience or lack of competence. In fact, the reverse is


true: It is comforting to have some silence and time for


reflection.


If you want to improve your listening skills, you can learn a


lot from the fields of psychology, sociology, and family


therapy. These disciplines have realized that to help people


with problems, you first have to understand what those people


mean by their words. In their book Clean Language, Wendy


Sullivan and Judy Rees talk about the power of “attending


exquisitely” to another person’s words. One of their hints


on improving listening skills is “Put your attention on what


the other person is actually saying rather than on the person


themselves, or what you think they might mean by their


words.” Another helpful piece of advice: “Repeat back some


of their words or phrases exactly as you heard them.” By


doing so, you demonstrate that you are, in fact, listening to


what that person is saying, and this feedback encourages them


to expand further on what they mean by their words.


Most of all, if you want to become a better listener, don’t


talk; develop an appreciation of silence.


Business Rules


## 第 657 页


Business rules are the internal “laws” of an


organization. They are self-governing; the organization


formulates them both for internal policy reasons and to


comply with industry standards and regulations, and of course


the laws of the country. They exist to direct operations,


people, and systems as to the rules they have to follow when


they do their work. Such rules can apply to any aspect of the


organization, from top management to the lowest-level


process. They can be as all-encompassing as “Employees are


directed not to commit any crime” or as detailed as “The


help desk employees will report to their supervisor any cases


that are still unresolved 48 hours after the first contact.”


Business rules can be written down, or they can be understood


by employees and verbally transmitted.


Some organizations have a process to methodically gather and


record their rules. Others approach this task less formally,


collecting business rules only as they arise during projects.


Sometimes new business rules that are discovered during a


project are recorded; other times, sadly, they are not. You


will find that business rules are expressed at varying levels


of specificity. You have to extract your requirements from


the business rules whatever state they are in.


Take this business rule as an example:


## 第 658 页


The maximum length of a truck driver’s shift is eight hours.


This business rule potentially affects the requirements for


solutions involved with the following:


• Establishment of a shift


• Monitoring shifts


• Who has to be informed


• Recording of each shift


• Scheduling trucks (you can’t schedule an assignment if the


driver cannot finish it within his eight-hour shift)


This means that your trawling uncovers requirements for


registering the beginning and the end of a shift, alerting


the depot management if any shift exceeds this limit, warning


the driver if he is approaching the shift limit, not


scheduling shifts longer than eight hours, and so on. The


point is that all business rules can give rise to


requirements, but first you have to find the business rules.


At the outset of the project, you should ask for the business


rules applicable to the project. Work through each business


use case and ensure that all appropriate business rules are


## 第 659 页


embedded into whichever model of the business use case you


are using. Business process owners are invaluable in helping


to find and interpret the applicable rules.


Your business use case scenarios (or other models) are a


sufficient and useful repository of the business rules. You


might consider recording new business rules as a by-product


of your requirements discovery. However, if the organization


does not have a formalized way of keeping its business rules,


then your business use case documentation is, for the moment,


a place to keep them. Be aware that some business rules apply


to more than one business use case, and for this reason,


among others, you should discuss with your management the


establishment of a central repository.


Rich Pictures


A rich picture is a graphical representation of your problem


space. Usually, a rich picture has a wider scope than just


the proposed product to be built and thus has the greater


value of showing the proposed product within its ecosystem.


There are no fixed conventions for rich pictures; you simply


draw whatever symbols, icons, or pictures you wish, or write


whatever text you feel is appropriate. All of these represent


## 第 660 页


elements that are used in the business. When you are drawing


a rich picture, you are forced to think deeply about the


problem to be able to represent it pictorially. This is an


exercise known as action learning. But let’s not talk about


pictures, let’s look at one.


The rich picture shown in Figure 24.2 identifies the problem


space for a project to build a dive computer. (Dive computers


are used by scuba divers to capture their time underwater and


their blood nitrogen levels, and to warn the diver when it is


time to start surfacing.) A rich picture is particularly


effective for capturing the scope of the problem. We


discussed this in Chapter 5, Goals-Scope-Stakeholders. Rather


than just focusing on the dive computer, the rich picture


identifies all the elements in the world that might have an


effect on the problem and the solution.


## 第 661 页


![embedded_p661_115.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p661_115.jpeg)


Figure 24.2 The rich picture of a scuba diving problem


space. Various elements and actors are shown, together with


some of their connections.


## 第 662 页


A technique for drawing a rich picture is to choose one


element of the problem. Start with the most obvious one—in


this case, the Dive Computer. Take a wider view by asking the


question: What else in the problem space might have


requirements that affect the dive computer? Suppose you say


the Diver has requirements about the different types of dive


computer. There are a number of existing Manufacturers. Some


divers want a connection between their Air Tank and the


computer; what sorts of air tanks exist? The diver might buy


a computer from one of the Dive Shops…and so on. You keep on


expanding the problem space by asking why you want to know


about each element and whether it raises requirements that


are relevant to the problem space. If you are not sure


whether an element should be included in the rich picture,


then include it but only until you are sure it has nothing to


do with the problem you are trying to solve.


Rich pictures are used at the beginning of a project to


ensure that all the stakeholders concur that it is an


accurate portrayal of the scope and activity of the


customer’s problem.


Creativity Workshops


## 第 663 页


Asking people what they want doesn’t always result in the


best future solution. Companies have gone out of business by


providing only what their customers ask for. This is because


customers ask for incremental improvements to what they have


at the moment. People generally don’t know what they want


until they see it. However, as soon as they see a new and


innovative solution, they will abandon the old supplier and


buy from the new. And it’s not just high-tech companies


(Nokia, Motorola, Blackberry, etc.) that fall into this pit.


Companies providing everyday business solutions disappear


too.


So, for the moment, let’s put aside asking what is wanted


and see if we can come up with better ideas that might bring


better and more desirable solutions.


As a consumer, you buy new products or services if they offer


you a genuine differentiation and advantage over your


previous products, or they are things that were previously


unavailable. Part of the task of a business analyst is to set


aside the presumed or asked-for solution and try to discover


something better.


The fundamental idea of a creativity workshop is to make use


of the group effect. There is the myth of the lone inventor


## 第 664 页


working in isolation in a lonely attic, but it is only a


myth. Almost all innovation comes from a team. Thomas Edison


is credited with hundreds of inventions, but it was Edison’s


team of engineers who were doing all the hard work. Edison


owned the company and got most of the credit, but it’s his


team that deserves it.


You must also be prepared to work hard, and to fail. Thomas


Edison’s tongue-in-cheek comment, “I have not failed. I’ve


just found 10,000 ways that won’t work” sums up working and


failing. But “failing” only means that an experiment


didn’t work, and you learn from it. The “failure” prompted


you to try again. In the end, you find something that works,


and works better than what your customer has at the moment.


The rules of running a creativity workshop are simple.


Get the right people. You need at least four, but don’t go


over about eight. Imaginative people are naturally the best


ones, but as long as you avoid obviously negative people,


you’ll find that most people will contribute.


Make sure everyone understands the topic. They have done


their homework and have come to the workshop with knowledge


of the problem and the goals of the project. You’re wasting


## 第 665 页


time if you have to spend the first half of the workshop


explaining what you need to achieve.


No evaluation, no criticism, no debate, no idea killers.


Nothing stops creativity more than a naysayer pouring cold


water on ideas. It doesn’t matter if an idea is not viable,


would cost too much, would be too disruptive, is not “our


way of doing things”—the idea will lead to another, better


one. For the moment, any idea is a good one. Later, you can


sort the gold nuggets from the chocolate teapots.


Have wild ideas and lots of ideas. Not all of these ideas


will turn out to be useful, but the more ideas you have to


play with, the more likely it is that one of them will turn


out to be the game changer.


Combination and improvement are encouraged. Build on other


people’s ideas and use their ideas to trigger your own.


Remove constraints. Pretend, for the moment, that a


constraint is not a fact of life. What happens if you remove


it, or carry on as if it were not constraining you? What


ideas come from the new situation?


Combine ideas. Take the phone and the camera, for example.


Who would have thought that two such disparate things could


## 第 666 页


be combined to universal popularity?


The thrust of the creativity workshop is to find innovative


solutions that are demonstrably better than the current


situation or any presumed solution that has been put forward.


It is only by innovation that we advance. Consumer technology


would still be in the 19th century if we gave people only


what they asked for.


Document Archeology


Document archeology is a technique of searching


through existing reports, documents, and files,


looking for underlying requirements. It is best


used when you have some existing or legacy


system, and plan to modify or renew it.


Documents can be paper documents, electronic files, or


screens. Doing archeology on them intends to uncover their


underlying requirements. Document archeology entails


reverse-engineering new requirements from the documents used


or produced by the current work. Along the way, you look for


requirements that should become part of the new product.


## 第 667 页


Obviously, not all of the old work will be carried forward;


because something exists in a document does not mean that it


automatically has to be part of a new solution. Nevertheless,


where a current system exists, it will always provide plenty


of material that is grist for your requirements mill (see


Figure 24.3).


![embedded_p667_116.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p667_116.jpeg)


Figure 24.3 In document archeology, you start by collecting


samples of all documents, reports, forms, files, and so on.


Gather anything that is used to record or send information,


including regular telephone calls. User manuals are rich


sources of material—they describe a way to do work. Help


desk records tell you what has gone wrong.


## 第 668 页


Inspect the documents (for simplicity’s sake, the term
