“document” means anything you have found), looking for


nouns, or “things.” These can be column headings, named


boxes on forms, or simply the name of a piece of data on the


document. If you hearken back to Chapter 23, Stored Data,


you’ll recognize that these “things” can be data entities


or attributes of entities. For each “thing,” ask several of


these questions.


• What is the purpose of this thing?


• Who uses it and why?


• What are all the uses the business makes of this thing?


• Which business events use or read this thing? If you have


built a CRUD table, it will help here. Alternatively, this


will help you build a CRUD table. (The CRUD table is


discussed in Chapter 37, Completeness Check.)


• Can this thing have an alphanumeric value? For example, is


it a number, a code, or a quantity? This indicates whether it


is an attribute or an entity.


• If it is an attribute, to which entity does it belong?


## 第 669 页


• Does the document contain a repeating group of things?


• If so, what is the collection of things called? This is


most likely an entity.


• Can you find a link between things? These can be


relationships on your data model.


• Which process makes the connection between them? Check your


business use cases.


• Which business rules are associated with each thing?


• Which processes ensure that these rules are obeyed?


• Which documents give users the most problems?


These questions will not, in themselves, reveal all the


requirements for the product. They will, however, give you


plenty of background material and suggest directions for


further investigation.


When doing document archeology, you search for capabilities


from the current work that are needed for the new solution.


This does not mean you have carte blanche to replicate the


old one. You are, in fact, gathering requirements because you


plan to build a new solution. Nevertheless, an existing


## 第 670 页


system will usually have some capabilities in common with its


replacement.


We suggest that you incorporate document archeology into your


data modeling approach, because most of the answers from the


questions listed earlier are commonly used in the latter


discipline.


Customer Experience Analysis


Consider customer journey maps as a trawling tool. Customer


journey maps, or customer experience diagrams, are a


simulation of your customer’s interaction with the


organization for a given set of transactions to achieve a


goal.


Customer experience might sound a little touchy-feely, but it


pays to keep in mind that customer experience has emerged as


a crucial factor in achieving success for most organizations.


As a business analyst, you are concerned with how your


customers see your organization, and through that vision you


determine their needs.


The customer journey map is drawn from the customer’s, or


external, point of view. It does this by breaking a


significant transaction—sometimes a set of transactions—


## 第 671 页


into the steps that a customer (not the organization) makes


to reach her objective. Having made the map, you analyze each


touchpoint and identify the customer’s needs and problems


for that point. In other words, the map gives you a


methodical guide for your trawling.


Consider the customer journey map shown in Figure 24.4.


We’ve taken a reasonably uncomplicated scenario by way of


illustration; there is no need to have anything more complex


to see how this works.


## 第 672 页


![embedded_p672_117.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p672_117.jpeg)


Figure 24.4 A customer journey map showing the steps to


having your refrigerator repaired


Note the symbols beside each touchpoint on the journey map;


they indicate the potential needs of the customer through


both the happy and painful points. You can travel the


customer’s journey and analyze and derive the requirements


## 第 673 页


for each step. Sometimes you might have to observe the


customers in action to see their needs.


The journey map can give you a different perspective for


discovering your customer’s requirements. It is drawn from


the customer’s point of view, so it is an external portrayal


of the business. Wherever there is a touchpoint, it probably


means that there is some internal process to handle it. These


internal processes would be investigated, perhaps using


process models or one of the other techniques mentioned


above.


An example: Let’s say that you work for a repair service,


and your project is to improve the service experience. The


relevant customer segment receives value when the


refrigerator is once again in good working order and is


repaired at a cost the customer considers reasonable.


Let’s walk through the journey map shown in Figure 24.4.


Start at the point where the fridge breaks. This is an


unhappy experience, but there is little that you as a repair


service can do about the fact that it broke. You didn’t make


the fridge, but you will fix it. Next up is the customer


finds a repair service step. At this point, the customer has


a need for information. Consider what kind of information


## 第 674 页


would be most useful and what you, as the repairer, should


supply. Makes and models of fridges and the most likely quick


fixes for them would be at the top of the list. You might


also consider warranty conditions. Think about other


informational needs. If you supply better information than


the competition, your service becomes superior to theirs, and


presumably attracts more customers.


Arrange engineer’s visit also has information needs. The


customer needs to arrange a mutually agreed time, find out


what repairs will cost, and determine if she should do


anything before the engineer arrives.


Unloading the fridge is never pleasant, because the customer


must find a place for all that food, and unless she can


borrow space in the neighbor’s freezer, a lot of the frozen


stuff is going to be wasted.


Next is the engineer’s inspection. This has been tagged for


unknown or unclear needs. Think about what the customer is


doing when the engineer is inspecting the refrigerator and


assessing the repairs. Is there any useful information that


can be given to the customer? Is there a need for the


customer to arrange entry for the engineer if the customer is


not at home? Is there a need for clear explanations of what


## 第 675 页


has to be done? Does the engineer need additional material or


information to explain things to the customer?


For the step receive engineer’s quote for the work, put


yourself in the place of the customer. What do you need to


know? How should the quote be delivered? What additional


information would be beneficial for the customer to receive?


Examples could include time to complete; alternatives to


repairing the appliance; warranty; payment options; cost of a


replacement appliance; and access conditions for the


engineer.


We’ll leave you to follow the remainder of the journey to


the end, but we want to mention one touchpoint: Waiting to


see if working properly has unknown needs. Is there a need to


give the customer information to help test whether the fridge


is working? Or perhaps information on how to correctly adjust


the fridge now that it is working again?


Travel the Same Journey as Your Customer


A customer journey map illustrates how a customer sees your


organization. There is no need for your customers to


understand the internal workings of your organization, but


you need to. The journey map gives you a structure for


## 第 676 页


discovering both the customer’s and your organization’s


needs.


If you, as a service organization, are serious about finding


all your customer’s needs, and through that improving your


service, be your own customer. Make calls to your own


customer support team. Try to sign up for an account at your


own online service. Disable your own fridge and call the


company. Be the customer and critically consider each step of


the way, asking what processes your organization initiates,


whether you could make the customer’s experience better,


whether the process could break down, what risks you and the


customer face at each step, what is needed to make the


journey better and more effective, and what can be eliminated


or changed to make the path smoother.


Review


In this and preceding chapters, we looked at the techniques


used when you’re trawling for requirements. There are other


techniques, but the ones we have covered are the ones you are


most likely to use, and also the most effective. If you are


thirsty for knowledge of business analysis techniques, then


James Cadle, Debra Paul, Adrian Reed, and others have


produced a book titled Business Analysis Techniques—123


## 第 677 页


Essential Tools for Success. As the title attests, this book


has plenty more techniques if you feel the need. This book is


listed in the Resources section.


You will probably use a combination of techniques, switching


between them as circumstances dictate. You are working with


your customers and stakeholders, so you must be sensitive to


their ways of working and choose the techniques that your


customers react best to and thus give you the best return for


your trawling efforts.


Another use for the Brown Cow model that you met earlier is


to be a guide to techniques you might use in each quadrant.


While you are at perfect liberty to use whatever you want


wherever you want, this guide might be useful. Figure 24.5


shows the Brown Cow matrix and the suggested techniques for


each quadrant.


## 第 678 页


![embedded_p678_118.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p678_118.jpeg)


Figure 24.5 Suggested trawling techniques for each Brown Cow


quadrant


You don’t have to trawl the entirety of the problem space


before moving on. The intention is to do as much as necessary


for your team to make a start on subsequent activities. If


you are trawling each business event at a time, then as you


## 第 679 页


find the requirements for each one, the later activities


shown in the Volere requirements process (see Figure P4.2)


can begin, and by the time that business event is


implemented, you have completed requirements discovery for


the next one.


Trawl for Requirements—Design—Develop—Repeat.

Contextual Design: Defining Customer-Centered Systems by Hugh

## 第 682 页


Part V: Writing Good Requirements


and Stories


Think of your developers as housebuilders. To get the house


you want—whether they are building it from scratch or


renovating an existing structure, and whether they are using


traditional construction materials or putting together a


modular home—you must tell them exactly what you want. If


you don’t specify where you want the windows and doors, how


high the roof should be, and what ready-made fittings


(windows, floor coverings, heating, etc.) you want, the


builders will build pretty much whatever they want, and it


almost certainly will not be what you want. It is obviously


not practical to let them build something and if you don’t


like it, have them demolish it and start over. Yet that is


close to what some software projects do. (The analogy is


appropriate, as many software projects cost about the same as


building projects.)


It is safe to say that to get the end result you want, you


must specify what you want. If you want a double-width entry


door, you must say so. Otherwise, if your request is open to


interpretation, the builders might give you a single door, or


## 第 683 页


perhaps they will gold-plate their efforts and give you a


triple-width door. You also must tell the builders the


purpose of what they are building so that they can select the


best set of materials and construct the product in the most


appropriate way. If you fail to tell them that your building


will be used to store heavy machinery, then you might well


find that the floors collapse under the weight. Similarly,


the environment comes into play: You would like your bedroom


to be on the east side of the house to catch the morning sun.


The instructions you give to the builders are parallel with


the requirements and stories you give to your developers.


They must be clear, be unambiguous, and indicate why whatever


it is they specify is needed. Your developers, like the


builders, will build you the correct solution if they


understand your requirements and understand why they are


building it.


Moreover, your requirements must be testable. For the


builders, this is straightforward. When you want a window


opening, you give them the measurements—6 feet wide by 4


feet high, or 180 by 120 cm. You can measure whatever they


build to test for compliance with the specification.


Similarly, requirements for software or any other solution


must carry a measurement to allow testing. It’s a little


## 第 684 页


more difficult than saying 6 by 4, but the ability to test a


requirement is well worth the effort to find the right


measurement. We’ll come back to measurements and acceptance


criteria (they’re more or less the same thing) in a few


chapters.


Over the next few chapters, we look at requirements and


stories and explain how you can write better ones. Please


note that if you normally write stories, even though the next


three chapters appear to be talking about traditional


requirements, there is plenty of information that is also


applicable to stories.


By the way, writing requirements and stories is not a


separate activity. You would be writing them as you discover


them during any of the requirements activities.


## 第 685 页


Chapter 25. Functional Requirements


Functional requirements are what the software product must


do; what actions it must take to satisfy the business need.


For example, it might be to calculate a premium, or plot a


trajectory, or record a transaction, or check a password, or


any of the almost infinite number of things that our software


solutions do. It’s a functional requirement because it


describes some activity, whereas a non-functional requirement


(covered in the next chapter) describes the qualities or


properties of that functionality.


Functional requirements come from the business activity that


you discover when you are trawling or prototyping. From that


activity—a mix of current and proposed future activities—


you determine how much of it is to be done by the software.


Let’s look at how you write functional requirements so that


the developers can build the right software. Figure 25.1


depicts the process.


## 第 686 页


![embedded_p686_119.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p686_119.jpeg)


Figure 25.1 The required functionality is discovered by the


Trawling and Prototyping activities. The output from


discovery is converted into detailed functional requirements.


As an example of a functional requirement, the following


describes an action that the product must do to provide value


to its customer:


## 第 687 页


The product shall predict which road sections will freeze


within the selected time parameters.


You write many such requirements. The complete collection


serves as the specification of the product to be built. When


your requirements are the right requirements, the developers


have no trouble understanding them, and they build the right


product: one that solves your customer’s business problem.


Uncovering the Functional Requirements


When you are trawling or prototyping (we talked about these


earlier) you are working with your stakeholders and


customers. You’ll find that they mainly talk about


functionality:


I need a solution to manage the food on the shelves. It has


to alert staff when any item falls below its threshold, and


also to identify which products have passed their “display


until” date. Of course, the solution has to provide the


total wholesale value of the entire store and the turnover


for each hour.


Your customer is describing desired functionality. For the


parts of the functionality that you and she decide to


automate, you write functional requirements.


## 第 688 页


It is of course possible to write these functional


requirements at the time your customer describes the needed


functionality, but that would result in a disconnected,


incoherent, and incomplete set of requirements. You cannot be


certain when the customer describes her situation that she


has told you everything, and you cannot know how any one


requirement would impact another.


To organize your requirements, we suggest that you take


rational slices of the whole of the solution’s functionality


and write the requirements for each slice. It will come as no


surprise that business events are the proposed way of slicing


the functionality.


Every business event (we have discussed these several times


before) has a functional response we call a business use


case (BUC). The BUC can be set down in several ways, but the


easiest one of these to discuss is the scenario. (We covered


scenarios in Chapter 20, Scenarios.)


The scenario is made up of a limited number of steps, each of


which is a slice of the BUC’s functionality. These steps are


generally small enough that it is a straightforward task to


write the atomic functional requirements from them.


## 第 689 页


The word “atomic” is used to say that while there are


components of the requirement—subatomic particles—there is


no need to divide the requirement into smaller slices.


If you are using prototypes to uncover the needed


functionality, then a prototype might involve more than one


business event. Depending on the kind of prototype you have


built—process model, screen wireframe, storyboard, video,


and so on—you can separate its business use cases, and from


there write its functional requirements.


For ready-made solutions (as previously mentioned, these are


also called off-the-shelf solutions, software as a service,


cloud solutions, and other names), functional requirements


are written for any needed configuration or modifications to


the ready-made. There is a distinction between the two.


Configuration means you’re using the ready-made’s


functionality as intended. That is, you are adjusting


parameters supplied by the vendor to adapt the ready-made to


your particular situation. Modification means making changes


to the ready-made that cannot be done by configuring


parameters. There are also requirements for auxiliary


applications needed as front-end or back-end processes for


the ready-made.


## 第 690 页


Deciding the Solution’s Functionality


Functional requirements specify the actions that your


solution has to take to support your customer’s business,


whatever that may be. So far, the discussion has been


concerned with the customer’s business, but your customer


may not always desire to automate the entirety of the


business. So, you and your customer determine the extent of


the automation.


Consider Figure 25.2. The process model (shown as a data flow


diagram, but any notation works equally well) shows a BUC.


The business event happens, and the triggering data flow


enters the workspace and sets off a chain of activities to


respond accordingly to the event. This is standard for any


business.


## 第 691 页


![embedded_p691_120.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p691_120.jpeg)


Figure 25.2 Determining the product boundary


Let’s say that the customer wishes activity A to be done by


a human. There are reasons for such a decision: registering


incoming visitors, checking credentials, and so on. This


means that activity A is outside any automated product.


Activity B uses the data from activity A to access data that


is stored digitally (on an in-house server or the cloud), so


the accessing activity must be automated. Activity C is also


part of the automated product, for the same reason. This


## 第 692 页


results in the product boundary being drawn between


activities A and B.


Alternatively, you might move the product boundary so as to


include activity A in the automated product—let’s say that


it does not have to be done by a human after all. So now the


product includes all of the work’s response to the business


event. This is quite common—online shopping, a telephone


banking app, email, and so on—and you will want to have such


a product boundary many times in your requirements work.


You could also move the boundary to the right and include


less of the BUC in your product. There are many


possibilities, and there is a lot more on this in Chapter 31,


Determine the Extent of the Automation.


Let’s say that you and your customer have agreed on the


product boundary. The activities inside this boundary make up


the product use case (PUC). You write the requirements for


all the activity contained by the PUC.


Figure 25.3 illustrates the part of the Requirements


Knowledge Model that shows how BUCs, PUCs, and atomic


requirements fit together. It also shows the equivalent


components if you are using stories. These story components


## 第 693 页


are explained in Chapter 28, Writing Good Stories. Note that


the complete Requirements Knowledge Model is in Appendix C,


Volere Requirements Knowledge Model.


![embedded_p693_121.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p693_121.jpeg)


## 第 694 页


Figure 25.3 The part of the Requirements Knowledge Model


under discussion. The asterisks indicate that many instances


of an entity (also called class) participate in the


relationship.


You see in this partial model how either the BUC or the


business event story is the response to the business event.


The product use case or functional story indicates the part


of the response you choose to include within the scope of the


product. This is then broken down into its atomic functional


requirements, or detailed tasks for stories.


Before we leave this, we should mention the part of the BUC


that fell outside the product scope. This is the


activity/activities to be done by humans. The requirements


for this should be written or assembled so that they become


part of an operations manual. This manual could include


different artifacts such as a list of instructions, business


process models, activity diagrams, flow diagrams,


screenshots, example forms, functional requirements, or


anything else that explains to the humans what they are


intended to do. In whichever way it is assembled, it should


describe the functionality to be done by the human workforce.


You can think of it as a requirements specification for


humans.


## 第 695 页


Now let’s look at how you would write the functional


requirements.


Writing the Requirements


To write requirements we need something to write about.


Fairly obviously, this is the functionality needed by the


solution to support your customer’s business. As mentioned


previously, a scenario describing the functionality of a


product use case is a good place to start. We discussed


scenarios in Chapter 20.


Simply put, each step from the scenario is converted to


functional requirements. This is illustrated in Figure 25.4.


## 第 696 页


![embedded_p696_122.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p696_122.jpeg)


Figure 25.4 Each of the scenario’s steps is decomposed into


its functional requirements. The collection of functional


requirements specifies what the product must do to fulfill


the business outcome of the PUC.


The following scenario describes a product use case for a


solution that predicts when ice will form on roads and sends


a schedule to the truck depot showing which roads have to be


treated and when. You have seen snippets of this previously.


Product use case: Produce Road Deicing Schedule


## 第 697 页


1. Engineer provides a scheduling date and district


identifier to the product.


2. Product retrieves the relevant thermal maps.


3. Product uses the thermal maps, district temperature


readings, and weather forecasts to predict temperatures for


each road section in the district.


4. Product predicts which road sections will freeze and when


they will freeze.


5. Product schedules available trucks from the relevant


depots.


6. Product advises the engineer of the schedule.


Including three to ten steps in the scenario


should give a reasonable level of detail, without


making it too complex for nontechnical


stakeholders.


The steps in this product use case scenario describe the


product’s response to the business event, Time to schedule


deicing. Having a limited number of steps—we suggest between


three and ten—in the scenario prevents you from getting


## 第 698 页


enmeshed in details and ensures that the scenario is written


in stakeholder-friendly language.


Once you and your stakeholders have agreed on the scenario,


for each of the steps ask, “What does the product do to


complete this step?” For example, the first step in the


scenario is:


1. Engineer provides a scheduling date and district


identifier.


What does the product do to complete this step? The first


thing is fairly obvious, so this is your first functional


requirement:


The product shall accept a scheduling date.


When you ask the stakeholders whether there is anything


special about the scheduling date, they tell you that due to


imprecise forecasts, they schedule no more than two days in


advance. This information suggests another functional


requirement:


The product shall warn if the scheduling date is neither


today nor the next day.


## 第 699 页


Another requirement from the first step is:


The product shall accept a valid district identifier.


You discover another requirement when you inquire what is


meant by “valid.” The identifier is valid if it identifies


one of the districts for which the engineer has


responsibility. It would also be valid if it is the identity


of a district that is intended by the engineer. This leads us


to two more functional requirements:


The product shall verify that the district is within the


deicing responsibility of the area covered by this


installation.


The product shall have the engineer verify that the requested


district is accurate.


The objective is to write enough functional


requirements for your developers to build exactly


the product that your client is expecting and


that your user needs to do the work.


The number of requirements you derive from any step is not


important. However, it can sometimes be an indicator of too


## 第 700 页


much or too little granularity. Experience tells us that it


is usually fewer than six. If you uncover only one


requirement from each step, it suggests either the level of


detail in your scenarios is too granular or your functional


requirements are too coarse. If you find you are writing more


than six requirements per step, it suggests that either your


requirements are too fine-grained or you have a very complex


use case. There is no hard rule here, but it is worthwhile to


pay attention to the granularity of your requirements.


Regardless of granularity, the objective is to write enough


functional requirements for your developers to build exactly


the product that your client is expecting and that your user


needs to do the work.


Let’s consider another of the product use case steps from


our example scenario:


4. Product determines which roads will freeze and when they


will freeze.


This step in the PUC scenario leads us to write three


functional requirements:


The product shall determine which areas in the district are


predicted to freeze.


## 第 701 页


The product shall determine which road sections are in the


areas that are predicted to freeze.


The product shall determine when each road section will


freeze.


Now continue in the same vein, working through each step from


the scenario. When you have exhausted the steps, you should


have written all the functional requirements for the product


use case. You should test whether you have completed the PUC


by walking through the requirements with a colleague and


demonstrating that the product use case provides the correct


outcome for the customer.


You can do the same thing using a process model. Figure 25.5


illustrates this.


## 第 702 页


![embedded_p702_123.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p702_123.jpeg)


Figure 25.5 The activities on a process model are able to be


decomposed to a collection of functional requirements.


The Snow Card


So far, the requirements have been no more than “the product


shall...” statements. You need more detail. The best way to


do this is to introduce the snow card. Figure 25.6 shows one.


## 第 703 页


![embedded_p703_124.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p703_124.jpeg)


Figure 25.6 The snow card carries the attributes of a


requirement.


The snow card shows the attributes of a requirement. It is an


idea borrowed from American architect William Peña. Peña was


an advocate of architectural programming, which has many


## 第 704 页


parallels with requirements discovery and recording. Peña’s


teams used blank cards that they taped to a wall for


recording requirements and issues for the buildings they were


designing. We adapted his idea by adding field headings such


that when a card is filled in, it provides a rigorous


definition of a requirement.


We are not for a moment suggesting that requirements work is


filling out forms. We are suggesting that you can make use


of the snow card’s fields to write better requirements.


Similarly, we are not suggesting that requirements should be


written on paper cards; most people find an electronic


“card” is easier to work with and share.


In any event, it is not the medium of the card but its


contents that are important to us. We will get to all of the


content in good time, but first consider the Description and


the Rationale. These are the “what” and the “why” of a


requirement.


The examples shown above are the description of the


requirement, but there is more to a requirement than that. We


suggest—strongly suggest—that you add a rationale to your


requirements to show why the requirement exists. In some


## 第 705 页


cases, this might be obvious, but in many circumstances, it


is a crucial component of the requirement.


For example:


Description: The product shall record roads that have been


treated.


This might seem at first glance to be a routine requirement


and of no great importance. Now let’s add the rationale for


this requirement:


Description: The product shall record roads that have been


treated.


Rationale: To be able to recognize untreated roads and


highlight potential danger.


The rationale indicates whether the requirement


is worthy of some special attention.


Now it looks a little more serious—human lives could


possibly be at risk, or at the very least, the owner of this


product would not be carrying out his statutory duties. With


the inclusion of the rationale, you give the developer the


opportunity to build a better solution; one that makes this


## 第 706 页


information readily accessible to the functionality that


discovers the untreated roads. Clearly, the rationale


indicates that this requirement is worthy of some attention.


Now consider this example:


Description: The product shall record the start and end time


of a truck’s scheduled activity.


This is a normal kind of requirement, one that would not


cause much comment. But does it contribute any value to the


product? Let’s look at two possible rationales:


Rationale: The truck depot foreman wants to know which trucks


are being most used.


Or:


Rationale: Trucks are to be scheduled a maximum of 20 out of


24 hours to allow for maintenance and cleaning.


Now we are getting somewhere. The first rationale says that


the requirement is low priority and might not be worthwhile


implementing. After all, the depot foreman can discover the


trucks’ usage simply by reading their tachometers. However,


the second rationale indicates that this is a valuable


## 第 707 页


requirement: If it is not implemented, then the truck fleet


will suffer.


By knowing why something is there, the developers


and the testers know much more about the effort


they should expend on it.


By including a rationale with the description, the


requirement itself becomes more useful. By knowing why


something is there and how important it is, the developers


and the testers know much more about the effort they should


expend on it. It also indicates to future maintainers why the


requirement exists in the first place.


The rationale also helps to overcome the possibility of


inadvertently writing a solution instead of the real need.


For example, the following requirement description is written


for a machine to sell bus tickets for a city bus company:


Description: The product shall provide the bus network route


map on a touchscreen.


The description is actually a solution to the problem. When


the rationale is added, the real need becomes visible:


## 第 708 页


Description: The product shall provide the bus network route


map on a touchscreen.


Rationale: Passengers have to provide their destination for


the fare to be calculated.


The rationale indicates that the real requirement is for


passengers to provide a destination. How they do so is best


left to the user experience designer and the solution


architect. The touchscreen might be the best way to


accomplish this goal, but then again, it might not. If


tourists were prominent users of the buses, then they would


not be familiar with the layout of the network, and finding


the stop on a map might be a very slow process. This would


not please passengers standing behind them in the queue to


buy tickets. Also, if the network is divided into zones for


charging purposes, then for regular commuters, it might be


more efficient to have a way to indicate the number of zones


to be covered and to ignore the actual stops. After all, a


destination can be a stop or a zone.


Regardless of how the need is finally


implemented, it is clear that writing both the


description and the rationale leads to discovery


of the real requirement.


## 第 709 页


Why is this aspect of requirements development important?


Because it is far too easy to hide important functionality by


describing an implementation, and it is far too easy to


select the most obvious implementation when better ones may


exist. Regardless of how the need is finally implemented, it


is clear that writing both the description and the rationale


leads to discovery of the real requirement. It also leads to


more accurate requirements. Often, the rationale clarifies


the requirement and you then update the description. You


might also find that when presented with your proposed


rationale, your customer realizes that you have been given


the wrong description. And so it goes.


We have not yet talked about how to ensure that each


requirement is measurable and hence testable. We do this by


adding a fit criterion, and this is so crucial that we have


devoted Chapter 27, Fit Criteria and Rationale, to it. There


are more attributes to a requirement; they are shown on the


snow card in Figure 25.6. We shall come back to these later,


so for the moment, we can leave the functional requirements


as a description and rationale only.


Technological Requirements


## 第 710 页


Technological requirements specify functionality that is


needed purely because of the chosen technology. In the


example of the PUC that produces the deicing schedule, the


product interacts with an external thermal mapping database.


Suppose the designer decides that handling this interaction


via an internet connection is the best option. Because of


this technological choice, the product has a need to


establish a secure connection. This need is a technological


requirement; that is, it arises purely because of the chosen


technology. If the designer had selected a different


technology to handle this part of the work, the result would


be different technological requirements.


The technological requirements are not there for business


reasons, but rather to make the chosen implementation work.


We suggest that the technological requirements are identified


as such. Stakeholders must clearly understand why a


requirement appears in the specification, so it is important


that the technological requirements are not introduced before


the business requirements are fully understood.


Level of Granularity


Requirements are written as a single sentence


with a single verb.


## 第 711 页


Note the level of detail or granularity in the preceding


examples—the requirements are written as a single sentence


with a single verb. When you write a single sentence, you


make the requirement readily testable and far less


susceptible to ambiguity. The functional requirement


describes an action, so there is always a verb, and


preferably a single verb. The action is what the product must


do to satisfy a business need.


Functional requirements are verifiable by your business


stakeholders. This is not to say that you have to show every


requirement to them, but when you need to, you want them to


understand enough to come to an agreement as to whether this


is the real business requirement.


Additionally, a reasonable developer is able to build the


correct product. “Reasonable” might be arguable, but


today’s developers are, for the most part, pretty good. If


your developers say they cannot build from the requirement,


then you must suspect that your requirement is too vague or


ambiguous.


Note the form “The product shall...”; it makes the sentence


active and focuses on communicating what the product is


## 第 712 页


intended to do. It also provides a consistent form for the


developers and other stakeholders who need to have a clear


understanding of what the product is intended to do. You can


of course substitute “will” for “shall” (some people


claim it is grammatically better), but be consistent with


whichever you choose. Some people prefer to omit “The


product shall” and write:


Record the salt capacity for each truck added to the fleet.


Use a separate component of your requirement to


indicate the priority of the requirement.


Please don’t try to use the description to indicate


priority. Sometimes people use a mixture of “The product


must,” “should,” or “could” to indicate the priority of


a requirement. This practice results in semantic confusion,


and we advise against it. Instead, use one consistent form


for writing your requirements’ description (“The product


shall . . .” is probably the most common), and use the


priority attribute on the snow card to indicate its priority.


Conditional Requirements


## 第 713 页


Sometimes you need to add a condition to a requirement. This


happens when the requirement comes into play when certain


processing circumstances have occurred. For example:


If a road scheduled for treatment has not been reported as


treated within 30 minutes of its scheduled time, the product


shall issue an untreated road alert.


Alternatively, you might find that the requirement reads more


easily if you write it with the condition at the end:


The product shall issue an untreated road alert if a road has


not been treated within 30 minutes of its scheduled time.


Avoiding Ambiguity


Whether the sources of your requirements consist of written


documents or verbal statements from interviews, you should be


aware of the enormous potential for ambiguity and the


misunderstanding that ambiguity can cause. Ambiguity arises


from several sources.


First, the English language is full of homonyms. English


contains an estimated 500,000 words in normal usage and about


the same number of technical, scientific, and other


specialized words. Normal-language words have been randomly


## 第 714 页


added by many different people and from many sources over a


long period of time. This growth has led to different usages


and meanings of the same word.


It is difficult to imagine why, when the language


contains a huge number of words, so many of them


have multiple meanings.


Consider the word “file,” which is used so commonly in


information technology. In addition to meaning an automated


storage place for information, it means a metal instrument


for abrading or smoothing; a collection of documents; a row


of people, as in “single file”; a slang term for an artful


or shrewd person; a verb meaning to rub away or smooth; and


more recently a verb used by lawyers when they “file suit.”


Of course, “suit” itself also means the clothing the lawyer


wears in court, as well as a set of playing cards such as


hearts, diamonds, spades, and clubs. It is difficult to


imagine why, when the language contains so many words, so


many of them have multiple meanings.


When writing requirements, we have to contend with more


challenges than just homonyms. If the context of your product


is not clear, then it will also lead to ambiguity. Suppose


you have the following requirement:


## 第 715 页


The product shall show the weather for the next 24 hours.


The meaning here depends on the type of requirement and what


is near it in the specification. Does the requirement mean


the product is to communicate the weather that is expected to


happen in the forthcoming 24 hours, or must it communicate


some weather and continue to do so until one full day has


elapsed?


We advise you to group your requirements by product use case


and write your requirements one PUC at a time. This system of


organization will, to a large extent, reduce ambiguity. For


example, consider this requirement:


The product shall communicate all roads predicted to freeze.


Does “all” refer to every road known to the product? Or


just those roads being examined by the user? The PUC scenario


tells us that the user has previously identified a district


or an area within the district. Thus, we may safely say that


“all” refers to the geographical area selected. In fact,


the meaning of almost any requirement depends on its context.


This is quite a good thing because we do not need to waste


time by laboriously qualifying every word of every


requirement. While anything has the potential to be


## 第 716 页


ambiguous, the PUC scenario, by setting a context for the


requirement, minimizes the risk of ambiguity.


You can also make your requirements less ambiguous by


including a glossary of terms in your specification. This is


why section 4 of the Volere Requirements Specification


Template—Naming Conventions and Terminology—exists. The


terminology you define there should be used consistently


throughout your requirements definitions.


You should try to eliminate pronouns from your requirements


and replace them with the subject or object to which the


pronouns refer. (Note the potential ambiguity of the


preceding sentence if we had said “they” instead of “the


pronouns.”)


When you write a requirement, read it aloud. If possible,


have a colleague read it aloud. Confirm with your stakeholder


that you both reach the same understanding of the


requirement. This may seem obvious, but “send the bill to


the customer” may mean that the bill goes to the person who


actually bought the goods or that the bill is sent to the


account holder. It is also unclear whether the bill is sent


immediately after the purchase or at the end of the month.


And does “bill” refer to an invoice, a bill of materials,


## 第 717 页


or a bill of lading? A short conversation with the


appropriate stakeholders about the definition and consistent


use of terminology will clarify the intention.


Grouping Requirements in Your Specification


We have spent a fair amount of time talking about business


events and how they make the discovery of the requirements


easier. What they also make easier is the development of the


product. We discussed deriving a product use case from the


business use case (from a BUC to a PUC), and suggested that


you write your requirements one PUC at a time. The PUC is a


separate and distinct amount of functionality. It is a


natural choice to be a unit of development.


This leads to saying that because you are probably writing


your requirements from a scenario or a process model, as


discussed above, you keep the requirements grouped in their


PUCs. This gives a context to the requirements, making it


easier for the developers to understand what is needed.


Additionally, grouping by PUC makes any specification easier


to read.


Requirements for Ready-Made Products


## 第 718 页


Requirements for solutions using ready-made components are in


effect no different from requirements for custom-built


solutions. Some of the requirements are written to configure


or customize the ready-made product, but they are still


written in the form “The product shall...”.


Functional requirements written about the configuration of


the ready-made product specify what the product will do when


it is configured. “The product shall...” tells the


developer what functionality is needed, and she uses the


configuration capabilities of the ready-made to make it


perform as desired.


You also must specify any needed customization. Here the


functional requirements specify the required changes to the


ready-made. They are the same as before in that they specify


needed functionality, and the developer builds that into the


ready-made. It is necessary to make it clear to the developer


which parts of the ready-made are being changed, and


additionally what ready-made functionality has to be removed.


Integrating the ready-made with existing IT solutions and


their operating environment is usually a major part of your


requirements work. Here you write requirements for any


changes needed to the ready-made to make it compatible with


## 第 719 页


existing databases. This entails mapping the ready-made’s


data to existing corporate data. Required changes to either


the ready-made or existing interfacing systems are specified


with functional requirements.


In some cases, you need to build front-end or back-end


applications to provide data to or receive data from the


ready-made. These are partly the same as regular apps but


need additional functionality to integrate the data. A front-


end application would normally be acquiring data to populate


the ready-made’s databases. Here you write requirements to


ensure smooth integration between the incoming data and the


ready-made. On the other side, the back end, many of the


requirements have to do with making the ready-made’s data


work with existing systems.


In these cases, requirements are written as we have been


describing them.


Review


Functional requirements specify what the solution must do to


satisfy the business need. They are written as an action:


“The product shall...”, followed by a verb. The functional


## 第 720 页


requirements should be a complete and unambiguous description


of the product’s functionality.


Functional requirements are derived from the product use


cases—the portion of the business use case that is to be


done by the product. The most convenient way we have found to


generate the functional requirements is to write a scenario


that breaks the PUC into a number of steps. Examine each step


and ask, “What does the product have to do to accomplish


this step?” The things that it does are the functional


requirements.


A process model achieves the same result. You examine each of


its activities and ask the question as above. You write the


functional requirements from the answers.


We suggest that you write these requirements (for the moment)


using two components: a description and a rationale. As we


work through the book, we discuss how to formulate the rest


of the requirement’s attributes.


One thing that you will probably notice is that your


requirements sometimes evolve. We mentioned above that when


you write the rationale for the requirement, it sometimes


causes stakeholders to reconsider what they have asked for.


## 第 721 页


You update the description accordingly. You might also find


that as you specify more and more of the product, you revisit


existing requirements and reconsider and, sometimes, change


them. However, by saying this, we are not advocating


uncontrolled requirements hacking. Rather, we advocate that


you keep an open mind about your requirements and be prepared


to change them if circumstances warrant a change.


When you have sufficient functional requirements to achieve


the outcome of a product use case, it is time to move on to


the next one. As you progress through these PUCs, you may


discover that a requirement you defined for one PUC also


applies to other PUCs. Reuse the requirement you have already


written by cross-referencing it to all relevant PUCs.


When all of the product use cases have been


treated, you will have defined the requirements


that completely and unambiguously specify the


functionality of the product.


When all of the product use cases have been treated this way,


you will have defined the requirements that completely and


unambiguously specify the functionality of the product.


Resources


## 第 722 页


The best resource for writing functional requirements is the


template packaged in Appendix A, The Volere Requirements


Specification Template.


## 第 723 页


Chapter 26. Non-functional Requirements


Non-functional requirements can make or break your solution.


The non-functional requirements (NFRs) specify the qualities


your product must have if it is to succeed with your


customers, in the marketplace, in the office, and in its


operating environment. Non-functional requirements specify


how well your solution performs its functional requirements.


Imagine for a moment that you are an engineer. You work for


the electricity company that supplies a city and the


surrounding area. Your job is to monitor the flow of


electricity in the city and make adjustments to the supply as


demand ebbs and flows over the day and from season to season.


Your IT people are building a new solution to provide you


with the functionality that allows you to see the supply in


real time on an array of screens. This information should


allow you to intervene whenever you detect some abnormality


that needs your correction. Some of this monitoring


functionality will be automated, but the role of the engineer


is to intervene and make adjustments if the situation becomes


critical.


## 第 724 页


Now imagine the non-functional requirements that apply to


this electricity monitoring and correcting solution. Non-


functional requirements are designated by types, and these


types are shown in the following list.


10 Look and Feel: The appearance and style of the solution


11 Usability and Humanity: The solution’s ease of use, and


any special considerations needed for a better user


experience


12 Performance: How fast, how many, how available, how


scalable, how accurate the functionality must be


13 Operational and Environmental: The operating environment


of the solution, and any considerations that must be


considered for this environment


14 Maintainability and Support: Expected changes, and the


time needed to make them; also, specification of the support


to be given to the solution


15 Security: Access, integrity, privacy, recoverability, and


auditability of the product


## 第 725 页


16 Cultural: Special requirements that come about because of


the culture and customs of people who come in contact with


the solution


17 Compliance: The laws and standards that apply to your


solution


The requirements types you see on this list have been derived


from a large collection of specifications. that we have


written over the years. From these we extracted the most


useful properties for solutions to have. For convenience, we


grouped them into eight major non-functional requirement


types, and within those, subtypes or variations on the type.


You can see the complete list and discussions on all the non-


functional types in the Volere Requirements Specification


Template. You find this in Appendix A.


Later in the chapter we’ll discuss each of these requirement


types fully. For now, we’ll introduce them by looking at


some practical examples. We’ll choose some of the NFRs that


are relevant for the electricity solution. Let’s go back to


our engineer.


Think of the functional requirements as those


that cause the product to do the work and the


## 第 726 页


non-functional requirements as those that specify


the quality of that functionality.


The obvious first choice of non-functional requirement for


your electricity solution is Security. Unless you are a


highly qualified engineer you have no right to be messing


around with the city’s electricity supply. Thus, the obvious


security requirements must include provisions for preventing


unauthorized people from accessing this solution. You also


need security requirements to warn an operator if the


consequences of her actions could be detrimental.


An even greater threat to the city’s electricity supply


comes from cyberattacks. Hostile actors with bad intentions


can bring down an electricity grid, so some of your security


requirements are aimed at keeping the grid safe from any


variation of a cyberattack.


Next up is Operational and Environmental. These have to do


with the operating environment of a solution. In this case,


your solution would need to connect to and interact with the


statewide or national electricity grid, with each of numerous


suppliers putting electricity into the grid, along with some


city-owned systems that supply information about traffic,


human movement, weather, and other factors.


## 第 727 页


Compliance requirements would also be high on the list.


These have to do with laws that apply to your solution. In


this case, the electricity monitoring solution would be


subject to various city and state regulations applicable to


the electricity supply. The engineer wants to be certain that


her actions are within the law.


Look and Feel non-functional requirements are significant.


The engineer would not want screens with a cartoonlike


interface. Like most engineers, she wants a professional or


engineering look to the solution. Its appearance must also


make her feel that it is reliable.


The UX designer would work with you to design the final


screens, but first you need to determine the requirements for


the look and feel. Most of all, you want the interface to fit


seamlessly into the engineer’s world so that it feels like


the natural way for her to do her work.


Let’s look at a different situation to see some other


examples. This time you are an insurance adjuster working for


an insurance company specializing in automotive insurance.


You are responsible for processing insurance claims made when


policyholders damage their cars.


## 第 728 页


Usability and Humanity requirements are important here.


Although you are a skilled adjuster, you need usability that


gives you convenient access to all the information you need


in order to settle insurance claims. You need to be able to


see the police report on the accident and the body shop’s


quote for repairs (possibly several of these), and you need


to consider any personal statements made by people involved


in the accident. So, the usability requirements specify a


solution that allows you to process the claims quickly and


accurately.


Cultural non-functional requirements are important to you,


or at least to your employer. This loss adjustment solution


is to be used in different states and in different countries.


Local culture must be taken into account to ensure that no


matter where they are, adjusters can understand the language


and the technical terminology being used.


Look and Feel requirements specify that your adjustment


solution is compatible in appearance with the other


applications that you use. The insurance company has


interface standards, and these non-functional requirements


specify conformity with them.


## 第 729 页


Compliance requirements are important because the solution


naturally would have to comply with insurance law applicable


to the country or state of the insured’s motor vehicle.


Privacy, which comes under the heading of Security, must


also be specified. The privacy requirements would specify


that personal information about the policyholder is not


released or available to anyone except the insurance adjuster


and his supervisor.


Some of the other types are also applicable to this example,


but now let’s turn to a more general look at non-functional


requirements. To understand the significance of non-


functional requirements it’s useful to consider a company


that early on recognized the impact that non-functional


requirements can have. The most obvious example of such a


company is Apple. Apple’s attention to look and feel,


usability, security, operability, and so on has made its


products both extremely popular and much imitated. People are


willing to pay a premium to have them.


Similarly, your choice of household appliances is often based


on non-functional requirements. All dishwashers wash dishes—


it’s their ease of use, their speed, and their environmental


credentials that make the difference to consumers.


## 第 730 页


Non-functional properties may be the difference


between an accepted, well-liked product and an


unused one.


Spend a moment thinking of the end users of your solution.


You have to provide the functionality that is needed for them


to do their work. The non-functional requirements are those


that make the product fit into the users’ world. If you get


the right non-functional requirements, they bring about


solutions that are readily, even enthusiastically, welcomed


by their intended users.


PUCs and NFRs


A product use case, a PUC, is the part of the response to a


business event that is done by the automated product. In the


previous chapter, we discussed how a scenario can be used to


describe the product use case by showing it as a number of


processing steps, and for each step, you determine the


functional requirements.


Non-functional requirements, however, do not fit so neatly


into this way of partitioning. Some of them can be linked


directly to a functional requirement, some apply to the


product use case as a whole, and some apply to the entire


## 第 731 页


product. Figure 26.1 shows possible links between the


functionality and the associated non-functional requirements.


## 第 732 页


![embedded_p732_125.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p732_125.jpeg)


## 第 733 页


Figure 26.1 In this example, the product use case has three


functional requirements, each having some non-functional


properties. The use case as a whole must meet certain


usability requirements, whereas the look and feel


requirements relate to the entire solution.


Non-functional Requirement Types


Let’s look at each type of non-functional requirement in


detail.


As you read through these requirement types, keep in mind


that sometimes it is difficult to say exactly which type a


requirement is. When this sort of uncertainty arises, it


could indicate that you have several requirements posturing


as one, or that you have one of those not-uncommon


requirements that is just too difficult to categorize. If


this bothers you, then you can give a requirement multiple


types. Don’t sweat it. The category is not important. The


requirement is.


There is one other thing to keep in mind as you go through


the various non-functional requirements: For the moment, we


are dealing only with the description and rationale of the


requirement. Some of the examples we give might seem a little


## 第 734 页


vague, ambiguous, or loosely worded. The method of attack is


to initially capture the stakeholder’s intention for the


requirement. Later you will add a measurement—this is the


fit criterion—to the requirement to clarify it and make it


testable. For example, you might write a fit criterion for a


usability requirement that specifies how quickly a first-time


user can learn to use the product and achieve certain tasks.


Or you might specify the improvement in usability and thus


efficiency that the new product must achieve.


We discuss fit criteria in the next chapter, but for the


moment we ask you to accept that it is possible to measure


such things as “attractive,” “exciting,” “easy,” and


other adjectives that appear in the descriptions of non-


functional requirements.


Look and Feel Requirements: Type 10


The Type number refers to the section of the


Volere Template in Appendix A.


Look and feel requirements describe the intended spirit, the


mood, the style of your solution’s appearance. Keep in mind


that these requirements are about the intention of the


appearance and are not a detailed design of an interface.


## 第 735 页


For many projects, the prime look and feel requirement would


be something like this:


Description: The product shall comply with corporate branding


standards.


Or:


Description: The product shall conform to the established


look and feel of the owning organization’s products.


These requirements do not in any way attempt to say that the


company logo must occupy 10% of the screen, nor do they talk


about the colors or the typefaces to be used. They simply


state that the product must comply with the established


branding standards. These standards are published elsewhere—


your organization has a department (usually the


communications department) or group responsible for these


standards—and you and your UX designer have access to them.


Sometimes the look and feel requirements have nothing to do


with corporate standards. For example, they might have to


specify the appearance of an app. Appearances matter, and


first impressions are important. Think of your favorite app,


on either your computer, tablet, or phone. Why do you like


it? The answer to that might be complex, but a significant


## 第 736 页


part of it has to do with the way it looks. It does not have


to be beautiful, but its appearance must be consistent with


what it is doing. You don’t want your bank app to look like


your music app, which in turn should not look like your


office apps. In some cases, you might have a particular


situation where the appearance of the solution is crucial to


its success.


Look and feel requirements specify the spirit of


the solution’s appearance. They are not the


design of the interface.


Let’s say that you are discovering the requirements for a


solution to be used by a police force. In this case, you


would write a look and feel requirement that the solution


must have “a police look and feel.” Perhaps it would be


more helpful to write the requirement as “Similar to the


look and feel of existing solutions at police headquarters.”


This kind of requirement might seem mere and obvious, but


imagine if you had not specified any look and feel, and the


developers implemented the solution with an inappropriate


appearance. Cops are cops, and they want their gear to look


like police gear. You don’t have to describe how to achieve


a “police look,” but you must specify it.


## 第 737 页


Can you measure and test whether it has a “police look and


feel”? Yes. You could measure the product’s approval or


acceptance by a test panel of police officers. Or you could


measure its adherence to established police solutions. The


reason for the product having a “police appearance” is to


have it accepted and used by police officers. If your test


panel accepts it and uses it, then you have achieved a


solution that fits the requirement. By the way, you would


probably test the “police look” of the product using


mockups and prototypes, and thus avoid the expense of


building the real thing and risking it being rejected.


Consider whether some of the following sample look and feel


requirements are appropriate for your current or next


project.


The product shall


• Appear simple to use


• Be approachable so that people do not hesitate to use it


• Appear authoritative so that users feel they can rely on it


and trust it


• Conform to your customers’ other products


## 第 738 页


• Be attractive to children or some other target audience


• Be unobtrusive so that people are not aware of it


• Appear innovative and state of the art


• Be professional looking


• Be conservative


• Appear intriguing


• Be exciting


• Be cool


If you’re thinking that some of the above are vague and


untestable, then please withhold judgment until we have


talked about fit criteria. We’ll get to that in the next


chapter, where we discuss how you can add a measurement to


the requirement that allows any of the above to be tested. So


initially, your look and feel requirements might appear to


lack substance, but your intention is to capture the desired


feel of the solution, and later you make it measurable, and


thus tangible.


## 第 739 页


Today, in some application areas, software has become a


commodity, and the distinction between the functionality of


competing products has largely disappeared. In such cases, it


falls to the non-functional requirements to differentiate one


product from another. Usually, the noticeable and exceptional


products have a distinctly superior look and feel.


You should always consider the audience for your product and


whether they require some special appearance or feel to the


solution. Your client has in mind the kind of experience she


wants visitors to the site to have, and much of that


experience is down to your look and feel requirements.


If you have a few moments and wish to amuse yourself to good


avail, think of a product and come up with look and feel


requirements for one or more of the following customer


segments:


• Gen-Z


• Sailors


• Vampires


• Mothers


## 第 740 页


• Taylor Swift fans


• Submariners


• Gormogons


• Residents of Coober Pedy


• Heavy metal streaming audience


To reiterate the key point, the look and feel requirements


describe the intention of the appearance and are not the


design of the interface. To design the product at this stage


would be premature—you do not yet know the complete


requirements of the product. Designing is the task of the


product’s designers and UX designers, once they know the


requirements.


Usability and Humanity Requirements: Type 11


How many times in the past year or so have you downloaded an


app to your device, used it for a few days, a few hours, or


perhaps a few minutes, and then deleted it? The first reason


for deleting it would be that it lacked the functionality you


needed or it asked you to pay for something that was not


valuable to you. The next reason would be its poor usability:


## 第 741 页


You found it so awkward or opaque to use that you just gave


up on it.


Why was it unusable?


• Sheer incompetence (there is nothing in this book that can


help with that).


• The app’s builder never thought about usability


requirements (there is a lot in this book that can help with


that).


• The builder didn’t bother to find out anything about the


kind of people who would be using it or the circumstances


under which they would be using it.


This can happen at any time, but it shouldn’t. As consumers,


we have become intolerant of poor usability and demand that


the products we use, whether they are software, consumer


goods, or services, be easy to use and likable. Usability


might be one of the key factors that determine whether your


customers accept or reject your solution.


Usability requirements make the solution conform


to the user’s abilities and expectations of the


user experience.


## 第 742 页


The usability and humanity requirements specify a solution


that conforms to the users’ human abilities and


expectations. So, you must consider your target customer


segment. What kind of people are they? What kind of product


do they need to do their jobs? The usability and humanity


requirements ensure that you make a successful solution for


them. This is illustrated in Figure 26.2.


![embedded_p742_126.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p742_126.jpeg)


## 第 743 页


Figure 26.2 Consider the capabilities, knowledge, and


circumstances of your intended audience when writing the


usability requirements. Imagine what it’s like to do this


job. Ask what would make this product fit most seamlessly


into this person’s world.


As an example of usability requirements in real life, let’s


look at Amazon. The Amazon site is easy to navigate, which


makes it easier for customers to find things—this, of


course, being the purpose of the site. It is also friendly


and makes you feel like a valued customer. You can write


reviews, get guidance from fellow customers and Amazon’s


recommendations, check out and arrange delivery easily,


return products conveniently, see your past orders, and so


on. Amazon’s attention to the non-functional requirements


has made it so attractive to shop at its site that people do


just that. Many people. As a result, Amazon has become the


world’s largest online retailer and has made its owner


staggeringly rich. (We are not promising Bezos-like riches if


you pay attention to non-functional requirements, but it


might help.)


The circumstances of your intended customers have an impact


on your usability requirements. Will your customer be


juggling other apps at the time of using yours? Will she need


## 第 744 页


to consult the grocery shopping list, send a photo of a


product to her spouse, and make a payment at more or less the


same time?


Does the customer for your product have a disability? For


example, customers who are partially sighted or have poor


eyesight should be considered. Seniors sometimes struggle to


use some apps, not because the seniors are incapable but


because they just can’t read the miniature typefaces on the


screen. Colorblindness can hamper a customer’s ability to


use a solution. About 1 in 12 males are red-green colorblind


(yes, these are the important traffic light colors) and might


be part of your usability requirements.


The usability of a product affects productivity, efficiency,


error rates, and so on. It also affects acceptance: whether


people actually use the product or are able to use the


product. Carefully consider what your customer is trying to


achieve with the product before writing usability


requirements. For example, you might write one of the


following sample requirements:


The product shall be usable by customers with no previous


experience of it.


## 第 745 页


The product (an accounting solution) shall be usable by


people with no formal accounting training.


The product shall be used in cold conditions and the operator


might be wearing heavy gloves.


The product shall be used by office staff with ten years of


schooling and fluency in English or Spanish.


The product shall be easy to learn by certified mechanical


engineers.


“Easy to use” and “easy to learn” are slightly different


characteristics. Easy-to-use products are designed to


facilitate an ongoing efficiency, so perhaps some training is


necessary before using the product. For example, suppose you


were specifying a product to be used for some repetitive


tasks in an office by clerical workers. You would be well-


advised to make it easy to use, even if the ease of use means


training people to use the product. The ongoing efficiency


will pay for this extra effort many times over.


Adobe Lightroom (Photoshop, or any of the other professional-


level photo manipulation products) is a case in point.


Lightroom is a comprehensive product that offers an amazing


wealth of options for the manipulation of digital images to


## 第 746 页


its intended audience of photographers. The Lightroom


learning curve is a steep one: There is a lot to be learned,


and we would venture to say that it is not particularly easy


to learn (at least it was not for one of your authors).


However, once learned, Lightroom’s features make


manipulating images a straightforward—even easy—task. Given


the depth of functionality needed to do the task and its


inherent complexity, Adobe has made its product easy to use


once you have learned how to use it.


By contrast, easy-to-learn products are aimed at those tasks


that are done infrequently and, therefore, may be forgotten


between uses—yearly reports, rarely used features of a


software product, and so on. Products that are used by the


public for which no prior training is feasible—telephones,


internet connections in public places, and dispensing


machines—need to be easy or quick to learn.


Your requirement might be as follows:


Description: The product shall be easy to use by a member of


the public on the first attempt without training.


Rationale: This new checkout product will save a considerable


amount on the cost of transactions, so we need our retail


## 第 747 页


customers to voluntarily switch to using it.


The rationale provides a justification of the customer’s


need, and also provides rich information to the builder of


the solution. In this case, the rationale says that this has


to be a solution that attracts people to use it; otherwise,


there is no point in building it.


We had a client who asked for the product to be “friendly.”


Because we could not immediately think of a suitable


measurement for this requirement, we felt, naturally enough,


that we could not write the description as “friendly” and


leave it at that. Some questioning revealed that the product


the client wanted would appeal to the personnel consultants


who were to use it. He knew that the consultants would be


more productive if they switched to the new product, but he


also knew that they would not use it, or would use it badly,


if they didn’t like it.


With that understanding, the requirement began to look like


this:


The product shall be liked by the personnel consultants.


We suggested to the client that we could measure the number


of consultants who, after an initial training period,


## 第 748 页


preferred to work with the new product rather than their old


way. The client agreed with this plan: He said that he would


be satisfied if 75% of the consultants were using the product


after a six-week familiarization period.


Thus, we had the description and rationale for our usability


requirement:


Description: The product shall provide the preferred way of
