working for the personnel consultants.


Rationale: To build the consultants’ confidence in the


product and achieve a 75% take-up rate


Usability and humanity requirements can cover areas such as


these:


• Rate of acceptance or adoption by the users


• Productivity gained as a result of the product’s


introduction


• Reduction of error rates


• Usage by people who do not speak the language of the


country where the product is to be used


## 第 749 页


• Personalization and internationalization to allow users to


change to local spelling, currency, and other preferences


• Accessibility to people with disabilities (this is


sometimes mandated by law)


• Use by people with no previous experience of the product


(an important, albeit often-forgotten consideration)


• Able to be used during the hours of darkness (this caters


to vampire users)


Usability requirements are derived from what your client is


trying to achieve with the operability of the product, and


from which kind of experience the users expect. Naturally,


the users’ characteristics and circumstances make a


difference to their expectations. You, as the requirements


analyst, have to discover these characteristics and determine


which levels of usability will turn the product into a useful


and pleasant experience for them.


Before you write your usability requirements, it is essential


to have a very clear picture of who will be using your


product. In Chapter 6, Customer Segments, we discussed the


process of constructing a persona: a virtual person that is a


distillation of the majority of your users. You survey your


## 第 750 页


user community, to derive this archetypal character to


represent that community. As a consequence, you write the


usability requirements to suit the persona—the embodiment of


almost all of the people who will actually use your product—


instead of writing them to suit your own personal preferences


or the preferences of just one or two of the loudest users.


Take a break and amuse yourself with usability requirements


for some of these users. The product can be anything you


choose:


• Round-the-world sailors


• Circus clowns


• Rock concert attendees


• Zombies


• Members of the US Lawn Mower Racing Association


• The most boring people in the world


Pay attention to usability, as it often leads you to discover


the differentiating factor between yours and competing


products.


## 第 751 页


Performance Requirements: Type 12


Performance requirements are written when your product needs


to perform some tasks in a given amount of time, or do some


tasks to a specific level of accuracy, or have certain data


storage capacity, or achieve a certain volume of throughput.


Think about the performance needs of the product if it is to


be successful. For example:


The product shall identify whether an aircraft is hostile or


friendly within 0.05 seconds.


Capacity is another performance requirement. This requirement


is one of the most critical ones for an ATM network, or other


distributed solutions:


The product shall support 50,000 concurrent users.


We previously mentioned a solution that predicts when ice


will form on roads and schedules trucks to treat them with


deicing material. The client for this solution wants to sell


it to road authorities around the world. These authorities


are responsible for geographical areas of varying sizes, so


the client needed to ensure that the product could handle the


## 第 752 页


largest area covered by any potential client. Initially, we


would have written the requirement as follows:


The product shall accommodate the largest geographical area


of any road authority in the world.


Of course, this is not a practical requirement to hand over


to a designer, so eventually we refined it:


Description: The product shall be able to analyze 5,000


roads.


Rationale: This is the anticipated maximum number of roads in


the area of any potential customer for the product.


When you are thinking about performance requirements,


consider such aspects as these:


• Speed to complete a task


• Accuracy of the results


• Safety to the operator


• Volumes of data to be held by the product


• Number of concurrent users or transactions at peak times


## 第 753 页


• Minimum acceptable performance


• Ranges of acceptable performance


• Throughput, such as the rate of transactions


• Efficiency of resource usage


• Reliability, often expressed as the mean time between


failures


• Availability—the uptime or time periods when users can


access the product


• Fault tolerance and robustness


• Scalability of most of the above


• Performance that is an improvement over any current


solution by a specified percentage


The last aspect mentioned would require your organization to


benchmark the performance of any previous system. Without


such a benchmark, it would be impossible to tell if a new


solution outperformed the old one. You might consider


benchmarking the system to be replaced during your Blastoff.


This way, you and your developers have a target to aim at.


## 第 754 页


Performance requirements can include the risk of damage to


people or property. If your product is a lawn mower, then


there is a genuine need for the product to avoid cutting off


the user’s toes. Isaac Asimov included the following


requirement in his laws of robotics:


A robot shall not injure a human being or, through inaction,


allow a human being to come to harm.


Hardware is not the only potential source of damage. You


should consider whether your software product could cause


damage, either directly or indirectly. The ice-predicting


product schedules trucks to spread deicing material on roads.


Because environmental damage from this material can be


serious, the following requirement is necessary:


Description: The product shall schedule deicing activities so


that the minimum necessary amounts of deicing material are


spread on roads.


Rationale: To minimize environmental damage to the area


adjacent to treated roads


In some cases, you may want to specify a performance


requirement for the outcome of a product use case. For


example, we found this performance-related requirement:


## 第 755 页


Description: When a scheduled truck reports that it has


broken down, the product shall provide a substitute truck


that can arrive at the breakdown within 30 minutes of the


breakdown notification.


Rationale: To make the road safe as soon as possible


Performance requirements come mainly from the operating


environment. Each environment has its own set of


circumstances and conditions. The people, machines, devices,


environmental conditions, and so on all place demands on the


product. The way your product responds to these conditions—


how fast it has to be, how strong, how big, how often—


dictates the appropriate performance requirements.


Operational and Environmental Requirements: Type 13


Operational requirements specify what the product has to do


if it is to operate correctly in its environment. In some


cases, the operating environment creates special


circumstances that have an effect on the way the product must


be constructed:


Description: The product shall be waterproof, shockproof, and


able to withstand freezing temperatures.


## 第 756 页


Rationale: The product shall be used in and around trucks at


night and during rainstorms, snow, and freezing conditions.


Not all products must operate in extreme environments; most


products are built to operate on laptops or workstations


installed in offices with an uninterruptible power supply.


However, within any office, it is almost always necessary to


interoperate with existing solutions. The operational


requirements in these cases specify what your product must do


to successfully collaborate with other products.


Sometimes the collaboration is with external systems, or


there is a need to access external databases. These items


show up as adjacent systems on the work context model:


The product shall interact in compliance with the Visa


International and Regional Operating Regulations issued


January 15, 2023.


To find the operational requirements, look at your product


boundary and consider the needs of each adjacent system.


Interview the representative of each of these systems to find


its interoperational requirements.


If you are intending to use ready-made products as part of


your solution, then here is where you specify the


## 第 757 页


interoperability requirements. These requirements would


specify what is needed to achieve correct interfacing between


the products, or what customization or configuration is


needed to complete the solution.


You should also consider the uniqueness of the environment


when using ready-made solutions. Because something works in


one place does not mean it works in another. For example, a


ready-made that works perfectly well in a UK hospital might


be unsuitable for a US hospital. The environment and work


practices would be quite different.


The people who make up the workforce are considered part of


the operating environment. Our colleague Aase Tvieto works at


a Norwegian university. She told us about the installers of


an accounting system who were not told that a lot of people


from outside Norway worked at visiting academic jobs at the


university. These people were contracted to receive their


payments in foreign banks. This omission led to a system that


struggled to account for foreign currencies, and caused a


considerable amount of frustration and inconvenience to both


the visiting academics and the university’s administrative


staff.


## 第 758 页


You might have to describe the physical environment affecting


the users when they use the product. This often means special


constraints are placed on the way the product is constructed.


For example, if the product will be used by people in


wheelchairs, or while people are driving, in the dark


(remember the vampires), in a hurry, and so on, then you must


specify that constraint.


Mobile devices have their own special set of requirements:


The product shall survive a drop of 10 feet (3 m) onto a hard


surface.


The product shall be usable in variable lighting conditions.


The product shall conserve battery life.


If you are building products for sale, you should include any


requirements needed to turn the product into a distributable


or saleable item. It is also appropriate to describe any


requirements that relate to the successful installation of


the product.


Maintainability and Support Requirements: Type 14


## 第 759 页


Usually, at requirements time you do not know exactly how


much maintenance your solution will undergo in its lifetime,


nor do you always know which type of maintenance it will


need. But you do know, beyond any uncertainty, that it will


need maintenance. Almost anything you build today will still


be around in five years (and probably more). Despite the


unpredictability of events during the life of your solution,


you can, to some extent, foresee some of the maintenance for


certain products. Consider whether any changes might occur in


the following areas:


• The organization that deploys your solution


• The technology used by your solution


• Other technology that affects your solution


• The operating environment


• Attitudes within the marketplace


• Laws that apply to the product


• Changes to the government (either by democratic or


revolutionary means)


• User demographics


## 第 760 页


• Business rules


If you know or strongly suspect that the product will undergo


relatively heavy maintenance due to expected changes, then


specify the types of expected changes and the amount of time


allowed for those changes.


If you are creating a software product that should be able to


run on several different operating systems, then specify


them:


Description: The product shall be readily portable to Android


and iOS.


Rationale: We anticipate moving into the mobile device


market.


Here you are saying to the developer that you want to be able


to implement the product on another platform at some point in


the future, and that you will hold her accountable for the


adaptability of the product to a new device. When you attach


the fit criterion (coming up in the next chapter) to this


requirement, you should specify the characteristics of the


device and the expected time or effort necessary to make the


transition.


## 第 761 页


The deicing product had this requirement:


The product shall be translated into various foreign


languages. As yet, the languages are unknown.


This requirement had a major effect on the product’s


designers. They designed the interface in such a way as to


make it easy to add new languages and new alphabets. Also,


they took into account the fact that different languages


sometimes mean different cultures and different ways of


presenting data.


As well as specifying that the solution must be able to be


opened up, requirements might also impose constraints. For


example:


Description: The product shall be written using the


organization’s standard technology stack.


Rationale: Developers can maintain the codebase.


Support requirements are also covered in this section of the


requirements specification. In some cases, your client may


indicate that the product will be supported by the existing


help desk; in other cases, the product must be entirely self-


supporting. By making this point clear at requirements time,


## 第 762 页


you ensure that the designer builds in the appropriate


mechanisms for contacting the help desk or providing answers


for questions likely to arise with usage.


Security Requirements: Type 15


There are a number of ways to look at security. The “CIA


trinity”—confidentiality, integrity, and availability—has


become quite standard. Confidentiality covers access and


privacy; integrity covers both integrity and audit;


availability covers the acceptable amount of downtime that a


solution is allowed. This also covers how much loss of data


is acceptable. We have presented these in a slightly


different order below, and we have also considered that


availability is covered as a performance requirement (see


above).


We also refer you to the National Institute of Standards and


Technology (NIST; https://www.nist.gov) and suggest you check


its Cybersecurity Framework.


Shari Lawrence Pfleeger, a security consultant, points out


that security can be thought of as having four aspects.


1. Access: The product’s data and functionality are


accessible to authorized users and can be produced in a


## 第 763 页


timely manner. Other access requirements focus on denying


access to unauthorized people.


2. Privacy: Data stored by the product is protected from


unauthorized or accidental disclosure. Privacy can also be


considered to be a compliance or legal requirement, but we


will deal with it here as a security issue. Privacy also


includes specifying how long data can be retained.


3. Integrity: The product’s data is the same as the source,


or authority, of the data, and is protected from corruption.


4. Audit: This is what the product has to do to allow


complete verification of its operations and data.


Access


Access means the solution’s data is, well, accessible. In


other words, the product stores its data in a way that users


can get at it and understand it.


In a security context, access requirements specify what the


product has to do to ensure that the product’s data is


available only to authorized users. At the same time, the


security employed must not hinder or unreasonably delay the


## 第 764 页


authorized users from getting what they want when they want


it.


When you write this kind of requirement, you are specifying


the allowable access—who is authorized, under which


circumstances authorization is valid, and which data and what


functions are accessible to each authorized user. For


example:


The product shall ensure that only authorized users have


access to the [name of] data (or function).


The term “authorized” may also need some further


explanation. For example, are all authorized users authorized


all the time? Does access depend on the time of day or the


location of the user at the time of access? Is there a need


for some kind of emergency override? Must a user collaborate


with another authorized user to gain access? In other words,


is the authorization conditional? If so, write these


conditions as a requirement.


Alternatively, you might write this kind of requirement as a


roles and permissions table. That is, roles on one dimension,


functions on the other and intersections showing who can


access what parts of the solution’s functionality and data.


## 第 765 页


You don’t normally specify security technology. However,


your client might have already implemented some security


technology—biometrics, passkeys, and so on. In this case,


your security requirements should specify this technology as


a technological constraint.


Privacy


Privacy is a concern to more and more people, and


particularly to organizations. We are dealing with privacy


under the heading of security, but these requirements could


also be envisioned as compliance requirements. Most Western


countries have laws governing privacy of personal information


held within computer systems. The European Union’s GDPR


(General Data Protection Regulation) is being adopted by more


and more countries—including the United States—as their own


law. GDPR is regarded as the toughest privacy and security


law in the world, hence the take-up by other countries, not


just those processing data within or exporting data from the


EU.


We suggest that you speak with senior management to determine


how serious they are about privacy. For example, is


management 100% committed to the privacy of customer data, or


are they prepared to sail a little closer to the wind? You


## 第 766 页


also need to spend some time with the company lawyers and


standards custodians, and work with them to interpret the


relevant privacy laws whether they be GDPR or local


regulations. This is done so that you can specify privacy


requirements in a way that they are both adequate for their


purpose and understandable to the developers.


If GDPR is too far-reaching for your needs, then you would


write requirements for what the product has to do to ensure


the privacy of its data. This capability is partly controlled


by access, as we discussed earlier, and partly by the product


ensuring that its data is not sent or distributed to


unauthorized people. This means the product must have control


over what copies—including printing—of the data can be made


and distributed.


Privacy breaches can lead to loss of customer confidence, to


penalties, and to fines. If your solution holds personal


information about the organization’s customers, then it must


protect that information. Significant fines can be levied if


that private information is ever released, either


accidentally or intentionally, from the organization.


For your own amusement, try some privacy requirements for the


following:


## 第 767 页


• Politicians


• Crooks


• Girlfriends or boyfriends


• Chefs


• Cats


Integrity


Integrity means that the data held by your solution


corresponds exactly to what was delivered to the product from


the adjacent system. The adjacent system is the originator,


and therefore, the authority for the data. You must consider


requirements for preventing the loss or corruption of data


and, should the worst happen, what the solution does to


recover lost or corrupted data. You might also consider what


happens when the original data changes. Does your version of


the data remain, or should it be updated to reflect its new


status?


In our deicing example, weather stations send data about


temperature and precipitation to the deicing solution. The


weather station originates the data so that any copies stored


by the deicing solution must be faithful to the weather


## 第 768 页


station’s version. Here is the appropriate integrity


requirement:


The product shall ensure that its road temperature data


corresponds exactly to the data transmitted by the weather


station.


You should also consider other integrity requirements, such


as those that cause the product to prevent unintentional


misuse by authorized users—the most common form of data


corruption. Naturally, the product must protect itself


against improper usage by outsiders as well. It must also


protect itself from bad data being imported.


Integrity also covers those requirements to prove the


integrity of the product after some abnormal happening. These


events can include such things as a power failure, an


exceptional operating condition, or unusual environmental


conditions such as a fire, flood, or bombing.


Immunity is also the concern of the security requirements.


You specify requirements for the product to protect itself


against malevolent software such as viruses, malware, denial-


of-service attacks, Trojan horses, and any of the many other


variations on the theme of attacking a computer system.


## 第 769 页


Backup, recovery, and archiving requirements are needed to


maintain the integrity of the product’s data in the event of


any unwanted disruption. You should talk to your operations


people to determine what steps are needed by the product to


prevent loss of data. You need to speak with your accountants


and legal team to determine what archiving is needed.


Auditing


Auditing is part of the security section of your


specification. Most accounting products have a requirement


that they be able to be audited. This should ensure that no


mistakes are made and that the results shown by the product


are correct. Audits are also used to detect fraud or misuse,


so audit requirements are often written to say that the


product must leave an audit trail. The precise nature of your


audit requirements must be negotiated with your own auditors,


who naturally are stakeholders for your project.


Audit requirements are standard for any product dealing with


money or valuable information or assets. Their inclusion


often results in requirements for the product to retain its


records for a given time.


Audit may also mean that the product maintains data on who


has accessed which information. The intention of this kind of


## 第 770 页


requirement is to ensure the integrity of the product’s


information:


Description: The product shall retain a journal of all


transactions for the statutory period.


Rationale: This is required by the auditors and by


accountancy laws.


...And No More


Charles Pfleeger, a security consultant, suggests adding


“...and no more” to your requirements. This phrase means


that the product must do exactly what the requirement


specifies and no more than it specifies. For example, if the


requirement is to find a name and address from a file, then


the product must not change the name and address after


finding them, or transmit the name and address in


contravention to the privacy requirements as discussed above.


Consider this access requirement:


The product shall allow access to authorized users.


The “...and no more” heuristic yields a complementary


requirement:


## 第 771 页


The product shall ensure that only authorized users are able


to gain access.


For security reasons, you might consider adding an overriding


requirement to your specification:


The product shall not do anything except that which has been


specified as a requirement.


Sometimes well-meaning product builders make the product


perform faster or be bigger than specified, or they add


unspecified features. While these properties may be


beneficial to one or more parts of the product, they may well


have a detrimental effect on the product as a whole or on the


security of the product. We know of several cases where


unauthorized or unspecified features added to a bank’s


website opened serious security loopholes. Make sure that


your development team does not build in extra features or


properties without first negotiating their inclusion as


requirements.


Clearly, security is essential. It should be assigned a


priority that reflects the value of misusing the product. For


example, if your product is to be used by a bank, or if it


processes credit card or financial trading transactions, then


## 第 772 页


the value of misuse (in financial terms) is high. Similarly,


if your product is intended for the military, then misuse may


result in loss of life (perhaps even your own) or loss of a


military advantage. Thus, for financial, military, or life-


support products, security has the highest priority, and


consumes more of the budget, than many commercial systems.


You should consider calling in a security expert as a


consultant stakeholder. Software developers are not usually


trained in security, and the security of some functionality


and data is so important that you need experts to advise on


the security requirements.


Cultural Requirements: Type 16


Cultural requirements specify special factors that would make


the product unacceptable because of customs, religions,


languages, taboos, prejudices, or almost any other aspect of


human behavior. Cultural requirements are needed when you try


to sell a product into a different country, state, or


organization, particularly when its culture and/or language


is different from your own.


While “hello” and “stop” are almost universally


recognized words and have the same meaning in all cultures,


## 第 773 页


most other words don’t. In English we have a single word for


“you,” whether we are speaking to one or many people


(excluding the Southern “y’all”). Many other languages,


however, have a different word for the plural and singular


“you.” Matters become even more complicated in those


languages that have a different “you” depending on the


familiarity of the contact. In French, for example, you use


the formal vous to speak with people in a business situation


—especially superiors—and tu when speaking to family and


close friends. To use tu too soon in a relationship can be


thought of as rude. In Denmark, the familiar du is used


almost always except when speaking to old people, when you


say de. To use the formal de is considered stiff and


unnatural by most people.


Sometimes cultural requirements are not immediately obvious.


We take our own culture for granted, and we don’t give a lot


of thought to how other people might perceive our products


and ourselves. If your product is to be used outside your own


country, and in some cases outside your own local region or


state or even your own organization, consider whether you


should call on the services of a cultural expert.


Cultural requirements are often unexpected, and at first


glance they sometimes appear to be irrational, such as


## 第 774 页


vampires will not enter your house unless you invite them in.


But you have to keep in mind that the reason behind the


requirements lies outside your own culture. If your reaction


is “Why on earth do they do it like that?”, the answer is


probably culture. It is also worth noting that different


professions might have cultural differences. The culture of,


say, engineering is quite different from that of marketing.


Following are some cultural requirements you might consider.


Religious observances:


The product shall not display religious symbols or words


associated with mainstream religions.


Cultural sensitivity:


The product shall not display terms, icons, or images deemed


unsuitable by the communications director (or whoever makes


that kind of decision in your organization).


Spelling:


The product shall use American spelling.


Forcing political or cultural alignment:


## 第 775 页


The product shall offer the choice of language in the order


appropriate for the region of the country.


This last requirement comes from Belgium, where three


languages are spoken; each region naturally considers its


language to be the most important. It is considered


inappropriate to offer French before Flemish if the user is


logged in from Flanders.


The more we build products for use in different walks of


life, by different professions, and for different


socioeconomic groups in different countries, the more we need


to consider cultural requirements.


Cultural diversity and inclusion mean that your solution


should not discriminate or fail to include minorities.


Sometimes this means that you must allow individual users to


nominate their own titles, pronouns, and honorifics. In any


event, there is an overarching requirement:


The product shall not discriminate against recognized


segments of society.


Bear in mind that some of these cultural diversity and


inclusion requirements might also be compliance requirements.


## 第 776 页


Compliance Requirements: Type 17


The cost of litigation is one of the major risks for OTS


software and it can be expensive for other kinds of software


as well. You must make yourself aware of the laws that apply


to your kind of product and write requirements to ensure that


the product complies with these laws. Even if you are


building software for use inside your own organization, be


aware that laws applying to the workplace might be relevant.


A compliance requirement looks like this:


The product shall comply with the Americans with Disabilities


Act.


This is a very broad requirement, and you would need to sit


down with lawyers to determine all of the parts of the ADA


that are applicable to your product. That would probably


result in you writing multiple requirements to ensure


compliance. You need to consult with your lawyers to


determine what these requirements should be.


You are required by law to display copyright notices,


particularly if you are using other people’s products.


Additionally, products are required by law to display warning


messages if there is any danger that some dim-witted user


## 第 777 页


might do the wrong thing with it. For example, a blanket made


in a southeast Asian country carries this warning:


Warning. Do not use this blanket as a hurricane shelter.


A label on a child’s scooter:


This product moves when used.


Start with your company’s lawyers; they have far more


experience with the law than you. Here are several things


that you can do to facilitate compliance.


• Examine adjacent systems or users—that is, the entities


that have contact with your product. You can use your context


diagram to identify them.


• Consider their legal requirements and rights. For example,


are any of the disabled-access laws applicable? Does the


adjacent system have any rights to privacy for the data that


you hold? Do you need proof of transaction? Or nondisclosure


of the information your product has about the adjacent


system?


• Determine whether any laws are relevant to your product.


For example, are data protection, privacy laws, guarantees,


## 第 778 页


consumer protection, consumer credit, or right to information


laws applicable?


• Check laws like the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX), Health


Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), Privacy


and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations,


General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), EU Consumer Laws,


Federal Trade Commission Act, Financial Services and Markets


Act, and more.


There’s more. Lots more. We urge you to consult your


organization’s lawyers. After all, they are paid to give


advice on matters of legal compliance.


Standards


Compliance requirements are not limited to the law of the


land. Some products must comply with industrial or


professional standards. For example:


The product shall comply with our ISO 9001 certification.


There is also the possibility that your solution must comply


with organizational policies. There may be internal standards


or there might be rules that apply to your or your


customer’s organization. For example, there might be rules


## 第 779 页


about improper use of the solution, or there might be


standards over and above any national standards.


Now that we have considered the content of the non-functional


requirements, let’s look at ideas for finding them.


Finding the Non-functional Requirements


Like all requirements, the non-functional ones can come to


light at any time. Nevertheless, there are certain places to


look that provide better opportunities to discover them.


Business Use Cases


We have stressed the efficacy of business events for the


discovery of requirements, and they will pay off once again


here. The business use case, the BUC, is the response to a


business event. It is the functionality that is triggered by


an external adjacent system (when the business event happens)


and continues to execute until the functionality needed to


achieve the outcome of the business event has been completed.


If you look closely at this functionality and the triggering


adjacent system, the non-functional requirements become


easier to see.


## 第 780 页


Take, for example, the BUC shown in Figure 26.3. This diagram


plays loosely with diagramming notation, but that is


deliberate to illustrate the point.


![embedded_p780_127.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p780_127.jpeg)


Figure 26.3 A business use case that is triggered by an


adjacent system, in this case a nurse in a hospital. The BUC


accesses a database of patient records and other medical


information.


Now let’s look at the adjacent system, the nurse, and ask


what non-functional requirements are needed for her.


Usability requirements would be high on the list. Nurses are


typically busy, and solutions aimed at them must be highly


## 第 781 页


usable, highly efficient, and with a logical workflow. Usable


solutions are responsible for fewer errors being committed,


which for hospital work is pretty important. For example:


Description: The product shall have a logical workflow.


Rationale: Hospital experience has shown that familiar


working practices result in fewer errors.


There is also a usability requirement to do with your


solution being consistent with other solutions that she


operates:


Description: The product shall appear familiar to nurses.


Rationale: Nurses are too busy to learn new interfaces. We


want nurses to start using the solution on their first


exposure to it.


Of course, you could think of this requirement as a


learnability requirement. The types of requirements often


overlap.


Look and feel requirements also come into play. The


appearance has to be medical—a nurse would not want to


operate a solution that looks like a game:


## 第 782 页


Description: The product must have a medical or clinical


appearance consistent with other hospital products.


Rationale: Nurses will feel more confident and be more


willing to use the solution if it has an appearance that is


compatible with the nurses’ work.


This requirement is slightly more difficult to quantify, but


you will be able to write a suitable fit criterion for it


after you have read Chapter 27, Fit Criteria and Rationale.


Operational requirements are also there to be discovered.


This business use case will probably have to operate by


linking to several databases, several medical devices, and


imaging devices, and of course must be available throughout


the hospital. You would write quite a few operational


requirements to accommodate the interfaces with these other


devices.


Privacy requirements must be treated very carefully. This is


a medical solution, so there are probably patient records


available to it. These are highly confidential, and there are


severe penalties for disclosing them. To get the privacy


requirements, you must sit down with the hospital


## 第 783 页


administrators and lawyers and probably several other


specialists.


Compliance requirements are needed to ensure that the


product does not transgress relevant laws and standards that


apply to medical solutions. Again, the lawyers are valuable


stakeholders.


Of course, there would be a lot more to it than space permits


here. The point is that you can take each business use case


individually, and by inspecting its functionality and its


adjacent systems, dig out its non-functional requirements


using the checklist in the template to help you.


The Template


The Requirements Specification Template in Appendix A has


more explanation and examples of the non-functional


requirements. You can use this template as a checklist of


non-functional requirement types when interviewing your


stakeholders. Go through the template looking at each of the


subtypes of non-functional requirements and probe for


examples of each.


Prototypes and Non-functional Requirements


## 第 784 页


You can use prototypes to help uncover non-functional


requirements. At requirements time, the prototype usually


takes the form of a whiteboard sketch, a paper prototype, a


wireframe, or some other quick-and-dirty mockup of what the


product might be like. The intention here is not to design


the product, but rather to ensure that you have understood


the needs by reverse-engineering the requirements from the


prototype. We discussed this process in Chapter 10,


Generating Sacrificial Candidate Solutions.


In the case of the road deicing solution, let’s say your


stakeholders respond favorably to a sketch of a screen


showing the roads to be treated in a glowing, cold blue


color, the safe roads in green, and the treated roads in


yellow. This is illustrated in Figure 26.4, albeit without


the color. This prototype yields at least these usability


requirements:


Description: The product shall clearly distinguish between


safe and unsafe roads.


Description: The product shall make any unsafe roads obvious.


## 第 785 页


![embedded_p785_128.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p785_128.jpeg)


Figure 26.4 A sketched prototype of a screen for the road


deicing solution. The screen is a proposal for the engineers


and is used to elicit requirements.


You do not yet know that “a glowing, cold blue color” is


intuitive—you need some ergonomic input, help from a UX


designer, or user surveys for that. Nevertheless, the


intention is clear from the prototype.


## 第 786 页


Go over your prototypes using the template. For each non-


functional type, which requirements does the prototype


suggest? Go through the prototype carefully, keeping in mind


that the prototype is not the requirement, but rather a


simulation of the requirements.


The Client


The client for the product may also have expectations that


are relevant to your quest for non-functional requirements.


In many cases, the reason for building a new product is to


provide a service to the users or to the customers of the


business, and the attractiveness of that service depends on


its non-functional qualities. For example, providing


portable, highly usable, or secure functionality may be


crucial to the development effort. Alternatively, your client


may say that if you cannot provide a live, interactive


display of the current trading position, then he does not


want the product. Thus, your client becomes the prime source


of the critical non-functional requirements.


Once the functional requirements are met, the non-functional


qualities may be what persuade potential customers to buy


your product. After all, your own buying decisions are often


influenced by the non-functional properties of the products


## 第 787 页


you bought. Also think about the non-functional requirements


of products that you admire.


Table 26.1 summarizes the questions to ask for a use case or


a functional requirement. Ask your client to what degree


these questions are relevant to the product you are


specifying. Your client, or the marketing department, is the


source of information about what will make customers buy the


product.


Table 26.1 Finding Non-functional Requirements


## 第 788 页


![embedded_p788_129.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p788_129.jpeg)


## 第 789 页


![embedded_p788_129.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p788_129.jpeg)


For each use case or the product as a whole, consider the


factor in the first column of Table 26.1. When you have


adequate knowledge of this factor, use it as a trigger to


start questioning your stakeholders about the requirement


types in the second column.


Don’t Write a Solution


We have already mentioned the inadvisability of writing a


solution instead of a requirement. This practice is so


widespread (especially with non-functional requirements) and


potentially so serious that you will forgive us if we mention


it again.


Don’t presuppose a solution or enforce a solution by the way


you write your requirements. By the same token, don’t adopt


a current solution to a problem and write that as the


requirement. Suppose, for example, that you write a security


requirement like this:


The product shall require a password to access account data.


## 第 790 页


Now the designer is forced to use a password in the solution.


As a result, even if a better security device than passwords


is available—and there absolutely are—the product builder


may not use it. In this case, writing a solution as the


requirement prevents the designer from searching for an


alternative, and probably better, solution.


By writing:


The product shall ensure that account data can be accessed


only by authorized users.


you are asking the product designer or a security consultant


—people qualified to do this—to find the most effective


security solution.


Apart from potentially solving the wrong problem, one of the


main concerns with writing a solution instead of a


requirement is that technology is constantly changing.


Solutions lock you into one technology or another, and


whatever you choose may be out of date by the time the


product is built. By writing a requirement that does not


include any technological component, you not only allow the


designer to use the most appropriate, up-to-date technology,


## 第 791 页


but also allow the product to change and adapt to new


technologies as they emerge.


To follow the guideline of not writing solutions, examine


your requirements. If any of them contain an item of


technology or a method, ask why the requirement exists.


Rewrite the requirement to suit your answer, and ask why


again. Do this three times. At that stage, the requirement is


as good as it is ever likely to be.


Review


Imagine a world where an automated process takes longer to do


than if you had done it manually; where your phone was so


difficult to use that it required you to frequently refer to


the instruction manual in order to use it; where your


neighbor could see your transactions whenever you used your


online banking; where the appearance of your mail app so


repulsed you that you stopped using it; where the websites


you visit use questionable cultural language; where your


notes app does not connect to any other app and cannot


receive messages from the internet; where the internet must


be reconnected each day, and then runs slowly and


intermittently; where none of your household appliances are


easy or pleasant to use.


## 第 792 页


This dysfunctional world is where nobody thinks about non-


functional requirements.


Despite their obvious importance, you should not overly worry


about what type of non-functional requirement one is. Take,


for example, an NFR about colorblindness. Is it a usability


requirement, or is it about accessibility? Or perhaps


compliance? It doesn’t matter. As long as you have


discovered the requirement, it’s fine whatever you call it.


For example, take the case of a non-functional privacy


requirement about compliance with GDPR (which you could


consider to be a security requirement or a compliance one).


Complying with GDPR uncovers a range of associated


requirements, both functional and non-functional:


The solution shall allow a manager to create a Subject Access


Request report and send it to a Data Subject on request.


That is a functional requirement. The following one looks


like a functional requirement but is actually a compliance


non-functional requirement:


The solution shall store all data within the European Union.


## 第 793 页


(You might find an equivalent requirement within the United


States.)


The solution shall allow corrections to be made to data where


a Data Subject notifies the company of an inaccuracy.


(Functional requirement)


The moral of the story is to not worry about whether a


requirement is functional or non-functional, but to worry


about finding all the requirements.


Resources


The Requirements Specification Template packaged in Appendix


A of this book is the most comprehensive source of non-


functional requirements available. And you already own it.

the qualitative aspect into the eight most important system


qualities.


The Quest for Software Requirements by Roxanne Miller


(MavenMark Books, 2009). This book is an excellent guide to

## 第 795 页


Chapter 27. Fit Criteria and Rationale


Why do we need to measure? Remember when you bought your


phone? One of the factors you considered was its storage


capacity—you needed one with enough storage. When you went


to the phone shop or went online, “enough storage” was not


listed as an attribute of any of the phones on offer.


However, “enough storage” is one of your requirements.


Storage costs money, so you don’t splash out and buy the


largest capacity they have. Instead, you calculate how big


your photo and video collection is, how much music you want


to hold in the phone, how many apps you have and their data


amounts, and so on. From all of this you arrive at a number,


and let’s say the number is 512GB. So now you go looking for


a phone with 512GB of storage, as this fits your requirement.


Note what happened. Without thinking too much about it, you


converted an imprecise requirement, “enough storage,” into


a precise requirement, 512GB. This precision enabled you to


go forward with your purchase.


Another requirement is that you don’t want to spend too much


money on the phone; you have plenty of other things to do


with your money. Here we have numbers again—you are willing


to spend, say, 500 dollars/pounds/euros, and so look for


## 第 796 页


these numbers displayed alongside the phones. Nobody lists


the phone as costing “not too much money.” Once again, you


translate a human requirement into numbers.


That was easy. Let’s be a little more ambitious. Let’s for


an enjoyable moment say that a proverbial rich uncle has


bequeathed you a considerable amount of money, and you and


your partner decide to use the money to build your dream


house. You purchase a block of land and hire a well-regarded


architect.


You now have to turn your needs into numbers. You have lots


of friends, so “A kitchen big enough to cook for my


friends” needs to be converted to measurements (as does the


dining space). How much space do you need between the center


island and the cooktop? You don’t want to take too many


steps between the two, but you want your partner to be able


to walk behind you without having to squeeze through.


(Squeezing your partner should probably be left until after


dinner and the guests have departed.)


You want a pantry cupboard “big enough to hold the spice


collection; the bottles of vinegars, oils, and sauces; other


ingredients, and a week’s supply of food.” This has to be


converted to measurements. As does the wine cellar where your


## 第 797 页


newfound wine collection is to be stored (Uncle Albert left


you his extensive wine collection along with the money).


It is the architect’s task here to find out what you need,


and to develop precise plans with measurements so that the


builders build exactly the house for you. See Figure 27.1.


Unless they have precise measurements, the builders will


build what they imagine you want or what they feel like


building. Additionally, if they do not build exactly to the


measurements, there is a possibility of running afoul of


local construction codes and having to demolish and rebuild.


## 第 798 页


![embedded_p798_130.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p798_130.jpeg)


Figure 27.1 Architects’ plans naturally include detailed


measurements to ensure that construction is done to match the


## 第 799 页


requirements.


This is analogous to what happens in software construction.


Unless you hand over a precise measurement of how you intend


to measure the delivered product, the results are almost


certain to be at best disappointing, and at worst a complete


waste of time. The latter means you probably have to demolish


and rebuild.


Architects use feet and inches or millimeters, but


requirements can’t be measured that way. We need another way


to measure, and this is the role of the fit criterion.


Why Does Fit Need a Criterion?


When you have a requirement for the product to perform some


function or to have some property, the testing activity must


demonstrate that the product does indeed perform that


function or possess the desired property. To carry out such


tests, the requirement must have a benchmark such that the


testers can compare the delivered product with the original


requirement. The benchmark is the fit criterion—a


quantification of the requirement that demonstrates the


standard that the product must reach.


## 第 800 页


“The idea is for each requirement to have a


quality measure that makes it possible to divide


all solutions to the requirement into two


classes: those for which we agree that they fit


the requirement and those for which we agree that


they do not fit the requirement.”—Christopher


Alexander, Notes on the Synthesis of Form


You should also consider the builders of the product. It


stands to reason that once they know the criterion for the


product’s acceptance, they will build to that standard. If


they are told their product will be used underwater, and the


acceptance criterion is that the product must operate for as


long as six months at a depth of 3,000 feet (900 m), then


they are unlikely to deliver something with a sunroof (see


Figure 27.2).


## 第 801 页


![embedded_p801_131.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p801_131.jpeg)


Figure 27.2 If they know the performance criterion that the


product must meet before it is accepted, the builders will


strive to build a product to meet that criterion.


Possibly the most challenging part of testing a requirement


against an agreed-upon measurement is defining the


appropriate measurement for the requirement. It is tricky,


but certainly not impossible.


Let’s suppose that your stakeholder is inexperienced and


asks for a product that is “user friendly.” This is an


incredibly vague and overused phrase, and what it means to


## 第 802 页


you is likely not the same thing as what it means to your


stakeholder. However, once you can measure “user


friendliness”—that is, put numbers against it—then you and


the stakeholder are able to arrive at an identical


understanding.


Additionally, the measurement of friendliness is passed along


to the developers, who treat it as a benchmark. They now know


how you and your stakeholder will test the delivered product:


You will measure it against the fit criterion.


So how do you find a measurement for “user friendly”?


First, you need to understand the reason for the requirement.


This is where the rationale comes into play. The rationale


is the same as the “So that” part of a story. Please use


whichever term you prefer. Ask the question, “What is the


justification for this requirement?”, or as that seems a


little formal, “Why do you have this requirement?”


Suppose that after some interrogation, your stakeholder


reveals that as far as he is concerned, “a user-friendly


product will be liked by the customers who are intended to


use it.” A little more probing reveals that “liked by the


## 第 803 页


customers” means they voluntarily change over to this new


product, and don’t hesitate before using it.


Description: The product shall be user friendly.


Rationale: We need customers to voluntarily change to the new


product, and not hesitate before using it.


This explanation gives us something to measure: the duration


of hesitation before using the product, the time elapsed


before complete adoption of it, or the user satisfaction


level after a period of usage.


Fit Criterion: On average, customers commence using the


product within five seconds of encountering it for the first


time.


Or:


Fit Criterion: Eighty percent of customers are voluntarily


using the product within six months of its release.


Or:


Fit Criterion: Customer surveys between six months and a year


after launch give a satisfaction rating of greater than 75%.


## 第 804 页


Some of these criteria might seem a little expensive to test,


but this is an important requirement. The rationale tells you


that customers should start using the product voluntarily. If


customers do not switch over to the new product, then the


project is a failure. With a requirement this important, it


is worth putting some effort into its development and


testing.


All of this goes to say that to make it precise, a


requirement cannot be just a text description. It also needs


a rationale and a fit criterion to be complete.


A fit criterion and the acceptance criteria for a story are


more or less the same thing. We’ll come back to acceptance


criteria later.


The Rationale for the Rationale


Quite often, stakeholders tell you their


perceived solution to the problem, rather than


their real need.


The rationale is the reason, or justification, for a


requirement. We have found that attaching a rationale to the


requirement makes the real need become apparent. Quite often,


## 第 805 页


stakeholders tell you their perceived solution to the


problem, rather than their real need.


For example, suppose the dialogue with your client goes


something like this:


“I need a screen to show me where all of my trucks are.”


You need a rationale for this. One approach is to ask why.


“So that when I get a request from one of my customers to


pick up some goods and transport them, I can find the truck


closest to the customer.”


“Why send the closest one? Could it be occupied at the


time?”


“Well, yes, I need vacant truck.”


“What about the destination? Do all trucks go to all


destinations?”


“No, some of them won’t go interstate. This is because of


their license.”


“So can we say that the reason—the rationale for this


requirement is not to see all the trucks but to find the


## 第 806 页


nearest available, suitable truck?”


“Yes, that’s really what I need.”


So now you have the requirement like this:


Description: The product shall assign the nearest available


suitable truck to the customer.


Rationale: The truck should arrive at the customer’s


location as soon as possible.


Finding the requirement’s rationale is the first step in


discovering the real need. And discovering the real need is


really the rationale for your job as a business analyst.


Sometimes, instead of giving you a solution as the supposed


requirement, your stakeholder gives you a requirement that is


so vague as to be (for the moment) unusable. In the example


given previously, the client asked for a “user-friendly”


product, but you could make sense of it when you learned that


the rationale was that the project needed the users to


readily adopt the product.


Suppose the rationale had been different. Say, instead of


ready adoption, the client gave you a rationale that


## 第 807 页


indicated a “user-friendly” product is so easy to use that


its users make fewer errors than they do with the current


product. The corresponding requirement has a different


meaning, and the resultant fit criterion is completely


different.


Description: The product shall be user-friendly.


Rationale: Users must find the new product easier to use than


the current product so that they make fewer errors.


Fit criterion: The average error rate for all user input


shall be less than 1.5%.


The rationale is not only a guide to help you find the fit


criterion, but also a means to help you know when you have


several different requirements masquerading as one. One


stakeholder says “user friendly” means the product is


pleasant to use, another says “user friendly” means the


product is exciting, and yet another says a “user-friendly”


product encourages users to make return visits to it. In this


case, you have three different requirements, each with its


own fit criterion that measures the desired property.


You must communicate a way to measure the


requirement’s real meaning.


## 第 808 页


Additionally, the rationale provides the basis for making


decisions about how to implement the requirement. Put


yourself in the developers’ shoes: You usually must choose


between several possible solutions, and if you understand the


thinking underlying the requirement, you can come up with the


most appropriate solution. Also, when you need to make trade-


off decisions, it helps if you understand the relative


importance of the requirement to the business, and the effect


that it will have if the requirement is not correctly


implemented.


Description: The product shall ensure that the buyer is


connecting from an approved country.


Rationale: Some countries do not have copyright laws, and our


suppliers prohibit us from selling into those countries.


Let’s not forget the testers’ need for a coherent


rationale. There are many ways to design tests for


requirements’ fit criteria, some of which involve much more


time and expense than others. A tester needs to understand


the reason for a requirement if she is to make the best


decision about where to spend testing time and money. We have


more to say about testing in Chapter 36, Quality Thinking.


## 第 809 页


Later, when a product is being used and maintained, the


rationale still has a vital role. You can work out what a


software product is doing by reading the code and observing


the people who use it. But suppose you need to make a change


to a product: If you do not understand why the product does


what it does, you reduce the odds that you will make the


correct change and increase the odds that your changes will


corrupt some related but distant part of the product—the


ripple effect. The problems that arise from a lack of


understanding of the rationale partly explain why software


maintenance is so time-consuming and expensive.


The rationale is the cognitive thread that connects your


customer’s business and the delivered product. It is


through knowing why something exists that the business


analyst/product owner is able to discover the correct


statement of need and the developers are able to construct


the correct product.


When asking stakeholders for their rationale for a


requirement, you might appear to be like the child constantly


asking a parent, “Why?” So be it—that is the role of the


requirements analyst. You have to ask why, and keep on asking


why, until you get to the real reason for the requirement.


But you haven’t finished yet, because you still have to pass


## 第 810 页


along a way to measure the requirement’s real meaning. That


is why you derive its fit criterion.


Finding Fit Criteria


To find an appropriate fit criterion, start by analyzing the


description and rationale you have established for the


requirement.


Description: The product shall make it easy for a buyer to


find his chosen music.


Rationale: Music buyers are familiar with the internet and


are accustomed to convenience and fast response times. They


will not tolerate slow or awkward searches for their chosen


music.


The rationale tells you that the requirement is about speed—


which is fairly easy to quantify—and awkwardness—which is


about complexity and perceived ease. For the speed component,


imposing a time limit for a search is appropriate. Suppose


your market research personnel tell you 9 seconds is the


limit of the target audience’s tolerance; to be better than


the competition, you are aiming for 6 seconds for your own


product. Keep in mind that this is measuring the customer’s


actions, not the time taken to search the catalog.


## 第 811 页


In terms of “awkwardness” mentioned in the rationale, your


ergonomics people and market research both say that buyers


must be able to find a wanted piece of music in no more than


three actions (an action here means a click, a gesture, a


menu selection, voice command, or some other conscious action


on the user’s part).


Your measurement for these, expressed as a fit criterion, is


this:


Fit Criterion: An average music buyer shall be able to locate


any piece of music within 6 seconds, using no more than three


actions.


Note that the time limit of 6 seconds also directs the


designer to make it obvious to the music buyer what has to be


done to find the music. A limit of 6 seconds means that there


is very little time for hesitating and figuring out what to


do next.


If you can’t measure a requirement, it is not


really a requirement.


Some fit criteria may, at first, be unattainable because of


business or real-life constraints. In other cases, your


## 第 812 页


client may not be willing to spend the amount required for


the implementation to meet the criterion. Thus, sometimes you


might negotiate an adjustment to the fit criterion so that it


allows for the product’s operating environment, the intended


usage, and the client’s budget. Think of these adjustments


as business tolerances. As you are certain that some of the


intended users of the product will be below-average


performers, you would adjust the fit criterion to read as


follows:


Fit Criterion: Ninety percent of music buyers shall be able


to locate any piece of music within 6 seconds, using no more


than three actions.


Scale of Measurement


Any requirement can be measured. All you have to


do is find a suitable scale with which to measure


it.


The scale of measurement is the unit you use to test the


conformance of the solution to its requirement. Take, for


example, a usability requirement. You can measure the time


needed to learn a product, or the time taken before achieving


## 第 813 页


a particular level of competence, or perhaps even the error


rate of the work done using the product.


You can measure anything.


Scales of measurement exist for all non-functional


requirements. Performance requirements can be measured by


time taken or availability percentages. Compliance


requirements can be measured against the relevant laws and


regulations. Look and feel requirements can be measured by


conformance to preexisting corporate branding standards.


Operational requirements can be measured by the accuracy and


exchange speeds between processors in the operating


environment. Cultural requirements, because they have to do


with human acceptance, are usually measured by acceptance


from marketing and customer relations.


So far, the only thing that we have not been able to find a


scale of measurement for is love. We cannot find any way of


measuring how much you love someone. Readers are welcome to


send suggestions.


Fit Criteria for Non-functional Requirements


## 第 814 页


A non-functional requirement is a quality that the product


must have, such as usability, look and feel, performance, and


so on. The fit criterion is, therefore, a measure of that


quality. Here we examine fit criteria for all the different


types of non-functional requirements.


Let’s look at an example. Your authors came across this


requirement for a consumer electronics product aimed at a


teenage market:


Description: The product shall be cool.


Even vague, ambiguous requirements can be


measured.


This requirement at first sight might seem hopeless and


unable to be measured; there is no deterministic scale of


coolness. If you look a little bit more closely, however, you


find that “cool” is a term often used to mean “something


that is desirable or impressive to have, or to be.”


When we asked why the product had to be “cool,” we were


given a rationale that consumers had to be attracted to the


product, and to want to own one and be seen to own it. To


satisfy this need, we had to first measure the product’s


## 第 815 页


attractiveness to its intended audience. The first attempt at


a fit criterion was this:


Fit Criterion: Forty percent of the people who see the


product on display in a store pick it up.


Naturally, you would not go live with the real product and


see if it met the test; you would follow the lead of most


electronics companies and test mock-ups with representative


groups of the target audience.


We improved the fit criterion to this:


Fit Criterion: Forty percent of the target audience who see


the product on display in the store pick it up and hold it


for at least 5 seconds.


We also felt that if the person who had picked up the product


showed it to someone else, it indicated that she felt that


the product was desirable. The “Hey, look at this” gesture


indicated the value she put on the product. Thus:


Fit Criterion: Forty percent of the target audience who see


the product on display in a store pick it up, hold it for at


least 5 seconds, and show it to a companion (if one is


present).


## 第 816 页


Of course, an even better fit criterion would have been a


measure of whether people actually bought the product, but


given the target market, we had to take into consideration


the fact that not everyone would be able to afford it.


Therefore, simply picking up, holding, and showing the


product was seen as the first test of how desirable it was,


or how envious nonowners would be. The client called this the


product’s coolness.


Of course, “coolness” must go beyond the store display. We


needed to add other requirements that specified how


convenient the product was to use. Clearly, a cool product


must be very convenient—cool—to use.


Earlier in this chapter, you saw an example of a requirement


that specified a “user-friendly” product; the client said


that “user friendly” meant the staff liked it. You can


measure “like”: If the staff likes the product, they will


use it. You can measure how quickly they start using it, how


much they use it, or how soon word gets around that the


product is good and users encourage one another to use it.


All of these criteria quantify the client’s desire that the


staff like the product and use it (see Figure 27.3).


## 第 817 页


![embedded_p817_132.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p817_132.jpeg)


Figure 27.3 You can measure your users’ liking for a


product by surveying their work practices before and after


the product is introduced, by measuring how long it takes


them to start using the product once it is available, or by


surveying them after a period of use to ascertain their


liking for the product.


You could write a fit criterion like this:


## 第 818 页


Fit Criterion: Within three months of introducing the


product, 60% of the users shall be using it to carry out the


agreed-upon work. From those users, the product shall receive


a 75% or more approval rating.


Note how you clarify the requirement when you add its fit


criterion. By negotiating a measurement, you transform the


requirement from a vague and somewhat ambiguous intention


into a fully formed, testable requirement.


You will find that it is usually not possible to get the


complete, measurable requirement from your first interview.


Indeed, it is highly unlikely that your stakeholders will


express themselves in such precise terms. We suggest you go


with the flow; don’t slow down your requirements-discovery


processes to make the requirement measurable, but rather get


the stakeholders’ intention—you write this as the


description—and the rationale. Then, analyze your


understanding, write your own best interpretation of the fit


criterion, and improve it by discussing it with your


stakeholder. You both need to agree that your proposed fit


criterion is an accurate measurement of the requirement.


Product Failure


## 第 819 页


The fit criterion might be determined by asking your


stakeholder, “What would you consider a failure to meet this


requirement?” Suppose you have this requirement:


Description: The product must produce the road deicing


schedule within an acceptable time.


Clearly, the scale of measurement here is time. Your client


can tell you how much time she thinks would constitute a


failure. For example, the client would consider the product


unacceptable if the engineer has to wait more than 15 seconds


for the schedule to become available. This means you have the


following fit criterion, with suitable business tolerances


applied:


Fit Criterion: The road deicing schedule shall be available


to an engineer within 15 seconds of the request being made


for 90% of the times that it is produced. It shall never take


longer than 20 seconds.


Sometimes, however, you may discover there is no agreement on


a quality measure, and hence there can be no fit criterion.


In these circumstances, it is probable that the original


requirement is not really a requirement. Perhaps several


requirements have been lumped together into one requirement;


## 第 820 页


in this case, each of the sub-requirements would then have


its own measurement.


Alternatively, perhaps the requirement is so vague, and its


intention so unrealistic, that it is not possible to know


whether it has been satisfied. For example, there is no


possible fit criterion for this requirement, and so it must


be rejected:


Description: I want a product my grandmother would have liked


if she were alive today.


Subjective Tests


Some requirements have to be tested using subjective tests.


For example, if a cultural requirement for a product to be


used in the public domain is “not offensive to any group,”


then the fit criterion must be along these lines:


Fit Criterion: The product shall not be offensive to at least


85% of a test panel representing the makeup of the people


likely to encounter the product. No more than 10% of the


interest groups represented in the panel shall report that


they felt offended.


## 第 821 页


The business tolerance here allows for the fact that you


cannot count on 100% of humans passing any test. In this


case, the business tolerances shield the product from the


lunatic-fringe extreme views, while at the same time allowing


“offensive” to be measured.


Although fit criteria are measures of the


product’s performance, it is sometimes more


cost-effective to test prototypes built


specifically for the purpose.


For this kind of testing, it is usually more cost-effective


to test prototypes or simulations built specifically for the


purpose than to test the delivered product itself. You would


hate to put in the effort to build the real thing and then


find your audience thought it offensive.


You can use subjective tests for your fit criteria, but the


numbers you use in fit criteria are not subjective. Suppose


you have a fit criterion of “reduce the time to perform


[some task] by 25% of the current time.” This means that the


current time must be known and documented, not just guessed.


The reason for the target of a 25% reduction must be well-


understood and agreed to by the client, and not just your


subjective feeling as to what is acceptable. The reasoning


## 第 822 页


behind wanting 25% —and not 20% or 30% —should be backed by


empirical data taken from a study of the business.


Standards


Sometimes numbers are not appropriate, or you can create a


better fit criterion by citing a standard. For example, the


requirement mentioned earlier that the product is “not


offensive to any group” could be handled by citing your


organization’s standards of conduct. Alternatively, your


communications department might have standards for what is


and what is not allowed to be said or displayed for public


consumption. By citing that the product must comply with that


standard, you are in effect setting the benchmark for lack of


offensiveness.


Sometimes other standards may apply to the kinds of products


you might be developing. As an example, the ISO 9241-11:2018


standard covers the ergonomics of human interactions with


computer systems. A short glance at the ISO list of standards


reveals many others that you might cite in your fit criteria.


Compliance requirements have a built-in standard: the law.


You could cite the appropriate law as your fit criterion, but


as it is likely to be unfathomable to you and your


development team, the simple approach is to allow your legal


## 第 823 页


department to give their opinion that the solution matches


the standard of the law.


Let’s look at each type of non-functional requirement and


consider how you might write the appropriate fit criterion.


Look and Feel Requirements


Look and feel requirements specify the spirit, mood, or style


of the product’s appearance and behavior, and the impression


the user gets when using the product. Additionally, many


companies require their products to be cloaked in company


colors. The rationale for this requirement is either


adherence to branding standards or a desire to enhance


customer recognition. These two points are slightly


different, however.


Let’s look at branding standards first. Your organization


has a communications department, which is responsible for the


branding standards. Thus, the fit criterion should specify


the target standard and state who or what is to certify the


product’s compliance.


Fit Criterion: The product shall be certified as complying


with this year’s corporate branding standards by the head of


communications.


## 第 824 页


Where the rationale is customer recognition, we suggest a fit


criterion along these lines:


Fit Criterion: Sixty percent of the target audience will


recognize the product as belonging to the corporation within


5 seconds of encountering it for the first time.


Look and feel requirements may start out as touchy-feely
