statements of intent. However, by determining the rationale


and looking for its measurable aspects, you will always find


a suitable fit criterion.


Usability and Humanity Requirements


Usability and humanity are the requirements for the


customers’ experience when using the product—in other


words, the fitness for use by its intended users. Products


are typically required to be easy to use, easy to learn, able


to be used by certain types of users, and so on. To write the


fit criterion for each of these requirements, you must find a


measurement scale that quantifies the objective of the


requirement.


Some examples:


Description: The product shall be intuitive.


## 第 825 页


To measure “intuitive,” you must consider the people to


whom the product must be intuitive. In the road deicing


example, you are told the users/actors are the road


engineers; they have engineering degrees and meteorological


experience.


Rationale: The road engineers must find it easy and


intuitive; otherwise, they will not use it.


Now that you know this rationale, “intuitive” is much


better defined.


Fit Criterion: A road engineer shall be able to produce a


correct deicing forecast within 10 minutes of encountering


the product for the first time, without reference to any out-


of-product help.


Sometimes “intuitive” really means “easy to learn.” In


this case, you ask how much time can be spent in training,


and the resultant fit criterion might look like this:


Fit Criterion: Nine out of ten road engineers shall be able


to successfully complete [list of selected tasks] after one


day’s training.


## 第 826 页


Look for the real meaning of the requirement, and


confirm it by having your stakeholders agree that


your proposed fit criterion is the correct


measurement of that meaning.


Fit criteria for usability requirements might also quantify


the time allowed for given tasks, the error rates allowed


(quantifying ease of use), the satisfaction rating awarded by


the users, ratings given by usability laboratories, and so


on. Look for the real meaning of the requirement, and confirm


it by having your stakeholders agree that your proposed fit


criterion is the correct measurement of that meaning.


Description: The product shall be pleasant to use.


Rationale: We want people to enjoy using it so that they


continue to visit our site.


Fit Criterion: Seventy percent of a representative test panel


return to our site more frequently than they do to the 10


other similar sites available to them.


Accessibility requirements specify how easy it should be for


people with common disabilities to access the product. This


could result in a fit criterion like this:


## 第 827 页


Fit Criterion: The product shall be certified to be in


compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).


It may also be necessary to specify the relevant parts of the


act and the body responsible for certifying compliance.


Performance Requirements


Most of the time, your performance requirements will be easy


to quantify; we tend to use numbers when we describe things


such as speed, accuracy, capacity, availability, reliability,


scalability, and similar characteristics of the product.


Typically, then, the nature of the performance requirements


will suggest a measurement scale. Let us look at some


examples.


Suppose you have this requirement:


Description: The response shall be fast enough to avoid


interrupting the user’s flow of thought.


The word “fast” indicates you should measure time. Here is


a suggested fit criterion:


Fit Criterion: The response time shall be no more than 0.25


second for 95% of responses, and no more than 1 second for


the remainder.


## 第 828 页


Similarly, the fit criterion for an availability requirement


might be written as follows:


Fit Criterion: In the first three months of operation, the


product shall be available for 98% of the time between 8 a.m.


and 8 p.m.


A fit criterion may be shown as a range. This is particularly


appropriate for performance requirements. For example:


Fit Criterion: The product shall allow for 30,000 downloads


per hour, although 50,000 per hour is preferred.


The point of using a range is to deter the developers from


constructing a product that could be overly expensive, and to


make the best design trade-offs to fit the budget and design


constraints.


If the requirement is given to you in correctly


quantified terms, then the fit criterion and the


requirement are the same.


As most performance requirements are themselves quantified,


it should be straightforward to write appropriate fit


criteria. If the requirement is given to you in correctly


## 第 829 页


quantified terms, then the fit criterion and the description


of the requirement are the same. In that case, write one or


the other.


Operational and Environmental Requirements


Operational requirements specify the environment in which the


product will operate. In some cases, the product must be used


in adverse or unusual conditions. Recall our example from the


road treatment solution:


Description: The product shall be used in and around trucks


at night, and during rainstorms, snow, and freezing


conditions.


The fit criterion for an operational requirement is a


quantification of the successful usage in the required


environment. For this operational requirement, its fit


criterion quantifies the ability of the product to withstand


the conditions. For example:


Fit Criterion: The operator shall successfully complete [list


of tasks] within [time allowed] in a simulation of a five-


1


year storm, and the product shall function correctly after


24 hours’ exposure.


## 第 830 页


1


This is an accepted quantification of meteorological


conditions. It means that (theoretically) you experience this


severity of storm once every five years. Unfortunately,


climate change means that five-year storms now happen more


frequently.


Operational conditions may also specify that the product must


coexist with partner, or collaborating, systems. The fit


criterion in this case will cite the specification of the


partner system or the way to communicate with the partner:


Fit Criterion: The interfaces to the Rosa Weather Station


shall be certified as complying with the National


Transportation Communication ITS Protocol (NTC/IP).


This criterion is testable—by engineers from NTC—and points


the product’s builders toward a known and accepted standard.


Additionally, most things in your operating infrastructure


have standards. For instance:


Fit Criterion: The product must comply with HTML Living


Standard 2024.


Maintainability and Support Requirements


## 第 831 页


Maintainability requirements specify expectations about the


maintenance of the product. Usually, the fit criteria for


these requirements quantify the amount of time allowed to


make certain changes. This is not to say that all maintenance


changes can be anticipated, but where changes are expected,


it is possible to quantify the time allowed to adopt those


changes.


Fit Criterion: All functionality must be migrated to the new


website with no more than 10 minutes of unavailability of the


site.


Security Requirements


Security is too important to be left to the whims or the


goodwill of the developers. Your organization probably has


some security standards in place, either specific to the


industry or specific to your type of product. Alternatively,


you might make use of existing international standards. For


example:


Description: The product shall comply with ISO/IEC


27002:2022.


Fit Criterion: The product shall be certified as complying by


an appointed certification body that is compliant with ISO


## 第 832 页


17021.


The example is very general, and you might need more detailed


requirements. However, the point is that the fit criterion


ensures that your security requirement is testable.


We treat access as part of security. Here you might write


your fit criterion for an access requirement in the form of a


table. The table would show the roles or names of authorized


people, together with the type of access


(read/add/change/delete) each is allowed.


Cultural Requirements


Cultural requirements, by their nature, are subjective and


slightly more difficult to quantify. The fit criterion is


usually based on who or what will certify the product’s


acceptability.


Description: The product shall not display religious symbols


or words associated with mainstream religions.


Fit Criterion: The communications department shall give the


opinion that the product displays no words or symbols that


could be construed as religious.


## 第 833 页


In almost all cases, your communications or HR department can


be considered to be the authority when dealing with cultural


issues. This fit criterion is a general-purpose one that


could be included in most specifications:


Description: The product shall not discriminate against any


segment of society.


Fit Criterion: The communications department/HR shall certify


that the product is culturally acceptable for all segments of


the target audience.


Compliance Requirements


Compliance requirements specify which laws the product must


conform to. As a result, this fit criterion applies to most


compliance requirements:


Fit Criterion: Your client will win a court case brought by


someone who uses your solution.


However, fit criteria must be able to be tested in a cost-


effective manner, and court cases are too expensive to be


indulged in lightly. Thus, the majority of fit criteria will


be along the following lines:


## 第 834 页


Fit Criterion: The legal department/company lawyers shall


certify that the product complies with the [appropriate


laws].


A compliance requirement that applies to almost anything you


do is GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation). This


originated with the European Union, and it applies to all


member countries and to all organizations doing business


within the EU. GDPR is considered to be the gold standard for


data protection, and as such it has been adopted, either


wholly or in a slightly modified state, by many other


countries and states. Just one example: the California


Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) has many similarities with the


GDPR.


The requirement would be:


Description: The product shall comply with GDPR (or the local


equivalent).


Fit Criterion: GDPR compliance shall be certified by [the


name of your organization’s compliance department].


Smaller organizations probably do not have their own


compliance sections, in which case it is down to the business


analysts and especially the product owner to ensure


## 第 835 页


compliance. There can be significant penalties for


noncompliance with privacy laws.


Compliance requirements are also written to ensure that the


product complies with cited standards. Most standards are


written by organizations that either have people who certify


compliance—“standards lawyers”—or issue guidelines as to


how you can certify compliance for yourself. In either case,


fit criteria can be written to specify how compliance with


the standard is to be verified.


Fit Criteria for Stories


The normal form for stories (As a - I can - So that) does not


include provision for fit criteria as we have been describing


them here. However, that is no reason to disregard measuring


your stories. As you are reading this, keep in mind that we


discuss acceptance criteria in Chapter 29.


This depends on whether you write separate non-functional


stories or add non-functional qualities to your functional


stories.


For separate non-functional stories, the fit criterion and


the acceptance criteria are the same thing. Write it


## 第 836 页


whichever way you choose. We will also look at acceptance


criteria for stories in a few chapters.


Some non-functional requirements are solution wide. For


example, security requirements or look and feel requirements


apply to the whole of your solution. However, in some cases


you would append non-functional requirements to functional


stories. In these cases, we suggest that you add a fit


criterion along with each one. This leaves the developers in


no doubt as to what is required to complete the functional


story.


Fit Criteria for Functional Requirements


A functional requirement is something that the product must


do—an action it must take. The fit criterion specifies how


you will know that the product has successfully carried out


that action. For functional requirements, there are no scales


of measurement—you can’t use numbers here. The action is


either completed or not completed.


For example, suppose that you have this functional


requirement:


Description: The product shall keep the music subscriber’s


listening history.


## 第 837 页


Rationale: The product must be able to recommend new music


based on the apparent preferences of the subscriber.


The rationale is enlightening; it tells us that we have to


know not just what the music fan has listened to, but the


type of music it is. The product must be able to find new


musicians that perform the kind of music the buyer likes.


This would give you the following:


Fit Criterion: At the end of a listening session, the product


shall have added the listened-to artists, the songs, the


genre, and the mood of the music to the subscriber’s


history. The history data can be ranked to provide the best


recommendations.


Another one:


Description: The product shall stream the subscriber’s


selected music.


Rationale: This is what the subscriber is paying for, and how


the artists earn their money.


Fit Criterion: The music is streamed; after 2 minutes the


artist royalty is recorded, the stream is added to the


subscriber’s history, and similar music will be played at


## 第 838 页


the end of the chosen stream if there are no more subscriber


selections.


Here the fit criterion is elaborating on the simple


description, and in doing so, is setting down the post


conditions for when the requirement is executed.


Fit Criteria and Data


For many functional requirements, completion depends on


satisfying an authority that the product has correctly


performed the action. The authority in this case is either


the source of the data or the adjacent system that initiated


the action.


If the action is to record something, then the fit criterion


is that the recorded data complies with the data as it is


known to the authority. For example:


Description: The product shall record the weather station


readings.


Rationale: The readings are necessary for preparing the


deicing schedule and must be kept for audit purposes.


Fit Criterion: The recorded weather station readings shall be


identical to the readings as recorded by the transmitting


## 第 839 页


weather station.


The authority in this case is the weather station: It


initiated the action, and it is the source of the data. You


can say the requirement is for the product to faithfully


store the data (allow for the product to make necessary


manipulations to the data) as sent from the weather station.


If this procedure is done correctly, then the product’s data


conforms to that transmitted by the station.


The fit criterion does not indicate how this conformance is


to be tested. Instead, it is simply a statement that the


tester uses to ensure compliance.


If the functional requirement is to make some calculation,


then the fit criterion says the result of the calculation


must be consistent with the authority’s view of the data.


Where the requirement is “the product shall check…,” the


fit criterion is “the checked data conforms with…” and


again cites the authority for the data. “The product shall


calculate…” results in a fit criterion of “the result


conforms to…” and gives the algorithm (or source of the


algorithm) for the result.


## 第 840 页


The general rule for functional requirements is that the fit


criterion ensures that the function has been successfully


carried out.


Defining the Data


For the fit criteria to be complete, your


specification must contain definitions of the


terms used in the fit criteria.


Because functional requirements often have to do with


manipulating data, it is as well that we take a quick look at


defining that data. This means making use of the data


dictionary. The dictionary is found in section 7 of the


Volere Template in Appendix A. The dictionary gives


definitions of the data by defining the content of data flows


and data entities.


For example, within the Ice Breaker solution there are


references to something called Road Section. If you were to


look in the data dictionary for the specification of this


solution, you would find this definition:


Road Section = Road Section Identifier + Road Section


Coordinates


## 第 841 页


You can then expect to find a definition of each attribute of


Road Section. For example:


Road Section Identifier = *Unique identifier for 500 meters


of road. The maximum number of road sections per road is


10,000. *


Another strategy for defining the data is to define each term


as part of the fit criterion of each individual requirement.


However, as you will usually reference the same term in more


than one requirement, it makes sense to maintain a central


dictionary that can act as a cross-reference between


requirements. Your growing understanding of the data means


that you progressively build a business data/information


model that specifies the essential stored data for the


requirements you are specifying.


Test Cases


You might find it feasible to write test cases


for your functional requirements.


You might find it feasible at this stage to think about


writing test cases for your functional requirements. This


approach is promoted by several agile techniques wherein the


## 第 842 页


tests are written before the code is. The basic idea is to


focus the developer to concentrate on learning the fit


criterion for any part of the functionality.


You can do the same thing with your requirements discovery:


You can write test cases. However, we understand that many


business analysts feel they should not be writing test cases.


If you like the idea but don’t want to do it, might we


suggest talking to your testers. In our experience, testers


are really happy to add test cases to requirements. There is


a benefit to you that comes from sitting beside testers while


they write test cases: They can only do it if they are


certain of the real intention of the requirements. This gives


you the opportunity to verify that you do have the right


requirement—the one that satisfies the real business need.


When you see how the tester intends to validate the


requirement, you can be certain that the delivered solution


will indeed satisfy the business need.


This is “testing before testing.” That is, the tester is


testing the requirement before the solution is built.


“Testing before testing” is most effective, and involving


the testers early in the development cycle is always


beneficial. And by the way, testers are the best people to


## 第 843 页


tell you whether or not your functional requirements are


testable.


Testers are the best people to tell you whether


or not your functional requirements are testable.


Fit Criterion for Project Purpose


We have already discussed writing the fit criterion for the


project’s purpose. We didn’t call it a fit criterion back


in Chapter 5, we called it a measurement. However, it’s


really the fit criterion for the project. Let’s look quickly


at this idea again: The project’s purpose is a statement of


the reason for making the investment in the project. If you


go to the trouble and expense of developing a product, then


it makes sense to have an objective benchmark to measure the


delivered product against.


The measurement of the purpose is the same as a fit criterion


for an individual requirement. The difference is that the fit


criterion measures a single requirement, whereas the


purpose’s measurement is the benchmark for the entire


solution.


Fit Criteria for Solution Constraints


## 第 844 页


Constraints are a special type of requirement—they are


global requirements—and they need to be specified correctly


just like any other type of requirement. Section 3a of the


Volere Template (Appendix A) includes the solution


constraints. These constraints place restrictions on the way


that the problem must be solved; you could also say they


mandate a solution to the problem. For example:


Description: The software part of the product must run on


Android and Apple iOS.


This requirement reflects management’s decision to use the


two most popular mobile operating systems. This decision may


or may not have a sound technological basis, but that is


beside the point for our purposes here. You are being told


that any solution you deliver has to comply with this


constraint.


We can test compliance—either you comply with the


requirement, or you don’t—as long as whatever it is that


you have to comply with is measurable. For example, you can


test whether you have complied with a law, but you can’t


test whether you have complied with a constraint that states,


“You shall be happy.” In the case of the mobile OS


constraint, you could write the following criterion:


## 第 845 页


Fit Criterion: All functionality of the software shall


operate as specified when run using Android 12 and later and


iOS 16 and later.


Similarly, all other constraint requirements—for example,


implementation environment, partner applications, commercial


off-the-shelf software, open-source software, workplace


environment, time budget, and financial budget—have fit


criteria.


Review


The fit criterion is an unambiguous benchmark


that the product has to meet.


A fit criterion is neither a test nor the design for a test,


but rather a benchmark that the delivered product must be


tested against. It is used as input to build test cases


through which the tester ensures that each of the product’s


requirements complies with its fit criterion.


Quantifying or measuring the requirement gives you a better


opportunity to interact with your stakeholders. By agreeing


on a measurement, you confirm that you have understood the


requirement correctly, and that both you and your


## 第 846 页


stakeholders have an identical understanding of it. As a by-


product, you will also find quantifying it ensures that the


requirement is both wanted and necessary.


Including a fit criterion in a requirement or a story


encourages testers to participate in the requirements


process. Testers should be involved early in the development


cycle, and they are particularly helpful at requirements time


when you are writing your fit criteria. This is not to say


that the testers must write the fit criteria for you, but


just that testers are the best source of knowledge about


whether something can be tested and whether the fit criterion


contains the appropriate quantification. In other words, the


testers are excellent consultants for the fit criteria.


The fit criterion is the real requirement.


The fit criterion, not the description, is the real


requirement. The description you write is the stakeholder’s


way of stating the intention of the requirement. If your


stakeholders are like most of us, they speak using everyday


language, which is, unfortunately, often ambiguous and often


not precise enough. You need to clarify the requirement with


a fit criterion that is stated in unambiguous, precise terms


## 第 847 页


and probably uses numbers or a measurement to convey its


meaning.


Fit criteria are also a vehicle for reaching a consensus


among multiple stakeholders. Your attempts to clarify and


measure will almost always result in hidden meanings becoming


visible, hidden requirements bubbling to the surface, and,


most importantly, the stakeholders agreeing on what is


needed.


You derive the fit criterion by examining the


requirement’s description and rationale, and


determining which quantification best expresses


the user’s intention for the requirement.


Fit criteria are usually derived after the requirement


description is written. You derive a fit criterion by


examining the requirement’s description and rationale, and


determining which quantification best expresses the user’s


intention for the requirement. You may sometimes find that


this close examination results in changes to the requirement,


but these changes are for the better and should be considered


quite normal; their occurrence simply means the requirement


was not properly understood in the first instance. With


patience and persistence, and with the wise use of


## 第 848 页


measurements, you can ensure that each of your requirements


is unambiguous, testable, and real.


Resources


Requirements Engineering: From System Goals to UML Models to


Software Specifications by Axel van Lamsweerde (Wiley, 2009).


This is a comprehensive overview of requirements engineering,


including discussions on specifying and validating


requirements with measurable criteria.


Notes in the Synthesis of Form by Christopher Alexander


(Harvard University Press, 1964). Alexander introduced the


concept of “fit” to measure the fit of architectural


designs against the way people needed to live.


## 第 849 页


Chapter 28. Writing Good Stories


This is a book about requirements and business analysis, so


when we talk about stories, we talk about them in a way that


is useful for the business analyst. The prime task of the BA


is to understand the business problem. As this understanding


matures, the analysts and appropriate stakeholders determine


the solution that best solves the problem.


In Chapter 21, Stories, we described the business event story


and how you can use it to determine the beneficiary and


outcome of the business events. This means that a business


event story is the linchpin of the analysis that follows. The


story’s event is isolated, and the analyst trawls,


interviews, models, prototypes, and does whatever else is


required to discover the set of requirements needed to


respond to the event.


In this chapter, we want to revisit business event stories


and discuss what makes a good, and therefore valuable, story.


But before doing so, we need to make clear the intention of


these stories.


First, these are not “user stories.” Normally, stories are


used as descriptors of some action that a user does with a


## 第 850 页


computer. The problem with this is that it assumes a


solution: If there is a user, then there is a solution for


the user to use. Assuming a solution also assumes that the


problem is known and understood. We have learned from bitter


experience that at requirements time, the problem cannot be


assumed, that the stakeholders do not always understand the


real problem, and that rushing into a presumed solution often


—too often—produces a result that is an almost complete


waste of time.


But you know that. You are reading a book about business


analysis and requirements, which you would not be doing


unless you understood the facts of business analysis life.


So, let’s press on and talk about business event stories,


and what makes a good one.


Business Event Stories


Back in Chapter 21 we discussed the format of the business


event story. It’s the same format as the user story, but it


has important differences in meaning. The format we’re


talking about is this:


As a [customer segment]


## 第 851 页


I can [some functionality that responds to my business event]


So that [received business value].


Let’s start by looking at a bad story and making it better.


We’ll take this example of a solution for an employment


agency that matches applicants to jobs. It has this story:


As a user


I can search for jobs.


On its own, this is of little use. You don’t know whether to


include the story in the solution or not. You don’t know who


a “user” is or why users would want to search for jobs.


Having a facility for someone to search for jobs does not


necessarily provide value. So, let’s step back.


The employment agency wants to match the best candidates with


suitable jobs. Value to this client comes when the best


candidates are put forward to the employer. Obviously,


employers will stop using the agency if it sends along


unsuitable candidates. So, we can improve the story to this:


As a candidate


I can search for jobs.


## 第 852 页


What is the justification for this story? Why does a


candidate want to search for jobs? Let’s say that the


candidate wants to search for jobs so that he can find


prospective employment. Keep in mind that “searching” and


“finding” are two different things. The candidate does not


want to search for jobs, the candidate wants to find a job.


So let us modify the story so that it provides some relevant


value to the candidate:


As a candidate


I can find jobs that meet my and the employers’ criteria


So that I will have the best chance of being called for an


interview for the job I want.


The candidate’s criteria would be attributes like location,


salary range, job description, type of company, employment


conditions, social activities, and so on. The employer’s


criteria would have attributes like experience required,


other skills, attitude toward work, past employment,


salaries, and other first-line determinants that provide some


filtering of candidates. You can define these criteria in the


data dictionary (section 7 of the template in Appendix A).


## 第 853 页


Now we’re getting somewhere.


We have moved from searching to finding, which implies that


the solution will do the matching, not the candidate or the


employer. Naturally, a good solution would provide an


override, but for the moment, we can say that most of the


employment would be done by matching the most suitable


candidates to the available positions.


When the story talked about searching, it was talking about a


solution to the problem, and as such, it masked the essence


of the problem. Additionally, when the story was changed to


“find,” it suggested that candidates don’t have to log on


each morning and search for jobs; they can be notified when


the solution makes a match. This gives more time for the


candidate to polish or enlarge her skills and become more


attractive to employers.


We will need other stories for the employment agency. A


candidate must be able to post her profile to show her


attributes, and the employer needs to post job vacancies with


the desired attributes for candidates. There would also be


stories so that employers and candidates can modify or delete


their job postings and candidate profiles.


## 第 854 页


Going a little further with these employment stories gives us


the following:


As an employer


I can post a precise job profile


So that I can find a limited number of the best candidates


for the position.


The “So that” line is important. It demonstrates the value


that the story delivers to the beneficiary. The employer does


not want to waste time interviewing unsuitable candidates,


she wants the best of them. Also, she does not want to


interview dozens of people for the job; there is no time for


that.


Admittedly, the “finding” story would be harder to


implement than the simplistic “A candidate can search for


jobs,” but it provides real value to the candidates, the


employers, and the owner of the solution. The latter is


significant, as its business viability is at stake here.


So, let’s look deeper into stories and what makes a good


story.


## 第 855 页


Properties of Good Stories


We are talking about writing good business event stories as


an aid to discovering the requirements. The story will help


you if it concentrates on the customer’s business problem.


Here we look at each component of a story, how to discover


them, and how they work together.


We start with the beneficiary of the story.


As a [Customer Segment]


The customer segment gives an indication of what that person


or thing is wanting to accomplish, and what functionality is


appropriate.


As an occasional flier


As a regular flier


As a platinum-level frequent flier


These are different customer segments and would have


different functionalities available to them. For example,


platinum flyers can book their seats in advance, and


occasional flyers have to pay if they want to select their


own seats.


## 第 856 页


The customer segment is the first part of the information


your story has to communicate. The next part looks at what


the segment needs to do.


I Can


Note that you should write “I can” and not “I want.”


Writing “I want” often results in a solution. For example:


As a cyclist


I want to follow my friends’ cycling routes


So that I can join them on rides.


After “I want,” the writer launches into an assumed


solution. Perhaps she envisioned a map with the cycle routes


highlighted. Who knows? What she really wants to do—this is


the business problem—is to cycle with her friends. But


let’s think about that for a moment. What do you need if you


are to cycle with your friends? The thing that jumps out is


that your friends have to tell you their cycling intentions


before they set out. There is little point in knowing that


Sally and Fatima like cycling along the canal towpath unless


you know when they next plan to do so. In other words, the


route without a start time is useless.


## 第 857 页


Instead of “I want,” let’s try “I can.” What must a


cyclist be able to do if she is to cycle with her friends?


The answer is she needs to know her friends’ intentions;


that is, when and where they plan to cycle.


However, that suggests that our cyclist is willing to go


along with whatever the friends suggest. Perhaps what she


needs to be able to do—this is the “I can” part of the


story—is to arrange a cycling outing with the friends she


wants to cycle with. Perhaps some of her friends are planning


a mountain route, but this weekend she wants something


gentler.


So, the story really is about making arrangements:


As a cyclist


I can arrange a mutually acceptable cycling excursion


So that I can cycle with my friends.


Note that the original proposed solution masked everything—


there is no need to build an app or anything at all. Simply


forming a cycling group on one of the messaging apps would


allow our amiable cyclist to find riding companions. In


requirements discovery terms, this is great. By discarding


## 第 858 页


the assumed solution and unearthing the real need, the good


story writer has found a business problem that requires


almost no development activity.


To summarize, “I can” must show a business result. It


should show some functionality that enables the customer


segment—the “As a” line—to achieve the story’s business


value. A statement of this value comes next.


So That


So that... is important. This is the part where you specify


the value, or benefit, of the story. If the story lacks


value, it should be discarded. If the story demonstrates high


value, then it should be prioritized to a higher rank. The


value of a story helps the product owner/team leader plan the


development; it helps the developers understand the rationale


of the story and thus influence some of the features; it


tells the testers how much effort to put into testing the


product. In short, knowing the value of a story is valuable.


The following is a bad story we found, and it shows why


getting to the real value is crucial:


As a bank account holder


## 第 859 页


I want to check my balance online


So that I can keep a daily balance 24 hours a day.


First, let’s get rid of the “I want” line; it’s an


assumed solution and has little to do with the value of this


story. The writer is assuming that logging on is the only way


to achieve the need, but it’s not necessarily the way to do


it.


The “So that” line, the justification, is also wrong: “24


hours a day”? Only insomniacs want to know their bank


balance at 3 a.m. But “daily balance” is the part that


raises the serious questions.


Asking why repeatedly is almost always the thing to do. If


you ask this account holder why he wants to keep a daily


balance, what answer could he give?


• I’m filthy rich and want to see all my money and gloat.


• I want to know if anybody has fraudulently taken money from


my account.


• I’m quite poor and want to know how much is left in the


account.


## 第 860 页


• I want to know if I can afford the new iPhone.


• ...and possibly more.


Working through each of these possibilities, we start with


the filthy rich justification. This is unlikely to be true


because anybody who is filthy rich would have most of their


assets tied up in investments and property. The bank balance


is only part of, and probably a very small part of, their


total wealth.


Obviously, fraud is a concern of most bank account holders,


but knowing just the balance is only partially helpful. To


know if somebody has plundered your bank account, you need to


know all the transactions that have occurred since you last


looked at the account.


The next two answers come down to the same thing: Simply


knowing the balance is not necessarily helpful. What account


holders need to know is how much money will be left after


all the contracted payments have been made. Contracted


payments are things like the electricity bill, the phone


bill, insurance, the car payment, rent and so on. The


information that is valuable to the account holder is what


will be left until the next payday. The phone lover wants to


## 第 861 页


see if he can afford the iPhone; the poor person needs to see


if there’s enough for new shoes for the kids.


So, our story needs drastic surgery. We suggest this:


As a bank account holder


I can be aware of my bank situation


So that I know my current and discretionary balances.


The story now provides something that is valuable to the


account holder. Of course, it is now more difficult to


develop than the original assumed solution. However, the


original provided so little value that developing it would


not provide much of a return to the bank. All banks offer to


hold your account so that you can access it online or by


phone. The bank that provides the more valuable facility as


shown in the final story is much more likely to attract


customers in the competitive market.


The bank account holder also mentioned that he wants to check


for fraudulent activity. The assumed solution for that is to


provide a list of recent transactions. The account holder


would have to scan the list looking for abnormalities.


However, most of what he looks at are the normal


## 第 862 页


transactions: paying the electricity bill, direct payments of


subscriptions, payments to known tradespeople, legitimate


shops, and so on. These fit into a pattern of certain amounts


for certain things. Look at your own bank transactions, and


you’ll see that they are the same or similar every month.


So, to know about fraudulent activity, the account holder


really needs to be alerted when there are any transactions


outside her normal pattern. The resultant story is this:


As a bank account holder


I can be aware of any abnormal transactions on my account


So that I can know immediately if fraudulent activity has


taken place.


When you look at any value statement in a story, ask why that


is valuable. And keep asking why until there is no further


answer. “Why do you want to know your discretionary


balance?” “I want to know if I can spend money.” It’s the


same thing; in other words, there is no further answer to the


question.


In earlier chapters, we discussed the essence of the problem,


and essence applies here. Is the value statement getting to


the essence of the business problem? If not, ask why a few


## 第 863 页


more times. Does the “So that” line leave the solution to


the problem unsolved? This example is taken from an energy


monitoring situation:


So that I can see my daily energy usage


This is not solving the real problem. Knowing your daily


usage is not all that helpful. Knowing which appliances and


which heating/air conditioning levels consume the most energy


is useful. Knowing how to use your heating/air conditioning


more economically is more useful. Knowing which alternative


suppliers are cheaper and provide a comparable level of


service is still more valuable. The “So that” line should


read as follows:


So that I can find the cheapest source of energy


To get to genuinely useful stories, you must


• Ask why, and ask it repeatedly.


• Get to the essence of the problem.


• Discard any assumed solutions.


Recognizing real value is your job; this is requirements


discovery. You discover what is really needed and record it


## 第 864 页


in a way that everybody can understand the need, and what a


solution must do to satisfy that need.


INVEST


The INVEST acronym was coined in an article by Bill Wake, and


it is useful for our requirements discovery purposes here.


The following inspection of the INVEST elements does not put


exactly the same meaning as Wake used, but then he was


approaching stories from a developer perspective. This is how


it works from a requirements perspective.


Independent


For use with requirements, a story should be a separate piece


of functionality, and one that is recognized as being able to


stand alone. That is, the customer and the BA can explore it


and find its requirements without having to refer to other


chunks of functionality. Business events have this


attribute.


Naturally enough, independence makes stories based on


business events ideal units for development. In some cases,


they will be too large for one development iteration and need


to be split, but each of the sub-stories are functionally


related and would be ideal targets for subsequent iterations.


## 第 865 页


We are suggesting that initially, you write stories for each


business event and take advantage of its independence.


Negotiable


Negotiable means that the initial business event story is a


placeholder for requirements, and the detailed requirements


are negotiated with the customer. The story written at the


business event level is not a detailed story, nor is it


incomplete. It is a placeholder waiting for its detailed


requirements to be discovered.


Valuable


Stories have to provide some value. Otherwise, you are


wasting yours and your client’s time.


The value of a story comes in the “So that...” line of the


story.


But not all stories are equally valuable. By having the value


as part of each story, it allows you to prioritize your


stories. This allows you to work on the most valuable stories


first, leaving the less valuable ones until later (if at


all).


Estimable


## 第 866 页


For developers, this means that they can estimate the effort


needed for development. This is needed for planning


iterations and other development tasks. It is less important


for the requirements discovery activity. Besides, when you


are writing a business event story, you really have only a


vague idea how much effort it would take to implement that


story, but this is probably enough to help with


prioritization of your business event stories.


Small


This quality applies only to the development activity, where


small stories are needed for iteration planning. For our


needs here, the business event story is whatever size it is.


Later, when we talk about story maps, we will demonstrate how


to break down stories to make them small enough for


development planning.


Testable


Requirements stories are testable in that the value line of


the story can be tested. If the story reads “So that I can


continue my insurance coverage,” then you are able to test


whether the insurance is in fact continuous.


## 第 867 页


A better meaning for “testable” is that the story enables


the customer to identify its value and confirm that the


story’s functionality is something needed by the business.


Please don’t feel that you have to run each story you write


past the gauntlet of an INVEST test. These attributes are


here to give you some guidelines on writing good stories.


Non-functional Properties


All the stories that you have seen so far in this chapter


specify the solution’s functionality. We know that for a


solution to be successful, it must be usable, attractive, and


secure; fit seamlessly into its operating environment; comply


with any relevant laws and electives; and so on. These are


the non-functional properties.


Back in Chapter 26, we discussed non-functional requirements.


Everything in that chapter applies to stories. However, if


you and your team are writing stories, then you need a way to


record the non-functional requirements.


You have some options.


1. Append the non-functional requirements to each appropriate


functional story.


## 第 868 页


2. Some non-functional requirements are solution wide. Write


these as we set out in Chapter 26.


3. Write separate non-functional stories.


Option 1 is preferable, as each non-functional requirement


then carries its own fit criterion.


Option 3 would look like this as a usability requirement:


As a cabin attendant


I can easily understand the cabin control panel


So that I can use it correctly after one day’s training.


It would look like this as a compliance requirement:


As a human resources officer


I can securely access employees’ records


So that the company complies with all GDPR provisions,


However you decide to do it, ensure that the non-functional


requirements are not left to chance or to the goodwill of the


developers.


## 第 869 页


Review


As a reminder, we are using stories to help with requirements


discovery. We suggest that the stories are written one for


each business event. The format of the story helps you to


ensure that you have discovered the right business events.


For example, the “As a” line nominates the customer segment


for the story. The customer segment is the beneficiary of the


story, and you must determine that this is a worthwhile


beneficiary.


The “I can” line is an overview of the functionality of the


response to the event. Elsewhere we refer to this as the


business use case. We cannot stress enough that this line


should not be a solution to the problem. If it is a solution,


it is likely masking the real business need of the story.


The “So that” line justifies the story—it is the business


value of the story. You can think of this as the benefit


provided to the customer segment in the first line. You


should examine this line carefully. Any stories where the


stated value is weak (or missing) can be either given a low


priority or discarded.


## 第 870 页


Business event stories are high-level stories. They are there


to guide your requirements discovery. That is, for each


story, you trawl or build prototypes to drive out the


detailed requirements.


Later, we will look at how you can make use of these stories


when you build a story map. The map is simply another way to


uncover the details from the business event story.


Resources


User Stories Applied: For Agile Software Development by Mike


Cohn (Addison-Wesley, 2004). Cohn is one of the best writers


on stories, and this is a comprehensive treatise on the


subject. It covers the principles of user story writing,


along with various techniques and best practices.


The Agile Samurai: How Agile Masters Deliver Great Software


by Jonathan Rasmusson (Pragmatic Programmers, 2017). This is


a comprehensive introduction to agile software development


and includes practical guidance on writing user stories.


If you need more on writing stories than we have provided in


this chapter, there is a huge amount of information to be


found online. Be aware that the different authors have


## 第 871 页


different takes on user stories, and not all of them are


suitable for requirements discovery.


Agile Alliance (https://www.agilealliance.org).


Scrum.org (https://www.scrum.org).


YouTube. There are lots of video tutorials and presentations


on user stories on YouTube.


## 第 872 页


Chapter 29. Acceptance Criteria


Acceptance criteria are a way to set a benchmark, a standard,


that any delivered solution must meet. Naturally, it must be


clear and binary. Clear in that the customer agrees that she


is willing to accept a solution that meets the criteria, and


binary in that either the delivered solution meets the


criteria or it is rejected.


In Chapter 27, we looked at fit criteria. Acceptance criteria


are more or less the same thing: Both are concerned with


making requirements measurable and testable. The difference


is mainly in how you write them.


Stories are written to describe something—some functionality


or non-functional attributes—that the customer needs to be


included in the delivered product. The acceptance criterion


looks in the other direction. It states whether that thing,


whatever it is, has been successfully included in the


delivered product.


Acceptance criteria should be written in the customer’s


voice. The criteria should demonstrate the scope and the


functionality that the customer needs from the story. They


should also be written early. They give precision to your


## 第 873 页


stories; just as fit criteria bring precision to your


requirements. Try writing acceptance criteria in parallel


with writing the business event story. It’s a great way to


drive questions out early.


Write acceptance criteria in parallel with


writing the business event story.


Let’s look at how to write acceptance criteria.


Given/When/Then


Given/when/then (from now on, we’ll call this GWT) is one of


the most common forms of writing acceptance criteria (which


we can abbreviate to AC) and is quite suitable to use when


discovering requirements. And it works extremely well with


business event stories.


Given/when/then is a construct that defines the start and end


states of, well, anything, but in our case, we’ll use GWT


for our business use cases. You write a GWT statement so that


the stakeholders can understand the transaction and confirm


that the GWT conditions are what they desire. The statement


is as follows:


## 第 874 页


Given that [a context]


When [an action is carried out]


Then [a set of observable outcomes should occur]


Let us say that we have a business event, “A potential


customer wants to subscribe to our streaming service.” The


following is the business event story for this:


As a movie fan


I can subscribe to the service


So that I can stream movies as I wish.


“Given” specifies the state of the solution’s universe


before the story begins to execute. For example, you could


say:


Given the potential subscriber is a real and identifiable


person, living in an approved country, with an acceptable


means of payment


“When” is an action that takes place, and “Then” is the


result of that action. For business event stories, read the


## 第 875 页


“When” part as the business event. For the above movie


streaming service:


Given the potential subscriber is a real and identifiable


person, living in an approved country, with an acceptable


means of payment


When a potential customer wants to subscribe to our


streaming service


Then an account is established for the subscriber, his


payment method is charged for the first month’s


subscription, and he is given logon details.


Let’s take this example of a story:


As a road engineer


I can generate a road treatment schedule


So that the depot and the truck drivers are made aware of


which road sections are predicted to freeze within the


selected time parameters.


You could write the acceptance criterion thus:


## 第 876 页


Given the weather forecast is available and was forecast


within the previous 15 minutes, and all weather stations are


online


When an authorized engineer supplies the appropriate time


parameters and areas to be forecasted


Then the product produces a schedule of road sections where


temperatures are 32°F (0°C) or below, and either moisture


is present or precipitation is predicted within the next


hour.


Another example:


Given a road is part of the district being monitored by the


product


When the driver reports the road has been successfully


treated (roads are treated by trucks with a human driver)


Then the road status is changed to “safe” and the road is


removed from the predicting activity for the next four hours.


You can see that the acceptance criteria and the story are


both saying the same thing (as they should). Some teams


## 第 877 页


prefer to replace the story with the AC in its Given-When-


Then form.


That’s fine when you are working at the business event


level. As the business event story moves into development, it


is sliced into smaller units of functionality to make


implementation more manageable. This means that your


acceptance criteria become more detailed—they are specifying


a subset of the business use case—and they begin to focus on


more technical matters.


However, you must always keep in mind that requirements,


whether they are written as stories or acceptance criteria,


must be testable. If something is not testable, then it has


no place in your solution.


When you write the acceptance criteria for a story, the GWT


statement is setting down the testable end conditions for the


functionality it covers.


This is the GWT for the business event “Customer wants to


watch a movie”:


Given a customer has an account and is correctly logged on


When a customer wants to watch a movie


## 第 878 页


Then the movie will be streamed until it ends or is paused


or stopped by the customer.


The “Then” line is testable. You can determine absolutely


that a movie is streaming to the right destination, you can


test that it runs to its ending and the credits have rolled,


and you can test the other “Then” conditions. Moreover,


your stakeholders can agree that what they need to happen


does in fact happen.


Another example:


Given the customer’s payment method is current and there


are items in the basket


When the customer signals that she wants to check out


Then the delivery address is confirmed, the customer’s


chosen payment method is debited, and the items in the basket


are recorded as sold and transferred to the fulfillment


system.


We have been talking about GWT statements at a business event


story level. This is intentional, as it is at this level that


GWT is most effective. As mentioned, the “When” part is


when the business event happens. The “Then” statement is


## 第 879 页


the outcome and must be agreed to by the stakeholders that


this is the outcome they need. If there is no agreement, then


you have more work to do to discover the real intention of


this business event. This is a crucial part of your


requirements discovery.


Later, your stories are broken down for implementation


reasons, and you can still write GWT statements for all of


the lower-level components. However, keep in mind that these


lower-level components contribute to the goal of the business


event. So, in many cases, you can abbreviate the acceptance


criteria to a checklist of items to be achieved by whatever


unit of functionality you are dealing with.


A word of caution: Some teams end up writing GWT statements


to such a granular level of detail that each story ends up


looking like a huge requirements document. Try to avoid this;


the purpose is to produce a testable set of stories, not to


produce a specification longer than The Lord of the Rings.


Who Writes the ACs, and When?


Business analysts are the ideal people to write the


acceptance criteria for stories. Business analysts—the


requirements discoverers—are the people closest to the


customers and what they need to achieve. Most of what you


## 第 880 页


have read so far in this book is about understanding the


customers and what is needed for their work. In some cases,


product owners or product managers write ACs, but care must


be taken that they are written from the perspective of the


customer and not based on the needs of the product.


We strongly suggest that you write acceptance criteria early


in the project at the point you establish the business


events. If each business event has its GWT statement,


everybody understands the importance and the effect of each


of the business events.


It also gives your client the information she needs to assess


the value of the project overall. GWT deals in outcomes, so


having them for all business events enables the development


team and the client to agree on the necessary outcomes for


the delivered solution to fulfill the client’s requirements.


Review


Given/when/then is not the only way to write your acceptance


criteria, but it is effective and so widely used that there


is little point in talking about alternatives. How you write


your acceptance criteria is not important; that you write


acceptance criteria is very important.


## 第 881 页


Your acceptance criteria set down the litmus test for the


business use case that responds to a business event. In other


words, GWT says that when this business event happens,


providing the solution space is in the nominated state, the


solution provides this desired outcome.


Without specifying the outcome, you cannot be sure that your


solution is what is needed. It is the acceptance criteria


that set down what your customer will accept.


Resources


Discover to Deliver: Agile Product Planning and Analysis by


Ellen Gottesdiener and Mary Gorman (EBG Consulting, 2012).


The authors mention how GWT can be used in business analysis.


## 第 882 页


Part VI: Designing Business


Solutions


A business solution—you might also call it a business system


—is an end-to-end assembly of components—devices, software,


people, communications, machines, and so on—that are put


together in such a way that they fulfill the requirements and


produce the desired outcome for the business.


A software solution—which we usually call the “product”


and some people confusingly call a “system”—will most


likely be a part, and probably a significant part, of the


business solution.


Designing is where you use the requirements to decide what to


build, what to buy, what to borrow, and what combination of


software, hardware, people, devices, and so on make up your


solution. This is where you decide if ready-made components


are the best fit for your solution, and whether to modify the


organization or modify the ready-made. Whether it is more


efficient to build a new piece of software or modify an


existing one. Whether to automate or do something manually.


## 第 883 页


“Design is not just about what it looks and


feels like. Design is how it works.”—Steve Jobs


When we talk about design, we are not talking about screen


layouts, or selecting colors or typefaces or button styles.


We have people better qualified than business analysts and


users to do that. In any event, the appearance of the


solution is only important once you know what it has to do


and who will be doing it.


Design permeates every activity in the development cycle.


Consider the Volere process shown in Figure P6.1.


## 第 884 页


![embedded_p884_133.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p884_133.jpeg)


Figure P6.1 The Volere process showing the activities for


discovering the requirements through to developing the


solution. Although it is shown as a separate activity, design


plays a part in the other activities.


## 第 885 页


You are designing in almost every part of the Volere process,


so let’s look at it from the beginning. During the Project


Blastoff activity, when you select the scope of the work to


be investigated it is a design decision. You select a scope


that isolates a part of the organization in need of renewal


or repair. Or perhaps your scope is of a completely new piece


of business. Either way, you are making design decisions as


to the extent of the scope of the problem space. Do you have


a larger scope to achieve a more comprehensive solution, or


do you have a smaller scope to produce a more focused


solution?


Then, as you derive sacrificial prototypes in the Prototype


for Requirements activity, you make design decisions. These


sacrificial or conceptual sketches of business processes are


to explore the problem space and drive out new ideas. You


discover requirements by designing potential solutions. Then,


in conjunction with your customers, you determine whether or


not they would solve the business problem and whether or not


it is the right problem to solve. Paradoxically, you use


design thinking to explore the problem space.


If you intend to deploy ready-made components, you are


designing when you make your selection as to which ready-made


is the best fit with the business problem. You are designing


## 第 886 页


when you decide whether to customize a ready-made solution


and leave the organization as it is, or use a ready-made and


change the organization to fit it. These are design


decisions.


You make an important design decision when you select the


scope of the solution. This is when you decide how much of


the work or the problem space should become the business


solution. Some of the business solution will be made up of


automated products. The scope decision you are making here


determines which parts of the original problem benefit from


being automated and which should be done by humans.


When the solution is being developed, the developers make


design decisions. These are at a lower level than the broad-


brush strokes of the business analyst, but nevertheless, they


have an impact on the resultant business process.


“Design adds value faster than it adds


costs.”—Joel Spolsky, web programmer, writer,


and creator of Trello


Designing business solutions is an iterative, nonlinear


process. Design is part of most of what we do, and so it is


vital for the business analyst to be involved in design. You


## 第 887 页


might not call it design, you might not think of it as


design, but when you consider that design is necessary to


make your solution work properly, you see that part of your


requirements discovery involves design.


Getting the requirements right is one part of the deal.


Designing, the other part, is deciding on the best possible


way to implement those requirements in the real world of your


customer.


## 第 888 页


Chapter 30. Business Solutions


The task of business analysis is sometimes seen as producing


a set of requirements from which to build a piece of


software. However, it has to be more than that. The software


by itself is probably not useful until it becomes part of a


wider business solution. Unless the software satisfies the


needs of the entity supplying input to it (part of the wider


business) and provides outcomes that are valuable to the


receivers of its outputs (also part of the business), then it


is of little value.


So let us take a broader look at business solutions and their


components, and why you are solving a wide problem, not a


narrow one.


A business solution is a physical reality. Which means that


we must move away from the abstract world above the line—the


essence of the problem—and think about the physical world of


machines, IT systems, people, and devices below it. The


“line” we are referring to is the horizontal line on the


Brown Cow model (you met this model back in Chapter 18)


separating what from how. This is illustrated in Figure


30.1.


## 第 889 页


![embedded_p889_134.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p889_134.jpeg)


Figure 30.1 The Brown Cow model highlights the transition


from the essential view above the line to the physical


reality below it.


## 第 890 页


A lot of business analysts find this model useful when they


are discussing requirements. “Are we talking above the line,


what the requirements are, or below the line, how they will


be implemented?”


In this chapter, we are talking about below the line, as we


are now concerned with how to implement the requirements.


Business Outcomes


Business solutions are what is needed to produce the


desired business outcomes. A business outcome is the end


result of activity within the business. Naturally enough, you


would like the outcome to be valuable to the organization. In


most cases, value comes when the business can produce its


products or services effectively and economically. You are


designing a business solution to do that.


But your client organization is probably already in business


producing those products and services, so now you are tasked


with designing a better way of doing it. That is, your


business solution might be designed to be 10% faster or


cheaper, or be more convenient, or utilize technology to make


it easier for customers to buy the products or services.


Achieving this business outcome is the goal of your project.


## 第 891 页


Or to say it another way, you are designing a business


solution to achieve a desired outcome.


A business solution is usually made up of multiple


components. It almost always uses software working with other


types of components including hardware components, people,


electronic devices, and anything else that can be used to


meet the requirements. Figure 30.2 shows the possible


components for a business solution.


## 第 892 页


![embedded_p892_135.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p892_135.jpeg)


Figure 30.2 A business solution is usually made up of one or


more components. These components can be anything needed to


achieve the desired business outcome.


Your task as the designer of the business solution is to


assemble the pieces that fulfill the business requirements.


The process of designing a business solution includes making


decisions about these pieces—what to build, what to buy,


## 第 893 页


what to reuse, what to do manually, and so on. This is


illustrated in Figure 30.3.


![embedded_p893_136.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p893_136.jpeg)


Figure 30.3 The assembled pieces make up the business


solution.


Consider this little example of a business solution: Your


authors recently bought a floor-standing reading lamp from an


online retailer. This is a lamp with a requirement that it


must be tall enough to illuminate the book of someone sitting


on the sofa and reading. Possibly an image that sprang to


your mind, as it did to ours, was that the delivery carton


would be a tall, awkward package. Not so.


The business analysts working for the lamp company had


correctly identified the real scope of the business


solution. That is, they found that the lamp would be sold


online, and so would need to be delivered by a courier or


mail service. This meant they had a requirement that the lamp


## 第 894 页


could be conveniently packaged. The product designers


produced a solution to this requirement by designing a lamp


whose central stalk is in sections and can be screwed


together. When assembled, the joins are all but invisible.


The lamp, which stands about 5 feet high (1.5 m) when


assembled, comes in a box the size of a large chocolate box.


(They enhanced this metaphor by printing a ribbon on the box.


See the photo in Figure 30.4.) This box fulfilled another


business solution design requirement—that the package is a


regular shape. Regular shaped packages are easier to handle,


making the product attractive to online retailers. It can be


readily stacked, it fits nicely into warehouse shelving, and


it’s easier to ship. Attracting online retailers, as well as


brick-and-mortar stores with their limited storage space,


adds to the success potential of the product.


## 第 895 页


![embedded_p895_137.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p895_137.jpeg)


Figure 30.4 The packaging for the reading lamp. The box is


about 16 inches (40 cm) on the longest side.


## 第 896 页


It gets better: The protective wrapping that surrounded the


stalk was easily torn away, making it very convenient to


assemble the lamp. We had it up and running in a few minutes.


Note that the business analysts did not design the product


but discovered the extent of the business solution. In this


case, it extended from the manufacturing process, through


fulfillment, and all the way through the mailbox to the


customer assembling it. Looking at the breadth of this


business solution meant that the business analysts discovered


the requirement that the product had to be able to be shipped


in a smallish box. It was then up to the product designers to


find a way to achieve that.


Business solutions are a collection of the


elements needed to achieve the desired business


outcome.


In the example of our reading lamp, the desired business


outcome for the company is to sell enough lamps to run at a


profit. The business solution to achieve this is made up of


all the needed elements—design, the manufacturing process,


sales, shipping, payments, customer relations, and so on.


## 第 897 页


However, you will rarely be asked to design a business


solution for the entire organization. Except for startups,


organizations are usually too large and too complex to be


taken on at one time. Most likely you would be designing at a


smaller scale, a part of the organization, or a new feature


to be added to the existing solution.


Shoe Fitter


As another example of a business solution, a sports shoe


company selling athletic shoes online wants to reduce the


number of returns. Analysis shows that many of the returns


are because the customers find that the shoes they bought are


not a comfortable fit.


The company wants to include a shoe fitting process as part


of its online selling, which means that the business analyst


must discover the requirements and design a business solution


to solve this problem. You can overcome the problem of poorly


fitting shoes by having a brick-and-mortar shop where the


customers can try on the shoes before they buy. This is not


an option for an online retailer, so the business analyst


needs to find the requirements and design a business solution


that simulates the customer trying on the shoes in the shop.

Having discovered the requirements, the business analyst’s


proposed solution is shown in Figure 30.5.
