Figure 30.5 The business solution that enables customers to


find the running shoe with the best fit. The box icons


indicate ready-made components.


A walk-through of this solution is needed.


The solution is an add-on to the company’s existing e-


commerce site. It starts with the customer specifying their


1


gender, the kind of surface (road, trail, track), and the


amount of money available to spend on the shoes. The customer


then prints a grid, which the website supplies. He then


photographs his feet on the grid in various positions.


1


Shoes for females are designed to a different shape. For


the same length shoe, the version for males has a wider heel


and toe. This makes it a poor fit and inadvisable for a


female to run in a shoe intended for males.


Once the customer has taken sufficient photographs (he is


guided on how to do this by the site), he uploads them for


analysis. This part of the business solution analyzes the


shape and size of the customer’s feet. From the database of


available shoes and their characteristics, the solution finds


a short list of the shoes that provide the best fit.


## 第 900 页


The customer browses the short list and can call up more from


the inventory if required.


Once he selects his shoes, the next component in the business


solution is a ready-made ordering system that takes the


order, and once processed, hands it off to the client’s


existing payment process. Once the payment is made, the


existing fulfillment system picks the shoes from the


warehouse and dispatches them to the customer.


The business solution has almost designed itself. Once the


requirements are discovered, the pieces of the solution fall


into place. The innovation here is being able to determine


the precise shape and size of the feet by photographing them


on the grid. After that, processes are more or less evident,


and the ready-made systems are brought into the picture. The


company has been in business for some time, so these ready-


made components are available and can be used as is, or with


minimal modification.


The important thing is not to rush into a solution, but to


discover the real business need and then find the right


business solution for it. Well-designed business solutions


are, after all, the engine rooms of successful businesses.


## 第 901 页


Review


A business solution is what a business does to achieve its


desired outcomes. You might be designing a business solution


for the whole of the business, but more likely your solution


is for a part of the business. Whatever the apparent size of


the problem, it is necessary to step back and see its real


extent. We referred earlier to this as finding the real


scope of the business problem.


All too often, designers fail to appreciate that their design


has to fit into an ecosystem. This ecosystem is made up of


other parts of the business, and sometimes parts of the


outside world. By concentrating on just the software part of


the solution, the designer produces a result that fits badly


into its surroundings.


To design well, you must step back and see the entirety of


the business problem. Once you have the big picture, you put


together the components that are needed to solve the problem.


These components can of course be software, but can also be


people, devices, networks, ready-made components, and


anything else that can do the job.


Resources


## 第 902 页


Sprint: How to Solve Big Problems and Test New Ideas in Just


Five Days by Jake Knapp, John Zeratsky, Braden and Kowitz


(Simon & Schuster, 2016). The authors, from Google Ventures,


show how you cause the Sprint design process to design, build


prototypes, and test business solutions. It’s an excellent


resource for teams looking to rapidly prototype and validate


product ideas.


Design a Better Business: New Tools, Skills, and Mindset for


Strategy and Innovation by Patrick Van Der Pijl, Justin


Lokitz, Lisa Kay Solomon, and Erik Van Der Pluijm (Wiley,


2016). This book offers a holistic view of innovation and


prototyping in the business context. It provides tools and


methodologies for creating prototypes and testing them as


part of a broader innovation strategy. It includes case


studies and real-life examples from both large and startup


organizations.


Business Model Generation: A Handbook for Visionaries, Game


Changers, and Challengers by Alexander Osterwalder and Yves


Pigneur (Wiley, 2010). This introduced the Business Model


Canvas (which has been much imitated) for designing your


business process. The Canvas is a one-page framework that


presents key elements of a business model in a visual way and


## 第 903 页


helps you think about the components of your business


process.


The Design of Everyday Things by Don Norman (Basic Books,


2002). This has been around for some time and remains the


definitive text on design principles and how they apply to


everyday objects. The same principles also apply to


information and functionality design.


## 第 904 页


Chapter 31. Determine the Extent of the
Automation


Most of the time in this book we have been talking about


requirements in a fairly abstract way. Now we need to think


about how these abstract requirements might be brought into


the physical world. We usually do this by automating them.


There is a caveat. When you decide on your automation, no


matter how attractive the technology may be, you still have


to satisfy the essence of the business problem. Designing


business solutions is not about selecting the coolest


technology and making beautiful products. It is about coming


up with the most effective solution for implementing the


essence. In this case, the objective is to determine an


automated product that, apart from satisfying the


requirements, is desirable to its customers, provides a


business benefit, and is something the organization has the


capability to build.


What Should You Automate?


An early step is to consider the extent of the automation.


Working on the assumption that there is an intention to meet


some or all of the requirements with automation, we now need


## 第 905 页


to consider which requirements can be included in the


automated solution. In other words, we are looking at where


to place the automation boundary.


Let’s start with the simple example illustrated in Figure


31.1. Here you see a business process. The solution designer


has, in conjunction with the client and the end user, decided


that the first activity in the business process should be


manual. The remainder of the activities in the process are to


be automated.


![embedded_p905_139.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p905_139.jpeg)


Figure 31.1 A conventional design for a business process.


The first activity in the business process is manual, and


thereafter, the activities are automated.


## 第 906 页


This solution is a fairly conventional one; you see it all


the time. Let’s say that a customer phones the organization


with a simple request. Because it’s a telephone call coming


from a human customer, the designer decides that the best


solution is to answer the call using a human. Of course, it


could have been automated, but in this case a service


representative needs to talk to the customer until the rep is


certain that she understands what the customer wants. At that


stage, she inputs the customer’s request into the automated


solution.


That was a simple solution. Now let’s look at something a


little more sophisticated. This is a scenario of a hospital


nurse treating one of her patients. This is a How-Now


scenario that describes the current way of working.


1. Nurse retrieves the patient’s medical records.


2. Nurse approaches the patient and decides if this is a good


time to visit.


3. Nurse uses the information from the medical records and


examines the patient. She considers the state of the patient.


4. Nurse decides on the appropriate treatment: whether the


treatment is emergency or routine, whether to summon a


## 第 907 页


doctor, and whether further tests have to be run.


5. Nurse treats the patient, either alone or with the help


she has summoned. The treatment can be entirely manual or


might involve medical devices.


6. Nurse records the treatment.


7. Nurse decides if there is a need for follow-up treatment,


or whether the situation can be covered by routine visits.


8. Nurse records her follow-up treatment decisions.


For this scenario, go through each step and decide if it is a


suitable candidate to be either fully or partially automated.


Step 1 should be automated—patient records are most likely


to be digital files, and indeed are more usable if they can


be processed by some automation. Possibly your choice here


relies on the existence of digital records, or a commitment


to build another business process that will digitize the


medical records. The lack of an automated medical records


system could of course mean that you have no choice but to


make this activity a manual one.


## 第 908 页


Obviously, step 2 is a human activity—the nurse is the best


judge as to whether now is the time to visit the patient.


Step 3 is where the nurse considers the state of the


patient. Automate? Or use the skills of the nurse to make


the assessment? To make a judgment you need to ask what the


nurse is looking for when she examines and assesses the


patient. The scenario is not detailed enough as it is, so you


need to look deeper into this activity. Is she making a


subjective judgment based on the demeanor of the patient? Is


there other patient health data that would help her make the


assessment? Could this activity be entirely automated using


data collected from patient monitoring devices?


Analytical skills are needed here to determine the true


nature of this activity. Although it is attractive to


automate as much as possible (saving labor costs, possible


improvement in accuracy, speed, etc.), there might be some


parts of this activity that should always be done by a human


professional. Possibly a physical examination by a competent


nurse is the best of all solutions.


And so on through the remainder of the scenario. Please take


a moment to go back over the scenario and consider your


choice for each of its steps. Some of these will be easy


## 第 909 页


choices, and some will make you pause and think about the


problem more deeply. If you have never been in a hospital as


a patient and don’t know any nurses or doctors, then try to


imagine what it would be like if you were a patient. Or you


might stream a few medical shows and see what you learn. We


hasten to add that business analysis is not normally done by


watching television, but in some cases, it might be a useful


discovery technique.


In situations such as the one discussed above, you will


probably end up with a design like that shown in Figure 31.2.


Here you see that most of the activities are partially


automated, shown by the shading of the activities. Most of


them show that the nurse uses automated assistance to


complete the activity. The one at the right-hand end of the


process is fully automated.


![embedded_p909_140.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p909_140.jpeg)


Figure 31.2 The automated portion of the activities is shown


in a darker shade.


## 第 910 页


Iterative and Evolutionary Design


Design is an iterative activity: It is rarely a straight-line


trajectory from the beginning through to the final product.


You must allow for this and take advantage of it. As you


design more, you learn more, and you change your design to


fit the new circumstances.


As you are working through your automation decisions, you


find that automating one part of a process causes you to


reconsider your choice for another part of the process. You


revise and continue. This is not a bad thing; all good


products evolve from their earliest incarnations.


However iterative and evolutionary it might be, design is


not endless. You should always, albeit reluctantly, either


set up a time box for it or define exit criteria so that you


have an agreed endpoint. But while you are designing, at


various times—perhaps these can be pegged to your


development cycle—it pays to step back and review your


design by asking yourself the following questions.


• Does the component or process I am designing fit


comfortably into the overall business solution?


## 第 911 页


• Is the design evolving into the best possible solution for


my customer segment?


• Is there some enabling technology that would make my design


better?


• Can I make use of AI for some of my processes?


• Can my customers help me improve the design?


• Can I find an even better way to design this solution?


• Am I still solving the right problem? Or is my design


becoming irrelevant?


Sometimes when you step back, you see a problem that requires


you to rework the design. This is no bad thing, provided you


are still within your time box. When you are forced to


rework, you will almost always find your subsequent design to


be better than your initial design. Such is the effect of


iteration.


Change happens. Part of stepping back is looking over your


shoulder to see if there are changes in your organization or


in the outside world that impact your design. There will be


at some stage.


## 第 912 页


Changes do not always come from outside your project. Your


design activity overlaps your discovery activity, and the


possibility of discovering some new facet to the problem is


always there. As you design, you raise more questions, the


answers to which might cause a change to the design. So be


it.


Prototypes Can Help


We looked at prototypes in earlier chapters. Keeping in mind


that we are using the term “prototype” to mean some kind of


sacrificial model, you can make use of prototypes when you


decide the extent of the automation.


For instance, Figure 31.3 shows a simple process model where


the designer is experimenting with different automation


boundaries. The designer has looked at the activities and


considered how much of the process can be automated. Working


from right to left, the designer proposes the extent of the


automation by drawing an automation boundary (shown by the


dotted lines). For each proposed automation boundary, the


designer has sketched the interface that would result from


implementing that proposal. The intention is to demonstrate


the possibilities of different automated solutions and to


## 第 913 页


help the stakeholders make their decisions on the extent of


the automation.


![embedded_p913_141.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p913_141.jpeg)


Figure 31.3 The designer is experimenting with different


automation boundaries and sketching the resultant interface


for each of them.


That’s a very abstract example. Let’s look at something a


little more concrete. We previously looked at a nurse in a


hospital, so let’s revisit that idea, but this time we’ll


look at another part of a nurse’s duties.


## 第 914 页


Nurses make scheduled rounds of their wards administering


medication to patients two or three times a day. There is an


overriding concern that the right medication is administered


to each patient. The nurses feel that while they could use


some automated help, it is vital that they are the people to


administer the medications and ensure that each patient is


properly treated.


A prototype of this process is shown in Figure 31.4. Let’s


walk through it.


## 第 915 页


![embedded_p915_142.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p915_142.jpeg)


Figure 31.4 A prototype of a business process that


administers medication to hospital patients


## 第 916 页


Here you are considering the extent of automation when


designing business solutions. You must start with two


questions.


1. How much of this can you beneficially automate?


2. How much does your client want you to automate?


Let’s look at the process and see if we can answer those


questions. The process begins when a nurse is assigned her


rounds. (It is common practice in hospitals for two nurses to


be assigned to this so that they can check each other, but


let’s simplify the prototype by having a single nurse.)


When the nurse is assigned, the proposed automation (shown as


the first shaded ellipse) sends her assigned rounds and the


needed medication to her tablet. At the same time, the auto


solution sends a list of the medications needed to the


dispensary. The patient records and the patients’


medications would already be digital files, so this is an


area of activity that you would automate. Besides, nurses


should not be doing routine clerical work.


The nurse checks the medications out of the dispensary. This


has potential for automation. It is simple enough for a


robotic solution to collect the needed meds and assemble them


## 第 917 页


for the nurse. Many retail pharmacies have this capability.


Does hospital management want to automate this step? Or do


they want to keep some human control here?


Once she has the required medications, the nurse begins her


rounds. For each patient, she assembles the prescribed pills


or medicines. She would be wheeling around a trolley with


each separate medication in its own container. Here she has


to assemble one pink pill, a blue one, and two yellow ones


(or whatever is prescribed for this patient). She then


ensures that the patient takes the medication (and doesn’t


spit out the nasty-tasting pink one) before checking him off


on her rounds assignment.


This is repeated for each patient until she has come to the


end of her rounds.


The hospital has expressed a preference for this part to


remain a manual operation. You could use a robot to run


around and dispense medication, but the hospital wants


patients to receive a smile and a cheerful word or two from a


nurse.


At the end of her rounds, the nurse hands back any unused


medications. This brings up a possibility for further


## 第 918 页


automation. When the nurse checked the medications out of the


dispensary, she was given the medications in bulk. When she


arrived at a patient’s bedside, she had to assemble the


patient’s prescribed medication from her bulk containers. A


possible automated solution could be used in the dispensary


where each individual patient’s medication is assembled


robotically. Would the cost of building or buying the robot


provide enough benefit to be worthwhile? Is it better for the


nurse to carefully hand-assemble the medication for the


patients or simply give out preassembled packages?


Consider the prototype a little, and feel free to mark up


your own automation proposals—which is exactly what you


would do in a workshop with the nurses and hospital


administrators. The objective is to find the most beneficial


and acceptable extent of any automation.


Architecture


Architecture comes into play during solution design. Your


organization probably has people looking after both


enterprise architecture and solution architecture. These are


constraints on your design work—you must form your business


solution to incorporate their restrictions. It is well beyond


the scope of this book to describe how architecture is done.


## 第 919 页


However, we should point out that the business analysts must


liaise with the architects when designing business solutions.


Enterprise architecture imposes one lot of restrictions. The


enterprise architect is concerned with the various solutions


that make up the structure of the organization, and with the


parts of the organization that produce or consume business


data. Enterprise architecture is there to ensure that all the


solutions work harmoniously together. Any solution you


propose must fit seamlessly into the enterprise.


Solution architecture is similar except that it is concerned


with only the solution under development. The solution


architect ensures that all the components and mechanisms of


the proposed solution are able to work cooperatively to


produce the desired outcomes.


“Always design a thing by considering it in its


next larger context—a chair in a room, a room in


a house, a house in an environment, an


environment in a city plan.”—Eero Saarinen,


Finnish-American architect and industrial


designer


## 第 920 页


Some architecture decisions should be made early in the


project. These are actually some of the non-functional


requirements we looked at earlier, like interoperability,


scalability, availability, security, and so on. These apply


to the entirety of the solution and determine some of your


later architecture decisions, which means that these


decisions come early in the project.


Each organization has its own unique approach to


architecture. These range from anarchic to highly organized,


often dependent on whether the organization is in start-up


mode or sustainability mode. It is therefore impossible to


offer any specific advice in dealing with your own


architectural situation. However, there are people in your


organization who can help you fit your solution into the


established architecture.


Review


As a business analyst, you might be discovering the


requirements for consumer products or services, but most BAs,


most of the time, are discovering requirements for software


that fits into a business solution. You start by looking at


the whole of the problem space and analyzing it. When you


## 第 921 页


have a satisfactory understanding of it, you and your client


determine which parts of it can be beneficially automated.


It is prudent to not assume automation at the outset and not


discover requirements only for the software part of the


solution. Instead, concentrate on discovering the essence of


the requirements for the business problem, and then decide if


automation provides the best solution.


Along with the decision of whether to automate, you are


deciding the characteristics of your solution. Some examples


include


• Making the solution as elegantly simple as possible.


• Presenting the solution’s information in a logical,


natural order.


• Keeping your solution consistent with other solutions used


by the customer.


• Orienting the solution toward the people who are to use the


solution. Keeping people at the center of your design


thinking will give you the best solution.


## 第 922 页


And then there is the holy grail of design: useful, usable,


used.


Your solution must do something useful for your customer.


1


Otherwise, it joins the Yottabytes of unwanted software in a


cloud somewhere. Usefulness is largely determined during


Blastoff when you set measurable goals for the project.


1


Approximately a million trillion megabytes.


Being usable is partly down to the UX designer (see the next


chapter) and partly down to the way that you, the business


analyst, understands the user and arranges the business


events and the processes that respond to the events.


A solution will be used if it achieves the two properties


above.


Resources


Business Process Management: Concepts, Languages,


Architectures, Fourth Edition, by Mathias Weske (Springer,


2024). This book provides a comprehensive overview of


business process management, including the role of


## 第 923 页


automation. It can help you understand the fundamentals of


business process analysis and automation.


Arc42 (https://arc42.org) is a website about solution


architecture. A lot of it is in German, but you might like


the company’s free template.


The Harvard Business Review website (https://hbr.org) has


articles on automation, business process optimization, and


decision-making in the context of digital transformation.


## 第 924 页


Chapter 32. Designing Information and
Functionality


You are designing a business solution; something that is used


by an organization to do work. That much is obvious. However,


some of that work will be done by humans, and usually by


humans interacting with computers. Humans have different


needs from computers: Computers can process huge amounts of


data, but humans can’t really process data. They need


information.


So far in your exploration of the problem space, you have


been thinking in terms of abstract functionality and data. We


have been urging you to think of the essence of the problem,


and not worry too much about how this essence could be


installed into the real, physical world.


Now comes the time to turn abstract functionality into usable


interactions and turn abstract data into information. See


Figure 32.1. Your design should enable your users to


understand what they are dealing with; to understand what


they can do with it and what it can do for them. Further, it


should enable them to easily find the information and


functionality they need to do their tasks.


## 第 925 页


![embedded_p925_143.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p925_143.jpeg)


Figure 32.1 Your business analysis so far has concentrated


on understanding and documenting the essence of the problem.


## 第 926 页


Now you have to turn that abstract essence into real-world


interactions and human-understandable information.


User Experience = Information + Functionality


We are reaching an area of design where the business analyst


is collaborating with a user experience (UX) designer.


UX designers are employed to produce a solution that makes


people want to buy it and/or use it. User experience design


is a significant topic and one that we consider to be beyond


the scope of this book. However, we take a brief look at it


here because this kind of design plays a large part in


solution development, and it has some parallels with your


role as a business analyst.


UX design aims to produce a usage experience that is pleasing


and interesting, usable and intuitive, as well as relevant to


the culture and aspirations of the user. Simply put, if you


provide a pleasing experience that users enjoy and wish to


repeat, then those users are far more likely to accept your


solution. They will willingly use it, not ask for changes,


and they will work effectively with it. This means you have


produced a solution that works the way your users feel it


should work.


## 第 927 页


UX design should not be left to amateurs. It comprises a


combination of several disciplines and, if it is to be done


properly, should be handled by experienced or professional


people. UX design usually involves cognitive psychology, user


interface design, human–computer interaction, and a liberal


amount of prototyping.


The business analyst is not expected to be a UX designer: Her


domain is the essential business functionality and non-


functionality, which are the foundation for UX design. The


essence is augmented by the personas that you or the UX


designer generated and by observations of users during


requirements discovery. You have gained insights into their


way of working, the kind of people they are, their knowledge,


how much pressure they experience when they work, their


preferences, and so on. You also know what they need to


accomplish with this solution.


That is what you as a business analyst bring to the table.


Figure 32.2 illustrates how the UX designer and the business


analyst meet. The BA brings knowledge of the required


functionality and data. The designer brings UX skills.


Together they bring about the most usable solution.


## 第 928 页


![embedded_p928_144.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p928_144.jpeg)


Figure 32.2 Where the business analyst and the UX designer


meet


## 第 929 页


Let’s step back from the UX designer role for the moment and


consider what is being designed.


Let’s start with information. Information is what we use to


make decisions. Information about the weather enables you to


decide whether to take an umbrella. Information about


different running shoes (lightness, flexibility, stability,


cushioning, etc.) enables you to decide which is the best for


you. Information about an insurance claim and its background


enables the claims adjuster to make decisions about the


company’s liability.


The user has a mental model of the information, and you


should present the information to fit this mental model. If


you, as a customer of an online retailer, have ever struggled


on a website to find the next piece of information you need,


it is because the designer’s mental model of the information


is different from yours. For example, you might want to know


the shipping costs before entering your credit card details.


You might think that entering your delivery address should


come before selecting a carrier. The task of the business


analyst (and that of the UX designer) is to understand the


user’s mental model and design accordingly.


## 第 930 页


As a business analyst, you know the data stored by the


solution space. For example, you might have built a data


model (class diagram, entity model) to demonstrate this data.


Each class on the diagram has a unique identifier—we looked


at this in Chapter 23, Stored Data. Let’s say that you have


a class of data called Subscriber, and its unique identifier


is Subscriber Number. This class is part of Figure 32.3.


![embedded_p930_145.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p930_145.jpeg)


Figure 32.3 A partial data model showing a few of the


classes needed for a subscription solution


Back to the user’s mental model. Let’s say that your user


is an employee of a music streaming service. What is her


mental model of the data? How does she want to see it? Does


she want to see a list of subscribers in Subscriber # order?


Most likely not, as that is the order in which people


subscribed, and that is probably of no use. So, what sequence


## 第 931 页


of information would conform to a user’s mental model? A


group of subscribers by area? All the subscribers to a


particular Service? Subscribers whose subscription


anniversary is approaching (to alert them that it’s time to


renew)? For any of these options to make sense, you need to


know what the user is doing and why she is doing it.


But you already know that. Any user activity is part of the


response to a business event. For each business event, there


is a business use case that describes the activity of the


response. We talked about this earlier, and you might have


built a process model or a scenario, or some other way to


model and understand the functionality of response. You might


have UX people working alongside you when you are discovering


this functionality.


Now you and the UX designer collaborate to put the data and


the functionality together. You are designing how the user


can make use of the functionality and the data to achieve the


desired outcome of the business event.


Your role here is to feed your requirements knowledge to the


UX designer. But it’s more than that. The UX designer looks


at the problem from the point of view of the user. You, on


the other hand, look at it from the point of view of the


## 第 932 页


business. These two views have to come together. The business


objectives have to be met, and the user has to have a


solution that she finds pleasant and convenient to use.


Otherwise, she will not use it or will use it badly. Either


one can subvert achieving the business outcome.


On the other hand, a solution whose functionality is exactly


what is needed, and whose usability is excellent, guarantees


that the desired outcome is achieved in the best possible


manner.


What happens if your organization does not employ a UX


designer? In this case, you as the business analyst are the


person best placed to fill the role. You have accumulated


knowledge of the problem through your prototyping and


trawling activities. You have become acquainted with the


people who are to use your solution; you might have built a


persona for some of the customer segments. You understand the


desired outcomes for the business events. All of that is the


raw material for the design of the product.


The next step is to collaborate with the user to work through


her interactions. You have to walk a fine line between seeing


the problem from the user’s point of view and listening to


## 第 933 页


that person so hard that you end up with an idiosyncratic


solution that pleases only one person—that particular user.


The design process is iterative, and we suggest that you do a


lot of your collaborative designing on a whiteboard. Yes,


there are software screen prototyping tools, but the task is


to design a flow for the activity, not fiddle with the colors


of the buttons.


We strongly recommend that if you are to undertake the UX


responsibilities, you read as much as you can and attend a


few training courses. UX is not as easy as it looks. You can


see this by all the examples of poor UX design. This


chapter’s Resources section has some suggestions for UX


information. Nothing you do without UX training will be as


good, but your BA training is the next best thing.


Review


Designing the information and functionality is where your


requirements discovery comes face-to-face with your


customers. Literally. You (and your UX designer) are crafting


the way that the customer will use the data you have


discovered, and the functionality that you have trawled,


prototyped, probed, challenged, and invented. Your


## 第 934 页


requirements discovery provides the raw materials for


designing the information and functionality.


We have suggested that designing the information and the


functionality is important enough to have a UX designer


collaborate with you, the business analyst. This ensures that


the customer gets to reap the benefit of your requirements


work by having a product that does exactly what he needs it


to do.


Resources


User Experience Foundations by Nick de Voil (BCS, The


Chartered Institute for IT, 2019). The author provides a


straightforward but authoritative description of UX and


explains why it works. His chapter on interaction design is


worth the price of admission.


Paper Prototyping: The Fast and Easy Way to Design and Refine


User Interfaces by Carolyn Snyder (Morgan Kaufmann, 2003).


The author is a usability engineer, and here she shows how to


create and test paper prototypes for different kinds of user


interfaces.


Interaction Design: Beyond Human-Computer Interaction, 3rd


Edition, by Helen Sharp, Yvonne Rogers, and Jenny Preece


## 第 935 页


(Wiley, 2011). This book advocates a multidisciplined


approach to interaction design; one that should resonate with


business analysts. It sets out the principles of interaction


design and how to apply them.


About Face: The Essentials of Interaction Design, 4th


Edition, by Alan Cooper, Robert Reimann, David Cronin, and


Christopher Noessel (Wiley, 2007). Cooper is one of the


pioneers of interaction design. This edition expands the


topic to include interactions with smartphones and tablets.


The User Experience Team of One by Leah Buley (Rosenfeld


Media, 2013). This is a lightweight approach to UX design


that business analysts might find to be a useful addition to


their requirements practices.


Seductive Interaction Design by Stephen Anderson (New Riders,


2011). This looks at how to make your product more engaging


and what motivates your customers to interact with your


product.


The UX Collective website (https://uxdesign.cc) offers a


wealth of articles and resources for UX design.


The website for the Nielsen Norman Group, founded by Jakob


Nielsen and Don Norman, has an extensive collection of


## 第 936 页


articles, reports, and usability guidelines (see


https://www.nngroup.com).


## 第 937 页


Chapter 33. Designing Using Ready-Mades


Most likely, the next development effort you are engaged in


will involve some ready-made components. These can be very


small things, such as a module of plug-in code, or something


quite large, such as a customer relationship management (CRM)


system that spans the whole of the customer life cycle. Or


they can be something between these two. In some cases, you


install the ready-made solution on your in-house servers, and


in some cases you use cloud services or you outsource the


functionality to a provider. In other cases, you reuse


components from an existing legacy system. Sometimes you pay


for your ready-made either by purchase or by subscription


fee, and other times it is open source and free. Ready-made


solutions and components are varied, but they have one thing


in common: They have to provide the functionality and data


needed to produce, partially or fully, a workable business


solution for your client.


We use the term “ready-made” to refer to any


component or complete solution, no matter what it


is. This is off-the-shelf (OTS) software that you


might buy, borrow, or reuse. In fact, it is


anything you don’t build yourself.


## 第 938 页


The task of designing is different when you are using ready-


mades. Here the task is to select, assemble, and integrate


the optimal collection of ready-mades. The aim, as always, is


to devise the business solution that best solves the business


problem.


In some cases, the optimal solution might be to deploy the


ready-made straight out of the box, in other cases the ready-


made needs customization or configuration to fit the


organization, and in some cases, it is best to adopt the


ready-made and modify the organization to fit it. The same


process applies if you are using an open-source (or any


other free) product. The only difference is that a request


for proposal (coming up next) is not used. You just download


the product and evaluate it.


Let’s look at how you go about designing your business


solution using ready-mades.


The Request for Proposal


A request for proposal (RFP) is a document that you generate


to invite vendors of ready-mades to propose their solution


to your business problem. You can invite any number of


## 第 939 页


vendors depending on the likelihood of their having suitable


ready-mades to propose.


Before we get into RFPs, we should mention two other


documents that can be used when dealing with ready-made


vendors. We mention them briefly here, as you will probably


come across them, but we don’t intend for this chapter to go


into the minutiae of each possible document.


If you are working for a government organization, you might


augment or replace the request for proposal with an ITT,


invitation to tender. The intention of both documents is


close enough that we will deal only with RFPs here.


An RFI, request for information, is a document sent out,


usually to a wide audience of potential vendors, requesting


information about their products. This is used in some early


stages to examine possibilities and try out potential


approaches to a solution. The form of an RFI can be pretty


much whatever you want it to be. It can be much less


constrained than an RFP, as you are casting your net very


wide looking for possibilities.


Let’s go back to the request for proposal. From a business


analyst’s point of view, your responsibility is to provide


## 第 940 页


enough information in the RFP for vendors to make sensible


proposals. The information should be complete enough for the


vendor to correctly understand the problem, yet not so


restrictive that you cut off creative solutions to the


problem.


Once you have received the vendors’ proposals, the task then


switches to evaluating the proposed ready-mades. You are


evaluating whether the ready-made is a perfect fit (it almost


never is), how much configuration and/or customization is


needed to make it fit, or whether it is better and cheaper to


change the business process to fit the ready-made. Having


looked at an array of ready-mades, you might decide that


building your own solution is your best option.


Figure 33.1 illustrates the usual way of generating an RFP.


## 第 941 页


![embedded_p941_146.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p941_146.jpeg)


Figure 33.1 The artifacts used to generate a request for


proposal


The first and probably most important artifact that you


produce is a model of the scope of the problem. You do not


want vendors proposing solutions to the wrong problem, nor do


you want them to be unclear about the solution you are


seeking. The scope model tells the vendor precisely where you


want their ready-made solution to fit into your business


organization.


## 第 942 页


Let’s look at an example where your client wants to buy a


ready-made warehouse management solution. Your client


considers that building a system from scratch is expensive,


and he wants the solution up and running as soon as possible.


Obviously, whatever you buy must fit into the client’s


existing organization.


Start with the scope of the problem. Figure 33.2 is a context


diagram for a proposed warehouse management system.


## 第 943 页


![embedded_p943_147.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p943_147.jpeg)


Figure 33.2 The context diagram for a proposed warehouse


management solution. This example has been simplified for


brevity’s sake. The context diagram is used to help generate


the RFP.


## 第 944 页


Here are some things to note. First, your client has an


existing logistics system (shown on the right side of the


diagram). This means that any proposed ready-made should not


include logistics but must interface with the existing


logistics system. Your client wishes to retain manual


warehouse workers to store deliveries of new incoming goods.


This means that any ready-made must be able to compute the


optimal positioning of new stock and generate the appropriate


instructions for the warehouse staff. Of course, there is a


lot more to warehouse management, and we will see some of it


as we press on.


Also note that warehouse management is only one component of


your client’s overall business solution. You are looking for


the ready-made that is the best fit with the existing


systems.


As you look at the context model, consider the flows of data


into and out of the solution space. The data content of each


of these flows should be defined in your data dictionary


(section 7 of the Volere Requirements Specification Template;


see Appendix A). Why? Because when you send out your RFPs,


you want the vendors to know what data is available and what


data you want their solution to produce. You also need to


## 第 945 页


ensure that the vendor clearly understands your data-related


terminology. Misunderstandings are both common and costly.


If you look back at Figure 33.1, you see that there are other


artifacts that are needed to produce the RFP. The first is a


list of the business events. (We discussed earlier how the


flows of data on the context model indicate the business


events.) These business events represent transactions to be


processed as part of the warehouse management solution. Some


of these originate outside the business, and others come from


other parts of the client’s organization.


The list of business events tells the vendor what events the


ready-made has to handle. The names of the events will


differ, but it is straightforward enough to find the


equivalence between your context diagram and the vendor’s


list of events. Comparing the outcomes of each business event


is the clearest way to determine how closely the vendor’s


solution matches your requirements.


Some of the business events might be complicated, or peculiar


to your client’s organization, and will need more detail


than just its name and its input and/or output data. For


these events, you can write a scenario and sometimes a few


(or a lot) of the detailed requirements. It should not be


## 第 946 页


necessary to write all of the detailed requirements; you


don’t really care how the ready-made produces its outputs,


just that the outcome matches what is needed.


RFP Contents


RFPs vary, and no doubt your organization has its own way of


writing one. We cannot override that, but we can suggest some


things that should be part of any RFP. There would of


course be more things than we show below, but those would be


specific to your organization.


You as a business analyst might not be the person ultimately


responsible for writing and sending out the RFPs, but your


requirements discovery is the most important contributor to


it. We suggest that you include the following items in your


RFPs:


• An introduction to the project—a half-page overview.


• The goals of the project; that is, the measurable outcome


the organization wants to achieve.


• A brief introduction to the organization, what it does, and


what its aspirations are.


## 第 947 页


• A context diagram that defines the scope of the business


activity to be done by the ready-made.


• A data dictionary of the data flows on the context diagram.


This gives you a better comparison with the ready-made’s


inputs and outputs.


• A list of business events. The vendor needs to determine if


its solution provides for the transactions you need to


process.


• The outcomes expected from each business event. Note that


these are outcomes, not outputs.


• Scenarios—but only for those cases where you need to


explain the response to a business event.


• Requirements—as many as are needed to explain specific


parts of the problem space.


There will also be some other corporate stuff, but this falls


outside your remit as a business analyst. These are items


like


• Bidding process


• Contractual issues


## 第 948 页


• Timetable for responding and for delivering


• And so on


Once the RFPs have been sent out and the vendors have


responded, it’s time to evaluate the proposed ready-mades.


Selecting the Best Ready-Made


You will make many decisions based on the closeness of the


match between your context model and the vendor’s ready-


made solution.


The task is to get the optimal fit. This can mean the


ready-made causes the least disruption to the organization,


or it can mean that it is more economical to adopt the ready-


made as is and reorganize the organization. In most cases,


you find the ready-made that best matches your business


process and modify it where the match is imperfect. Figure


33.3 illustrates the matching part of this.


## 第 949 页


![embedded_p949_148.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p949_148.jpeg)


## 第 950 页


![embedded_p949_148.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p949_148.jpeg)


Figure 33.3 You start with a likely looking candidate ready-


made. However, you have to look under the hood to see if it


is a real match. The scope and the business events are


crucial. These should be a close match to avoid unnecessary


customization.


Scope


Scope is the obvious place to start. During the Blastoff


activity, you produced a context diagram showing the extent


of the problem space and indicating its functionality. You


provide this context diagram to the vendors and ask them to


demonstrate how their ready-made achieves the required


functionality. You also ask how their ready-made treats each


of the business events.


You have to know how much of the ready-made is usable within


your business solution. See Figure 33.4. It does not have to


be, and probably won’t be, a perfect match. You can build


any missing pieces yourself or disregard any pieces of the


ready-made that are surplus to your requirements. However,


the scope of the ready-made should be such that it


substantially matches your business problem space, or the


parts of it that you want covered by the ready-made.


## 第 951 页


![embedded_p951_149.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p951_149.jpeg)


Figure 33.4 The scope of the proposed ready-made (shown as


shaded) is not an exact match with the client’s problem


space. The shortfall would have to be made up with custom-


built software, or the organization would have to change to


match the ready-made.


Business Events


## 第 952 页


Business events represent the work that your business


solution has to do. That is, each business event happens


because someone or something needs your solution to do


something such as produce data or a product; thus, it is


important that the ready-made responds to the “same”


business events that the solution you are designing calls


for. Of course, they are not the same, at least initially.


The ready-made is designed to be customized to fit each


unique customer’s needs, so the names start out as generic


names. Take, for example, “Create new customer.” You might


rebadge this to be “Enroll new subscriber.” This would be a


standard workflow to process new customers. You would


customize it if you had several types of customer with


variations of the workflow for each. This customization would


hopefully be done by configuration. The result is that the


ready-made provides business events that can be adapted to


cater to your business events.


You are not just looking at functionality. It is the outcome


of the business event that matters most. If you have not


already done so, it is now worthwhile to write the outcome or


rationale for your events. If you wrote business event


stories, the “So that” part is what is needed here.


## 第 953 页


The ready-made will not be a perfect match as it comes out of


the box, but you are matching the outcome of the configured


ready-made with the outcome you need. Non-functional


requirements also come into play; they are also part of the


outcome. The vendor’s version (after configuration) of the


business event must implement all the non-functional


requirements that you have discovered.


The point of this exercise is to determine if the ready-made


outcomes can be made to match your client’s business events,


either by configuration or by customization. You are


determining whether the ready-made is able to bring about the


correct business outcome for the problem space.


Requirements


There is no doubt that the ready-made must match the


requirements. After all, the requirements specify what any


solution must do to satisfy the business need. Why have we


not discussed this seemingly important issue?


Because it is usually possible to operate at the business


event level. If the ready-made—configured or customized—has


the same outcome as you have specified for each business


event, then there is usually no need for the lower-level


requirements to come into play.


## 第 954 页


The non-functional requirements are different. Security,


cultural, and compliance requirements are paramount here.


Examine these requirements thoroughly, especially when the


ready-made comes from another country. Other countries have


different laws and some of these might be showstoppers. For


example, privacy laws differ between the United States and


Europe. GDPR, an EU regulation, prohibits data from being


exported to the United States with its less stringent privacy


laws.


There are some situations where you have specialized


requirements. For example, you might have requirements about


how a calculation is done; your organization might calculate


loan interest in a nonstandard way. You might have


requirements to do with corporate governance, and these are


unique to the company. In these cases, the ready-made must be


able to have the facility to include custom-made


modifications. There are some ready-mades that prohibit


customers from changing the code, which would disqualify them


if the need for customization arose.


It is the closeness of the match between the


outcomes of the business events that determines


the fit of the ready-made to your problem space.


## 第 955 页


But by and large, it is the closeness of the match between


the outcomes of the business events that determines the fit


of the ready-made to your problem space. If the outcomes fit,


then there is little need to investigate how the ready-made


achieves its outcomes.


Scoring


Whatever scoring technique you use, keep it simple. We


suggest that for each business event, compare the required


outcome with the outcome provided by the ready-made. Award


points something like this:


4—meets the outcome “out of the box.”


3—meets the outcome when configured.


2—meets it with a small amount of customization. You have to


set your scale of what “small” means in terms of hours/days


of effort.


1—meets the outcome with a large amount of customization


(you decide what “large” is) or with integration with other


existing solution components.


0—cannot meet the outcome.


## 第 956 页


If you have prioritized the business events (and you should


have), then their priorities become multiples of the score.


Use the MoSCoW scale (described in Chapter 8, Prioritizing


the Business Events) for the following:


Must Haves—multiply the score by 3.


Should Haves—multiply by 2.


Could Haves—multiply by 1.


Won’t Haves—you should not be considering these at all for


a ready-made.


You might also consider whether the Must Haves should have a


minimum score of, say, 6 to receive further consideration.


There are other factors that you might consider including in


your scoring. All constraints must be met, and the non-


functional requirements play a significant part. Your


security team should assess the security of the ready-made.


A failure in the security area disqualifies a candidate, as


does any shortfall in compliance requirements. Any ready-


made that does not comply with privacy laws must be counted


out. Cultural fit is important—does the ready-made work in


## 第 957 页


a way that is compatible with your workforce? If it is too


alien, then people will be reluctant to use it.


Most vendors intend to make their products usable, but there


are some more sophisticated products that have a long and


expensive learning curve. Here you are trying to assess how


quickly and easily the ready-made will become an accepted


part of your business. Does the vendor offer training in some


way to ease the transition? Usability in all its meanings


should be part of your scoring.


And while we are speaking of the vendor, you might consider


scoring each vendor on their willingness to collaborate while


you get the ready-made up and running. Part of this score


should be allocated to the level of, and the expertise of,


the support offered.


Scoring should also include a cost-benefit analysis and a


risk assessment. However, these two are usually the


provenance of your management team.


Configure or Customize?


Once you have chosen your ready-made, you know the gaps


between the desired business solution and the ready-made


component. These can sometimes be filled by configuring the


## 第 958 页


ready-made. This is perfectly normal and is expected. Ready-


mades are designed to be configured. You specify the required


parameters to be adjusted, and what result the ready-made


should produce once configured.


When configuration is not enough, you need to customize the


ready-made code. The latter should not be undertaken lightly,


as it puts you out of step with future releases of the ready-


made. You will have to reinsert your customization for every


upgrade.


Despite that, there are circumstances when customization is


advantageous. If customizing the ready-made gives you a


competitive advantage, or if it is mission critical, then


naturally you should do it. Consider the purpose-based


alignment model shown in Figure 33.5.


## 第 959 页


![embedded_p959_150.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p959_150.jpeg)


Figure 33.5 The purpose-based alignment model. You use this


to help make decisions about configuring or customizing.


Diagram from Kent McDonald.


First, let’s consider the scales at the bottom and sides of


the model. Whether the business event is mission critical is


the place to start. This gives you a very clear indication as


to whether spending money customizing the ready-made is a


good investment or not. This scale is tempered by the


vertical scale of differentiation.


## 第 960 页


Differentiation is not the same as different. You can make


something different by painting it a different color.


Differentiation is having a product that has a clear gap


between it and its competitors. For example, there is a


differentiation between electric and internal combustion


cars. If differentiation is important to you—that is, you


want your solution to have a clear advantage over your


competitors’—then you measure your business event along the


vertical scale. Is it high or low?


Having assessed the business event on both the mission-


critical and the differentiation scales, what quadrant does


it occupy? For the Differentiating quadrant, the business


event is important enough to go to the expense of customizing


the ready-made. The Parity quadrant means that you are happy


enough to end up on par with your competitors, so you would


probably take the cheaper option of configuration.


The Partner quadrant means that this is not mission critical


to you, but if you can find a partner organization, you can


use its abilities to exploit the differentiation. The Who


Cares? quadrant is fairly self-explanatory. Here you do the


minimum possible with the ready-made.


## 第 961 页


There is a reference to the University of Alaska’s white


paper in this chapter’s Resources section. This gives a


fuller explanation of the model.


Requirements for Adaptation


You have to specify the requirements for either the


configuration or the customization. Configuration, as


mentioned above, needs you to specify which configuration


adjustments have to be made, and the intended outcome of the


configured ready-made.


Customization requirements are more serious but are


essentially the same as the requirements you have been


gathering from your stakeholders. Each business event has its


own Mini Blastoff, and you go about trawling for the


requirements just as we described earlier.


The difference this time is that you see the ready-made as a


set of constraints, and your requirements must cater to those


constraints. You still need to get to the essence of the


problem, and we have been urging you to write your


requirements from the point of view of the business and not


the technology. That changes, because now you are writing


requirements for additions and adaptation of the ready-made.


## 第 962 页


Reorganizing the Organization


When the ready-made is a larger-scale solution, it sometimes


means that the optimal approach is to buy the ready-made and


adapt the organization to fit it. For example, suppose that


you are looking at a ready-made for an insurance client. The


ready-made is a total solution that provides processes for


all of the business of insurance. The current organization


has been using a collection of different applications to do


its work up until now. Installing the ready-made means


disrupting the way people work, but it will, in the long


term, provide benefits.


This is largely an economic decision. Is it cheaper to


customize the ready-made, or to restructure the organization?


Is the ready-made so advantageous that it warrants the


disruption of changing the organization?


Changing the organization is fairly serious. You might


involve human resources (HR) to help you with estimating the


time and effort needed for the reorg. You also have to factor


in the stunning lack of enthusiasm you will encounter for


this exercise, and that should be factored into this


decision. You may also need to consult higher management. See


Figure 33.6.


## 第 963 页


![embedded_p963_151.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p963_151.jpeg)


Figure 33.6 How to accommodate the ready-made: The


organization surrounding it is changed.


## 第 964 页


Every organization is different, so it is impossible to


describe exactly what you have to do. However, we suggest


that you look at each business event. The ready-made will


process more or less the same business events as you do at


the moment. It will sell goods, renew policies, predict crop


prices, or do whatever your current business does.


For each business event, look at what human activity is


needed. Is there any front-end processing or back-end


activity? Is this different from what went before? If so, you


need to describe the human tasks. This is regular business


analysis—you study the activity and write requirements for


it. Instead of the requirements being used to write some


software, your requirements are used to write instructions


for a human to do a task. We suggest that usually a scenario,


with a few detailed requirements, is sufficient to guide a


human on what to do. When the organization has a specific way


to do a calculation, or the rules are complicated for whether


or not to accept an application, you need to augment the


scenario with detailed atomic requirements. This is


illustrated in Figure 33.7.

Figure 33.7 Specifying the activities that need to be


changed to accommodate the ready-made


Review


Designing using ready-made components or solutions is a


regular part of business analysis. Many of the projects you


work on will involve, to a greater or lesser extent, the use


of ready-mades.


We have set down the business analyst’s responsibilities


with ready-mades. While you may not get to make the final


choice of the ready-made product, your input to the process


## 第 966 页


is crucial. In order to assess the optimal ready-made, you


need more than the glossy brochure or the slick website and


their promises of boundless productivity gains and


everlasting corporate bliss. You need to understand the


business being done and what impact the ready-made has upon


that business. This is the task of the business analyst.


It is impossible to specify a definitive process for doing


this. Organizations and ready-mades are far too varied for


any one set of directions to cover all variations. However,


we hope the general guidelines we have provided will help in


your selection and deployment process.


The better the RFP is, the better the vendors’


responses will be.


While organizations differ, the request for proposal is


almost constant. This document is soliciting candidate ready-


mades, and it stands to reason that the better the RFP is,


the better the vendors’ responses will be. A large part of


designing with ready-mades is to make the best selection. An


analogy to this is building something complicated using LEGO


bricks. You are searching for the best pieces to make the Taj


Mahal, and some pieces fit your construction better than


others. The RFP is designed to find the best pieces, so a lot


## 第 967 页


of your effort should go into the RFP that will get you the


most appropriate ready-made solution.


Resources


The Purpose-Based Alignment Model, originally from Alaska


University, is a useful guideline to help you determine


whether to configure or customize your ready-made (see


https://insideproduct.co/purpose-based-alignment-model).


## 第 968 页


Part VII: Requirements Repository


The requirements repository is central to everything. As you


can see in the schema shown in Figure P7.1, all the


activities both feed into and feed from the requirements


repository.


## 第 969 页


![embedded_p969_153.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p969_153.jpeg)


Figure P7.1 The requirements repository is central to your


requirements discovery activities. All the activities feed


into, or draw from, the knowledge of the requirements stored


in the repository.


## 第 970 页


The requirements repository is like any other: It’s a place


to store knowledge. The repository can take several forms. It


can be a specification, a story map, a backlog, a collection


of artifacts, or some other form of database of requirements.


We will discuss these later, and of course the choice of


format for your repository is up to you and your requirements


team. In this part of the book, we shall set out some options


and help you decide which best fits your way of discovering


requirements.


The fundamental idea of a requirements repository is this: As


you are going about your requirements discovery and


elicitation, you are uncovering information that you must


store somewhere for later use. For example, you might build a


scenario of a process, and as this model conveys information


about the problem space or solution space, it is appropriate


to store it in the repository. Similarly, when you are


writing requirements or stories, these are also stored in the


requirements repository. This constant usage means that the


repository is a dynamic store of the requirements information


you are collecting.


Your requirements repository is the physical


incarnation of the Requirements Knowledge Model.


## 第 971 页


The Volere Requirements Knowledge Model is a language for


communicating and managing the knowledge that you discover


during requirements-related activities. It is also a model of


the knowledge you keep in your repository. Or you could say


that the requirements repository is the physical incarnation


of the Requirements Knowledge Model.


Appendix C contains the Requirements Knowledge Model along


with a detailed definition of all its classes of knowledge


and the relationships between them. You have come across this


model earlier in this book, but here we revisit it to explain


the contents of the requirements repository. It is shown in


Figure P7.2.


## 第 972 页


![embedded_p972_154.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p972_154.jpeg)


## 第 973 页


Figure P7.2 The Requirements Knowledge Model in the form of


a simplified class diagram. Each class on the model


represents an artifact that could be part of your


requirements discovery. The connecting lines represent the


relationships or associations that locate the artifact within


your requirements knowledge.


If we start at the top left, we see the class (or entity, if


you prefer) of the Work Scope. The work of the customer’s


business and the problem space are the same thing. We have


called it “work” here, as it is a more representative


description. Whatever you call it, you would probably record


this class using the artifact of a context diagram. Then, as


we discussed earlier, you would break the work scope into a


number of Business Events. The asterisk on the association


connecting these work scope and business events indicates


that there are many Business Events for a Work Scope. A


business event happens, and the connected Business Use Case


or Business Event Story, describes the response of the Work


to the business event. So, this class would be recorded using


an artifact such as the story, a scenario, perhaps a process


model, or whatever else you feel appropriate to document the


response.


## 第 974 页


The purpose of revisiting the model is to discuss storing the


artifacts that you collect as you go about your requirements


discovery. You will collect or generate an artifact—a BUC


Scenario, a Story, a Requirement, and so on—for all or most


of the classes in the model. Having a picture of how your


artifacts fit together should prove useful when you’re knee-


deep in the products of your requirements discovery.


You should give some consideration to the physical


incarnation of your repository, especially your


specifications and story maps. For example, some teams prefer


to have their story maps in the form of paper cards stuck on


the wall. Others prefer a software tool of some kind. Many


requirements teams are happy using a collaborative word


processor or spreadsheet for their requirements


specification. Others prefer to use a specialized software


tool to store their requirements.


There are a variety of requirements tools, with a variety of


capabilities. It is important to match the tool’s


capabilities with the way in which you prefer to manage your


requirements. In some cases, a tool will offer tracing


capabilities so that you can track requirements through


implementation and testing. In other cases, being able to


collaborate with a dispersed team is more important.


## 第 975 页


It is well beyond the scope of this book to discuss the


available requirements tools. However, if you are choosing a


tool, choose carefully. Some of them lock you into a way of


working that you and your team may find irksome. The tool is


there to support you, not the other way around.


One aspect that we suggest you look for in a tool is how


closely its database can be made to implement the


Requirements Knowledge Model, and whether it can be


configured to accommodate the snow card format for your


requirements.


The following chapters discuss some of the options you have


for the content and arrangement of the knowledge in your


requirements repository.


## 第 976 页


Chapter 34. Requirements Specification


If you are using stories for your requirements, then please


skip to the next chapter. Here, we’ll start discussing the


requirements repository with the conventional requirements


specification. This requirements document has been with us


for quite some time, but longevity does not mean feeble. The


specification plays a vital part in solution development


today.


The specification is typically a complete description of the


solution to be built. It is generally made up of hundreds,


perhaps thousands of functional and non-functional


requirements. This document is also known as the software


requirements specification, or SRS.


The specification is often criticized because it typically


takes time to complete it. Some critics like to point out


that by the time the specification is complete, the original


problem may have changed. This can be true in some


circumstances; however, it must be balanced against the time-


saving effectiveness of understanding the problem and having


a precise specification of what to build. But you should also


adapt the way you build requirements specifications to ensure


## 第 977 页


that you don’t end up with an out-of-date specification.


We’ll look at one way of doing this in a moment.


A complete requirements specification is sometimes necessary.


In some cases, if you are outsourcing the development of the


solution, you would need a complete specification before your


outsourcer can start work. In other cases, the outsourcer can


start construction and work in an agile way with progressive


requirements being fed as needed.


Your work might involve some kind of military application,


medical appliance, scientific application, security, or some


other situation where it is necessary to prove that the


requirements are complete and can be traced to the


implementation. In these cases, a complete specification is


required. Your organization might have development standards


whereby the specification must be complete and provable


before construction begins.


So, as we go through this chapter, what we are discussing is


relevant whether you are building a complete specification or


building your specification incrementally.


The requirements we are talking about in this chapter are


those you have met in previous chapters—functional and non-


## 第 978 页


functional requirements. These are the conventional


requirements that are typically written as a statement, “The


product shall…”, and you can expect to write quite a few of


them.


We strongly suggest you use the Volere Requirements


Specification Template that you find in Appendix A as a


guide. This is a complete description of a requirements


specification and its contents. We will visit parts of it in


this chapter.


Structure of the Specification


The template is set out so that the atomic requirements are


grouped together by type. That is all the functional


requirements, followed by the look and feel requirements,


then the usability requirements, and so on and so on.


While there might be value in doing this, it is just one way


of arranging your requirements knowledge. The specification


does not have to be written that way, and it is probably


preferable that you write yours one business event at a time.


Let’s look at why.


People often speak of “high-level requirements” and “low-


level requirements.” While this is usually well-intentioned,


## 第 979 页


the problem is that it is quite arbitrary, and nobody is


quite sure exactly or can agree on what is “high” and what


is “low.” Of course, you can say that a high-level


requirement is one that has lower-level requirements attached


to it, but that is close to meaningless and does not locate a


requirement in any kind of hierarchy.


However, we do know exactly what a business event is—where


it starts, where it ends, and what happens in between.


So, we suggest that you use each business events as your


“high-level requirement” and attach the atomic


requirements to the business event. This gives your


specification a usable structure. Business events are self-


contained, so there is no overlap between them. Readers of


the specification can select whichever business event they


are interested in and focus on its details without


distraction.


Let’s look at the specification as a whole. Drawing from the


Volere template, we suggest that you have a structure along


these lines. You can relate these headings to the template:


Area 1: The Problem


Goals


## 第 980 页


Stakeholders


Glossary of terms


Scope of the problem space


Business data and dictionary


Area 2: The Solution


Scope of the solution


Area 3: The Business Events


List of business events


Business event 1


{functional requirement}


{non-functional requirement}


Additional material


Business event 2


{functional requirement}


{non-functional requirement}


## 第 981 页


Additional material


etc.


where { } enclose multiple requirements


Area 1: The Problem sets out the goals of the initiative and


the problem to be solved. Most of this comes from the


Blastoff, which we discussed earlier. It is crucial that


everybody on the project has the same understanding of the


problem to be solved, so it is appropriate that this is the


beginning of your specification.


The scope of the problem should be defined using a context


model, but whatever you use, it should unambiguously define


the boundaries of the problem space. It must be clear to


everybody on the team what is inside and what is outside the


business problem you intend to solve.


Area 2: The Solution deals with how much of the problem that


you choose to automate. This should be defined with a second
