context model, showing the extent of the IT product to be


developed and what remains outside the scope of automation.


Area 3: The Business Events should begin with a list of


business events. Following this, for each business event, you


## 第 982 页


write your functional and non-functional requirements. We’ve


described how to write these requirements in previous


chapters.


For each business event, you should include any additional


material, such as a scenario or process model of the business


use case. This helps readers and developers understand the


response to the event. You can also include any additional


information that you think will be helpful. You will need to


refer to the dictionary of the business data defined in Area


1.


Some of your non-functional requirements will overlap between


other business events. This is not serious. You can, if you


like, write them once and tag them as belonging to other


business events, or duplicate them for each of the relevant


events. The second approach makes it easier for the


developers, as each event is a complete package. You might,


as a courtesy, flag the requirements as duplicated elsewhere.


As you can discover and write the requirements one business


event at a time, it makes sense to build the solution the


same way. Figure 34.1 illustrates this idea by showing how a


requirements specification can be built iteratively.


Construction of the solution starts as soon as the


## 第 983 页


specification of that event is complete enough. In the same


way, you can develop a business event part by part. For


example, you can build the main flow first and the exceptions


and alternatives later.


![embedded_p983_155.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p983_155.jpeg)


Figure 34.1 The business analysts discover the requirements


for a business event. These requirements are added to the


specification. Developers begin construction as soon as the


requirements for each business event are ready. Construction


continues while more discovery is taking place.


The requirements specification defines the solution you want


to develop. It should describe exactly what you and your


## 第 984 页


stakeholders intend.


Resources


Software Requirements, Third Edition, by Karl Wiegers and Joy


Beatty (Microsoft Press, 2013). This book presents a slightly


different way of writing a specification.


The template packaged in Appendix A, The Volere Requirements


Specification Template, demonstrates a complete requirements


document.


## 第 985 页


Chapter 35. Story Map


The story map is a better way of organizing your backlog of


stories. It provides a structure that is an understandable


overview of the solution to be implemented—understandable to


the business stakeholders as well as the development team.


The stories for the map are those that we described in


Chapter 28, Writing Good Stories. You would have written


these as you went about your requirements discovery. A


backlog, more correctly a product backlog, is a collection


of stories awaiting development. Here we are discussing how


your requirements repository could be a story map, and how


that can be an effective way of collecting and communicating


your stories.


We attribute the story map to Jeff Patton; he introduced them


in his book User Story Mapping. We are not using story maps


here exactly as Patton described them. We have adapted the


map to be more oriented toward requirements discovery, and


(for good reasons) some of the terms we use differ. However,


the spirit of story maps and how they are used remain the


same.


The first thing to notice is that a story map is built and


used iteratively. You write stories and add them to the story


## 第 986 页


map as you discover them, and the development team uses the


stories to progressively feed their development. So, you can


think of the story map as a focal point for the whole effort,


or as we are talking about here, a dynamic requirements


repository.


The illustrations in this chapter show the story map as if it


were being built along a wall using cards or Post-it notes.


Indeed, many teams prefer to build their maps this way, as it


gives them a large visual representation of the solution. Of


course, dispersed teams use collaborative online tools for


their maps.


Let’s look more closely at the story map and how you might


use it.


The Story Map


Let’s start with what it looks like. Figure 35.1 shows the


structure of the story map. Across the top you see Business


Event Stories, one for each business event. The diagram shows


three business events; you would probably have ten times that


many, but space prohibits showing that many here.


## 第 987 页


![embedded_p987_156.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p987_156.jpeg)


Figure 35.1 The structure of the story map. The annotations


are the terms we are using for the components of the map.


The top row of the story map gives you and your stakeholders


an overview, or the breadth of, the solution you intend to


build. It does this by showing all the Business event


stories. The problem space, and as a result the solution


## 第 988 页


space, responds to business events, and each one has a


business event story.


Each business event needs some automation built for it, and


this is specified by the lower-level stories under each


business event story.


The first lower level is the Functional stories. These break


down the business event story into recognizable chunks of the


functionality needed to complete the response to the business


event.


Below each functional story are the Detailed tasks. This is


quite a granular breakdown of the functionality, and there is


no need for any further breakdown.


Business Event Stories


The top row of the map shows the business event stories. It


is appropriate that these stories make up the top row of the


map because collectively they give a complete narrative on


what the solution does.


Consider this: Every business responds to business events.


That’s all it does; it responds to the prompts and requests


that come from external sources. For example, a customer


## 第 989 页


wants to join a gym, the customer wants to change her method


of payment, suspend her membership, re-sign her membership,


enter the gym through the turnstile, request a personal


instructor session, or any of the other things triggered by


outside entities. There are also, as we discussed earlier,


time-triggered business events: time to bill the customer for


another month, time to send out fitness newsletters, and so


on.


By building the top row from stories that describe (at a high


level) each business event, the map describes the whole of


the business—or more accurately, the whole of the solution


that automates the business.


As they are about business events, these stories can be


derived directly from the context model, as shown in Figure


35.2.


## 第 990 页


![embedded_p990_157.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p990_157.jpeg)


Figure 35.2 Much earlier we discussed how the business


events are derived from the flows on the context model.


Instead of building a list of the business events, you write


a business event story for each of them and add those to your


story map.


Each business event story describes one business event. Using


the format of the stories as previously discussed, it looks


like this:


As a [adjacent system]


I can [brief description of the functionality of the BUC]


So that [the business benefit, or outcome, of the story].


## 第 991 页


This is a brief, but for the moment, sufficient description


of each business event. By reading the top line of the story


map, a stakeholder becomes aware of the complete


functionality of the solution, and what it will do to achieve


the goals of the development effort.


Functional Stories


The business event story is a summary. The next level below


it is made up of the functional stories. These represent the


first breakdown of the business events. Each one is a


recognizable chunk of the functionality needed to complete


the work of the business event. You are breaking down to this


level to provide more convenient chunks to develop.


The task is to find the main chunks of functionality. There


should not be too many of them—two, three, four, or perhaps


five—as these will later be broken down, or sliced, into


still smaller chunks.


There is no need to write these stories in the usual format


of “As a-I can-So that,” because the business event story


has already set down the beneficiary and the benefit, and the


functional story inherits them. All that remains for the


functional story is to describe that particular chunk of


functionality.


## 第 992 页


Note that in Figure 35.3, the traveler wishes to choose her


own flight based upon preferences of time, airline, seating,


and airport. So, it is necessary to collect all available


information about possible flights and let the traveler


review and model the possibilities.


![embedded_p992_158.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p992_158.jpeg)


Figure 35.3 The business event story sets out the


beneficiary and benefit, and indicates the functionality


## 第 993 页


needed to deliver that benefit. The functional stories break


down the needed functionality into convenient chunks.


The functional stories also illustrate that once the optimal


flight has been found, a reservation will be made with the


airline and the traveler pays for her flight.


If you had been building prototypes earlier, you might have


built a process model for this business event. In this case,


the functional stories are likely to be activities from your


process model. In any event, it is straightforward enough to


find chunks of functionality that are small enough to be


useful but large enough that you do not have too many of them


under the business event story.


The thing to note about the functional stories is that they


provide an overview of the functionality that responds to the


business event. At this stage, informed business stakeholders


should be able to read and understand what the delivered


solution is intended to do for them.


Detailed Tasks


Below each functional story are the detailed tasks. These are


the basic units of functionality. Their purpose is to show


the low-level functionality (also the non-functionality) that


## 第 994 页


completes the work of the functional story. You might think


of them as the components of the functional story. You might


also think of them as atomic requirements as we describes


them back in Chapter 25, Functional Requirements, and Chapter


26, Non-functional Requirements.


The detailed tasks belonging to a functional story will


probably be executed by the solution in the same continuous


piece of time. If you were using the solution that carries


out these tasks, you would probably not stop before


completing them. If there is a need to stop, it would


indicate the need for a separate functional story.


Let’s look at the detailed tasks for the functional story


“Find flights to/from destination,” as illustrated in


Figure 35.4.


## 第 995 页


![embedded_p995_159.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p995_159.jpeg)


## 第 996 页


Figure 35.4 The detailed tasks are arranged in a column.


These are the base units of functionality needed by the


functional story.


You can see from these detailed tasks that as you descend,


they add elaboration and sophistication to the functional


story. The first two are the fundamental ones; the last three


are there to make a better experience.


You prioritize the detailed tasks by putting the most


important tasks highest in the column. You could, for


example, release a minimal product by delivering only the top


two detailed tasks. You would do this to demonstrate the


solution’s range of functionality, rather than its depth, as


a showcase of the complete solution yet to come.


No doubt, some of the detailed tasks will have been


discovered during the investigation and design activities


that preceded story mapping. Provided they fit the intentions


of the functional story, you can add them to the map at any


time.


Having worked on one functional story, you would then move on


to add the detailed tasks for the others. You might do this


right away, you might wait and do it in a just-in-time


## 第 997 页


manner, or you might, depending on your way of working, leave


the detailed tasks for the team to do at development time.


Growing the Map


Now that you have done this for one business event, you do it


for the rest of them, but probably not all at once. You are


constantly prioritizing the business events, which means that


you are always working on the most valuable or most urgent


ones. Some of the low-priority events could be delayed for


some time.


Additionally, because the detailed tasks that are lower in


the column are the more sophisticated and refined tasks, you


might choose to leave these until later and add them when you


reach a suitable point in your delivery.


Figure 35.5 illustrates a more complete map. Your map would


only look like this close to the completion of delivery.


Until then, it would be built on demand according to your


priorities.


## 第 998 页


![embedded_p998_160.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p998_160.jpeg)


Figure 35.5 A more complete story map. The cluster of


stories under each business event story provides the needed


functionality and is in increasing levels of sophistication


as you descend in the map. Your maps will be much wider (and


possibly deeper) than this illustration.


The discovery activities overlap and iterate—you are


constantly jumping between them. The construction of the map


can start as early as you like; perhaps as soon as you know


the customers and their values. As you go about your


investigation, you are learning more about the problem space


and can use the map as the repository of your increasing


knowledge.


## 第 999 页


The point is that writing the stories and building the map


are not separate activities; they are concurrent with other


activities that are themselves concurrent activities. This is


illustrated in Figure 35.6.


![embedded_p999_161.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p999_161.jpeg)


Figure 35.6 The story map is intended to be a living


artifact, constantly being added to, modified, and used,


hence the two-way arrows.


## 第 1000 页


Enhancing the Map


The map is not restricted to stories. There is other


information it can carry.


You know the customer segment for your story. It’s the same


as the adjacent system, and it is what you wrote in the “As


a...” line of the story. The customer segment is the entity


making the demand upon the solution, so it is most likely to


be the eventual end user, or beneficiary, of this part of


your solution. In Figure 35.7, the beneficiary is the


traveler. This information comes from your investigation of


the solution space and from your original determination of


the customer segments. You can annotate the story with


expectations about the users, or a profile, or a persona,


to help the designers and developers make this story more


usable and convenient.


## 第 1001 页


![embedded_p1001_162.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1001_162.jpeg)


Figure 35.7 This story map has been enhanced with a profile


of the intended customer segment and a wireframe with some


suggested interface ideas.


You might consider enhancing your story map with a wireframe


sketch of the interface. The intention is not so much to


design an interface, but to guide the designers. Keep in mind


that, to a user, the interface is the product; by sketching


## 第 1002 页


an interface, you are sketching the user’s perception of the


product. This paper-and-pencil approach is quick, and most


importantly, it gives no indication that the wireframe is


anything but a guide.


Stakeholders relate to sketches. Some stakeholders have


trouble saying what they envisage, but a sketch done while


they are in the room with you can, and probably will, elicit


their needs. Sketches invite stakeholders to discuss it and


make improvements to both the wireframe and the story map.


Adding Non-functional Requirements to the Map


Non-functional requirements can, and should be, added to your


map.


When you investigated the solution space for your proposed


business solution, you were partly appraising the solution


for its suitability within its environment, and partly


appraising the people in and around the problem space. It is


these people who you must satisfy, and it is the non-


functional requirements—its usability, security, look and


feel, performance, and so on—that determine whether they


accept or reject your solution.


## 第 1003 页


In short, provided the functionality is met, it


is the non-functional qualities that determine


the acceptance or rejection of your product.


Please don’t think that the non-functional requirements are


something that can be left until late and then bolted onto a


story map. You should have discovered most of the non-


functional requirements during your investigation while you


were discovering the required functionality.


Non-functional requirements are discussed fully


in Chapter 26.


When you are building your story map, we suggest that the


non-functional requirements are appended to the appropriate


stories and tasks on the map. This is shown in Figure 35.8.


## 第 1004 页


![embedded_p1004_163.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1004_163.jpeg)


## 第 1005 页


![embedded_p1004_163.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1004_163.jpeg)


Figure 35.8 This shows a single business event and one of


the subordinate columns. The non-functional requirements have


been attached to the stories and detailed tasks. The non-


functional requirements are not stories but needs or


constraints that apply to the stories. You might consider


using different colored cards for these.


Non-functional requirements are inherited. That is, if the


business event story has a compliance requirement, then every


story or task belonging to that business event inherits the


same compliance need. Similarly, a look and feel requirement


attached to a story high in the stack applies to every task


below it.


## 第 1006 页


Some non-functional requirements can be solution wide. For


example, security requirements usually apply to the solution


as a whole. Either repeat the requirement for this business


event or tag it to say that there is a solution-wide


requirement for this event or treat solution-wide


requirements as a separate category of requirements as long


as you ensure that they are part of the final product.


Similarly, there are non-functional requirements that apply


to more than one business event story. We suggest that you


add the requirement to each relevant event story and tag the


requirement to say that it is a duplicate.


Prioritizing the Map


Prioritizing means that you are always working on the most


valuable part of your problem space and solution space.


We suggest that the best way to start is by prioritizing the


business events. You might have done this as you were


discovering the events during the Blastoff. We discussed this


in Chapter 8, Prioritizing the Business Events. So, let’s


assume you know the business events (or most of them) when


you start your map. This gives you a map with the business


events lined up, say, left to right in priority order. You


## 第 1007 页


know that priorities often change as you progress, so it pays


to revisit your priorities and reorder the business event


stories if needed. As you work on requirements discovery for


the highest-priority events, you fill out the story map by


adding functional stories, detailed tasks, and non-functional


requirements.


You also prioritize the detailed tasks. MuSCoW


prioritization is useful here. The categories are


Must have—non-negotiable needs


Should have—not vital to have immediately but are required


prior to the solution being considered complete


Could have—nice to have but can be omitted


Won’t have—not a priority at this time


The “Could haves” and the “Won’t haves” can be pushed to


the bottom of the map, or, if time is extremely short,


discarded. The map shown in Figure 35.9 is fairly complete,


but you would not wait until you have a complete map to start


prioritizing.


## 第 1008 页


![embedded_p1008_164.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1008_164.jpeg)


Figure 35.9 A story map showing a possible prioritization


approach. The business events on the top row have been


prioritized, and then the product owner has decided to


develop and release the solution in the order shown by the


shaded shapes.


## 第 1009 页


As mentioned, the business event stories should be


prioritized early, and then the detailed tasks prioritized


almost as soon as you add them.


The releases shown as shaded areas are decided mainly by the


product owner, as this is now moving firmly into his


territory. Some of the prioritization might now be based on


the needs of the product. For example, you might need to


implement some parts of the story map to provide data for


other releases. But keep in mind that the requirements


discovery activity contributes significant knowledge of the


business value of the artifacts on the map.


Note how for some of the events, the functional stories have


been prioritized such that a release is not for a complete


business event story. You might do this, for example, to get


early feedback without building the whole event. You might


also do it to put out a minimum viable product (MVP). The


MVP is used mainly as a proof of concept and should not be


used as a substitute for doing the real work.


The usual prioritization criterion is value. Value means


value to the customer segment (which most times is the user


of your solution). Value might equate to frequency of use (if


people use something a lot, they probably value it), it can


## 第 1010 页


be convenience, or it can be the take-up of the product.


Value is value to your client or to the owning organization.


Your client’s priorities are first legal compliance (it’s


valuable to stay out of jail), contractual obligations


(don’t get sued), supplying the client’s products or


services, and then gaining revenue or saving costs.


Although value is the most common criterion for assigning


priority, you must consider others. You might think about


proof of concept, time needed to develop, risk (do the


riskiest business events first), politics, or almost anything


else. Whatever your priorities are, they change often; it


pays to revisit prioritization frequently.


When we prioritize, we automatically think of the glamorous,


high-priority items. But there’s value to you at the other


end of the scale. Assigning a low priority to something


optimizes your project time; the low-priority items do not


have to be built right away, and perhaps they will never be


built.


Using the Map Iteratively


The story map is your central repository for requirements


knowledge. The map is loaded by the discovery activity,


## 第 1011 页


refined by the product owner, and used by the delivery


activity.


Figure 35.10 demonstrates how you might use a story map to


synchronize the requirements discovery with the solution


delivery, but it requires some explanation. The numbers in


the text refer to the circled numbers in the diagram.


## 第 1012 页


![embedded_p1012_165.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1012_165.jpeg)


Figure 35.10 Using the story map for iterative development.


The text contains a commentary on how this works.


1. The business analysis activity has scoped the solution


space and has determined the business events. These are added


to the story map as business event stories. There will of


## 第 1013 页


course be many more than three events, but three will do for


the purposes of illustration.


2. The product owner is responsible for prioritization of the


stories, which is best done at the business event level.


Let’s say that the product owner has prioritized the map and


made the middle business event the highest priority.


3. The business analysts do a more detailed discovery for


this event. This results in adding the functional stories and


some of the detailed tasks. As soon as they are added, the


delivery activity starts to develop the solution, which, for


the moment, remains an incomplete or partial solution.


4. Meanwhile, the product owner selects the next-highest-


priority business event, the business analysts go to work


discovering the requirements for this event, and as they add


the details, the delivery team uses them to build more of the


partial solution.


This process continues to iterate until both the map and the


solution are complete, or any remainder is such a low


priority that the team agrees not to continue with it.


Naturally enough, the requirements discovery activity must be


quick enough to feed the map at a rate that does not delay


## 第 1014 页


the delivery. Also, naturally enough, if the stories added to


the map are the right stories, then delivery will save time


by having the correct understanding of what is needed.


The moral of the story here is that when you are using


stories, the story map is the most versatile and useful way


to keep them.


Review


We like the story map because it is a very visual


presentation of the requirements. It has an overview of the


solution along the top row of the map. These are the business


event stories and it is the business events with which the


stakeholders will be most familiar. By walking your business


stakeholders along the top row, you can explain the entirety


of the proposed solution.


The functional breakdown of the business, of its stories, is


shown by the lower-level functional stories, detailed tasks,


and/or atomic requirements that are attached below each


business event story. These can be broken down gradually to


the level of granularity that you feel is appropriate. There


are no hard-and-fast rules about functional breakdown; you do


## 第 1015 页


it to give your developers the information they need to


proceed with constructing the solution.


As we discussed above, you can enhance your story map with


non-functional requirements, wireframe sketches, user


profiles, and almost anything else you feel is appropriate to


convey the requirements to the developers.


Prioritization is made easier by having the visual display


that the story map provides. When you start to build a story


map, you are at the beginning of implementation, and so your


prioritization will be based on both business needs and the


needs of the emerging product. That is, the product owner


decides priorities for the stories, according to whatever


will make the most coherent and useful partial solution.


An operational advantage of the story map is that it is built


iteratively in sync with the requirements discovery. The


business analysts add their newly discovered requirements and


functional breakdowns to the map in time for the developers


to take these stories from the map and use them to produce


the growing incremental solution.


Resources


## 第 1016 页


User Story Mapping: Discover the Whole Story, Build the Right


Product by Jeff Patton (O’Reilly, 2014). This is the book


that introduced story maps and remains the definitive work on


the subject.


You can also find useful information about story maps at Jeff


Patton’s website (https://jpattonassociates.com/story-


mapping), which includes articles, videos, and workshop


resources, as well as the original blog post in which he


first described story maps.


Other books on agile development mention story maps, but


Patton’s book is the most direct source of information.


## 第 1017 页


Chapter 36. Quality Thinking


In this part of the book, we are discussing the


requirements repository. This is the place where all your


requirements—regardless of whether they are conventional


requirements, stories, models, or anything else—are stored.


This repository contains the information needed to develop


your solution.


We must start with the premise that if the requirements are


not fit for purpose, then neither will be the solution you


deliver. Here we look at how you can ensure that your


requirements are what they need to be. That the specification


(in whatever from) is a precise, complete, and unambiguous


statement of the real need. Anything less negates the reason


for discovering the requirements.


We by no means suggest that you only start to think about


quality when you have all the requirements in a repository.


Quality thinking starts early and ends late—it covers


everything you do. So, while we talk about testing the


requirements, please think of this as a task that forms a


natural part of your requirements discovery, and not


something done once at the end.


## 第 1018 页


So, let’s talk about testing the requirements with the above


caveat. This is testing before building. Testing before


building is not a radical idea; most industries test their


requirements before building anything. For example, any


bridge you drive over was tested before it was built. The


testing engineers went over the plans, perhaps ran some wind


tunnel tests, some stress tests, traffic simulation tests,


and a whole lot more. The point is that the road authority


has to be certain that when the bridge has been completed, it


will bear the weight of the traffic flowing over it, and it


will not collapse due to vibrations caused by vehicles or


excess movement caused by environmental factors. Put it this


way; would you happily drive over a bridge knowing that it


was not tested before construction, that it might not carry


the weight of your vehicle, and that there is a possibility


of it collapsing before you get to the other side?


Testing the requirements means you are ensuring that they are


the right requirements and that the resultant solution is the


right solution.


Following are tests you can apply to ensure the quality of


your requirements.


Within Scope?


## 第 1019 页


A fairly common problem with development efforts is out-of-


scope requirements. It is all too easy for your stakeholders


to become overenthusiastic and start generating requirements


that are irrelevant to the purpose of your solution.


Scope creep refers to the situation where more and more


requirements are added to the solution so that its scope


grows beyond what was originally intended. Uncontrolled scope


creep usually leads to late and over-budget delivery. And


worse, the solution might not provide what was intended in


the first place. Naturally, there are times when increasing


the scope of a solution brings benefits to the customer.


However, scope creep as we are discussing here is not a


welcome phenomenon.


Use the context diagram to determine whether a


requirement is within scope.


Back in Chapter 5, Goals-Scope-Stakeholders, we discussed how


to determine the scope of the problem space by building a


context diagram. Here we present another use for the context


diagram; this time we use it as a model of the IT solution


space, or product, to judge whether a requirement is in or


out of scope. Figure 36.1 shows the context model of a


product for predicting when ice will form on roads and


## 第 1020 页


scheduling trucks to treat the roads before they freeze. You


have already seen examples from this project.


## 第 1021 页


![embedded_p1021_166.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1021_166.jpeg)


## 第 1022 页


Figure 36.1 The context model shows the scope of the


solution and the flows of data that enter and leave it.


You have seen how the flows of data that enter and leave the


solution space determine its functionality. Naturally enough,


when you choose to automate this functionality, you must


write requirements for it.


Suppose you are inspecting the requirements for this product,


and you have been given this requirement:


The product shall pay truck drivers for working overtime.


Look at the context model in Figure 36.1. There is no data


flowing into the product that provides any information


about drivers. The product knows about trucks, but not who


is driving them. Thus, to accommodate this requirement, you


would need to add a number of flows—driver information, work


hours, rates of pay, deductions, paychecks, and many other


things. Clearly, all of these would bloat the scope of the


product.


Either this requirement is out of scope or the scope of the


product is incorrect. Given the nature of the other data


flows entering and leaving this product, you would almost


certainly decide that paying drivers is out of scope.


## 第 1023 页


Now suppose you had this potential requirement:


The product shall record the hours that the trucks are


active.


To determine if this requirement is in or out of scope, you


need the rationale for the requirement. If the rationale is


to provide some kind of report on truck activity, then we can


say it is out of scope—there is no flow on the context model


that carries such information. On the other hand, suppose the


requirement has this rationale:


Description: The product shall record the hours that the


trucks are active.


Rationale: Trucks may not be scheduled for more than 22 out


of 24 hours to allow for maintenance and cleaning.


The rationale says that the data is kept and used inside the


product, and thus there is no reason to add another data flow


to the context model. Given this rationale, you can conclude


that the requirement is within scope.


The rationale must also make sense within the context of the


solution, as creeping requirements often have a rationale


## 第 1024 页


that indicates the requirement is out of scope or is beyond


the original goal of the solution.


Relevancy


While the context model is a clear indicator of scope, you


also have to consider the relevancy of any requirement.


In Chapter 3, Understand the Real Problem, we discussed how


you identify the purpose of the project and record it as a


statement of quantified goals. These goals serve to determine


relevancy of requirements throughout the project.


Does this requirement contribute to the purpose


of the project?


To test a requirement for relevancy, compare its intention


with the project goals. The test is fairly simple: Does this


requirement contribute to the purpose of the project? Does


this requirement help make the solution, directly or


indirectly, meet the project’s purpose?


Let’s go back to the deicing product. Suppose you are


testing its requirements and you encounter this one:


## 第 1025 页


Description: The product shall maintain a lookup table of the


times of sunrise and sunset throughout the year.


At first this requirement appears to be relevant. The product


predicts the formation of ice on roads, and ice usually forms


at night. Thus, this requirement appears to contribute to the


project goal:


Project Goal: To accurately predict when ice will form on


road surfaces and to efficiently schedule the appropriate


deicing treatment.


However, if you dig a little deeper, you discover that the


temperature of the road surface is the determinant of whether


ice will form, and road temperature is monitored and


transmitted by weather stations. Whether it is night or day


does not override the actual temperature. As ice is perfectly


capable of forming during the daylight hours, there is no


apparent reason for the product to have any knowledge of day


or night.


Requirements sometimes do not initially appear to be


relevant. The requirement may call for the product to do


something that seems to have no immediate connection to the


purpose. However, without this requirement, the product could


## 第 1026 页


not do what it needs to do. As an example, consider this


requirement:


Description: The product shall record the salt capacity of


the trucks.


At first glance, this requirement appears to have nothing to


do with the goal of the product, which is to efficiently


schedule trucks to treat roads with deicing salt. But look at


the rationale for this requirement:


Rationale: Different trucks have different capacities. The


scheduling of trucks depends on their capacity to treat the


number of road sections predicted to have ice formation.


Now that the reason for the requirement is apparent, you can


say that this requirement is a valid one: It contributes to


the goals of the project.


When considering relevancy, pay particular attention to the


following sections of your requirements specification.


• Users (Section 2): Who are you building the product for,


and is it a product suitable for these users?


## 第 1027 页


• Requirements Constraints (Section 3): Is the product


relevant within the constraints? Have all the constraints


been observed by the requirements?


• Relevant Facts (Section 5): Have the requirements failed


to account for any external factors?


• Assumptions (Section 5): Are the requirements consistent


with any assumptions you are making about the project?


Completeness of a Requirement


The snow card (see Figure 36.2) gives you a comprehensive


way to formulate a requirement. There are references to the


snow card in other chapters in this book; here we look at how


you can use it as a requirements completeness checklist. By


the way, it does not matter whether you are using paper cards


or a digital version, we’ll continue to call it a snow card.


It’s the attributes of the card and their completeness that


we are interested in.


## 第 1028 页


![embedded_p1028_167.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1028_167.jpeg)


Figure 36.2 An example of a complete atomic requirement


using the Volere snow card. All of the attributes are


present, and the analyst has marked the requirement as having


no known conflicts with other requirements. This requirement


passes the completeness test.


## 第 1029 页


Are There Any Missing Attributes?


The snow card is packaged as part of the Volere


Requirements Specification Template in Appendix


A.


The first test for completeness uses the snow card as a


checklist to ensure that all relevant attributes are present.


The snow card is shown in Figure 36.3. The annotations


explain the attributes of the card, and in some cases, they


suggest a quality check. You should ensure that all the


relevant attributes are completed.


## 第 1030 页


![embedded_p1030_168.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1030_168.jpeg)


Figure 36.3 The annotations explain the meaning of the snow


card’s attributes.


Being relevant is important, as sometimes some of the


attributes are not necessary, and the card should never be


## 第 1031 页


used as a form-filling exercise. If something is not needed,


then leave it out. For example, sometimes the description


makes it obvious why the requirement is important, and there


is little point in writing the rationale. Sometimes the


description can be dropped because a clear and readable fit


criterion is provided. Sometimes there are no supporting


materials.


Naturally, if one of the attributes is missing, then its


omission should occur because it is not necessary rather than


because it is too difficult or has been overlooked. If the


attribute is missing because you are still investigating it


(and perhaps waiting for an answer from someone), then


include that information in the requirement to keep everyone


informed and to forestall unnecessary questions:


Supporting Materials: Waiting for county engineers to supply


details of road treatment volumes


The completeness test says that each requirement must have


all relevant attributes. If they are not part of the


requirement, their absence should be obvious or explained.


Testing the Fit Criteria


## 第 1032 页


See Chapter 27, Fit Criteria and Rationale, for a


full explanation of how to write fit criteria.


Requirements can be ambiguous. In fact, any English (or any


other language) statement is potentially ambiguous in some


way, as well as vulnerable to being misunderstood. To


overcome ambiguity, you add a fit criterion to the


requirement. This enables you to measure the requirement and


so make it both precise and testable.


A fit criterion for an atomic requirement and an acceptance


criterion for a story are, in essence, the same. We’ll just


talk about fit criteria here, but everything applies to


acceptance criteria.


The fit criterion allows the solution to be


objectively tested against its requirement.


The quality check here is to ensure that the fit criterion is


a reasonable measurement of the requirement—one that allows


the solution to be objectively tested against its


requirement.


The first question is “Does the requirement have a correctly


defined fit criterion?” If not, it is probably not


## 第 1033 页


understood well enough. The next question for the fit


criterion is “Can it be used as input when designing


acceptance tests?” You should also consider whether a cost-


effective (within the project’s constraints) way of testing


a solution against this requirement exists.


The fit criterion must also meet the purpose of the


development effort. We have discussed how the requirement


must conform to the project purpose, so it makes sense that


the measurement of the requirement must likewise conform to


this purpose.


While the fit criterion uses numbers to express the


requirement, the numbers themselves must not be subjective;


they must be based on evidence. For example:


Description: The product shall be easy to learn.


Fit Criterion: A user shall be able to learn to process an


insurance claim within 30 minutes of starting to use the


product for the first time.


First ask, “Is this a reasonable measurement of ‘easy to


learn’?” Then ask, “Where did the 30 minutes come from?”


Is it simply the whim of a stakeholder or the requirements


analyst? Or is it based on evidence that a learning curve


## 第 1034 页


longer than 30 minutes means the users become discouraged and


give up? It is of course useful if the requirement writer has


included a reference to the evidence in the Supporting


Materials component of the requirement.


Supporting Materials: Internal company document: Brenton


Workflow Study, 2022


A fit criterion can also be written using a predefined


standard. For example, when the requirement specifies that


the product is to conform to corporate branding standards,


the fit criterion should cite these standards and refer to


the communications department for verification. In this case,


your quality check asks if company branding is the correct


measurement for the requirement.


Security requirements would probably also use a standard as


the fit criterion—either an industry-specific security


standard (such as ISO or NIST) or the organization’s own


internal security standards.


Where a standard is used, you should check that the standard


is appropriate for the requirement and that it is accessible


enough for the developers to deliver a product that complies


with it.


## 第 1035 页


Whether the fit criterion uses numbers or cites a standard


depends on the type of requirement. Performance and usability


requirements normally use numbers, whereas look and feel,


security, and cultural requirements mostly use standards.


In any event, if a requirement lacks an appropriate fit


criterion, you need to revisit it and talk to the stakeholder


(shown on the snow card as the Originator).


Consistent Terminology


When a poet writes a poem, he intends that it should inspire


rich and diverse visions in anyone who reads it. The


requirements analyst has the opposite intention: She would


like each requirement to be understood in precisely the


same way by every person who reads it.


Requirements specifications are not poetry—they are not even


novels where the reader uses his imagination to “see” the


story being told. Requirements must have only one


interpretation; otherwise, there is a high risk of building a


product that satisfies the wrong interpretation of the


requirement.


Does the specification contain a definition of


the meaning of every essential subject-matter


## 第 1036 页


term within the specification?


To specify a requirement such that it has only one meaning,


you need, in addition to a fit criterion, to define the terms


and the meanings of those terms within the context of the


specification. Section 4 of the Volere Requirements


Specification Template is called Naming Conventions and


Terminology. This section acts as a glossary of the words


specific to this project and provides a starting point for


understanding the language.


Eventually, each term used in the atomic requirements is


defined in section 7, which includes the data dictionary. The


terms are given a nonambiguous definition that is agreed on


by the stakeholders, and these terms are then used to write


the requirements.


Is every reference to a defined term consistent


with its definition?


The next test of consistency is to check that each


requirement uses terms in a manner consistent with their


defined meanings. As an example of inconsistency, the


requirements for a television solution that we audited used


## 第 1037 页


the term “viewer” in many parts of the specification. Our


audit identified six different meanings for the term,


depending on where it was used. Had the requirements using


this term been allowed to continue in their ambiguous way,


the end product would have had some serious problems.


Without an authority—in this case, a data dictionary—that


defines the meaning of terms used in the requirements,


everyone on the project will make their own interpretation.


If the requirements mean different things to different


1


people, the project descends into Babel.


1


The Tower of Babel is a biblical story in which the


construction of a huge tower had to be abandoned because all


the builders spoke different languages. Is that anything like


your development project?


Viability


Viable requirements are those for which it is possible to


develop and implement a product in a cost-effective manner,


and when implemented, the product is operationally


successful. In addition, the product must be able to be


implemented within the constraints for both the design of the


product and the budget for the project.


## 第 1038 页


For example, this requirement is not viable, because it could


not be operationally successful:


Truck drivers shall receive weather forecasts and schedule


their own deicing.


The problem is that truck drivers do not have the information


necessary to predict the time that a road will freeze—they


cannot know which roads have been treated and which are in a


dangerous condition. Coordinating a number of trucks treating


multiple roads stretching over the whole of a county is a


matter for centralized control.


Viability is sometimes determined by the intended users.


For example, it is probably not viable to pay pensions to the


very elderly using cutting-edge, high-tech mechanisms. People


who matured at a time when technology was nowhere near as


sophisticated as it is now might struggle if your product


requires both manual dexterity and a high level of


technological skill to operate it.


You might also consider whether the organization is mature


enough to cope with a requirement. There is little point in


specifying a product for users who need to have engineering


## 第 1039 页


degrees to use it when you are employing minimum-wage manual


laborers.


Do you have the technological skills to build the


requirement? It is an easy matter to write a requirement, but


it is often a different, more difficult task to construct a


working solution for it. There is little point in specifying


a product that is beyond your development capabilities.


Do you have the time and the money to build the


requirement?


Do you have the time and the money to build the requirement?


Here you have to estimate the cost of meeting the requirement


and to assess it as a share of the total budget. (The budget


should be shown as a constraint in section 3 of the


requirements specification.) If the cost of constructing a


requirement exceeds its budget, then the customer value


attached to the requirement indicates how you should proceed:


High-value requirements are negotiated, while low-value


requirements are discarded.


Is the requirement acceptable to all


stakeholders?


## 第 1040 页


Is the requirement acceptable to the stakeholders? If a


requirement is very unpopular with a significant section of


the stakeholders, then history tells us that it is futile to


include it in the product. Stakeholders have been known to


sabotage the development or operation of products because


they disagree with part of it. Users have been known to


ignore and not use products because not all of the


functionality was as they thought it should be.


Do any other constraints make the requirement nonviable? Do


any of the partner applications or does the expected work


environment contradict the requirement? Do any solution


constraints—constraints on the way that a product is


designed—make the requirement nonviable because it is


difficult or impossible to achieve?


Requirement or Solution?


The description of a requirement, or the “I can” line of a


story, is unfortunately often stated in terms of a solution.


We all unconsciously talk about requirements in terms of how


we think they should be solved. This is usually based on our


personal experience. The result is a statement that focuses


on one possible solution—not necessarily the most


appropriate one—and usually hides the real requirement.


## 第 1041 页


The problem with requirements that state a solution is that


you cannot always know what problem it is solving. For


example:


Description: The product runs on the latest version of


Chrome, Safari, or Edge browser on Windows, Linux, and Mac.


By nominating specific browsers, the writer has written a


solution and not a requirement. What business problem is this


trying to solve? Is there a specific reason for using Chrome


and Firefox? Or is the writer trying to use the most popular


browsers? Then you must ask what happens when new browsers


are introduced.


Perhaps—we can’t be sure, but it’s likely—the requirement


should be rewritten thus:


Description: The product shall run on the browsers used by


90% of the Web population.


This solves the business problem—reaching the maximum


audience—and leaves the browser selection to whatever is


popular at the time:


Description: The product must allow users to reset their


password by clicking “I forgot my password” and receiving a


## 第 1042 页


link to their verified email address.


This kind of requirement might be well-meaning but is so


solution heavy that it cripples the product. It invokes


passwords and prescribes a process that leaves no room for


anything better. The fact that people forget their passwords


suggests that passwords might not be the best solution for


customers to access their accounts. Unless there is a


constraint that mandates this approach, you should go back


and reexamine the problem that this requirement is trying


(and possibly failing) to solve. You could almost certainly


find a better solution.


The point of this is to ensure that you are solving the right


business problem, and not invoking some solution that might


well be solving something else.


Value of the Requirement


The customer satisfaction/dissatisfaction ratings


indicate the value that the customer places on a


requirement.


The customer satisfaction and customer dissatisfaction


ratings attached to a requirement indicate the value the


## 第 1043 页


customer places on a requirement. You can see these on the


snow card illustrated in Figure 36.3. The satisfaction rating


measures (from 1 to 5) how happy the customer will be if you


successfully implement the requirement, and the


dissatisfaction rating measures (from 1 to 5) how unhappy the


customer will be if you do not successfully deliver this


requirement.


Requirements that are absolutely essential have a high


dissatisfaction rating: The client will be justifiably


annoyed if this requirement is not part of the final product.


There are also lots of requirements that are run-of-the-mill.


These are the things that are normal for the organization, so


nobody gets excited when they are part of the solution. These


often have a low satisfaction rating to reflect the humdrum


nature of the requirement but have a high dissatisfaction


rating to show that they must be part of the delivered


product.


Stories typically don’t carry satisfaction and


dissatisfaction ratings. It is okay to use MuSCoW ratings


instead.


It is important to give the developers and testers a clear


indication of the importance of each requirement. Through


## 第 1044 页


this, they know how much effort to expend developing and


testing each requirement. Naturally, the effort expended


should be proportional to the value of the requirement.


The value of individual requirements also plays a part in


your prioritization activities. In fact, we strongly suggest


that an indication of value is attached to all requirements


or stories, or at the very least to the business use case.


Gold Plating


The term “gold plating” comes from the desire of some


billionaires or movie stars to have gold-plated bathroom


taps. The water does not flow out of gold-plated taps any


better than it does from the chrome-plated ones that you or I


use, and the water is exactly the same water. The difference


is that the gold-plated tap costs more, and might, to some


eyes, look a little better. They might also be a way of


signaling the wealth of the owner. The term “gold plating”


has been taken up by the IT industry to mean unnecessary


features or requirements that contribute more to the cost


of a product than they do to its usefulness.


Let’s look at an example. Suppose there is a requirement


that when a user logs on to the product, it greets her by


## 第 1045 页


name. Is that necessary, or is it gold plating? How about if


the product accompanies the personalized greeting with a


couple of bars of Mozart (or Taylor Swift according to


preference)?


Does it matter if this requirement is not


included?


While both of the above requirements might be “nice to


have,” or “Could have” on the MuSCoW scale, neither of


them enhances the functionality or usability of the solution.


Would anyone really mind if these requirements were omitted?


A low dissatisfaction rating indicates a


requirement that is probably gold plating.


The next, and perhaps more reliable, test is to look at the


customer dissatisfaction rating attached to the requirement.


A low dissatisfaction rating indicates the requirement is


probably gold plating even if it has a high satisfaction


rating (who doesn’t like a little gold plating?). After all,


when the customer says that it does not matter if this


requirement is not included, he is signaling that the


## 第 1046 页


requirement does not make a vital contribution to the


product.


Also, consider your prioritization. If you have been


prioritizing your business events, your requirements, your


stories, and the detailed tasks, then the gold-plated ones


would have consistently been pushed to the bottom of the


pile. If it never reaches the top of the stack, then it is


sure to be unwanted, and pretty sure to be gold plating.


We hasten to add that there is a difference between


unnecessary gold plating and cool features that either sell


the product to the consumer or make it far more acceptable to


the user. Some of these features could be considered to be


gold plating, but before you delete them, ask whether they


add to the appeal of the product or merely add to the cost.


The point is that you should know whether a requirement is


gold plating. If so, and you decide to include it, then it


should be a conscious choice.


Scope Creep and Your Project


We mentioned scope creep earlier and would like to revisit


it, but this time look at the effect of creep on your


project. Obviously, if your project is to build a bookshelf


## 第 1047 页


and you find yourself repainting your study and adding a new


window, then your project is late, over budget, and


potentially building something that nobody needs.


The effect of scope creep is shown in Figure 36.4, where the


graph depicts the cost of delivering functionality. Look at


what happens when the size of the product creeps up by 35%.


According to many commentators, this is about the average for


most projects. After creep, the effort needed expands by even


more than 35%—and yet this is the part of the product that


somebody expected to get for free. When the requirements grow


beyond what was originally anticipated, the budget must grow


in tandem. But how often do you hear, “Just one more little


thing—it won’t affect the budget”?


## 第 1048 页


![embedded_p1048_169.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1048_169.jpeg)


Figure 36.4 The ratio of cost to size is not a straight


line: Cost increases exponentially as size increases because


more effort is needed for integration work. It is this


disproportionate increase in effort that causes many projects


to fall way behind schedule or fail completely.


## 第 1049 页


Scope creep has a bad reputation, mostly because of the


disruption to the schedules and the bloated costs of product


delivery associated with this phenomenon. It is prudent to


look at some of the causes of creep and to discuss how we can


approach this problem.


Most creep occurs because the requirements were


never gathered properly in the first place.


The first thing to address is the scope itself. Perhaps the


scope was set incorrectly in the first place. Perhaps it was


set before the team and the stakeholders had the opportunity


to come to grips with the scale of the problem. Perhaps the


scope was not adequately communicated, and some stakeholders


did not have the opportunity to include needed functionality.


Scopes are sometimes wildly optimistic. For political


reasons, an inadequate scope that minimizes the effort and


cost is presented by the project committee. Then, as reality


catches up later in the project, the scope must be expanded


to incorporate the requirements that should have been part of


the scope all along.


Once you have addressed the scope, look at the goals of the


project. If the goals are unclear or unrealistic, it is very


hard to see a realistic scope. If there is a degree of


## 第 1050 页


uncertainty as to what the project is intended to achieve,


then the scope will almost certainly be wrong. In Chapter 5,


you saw the goals-scope-stakeholders trinity. These three


elements are interdependent, and if the goals or the


stakeholders are incorrect, then the scope is probably also


incorrect.


Of course, the scope can change. Changes can happen that have


an effect on the scope of the problem. In these cases, the


budgets must change to accommodate the new, enlarged scope.


Refer to Figure 36.4 for an explanation of the cost of


changing scope.


A lot of scope creep occurs because the requirements were


never gathered properly in the first place. If the


requirements are incomplete, then as the product develops,


more and more omissions must, of necessity, be discovered.


When stakeholders become aware that product delivery is


imminent, they ask for more and more “new” functions. But


are they really new? We suggest they are requirements that


should have been part of the product all along. They were


just not, until now, part of the requirements specification.


Similarly, if the users and the clients are not given the


opportunity to participate fully in the requirements process,


## 第 1051 页


then the specification will undoubtedly be incomplete. Almost


certainly the requirements will creep as delivery approaches


and the users begin asking for the functionality they know


they need.


We have also observed creep that arose because the original


budget was set unrealistically low (often for political


reasons). When creep sets in, it was not so much a matter of


the requirements creeping but of the product bringing itself


up to its correct functionality.


Requirements also change. Quite often they change because the


business has changed or because new technological advances


have made change desirable. These kinds of changes are often


seen as requirements creep. In truth, if changes that cause


new requirements happen after the “official” end of the


requirements process, then this type of requirements creep


could not have been avoided.


Your business analysis role in this situation is to make


project management aware that requirements creep is happening


and, if possible, to help determine the cause of this creep.


Review


## 第 1052 页


Quality is an attitude; it’s down to you. Quality is not


some happy-clappy manager with motivational speeches,


slogans, and emails telling you how important quality is to


the organization. It’s you, and importantly, your team. When


you work with a quality team your work is both excellent and


enjoyable, and your output is always as good as it needs to


be.


There is a happy equilibrium between doing just enough to put


out the necessary requirements, and “analysis paralysis”,


where you spend so much time refining the requirements that


nothing gets built. Quality thinking in requirements means


that you work on your requirements until you are certain that


they are the right requirements, and they are written such


that the developers cannot misunderstand them. And you do


this in a timely manner.


How can you know you have produced the right requirements?


There are several ways to know.


The first one is yourself. Are you satisfied that you are


writing requirements that, when implemented, will solve your


customer’s problem? Are you confident that you’re doing


good work, and not just churning out lots of requirements


## 第 1053 页


hoping that their sheer volume prevents anyone from knowing


they won’t do the job?


Quality starts with you.


You should test your requirements. You can, and we urge you


to do this, ask a friend to read and test your requirements.


Peer reviews are common and effective. They require an ego-


free approach to your work—you must be willing to both


criticize your colleague’s work and accept criticism about


yours.


You also test your requirements by going over the sections of


this chapter—relevance, completeness, gold plating, scope


creep, and so on—and checking that each requirement passes


those criteria. Is it a testable requirement? Does it have


the appropriate fit criterion or acceptance criterion? And is


it valuable? Does it contribute to the goals of the project?


You can, and some organizations do, have “guardians” for


the requirements repository. These guardians, possibly the


lead business analyst and a tester, check all the


requirements as they are added to the repository. The


guardians have the authority to reject incorrect requirements


and ask that they be redone.


## 第 1054 页


Having guardians of the repository mimics what happens in


most industries—the requirements are thoroughly tested


before any product is built.


A little sidetrack:


The Project Management Institute, in its PMBOK guide, has the


following definitions.


Validation: The assurance that a product, service, or system


meets the needs of the customer and other identified


stakeholders. It often involves acceptance and suitability


with external customers.


Verification: The evaluation of whether or not a product,


service, or system complies with a regulation, requirement,


specification, or imposed condition. It is often an internal


process.


You have a part to play in both of these quality aspects.


A lot of validation is done during the requirements activity.


You are ensuring that the requirements you write are meeting


the real needs of the customer.


## 第 1055 页


Validation also involves having the customer or client


agreeing that the delivered solution provides value based on


the assumptions and hypothesis in the business case and on


the goals of the project.


You might also check whether the delivered solution produces


the benefits expected of it. However, this is entering the


territory of benefits management.


Your verification task is to work with the testers to


determine whether the product in production does what you


specified it to do. Quality requirements make this easier by


including a correctly measured fit criterion or acceptance


criteria. Without that, verification becomes close to


impossible.


Quality is an attitude. You decide, and it’s only you who


can decide whether you want to do quality work. Wanting to do


good work almost always results in doing good work. And we


should mention that doing good work with your requirements is


always more effective and faster than having sloppy


requirements and making lots of time-consuming corrections


later.


Resources


## 第 1056 页


Mastering Software Quality Assurance: Best Practices, Tools,


and Techniques for Software Developers by Murali Chemuturi


(J. Ross Publishing, 2010). This is a comprehensive guide to


software quality assurance, from requirements quality through


to organizational quality.


The Art of Software Testing by Glenford Myers, Corey Sandler,


and Tom Badgett (Wiley, 2011). While this book is primarily


focused on software testing, understanding testing processes


and strategies is crucial for ensuring the quality of


software requirements.


Jama Software’s website (https://bit.ly/460LkWy) has some


good stuff on requirements quality under the “Requirements


Management and Traceability” heading.


## 第 1057 页


Chapter 37. Completeness Check


Your requirements repository is where you record your


requirements. Regardless of the way you store them—


specification, story map, backlog, requirements tool, and so


on—at some stage you will find it necessary to check if you


have a complete set of requirements. To point out the


obvious, if your requirements are incomplete, then the


solution you deliver will also be incomplete.


In this chapter, we are looking at a process to ensure the


completeness of the requirements. It is not intended to say


that you always wait until you reach a stage where you


declare the requirements complete and want to check that they


are. While this process works admirably well for that


purpose, we urge you to progressively apply the ideas in this


chapter to your scenarios and process models as you are


working on them.


As you work with your stakeholders on a business process, you


ask where the data comes from, where it goes, how it is used,


and so on. You are also looking at the process to see what


activities are needed, what problems can occur, and what to


do if a problem or error is encountered. You should try to


apply these ideas early in your discovery process.


## 第 1058 页


Let’s get back to checking for completeness. There are


several things you can do to start checking the completeness


of your repository.


The first should always be to check that you have the non-


functional requirements. These are often overlooked or


forgotten in the rush to get the new solution out the door.


Look through your business use cases and check if they have a


reasonable set of non-functional requirements.


For example, if you are developing a financial product but


there are no security requirements, something is definitely


missing. Similarly, a web solution that lacks either


usability or look and feel requirements is certainly in


trouble.


Use the Volere Requirements Specification Template (found in


Appendix A) as a checklist and guide to making sure that you


have the relevant non-functional requirements.


The functional requirements should be sufficient to complete


the work of each business use case. To check this aspect,


play through each of the business use cases as if you were


the solution. If you do everything the requirements call for,


do you arrive at the outcome for the business use case? Are


## 第 1059 页


your users (ideally, they are with you when you perform this


role-play) satisfied that the solution will do what they need


for their work?


Look for exceptions. Back in Chapter 20, when we looked at


scenarios, we covered exceptions and alternatives. Have you


generated enough exceptions and alternatives to cover all


eventualities, and do your functional requirements reflect


this coverage? If you have scenarios of the business use


case, revisit them and, for each step, determine whether


exceptions can occur there or whether an exception might


prevent that step from being reached.


But of course, all that depends on you having discovered all


the business events and their associated business use case.


What follows is a short process to ensure that you have a


complete set of business events.


Have All Business Events Been Discovered?


You have, at our urging, been discovering and exploring the


requirements one business event at a time. The business


events are found first by examining the context model and for


each flow of data either in or out of the problem space,


## 第 1060 页


determining what happened to trigger that flow. These


happenings are the business events.


Let’s start with the scope. Figure 37.1 shows the context


diagram, and hence the scope, for the deicing solution.


(You’ve seen this before.) This predicts when roads are


likely to freeze and dispatches a truck to treat the road


with an antifreeze compound (it’s mainly salt) before the


ice forms on the road’s surface.


## 第 1061 页


![embedded_p1061_170.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1061_170.jpeg)


## 第 1062 页


Figure 37.1 The context diagram for a solution that predicts


when ice will form on roads and schedules a truck to treat


the road before it freezes


A quick run around the data flows on this diagram yields the


following list of business events and their associated data


flows:


1. Weather Station transmits reading—Weather Station Reading


2. Weather Bureau forecasts weather—District Weather


Forecast


3. Road Engineering advises changed roads—Changed Road


4. Road Engineering installs new Weather Station—New Weather


Station


5. Road Engineering changes Weather Station—Changed Weather


Station


6. Time to test Weather Stations—Failed Weather Station


Alert


7. Truck Depot changes a truck—Truck Change


8. Time to detect icy roads—Road Deicing Schedule


## 第 1063 页


9. Truck treats a road—Treated Road


10. Truck Depot reports problem with truck—Truck Breakdown;


Amended Deicing Schedule


11. Time to monitor road deicing—Untreated Road Reminder


12. Thermal Map Supplier updates map—Thermal Map


That gives us 12 business events that cater to all of the


flows on the context model.


Now go over the list and look for non-events. The term


“non-events” is a play on words—it indicates an event that


happens if another event does not happen.


For example, business event 9 is Truck treats a road. What


happens if the truck does not treat the road? The work has to


do something, and what it does is a non-event (it happened


because another event did not happen). The non-event in this


case is event 11, Time to monitor road deicing. The work


responds to this (non) event by checking whether all roads


have been reported as treated and, if they have not, issues


an Untreated Road Reminder.


## 第 1064 页


You would then go over the list asking of each event, what


happens if this event does not happen? Mostly the answer is


nothing; occasionally the answer is that there is a new


business event to follow up on the non-happening.


Define the Business Data


The next part of the completeness check involves the


business data. This is the data that is stored inside the


solution space. It is stored by the incoming data flows when


they bring data in from the outside world. Later, this data


is read by other business events to do their work. In your


solutions, this data will be held by a database or some kind


of cloud storage. For the moment, let’s just look at the


data and ignore its implementation.


You can, if you wish, build a stored data model. You might


have already done this, or you might choose to do it for this


completeness check. You can use a class diagram, an entity


relationship model, a relational model, or any other data-


modeling notation you prefer, as long as it shows the classes


of data and the associations or relationships between them.


You might prefer to call these things a class of data, an


entity, a data object, a thing, or some other name. It does


## 第 1065 页


not matter—for the purposes of readability, we’ll use the


term “class” and define it like this.


A class of data:


• Represents a type of real-world thing, either concrete or


abstract, that is used by the business; for example, a truck,


a weather station, a contract, an account.


• Can be given a name that is recognized by the business. It


is something that the stakeholders know about.


• Has unique identifiers on each instance of the data in the


same class. For example, credit cards have numbers; accounts


have an identifying number, as do invoices and insurance


policies.


• Is something that needs to be stored and later read by the


solution.


• Is a collection of data attributes. The class itself is not


data (it has no alphanumeric value), but data is stored about


the class.


• Is named with a noun.


## 第 1066 页


• Can be an event that is remembered; for example,


agreements, contracts, purchases.


• Can be an adjacent system from the context diagram. The


solution most likely keeps data about the customers, banks,


suppliers, and so on that are found on many context diagrams.


Some business analysts prefer not to build a model of the


stored data, and if you are one of those, consider doing


this: Simply make a list of all the classes of stored data.


Do this by looking for all the named “things” that are


uniquely identified and qualify as a class according to the


above list of qualities.
