You can start with the flows of data entering and leaving the


road deicing context diagram shown in Figure 37.1, or the


list of business events and their data flows listed above.


The first incoming flow is Weather Station Reading. This


gives you two classes of data: Weather Station (there must be


more than one of these and so they are identified), and


Temperature Reading (again, there are many of them and they


are identified by the time and date of the reading).


The next flow on the list is District Weather Forecast. This


gives you two entities: District (there are many of them, so


## 第 1067 页


they are identified, and the solution needs to retrieve them,


so they will have a unique identifier); and Forecast (again,


something remembered by the solution).


The next flow of data is Changed Road, so the solution must


be storing data about roads. Roads are a nameable thing;


there are many of them and so they have identifiers. The


prediction processing needs to know about the roads, so you


add Road to the list of data classes.


Try looking at each of the remaining flows on either the


context model or the list of events and identify all the


things that you consider to be a class of data.


The list we have (in alphabetical order for the sake of


convenience) is as follows:


Depot


District


Forecast


Road


Road Section (we snuck that one in, as we guessed that roads


are too long and would need to be divided into sections to


## 第 1068 页


make forecasting more precise)


Temperature Reading


Thermal map


Truck


Weather Station


If you prefer to build a stored data model, then yours would


look something like the one in Figure 37.2. This is our view


of the stored data used by the deicing and predicting


solution.

![embedded_p1069_171.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1069_171.jpeg)


## 第 1070 页


Figure 37.2 This model shows the classes of data used to


predict and schedule the deicing of roads. The lines


connecting the classes are associations, or relationships,


needed by the business.


CRUD Check


Now we arrive at the best part. The CRUD (Create, Read,


Update, Delete) check is based on the fact that if there is


a class of data, it must be Created. It cannot suddenly


materialize out of thin air. There must be something to bring


it into the solution space. The something that does this is a


business event.


Glance back to the context model shown in Figure 37.1. The


incoming data flows are there because business events happen,


and when they do, they bring data into the solution via the


data flows.


For example, business event 1 on the list shown above is


Weather Station transmits a reading. The data flow—


conveniently called Weather Station Reading—brings data into


the solution where it is stored as the class Temperature


Reading. If you look back at the stored data model in Figure


37.2, you can see this class connected to the Weather Station


## 第 1071 页


class. This connection records which Weather Station


transmitted the reading.


Similarly, if you look over the list of business events, you


can deduce the classes of data that are created (this is the


C in the CRUD acronym) by each business event.


If the solution needs to create some data, then it must also


make use of that data. This is where the solution Reads the


data. Reading the data happens when a business event needs to


access some previously created data in order to do its work.


For example, the business event Time to detect icy roads


would need to read the classes: Roads, Temperature Reading,


Road Section, Thermal Map, Truck, and so on.


Some of the data is Updated. For example, there is a


business event Truck depot changes a truck. This would happen


if, say, the depot modified the truck to change its salt


capacity. This event results in some of the data attributes


of the Truck class being changed.


Finally, some data might be Deleted. This is not deleting


for the purpose of cleaning up the database, but because


there is some business reason for getting rid of some data.


For example, under most countries’ privacy laws, if a


## 第 1072 页


company holds personal data about you and you no longer wish


that to be the case, then if you request it, the company must


delete your data.


If you go through the list of data classes and


the business events that do something to them—


Create, Read, Update, Delete—then you can build


a CRUD table.


If you go through the list of data classes and the business


events that do something to them—Create, Read, Update,


Delete—then you can build a CRUD table. A suggested one is


shown in Figure 37.3.


## 第 1073 页


![embedded_p1073_172.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1073_172.jpeg)


## 第 1074 页


Figure 37.3 Each cell shows the identifier of the business


event that creates, reads, updates, or deletes the class.


Gaps in the table could mean that there are missing events.


Go over the CRUD table. This is a completeness check and you


are looking for missing business events. This is the reason


you built the CRUD table.


If a class is read without first being created, it means


you’ve somehow missed the creation event. If an entity is


created without being read, then either a reading event is


missing or some data has been created that has no purpose.


Some data classes—but not all—are updated. Sometimes there


is no reason why stored data should ever be changed, and


sometimes there is every reason. For example, if a customer


changes address (a common enough occurrence), then there must


be a business event that alters the address data held for the


customer. Look at each of the data entities and imagine their


attributes. Is there a reason to change any of them? If so,


is there a corresponding updating business event in the


table?


Similarly, with the Delete column. Not all data is deleted,


but you should check the entities and ask if there is a


## 第 1075 页


business reason to remove them from the solution’s stored


data. If so, find the appropriate business event.


Look for empty cells in the CRUD table—these might reveal


missing business events. For example, the classes Depot and


District do not have any creating business events, yet they


are read. Thus, the context diagram is incomplete: It lacks


the business events with their incoming data flows needed to


create these classes of stored data.


Many of the cells in the Update column are blank. Some of


these classes would not be updated; however, you should check


their attributes for data that is likely to change—names,


addresses, and so on—and add any missing business events.


When you find missing business events, you need to revisit


your stakeholders to discover what is needed. This should


lead to you updating the context diagram, the event list, and


the CRUD table. You might have to iterate once or twice


before you reach a stable situation.


Then, at the end of the CRUD table exercise, you can be


humanly certain that you have discovered all the business


events, and this will lead you to finding all the


requirements.


## 第 1076 页


Review


While we are urging you to build your requirements


specification iteratively, it is imperative that you can


reach a point where you can safely say that the specification


is complete. Moreover, you might find that there are times


when you want to be able to check that the part of the


specification you have built so far is complete. In other


words, you want to check the completeness of an incomplete


spec.


The CRUD check is a powerful weapon for checking


completeness. It’s powerful because it is founded on a


simple truth that data in the problem space (and in the


solution space) must be created, and if it is created, then


it must be used. The creation and the using are done by


business events.


The CRUD check neatly ties things together. The data flows on


the context model indicate the business events. The business


events bring data into or take data out of the work scope.


This shows up on the CRUD check as Creating and Reading the


data.


## 第 1077 页


We touched very lightly on data modeling, and a light touch


it must be. Data modeling is a subject in itself, and plenty


of books and training material have been written about it. We


felt it was beyond the scope of this book to have a full


treatise on data modeling. However, it is an area of business


analysis that we urge you to look into much more. There are


references in the Resources section that should be helpful.


Resources


Data Modeling Made Simple: A Practical Guide for Business and


IT Professionals, 2nd Edition, by Steve Hoberman (Technics


Publications, 2009). This is an introduction to data


modeling. It covers various techniques and provides real-


world examples to help you understand how to model data


effectively.


Data Modeling Essentials, 3rd Edition, by Graeme Simsion and


Graham Witt (Morgan Kaufmann, 2004). This uses entity


relationship diagrams to explain the concepts. ER diagrams


are slightly different from the class diagrams we have been


showing you, and they are good at explaining ideas that


business analysts can use.


## 第 1078 页


There are references to the CRUD check buried deep inside


books on database design. However, we do not suggest you read


any of them. They are concerned with the physical


implementation of the data, and not its business meaning.


## 第 1079 页


Chapter 38. Managing Requirements


We have been talking about discovering requirements, and


among other things, ensuring their correctness and


completeness. We also talked about storing them in a


repository. So now we turn to the topic of managing those


requirements. It is one thing to discover the correct


requirements; the next thing is to ensure that the


requirements are being properly used.


In this chapter, we discuss requirements management and how


you can trace your requirements to ensure that all of them


are implemented, and conversely, that the implementation


consists only of requirements.


We also talk about tracking the status of the requirements:


What state of development are they in? Are they only


suggestions for requirements, or have they been implemented


and tested? Or somewhere in between? Tracking is not only


about understanding the status of the requirements but doing


it in such a way that the entire team can see the


requirements and thus the status of the project. Visibility


is one of the objectives of requirements management.


## 第 1080 页


We also visit the thorny issue of changing requirements.


Change is good and bad. It is disruptive and it is helpful.


It costs effort and saves effort. And it is like fire—it can


consume you if you don’t control it. Later in the chapter


we’ll look at how you can manage change.


Let’s start with traceability.


Traceability


Requirements traceability is about establishing and


maintaining a link or trace between various project artifacts


and the requirements. The purpose of doing this is to ensure


that each requirement is consistently and accurately


represented throughout the project’s life cycle.


This at first seems bureaucratic, but you should consider


whether the benefits of tracing your requirements outweigh


the cost.


Traceability provides transparency and helps stakeholders


understand how requirements are interconnected with other


project artifacts, such as prototypes, design documents, and


the final code. Traceability helps with managing changes


(discussed below), and by showing the impact of modifications


on related requirements, design, and testing. By being able


## 第 1081 页


to see the linked artifacts, your change supremo is in a


better position to judge the impact of any proposed change.


Traceability of your requirements helps you to ensure that


each requirement is tested and validated appropriately. In


cases of military or medical projects, it is a legal


requirement that you can demonstrate that each requirement is


implemented and tested. Even for commercial or scientific


projects, validation of the requirements is important. After


all, what would be the point of discovering requirements and


then not implementing them? Apart from the low-priority


requirements you choose not to develop, all requirements


should end up as part of the delivered solution. Tracing the


requirements helps considerably in locating gaps in the


requirements or in the product.


We are using the word “requirement” when discussing


traceability. However, you know that individual atomic


requirements are assembled into business use cases or


functional stories, so you can trace them by one of these


groupings.


Tracing requirements can also create a record of how


requirements evolve over time.


Traceability Matrix


## 第 1082 页


A traceability matrix is used to document and visualize


traceability relationships. It is typically a table where


each atomic requirement (or business event, business use


case, functional story, or other grouping) is linked to


design components, test cases, and other relevant artifacts.


In its simplest form, it would show an identified


requirement, the associated test case(s), and the status of


the testing, and thus demonstrate the successful


implementation of the requirement.


The metric can, and usually should, be more elaborate. You


can include an identifier of the module(s) of code that


implement the requirement, any design documents, and any


prototypes that display information still current to the


implementation.


Figure 38.1 shows an example of a requirements traceability


matrix.


## 第 1083 页


![embedded_p1083_173.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1083_173.jpeg)


Figure 38.1 A simple requirements traceability matrix table


The product owner and project manager, and indeed the whole


team, use the traceability matrix to monitor the status of


the requirements, and how much of the product has been and


still remains to be built.


Now let’s look at another way to trace. This one is more


comprehensive.


Requirements Knowledge Model


## 第 1084 页


You met the Requirements Knowledge Model before—it is a


representation of the information you assemble when you


discover your requirements. This time we are using it to


demonstrate how it makes it possible for you to trace your


requirements. Without having such an underlying structure,


requirements tracing would be at best ad hoc, and possibly


nonexistent. Consider the model shown in Figure 38.2.


## 第 1085 页


![embedded_p1085_174.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1085_174.jpeg)


## 第 1086 页


Figure 38.2 The Requirements Knowledge Model. The classes of


knowledge you need to trace, and the links between them, are


highlighted.


This presentation of the Requirements Knowledge Model


highlights the traced classes along with the links between


them. Let’s start at the top left with the Work Scope. We


previously discussed how you use the scope to determine the


business events. This determination establishes that there is


a link between work scope and Business Events. This link is


shown by the line between the two classes, and the notation


along the line says that there are many business events


attached to one work scope.


The links between the elements are significant. In this case,


you have a work scope divided into a number of business


events. For traceability purposes, you need to keep a list of


these business events, and obviously, to which work scope


they belonged. You would most likely use a requirements


traceability matrix to keep track of this information,


The Business Use Case, or the Business Event Story (whichever


you are using), is linked to the business event and


represents the response that the solution makes to the


business event. The model tells us that there is only one of


## 第 1087 页


these for any business event. By giving a unique identifier


to each business event, you also identify the BUC or business


event story.


You would normally automate part or all of the BUC, which


might be done with one or more chunks. These chunks are the


Product Use Cases (PUC) or Functional Stories attached to the


BUC. The association between these classes establishes the


link you need for tracing.


The next breakdown is Atomic Requirement or Detailed Task.


The Volere snow card has a field for a requirement ID. It is


similarly possible to identify a detailed task. Tracing then


becomes a matter of maintaining the list of atomic


requirements/detailed tasks that belong to the PUC or the


Functional Story.


Thus, you can link the chain of classes from the original


work scope down to the atomic requirements or detailed tasks.


Naturally, you also link in the reverse direction.


Implementation Unit


The model shown in Figure 38.2 shows a link to a class called


Implementation Unit. The exact nature of this is not


important to our discussion here, but as its name suggests,


## 第 1088 页


it is a piece of the final implemented code. It might be an


entire application; it might be an identifiable unit of code


within the codebase. Its exact nature is not as important as


the association between the atomic requirement and the


implementation unit. This association is established


whenever the developers implement one or more atomic


requirements. In other words, it is the existence of the


association between the implementation unit and the atomic


requirement that tells you that the atomic requirement (or


the detailed task) has been implemented.


This is the final leg of the trace. You can now verify that


requirements have been implemented, and conversely, that


implementation units are the product of requirements.


Tracing


The Requirements Knowledge Model represents the requirements


for managing requirements. If you look back at the model in


Figure 38.2, you can see other potential traces. For example,


there is a link between Business Use Case and Stakeholder.


You might choose to trace which stakeholders are responsible


for which BUCs. There are also other potential links shown in


the model. You and your team choose which of these to


## 第 1089 页


maintain, depending on the size of the project in the budget


automation you have for this kind of management.


The model shown here does not include other classes of


knowledge that you might wish to incorporate in your own


model. For example, you can include a Test Case class that is


linked to the implementation unit and to the atomic


requirement. These links demonstrate that your requirement


has been both implemented and tested. You might also include


design documents, prototypes, or other artifacts that you


choose to trace. Your requirements knowledge model reflects


your team’s view of the requirements discovery activity.


You might be doing this using an automated tool, which you


would do for large and complex projects. If this is the case,


the tool keeps track of the traced classes and the links we


have been discussing, and automatically updates them as


project artifacts evolve. Lacking such a tool, you can use a


manual traceability matrix to satisfy the traces. If your


requirements are being handled using a physical medium such


as cards or Post-it notes attached to a wall—we spoke about


this in Chapter 35, Story Map—then you have a visual link


between the knowledge classes.


## 第 1090 页


Industries such as healthcare, aerospace, military, and


finance; regulatory authorities; and similar groups require


strict traceability to ensure that software meets safety and


quality standards.


Traceability is not a one-time activity. It should be


maintained throughout the software’s life cycle as


requirements evolve and changes are made to project


artifacts. Establishing and maintaining traceability is a key


responsibility of the requirements management team in any


project.


Tracking Status of Requirements


The status of requirements refers to the current state or


condition of individual requirements (or business events,


product use cases, or functional stories) throughout the


software development project’s life. Whereas traceability is


concerned with ensuring that requirements are tested and


implemented, status is concerned with the stage of


completeness that a requirement has reached. This is the


concern of a project manager, a product owner, and team


members who need to be aware of the state of their project.


Kanban


## 第 1091 页


You might include status in your requirements traceability


matrix, or you might find it more convenient to have a


separate status matrix. The best way, in our opinion, of


showing status is a Kanban board. Kanban originated in Japan


and was initially developed by Toyota for its manufacturing


processes. It has since been adapted and widely used in


various industries, and particularly in agile software


development.


The advantage of the Kanban board is that it is a visual


representation of the requirements and their stages of


development on their voyage through to implementation and


deployment. Each requirement is typically depicted as a card,


with different columns on the board representing various


stages of the workflow. Figure 38.3 shows an example of a


Kanban board.


## 第 1092 页


![embedded_p1092_175.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1092_175.jpeg)


Figure 38.3 A sample Kanban board showing the status of the


requirements (shown as documents) for the project. You can


choose to use PUCs or stories instead of requirements on your


Kanban board.


The Kanban board shows work in progress, and thus the status


of the requirements. Each small document icon on the board


represents either an atomic requirement, a story, a PUC or a


BUC, or possibly a business event. It is a matter for you to


## 第 1093 页


choose at what level you wish to track the status. For the


moment, let’s call them “requirements.”


Each column represents one stage that the requirement passes


through. There are no hard rules for categorizing the status


of requirements, but you might find the following useful.


These are the column headings shown in Figure 38.3.


• Proposed: Requirements that have been identified but have


not undergone formal review or analysis


• Analyzing: Requirements that are being discovered (you


might break this down further to reflect different stages of


requirements analysis)


• Design: Requirements for which there needs to be some


solution design


• Specified or Backlog: Requirements or stories that have


been written, have been quality-checked, and are now part of


the specification or product backlog


• Implementing: Requirements that are being developed


• Validating: Requirements that are in the validation and


verification process


## 第 1094 页


• Deployed: Requirements that have undergone testing or


validation to ensure that they meet their specified criteria


and are now deployed in production


At the risk of overloading your Kanban board, you might


include a column for requirements that are not currently


within the project’s scope but may be considered for future


releases. You might also keep track of rejected requirements


—those that you have considered to be unnecessary, out of


scope, or infeasible.


The Kanban board shows work in progress. It would be


necessary to add some indicator to the requirement to say


that it has completed that stage. You would also include some


information on why a requirement was changed, dropped, or


included. This might be needed later for verification


purposes.


One of the principles of Kanban is that work is “pulled”


from one stage to the next. Pull takes place when the


condition of the work item allows, and there is capacity in


the next stage that permits new work to be accepted. For


example, the Design column of the board is fairly full. This


indicates that the designers are overloaded and have become a


bottleneck—they cannot, at the moment, pull more


## 第 1095 页


requirements into their activity. At the other end of the


board, the Validating column has plenty of capacity, a signal


perhaps to up the tempo of Implementing.


Kanban allows you, or your management, to limit the number of


work items that can be in progress at any given time. This


limit is set for each column on the Kanban board according to


the capacity of the workers available for that task. You


limit work in progress to maintain a steady workflow, one of


the key factors in eliminating waste. When you can see the


requirements and their status you can reduce wait times,


minimize delays, and ensure that your requirements discovery


moves smoothly and efficiently through the workflow.


A Kanban board does not have to be a physical board. There


are many automated tools for maintaining a Kanban board


online and for using it for remote, collaborative working.


The key point is that it provides a visual representation of


the requirements discovery and delivery work in progress.


This visualization makes it easy for team members to


understand the current status of the requirements, the work


that has been done, and the work remaining to be done.


Requirement status should be monitored continually throughout


the project’s life cycle, from initial requirements


## 第 1096 页


discovery to post-release maintenance.


In summary, tracking the status of requirements is an


integral part of requirements management in software


development. It ensures that requirements are properly


reviewed, implemented, tested, and verified, contributing to


project success and effective communication among project


stakeholders.


Change Management


Change happens. We know that. But change is never free; it


always has some impact on the rhythm of the project or the


needed effort.


Many projects complain of ever-changing requirements, of


stakeholders changing their minds, or asking for changes


after something has been delivered, and so on. The litany of


complaints is almost endless.


But it does not have to be this way.


Changes happen for a number of reasons, and some of them we


cannot help you with. Corporate politics is one. Sometimes


you have stakeholders who align themselves with certain


requirements, and having their requirements supplant others,


## 第 1097 页


even late in the development, is a matter of demonstrating


corporate power. Sometimes the stakeholders change, and you


are suddenly dealing with new people who have very different


ideas from the old ones.


Some changes happen because of changes to external forces.


Sometimes mid-project the law changes, or regulations change,


or corporate business rules change. Sometimes technology


changes and it becomes obvious that the new technology offers


such benefits that the best thing to do is to make changes to


accommodate this advance.


You can’t do much to stop these types of changes happening.


But you can do things to accommodate them more easily.


Then there are other changes that should not happen.


For example, if the scope of the problem space is not made


reasonably accurate at the outset of the project, then


changes are almost certain to happen when stakeholders


realize during the project that needed functionality has been


excluded. It’s also possible that unneeded functionality has


been included. Both of these require changes that could have


been avoided.


## 第 1098 页


As you are going about your requirements discovery, you are


learning about the organization, the work, and the people who


do the work. The more you learn, the better position you are


in to make assessments of the areas that are likely to be


exposed to change. In the template, section 5 deals with


assumptions. This is where you record your assumptions about


anticipated changes. For example, you might assume that the


technology could change, or the marketplace could change, or


fashion and customers’ preferences could change. Assuming


the change might happen does not mean that it will happen,


but you would give this area a lower priority and develop it


later to avoid having to redo work if a change happens.


How many changes are you dealing with? If there are a lot of


changes, then it could be a sign of poor business analysis.


If stakeholders are constantly asking for new things, then it


suggests a poor definition of the scope or poor communication


during the discovery activities. In this event, it is


worthwhile for the team to meet and examine the nature of


changes with a view to changing not the requirements, but the


way the requirements are gathered.


Prototyping helps to avoid change. Having a mockup helps


those stakeholders who are not good at visualization.


However, some people fail to grasp what a sketched prototype


## 第 1099 页


is showing them, and for these people, you need the actual


product.


Incremental or partial development helps here. A proof-of-


concept version, or an MVP, or some other sample version can


help these people see what the final product will be like and


what it does. You are asking them if this is what they


imagine they need.


At this stage, if the sample product is a long way from


expectations, then we suggest you shut down the project and


determine what went wrong. The product will never be any good


if it is hacked into place by delivering something and then


changing it to meet the flood of user requests. It will only


be good if you build it on a solid foundation of a correct


and agreed scope and goals of the project, along with


requirements that are discovered by understanding the real


business problem.


The moral of the story is that good business analysis goes a


long way to preempting changes to the requirements, and it


requires much less effort than building something and later


changing it.


## 第 1100 页


So, let’s turn away from the causes of change and look at


how you might handle the change.


Managing Change


The first rule of managing change is that all changes are


communicated to a central person—let’s call her the change


supremo. This is probably the project manager, but it


depends on your organization. Your project is out of control


if stakeholders can bypass the supremo and bring their


requests to their favorite business analyst or developer.


The change supremo filters all changes. A quick triage


reveals whether the change is relatively nondisruptive or has


serious ramifications.


Is the change valid? Does it contribute to the goals of the


project and the organization, and also to the intention of


the product?


• How much effort is required?


• Does it negate any effort already expended?


• If accepted, would it change the scope of the problem space


and/or the scope of the solution?


## 第 1101 页


• Does the change affect only the product, or does it have


ramifications in the business?


• Does the change bring value to the project and/or the


organization?


• Is it trivial, or gold plating, and can be safely


discarded?


• If the change is ignored, what impact would that have?


If the change is accepted by the supremo, then low-impact


change requests can be handed off to a business analyst for


investigation and resultant requirements.


High-impact changes are those that have a serious consequence


on the project’s budget or that significantly alter the


outcome of the project. For these change requests, the


supremo must confer with a higher authority.


The change management process should be as nonbureaucratic as


possible without losing control of changes. A competent


change supremo who is close to, or part of, the project would


outperform a change committee any day.


## 第 1102 页


However it is done, the cost of incorporating all changes


must be recorded. It is vital for project leadership to


understand the cost and impact of change, and to warn


customers of potential delays to the delivery of the product.


It is also crucial that your project, and future projects,


make allowances for change when assessing their viability.


Without allowing for the additional cost of changes, it is


unlikely that project budgets can be taken seriously.


Finally, the most valuable part of change management is


learning where changes come from, and in what stage of the


development cycle. Changes made to requirements while they


are still being discovered are relatively cheap (or mostly


free). Changes made to products already in use are


significantly expensive.


By learning where and why changes originate, you are in a


better position to adjust your discovery and delivery process


to minimize change. You can never eliminate change, but you


can tame it.


Review


This book is about discovering requirements. Discovering the


right requirements is crucial if you are to deliver the right


## 第 1103 页


solution. However, there is a little more to it than just


discovery. You have to ensure that the requirements are


managed so that they provide the maximum usefulness to your


stakeholders and developers.


Managing requirements involves identifying the requirements


for traceability purposes, documenting them in a way that


makes their meaning clear, prioritizing them so that the most


valuable requirements are developed early, and controlling


them so that they provide the information needed for the


successful development of the delivered solution.


Managing can include ensuring that the requirements are


captured in a form that makes them understandable and useful.


Previously we looked at how you write stories and atomic


requirements. Managing requirements is concerned with


collecting all the requirements in a usable form.


Management also includes assessing the assembled requirements


to ensure that they are complete, consistent, and feasible.


Prioritization is constructive. It ensures that the


requirements are ranked according to their business value and


impact on the project or solution’s success.


## 第 1104 页


Traceability establishes and maintains links between


requirements and other project artifacts, which ensures that


all requirements are correctly treated and eventually


implemented.


Change happens throughout the project, and the requirements


management task is to evaluate the value and impact of each


change. Naturally, it is crucial to communicate the accepted


changes to the stakeholders and project team.


In summary, managing requirements is about monitoring and


controlling the requirements throughout the project and


ensuring that they are correctly developed. After all, you


put a lot of effort into discovering them. You should ensure


that they are used properly.


Resources


Requirements Engineering: Fundamentals, Principles, and


Techniques by Klaus Pohl (Springer, 2010). Pohl writes about


approved techniques for discovering requirements and goes on


to discuss validating and managing requirements for software-


intensive systems. There is additional material on the


book’s website, http://www.requirements-book.com.


## 第 1105 页


More information on the traceability matrix is available at


bit.ly/49tx7nJ.


Essential Kanban Condensed by David Anderson and Andy


Carmichael (Lean-Kanban University, 2016). This is a


distilled introduction, but it gives you all the principal


concepts and guidelines to Kanban.


The Effective Change Manager’s Handbook: Essential Guidance


to the Change Management Body of Knowledge by Richard Smith,


David King, Ranjit Sidhu, and Dan Skelsey (Eds.) (Kogan Page,


2014). This is a comprehensive treatise on the subject and


comprises chapters from established leaders in the topic.


## 第 1106 页


Part VIII: The Conduct of


Business Analysis


We’re getting close to the end of this book, and so far, it


has been talking about techniques for business analysis:


context diagrams, business events, requirements, stories,


models, prototyping, and others. We hope that you have found


a collection of techniques that will be helpful to you and


your work.


Before we part company, we want to look at the softer side of


business analysis: the people-focused side. We want to talk


about people and why they are important. We will also talk


about the process and how you might look at it before you


decide what your process is to be.


As part of the softer side, we also want to visit systems


thinking and how that might influence you when you’re


investigating and discovering your client’s problem space.


And finally, we’ll discuss how innovation makes an


incredible difference and should be part of every development


effort.


## 第 1107 页


The following (mainly short) chapters on the soft topics


don’t necessarily link together or follow any particular


sequence. But each provides insights that are intended to


make your business analysis better. Some of them show you


ideas that you might like to build into your own work


practices.


## 第 1108 页


Chapter 39. Your Process


Anarchy might be fun, but anarchists never build anything


useful. Can you imagine anarchists building the pyramids in


Egypt? “Listen up, guys. We’ve got these blocks of stone.


What do you think we can do with them?” No, the Egyptians


had a process that enabled them to put up structures that are


still standing 4,000 years later. Cut to today. Would you


happily catch the elevator to the 32nd floor if you thought


for one moment that the construction company had randomly


thrown together some steel, glass, and concrete, and kept


doing that until it looked like an office building?


To do anything meaningful, we usually need a number of


people. And as soon as you have more than one person involved


in your requirements and development effort, there is a need


for a process of one form or another. Simply put, if we want


multiple people to pull in the same direction, all of them


have to know what they’re supposed to be doing. This is the


role of the process.


That is not to say that a process should be fixed, rigid,


unvarying, and heavily enforced and leave no room for human


creativity. It should not be a process that must be


obediently followed to the point that the people using the


## 第 1109 页


process are reduced to automatons: “That’s step 47 done.


Tick. Now do step 48.” Any worthwhile process should be the


opposite of the robotic approach. It should be framed around


the people and the work they are doing.


It must also be flexible enough to adapt to unforeseen


happenings, because we know that we will almost always


encounter the unexpected. We can gather information to try to


reduce uncertainty, and the right information certainly does


that, but there will always be uncertainty. The best we can


do is to have a process that allows for deviations when the


unexpected happens, or when sticking to the plan would be


counterproductive.


Serial or Agile?


We are quite often asked, is the Volere process serial or


agile? The answer is yes. It is agile in that you jump from


one activity to another in response to happenings, and serial


when you ensure that the foundation is solid before moving on


to prototype or trawl. It is serial in that you understand


what has to be built before building it, and agile in that


you build as soon as you have enough confidence in the


requirements so far, and the product is built iteratively and


incrementally.


## 第 1110 页


Note the “enough confidence in the requirements.” This


implies that the business analysts have done their discovery.


Working code is not the cheapest way to explore the problem


and its proposed solution, nor is it the most effective. So,


it makes sense to postpone that code while there are cheaper


and more adaptable ways of exploring.


It is both serial and agile when it comes to change. But the


nature of change means that we must approach it differently


according to the reason for change. Iterative development


reduces the impact of change. If you have not built the


solution as one monolith, but are assembling it


incrementally, then you are reducing the odds that a change


will affect what you have already built.


However, the process is aimed at exploring portions of the


problem until the likelihood of change is minimized and the


risk is acceptable and then building that portion. A lot of


change happens because the wrong solution was built before


the real requirements were understood. Or it was built in an


attempt to display functionality to the stakeholders as a way


to discover the requirements. By sketching prototypes, using


models and other tools, the team experiments and explores the


problem. By working in tandem with the stakeholders, this


exploration establishes that the right problem is being


## 第 1111 页


solved and that the proposed solution will integrate with the


rest of the business. When you know these things—and only


when you know them—you can build a solution with the odds of


it needing to be changed greatly reduced.


Of course, change happens—technology, politics, and the


marketplace all change, as do the customers’ aspirations. We


cannot stop change, but we can use our Blastoff time to model


and anticipate the kinds of changes that could impact our


problem space and make allowances for it. In other words, by


being a bit more serial, and especially by establishing the


foundations first, we can make it easier to be more agile and


accommodate change.


A Common Language


When your airplane is coming in to land at a foreign airport,


the pilot and the air traffic controller speak English to


each other. You could be on an IcelandAir plane with an


Icelandic pilot landing in Reykjavik, and ATC and the pilot


still speak English. Why?


Because lives depend on the controllers, the pilots, and


everyone else involved understanding each other. By using a


common language, words have the same meaning. “Twenty nine


## 第 1112 页


right” means the same to both parties, and so there is far


less chance of a misunderstanding causing a potentially fatal


mishap.


Rarely does anyone die if people on your IT project


misunderstand each other (medical and military projects


excluded). But the project definitely suffers when the wrong


things are built.


One of the advantages of having a known process is that it


comes with a common language. The language of the process


itself—Blastoff, business event, description, rationale—is


defined and becomes known to everybody involved in the


process. Similarly, in the Volere Requirements Specification


Template, there is a glossary and a data dictionary. These


are there to define the business terms so that everybody on


the project has the same understanding of the words being


used. Without a common language, projects flounder, sometimes


producing the wrong solution but mainly living in an


inefficient state of misunderstandings and doubt.


As part of the common language, we refer you to the


Requirements Knowledge Model in Appendix C. This sets out the


artifacts that make up the knowledge you are accumulating


about the requirements. Using this model helps to standardize


## 第 1113 页


the requirements terminology and so makes for better


understanding and for your requirements process to flow more


smoothly.


Making It Your Process


Throughout this book, we have been showing you the Volere


process (shown again in Figure 39.1). There are a couple more


things that we still need to explain to illustrate how you


can make this your process.


## 第 1114 页


![embedded_p57_4.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p57_4.jpeg)


Figure 39.1 The Volere requirements process


Project Blastoff


Let’s start with the Project Blastoff activity. This is


where you set the foundation for your requirements efforts.


## 第 1115 页


We cannot stress enough how important it is to correctly and


honestly establish the scope of the problem and the goals or


benefits that the development effort is intended to deliver.


There is a lot more about this in the next chapter, where we


take a look at how to avoid some project disasters that came


about because the projects had no realistic goals or scope.


In order to discover the right scope and the right goals, you


might find it necessary to do some prototyping and


experimenting. Although we speak mainly about the Prototyping


activity as a way to discover requirements, you might find


prototypes useful for modeling the outcomes of different


scopes and goals. There are no precise rules for this kind of


prototyping, but you should not leave the Blastoff activity


until you and your stakeholders are rock-solid on what you


want to achieve.


We strongly suggest that your Blastoff achieves a well-


defined and universally agreed scope. Well-defined does not


mean inflexible. As you move along with your requirements


discovery, you usually uncover opportunities. Taking


advantage of the opportunity often means adjusting the scope.


So be it. As long as you remain in control of your scope and


the changes that you make to it, then all should be well.


## 第 1116 页


Although this is usually outside the responsibilities of


business analysts, you should be aware that the context


diagram—which we recommend as a way of demonstrating the


scope—can be used to make estimates. For a project to be


successful, you need to start out with realistic expectations


of how much effort is involved.


Prototype for Requirements


Prototyping is experimenting. You are not building a


prototype that is intended to be the forerunner of the final


product. Instead, you are sketching experimental solutions to


explore their outcomes. Prototyping means using quick models


to explore the problem space.


Another reason for prototyping is to find an alternative to


the presumed solution. Sometimes, at the beginning of the


project, someone presumes to know the solution. The project


is launched to build that solution without questioning it.


Distressingly often, the presumed solution is not what is


needed, so the effort expended building it is wasted.


Prototyping usually discovers the right problem to solve when


it demonstrates how alternative solutions yield far better


results.


## 第 1117 页


As you go about your requirements discovery, you will most


likely find yourself switching back and forth between


Prototyping and Trawling.


Trawl for Requirements


In Part IV, Trawling for Requirements, we presented a number


of techniques that are productive when working with the


stakeholders to discover their requirements. Not all the


techniques are relevant to all types of projects. However, we


encourage you to try techniques you have not used before and


see if they work for you and your stakeholders.


When you are trawling, you almost certainly will encounter


ready-made solutions. It is normal practice for organizations


to buy something off-the-shelf rather than build everything


from scratch. This means that your trawling needs to


encompass the ready-made product. This might also have


entailed writing the request for proposal (RFP). The most


significant part of using ready-mades is adapting them to fit


the organization or adapting the organization to fit the


ready-mades.


However, before you can use a ready-made solution, you need


to discover the real needs of the business. Additionally, you


need to decide which of those needs are best served by which


## 第 1118 页


ready-made, and how much adaptation is worth doing. This


probably means developing a scoring model to assess the


relative merits of competing ready-made solutions.


Trawling should not be seen as a stand-alone activity, but as


something that works with a close connection to the


prototyping and some of the design activity.


Keeping Requirements Knowledge


In some circles, documentation is a dirty word. However,


cooler heads know that a certain amount of it is needed.


Requirements are needed to give the designers and the


developers the best possible guidance on what they are to


deliver. Designers and developers need to leave behind enough


information about what they did and why they did it to enable


future generations to understand the solution.


Anything you develop today will probably have a life of at


least five years, and possibly more. This lifetime is needed


to give your sponsor or client enough time to get a return on


the investment. It costs money to develop solutions, and this


is recovered by the improvements to the business processes


that the solution enables. However, it usually takes years


before the development debt is paid off.


## 第 1119 页


During these years, the solution needs maintenance. Without a


guide to why the solution does what it does, the maintainers


are at a disadvantage. Understanding what something does is


relatively easy, but understanding why it does it is much


harder. Any documentation on why decisions were taken will be


very welcome in a few years’ time. If the decision was a


hard one, we suggest that writing a short piece on why you


chose one option over another can pay off later.


You have worked hard to discover the right problem to solve


and written the right requirements or stories. There is no


reason to discard this form of documentation once the


solution has been delivered. After all, each requirement or


story carries a rationale. This explains to future


generations why each requirement exists.


The requirements repository sits in the middle of the Volere


requirements process. Refer to the Requirements Knowledge


Model (Appendix C) for an explanation of the information that


should make up your repository. This repository can take


almost any form you choose: requirements specification, story


map, database, spreadsheet, a mixture of the above, or


something else. The form of the repository is a team or


organizational decision.


## 第 1120 页


Whatever you do, give more than a little consideration as to


what device or software you use for this storage, and what


form it will take. Your requirements knowledge is valuable.


Please don’t be careless with it.


Designing


Designing the solution should not be seen as a separate


activity that you arrive at once all the requirements are


known. Of course, there are some facets of designing that


cannot be done until the requirements are substantially


complete, but a lot of design is done well before then.


You are designing solutions when you’re sketching


prototypes. You’re designing when you’re thinking about and


modeling business processes. You’re designing when you are


in the Blastoff and deciding the scope of the problem and


what is the best problem to solve.


Design thinking should be part of your requirements


discovery. You have to constantly be looking out for


opportunities to design something better than what is being


proposed. You have to always be looking to see if a business


process could be improved by a better design. And let’s face


it, apart from the Parthenon and the Japanese Samurai sword,


most things could be improved by better design.


## 第 1121 页


Development


Development is beyond the scope of this book. As a business


analyst, you might be involved in writing code, but we don’t


aim to help you with Python or JavaScript or C#. What we can


help with is syncing requirements discovery with the


development activity.


We wrote about syncing earlier when we were discussing story


maps in Chapter 35. The main thrust is that when the


discovery and development are synced, the business analysts


are discovering the requirements on a just-in-time basis. See


Figure 39.2.


## 第 1122 页


![embedded_p1122_176.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1122_176.jpeg)


Figure 39.2 The development of the solution is synchronized


with the requirements discovery. This diagram was shown in


## 第 1123 页


Chapter 35 where there is a full explanation of it.


This requires the product owner, or someone organizing the


development activity, to find the parts of the solution that


should be the next to be developed. We have urged you to


manage your requirements discovery and your development one


business event at a time. This makes the synchronization


straightforward. The business analysts use the business event


as their unit of discovery, and when they deliver the


requirements for that business event, the development team


has a discrete unit to implement and test. There is usually a


small amount of overlap between business events; they share


data, and sometimes they have some common functionality.


However, this is usually easy to spot, and so the developers


can avoid implementing the same functionality more than once.


This assumes that you have an in-house development team, and


the solution is one that allows for incremental development.


Otherwise, it might be necessary to build the complete


requirements specification, and once done, the developers or


the outsource contractor starts the work.


The advantage of incremental development is that there is


only a short lag between the requirements and the delivery of


a partial solution. When the complete specification is


## 第 1124 页


written before any development starts, the lag might mean


that the specification is slightly out of date. On the plus


side, a complete specification gives you the opportunity to


check its completeness and correctness before committing to


development.


The choice of development tactics depends very much on the


nature of the solution, and your organization. The above


should help to make the best choice for you.


Review


“If you can’t describe what you are doing as a


process, you don’t know what you’re doing.”—


W. Edwards Deming


There is obviously a need for some kind of process if you are


to effectively discover the right requirements. Such a


process includes the activities needed to liaise with the


stakeholders, understand their work and future ambitions for


their work, and record and communicate those requirements.


However—and we cannot stress this enough—the process is


there to guide you. It is not there to rule you. We have


provided you with the Volere process. We have described the


## 第 1125 页


various parts and activities of this as we worked through the


book. This process works straight out of the box, or you can


adapt it to fit the circumstances of your workplace and your


team. We favor the latter. Volere is not intended to be a


lockstep process, but a framework for successful requirements


discovery.


Your development team probably uses Scrum or one of the agile


methods, so your process must fit in and work smoothly with


agile development. We talked in earlier chapters about how to


synchronize with your development team.


Finally, we should mention the track record of the Volere


process. It has been used by thousands of projects over many


years and continues to be adopted and adapted by


organizations in many parts of the world. When used wisely,


it opens the door to successful requirements discovery.

tools, techniques, and methodologies that are used by

Business Analysis by Debra Paul, Donald Yeates, and James

The Business Analysis Body of Knowledge (BABOK Guide) by the

This is an international work, and it offers a structured

framework for understanding and applying business analysis
