## 第 1128 页


Chapter 40. The Importance of the Early
Days


How many large government project (those costing tens of


millions, if not billions, of dollars/euros) finish on time


and on budget, and deliver all the promised benefits? Take a


minute to think about this. Or take as long as you like; your


answer will still be zero.


Think of large project disasters such as the California High


Speed Rail that was intended to whisk Californians from Los


Angeles to San Francisco in less than three hours. As of


2024, the project has been running for 16 years, and has


consumed over $11 billion, yet only a few miles of rail have


been laid and the project has been eviscerated down to a


section running between Merced and Bakersfield, two barely


known locations.


The Sydney Opera House’s original plan had four years to


completion and a budget of 7 million Australian dollars. It


took AU $102 million and 14 years to complete.


Denver International Airport—a new airport to replace


Stapleton—was years late and cost more than $5 billion. This


was a 300% increase from the original estimate.


## 第 1129 页


These are construction projects. What about large-scale IT


projects that failed? Same results—the answer to the opening


question is still zero. Start looking around and you’ll find


dozens (look long enough and you’ll find hundreds) of large


IT projects that finished late, were abandoned unfinished, or


were over budget and did not deliver the benefits that were


originally promised.


For example, the Canadian government’s Phoenix Pay system


proposed much but turned out to be an almost complete


disaster (only 20% of paychecks were accurate, and some


people were not paid at all). It was very expensive to fix.


Or take FoxMeyer’s Delta III disaster. FoxMeyer was one of


the top pharmaceutical distributors in the United States,


worth around $5 billion. Aiming to be more efficient, it


launched the $65 million Delta III project in 1993. Despite


its high-priced consultants, the delivered software was


woefully inadequate, and the company was bankrupt three years


later.


How about your own organization? How many IT projects finish


on time and on budget, and produce the target benefits? The


answer this time is probably not zero, but it is certainly


not 100% of the projects either. Large IT initiatives are


## 第 1130 页


among the projects most likely to fail—they are only


slightly less risky than building a nuclear power plant.


Why Do Things Go Wrong?


Why do most IT projects go wrong? Why do they run late, cost


more, and deliver much less than promised? The answer is


complex, as there can be a mix of different factors:


politics, psychology, poor management, incompetence,


inexperience, wrong stakeholders, unrealistic ambitions,


hubris, and so on. But there is one common factor for all


failed projects: They do not do what should be done in the


early days.


We spoke about the early days way back in the chapters


talking about the Project Blastoff. It is in these early days


of the project’s life that you decide on the things that


have the greatest impact on the success or failure of your


project.


For example, it is in the early days that you determine the


purpose of the project. That might seem blindingly obvious,


but it is not obvious at all to the people in charge of


failed projects. Consider the projects that set out to build


railway lines, or bridges, or roads, or public health or


## 第 1131 页


payroll IT systems, where nobody, or not enough people, asked


why they were doing it. Or if they did, the answer was so


vacuous that it only fooled the instigators of the project


and their political paymasters. And the politicians or high-


level executives were so keen to start building that they did


not want to hear anybody casting doubt on the purpose of the


project.


Good planning, the early-days activity we are talking about


here, starts with why. “Why are we doing this project?”


“What is its purpose?” “What do we want to achieve?”


Generally, the reason is to realize benefits to the


organization. It might take several (or more) iterations for


you and your stakeholders to agree on those benefits and make


them tangible and understood by everyone.


Planning before starting is the antithesis of “digging a big


hole.” This big-hole metaphor comes from large-building


construction such as office buildings, where before you can


build anything, you dig a big hole for the foundations. For


multistory buildings, you dig down to the bedrock.


You have probably seen the big-hole metaphor at your work.


There is a project on shaky foundations (if you will pardon


another building construction metaphor), with no proper


## 第 1132 页


costing and poorly defined benefits. The project team rushes


in and starts building something, anything (digging their big


hole), before any real planning can take place. The existence


of the “big hole” is expected to dissuade stakeholders from


stopping the project or changing direction. “We’ve already


started building, it’s too late to stop it.” It is also


meant to stop any delay while sensible people try to figure


out what it is supposed to deliver.


Similar to measurable objectives is having a rock-solid scope


for the project. By this we mean a context diagram with all


the input and output flows defined in the data dictionary. It


might seem pedantic to insist on this, but projects without a


clear and well-defined scope are headed for disaster. Ask


anybody who has started house renovations without a clear


scope and goals. They will tell you—all of them—that the


renovations cost twice as much as they thought and took three


times as long (these are conservative figures). Ask anybody


who has worked on an IT development project with no clearly


defined scope, and they will tell you the same.


For large government projects, the budgets—time and money—


are set artificially low. Politicians need to sell their


grandiose schemes to the taxpayers, and so the money and time


needed are set at levels that can be trumpeted to the public.


## 第 1133 页


They do this because people are not going to vote for a


project if they know the truth. Britain’s HS2 high-speed


rail project had an initial estimate of between £30 billion


and £36 billion. Four years after the project was signed off,


the price had risen to £56.6 billion. Current estimates are


in excess of £100 billion. Taxpayers would not have tolerated


a project with a price tag of £100 billion, yet that is what


they will end up paying. (As a side note, the ambitions of


HS2 have already been scaled back, cutting in half the hyped


benefits, “hugely enhanced capacity and connectivity,” but


not reducing the cost.)


That’s government. Does it happen in private organizations?


All the time. Project initiators need to sell it to the


board; predictably enough, costs are underestimated, and


benefits overstated. How many of these projects fail? All of


them. None of them finish within budget, none of them deliver


the promised benefits, and almost all of them deliver


benefits that are considerably less than the cost of the


project.


Why does this happen so distressingly often? Because people


avoid putting effort into the early days where you do your


planning. “Planning? That’s not real work. Requirements?


## 第 1134 页


That’s not real work. Let’s just get on with digging our


big hole.”


“Send ‘em to the movies” was the approach used by our


colleague Stephen Mellor. He was referring to the developers,


and how it is wise not to start building anything until the


planning is done. Another colleague, Steve McMenamin, ran


very large projects for several electricity companies. Steve


insisted that nobody do anything until a small group had


established the vision, plan, and scope for the project.


Steve’s multiyear projects always came in on time and on


budget.


The Role of the Business Analyst


You are most likely a business analyst, not a project


manager. What’s your role in all this? An important one. As


a business analyst, you must always challenge assumptions,


and where possible, provide evidence that the assumption is


wrong. IT projects make too many assumptions at the


beginning, many of them dangerous.


First, there is the assumption that this project is unique,


and what has happened to other IT projects will not happen to


this one. However, you can no more suspend the laws of


statistical probability than you can suspend the law of


## 第 1135 页


gravity. Your project is an IT project and the mean cost


overrun for IT projects is 73%, and 18% of projects achieve a


mean overrun of 447%.


The source of these numbers is Bent Flyvbjerg, a


consultant on more than 100 projects costing $1


billion or more, who has a database of thousands


of projects, why they worked, and where they went


wrong. See his book, How Big Things Get Done.


Now that you have seen those numbers, can you safely assert


that your project is so unique that it will not overrun by


something like 73%?


The planners of IT projects often assume that nothing will go


wrong. Another wrong assumption. A quick scan of other IT


projects tells you that on every project, things go wrong.


Key people unexpectedly leave, there are mismatches between


ready-made solutions and their expected behavior,


stakeholders become unavailable, managers become disengaged,


suppliers are unreliable, performance is less than expected,


and on and on. If you assume that nothing will go wrong, it


means your project budget has no contingency buffer.


Statistics tell us the buffer should be at least 50%.


## 第 1136 页


Setting out to build a presumed solution instead of solving a


business problem is a big project killer. Many projects start


by presuming to know the solution: We need to build a


website, a CRM system, a new payroll system, and so on.


Distressingly often, these presumed solutions turn out to


solve the wrong problem. As a business analyst, you must


challenge the presumed solution and constantly ask why the


project needs to be done. By asking why, and sometimes you


need to ask many times, you can arrive at the real reason—


the real goal of the project—and then start to find suitable


solutions.


Finally, and this is incredibly obvious but not always


observed, to determine whether the expected benefits will


outweigh the costs, you have to measure both of them.


Inflating one and minimizing the other always ends badly.


All of these things need to be done by business analysts and


project management in the early days, before someone starts


digging a big hole.


Resources


How Big Things Get Done by Bent Flyvbjerg and Dan Gardner


(Macmillan, 2023). This book talks through many projects that


## 第 1137 页


failed because they did not pay attention to the early days.


Flyvbjerg is a consultant with a database of thousands of


failed projects. He is called into multimillion-dollar


projects that get themselves into trouble. It’s also an


entertaining read.


The Mythical Man-Month by Frederick P. Brooks (Addison-


Wesley, 1995). This has been around for a long time and


remains the classic book on the challenges of software


project management. It provides insights into why projects


can go wrong.


Project Management for the Unofficial Project Manager


(Updated and Revised Edition) by Kory Kogon and Suzette


Blakemore (BenBella Books, 2024). This is a practical guide


for the business analyst who finds herself managing without


the official title of project manager.


The Project Management Institute website


(https://www.pmi.org) offers a wealth of resources, including


articles, webinars, and best practices related to project


management.


Harvard Business Review has articles and case studies on its


website (https://hbr.org) that can give insights into project


## 第 1138 页


success and failure.


## 第 1139 页


Chapter 41. People


So far, we have been talking about how to discover


requirements. We have looked at a process and techniques


that, when used well, make a difference to the effectiveness


of your work. Now it is time to talk about another element;


one that has a greater effect than any technique can hope to


achieve: the people element.


Projects (at the time of writing) are staffed by people who


discover the requirements and build the solutions. If the


employing organization wants these people to do a good job,


then it must align its values with the motivators of the


people.


In this chapter, we look at some of these organizational


values and how they affect the requirements discovery


process.


Drivers of Human Behavior


The following draws on work that we did in collaboration with


our partners in the Atlantic Systems Guild and that resulted


in the book Happy to Work Here—Understanding and Improving


the Culture at Work (listed in this chapter’s Resources


section).


## 第 1140 页


That book introduced the concept of culture drivers.


Culture, as we defined it, is a set of shared beliefs and


resultant behaviors. For example, if we all had the shared


belief that left-handed people are significantly more


intelligent, the resultant behavior would be that we would


all listen more attentively when a lefty started to speak.


So, what beliefs can an organization hold that have a


beneficial effect on the behavior of its people? We have


isolated four such beliefs, which we call culture drivers,


and although there are others, these are the four that have


the most impact.


The Perceived Value of People


How does your organization see its people? Are they an


inconvenient but necessary burden on the bottom line? Are


they seen as untrustworthy and error-prone? As lazy and not


very competent? If any of these are true, then apart from


suggesting you seek employment elsewhere, we propose that


this lack of value is having a negative impact on your


requirements discovery process. We’ll explore this as we go


along.


Does your organization acknowledge that people


are its most valued asset?


## 第 1141 页


On the other hand, if your organization acknowledges that its


people are its most valued asset, then it hires better people


and looks after them. This might seem incredibly obvious, but


you can observe whether it’s true by observing its hiring


process. Does it put a lot of effort into finding the right


talent, or does it simply fill vacancies with the first (or


cheapest) person to roll along? Is it more concerned with


people’s ability than whether there are enough people to


fill the available desks?


As part of valuing its people, does the organization


celebrate people for achieving something? Or is it more


focused on blaming people when something doesn’t work? There


is always an element of risk when people are innovating and


trying new things, but if failure is always punished, then


few people are willing to take any risks at all. In


requirements work, this translates to overly heavy


specifications and overly detailed descriptions of every


requirement; both of which are a waste of time for normal


projects.


Additionally, good, highly valued people are not managed on a


minute-by-minute basis. They make their own decisions about


what their requirements discovery process should be. They


## 第 1142 页


also make responsible decisions about when their requirements


are in a state that it is safe to move on, and when more


discovery needs to be done.


When they are valued, people gravitate toward processes that


are effective, rather than what is prescribed; they opt for


processes that are as light-touch as possible, without


compromising quality. They have greater flexibility when they


put together and use their requirements process.


The Perceived Value of the Team


The next culture driver has to do with teams. Teams are made


up of individuals, each of which has his/her own set of


skills, abilities, and ways of approaching their work.


However, when those individuals come together and form a


team, something mystical happens: The team forms its own


personality.


One trait of this personality is team self-confidence. Team


self-confidence means that the team always presses forward,


confident that it can overcome any obstacle that appears and


confident that it will recover quickly from any errors that


it makes. The self-confident team almost always selects a


process that involves prototyping and partial and frequent


development cycles that deliver incremental parts of the


## 第 1143 页


solution. In other words, the self-confident team selects a


riskier process that will deliver results more quickly. If


some of the risks result in partial failure, the team is


confident that it can recover the situation with no permanent


damage to the project. It should be kept in mind that self-


confidence is not the same thing as arrogance.


Another team personality trait is the value it puts on


excellence. An excellent team always tries to deliver the


best possible solution within the constraints. Second best is


not good enough for the excellent teams, which in turn


engenders pride in the team’s work. Moreover, excellence


attracts excellence. Organizations and teams that turn out


excellent work are desirable places to work. The best people


want to work there because they want to do good work. And so


this virtuous cycle means that teams become better and better


at adjusting their process to produce solutions that meet the


real requirements.


The Perceived Value of Knowledge


Knowledge is one organizational asset that is often handled


carelessly. Yet, the knowledge that an organization gathers


as it goes about its work is second only to people in terms


of value. If we look at this with regard to requirements,


## 第 1144 页


then the team or organization that values its knowledge


ensures that requirements (the foundation for product


development) are recorded in a way that will make sense ten


to fifteen years later.


It is tempting to say that the code is the best documentation


of what it does. In some, usually simple cases, this is true.


However, the code does not reveal why it does something, and


often—more than often—the rationale for a requirement is a


crucial part of the knowledge. If you understand why


something is the way it is, then you are in a position to


make improvements and respond to changes in the requirements


throughout the life of a product. Being able to pass along


the rationale for the requirements means that future


maintainers don’t accidentally introduce new problems when


making changes by failing to understand why the solution was


built that way.


Teams that understand the value of knowledge put


a great deal of emphasis on collecting that


knowledge in the first place.


Teams that understand the value of knowledge put a great deal


of emphasis on collecting that knowledge in the first place.


These teams understand that if you are to build the right


## 第 1145 页


solution, you must have a correct knowledge of the problem to


be solved. They don’t start building until they are


confident that they have enough knowledge. Moreover, every


team member and most of the stakeholders have equal access to


that knowledge.


This means that their requirements repository is carefully


curated, is progressively added to as knowledge is gained and


refined, and is constantly being accessed and used by team


members. Along the way, team members are constantly learning


and are sharing their knowledge with their teammates via the


repository.


Requirements knowledge can take many forms, but generally it


is a specification, a story map, a collection of individual


requirements, diagrams, and so on. Because they value


knowledge, and the quality of that knowledge, there is


nothing in the team’s repository that is not useful.


The Perceived Value of Time


Many projects are obsessed with time—everything is urgent.


This obsession mandates that getting the solution finished in


the least amount of time is the prime objective. Of course,


if aliens from the Yilktor 9 galaxy are traveling at warp


speed toward Earth with the intention of enslaving humanity,


## 第 1146 页


and your project is to deliver a force field for keeping them


at bay, then of course it’s urgent.


However, most of us are not being attacked by Yilktorians,


and most of us know that the right amount of time to be


allocated to a task is the time needed to produce a high-


quality product. We also know that allocating more time—up


to a point—improves the likelihood of producing a better


product. Having time means that the team can explore


alternatives to find a superior solution. It also means the


team has time to ensure that the requirements are accurate


and are drawn from a wider range of stakeholders.


More time increases the likelihood of producing a


better product, but . . ..


However, spending too much time on a project exposes it to


unnecessary risks. On overly long projects, there is a risk


that key team members leave; a risk that market conditions


change; or a risk that changes in technology mean the product


is no longer technically viable. Over time, management at our


organizations change. Sometimes this means that new managers


change the direction or goals of our projects.


## 第 1147 页


Allocating too little time for a project is also damaging to


the final product. Putting people under pressure to deliver


in ridiculously short time frames results in products that


are lower-quality, bug-ridden, missing some of the


requirements, not adequately tested, and so on. It also has


an adverse effect on people. People want to do good work, and


they resent it when, due to time pressure, they are unable to


do so. And if the time pressure is perceived as being


unnecessary, they lose respect for the organization and its


management.


Time has values that are more than the passing of hours and


days. It is a nonrenewable commodity that must be treated


carefully. Your choice of requirements process must therefore


balance the amount of time needed to achieve the right result


against allowing too much time and becoming victim to chance


happenings, boredom, and lack of interest.


Review


How you organize your requirements activities should not be


dictated by a set of rules or a rigid method. Paying


attention to the people and teams you have available and


determining which requirements activities are best suited to


the people will yield the best value to your situation.


## 第 1148 页


Having an excellent team for your project helps. It helps a


lot. But you only get excellent teams when people are given


the chance to flourish. Restricting people with unnecessary


procedures and rigid processes will not get you an excellent


team. On the other hand, allowing people to be flexible with


their processes, allowing sufficient time, and being


obsessive about producing excellent work attracts the kind of


people you need to make excellent solutions.

culture goes wrong, and what you can do to make it better for


the people at your work.


Adrenaline Junkies and Template Zombies: Understanding


Patterns of Project Behavior by Tom DeMarco et al. How do


people on your projects behave? You’re bound to find more


than one behavior pattern that applies to your people in this


book.


Leaders Eat Last by Simon Sinek. Anything by Sinek is worth


reading, and his website, simonsinek.com, has lots of


resources. In this book Sinek explores how creating a


## 第 1149 页


supportive and trusting environment leads to highly effective


teams.


TED Talks (ted.com). Look for talks leadership, teamwork, and


interpersonal skills. Checkout Simon Sinek, Brené Brown, and


numerous other thought leaders.


Harvard Business Review. Look for articles on team dynamics,


and communication to find relevant insights and case studies


about people on projects.


## 第 1150 页


Chapter 42. Systems Thinking


Many people reading this book have the job title “business


analyst” or something similar. Analysis means dissection:


breaking a system into its components in order to study them.


Contrarily, systems thinking is examining a system in its


totality. Instead of thinking about the components of a


system, you are looking at the connections between the


components and the effect that one component can have on


others. You are also looking at the outcome of the system and


you can think of the outcome as why the system exists.


Systems thinking starts by thinking about your business area


—your problem space—as an end-to-end system; that is, a


system made up of a set of components that produces something


that none of the components can do on its own. So, let’s not


look at the components but at the aggregation of the


components and the ways in which they interact.


But let’s not stop there. All systems are connected to other


systems. This is very apparent when you think of the


internet. Via the internet (a system), your phone (another


system) is connected to the system that is run by your bank,


which in turn is connected to your employer’s payroll


system. Think of that delicious moment when your monthly


## 第 1151 页


salary pops into your bank account, and try not to think


about that less-than-delicious moment when your energy


company uses your direct debit mandate (the direct debit


system is a subsystem within the bank’s system) to move your


monthly payment into its account (yet another system).


Given that everything is connected to everything else, your


systems thinking should include the adjacent systems that


surround your own problem space. Happenings in those can have


an impact on your space, just as happenings in your problem


space impact the outside world.


Thinking About Systems


As an example of systems thinking, imagine a clutch of


teenagers. Think of each of them as a component in the


following social system. Tracey tells Vijay that she is


breaking up with him. Later that day Vijay is approached by


his friend Billy, who asks Vijay if he wants to go to the


movies that evening. Vijay is in a bad mood from being dumped


by Tracey and so he says no. Billy wants to go to the movies,


so he asks Zuri (who he knows but is not particularly close


with) if she wants to go. She says yes but wants to bring her


friend Janice. Billy, Zuri, and Janice go to the movies;


Billy and Janice get on particularly well and make a date for


## 第 1152 页


the following weekend. Zuri loves the movie (she had not


heard of it before) and decides to find more of the


director’s movies on her parents’ streaming service. Enough


about teenagers, let’s stop there.


Now let’s consider that if even one of the components acted


differently, then the outcome of the system (the clutch of


teenagers) would be different. This time Tracey does not


break up with Vijay. Billy and Vijay would not have gone to


the movies, so Billy would not have met Janice. Zuri would


not know about the director and would not see his other


movies.


The point of the story is that Tracey’s action had an impact


on Zuri’s movie preferences, and if some of the other


participants had acted differently, it would have impacted


one or more of the others.


As another example, think of a website selling products


online. The website is a system made up of components: the


display area where the goods are shown to the customers;


checkout; payments; fulfillment; inventory control;


warehousing; delivery; returns; and support. (If you prefer,


you can think of “components”' as subsystems, features,


processes, activities, or whatever.)


## 第 1153 页


When you think systemically, you see the website and its


support processes as a network of interconnected


components. Connections in this case might be a direct data


flow, or it could be that one component stores data that is


used by one or more others. That they are connected means


that any component can affect almost any other component, and


any component is dependent on the actions of the others.


The online selling website is illustrated on Figure 42.1.


Imagine it in action and consider what happens with the


Checkout activity when someone is finalizing their purchase.


It has to ask the Delivery activity for an estimated delivery


time (to allow the customer to pull out of the sale if the


delivery time is too long), it checks with Inventory that


stock is available and asks for it to be reserved for this


sale, and it signals the Payments activity to collect the


customer’s money. When that is done it records the sale as


final on the database. This will be retrieved by the


Fulfillment activity that results in the product being


delivered to the customer.


## 第 1154 页


![embedded_p1154_177.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1154_177.jpeg)


Figure 42.1 Think of the website as a network of components


with direct or indirect connections between the components.


What happens in one affects one or more of the others.


Now consider the requirements. Suppose that you are renewing


the Checkout activity. Obviously, you need the requirements


## 第 1155 页


for checking out, but you also need the requirements for


interacting with the other activities. What data do you


retrieve from the Delivery activity? Does it calculate


delivery time, or is that a requirement for the Checkout


activity? If the Delivery activity does it, what data is


needed to do it? Similarly, the other activities have


requirements for how they will interact with the renewed


Checkout. You also need to look at whether any of those


activities impact any of the others and generate yet more new


requirements.


Systems thinking means that you are concerned with the wider


system. Although you are charged with renewing the Checkout


activity, you have to step back and take a wider, systemic


view of the big picture of the problem space.


Ripple Effects


There might also be ripple effects. You are probably aware


that the “ripple effect” uses the analogy of the ripples


spreading out from a stone thrown into a pond. Here we use it


to refer to the likelihood that an error in one part of a


system causes a failure in another part, which in turn causes


a further failure, which in turn...and so on. Ripples could


happen if your new Checkout activity had a fault, or


## 第 1156 页


introduced some new data, or removed old data, or put data


into the database, which in turn caused the Inventory


activity to produce incorrect results, which in turn caused


discrepancies in the Fulfillment activity. Sometimes you see


the ripples right away, but sometimes they travel a long way


before becoming apparent.


For the want of a nail, the shoe was lost


For the want of the shoe, a horse was lost


For the want of a horse, the rider was lost


For the want of a rider, the message was lost


For the want of a message, the battle was lost


For the want of a battle, the kingdom was lost,


1


and all for the want of a horseshoe nail


1


Ancient proverb that probably dates back to the 13th


century. Benjamin Franklin picked it up for his Poor


Richard’s Almanack in 1758.


## 第 1157 页


From the requirements perspective, it means looking outward


from the component you are building and determining which


other components can be affected by ripples.


To summarize so far, any business area for which you are


discovering requirements is never isolated. It has


connections to other business areas, which are in turn


connected to others. What you do with your business area can


affect others, just as those business areas can affect yours.


You have to look at the network and avoid constraining your


discovery. Your discovery is always wider and more intricate


than you first thought it would be.


Step back and see the bigger picture.


External Influences


Consider the following example, which is the ticketing


2


solution for the Mudville baseball team who play their home


games in Mudville Stadium. The initial context diagram for


this solution is shown in Figure 42.2. However, systems


thinking says that this is not a wide enough scope to


accommodate the external influences that can disrupt such a


system. Let’s see how this works.

The Wider View


How do you know that the context diagram shown in Figure 42.2


is complete? You use systems thinking. A useful entry point


for systems thinking is a quotation from American theoretical


meteorologist Edward Norton Lorenz:


“If a butterfly flutters its wings in Brazil could it cause


a tornado in Texas.”


## 第 1161 页


The quotation comes from a lecture Lorenz gave in December


1972. He was referring to the weather being a chaotic system,


and even small occurrences in one place could have a major


impact somewhere quite distant. The quotation gave rise to


the Butterfly Effect, a metaphor for the principle of chaos


theory. We are not dealing with chaotic systems, but we


should still consider small happenings that can have


significant effects elsewhere.


Even small occurrences in one place could have a


major impact on a distant part of the system.


An occurrence can be large or small. Consider these


happenings in Mudville. A water main on Casey Street bursts.


This causes the street to be closed until the main is dug out


and fixed. This would not be interesting to a ticketing


system, except that Casey Street is a major access route to


Mudville Stadium, and fans with tickets for gates on Casey


have to be advised to use alternative gates.


Another happening: During a routine inspection, the support


structures under blocks 2 through 5 of the East Stand are


found to be in an unsafe state. The stadium manager


immediately advises the ticketing solution to stop selling


## 第 1162 页


tickets in those blocks and notify fans who have already


bought tickets to negotiate an exchange of seats.


3


For really big games (Mudville versus Pittsfield is a very


well-attended match), the police might issue security


restrictions, and again, fans might have to be notified.


Additionally, the police have requested to be told when


ticket sales exceed a threshold, as they (the police) need to


assign extra officers for crowd control outside the stadium.


3


The first baseball game in the United States was played in


Pittsfield, Massachusetts, in 1791.


Coming back to the butterfly, one must have fluttered its


wings, because the weather forecasting service issued a


warning of an extreme weather event. A huge snowstorm is


predicted for game day, and the team managers of both teams


decide that for the safety of the fans and the players, they


will postpone the game. Now the team manager needs to notify


the ticketing solution, which starts the process of notifying


fans and issuing tickets for the rescheduled game.


So, we are seeing how happenings outside our problem space


can have an impact inside it. Using systems thinking during


the requirements discovery means that you step back as far as


## 第 1163 页


possible to see the happenings that can potentially impact


your solution. You have seen in the above example how you now


need requirements to exchange tickets, to notify ticket


holders of changes, of rescheduling tickets, and so on. There


are also requirements for notifying the police when ticket


sales reach a certain threshold.


Using Data to Find Missing Connections


You should also refer to the data. Look at the data


entities/classes, and for each one ask what could happen that


could impact that data. Here you can use the Create, Read,


Update, Delete (CRUD) checklist (described fully in Chapter


37, Completeness Check) to help you discover happenings that


you might have missed.


All of this means that the context diagram has to be


substantially revised. Figure 42.4 shows the revision.

![embedded_p1164_180.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1164_180.jpeg)


Figure 42.4 The revisions discussed above are shown using

## 第 1165 页


The changes to the context diagram have come about because


systems thinking says that any system is actually part of a


larger system, and therefore potentially subject to the


impact of happenings in that larger system. Equally,


happenings within the smaller system can have an impact on


the larger one.


For example, if the Mudville ticketing system sells lots of


tickets for a game, it advises the police, which would then


put crowd control measures in place. This might involve


closing off streets in the town or drafting in extra officers


to help manage the crowd. So, a humble ticketing system


causes the town police to act.


Any solution that you deliver has to slot into


its ecosystem.


As a business analyst, we suggest using systems thinking as


part of your requirements discovery. Any solution that you


deliver will have to slot into its ecosystem—the real world


that surrounds the solution. Which means that butterflies


fluttering their wings could have some meaningful impact on


your solution. It is part of your requirements discovery to


uncover the butterflies so that the solution is not subject


## 第 1166 页


to unforeseen happenings. All potential impacts should become


known at discovery time.


Review


Following are heuristics for systems thinking:


• Step back, and then step back further.


• Everything is connected.


• Ripples can travel a long way.


• Think of the holistic system.


• Your solution is part of an ecosystem.


• The solution’s data impacts and is impacted.


• Ask why the system exists.


• Butterflies can be dangerous.


Resources


Thinking in Systems: A Primer by Donella H. Meadows (Chelsea


Green Publishing, 2008). This is pretty much the standard


## 第 1167 页


text on systems thinking and how to apply it to real-world


problems.


Systems Thinking for Curious Managers by Russell Ackoff and


Herbert Addison (Triarchy Press, 2010). This presents


Ackoff’s f-Laws, 80 or more insights into systems thinking.


The Fifth Discipline: The Art and Practice of the Learning


Organization by Peter Senge (Crown Business, 2006). This


explores systems thinking as a key component of


organizational learning. Senge’s cause and effect diagrams


are useful.


The Systems Thinker Magazine (https://thesystemsthinker.com)


has articles and case studies on systems thinking and its


applications.


The Donella Meadows Institute (https://donellameadows.org)


offers resources, articles, and workshops related to systems


thinking and sustainability.


Systems Thinking, Systems Practice by Peter Checkland (Wiley,


1993). This book began it all when Checkland wrote about soft


systems methodology. This contrasted “hard” systems—which


can be engineered—with “soft” systems in which the focus


## 第 1168 页


is on making sure the process of inquiry into real-world


complexity is itself a system for learning.


## 第 1169 页


Chapter 43. Artificial Intelligence (AI)


Writing anything about artificial intelligence is doomed. The


field is expanding and changing so quickly that a lot of what


is written is obsolete almost before it is read. However, it


is something that will have an impact on all our lives and


will also impact the way we go about discovering


requirements. It is already doing both of those and will do


it to an even greater extent in the future.


Artificial intelligence (AI) is the name given to intelligent


machines, or bots (software, really), that mimic human


thinking capabilities. AI bots understand and process natural


language and images, and so respond much as a human would.


This is referred to as general or strong AI, as it can


reason, solve problems, and learn from experience, very much


like a human being. General AI is useful for your


requirements discovery tasks. You can chat with it, ask


questions, and ask for recommendations for requirements.


Narrow AI engines are specialized and designed to perform a


specific task. They can also learn from experience and make


decisions. Embedding this kind of AI in business processes is


beneficial. For example, you might embed AI in a warehouse


management solution to monitor stock as it comes into the


## 第 1170 页


warehouse and goes out as it is sold. Demand for different


items changes due to seasonal demand and fashion. AI would


learn which items are in demand, what trends are forming, and


predict popularity more accurately than a human could. It


would also suggest housekeeping routines whereby the popular,


and soon to be popular, items are moved closer to the


dispatch bays. Your task as a business analyst is to discover


opportunities to use AI as part of your customer’s business


process.


AI will establish itself as an essential part of our


businesses and business processes. To what extent it


transforms from being the faithful servant to controlling


more and more of a business remains to be seen. In the


meantime, we can get the best of the opportunity that AI


provides by using it as an intelligent and useful assistant.


Using AI for Requirements Discovery


You can ask one of the AI bots, such as ChatGPT from OpenAI,


to generate a set of requirements for the solution of your


choice, and the bot will search a large amount of data


looking for specifications for similar applications. It then


returns a proposed specification. Job done; take the


afternoon off. Or can you?


## 第 1171 页


It might work if you’re prepared to risk your customer’s


future business (and possibly your job and reputation) on the


accuracy of the AI bot. Also, consider that AI uses


historical data to generate its requirements. This means that


the AI-generated requirements probably won’t go beyond what


exists at the moment. Additionally, some AI bots have been


known to sometimes generate completely fictitious results.


However, all of that does not mean that AI cannot be useful


to you as a business analyst. It can be very useful indeed,


if you think of it as your assistant and not your


replacement.


Suppose that you are prototyping, and you’re looking for


ideas. You ask your AI chatbot for a process model by


prompting it with this:


“I am selling shirts. I need a process to


fulfill the orders from my customers. The


fulfillment process must include packaging and


shipping the shirts to the customers.”


We tried it, and ChatGPT came back with this:


## 第 1172 页


Sure! Here’s a process for fulfilling orders and


shipping shirts to customers:


1. Receive the order: Once an order is placed,


you will receive a notification from your e-


commerce platform or website.


2. Prepare the order: Locate the shirt(s) in your


inventory and check for any defects or quality


issues. If the shirt needs to be printed with a


design or logo, do so at this stage. Then,


package the shirt(s) securely, ensuring they are


protected during shipping.


3. Choose a shipping carrier: Decide on a carrier


for shipping the package. Popular options include


USPS, FedEx, and UPS.


4. Print shipping label: Once you have chosen a


carrier, print out the shipping label provided by


your e-commerce platform.


5. Mark as shipped: Mark the order as shipped in


your e-commerce platform, and provide the


customer with the tracking information.


## 第 1173 页


6. Deliver the package: Deliver the package to


the shipping carrier or schedule a pickup for the


package to be picked up at your location.


7. Follow up: Monitor the shipping status to


ensure the package is delivered to the customer


successfully. If there are any issues or delays


with delivery, communicate with the customer and


the carrier to resolve the issue.


Treat this as a starting point, and for each AI-generated


step in the process, ask the following questions.


• Is this touching a topic that you have not previously


considered?


• Does it suggest one or more processes that have not yet


been discussed with the stakeholders?


• Can this be used as is, or is it more useful if modified?


• Does the suggested process suggest that you are solving the


wrong problem and should revise your prompt?


• Does it require drilling down to find the details before


you can decide its usefulness?


## 第 1174 页


• Should you refine your prompt and see if the chatbot can


produce a better process?


• Or would it be profitable to abandon this process and


generate another using a different prompt?


The point is not to have AI generate your processes and


requirements, but to use it to generate input to your


analysis and innovation.


The point is not to have AI generate your


processes and requirements, but to use it to


generate input to your analysis and innovation.


There are other ways you can use AI for requirements


discovery.


You could also ask your AI chatbot to write preliminary


stories. Some of them might be useful for your story map;


others will need investigation and modification before they


become useful. The point is to generate input for your


analysis. If you prompt well enough, you could get valid


stories from the AI bot, but prudence says that you should


check everything carefully.


## 第 1175 页


Natural language processing (NLP) is part of AI and is used


to analyze large volumes of text and to identify patterns.


You can use this ability in your requirements discovery. For


example, you can ask your AI chatbot to analyze your support


tickets to determine common themes or patterns from the


customer difficulties registered by the support people. These


themes indicate the most important areas to deal with and


will probably suggest requirements that might not have been


obvious before. Similarly, your chatbot should analyze


customer feedback and user reviews to find the good, the bad,


and the ugly with the current business. Again, this analysis


should help you find previously undiscovered requirements.


Analyzing large volumes of customer feedback should give you


strong indications for your prioritization. Knowing, not


guessing, what is important to your customers should be one


of the prime drivers of the priority in which you discover


and develop requirements.


Machine learning (ML), another part of AI, builds models


from the supplied or training data. The models are


predictive; they help you identify potential future


requirements. This relies of course on having the right


training data. So, let’s suppose that you have the right


data on your and your competitors’ products. By analyzing


## 第 1176 页


the way that these products are used, it is possible for ML


to identify patterns of usage and make predictions on


different ways that your product could be used in the future.


ML would also identify the features or processes in the


products that caused the most complaints or that customers


found hard to use.


This is grist for your business analyst’s mill—these


predictions are the basis for requirements that can enhance


your current product or be incorporated in new products.


Business rules are sometimes hard to find, yet they must be


incorporated into any new solutions you develop. They are


hard to find in many organizations because there is no


central repository. If the organization is using a business


rules engine, then the problem is solved—all of the rules


are in one place and the only requirement is to consult the


business rule engine whenever the solution needs a business


decision. That is of course providing all the rules are in


the engine. On the other hand, if there is no central


repository, then natural language processing (discussed


above) can sift through huge amounts of data to uncover the


business rules for you.


## 第 1177 页


Data mining techniques can be used to analyze data from


various sources to identify requirements. Because there is so


much data to mine, you need the help of NLP or a chatbot to


do most of the work. You might start with your bot analyzing


your customer support tickets to determine the most common


problems and write requirements to alleviate or eliminate the


problems. You might have the bot trawl social media posts to


find what customers like and dislike.


If your customers are willing, chatbots can be used to


interact with them directly in a conversational manner. The


idea is for the chatbot to explore and uncover requirements


that might not have been obvious to you or your customers.


There is a caveat: You should never give confidential


information to a chatbot. The chatbot sees and remembers


everything, and you have no idea what it might do with your


confidential information.


AI has a role in requirements discovery if used wisely. It


should be seen—at least in the foreseeable future—as an


assistant to help you find the requirements. It can also help


you find new and innovative requirements that otherwise might


not have come to light. To do this, it is of course important


that the data you’re using is high-quality data and that the


AI algorithms are accurately trained.


## 第 1178 页


You can ask your AI assistant to check your requirements and


stories. It can root out ambiguous terms and inconsistent


terminology. It might (no guarantees) find gaps in the


requirements, or ambiguous or misdirected requirements.


AI is a powerful tool, and it has a future assisting you with


your business analysis and requirements discovery.


AI in Business Processes


The next facet of AI comes into play when you propose to have


AI as part of your solution. Suppose that you are working on


a traffic monitoring system. The intention is to control the


traffic lights of a major city, with the goal of maximizing


traffic throughput. When the lights are properly coordinated


throughout the city, traffic is able to move more quickly and


smoothly with fewer interruptions (such as being stopped at


the lights, or in gridlock).


Traffic volumes and the needs of drivers vary throughout the


day. After the morning commuter rush, delivery trucks with


their frequent stops take over, then this is replaced by the


lunchtime traffic pattern, and so on until the afternoon


commuters return home. Then, the evening pattern kicks in


with people going out for their entertainment.


## 第 1179 页


The regular usage patterns make programming traffic lights


more complicated, but what makes the task even harder is that


these patterns evolve and change over time. Sometimes these


changes are gradual, and sometimes they happen quite rapidly.


For example, people are coming into the office less


frequently, with some weekdays—particularly Fridays—having


very little commuter traffic. Seasonal sales can bring people


into the city to go shopping. Special events and public


holidays have an impact, as does the weather. We have also


seen how a pandemic can have a marked impact on traffic.


Enter AI. Your plan is to have a real-time AI component


learn the evolving traffic patterns and the volume of


traffic in different parts of the city. It will manipulate


the traffic lights to optimize the traffic flow according to


current conditions.


Now your business analysis skills come into play. AI can only


be as good as the questions it is asked. That is, the AI


engine has to correctly understand that your intention is to


optimize the traffic flow, and exactly what you mean by


“optimize.” Does that mean that a vehicle will get to its


destination more quickly, or does it mean that because of the


smooth flow of traffic, the driver perceives he is getting


there sooner, even if his speeds are actually slower? Does


## 第 1180 页


“optimize” mean that traffic coming from, say, the north,


is given higher priority than that from the west? Your bot


cannot “optimize” traffic unless the prompts you feed it


lead in the right direction.


Prompting


Prompt engineering, the term for working out the best


prompts or questions for AI, should now come up with a prompt


that optimizes traffic in the city. As indicated above, you


must be precise as to the meaning of “optimize.” The prompt


would be much longer than a single sentence, as you are


dealing with a complex problem. An embedded AI bot is


prompted once at the beginning. Thereafter—if you have


prompted correctly—it will learn about traffic and continue


to refine its behavior, resulting in a continual improvement


in the city’s traffic flow.


Let’s look at the learning part. As time progresses, the AI


bot learns what works and what doesn’t. It learns, for


example, that fires disrupt traffic, so it learns at which


times of the day fires are more likely to occur. It learns


how to set the traffic lights to get the fire engines to the


fire as quickly as possible.


## 第 1181 页


Your prompt would have had to tell the bot what you want it


to learn and what to do with what it learns. Your prompt also


tells the bot what it must never do (turn all the lights


green), and any other rules it must stick by.


This is a shift in the business analyst’s


responsibilities. You are now engineering prompts to produce


the optimal results from your AI bot. Your analysis is about


reaching a common understanding of the problem, and what role


AI is to play in the solution to the problem. AI is not smart


enough (yet) to understand what you are trying to achieve


unless you tell it.


Your ability to write the correct prompts determines the


value that your AI bot can deliver. Writing good prompts


starts with understanding the real problem, which is more or


less what we have been talking about throughout this book.


That is, find the real problem and write the right


requirements. Think of a prompt as the requirements for the


AI bot. You have already seen that the right approach to


requirements discovery leads to the right requirements. The


right approach will also, of course, lead you to write the


right prompts.


## 第 1182 页


BA skills will evolve over time as AI evolves, but whatever


happens, it will be exciting and promises some wonderful


business analysis opportunities.


Review


The greatest potential for artificial intelligence, as far as


the business analyst is concerned, is for it to be an


assistant for discovering requirements. It can assist by


suggesting lines of questioning, it can assist by suggesting


innovations, and it can assist by reviewing requirements


documentation.


AI will become part of most business processes. Your role as


a business analyst is to understand what AI can do as part of


those processes and to engineer the right prompts to cause


the AI bot to perform as needed. This, in a way, is what BAs


have been doing all along: discovering the correct problem to


solve, discovering the best solution for the problem, and


writing the requirements (in this case, prompts) to cause the


right solution to be built. Learn whatever you can about AI.


It is a significant part of your future.


Resources


## 第 1183 页


As we mentioned at the beginning of this chapter, anything


you write about AI is doomed to obsolescence. So, we feel it


is hardly productive to give you a list of books and other


resources that will be out of date by the time you read this.


At the time of writing, AI is showing explosive growth. New


books, articles, and websites are appearing almost by the


hour. Our best recommendation for getting an up-to-date list


of references is to ask ChatGPT (https://openai.com/chatgpt)


or one of the other bots to give them to you.


You might check out How to Create a Mind by Ray Kurzweil


(Penguin Books, 2013). This looks at reverse-engineering the


brain to understand it and using that knowledge to create


intelligent machines.


Sal Khan, the founder and CEO of Khan Academy, in his TED


Talk (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hJP5GqnTrNo) argues


that artificial intelligence will trigger the greatest


positive transformation education has ever seen.


## 第 1184 页


Chapter 44. Learning as You Go


Every time you do something you learn something, and you


reuse lessons that you learned in the past. Over time, every


individual builds up a store of knowledge, and the more


knowledge a person has, the more valuable he is to his


employer. However, when he goes home at night almost all of


his knowledge goes with him. Fortunately, his knowledge comes


back with him the following morning. Inevitably when he


leaves the organization, his knowledge leaves permanently.


This situation could be summed up by saying that people


learn, organizations don’t. That is, unless the organization


has a way of capturing and retaining knowledge as it is


acquired. The part of that knowledge we are concerned with


here is often called “lessons learned.”


Lessons learned is the process of capturing information about


what went right and what went wrong on a project. Learning


about successful projects helps other projects adopt the same


strategies and techniques. Learning about failures helps to


prevent other projects from repeating those mistakes in the


future. It is of course important that you are not operating


in a toxic blame culture, and that people feel confident to


## 第 1185 页


speak freely about their projects, knowing there will be no


recriminations.


“A lesson will repeat itself until learned.”—


Unknown source


Lessons Learned


Lessons-learned sessions are traditionally held at the end of


a project. However, by this time everybody is exhausted,


exhilarated, regretful, and probably unwilling to rehash a


project that has consumed their life for the last six months


or more. It is more likely the lessons will be better learned


if they are learned progressively.


Possibly the most valuable lessons-learned session is the


one you hold at the beginning of the project. Team members


can revisit similar projects from the past with a view to


avoiding the mistakes and making the most of the successes.


It is useful to keep in mind that even though you think of


your project as unique, it should be seen as one of many


projects of the same category or with the same


characteristics. Your project will be subject to the same


problems, setbacks, mishaps, staffing issues, and so on that


have plagued others of the same type. It is also worthwhile


## 第 1186 页


to look outside your own organization for lessons that have


been learned by other people’s projects.


“One of the strong points in IBM-s project


management model is lessons learned, which is


conducted on every project.”—John Capron,


technical team leader, IBM


It is of course profitable to have informal lessons-learned


sessions throughout the project. For example, members of a


Scrum development team meet at the end of each sprint for a


retrospective. These are short sessions where the team


discusses what went well, what problems were encountered, and


what they could do better. These improvements are


incorporated into the next sprint. This should be more or


less what you do throughout your requirements discovery. The


intention is that if things do go wrong, you and your team


learn about them as soon as possible and find a way to


prevent them for the rest of the project.


Lessons from Requirements


What lessons can you learn during a requirements discovery


effort? We suggest these (in no particular order).


## 第 1187 页


Scope creep: Is the scope creeping? Are new business events


being added? Are unexpected requirements occurring? Scope


creep is generally not a good thing—it interferes with


predictions on the duration of the effort, and in some cases


nullifies the point of the development project. It is also


useful to check previous projects for creep and from those


projects, see how much impact creep had on the project. The


extent of the creep is significant. There will always be some


creep, but once it starts to exceed 10% to 15% of the


original scope, there is cause for concern. When scope creep


becomes excessive—say, more than 45%—your project is out of


control and you should seriously consider abandoning it.


Effectiveness of requirements: Are the developers producing


the expected solution from your requirements? Do they


understand the requirements, or are they asking too many


questions? If they are, it suggests that the requirements and


their support documentation are inadequate. Requirements are


crucial to the development effort, and if there are problems


with them, the problems should be corrected before


significant damage is done.


Stakeholder behavior: Stakeholders, and the way they respond


to your requirements discovery, play a major role in the


success of the development effort. Are the stakeholders


## 第 1188 页


making themselves available, and cooperating when they do? Do


you have the right stakeholders? Are they competent and


knowledgeable enough to provide the information you need? Are


their expectations misaligned with the goals and timetable of


the project? If there are stakeholder problems, earlier


lessons-learned reports could have warned you about them.


Project timetable: Will you be able to meet the project’s


delivery dates? Lessons learned from previous development


efforts should warn of this. Some managers love to set


deadlines that are deliberately short, but allowing too


little time rarely produces the desired result. If your


project timetable leaves too little time for the work to be


done properly, then you are obliged to raise a red flag and


say that the required effort means that an on-time delivery


is impossible.


Changing requirements: The important lessons to learn from


changing requirements are the reasons they change. Sometimes


there are legitimate changes—the nature of the business has


changed, or a technological advance enables a different


business to be done. Otherwise, if the requirements are


frequently changing requirements, it signals that the


requirements are not correct in the first place.


Alternatively, the requirements might be solutions and not


## 第 1189 页


business requirements, and it quickly becomes clear that the


solution is solving the wrong problem. There are lessons to


be learned from changing requirements—much of the time the


problem lies with the requirements process.


Benefit shortfall: As you progress with your requirements


discovery, you should be constantly questioning whether the


cost of your efforts will outweigh the benefits the eventual


solution will bring. The initial enthusiasm for the project


often generates unrealistic expectations. The lessons learned


from this and previous projects should alert you that the


project is unlikely to deliver value.


What went well: It’s not all darkness and disaster. Your


lessons-learned sessions should reveal the aspects of your


requirements discovery that work well. If some team members


report that the stakeholders respond favorably to particular


techniques, then more of the team should try them. Similarly,


in lessons-learned sessions you will hear about the best


stakeholders to talk to, ways to write better requirements,


and anything else that the team finds productive and


effective.


Recording the Lessons


## 第 1190 页


Lessons learned must be recorded—they are too valuable to


leave solely in the heads of the team members. This


documentation need not be elaborate, but it should include


descriptions of the good things and the bad things, and the


recommendations on avoiding the bad things in the future.


This documentation should be made available to all


stakeholders, and they should be made aware that it exists.


There are several specialized automated tools for capturing


and disseminating lessons-learned knowledge. There are also


everyday document management systems (your organization


probably has one) and intranets and collaborative document


systems. If your organization does not already have an


automated way of storing lessons learned, given the


availability of tools, it should be relatively easy to set


one up.


Lesson learning is, or should be, organizational learning.


It is of such value to you and your team that it should be a


normal part of the way that you conduct your business


analysis. Sadly, many teams, and many organizations, ignore


the lessons of the past. Sadly, many teams and many


organizations repeat them.


Review

Figure 44.1 The virtuous circle of learning lessons. This is


a self-reinforcing cycle that continually builds


organizational knowledge.

The Fifth Discipline: The Art and Practice of the Learning

one of the early writers in the field. His diagramming of


cause and effect is excellent.


Black Box Thinking by Matthew Syed (Portfolio, 2015). This

industries.
