## 第 1193 页


Chapter 45. Requirements and Innovation


Not a lot of people think it is part of their job to be


innovative. And yet, it is your (and your team’s) ability to


produce fresh ideas that stands between your customer and


obsolescence. Without innovation, any solution will be more


or less the same as the one it’s replacing. New ideas are


needed to keep ahead of your competitors, and to provide


better solutions for your customers.


You, as a business analyst, have a responsibility here. You


should be constantly coming up with new ideas and not just


delivering what is asked for. Challenging the assumptions and


the presumed solutions is part of delivering a successful,


more valuable solution.


Innovation is most apparent during the Prototype the


Requirements activity. Here is where you are exploring the


problem space by sketching different solutions. If you are in


the early days of the project, novelty is highly valued. By


having new proposals, you are in a better position to guide


the team away from the presumed solution toward something


more beneficial. Innovation does not stop with prototyping—


it should be a part of all of your requirements discovery


activities. Your trawling, your design, and indeed your


## 第 1194 页


development all benefit from innovation. You will find that


there is almost a direct correlation between the amount of


innovation and the value of the delivered solution.


There is almost a direct correlation between the


amount of innovation and the value of the


delivered solution.


Dyson bagless vacuum cleaners, the World Wide Web, the


iPhone, graphical user interfaces, radar, the jet engine,


What3Words, software itself, and on and on—all of these


were, at the time of their invention, startlingly different


from what came before. All of them are valuable, some


incredibly so. All of them were, at the time, innovations. If


you look at the world’s most valuable companies, all of them


became valuable by being innovative. All of them have a


culture for innovation.


As a side note, you might have recognized the above list is


made up of things that people were not, at the time, asking


for. Yet, once people saw them, they realized how valuable


they were. This applies to you. Your innovation sessions


should produce solutions, features, and approaches that


people have not asked for. When you present them to the


## 第 1195 页


stakeholders, they could, and should, realize that they need


them.


You can learn to be innovative. You might not turn into the


next Steve Jobs or Thomas Edison or Ada Lovelace, you might


not invent the transistor or the telescope, but you can learn


to make fresh contributions to your project. You can


integrate innovation into your requirements discovery process


to make yourself and your team more creative, and to look at


problems in a more productive way.


The Value of Innovative Requirements


Innovation drives progress. It is progress that allows us to


advance and evolve. If we had no innovation, no progress, you


would ride a horse to work. Simply put, we need to innovate.


We need to find better solutions to our business problems. We


need to find ways to become more efficient. We need to


introduce fresh thinking to make our solutions valuable to


our customers.


Often, the business problem you are working on has an


existing solution, and your customer wants to renew and


refresh it. There are many reasons for wanting to do this:


changes in the marketplace, changes in technology, and so on.


## 第 1196 页


Most of the time, on renewal projects, the stakeholders ask


for what they have with some incremental improvements. Most


of the time, when this kind of solution is delivered, it is


met by disappointment. Disappointment in that it doesn’t


really provide enough benefit or do enough new things to be


considered valuable.


Your role, when you are discovering requirements, is to


listen to the stakeholders, but also to think about


innovations that could prove valuable to them. Business


analysts are not there to obediently record what the


stakeholders say they want. You need to innovate to get a


better result. So, your requirements should not be exactly


what was asked for, but improvements on what was asked for.


Earlier, in Chapter 13, Creative Candidate Solutions, we


discussed a number of techniques for having creative ideas.


In that chapter, we were talking about building prototypes.


However, the techniques from Chapter 13 can be used


throughout your requirements discovery process. When a


stakeholder asks for something, the innovative response is to


accept what is asked for and innovate ways to improve it.


As mentioned above, some of our best innovations are things


that nobody asked for. Unless your stakeholders are visionary


## 第 1197 页


people, they are probably not going to ask for solutions that


are a quantum leap over what currently exists. Which means it


is up to you, the business analyst and your team, to be the


ones to innovate. These innovations become part of your


specification or story map, and then part of the delivered


solution.


An Innovation Process and Requirements


It is difficult to say that something as creative as


innovation can be described by a process. However, if we look


at IDEO, a very successful US industrial design company, we


can see something of a process. It looks like this.


1. Observation: Here people from both IDEO and the client


observe the problem they are trying to solve. They also try


to experience the problem from the consumer’s point of view.


2. Brainstorming: IDEO mixes various stakeholders, clients,


and analysts to study the problem and come up with a number


of possible solutions.


3. Rapid prototyping: The engineers make quick-and-dirty


models to help with visualizing and understanding the problem


and the solution.


## 第 1198 页


4. Refining: Here they narrow down the choices to a few


possibilities.


Let’s look at how the IDEO process fits with the Volere


requirements discovery process. We have been looking at


this throughout this book, and it is shown again in Figure


45.1.


## 第 1199 页


![embedded_p1199_182.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1199_182.jpeg)


Figure 45.1 The Volere requirements discovery process.


Innovation plays a part in all its activities.


The process begins with the Project Blastoff. This is where


you work with the various stakeholders to define the problem


## 第 1200 页


and its scope. You also decide the goals of the project that


is setting out to solve this problem. It is during the


blastoff that you are observing and understanding the


problem.


In Part III of this book, we spoke about Prototyping for


Requirements, and how you create prototypes of candidate


solutions. We suggested that you can think of brainstorming


and rapid prototyping as the same activity.


Then comes IDEO’s refining and converging. Prototyping is


the activity where you are trying to generate as many ideas


as possible. In other words, you are having diverging ideas.


Then comes the probing activity, which we spoke about in


Chapter 14, Probing and Exploring the Candidates. Here you


are converging and narrowing down the candidates while


learning more about the problem.


The final design of the solution comes when you move into


the design arena. This is described in Part VI of this book.


Here you take what you have learned from Trawling and


Prototyping and craft the solution to be implemented. At this


stage there is still room for innovation. You can innovate


better ways to arrange components of the solution, better


## 第 1201 页


ways to carry out the requirements, better appearance and


better workability.


The moral of the story is that you can be, and should be,


innovative throughout the requirements discovery process.


A Culture for Innovation


A culture for innovation and a culture for effective


requirements discovery are the same. Culture, as we use the


term here, is a set of attitudes and behaviors that are


shared by your team of business analysts, developers,


stakeholders, and other people concerned with the


requirements and delivery of the correct and best business


solution.


Culture is a “soft” subject—it is impossible to measure,


but it can be observed. Let’s look at the observable


features of a culture for innovation.


Safety


First up is the organization’s attitude toward safety.


Innovation relies on taking risks by having new ideas. It


relies on trying things to see if they work. It relies on


## 第 1202 页


challenging the status quo and proposing new and different


solutions. It relies on fresh thinking.


None of these are possible unless people feel safe. If they


think that they will be ridiculed, criticized, or disregarded


for the rest of the project, they will naturally be reluctant


to propose any potentially risky ideas.


Yet, it is from these risky ideas that we have great


solutions. An obvious example is the touchscreen phone that


you, and most of the planet, carry around. Imagine the time


when the incomplete idea for the iPhone was first aired. What


would have happened if Apple’s management had dismissed it?


• “It will kill off the iPod market” (it did, but Apple


grew much richer).


• “This thing is more of a computer than a phone” (it is,


but that allows apps).


• “Nobody will want a phone without a keypad” (all phones


prior to the iPhone had an array of physical buttons to dial


with).


Fortunately, the Apple engineers operated in a safe


environment. They were allowed, even encouraged, to voice


## 第 1203 页


their incomplete ideas.


Consider Thomas Edison, one of the most innovative people


ever, and his tongue-in-cheek remark that he had not failed,


just found 10,000 things that didn’t work. Edison understood


that his engineers needed to take risks and that many of


their innovations would turn out to be unusable. But the


engineers worked in safety, knowing that they would not be


criticized or demeaned if their ideas were incomplete or a


prototype did not work.


Edison understood that risk was a necessary part of


innovation. His greatest innovation was not the light bulb


nor the gramophone, but the electricity distribution grid. He


understood that if people were to buy his light bulbs, they


first needed to have electricity in their houses.


“Hold on, Thomas, you can’t go running wires all over the


city. It’s never been done before. It’ll be expensive. The


wires might frighten the horses.”


It is hard to imagine not having electricity flowing reliably


into your home, but you have it because Edison was willing to


take the risk.


## 第 1204 页


Safety also means that it is safe to challenge conventional


thinking. The role of the business analyst is changing.


Challenging existing solutions and existing processes has


become very much a part of the new business analyst’s


responsibilities. It is by being willing to break the old way


of thinking that the business analyst can find new things.


Naturally, your organizational culture must make it safe to


criticize cherished beliefs or processes.


Blame


Safety also means freedom from blame. Consider this: When


something goes wrong at your organization, is the first


reaction to find what went wrong and why it went wrong? Or


is it to find out who went wrong? In other words, is it


organizational culture to find someone to blame? It often


does not matter whether the culprit is guilty or not—someone


must be blamed. In this kind of organization, nobody wants to


be impeached, so nobody takes any risks. Nobody challenges


the existing processes or solutions. Nobody proposes new


ideas. Nobody tries to do anything except conform as closely


as possible to the current state of affairs and conventional


solutions.


Democracies and Skunkworks


## 第 1205 页


Innovation works best in democracies. All the great


innovations have come from democracies rather than from


authoritarian regimes. The freedom to experiment is far more


effective than an authoritative regime dictating what must be


done.


In the same way, bureaucracies are authoritarian. If there is


a central planning committee, then it limits innovations to


what the committee can agree on. It is likely that very


little will be. To overcome their own bureaucracy, some


organizations create “skunkworks” projects. The name goes


back quite far, but the essence of the technique is to form a


small group who are outside the normal reporting hierarchy.


The group answers to a single person high in the management


structure and nobody else. This manager’s task is to be an


umbrella and shield the skunkworks project from any outside


interference.


An excellent example of skunkworks came when IBM decided to


build a personal computer. At the time, IBM manufactured


mainframe and minicomputers, and had a stranglehold on the


world’s computing market. But IBM saw that change was in the


air. Young people in their parents’ garages were building


personal computers that were becoming more capable by the


day, but none of them were thought suitable for corporate


## 第 1206 页


use. IBM knew that having the IBM badge on a machine would


add gravitas, and probable adoption by regular businesses.


IBM also knew that its bureaucracy would strangle the


development of something so outside its normal product line.


The chairman estimated that going through the normal channels


would take four years and 300 people before they had anything


like a viable product. If IBM was to get a foothold into the


PC market, it needed to get its product there quickly.


This prompted the IBM skunkworks project (it was actually


called “Project Chess”). A small number of engineers who


used non-IBM technology and non-IBM software were tasked to


create their machine in under a year. They even went outside


IBM for the operating system (OS). They found it in a Seattle


startup called Microsoft run by a 24-year-old Bill Gates.


Gates was happy to supply them with his QDOS (the QD is for


quick and dirty) operating system.


So, IBM went to market with an IBM badge on the outside of


their machine and Microsoft software on the inside. The


result was a raging success when very quickly corporate


America realized the value of putting a personal computer on


employees’ desks.


## 第 1207 页


If you work on a Windows desktop machine, it’s a direct


descendant of a skunkworks team working outside the


bureaucracy and being free to make its own decisions.


The Sanctity of the Incomplete Idea


Very few ideas are born fully formed—most of them are


embryonic. And just like a human embryo, they must go through


a gestation period and be nourished and cared for and


developed before they are ready to be born into the world.


Some organizational cultures immediately trash any idea that


is not obviously fully formed and viable. However, most ideas


are incomplete when they are first aired. Choking off


incomplete ideas restricts the flow of innovations and


discourages people from having ideas. By nurturing and


developing incomplete ideas, you get the advantage of group


improvement and the likelihood of new ideas emerging.


An example of an incomplete idea being nurtured until it was


ready for prime time is the Dyson vacuum cleaner. These


bagless cleaners have become the biggest-selling vacuum


cleaners in the world, but it took over 5,000 prototypes


before it was ready for the market.


## 第 1208 页


At some stage of your life, you will have used WD-40. This is


an all-purpose lubricant used to stop hinges squeaking, to


loosen rusted-in bolts and jammed door locks, separate stuck


LEGO parts, get crayon marks of walls, get chewing gum out of


your kid’s hair, and clean the stainless-steel splash panel


behind your cooktop. Despite its ubiquity, it is unlikely


that many people wonder about its name. WD is for water


dispersant, and 40 is the number of attempts the engineers


made before they hit on the right formula and had a product


suitable to release.


The airplane you fly in today is a descendent, in one way or


another, of the Wright Flyer. Orville and Wilbur Wright were


not engineers; they ran a bicycle business in Ohio. They were


curious about flight, and their curiosity gave them the idea


to build a heavier-than-air flying machine. Nobody else had


done it at the time. It took a few years, and Orville and


Wilbur went through many prototypes. Along the way, they had


setbacks, but whenever something did not work they went back,


studied the problem, and found a suitable solution. They


persisted with their incomplete idea until eventually the


Wright Flyer flew for 852 feet in December 1903, at Kitty


Hawk, North Carolina.


## 第 1209 页


Was the flying machine an incomplete idea? Sure. At the time,


nobody knew whether it was possible or not. Was it a safe


environment for Wilbur and Orville to innovate in? Sure.


Apparently, they used to argue a lot, but always about the


machine they were building; it was never personal. It must


have been safe to argue like this; the brothers stayed


together until they succeeded and remained close for the rest


of their lives.


Enlightened organizations know that their continued existence


relies on innovation. As all innovation starts with an idea,


these organizations are careful to offer a safe haven for


their incomplete ideas. One day they might turn into


successful products.


Innovation and Requirements


As much as you would like to, it is probable that you are not


going to invent something—such as the Wright Flyer or the


iPhone—that will change the world. But that doesn’t mean


you invent nothing. Your solutions should be made up of lots


of little—sometimes no so little—innovations that you and


your team created along the way.


## 第 1210 页


You are not a slave to your stakeholders. Because a


requirement is asked for does not mean that it is the final


word. It sometimes can be improved upon, or sometimes a


better, more innovative alternative can be created. You


should operate in the “blue zone.”


We wrote about the blue zone in a previous book, Adrenaline


Junkies and Template Zombies. It works like this: Your leader


gives you an assignment. This might be the whole project, or


it might be to investigate and write the requirements for one


business event. The assignment is your “green zone”; it has


a purpose and boundaries. The assignment might also have a


“red zone”—things that your leader has made specifically


off-limits and you should not concern yourself with them.


You start to work on your green zone, and fairly soon you


find yourself taking an interest in things outside it. You


are venturing into a new area. This is not the red zone; this


is a new area. This is the blue zone. The elements in the


blue zone are those that would be beneficial to investigate


with the potential of including them in your solution.


The criterion for venturing into the blue zone is the


potential for benefit to the project and the delivered


## 第 1211 页


solution. You don’t ask for permission to go into the blue


zone; you just know that it will be valuable.


One reason you might operate in the blue zone is the


difference between incremental and innovative. As discussed


earlier in this chapter, people, particularly users, tend to


ask for incremental improvements: “I need the three screens


I have with the current version, but I need a little more


data on two of them.” An innovative solution might replace


two of the screens with some automation, or it could do


almost anything else.


To put this into practice, you must be willing to challenge


almost everything you are told. Not by loudly and


aggressively attacking each proposal, but by quietly


questioning the value of them.


• Can you use any of the innovation techniques or creative


triggers from Chapter 13, Creative Candidate Solutions, to


generate something that either improves the requirement or is


a beneficial alternative?


• Ask what happens if you don’t include this requirement.


• Are you or your stakeholder making assumptions about the


requirement?


## 第 1212 页


• Can you approach it “laterally” and see if there is a


more creative requirement to be had?


• Is it a requirement or a solution, and what problem is it


solving? Is there a more beneficial problem to solve?


Of course, you would not do this to every atomic requirement.


Perhaps operating at the business event or functional story


level would be more productive. But you are still questioning


much of what you are told. You are not exactly being an


anarchist, just slightly subversive.


Your task, and here we are paraphrasing Denys Lasdun, an


architect, is not to give your customers what they ask for,


but to give them something that when they see it, they


realize it is what they wanted all along. This is giving


customers what they need.


Requirements discovery can be a creative activity. It is a


necessary activity and can be made more fulfilling when you


mix in a few innovations. Your solutions will be better for


it.


And that brings us to the end of the book. If you have read


it all the way through, then you have the authors’


admiration and gratitude. Along the way we hope that you have


## 第 1213 页


found something—preferably several somethings—that will


make you better at requirements discovery and make your


requirements and stories more precise and more valuable.


We set out to write this edition to bring you a reliable


companion for your requirements work. We also intended to


make a noticeable difference to the way that you see


requirements and go about discovering them and writing them.


We hope that you have enjoyed our book and found enough wise


words to make your investment in it worthwhile and


beneficial.


Our best wishes, James and Suzanne

Volere


Volere is the result of many years of practice, consulting,


and research in requirements engineering and business


analysis. We have packaged our experience in the form of a


generic requirements process, requirements training,


requirements consultancy, requirements audits, a variety of


downloadable guides and articles, a requirements knowledge


model, and this requirements template.


The first edition of the Volere Requirements Specification


Template was released in 1995. Since then, thousands of


organizations all over the world have saved time and money by


using the template as the basis for discovering, organizing,


and communicating their requirements.


The Volere website, https://www.volere.org, contains articles


about the Volere techniques, experiences of Volere users and


case studies, requirements tools, and other information


useful to requirements practitioners. Updates to this


## 第 1217 页


template and instructions for downloading are also available


there.


Requirement Types


For ease of use, we have found it convenient to think of


requirements as belonging to a type. Having types is an aid


to discovering the requirements and allows for groups that


are relevant to a specific expert specialty.


Functional requirements describe what the product has to do,


the rules that it has to carry out, what it has to remember,


and what processing actions it must take.


Non-functional requirements are the properties that the


functions must have, such as performance and usability. Do


not be deterred by the unfortunate name for this kind of


requirement; they are as important as the functional


requirements for the product’s success.


Constraints impose restrictions on the chosen solution.


These restrictions might apply to the whole project; for


example, budget, time, and skills. Other constraints relate


to the technology to be used to implement a solution or


business practices that must be conformed with.


## 第 1218 页


Project drivers are the business-related forces. For


example, the purpose of the project is a project driver, as


are all the stakeholders—each for different reasons.


Project issues define the conditions under which the project


will be done. Our reason for including them as part of the


requirements is to present a coherent picture of all factors


that contribute to the success or failure of the project and


to illustrate how managers can use requirements knowledge as


input to help manage a project.


Testing Requirements


The Volere philosophy is to start testing requirements as


soon as you start writing them. You make a requirement


testable by adding its fit criterion. This fit criterion


measures the requirement, making it possible to determine


whether a given solution fits the requirement. All


requirements can be measured, and all should carry a fit


criterion.


The Snow Card


The snow card is a guide to writing an atomic requirement. An


atomic requirement is not further decomposed. The components


of the snow card are identified below.


## 第 1219 页


The snow card can be on paper, which is convenient to use


when you are a face-to-face team, or automated, for when you


are a remote team. The snow card is shown in Figure A.1.


## 第 1220 页


![embedded_p1220_183.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1220_183.jpeg)


Figure A.1 The Volere snow card: a guide to the well-written


requirement


## 第 1221 页


The following discusses and provides examples for each


section of the Volere Requirements Specification Template.


Sections may have headings of Content, Motivation, Examples,


Considerations, and Form. These help explain the content.


1. The Purpose of the Project


The first section of the template deals with the fundamental


reason your client asked you to build a new product. That is,


it describes the business problem the client faces and


explains how the product is intended to solve the problem.


1a. The User Business or Background of the Project Effort


Content


A short description of the business being done, its context,


and the situation that triggered the development effort. It


should also describe the work that the user intends to do


with the delivered product.


Motivation


Without this statement, the project lacks justification and


direction.


Considerations


## 第 1222 页


You should consider whether the business problem is


significant enough to warrant the expense of solving it.


Perhaps there is not a problem, just a significant business


opportunity your client wishes to exploit. In this case,


describe the opportunity.


Alternatively, the project may seek to explore or investigate


possibilities. In this case the project deliverable, instead


of a new product, would be a document proving that the


requirements for a product can (or cannot) be satisfied.


Form


A short text description is often sufficient to provide an


understanding of the project. You can choose to support the


description with models and photographs.


1b. Goals of the Project


Content


This part of the specification describes what we want the


product to do and what advantage it will bring to the overall


goals of the work. Do not be too wordy in this section—a


brief explanation of the project’s goals is usually more


valuable than a long, rambling treatise. A short, sharp goal


## 第 1223 页


will be clearer to the stakeholders and improve the chances


of reaching a consensus for the goal.


Motivation


There is a danger that the goal gets lost along the way. As


the development effort heats up, and as the customer and


developers discover more about what is possible, the solution


can wander away from the original goals as it undergoes


construction. The goals should be very public, and the team


should periodically be reminded of them.


Examples


We want to eliminate delays between the customer ordering


online and the shipping of the goods.


To reduce road accidents by accurately forecasting and


scheduling the deicing of roads.


Measurement


Any reasonable goal must be measurable. This is necessary if


you are ever to test whether you have succeeded with the


project. The measurement must quantify the advantage gained


by the business through doing the project. For example, if


the goal of the project is:


## 第 1224 页


We want to eliminate delays between the customer ordering


online and the shipping of the goods.


you must ask what advantage meeting that goal brings to the


organization. If immediate shipping results in more satisfied


customers, then the measurement must quantify that


satisfaction. For example, you could measure the increase in


repeat business (on the basis that a happy customer comes


back for more), the increase in customer approval ratings


from surveys, the increase in revenue from returning


customers, and so on.


Ask whether your goal is one of the following.


• Service goal: This is measured by quantifying what it does


for the customer.


• Revenue goal: Quantify revenue or revenue growth over what


period. Alternatively, a revenue goal could be quantified by


market share.


• Legal goal: This is not a quantification, but a way of


knowing that the product conforms to a piece of legislation.


It is crucial to the rest of the development effort that the


goal is firmly established, is reasonable, and is measured.


## 第 1225 页


It is usually the latter that makes the former possible.


Form


You can use Purpose, Advantage, Measurement (PAM) to


structure your goal


• Purpose: One sentence to explain the organization’s


reason for investing in the project.


• Advantage: One sentence describing the benefit that the


organization will realize if the project is successful


• Measurement: One sentence or a graph or diagram that


quantifies how you will measure whether the benefit has been


achieved


Another form for your goals might be to use some kind of goal


model. For example, the Extended Enterprise Modeling Language


(EEML) includes a goal modeling technique. If your


organization is using enterprise modeling, then this provides


a connection between the enterprise’s strategic goals and


the goal of an individual project.


You can also use a value proposition statement as a way to


capture the overall goal of investing in a project. For


## 第 1226 页


example, a value proposition statement for the road deicing


project could be:


As a Road Authority


I receive value when accidents attributed to ice are no more


than specified by the European Road Safety Standard EU-1047-


AHG-4.


2. The Stakeholders


This section describes the stakeholders—the people who have


an interest in the product. It is worth your while to spend


enough time to find all the stakeholders. Missing


stakeholders usually means missing requirements.


2a. The Client


Content


This item gives the name of the client (sometimes referred to


as the sponsor). It is permissible to have several names, but


having more than three negates the point.


Motivation


## 第 1227 页


The client has the final say on acceptance of the product and


thus must be satisfied with the product as delivered. After


all, the client is the person who makes the investment in the


product. If you cannot find a name for your client, then


perhaps you should not be building the product.


Considerations


Sometimes, when building a product for external users, the


client is the marketing department.


Form


An annotated organization chart showing where the client fits


within the organization. A list of the decisions for which


the client will be responsible. You can also include a chart


showing the review checkpoints and itemizing what you will


provide for the client as progress indicators for the


project.


2b. The Customer


Content


The person intended to buy the product. In the case of in-


house development, the client and the customer are probably


the same person. The customer might also be the manager who


## 第 1228 页


decides whether the people for whom he is responsible will


adopt a new/changed product.


In the case of development of a mass-market product, this


section contains a description of the persona developed as


the archetypical customer for the product (see section 2e).


Motivation


The customer is ultimately responsible for deciding whether


to buy or recommend the use of the product. The correct


requirements can be discovered only if you understand the


customer and her aspirations when it comes to using your


product.


Form


A list of the decisions for which the customer will be


responsible. You can also include a chart showing the review


checkpoints and itemizing what you will provide for the


customer as progress indicators for the project. This might


include a list of possible prototypes or simulations that you


will provide for the customer during the progress of the


project.


2c. Other Stakeholders


## 第 1229 页


Content


The roles and (if possible) names of other people and


organizations that are affected by the product, or whose


input is needed to discover the requirements and build the


product. These stakeholders might work for your organization


or might be external.


Following are examples of stakeholders:


• Client/sponsor (refer to section 2a)


• Customer (refer to section 2b)


• Subject-matter experts


• Users of a current system


• Marketing experts


• Legal experts


• Security experts


• Domain experts


• Usability experts


## 第 1230 页


• Representatives of external associations


• Business analysts


• Designers and developers


• Testers


• Technology experts


• System designers


For each type of stakeholder, it might be useful to provide


the following information:


• Stakeholder identification (some combination of role/job


title, person name, and organization name)


• Knowledge that the project needs from that stakeholder


• The degree of involvement necessary for that


stakeholder/knowledge combination


• The degree of influence for that stakeholder/knowledge


combination


• Agreement on how to address conflicts between stakeholders


who have an interest in the same knowledge


## 第 1231 页


Motivation


Failure to recognize stakeholders results in missing


requirements.


Form


A stakeholder map supported by the name of the representative


of each role together with the knowledge to be supplied by


that role. Figure A.2 shows a generic stakeholder map that


you can use as a checklist. You would replace the role names


with the specific people/roles/organizations for your


project.


## 第 1232 页


![embedded_p170_23.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p170_23.jpeg)


Figure A.2 The stakeholder map or “onion diagram” used to


identify stakeholders.


## 第 1233 页


Another form you can use to identify the stakeholders is a


Stakeholder Analysis Spreadsheet. A sample is downloadable at


https://www.volere.org/templates/stakeholder-analysis-


download.


An annotated organization chart is also a useful form for


defining stakeholders.


2d. The Hands-On Users of the Product


Content


A list of a special type of stakeholder—the potential users


of the product. For each category of user, provide the


following information.


• User name/category: Most likely the name of a user group,


such as clerical users, schoolchildren, road engineers, or


project managers.


• User role: Summarizes the users’ responsibilities.


• Subject-matter experience: Summarizes the users’


knowledge of the subject matter/business. Rate as novice,


intermediate, or expert.


## 第 1234 页


• Technological experience: Describes the users’ experience


with relevant technology. Rate as novice, intermediate, or


expert.


• Other user characteristics: Describe any characteristics


of the users that have an effect on the requirements and


eventual design of the product. For example:


∘ Physical abilities/disabilities


∘ Intellectual abilities/disabilities


∘ Attitude toward job


∘ Attitude toward technology


∘ Physical location


∘ Education


∘ Linguistic skills


∘ Age group


∘ Gender


∘ Ethnic group/s


## 第 1235 页


Motivation


Users are human beings who interface with the product in some


way. Use the characteristics of the users to define the


usability requirements for the product. Without a thorough


knowledge of the users, you end up building a product that is


not connected to the real world. Users are also sometimes


known as actors.


Examples


Users can come from a wide variety of (sometimes unexpected)


sources. Consider the possibility of your users being


clerical staff, shop workers, managers, highly trained


operators, the general public, casual users, passers-by,


illiterate people, tradespeople, students, test engineers,


foreigners, children, lawyers, remote users, emergency


workers, and so on.


Form


A simple user characteristics list or spreadsheet containing


for each user: User Role + User Name/Representative + all the


relevant characteristics (see under Content above) for that


user.


2e. Personas


## 第 1236 页


Content


A persona is a virtual person produced using data and team


knowledge of the target audience. This section contains a


description of the persona, which might include the


persona’s name, age, job, family, hobbies, where they live,


favorite food, favorite music, likes, dislikes, where they go


on holiday, attitude toward technology, attitude toward


money, or any other characteristic that could influence the


way the persona thinks of the product. It helps if you


include a photograph or drawing of the imagined person.


Motivation


By having a persona, you can make the requirements specific


to the archetypical person your solution is aimed at. This is


a particularly effective technique if you are specifying the


requirements for a consumer product or a product to be used


by members of the public.


Form


A profile of the persona. Include a photograph of the


persona. You can download a suitable one from the internet.


2f. Priorities Assigned to Users


## 第 1237 页


Content


Attach a priority to each category of user. This identifies


the importance and precedence of the user and helps you plan


how to use your time. Prioritize the users as follows.


• Key users: They are critical to the continued success of


the product. Give greater importance to requirements


generated by this category of user.


• Secondary users: They will use the product, but their


opinion of it has no effect on its long-term success. Where


there is a conflict between secondary users’ requirements


and those of key users, the key users take precedence.


• Unimportant users: This category of user is given the


lowest priority. It includes infrequent, unauthorized, and


unskilled users, as well as people who misuse the product.


The percentage of the type of user is intended to assess the


amount of consideration given to each category of user.


Motivation


If some users are more important to the product or to the


organization, then this preference should be stated because


it affects the way that you design the product. For example,


## 第 1238 页


key customers represent a significant part of the


organization’s revenue and should be given preferential


treatment.


Some users may be listed as having no impact on the product.


These users will make use of the product but have no vested


interest in it. Any special requirements from these users


will have a lower priority.


Form


Include the user importance rating on your user


characteristics spreadsheet; see section 2d for the


information of the core project team. Depending on the


culture of your organization, you might need to treat this as


sensitive information.


2g. User Participation


Content


Where appropriate, attach to the category of user a statement


of the participation that you think is necessary for those


users to provide the requirements. Describe the contribution


that you expect these users to make; for example, business


knowledge, interface prototyping, or usability requirements.


If possible, assess the minimum amount of time that these


## 第 1239 页


users must spend for you to be able to determine the complete


requirements.


Motivation


Many projects fail through lack of user participation. When


people must make a choice between getting their everyday work


done and working on a new project, the everyday work usually


takes priority. This user participation requirement makes it


clear from the outset that specified user resources must be


allocated to the project.


Form


Include the estimated user participation time, together with


the type of knowledge you expect that user to provide, on


your user characteristics spreadsheet; see section 2d.


2h. Maintenance Users and Service Technicians


Content


Maintenance users are a special type of hands-on user who has


requirements that are specific to maintaining and changing


the product.


Motivation


## 第 1240 页


Many of these requirements will be discovered by considering


the various types of maintainability and support requirements


detailed in section 14. However, if you define the


characteristics of the people who maintain the product, it


will help to trigger requirements that might otherwise be


missed.


Form


Include the maintenance users on your user characteristics


spreadsheet; see section 2d.


3. Constraints


This section describes constraints on the eventual design of


the product. Constraints are restrictions that must be


satisfied.


Constraints are global—they are factors that apply to the


entire product. Often you know about the constraints, or they


are mandated before the project gets under way. They are


probably determined by management and are worth considering


carefully—they restrict what you can do and so shape the


product. Constraints, like other types of requirements, have


a description, rationale, and fit criterion, and generally


## 第 1241 页


are written in the same format as functional and non-


functional requirements.


3a. Solution Constraints


Content


This specifies constraints on the way that the problem must


be solved. Describe the mandated technology or solution. You


should also explain the reason for using the technology.


Motivation


To identify constraints that guide the final product. Your


client, customer, or user may have design preferences, or


only certain solutions may be acceptable. If these


constraints are not met, your solution is not acceptable.


Examples


Constraints are written using the same form as other atomic


requirements (refer to the atomic requirements snow card for


the attributes). It is important for each constraint to have


a rationale and a fit criterion, as they help to expose false


constraints (solutions masquerading as constraints).


## 第 1242 页


Description: The product shall use calls to mobile phones to


communicate with the drivers in their trucks.


Rationale: The client will not pay for a new radio system,


nor are any other means of communication available to the


drivers.


Fit criterion: All signals generated by the product shall be


understandable by all drivers.


Description: The product shall operate under Windows 10.


Rationale: The client uses Windows 10 and does not wish to


change to a later version.


Fit criterion: The product shall be approved as Windows 10


compliant by the Microsoft testing group.


Considerations


We want to define the boundaries within which we can solve


the problem. The solution constraints should only be those


that are non-negotiable, and not the whim of a manager.


Form


## 第 1243 页


Include the constraint requirements as a specific type of


atomic requirement in your requirements spreadsheet or


database.


Another form for constraints can be diagram(s) of the systems


architecture for the new/changed product—see sections 3b and


3c.


3b. Implementation Environment of the Current System


Content


This describes the technological and physical environment in


which the product is to be installed. It includes automated,


mechanical, organizational, and other devices, along with the


nonhuman adjacent systems.


Motivation


To describe the technological environment into which the


product must fit. The environment places design constraints


on the product. This part of the specification provides


enough information about the environment for the designers to


make the product successfully interact with its surrounding


technology.


## 第 1244 页


The operational requirements are derived from this


description.


Examples


Examples can be shown as a diagram, with an icon to represent


each device or person. Add interfaces between the processors


and annotate them with their form and content.


Considerations


All component parts of the current system, regardless of


their type, should be included in the description of the


implementation environment.


If the product is to affect or be important to the current


organization, then include an organization chart.


Form


A diagram that represents each hardware and software


component/subcomponent/device/building block that will be


used to implement the product. The diagrams that you use


depend on your organization and your projects’ ways of


working; the important point is that the implementation


environment is unambiguously understandable by the people who


## 第 1245 页


have to make decisions about how the functional and non-


functional requirements will be implemented.


3c. Partner or Collaborative Applications


Content


This describes applications that are not part of the product


but with which the product will collaborate. They can be


external applications, ready-made solutions, or preexisting


in-house applications.


Motivation


To provide information about design constraints caused by


using partner applications. By describing or modeling these


partner applications, you discover and highlight potential


problems of integration.


Examples


This section can be completed by including written


descriptions, models, or references to other specifications.


The descriptions must include a full specification of all


interfaces that have an effect on the product.


Considerations


## 第 1246 页


Examine the work context model to determine whether any of


the adjacent systems should be treated as partner


applications. It might also be necessary to examine some of


the details inside the scope of the work (see section 6) to


discover relevant partner applications.


Form


A diagram or table that identifies all the interfaces between


the product to be built and other adjacent systems. Bear in


mind that the adjacent systems might be software, human, or


hardware. Some adjacent systems are within your organization


and hence potentially more easily understood and perhaps


influenced. Other adjacent systems are outside your


organization and might be difficult if not impossible to


influence. A product scope diagram (see section 8a for an


example) is often used to define interfaces with partner or


collaborative applications.


3d. Ready-Made or Off-the-Shelf Software


Content


This describes ready-made components or solutions that must


be used to implement some of the requirements for the


product. This could be commercial, open-source, or any other


## 第 1247 页


off-the-shelf (OTS) or legacy software. It could also apply


to non-software OTS components such as hardware or any other


commercial product that is intended as part of the solution.


Motivation


To identify and describe any ready-made components to be


incorporated into the eventual product. The characteristics,


behavior, and interfaces of the ready-made are design


constraints.


Considerations


When gathering requirements, you may discover requirements


that conflict with the behavior and characteristics of the


ready-made solution. In light of your discoveries, you must


consider whether the ready-made product is a viable choice.


If the use of the ready-made software is not negotiable, then


the conflicting requirements must be discarded.


Note that your strategy for discovering requirements is


affected by the decision to use ready-made software. In this


situation, you investigate the work context in parallel with


making comparisons with the capabilities of the ready-made


product. Depending on the comprehensibility of the OTS


software, you might be able to discover the matches or


## 第 1248 页


mismatches without having to write each business requirement


in atomic detail. The mismatches are the requirements that


you will need to specify so that you can decide whether to


satisfy them by either customizing the ready-made solution or


satisfying the requirement in another way, such as modifying


the business environment.


Form


Models or written documentation that specifies the functional


and non-functional requirements that can be implemented using


this ready-made software product.


3e. Anticipated Workplace Environment


Content


This describes the workplace in which the users work and use


the product. It should describe any features of the workplace


that could influence the design of the product, and the


social and cultural aspects of the workplace.


Motivation


To identify characteristics of the workplace so that the


product is designed to compensate for any difficulties.


## 第 1249 页


Examples


The single office printer is a considerable distance from the


user’s desk. This constraint suggests that printed output


should be deemphasized.


The workplace is noisy, so audible signals might not work.


The workplace is outside, so the product must be weather


resistant, have displays that are visible in sunlight, and


allow for the effect of wind on any paper output.


The product is to be used in a library; it must be extra


quiet.


The user will be standing up or working in positions where he


must hold the product. This suggests a hand-held product, but


only a careful study of the user’s work and workplace will


provide the necessary input to identifying the operational


requirements.


Considerations


The physical work environment constrains the way that work is


done. The product should overcome whatever difficulties


exist; however, you might consider a redesign of the


## 第 1250 页


workplace as an alternative to having the product compensate


for it.


Form


A written description of the workplace; rich pictures showing


all the components in the workplace; photographs of the


workplace; videos of the workplace.


3f. Schedule Constraints


Content


Any known deadlines or windows of opportunity should be


stated here.


Motivation


To identify critical times and dates that influence product


requirements. If the deadline is short, then the requirements


must be kept to whatever can be built within the time


allowed.


Examples


To meet scheduled software releases.


## 第 1251 页


There may be other parts of the business or other software


products that are dependent on this product.


Windows of marketing opportunity.


Scheduled changes to the business that will use your product.


For example, the organization may be starting up a new


factory and your product is needed before production can


commence.


Considerations


State deadline limitations by giving the date and describing


why it is critical. Also, identify prior dates on which parts


of your product need to be available for testing.


You should also ask questions about the impact of not meeting


the deadline.


• What happens if we don’t build the product by the end of


the calendar year?


• What is the financial impact of not having the product by


the beginning of the Christmas buying season?


• What parts of the product are most critical for the


Christmas buying season?


## 第 1252 页


Form


A written statement giving the date of the deadline, the


reason for the deadline, and the effect of not meeting the


deadline.


3g. Budget Constraints


Content


This section shows the budget for the project, expressed in


money or available resources.


Motivation


The requirements must not exceed the budget. This limitation


may constrain the number of requirements that can be met by


the product. The intention of this question is to determine


whether the product is really wanted.


Considerations


The intention is to restrict the wildest ambitions and to


prevent the team from gathering requirements for an Airbus


380 when the budget can only buy a Cessna. Is it realistic to


build a product within this budget? If the answer to this


question is no, then either the client is not really


## 第 1253 页


committed to building the product or the client does not


place enough value on the product. In either case, you should


consider whether it is worthwhile to continue.


Form


A written statement giving the amount of the budget and the


source of the funding.


3h. Enterprise Constraints


Content


This section contains requirements that are specific to the


enterprise that is making the investment in your project.


Motivation


To understand requirements that sometimes appear irrelevant


or irrational because they are not obviously relevant to the


goals of the project.


Examples


The product shall be installed using only American-made


components.


## 第 1254 页


The product shall make all functionality available to the


CEO.


Considerations


Is there a company-wide edict that only specified browsers or


only specified mobile operating systems are to be used?


Is a director also on the board of a company that


manufactures products similar to the one that you intend to


build?


Whether you agree with these enterprise requirements has


little bearing on the outcome. The reality is that the system


must comply with enterprise requirements even if you can find


a better, more efficient, or more economical solution. A few


probing questions here may save some heartache later.


The enterprise requirements might be purely concerned with


the politics inside your organization. However, in other


situations you may need to consider the politics inside your


customers’ organizations or the national politics of the


country. Another way to think about the enterprise


requirements is that they are constraint requirements that


have been defined by strategic decisions that are outside the


obvious boundary of your project scope.


## 第 1255 页


4. Naming Conventions and Terminology


It has been our experience that all projects have their own


unique vocabulary that usually contains a variety of acronyms


and abbreviations. Failure to understand this project-


specific nomenclature inevitably leads to misunderstandings,


hours of lost time, miscommunication between team members,


and ultimately poor-quality specifications.


4a. Glossary of All Terms, Including Acronyms, Used by
Stakeholders Involved in the Project


Content


A glossary containing the meanings of all names, acronyms,


and abbreviations used by the stakeholders. Select names


carefully to avoid giving a different, unintended meaning.


If the work that you are studying already has a glossary of


terms, then use this as your starting point. This glossary


should be enlarged and refined as the analysis proceeds, but


for the moment, it should introduce the terms that the


stakeholders use and the meanings of those terms. This


glossary reflects the terminology in current use within the


work area. You might also get started by building on the


standard names used within your industry.


## 第 1256 页


For each term, write a description. The appropriate


stakeholders must agree on this description of the meaning of


the term.


We suggest you add all acronyms and abbreviations. We often


encounter situations where team members use acronyms but


admit they do not know the meanings of those acronyms. This


section gives you a place to register your acronyms.


Motivation


Names are very important. They invoke meanings that, if


carefully defined, can save hours of explanations. Attention


to names early in the project helps to highlight


misunderstandings.


As the detailed work progresses, the glossary provides input


to the more precisely specified business/work data model and


data dictionary—see section 7 of the template. As the


analysis data dictionary evolves, many of the definitions


from the glossary are expanded in the dictionary by adding


their data composition.


Examples


## 第 1257 页


Truck: A vehicle used for spreading deicing material on


roads. “Truck” is not used to refer to goods-carrying


vehicles.


BIS: Business Intelligence Service. The department run by


Steven Peters to supply business intelligence for the rest of


the organization.


Thermal Map: A region or other geographical area is surveyed


to determine the temperature differences at various parts of


the area. The resultant thermal map means the temperature at


any part of the area can be calculated by knowing the


temperature at a reference point.


Considerations


Make use of existing references and existing data


dictionaries. Obviously, it is best to avoid renaming


existing items unless they are so ambiguous that they cause


confusion.


From the beginning of the project, emphasize the need to


avoid homonyms and synonyms. Explain how they increase the


cost of the project.


Form


## 第 1258 页


An existing glossary of terms, or a pointer to industry


dictionaries, or a list of terms commonly used in the problem


domain, along with a sentence describing the meaning and


purpose of each term.


5. Relevant Facts, Business Rules, and Assumptions


Relevant facts are external factors that influence the


product but are not covered by other sections in the


requirements template. They are not necessarily translated


into requirements, but might be. Relevant facts alert the


developers to conditions and factors that have a bearing on


the requirements.


5a. Relevant Facts


Content


Factors that have an effect on the product but are not


mandated requirements or constraints.


Motivation


Relevant facts provide background information to the


specification readers and might contribute to requirements.


They will influence the eventual design of the product.


## 第 1259 页


Examples


One ton of deicing material will treat three miles of single-


lane roadway.


The existing application is 10,000 lines of C# code.


5b. Business Rules


Content


Business rules are the “laws” of the organization. These


are the rules that might have an impact on the


work/business/domain that is the source of the requirements.


Relevant business rules are the trigger for requirements.


Motivation


Business rules are mentioned at all stages of the


requirements discovery process. It is often difficult to


immediately ascertain whether a business rule is or is not


relevant to the project that you are doing. This section


provides a place to capture the business rules and, as


understanding of the work increases, to revisit them and use


them as triggers to discover relevant requirements.


Examples


## 第 1260 页


The maximum length of a truck driver’s shift is five hours.


The engineers visit the weather stations for maintenance once


a week.


Form


A written statement describing the business rule, the reason


for the rule, and the authority for the rule. Alternatively,


you can refer to the repository of the organization’s


business rules.


At the start of a new project, determine if there are any


relevant business rules that have already been recorded. When


your project discovers a new or changed business rule, it


should be recorded. The business rules are updated by every


project.


There are some specialized software tools, or business rules


engines, that can help with building a central repository of


the organization’s business rules.


5c. Assumptions


Content


## 第 1261 页


A list of the assumptions that the developers are making.


These assumptions might be about the intended operational


environment but can be about anything that influences the


product. As part of managing expectations, assumptions also


contain statements about what the product will not do.


Motivation


To make people declare the assumptions that they are making.


Also, to make everyone on the project aware of assumptions


that have already been made.


Examples


Assumptions about new laws or political decisions.


Assumptions about what your developers expect to be ready in


time for them to use—for example, other parts of your


products, the completion of other projects, software tools,


or software components.


Assumptions about the technological environment in which the


product will operate. These assumptions should highlight


areas of expected compatibility.


The availability and capability of ready-made components.


## 第 1262 页


Dependencies on computer systems or people external to this


project.


Considerations


We often make unconscious assumptions. It is necessary to


talk to the members of the project team to discover any


unconscious assumptions that they have made. Ask stakeholders


(both technical and business related) questions such as


these.


• What software tools are you expecting to be available?


• Will there be any new software products?


• Are you expecting to use a current product in a new way?


• Are there any business or environmental changes you are


assuming we will be able to deal with?


Assumptions are intended to be transient. That is, they


should all be cleared by the time the specification is


released—the assumption should have become either a


requirement or a constraint (or be proved irrelevant). For


example, if the assumption is related to the capability of a


product that is intended to be a partner product to yours,


then the capability should have been proven satisfactory and


## 第 1263 页


it becomes a constraint to use it. Conversely, if a ready-


made product is not suitable, then it becomes a requirement


for the project team to construct the needed capability.


Form


A written statement describing the assumption along with the


effect on the project if the assumption is false. Depending


on the complexity of the assumption, it might be necessary to


include references to other documents or people.


Understanding of assumptions can be explored and shared by


using cause-and-effect diagrams such as Peter Senge’s


dynamics models.


6. The Scope of the Work


The scope of the work, or the problem space, determines the


boundaries of the business area to be studied and outlines


how it fits into its environment.


6a. The Current Situation


Content


This is an analysis of the existing business processes,


including the manual and automated processes that might be


## 第 1264 页


replaced or changed by the new product. In terms of the


Volere Brown Cow model, you refer to this view as the “How-


Now” view. Business analysts might already have done this


investigation as part of the business case analysis for the


project. This is where it might be appropriate to build some


business process models. These are models of the processes


that the business uses to carry out the work of the


organization. The models include roles, individuals,


departments, technology, and procedures. They illustrate the


workflow and the dependencies between the components of the


process.


Motivation


If your project intends to make changes to an existing


system, you must understand the effect of proposed changes.


The study of the current situation provides the basis for


understanding the effects of proposed changes and choosing


the best alternatives. Business process modeling does not


always lead to building software. Instead, some changes in


procedures and the way roles are allocated might prove to be


the best way to make a necessary improvement.


Form


## 第 1265 页


There are many different notations suitable for building


business process models; for example, activity diagrams,


business process diagrams, swim lane diagrams, and data flow


diagrams.


6b. The Scope of the Work


Content


The work context diagram identifies the extent of the problem


space, or work, that you need to investigate. Note that the


work usually includes more than the intended product. This is


because you must understand the work that the product will


support if you are to build a product that will fit cleanly


into its environment.


The adjacent systems on the example context diagram (see


Figure A.3) indicate other entities that interact with your


work. The interfaces between the adjacent systems and the


work context indicate the data that travels between them.


Motivation


To clearly define the boundary for your study and hence the


requirements effort. Without this definition, you have little


chance of building a product that will fit seamlessly into


its environment.


## 第 1266 页


Examples


The work context model shown in Figure A.3 defines the


connections between the part of the world that is under


investigation and other people, organizations, hardware, and


software (referred to as adjacent systems). The inputs and


outputs represent the data and material that travel between


the work and other parts of the world. The work context is


the basis for partitioning the investigation and discovering


the requirements.


## 第 1267 页


![embedded_p1267_184.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1267_184.jpeg)


## 第 1268 页


Figure A.3 A work context diagram


Considerations


The names used on the context diagram should eventually be


defined in the data dictionary (see section 7). Without these


definitions, the context model lacks the required rigor, and


it may be misunderstood.


Form


A diagram showing the inputs and outputs that flow between


the work and the adjacent systems or a table that identifies


all the inputs and outputs that flow between the work and the


adjacent systems. These should be defined in the data


dictionary—see section 7b.


6c. Work Partitioning


Content


We use business events to partition the problem space. The


content of this section is a list showing all business


events to which the work responds. Business events are


happenings in the real world that affect the work. They also


happen because it is time for the work to do something: for


example, produce weekly reports, remind nonpaying customers,


## 第 1269 页


check the status of a device, and so on. The response to each


event is called a business use case (BUC); it represents a


discrete piece of the work. All of the work is made up of the


responses to business events.


The event list includes the following elements:


• Event name


• Input or triggering data flow from adjacent system


(identical to name on context diagram)


• Output(s) to adjacent systems (identical to name(s) on


context diagram)


• Brief summary of the BUC. This is optional, but we have


found it is a very useful first step in defining the


requirements for the BUC. You can think of it as a mini


scenario.


• Classes of business data relevant to this event (you won’t


know this early in the study of the event, but as you go into


detail, you will start to understand the essential data and


you can add it to the event list).


Motivation


## 第 1270 页


To identify logical chunks of the work that can be used as


the basis for discovering detailed requirements. These


business events also provide the subsystems that can be used


as the basis for managing detailed analysis and design. Each


business event has a BUC whose details can be studied


independently. However, all BUCs connect to each other


through shared interest in the stored business data (see


section 7a).


Examples


## 第 1271 页


![embedded_p1271_185.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1271_185.jpeg)


Considerations


## 第 1272 页


Attempting to list the business events and write a one-


sentence summary of each BUC is a way to test the scope of


the work. This activity uncovers uncertainties and


misunderstandings about the project and facilitates precise


communications.


We suggest you gather requirements for discrete sections of


the work. This means you need a way to partition the work. We


have found business events to be the most convenient,


consistent, functionally cohesive, and natural way to break


the work into manageable units and to be able to trace the


details back to the scope of the work.


Form


Business event list/table containing, for each event: Event


Number, Event Name, Name of Input, Name of Output(s), and


Summary of the business event response. For reasons of


traceability, the names of the inputs and outputs on the


business event list must match the names on the work context


model/table (see section 6.b).


6d. Specifying a Business Use Case


Content


## 第 1273 页


A specification of the details of how a BUC responds to a


business event. You can assess how well you understand the


BUC by attempting to write its business fit criterion. To do


this, ask yourself: How will I know whether this BUC has


carried out the intention of the business response to the


business event?


Motivation


To understand the detailed business response that must be


carried out when a business event takes place and provide a


basis for discovering the detailed requirements. The


understanding of the BUC also provides the basis for


discussing which parts of the BUC should be carried out by


the product that will be built. If you are using stories,


then the equivalent of a BUC is a business story.


Examples


In the sample specifications included with the download of


this template, you will find examples of BUC scenarios.


Business Event: Borrower wants to extend loan


Business Use Case: Decide on loan extension


Trigger: Loan Extension Request


## 第 1274 页


Preconditions: The borrower must have an existing loan for


the book in question.


Interested Stakeholders: Chief Librarian, Other Libraries,


Auditors


Active Stakeholders: Duty Librarian, Borrower


- The borrower gives the loan extension request to the duty


librarian.


- The librarian finds the book loan agreement for the


requested extension.


- The librarian finds any other books that are currently


loaned to the borrower.


- If the due return date on each of the books is later than


today’s date


then


the librarian tells the borrower there is a loan extension


approval.


the librarian records the loan extension.


## 第 1275 页


otherwise


the librarian tells the borrower there is a refused loan


extension.


the librarian records the refused extension.


the librarian asks the borrower to return the overdue books.


Outcome: A decision on book loan extension and the borrower


is informed


Considerations


Whatever approach you use to specify the details of a BUC,


you should stay within the boundary of the input and


output(s) for that business event. If you discover additional


input or output data, then it is an indication that you need


to make changes to the input/output data on the event list


and on the work context diagram.


Form


A BUC can be specified using any combination of models that


suits the analyst. The most common approaches are activity


diagrams, BUC scenarios, process flow diagrams, sequence


diagrams, business stories, mind maps, interview notes....


## 第 1276 页


The only caveat is that the inputs and outputs on your BUC


are precisely the same and hence traceable to the inputs and


outputs on the corresponding business event.


7. Business Data Model and Data Dictionary


The business data represents the business knowledge that is


stored, referenced, and maintained to satisfy the business


requirements. The business data provides a way to communicate


the essential subject matter independently of the technology


used to store the data.


7a. Business Data Model


Content


A diagram of the essential subject matter, business objects,


entities, and classes that are germane to the work that you


are investigating. It might take the form of a first-cut


class model, an entity-relationship model, or any other kind


of data model. Figure A.4 is an example of a business data


model.


Motivation


To clarify the system’s subject matter, thereby triggering


recognition of requirements not yet considered. To discover


## 第 1277 页


missing requirements, you can cross-check the data model and


the events using a Create, Read, Update, Delete (CRUD) table.


The data model is a specification for all the business data


that is relevant to the scope of the work.


Examples


This example is a model of the business system’s data using


the Unified Modeling Language (UML) class model notation.


This is all the data that is Created, Read, Updated, and


Deleted by processes within the scope of the work being


studied. See section 6 for more about the scope of the work.


## 第 1278 页


![embedded_p1278_186.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1278_186.jpeg)


Figure A.4 A business data model


## 第 1279 页


Each rectangle in Figure A.4 represents a class of business


data or a “thing” that the work you are studying is


interested in. The attributes of that class are defined in


the data dictionary (see section 7b). For example:


District = *A geographical area defined by the council*


District Name + District Size + District Coordinates


Similarly, each attribute is also defined in the dictionary.


For example:


District Name = *The unique name used by the engineers to


identify a district*


You can use any type of data or class model to capture this


knowledge. The issue is to capture the meaning of the


business subject matter and the connections between the


individual parts, and to show that you are consistent within


your project. If you have an established company standard


notation, use that, as it will help you to reuse knowledge


between projects.


For more examples of data models, look at the example


specifications that are packaged with the download of this


requirements template.


## 第 1280 页


Considerations


Are there any data or object models for similar or


overlapping systems that might be a useful starting point? Is


there a domain model for the subject matter dealt with by


this system?


Form
