Use the requirements that you have already specified as input


to designing the training. For example, you have specified


what a PUC must do. Use that PUC scenario or model as the


basis for building training for the users who will be


carrying out that task. You have defined all the terms used


in the requirements, so take advantage of this and use the


same definitions and dictionary in the user training.


26. Waiting Room


The waiting room holds requirements that will not, for one


reason or another, be part of the upcoming release of the


product. If you are competent at gathering requirements, your


## 第 1371 页


users may often be inspired to think of more requirements


than you can fit within the constraints of the project. While


you may not want to include all these requirements in the


initial version of the product, neither do you want to lose


them.


If you are doing iterative development, then the waiting room


is your story backlog.


Content


Any type of business event, requirement, or story at any


level of detail.


Motivation


To allow requirements to be captured, even though they will


not be part of the current development. To ensure that good


ideas are not lost. To manage a backlog.


Considerations


The requirements discovery process often throws up


requirements that are beyond the sophistication of, or time


allowed for, the upcoming release of the product. This


section holds these requirements in waiting. The intention is


to avoid stifling the creativity of your users and clients,


## 第 1372 页


by using a repository to retain future requirements. You are


also managing expectations by making it clear that you take


these requirements seriously, although they will not be part


of the agreed-upon product.


Many people use the waiting room as a way to plan future


versions of the product. Each requirement in the waiting room


is tagged with its intended version number. As a requirement


progresses closer to implementation, you can spend more time


on it and add details such as the cost and benefit attached


to that requirement.


You might also prioritize the contents of your waiting room.


Low-hanging fruit—requirements that provide a high benefit


at a low cost of implementation—are the highest-ranking


candidates for the next release. You would also give a high


waiting room rank to requirements for which there is a pent-


up demand. You can think of the waiting room as a way of


managing your backlog.


The waiting room means your users and client know the


requirements are not forgotten, but merely parked until it is


time to review them and make decisions about whether they


will be incorporated in the product.


## 第 1373 页


27. Ideas for Solutions


Ideas for solutions are obviously not requirements, but it is


impossible when gathering requirements not to get ideas for


how they might be implemented. Rather than discarding the


ideas or—even worse—writing them as if they are


requirements, a practical idea is to simply set aside a


section of your specification for these ideas. Record each


one in this area, and then hand them over, along with the


requirements, to your designer.


Content


Any idea for a solution that you think is worth keeping for


future consideration. This can take the form of rough notes,


sketches, pointers to other documents, pointers to people,


pointers to existing products, prototypes, and so on. The aim


is to capture, with the least amount of effort, an idea that


you can return to later.


Motivation


To make sure that good ideas are not lost. To help you


separate requirements from solutions.


Considerations


## 第 1374 页


While you are gathering requirements, you will inevitably


have solution ideas; this section offers a way to capture


them. Bear in mind that this section will not necessarily be


included in every document that you publish.


Form


The ideas for solutions are an ideal subject for a blog. This


is, after all, the place for ideas, and blogs are a great


place for creativity and building on one another’s ideas.


## 第 1375 页


Appendix B. Stakeholder Management
Templates


This appendix contains templates that are designed to help


you manage your stakeholders. Its aim is threefold:


1. To help you discover the relevant stakeholders for your


project


2. To help you identify gaps that are without stakeholder


representation


3. To help you agree on your decision-making structure


Stakeholder Map


Figure B.1 is a generic stakeholder map showing the potential


classes of stakeholders. Use it as an aid for discovering


your stakeholders. Refer to Part II, Project Blastoff, for a


discussion of stakeholder classes.

Figure B.1 This generic stakeholder map shows the various


classes of stakeholders. Use it as an aid to identifying your


stakeholders.

The following template is a sample checklist you can use to


identify and analyze your stakeholders. Note that the


template’s stakeholder classes correspond to those on the

have suggested common roles that represent the class. Of

probably be more convenient for you to do so using a


spreadsheet. An extract of the spreadsheet is shown in Figure


B.2. The complete version of the stakeholder template in the


form of an Excel spreadsheet can be found at


https://www.volere.org/templates/stakeholder-analysis-


download.

## 第 1379 页


Appendix C. Volere Requirements Knowledge
Model


The Volere Requirements Knowledge Model is a language for


communicating and keeping track of the knowledge that you


discover during requirements-related activities. Your model


specifies which requirements knowledge you plan to discover


and trace. Your own process must define who gathers which


knowledge, to what degree of detail, and how it will be


packaged and reviewed.


Using the Model


As with any language, communication is most effective when


everyone has the same understanding of the words that you


use. If your team agree on how they are going to communicate,


it will make for a more effective team. We recommend that you


start with one of the example knowledge models in this


appendix and use it as the basis for planning and monitoring


your project. If you find a term that has different meanings


for different team members, then it’s an indication that you


need to determine the consensus meaning and change the model


so that you remove the potential communication block.


Interpreting the Model


## 第 1380 页


A requirements knowledge model identifies the classes of


requirements knowledge and the relationships between them. An


extract is shown in Figure C.1.


![embedded_p1380_193.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1380_193.jpeg)


Figure C.1 Two knowledge classes and their relationship


In this example, the Work Scope and the Business Event are


both classes of knowledge. The relationship between the two


classes is that they identify the Business Boundary. There is


one (1) Work Scope related to many (*) Business Events.


Reading in the other direction, you see that each Business


Event is related to (1) Work Scope.


The precise meaning of every class and relationship is


defined later in this appendix.


Example Requirements Knowledge Model


You can use the example knowledge model as a starting point


for your own knowledge model (see Figure C.2). If you need


## 第 1381 页


to, you can make changes by adding or renaming the classes


and/or relationships, but remember that any change you make


should be reflected in the dictionary of definitions that


supports your model; see the sample dictionary in the next


section.


## 第 1382 页


![embedded_p1382_194.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1382_194.jpeg)


## 第 1383 页


Figure C.2 The requirements knowledge model showing the


classes of knowledge used for requirements discovery


The following knowledge classes are suited to projects in


which you specify individual atomic requirements:


• Business Events


• Business Use Cases


• Product Use Cases


• Atomic Requirements


OR


The following knowledge classes suit projects that use


Stories and are especially suited to agile development teams:


• Business Events


• Business Event Stories


• Functional Stories


• Detailed Tasks


Dictionary for Requirements Knowledge Model


## 第 1384 页


It is preferable if you have common agreement on what the


names of the classes mean. This requires a dictionary to


support the names you use. The following is a definition of


the classes of knowledge and the relationships between them.


The classes are listed in alphabetical order, followed by the


relationships in alphabetical order.


Knowledge Classes


Knowledge class: Atomic Requirement


Purpose:


An atomic requirement specifies a business need or want. It


has a number of attributes.


Attributes:


Requirement Number


Requirement Description


Requirement Rationale


Requirement Type


Requirement Fit Criterion


## 第 1385 页


Requirement Source


Customer Satisfaction


Customer Dissatisfaction


Conflicting Requirements


Dependent Requirements


Supporting Material


Version Number


Considerations:


Also see the requirement subtypes; namely, Constraint


Requirement, Functional Requirement, Non-functional


Requirement, and Technological Requirement.


Suggested Implementation:


Sections 9 through 17 of the Volere Requirements


Specification Template. Various automated tools are available


that allow team access to the requirements.


Knowledge class: Business Event


## 第 1386 页


Purpose:


A Business Event is a happening outside the work scope that


is a demand for some service provided by the work. Examples


of business events: Motorist passes an electronic tollbooth;


Customer orders a book; Doctor needs a scan of a patient;


Pilot lowers the landing gear.


Business events can also happen because of the passage of


time. For example, if a customer’s bill is not paid in 30


days, then it is time for the work to send a reminder. Or if


it is two months before an insurance policy is due to expire,


it is time to send a renewal notice.


Attributes:


Business Event Name


Business Event Adjacent Systems/Actors/Users


Business Event Summary


Considerations:


It is important to recognize the business event. Its nature,


the circumstances that exist at the time of the event, and


## 第 1387 页


the activity of the adjacent system at the time of the event


are all important indicators of the appropriate response.


Suggested Implementation:


Section 6 of the Volere Requirements Specification Template.


A list of the business events and their associated input and


output flows will suffice. It is practical to give each


business event a unique identifier.


Knowledge class: Business Event Story


Purpose:


A Business Event Story describes what activity is needed when


a business event takes place. A business event story is the


equivalent of a business use case, but it usually does not go


into as much detail. If you are working in an agile


environment, then it is likely that you are using business


event stories.


Attributes:


Role of Stakeholder


Name of Stakeholder


## 第 1388 页


Stakeholder Functionality


Reason for needing this functionality


Suggested Implementation:


As a [Name of Stakeholder, name of customer segment, adjacent


system name, or Role name]


I can [Something the stakeholder needs the work to do]


So that [The business reason for fulfilling this need]


Knowledge class: Business Use Case


Purpose:


A Business Use Case (BUC) is the processing done in response


to a business event. For example, A policyholder decides to


make a claim is a business event. The triggering data flow in


this case is that a Claim Request informs the BUC that the


event has taken place. The business use case contains all the


processing done by the work to approve or deny the claim.


Also see Business Event Story and Product Use Case.


Attributes:


## 第 1389 页


Business Use Case Name


Business Use Case Description


Business Use Case Trigger (this is the data flow that


triggers the BUC)


Business Use Case Outputs


Business Use Case Rationale


Business Use Case Priority


Normal Case Scenario


Exception Case Scenarios


Preconditions


Post or Exit Conditions


Considerations:


Business use cases are self-contained portions of the work


and can be studied independently. For this reason, they are


an important unit that project leaders use to structure the


analytical work.


## 第 1390 页


Suggested Implementation:


Section 6 of the Volere Requirements Specification Template.


An automated tool that allows sharing of the business use


case attributes is advisable. BUCs can be represented using


any combination of business process models, sequence


diagrams, activity diagrams, scenarios, or any other


representation that is acceptable to the people involved,


providing the Business Event Story is within the boundaries


declared for the Business Event.


Knowledge class: Constraint Requirement


Purpose:


A constraint is a type of requirement. It is a constraint on


the design of the solution or a constraint on the project


itself, such as budget or time restrictions.


Considerations:


Constraints are a type of requirement. They are imposed


because of organizational policy or technological needs.


Highlight them, as it is important that you and your


management are aware that they are constraints and not


customer-generated requirements.


## 第 1391 页


Suggested Implementation:


Section 3 of the Volere Requirements Specification Template.


Design constraints should be recorded in the same way as the


other requirements. See the Knowledge class Atomic


Requirement for the attributes.


Knowledge class: Detailed Task


Purpose:


The Detailed Tasks are chunks of functionality. You can think


of them as the things that have to be done to complete the


work of the Functional Story.


Suggested Implementation:


A sentence stating a cohesive unit of functionality: Get


Airport Information, Find Matching Address, Store Customer


Details....


Knowledge class: Fact/Assumption


Purpose:


An Assumption states an expectation on which decisions about


the project are based. For example, it might be an assumption


## 第 1392 页


that another project will be finished before this one is, or


that a particular law will not be changed, or that a


particular supplier will reach a specified level of


performance. If an assumption turns out not to be true, then


it indicates that there might be unknown effects on the


project.


A Fact is some knowledge that is relevant to the project and


affects its requirements and design. A Fact can also state


some specific exclusion from the solution and the reason for


that exclusion.


Fact/Assumption is a global class and could have a


Relationship with any of the other classes in your knowledge


model.


Attributes:


Description of the Assumption/Fact


Reference to people and documents for more details


Considerations:


Assumptions indicate a risk. For this reason, they should be


highlighted, and all affected parties made aware of the


## 第 1393 页


assumption. You could consider installing a mechanism to


resolve all assumptions before implementation starts.


Suggested Implementation:


Section 5 of the Volere Requirements Specification Template.


These can be written in free text. They should be regularly


circulated to management and the project team to help


everyone have the same understanding.


Knowledge class: Functional Requirement


Purpose:


A Functional Requirement is something that the product must


do; for example, calculate the fare, analyze the chemical


composition, record the name change, or find the new route.


Functional requirements are concerned with creating,


updating, referencing, and deleting the essential subject


matter within the context of the study.


Attributes:


This is a subtype of Atomic Requirement and inherits its


attributes.


Suggested Implementation:


## 第 1394 页


Section 9 of the Volere Requirements Specification Template.


See the Knowledge class Atomic Requirement for the


attributes.


Knowledge class: Functional Story


Purpose:


A Functional Story represents one of the pieces of


functionality that is necessary to implement a business event


story.


Functional stories are concerned with creating, updating,


referencing, and deleting the essential subject data within


the scope of the solution.


Attributes:


A simple verb-object statement.


Suggested Implementation:


If the functionality is simple enough for one development


cycle, then you can indicate the required functionality using


a verb-object statement like Make Reservation, Pay Invoice,


Find Suitable Flights....


## 第 1395 页


For more complex stories, you can use the common story


format:


As a [Name of Stakeholder or Role name]


I can [The functionality of the story]


So that [The business reason/rationale behind the need]


Knowledge class: Implementation Unit


Purpose:


The unit for packaging your implementation.


Attributes:


Implementation Unit Name


Considerations:


This could be what your customers refer to as a “feature,”


or if your product is a consumer item then it is possibly


called a “function.” The choice of Implementation Unit is


driven by a combination of your implementation technology and


your implementation process. When you tailor this part of the


knowledge model you might find that you replace the


## 第 1396 页


implementation unit with several classes. The important point


is that you can unambiguously trace your implementation unit


back to the relevant requirements.


Knowledge class: Naming Conventions and Data Dictionary


Purpose:


A Data Dictionary that defines the meaning of terms used


within the requirements. This dictionary will be added to


throughout the project to include terms that are related to


the implementation. This is a global class and could have a


Relationship with any of the other classes in your knowledge


model. Consistent use of the same terminology, as defined in


the dictionary, helps minimize misunderstandings.


Attributes:


Name of the Term


Definition of the Term


Suggested Implementation:


Section 4 of the Volere Requirements Specification Template;


this should be in the form of a glossary. Along with the work


context and the product context, this provides an


## 第 1397 页


introduction for new team members. In section 7 of the


Template, there is a formal dictionary that defines the data


in the inputs, outputs, and attributes within the scope of


the work and the scope of the product. The dictionary


provides a mechanism for connecting business terminology and


implementation terminology.


Knowledge class: Non-functional Requirement


Purpose:


A non-functional Requirement is a quality that the product


must have. For example, it must be fast, attractive, secure,


customizable, maintainable, portable, and so on. Non-


functional requirement types are Look and Feel, Usability,


Performance and Safety, Operational Environment,


Maintainability and Portability, Security, Cultural and


Political, and Legal. For more about non-functional


requirements, refer to the Volere Requirements Specification


Template in Appendix A.


Attributes:


This is a subtype of Atomic Requirement and inherits its


attributes.


## 第 1398 页


Considerations:


Providing the functional requirements are correct, the non-


functional properties are what make the customer accept the


product.


Suggested Implementation:


Sections 10 through 17 of the Volere Requirements


Specification Template. It is vital that you give all non-


functional requirements the correct fit criterion.


Knowledge class: Product Use Case


Purpose:


A Product Use Case (PUC) is a functional grouping of


requirements that will be implemented by the product. It is


the part of the business use case that you decide to build as


a product. If you are working with an agile development team,


you will likely use Functional Stories instead of Product Use


Cases.


Attributes:


Product Use Case Name


## 第 1399 页


Product Use Case Identifier


Product Use Case Description


Product Use Case Users


Product Use Case Inputs


Product Use Case Outputs


Product Use Case Stories


Product Use Case Scenarios


Product Use Case Fit Criterion


Product Use Case Owner


Product Use Case Benefit


Product Use Case Priority


Suggested Implementation:


Section 8 of the Volere Requirements Specification Template.


The product use cases are a good mechanism for communication


within the extended project team. PUCs might take the form of


models, user stories, scenarios, or anything else that suits


## 第 1400 页


the people involved. Whatever the type of representation, the


details of the PUC should be within the boundaries declared


by the PUC inputs and outputs.


Knowledge class: Project Goal


Purpose:


To understand why the company is making an investment in


doing this project.


Attributes:


Project Goal Description


Business Advantage


Measure of Success


Note that there might be several project goals.


Suggested Implementation:


Section 1 of the Volere Requirements Specification Template.


This is the basis for making decisions about scope,


relevance, and priority. It is the guiding light for the


project. Ideally, this should be defined as part of the


## 第 1401 页


project initiation. The project goals should be unambiguously


defined and agreed on before putting effort into discovering


detailed requirements.


Knowledge class: Solution Scope


Purpose:


The solution scope identifies the boundaries of the solution


that will be built. The solution scope is a summary of the


boundaries of all the product use cases OR all the functional


stories.


Attributes:


User Names


User Roles


Other Adjacent Systems


Interface descriptions


Suggested Implementation:


Section 8 of the Volere Requirements Specification Template.


This should preferably be a diagram: either a use case


## 第 1402 页


diagram or a solution context diagram. Some interface


descriptions might be supported by prototypes or simulations.


Knowledge class: Stakeholder


Purpose:


Identifies all the people, roles, and organizations that have


an interest in the project. This covers the project team,


direct users of the product, other indirect beneficiaries of


the product, specialists with technical skills needed to


build the product, external organizations with rules or laws


pertaining to the product, external organizations with


specialist knowledge about the product’s domain, opponents


of the product, and producers of competitive products.


Attributes:


Stakeholder Role


Stakeholder Name


Types of Knowledge


Necessary Participation


Appropriate Trawling Techniques


## 第 1403 页


Contact information (e.g., email address)


Suggested Implementation:


Section 2 of the Volere Requirements Specification Template.


Use the stakeholder map and stakeholder analysis template in


Appendix B to define the attributes for each stakeholder.


Knowledge class: Systems Architecture Component


Purpose:


A piece of technology, software, hardware, or abstract


container that influences, facilitates, and/or places


constraints on the design.


Knowledge class: Technological Requirement


Purpose:


A technological requirement exists because of the technology


chosen for the implementation. These requirements are there


to serve the purposes of the technology and are not


originated by the business.


Attributes:


## 第 1404 页


This is a subtype of Atomic Requirement and inherits its


attributes.


Considerations:


The Technological Requirements should only be considered when


you know the technological environment. They can be recorded


alongside the business requirements, but it must be clear


which is which.


Knowledge class: Work Scope


Purpose:


Defines the boundary of the business investigation necessary


to discover, invent, understand, and identify the


requirements for the product.


Attributes:


Adjacent Systems


Input Data flows


Output Data flows


Work Scope Description


## 第 1405 页


Considerations:


This should be recorded publicly, as our experience is that


it helps the team share a common understanding of the


business they are investigating. A context diagram is an


effective communication tool for defining the work scope.


Suggested Implementation:


Section 7 of the Volere Requirements Specification Template.


This is best illustrated with a context diagram.


Relationships


These relationships (associations, if you prefer) are shown


in Figure C.2.


Relationship: Automating


Purpose:


To identify which parts of the business problem will have an


automated solution.


Multiplicity:


For each Business Use Case there are many Product Use Cases.


## 第 1406 页


OR


For each Business Event Story there are many Functional


Stories.


Relationship: Business Boundary


Purpose:


To relate the work scope with the business events the work is


responding to.


Multiplicity:


For each Business Event there is one Work Scope.


For each Work Scope there are potentially many Business


Events.


Relationship: Business Relevancy


Purpose:


To ensure that there are relevant business connections


between the scope of the investigation, the project purpose,


and the stakeholders.


Multiplicity:


## 第 1407 页


The trinary Relationship is as follows:


For each instance of


one Work Scope and


one Stakeholder there are one or more Project Goals.


For each instance of


one Project Goal and


one Stakeholder there is one Work Scope.


For each instance of


one Project Goal and


one Work Scope there are potentially many Stakeholders.


Relationship: Business Responding


Purpose:


To connect the chunk of functionality that responds to a


business event.


Multiplicity:


## 第 1408 页


For each Business Event there is one Business Use Case.


OR


For each Business Event there is one Business Event Story.


Relationship: Business Tracing


Purpose:


To keep track of which requirements are generated by which


business use cases or Functional Stories.


Multiplicity:


For each Business Use Case there are potentially many Atomic


Requirements.


OR


For each Functional Story there are potentially many Detailed


Tasks.


Relationship: Design Guiding


Purpose:


## 第 1409 页


To keep track of which Systems Architecture Components affect


the Solution Scope.


Multiplicity:


The Solution Scope is potentially connected to many Systems


Architecture Components.


Relationship: Implementing


Purpose:


To keep track of which Implementation Units implement which


Atomic Requirements


OR


Detailed Tasks.


Multiplicity:


For each Implementation Unit there are potentially many


Atomic Requirements


OR


Detailed Tasks.


## 第 1410 页


Relationship: Owning


Purpose:


To establish ownership of the requirements. The idea of


“ownership” is to identify a person who takes the


responsibility for or is the most knowledgeable about the


requirement.


Multiplicity:


Each Business Use Case


OR


Business Event Story is owned by one Stakeholder.


Relationship: Product Boundary


Purpose:


All the product use cases together form the complete Solution


Scope.


OR


All the Functional Stories together form the complete


Solution Scope.


## 第 1411 页


Multiplicity:


For the Solution Scope there are potentially many Product Use


Cases


OR


Many Functional Stories.


Relationship: Product Inclusion


Purpose:


To establish which requirements are contained in which


product use cases


OR


Which detailed tasks are contained in which functional


stories, for the purpose of traceability and dealing with


change.


Multiplicity:


For each Atomic Requirement there is one Product Use Case.


OR


## 第 1412 页


For each Detailed Task there is one Functional Story.


Relationship: Supporting


Purpose:


To keep track of which systems architecture components


support which implementation units for the purpose of


tracking tests and assessing the impact of change.


Multiplicity:


For each Systems Architecture Component there are potentially


many Implementation Units.


For each Implementation Unit there are potentially many


Systems Architecture Components.


Knowledge Model Annotated with Template Section


Numbers


The Volere Requirements Knowledge Model is a formal structure


for identifying and relating classes of requirements


knowledge. The Volere Requirements Specification Template


contains many examples and guidance for content and form for


ways you can present the requirements knowledge. You will


## 第 1413 页


find the complete Volere Requirements Specification Template


in Appendix A.


Figure C.3 shows the knowledge model again, this time


annotated with the relevant sections of the requirements


template.


## 第 1414 页


![embedded_p1414_195.jpeg](robertson_images/embedded_p1414_195.jpeg)


## 第 1415 页


Figure C.3 The numbers on the classes point to the relevant

## 第 1416 页


Glossary


actor The person or automated system that interacts with a


product use case. Actors are also known as users and end


users.


adjacent system A system (customer segment, person,


organization, computer system) that provides information to


or receives information from the work that you are studying.


agile development A way of developing software using


iterative development. A variety of agile techniques exist,


including Scrum, eXtreme Programming, and Crystal. We use the


term “iterative” to mean any agile or iterative technique.


Agile Manifesto A set of principles that focus on the


delivery of working software to the customer, collaborative


working practices, and the ability to respond rapidly to


change.


artificial intelligence (AI) The name given to intelligent


machines or bots (software, really) that mimic human thinking


capabilities.


atomic requirement A requirement that is testable and does


not need further decomposition. See also functional


## 第 1417 页


requirement, non-functional requirement, constraint, snow


card.


attribute A data element that describes (and has been


attributed to) a class. Also used to mean the components of


an atomic requirement.


blastoff A technique for building the foundation for the


requirements activity by establishing the scope-stakeholders-


goals trinity and verifying the viability of the project.


Brown Cow model A technique for discussing and modeling the


work by using different system viewpoints. The viewpoints are


permutations of now, future, how, and what.


business analyst The role responsible for discovering and


communicating requirements among the project’s stakeholders.


Can be referred to as requirements analyst, requirements


engineer, and systems analyst.


business data model A model of the essential classes of


business data and associations between them necessary to


support the functional requirements within the scope of the


work.


## 第 1418 页


business event Something that happens to the business


(usually called “the work”) that makes it respond.


Examples: Customer pays an invoice, Truck reports all roads


have been treated, Time to read electricity meters, and


Customer wants to search website.


business process model A model of the processes within a


business; often used to understand the current processes so


that they can be improved. A variety of notations are used


for such models.


business use case (BUC) The work’s response to a business


event. It includes the processes and the stored data needed


to satisfy the request implicit in the business event. See


also product use case.


buyer See customer.


class A physical or abstract entity within a context of


study that has one or more attributes of stored data.


class model A model showing classes of data and the


associations between them. This is also known as a business


data model.


## 第 1419 页


client The person who is commissioning and paying for the


development effort. The client can be internal, and is


sometimes known as the sponsor. For example, the manager of


the audit department would commission you to build an audit


application. An external client would commission your


organization to build a solution for him. In this case, you


would be a development organization.


constraint A requirement, either organizational or


technological, that restricts the way you produce the


product. It may be a management edict on the way the product


must be designed—“It must work on a 5G mobile phone”—or a


budget that limits the extent of the product or a


characteristic of the current technology that constrains the


possible solutions.


context The subject matter, people, and organizations that


affect the requirements for the product. The context of


study, or the work context, identifies the business to be


studied and the adjacent systems that interact with this


work. The product context identifies the scope of the product


and its interactions with users and other actors.


context diagram A graphical model of the work scope showing


how the work to be investigated connects to the outside


## 第 1420 页


world.


customer A person who buys something from your client, or


buys your solution. “Customer” and “client” are often


used interchangeably.


customer segment A group of customers or end users who have


a unique set of requirements that separates them from other


customer segments. Typically you develop a solution for each


customer segment.


data dictionary Specification (to the elemental level) of


the terms used in the requirements specification.


data element A piece of data that has a defined range or set


of values within a context of study. Also called an


attribute.


data flow Data that moves from one process to another, or


from an adjacent system to the work. Usually represented by a


named arrow.


data model A model showing classes of data and the


associations between them. This is also known as a class


model. See also business data model.


## 第 1421 页


design The act of crafting a technological solution to fit


the requirements within the constraints.


developer Someone who is part of the technological


development or building of the product, sometimes called a


programmer.


domain analysis The activity of investigating, capturing,


and specifying generic knowledge about a subject-matter area.


end user The person who operates your solution to do her


work. Also called customer.


essential viewpoint A viewpoint that focuses on the


processes and data independently of any technological


implementation. Also referred to as “thinking above the


line”.


external event A business event triggered by a happening in


an adjacent system outside the work context. See also time-


triggered event.


fit criterion A quantification or measurement of the


requirement such that you are able to determine whether the


delivered product satisfies (fits) the requirement. This is


much the same as an acceptance criterion.


## 第 1422 页


function point A measure of the functionality of the work or


of a piece of software. Function points were first proposed


by Allan Albrecht; today the method for counting function


points is specified by the International Function Point User


Group.


functional requirement A requirement for the solution to


carry out some functional activity.


innovation Fresh thinking about the problem to find a new


and better way to do the work.


iterative development Strategies that facilitate repetitive


and continuous delivery of software solutions with current


business value.


lessons learned An examination of the project to date with


the intention of improving the requirements discovery


process. Also known as retrospective.


naming conventions The terminology (including abbreviations


and acronyms) that the stakeholders use when talking about


the work. This terminology is usually captured in a glossary


such as the one you are reading.


## 第 1423 页


non-functional requirement A property or quality that the


product must have, such as an appearance, speed, security,


accuracy, usability....


off-the-shelf (OTS) Software products developed by external


organizations. These can be commercial (COTS) or open source


products. See also ready-made.


owner See client.


persona A virtual person, archetypical of your users,


invented to help you discover the requirements.


problem space The scope of the study that is necessary in


order to understand the problem to be tackled by a project.


This is also called the work.


product The thing for which you are writing your


requirements. In this book, “product” usually means a


software product, but the requirements can be for hardware,


consumer goods, a service, or anything else you need to


specify. See also solution.


product owner The person responsible for the delivery of the


product. The product owner is responsible for prioritizing


## 第 1424 页


the product backlog and deciding on the sequence in which


parts of the product are developed.


product use case (PUC) The part of the business use case you


decide to automate. You write the requirements for each


product use case. See also business use case.


project blastoff See blastoff.


project goal The reasons for doing the project. The goal


must include a quantification of the expected benefit.


prototype A simulation of potential solutions using software


prototyping tools, low-fidelity whiteboards, or paper


mockups. Also referred to as a sketch. In this book,


prototypes are used to explore the problem space.


quality gateway A set of tests (relevance, ambiguity,


viability, fit, etc.) to assure the quality of individual


requirements before the requirements become part of the


requirements specification.


rationale The justification for a requirement. Used to help


understand a requirement, and to discover the underlying


reason for the requirement.


## 第 1425 页


ready-made A solution or a component that you do not build


yourself. This can be an off-the-shelf (OTS) solution, an


open-source solution or component, a legacy solution, or


anything else you don’t build. It can be installed in-house,


or it can be a cloud service or software as a service (SaaS).


requirement Something that the solution must do, or a


property that the product must have, that is needed or wanted


by the stakeholders.


requirements analyst The person who has responsibility for


producing the requirements specification. Depending on how


roles are defined in an organization, this individual might


be referred to as a business analyst, systems analyst, or


requirements engineer.


requirements creep The uncontrolled addition of new


requirements to the product after the requirements are


considered complete.


requirements knowledge model A conceptual filing system—


usually expressed as a data model—that establishes a common


language for communicating requirements. (An example appears


in Appendix C.)


## 第 1426 页


requirements specification A complete collection of


requirements knowledge for a specific project. The


specification defines the product and may be used as a


contract to build the product.


requirements repository A place for the project team to


store requirements knowledge. The repository can be one or a


combination of a specification, a story map, a backlog, a


collection of artifacts, a database of requirements, or any


other form that records the requirements.


requirements specification template A guide for gathering


and organizing requirements knowledge. (An example appears in


Appendix A.)


requirements tool A software tool capable of maintaining all


or part of the requirements specification.


scenario A breakdown of a business use case or product use


case into a series of stakeholder-recognizable steps.


sketch A quickly built model or prototype of a piece of work


or a candidate solution. Sketches are used to explore the


problem space.


## 第 1427 页


snow card A card—paper or digital—showing the attributes


of an atomic requirement.


solution A way of implementing the requirements. Also called


the product.


sponsor See client.


stakeholder Any person who has an interest in the product


and who therefore has requirements for it, such as the


client, a user, or someone with specialized knowledge who


builds the product. Some stakeholders are outside the


organization, such as an auditor, a safety inspector, or a


lawyer.


story A technique for discovering requirements by using the


guide: “As a [...] I can [...] so that [...].” Sometimes


called a user story or a story card.


system In the context of this book, a business or work


system, and not just a computer or software system.


systemic thinking Or Systems thinking. The technique of


understanding how components of a business solution affect


one another and affect the whole system.


## 第 1428 页


systems analysis The craft of modeling the system’s


functions and data. Systems analysis can be done in several


ways: data flow modeling, as defined by DeMarco; event


response modeling, as per McMenamin and Palmer; use cases, as


per Jacobson; or any of the many object-oriented methods,


most of which use the Unified Modeling Language (UML)


notation or the Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN).


technological requirement A requirement that is necessary


only because of the chosen technology; it is not there to


satisfy a business need.


thinking above the line Deriving and discussing the essence


of the work. The “thinking” refers to an exploration of the


possibilities without being constrained (for the moment) by


technological realities. The “line” is the horizontal line


on the Brown Cow model that separates the physical reality


(how) from the essential policy (what).


time-triggered event An event triggered by some time-related


policy. Examples: “Time to produce sales report,” “Time to


remind driver to renew license.” See also external event.


trawling techniques Techniques for discovering, eliciting,


determining, and innovating requirements.


## 第 1429 页


use case A chunk of functionality describing the interaction


between a user/actor and an automated system. In this book we


use business use case and product use case.


user The person or system that uses the product to do work.


Also known as an actor or end user.


user story A way of specifying functionality to be


developed. The form “As a [...] I can [...] so that [...].”


is used. See also story.


Volere A set of principles, processes, templates, tools, and


techniques developed to improve the discovery, communication,


and management of requirements. (Volere is the Italian verb


for “to wish” or “to want.”)


work A business area of the organization that your product


is meant to improve. The business analyst studies the work


before making decisions on the optimal product to do some or


all of the work. Work is also known as the problem space.


work scope The extent of the business area under


investigation. It is usually shown using a context diagram.
